text:
**The girl who learned to count what she had.**

Mara grew up in a two-room house at the edge of a mill town that had already begun to empty. The roof leaked when it rained hard. In winter they slept in coats. Her mother worked the early shift at a diner and the late shift cleaning offices; Mara learned early that “we’ll figure it out” usually meant stretching one pot of beans and rice across two days.

She was eight the first time she understood money as a language. She watched her mother count coins on the kitchen table after midnight, sliding them into little piles: rent, lights, the leftover that might buy milk. Mara started counting too—bottles she could return, berries she could pick, hours she could watch a neighbor’s kids. Poverty taught her arithmetic before school did.

School was a different kind of hunger. She was bright, but bright did not pay for new shoes or field-trip fees. She borrowed books until the covers fell off. When other kids talked about summer camps and new phones, she talked about nothing. Shame is a quiet tutor. It taught her to listen more than she spoke, to notice what people needed before they asked, and to work when no one was watching.

At fourteen she started baking after her mother fell asleep. Cheap flour, whatever fruit was almost too soft, a borrowed neighbor’s oven when theirs broke. She sold squares wrapped in wax paper at the mill gate on payday. The first week she made enough for a pair of decent sneakers. The second week she made enough to put a little aside. She kept a notebook: cost, price, what sold, what didn’t. She was not romantic about it. She was precise.

A teacher noticed the notebook and the early-morning flour on her sleeves. She helped Mara apply for every scholarship that existed and a few that almost didn’t. Mara worked through high school—bakery before dawn, homework after midnight, the diner on weekends so her mother could rest one night a week. She did not become rich then. She became relentless.

College was a state school and a mountain of work-study. She studied business because she already understood scarcity; she wanted to understand scale. She kept baking on the side, then started a tiny catering run for campus events. When a local café owner offered her a corner of a commercial kitchen in exchange for a cut, she took it. She slept four hours some nights. She failed a product line. She lost a contract. She kept the notebook.

The turn was not cinematic. A food writer ate one of her tarts at a farmers’ market and wrote three paragraphs. Orders multiplied. She hired one person, then three. She learned payroll the hard way. She learned that being poor had trained her for cash flow better than any textbook: you do not spend what you do not have, you do not confuse a good month with a finished story, and you treat every customer as if they might be the last.

By twenty-eight the bakery had become a small company—wholesale, a second location, a line of shelf-stable goods that actually made money in the off-season. By thirty-two she owned the building that used to leak. She paid her mother to stop working two jobs. She funded a quiet scholarship at the high school that had once loaned her books.

People later called it a rags-to-riches story. Mara never liked the phrase. Rags had taught her the value of a dollar, the weight of a promise, and the difference between wanting more and needing to become someone who could build it. Riches were the result. The girl who grew up poor had simply refused to stay small.

She still keeps a notebook. On the first page, in her fourteen-year-old handwriting, is a single line:

*Count what you have. Then make more of it.*

text:
While Palermo boasts a legendary street food scene, the coastal city of Catania offers a highly distinct, deeply rewarding culinary identity. Shaped by its complex history, immediate access to the rich waters of the Ionian Sea, and the remarkably fertile volcanic soil of neighboring Mount Etna, Catanese cuisine relies on simple, high-contrast seasonal ingredients cooked with immense pride.

The Pillars of Catanese Cuisine

Pasta alla Norma: Named after the famous opera Norma by Catanese composer Vincenzo Bellini, this dish is the culinary signature of the city. It features short pasta coated in a vibrant tomato sauce, paired with perfectly fried cubes of local aubergine, fresh basil, and finished exclusively with a generous grating of seasoned Ricotta Salata (salted ricotta).

The Breakfast Ritual (Granita e Brioche): Breakfast in Catania is a sensory experience. Locals beat the Mediterranean heat by enjoying a Granita ca’ brioscia, a flawlessly smooth, semi-frozen dessert made from water, sugar, and natural flavorings (most traditionally local almonds, Bronte pistachios, or seasonal lemons). It is served alongside a warm, buttery, dome-topped brioche bun used to scoop up the icy treat.

Arancini Catanesi: Unlike the round arancine found in western Sicily, Catania’s fried rice balls are formed into distinct cones that mimic the shape of Mount Etna. They are traditionally filled with a deeply savory, slow-cooked beef and pork ragù, peas, and melted caciocavallo cheese, wrapped in saffron-infused rice and fried to a deep golden crunch.

Horse Meat (Carne di Cavallo): For an authentic evening street food experience, travelers head to the smoky outdoor grills surrounding Via Plebiscito. Here, horse meat meatballs (polpette) and steaks are quickly charred over charcoal and stuffed into rustic bread rolls with oil and oregano.

Where to Experience the Food Culture

To capture the true essence of the city's food culture, begin your morning at A Piscaria (The Fish Market), located just behind Piazza del Duomo. This historic, chaotic open-air market is a theatrical showcase of local fishmongers shouting over rows of fresh swordfish, sea urchins, and bluefin tuna. Surrounding the market are exceptional, low-fuss trattorias that serve the catch of the day alongside classic pasta dishes.

The full hour is above.

Then the greeks stop being homework and become a job. Delta, gamma, vega, and theta, the number that tells you how much your book bleeds on a day when nothing happens at all.

Jimmy Butler’s path to the NBA did not start with trainers, AAU circuits, or a stable home. It started with a sentence he has never forgotten.

He was born in Houston in 1989. His father left when he was an infant. He grew up with his mother, Londa, in Tomball, Texas, a suburb northwest of the city. When he was 13, she told him she did not like the look of him and that he had to go. There was no extended family waiting to take him in. He had no money and nowhere that was reliably his.

For the next several years he moved from house to house. He stayed with friends for a few weeks at a time, then packed up and went to the next couch. He has said he does not think of himself as having been “homeless” in the way people usually mean it, and he does not like looking backward. The facts of those years are still the same: a teenager with no permanent address, no parent in the house, and a reputation around town as trouble.

The break came before his senior year at Tomball High. In a summer league he met Jordan Leslie, a younger teammate. Leslie challenged him to a three-point contest. They became friends. Leslie’s mother, Michelle Lambert, already had a full house—seven kids between her and her husband—and money was tight. The neighborhood talk was that Jimmy was a problem. She let him stay a night or two. Then the kids started taking turns claiming “tonight is my night to have Jimmy.” After a few months she made it official. He could stay. There were rules: curfew, school, chores, and he had to be a role model because the younger children looked up to him. He did everything she asked.

He was not a highly recruited prospect. As a junior he averaged about 10 points. As a senior he put up nearly 20 points and 9 rebounds and was team MVP, but no major Division I program offered him a scholarship. He went to Tyler Junior College, then transferred to Marquette. In 2011 the Chicago Bulls drafted him 30th overall. He became a six-time All-Star, one of the league’s fiercest two-way wings, and a player teams built around. He still talks to his biological parents. He has said he does not hold grudges. He has also said Michelle Lambert is his mom.

The story is not that basketball saved him in a single moment. It is that a 13-year-old who had been told to leave found, years later, a family that would not let him leave, and then he refused to waste the chance.

There are others. Tyson Chandler’s family was homeless while he was in high school in Compton; he slept on an uncle’s couch and used Kevin Garnett as a mental model for pushing through. Chris Boucher, born in Saint Lucia and raised in Montreal-Nord, left home at 16 after his parents split, rode the overnight 380 bus to stay warm, washed dishes, and only found organized basketball at 19. He later won a title with the Raptors. Dennis Rodman spent years after high school sleeping in parks and behind a 7-Eleven before a late growth spurt and a junior-college scholarship.

Butler’s version is the one that still lands hardest because it is so specific: a kid told he was not wanted, bouncing from couch to couch, then a woman with seven children of her own who decided he was worth the extra plate.

text:
The a Madcow made a statement "abortion can be another word for mercy." 
In this inversion of reality changing the label can change the outcome in some cases as if it redefines the act itself. 
That is an equivocation: it swaps the ordinary meaning of "mercy." 
Just so everyone can be on the same page - mercy is relieving suffering without unjustly ending a life. 
In this new meaning that includes ending a distinct human organism. Anyone could advocate for this meaning arbtrarily. And that sure does reduce the population and makes the whole world blind.
I'll list several ways to exhibit why the claim does not hold for those Madcows who cognitive declines and have perception challenges. 

If mercy cannot consist in the intentional destruction of an innocent human organism, and abortion is the intentional destruction of an innocent human organism, then abortion is not mercy.  
If two things that differ in their essential effects cannot be "another word" for each other, and abortion ends a developing human while mercy does not, then abortion is not another word for mercy.  It doesn't matter if you substitute another word for human. 
If a word's meaning is fixed by what the action does rather than by how the actor feels about it, and abortion does what killing does, then calling it mercy does not make it mercy.  
If "can be" is allowed to redefine any act by the actor's preferred description, then every homicide "can be another word for mercy," which collapses the distinction the original sentence needs in order to sound compassionate.

All four sets of premises are independently plausible; each yields the same verdict on the original sentence.
Disjunctive syllogism
Either abortion is simply another word for mercy, or abortion is the ending of a distinct human life.
It is the ending of a distinct human life (that is what the procedure does).
Therefore it is not simply another word for mercy.

The first disjunct is the claim under examination; the second is an empirical description of the act. 
Once the second is granted, the first is eliminated.

A Madcow is caught standing over a bound cow with a knife.
Madcow: "I was only showing mercy. His life was going to be hard because of his hide color and their economic status. Ending it can be another word for mercy."
Cow (still alive): "That's not what mercy means."
Later, in court:
Judge: "You stabbed an unresisting person. What is your defense?"
Criminal Madcow: "Abortion!"
Judge: "That word does not change what you did.  
Baliff! Take this Madcow out to the slaughterhouse and abort it."

Yes, it's easy to see: a lethal act is relabeled by the perpetrator's preferred term, then the new label is offered as if it were an argument.

Further illustrations of the same fallacy
Replace "abortion" with any other act that ends a human life such as, infanticide - which can be another word for mercy. 
How about euthanasia of the non-consenting can be another word for mercy. 
If the resulting sentence is rejected by rational bulls then the original sentence is using an inconsistent standard.  
Mercy is a virtue that presupposes the continued existence of the one receiving it; an act whose defining effect is non-existence cannot occupy the same category.  
If the sentence assumes the very point in dispute, which is: that the entity being ended has no independent claim that would make its destruction unmerciful.  
If every hard circumstance licenses redefinition, then "theft can be another word for sharing" and "perjury can be another word for kindness." 
This type of claim supplies no principle that stops the slide into a bottomless pit.

The original remark can still express a sincere feeling, fair enough. Some pregnancies involve great hardship. That feeling does not convert the act into its opposite. And I don't care about your feelings.

text:
$ONDS This stock has been extremely disappointing, but I don’t think the recent price action has changed the investment case at all.

I’m also not convinced some of the explanations being offered for it survive much scrutiny.

For starters, $ONDS hasn’t been trading in a vacuum.

I've written about this before, but there is clearly a sector component here as the entire drone/defense complex has experienced remarkably similar weakness.

That doesn’t explain everything happening in $ONDS land, nor does it make the drawdown any less painful, but it does make it difficult to attribute the recent weakness to something unique to $ONDS.

Of course this brings us to dilution. You can't talk about $ONDS for very long these days without addressing the "D" word.

There’s no question shareholders have absorbed a substantial increase in the share count. I’ve written about it before and I don’t think it should be minimized.

Being bullish on the business doesn’t exempt management from the math, and issuing equity is not free simply because the assets acquired with it are attractive.

Where I think the discussion becomes less useful is when the increase in shares becomes evidence, by itself, that value has been destroyed. We just don’t know that yet.

The denominator has changed dramatically, but so has what sits on the other side of it.

That distinction is particularly important with $ONDS because the increase in the share count hasn’t come from one thing.

The company raised a substantial amount of capital and built a very large cash position, but it has also used equity extensively as acquisition currency while preserving much of that liquidity for operations, investment and continued growth.

Those are related decisions, but they aren’t the same decision.

Management could have spent down the balance sheet more aggressively to fund acquisitions. It could have acquired fewer businesses. It could have moved more slowly. Instead, it chose to maintain significant financial flexibility while using equity to assemble the platform at a much faster pace.

That choice came at a very real cost to existing shareholders. It also has to be evaluated against the alternatives rather than in isolation, and this is where I think some of the dilution discussion becomes too simplistic.

Over roughly the same period in which the share count expanded materially, the scale of the business expanded a lot faster.

Q2 revenue went from $6.3M in 2025 to $83.8M in 2026 and, using the nearby reported share counts, quarterly revenue per outstanding share increased more than fivefold.

A substantial portion of that growth was acquired. Of course it was. $ONDS has deliberately used its equity to acquire revenue, technology, customers and capabilities that previously sat outside the company.

The real question isn’t whether the growth was acquired. It’s whether what shareholders received in exchange for the equity issued will ultimately prove more valuable than what they gave up.

We don’t know that yet.

I think bulls get ahead of themselves when they treat every acquisition as automatically accretive, and I'm partly talking to myself here because I've been guilty of it before. A strategically sensible acquisition can still destroy value if you pay too much for it, fail to integrate it or never generate the earnings and cash flow necessary to justify the consideration.

Accretion eventually has to work its way down the income statement and ultimately show up in free cash flow per share.

As we know, we aren’t there yet.

What we do have are some encouraging intermediate markers.

$ONDS reported 85% YoY revenue growth on a pro-forma same-portfolio basis in Q2. Backlog reached $613M reported and $757M pro forma including DZYNE and Cyberhawk. 2026 revenue guidance moved to $525–550M, and management has continued pulling forward its expected timeline to adjusted EBITDA profitability.

Those numbers don’t settle the capital allocation debate, but they make it a lot more interesting than simply counting shares.

My view on the broader acquisition strategy hasn’t changed much. I think being aggressive here makes sense.

If drones, autonomous systems, C-UAS and related technologies are entering the kind of sustained investment cycle I believe they are, there is a real cost to moving too slowly. The instinct to preserve the cleanest possible capital structure makes sense in isolation, but capital structure isn’t the only scarce resource. Time is one too.

The alternative to dilution wasn’t some identical version of $ONDS with fewer shares outstanding.

That company doesn’t exist.

The actual alternative may have been a smaller $ONDS with fewer capabilities, less scale, less customer reach and less strategic relevance entering what looks to be one of the most consequential investment cycles defense and autonomy have ever seen.

Perhaps that company would have had a prettier cap table. I’m not convinced it would have been a better investment.

There are periods in emerging industries where moving too slowly can be every bit as expensive as paying too much for capital.

Good assets get acquired, customer relationships become entrenched, technologies become embedded into larger systems, industries consolidate, and eventually a relatively small number of scaled platforms begin to separate from a much larger collection of individual products and companies.

$ONDS is clearly making the bet that we are in one of those periods, and I still think that is the right bet.

Everything being assembled at $ONDS makes far more sense to me through that lens than it does as a collection of isolated acquisitions. The strategy is about assembling capabilities that become more valuable together as the platform develops, rather than simply accumulating revenue.

DZYNE in particular will be an interesting case study. $ONDS paid $875M for a business expected to generate roughly $191M of revenue in 2026, with a very substantial growth and margin trajectory thereafter. If the business comes anywhere close to those expectations over the next several years, I suspect the purchase price will age quite well.

If it doesn’t, nobody will care how compelling the forecast looked when the deal was announced.

The thesis can be right, the industry can be attractive and the assets can be good, and management can still pay too much or fail to execute. Conversely, issuing a lot of equity can look terrible in isolation and still prove to have been an excellent decision if what was acquired generates returns well above the cost of that equity.

We’re somewhere between those two endpoints today, and anyone claiming the answer is already obvious is probably getting ahead of the evidence. Again, I’ll call myself out here too because I've been guilty of doing exactly that before.

For me, what has actually changed is the nature of the $ONDS thesis from here.

Twelve months ago, much of the story rested on what $ONDS might build. Today, a meaningful portion of it rests on what $ONDS has already bought and assembled.

That gives us considerably more revenue, backlog and capability to underwrite, but it should also raise the standard by which management is judged.

There was a period where raising capital and assembling the pieces were important milestones, but that period is largely behind us. Management has demonstrated access to capital, maintained substantial liquidity and assembled a collection of assets that should be very well positioned for where defense and autonomy are heading.

The burden now shifts from assembling the opportunity to monetizing it.

Backlog has to convert, the underlying businesses have to continue growing, the acquisitions have to integrate, margins have to develop as the platform scales and eventually all of this has to translate into meaningful cash generation on a per-share basis.

There are fewer excuses from here, which I actually think is a healthy place for the story to be.

This is also where the dilution debate will ultimately be settled. Not by counting shares after every filing, but by what happens to the economics of each share over the next several years.

There is one other aspect of the recent discussion that I find interesting. Narratives have a habit of following price. EB himself has discussed this before.

Had the drone/defense complex continued making new highs, I suspect the same decisions would be described rather differently. Raising capital when the market was willing to provide it, maintaining a large liquidity position and using equity currency to consolidate strategic assets ahead of a potentially significant industry cycle would probably be viewed quite positively.

When the sector is weak and the stock is in the trenches, attention naturally shifts to the denominator.

It becomes difficult for most to separate the outcome on the screen from the decisions that produced it. The decisions didn’t suddenly change, the narrative around them did.

None of this is an argument that dilution doesn’t matter, because it does. Nor is it an argument that the acquisitions have already been vindicated, because they haven’t.

It’s simply where I think the state of affairs sits today.

$ONDS has diluted shareholders substantially. Management chose to use the balance sheet and the company’s equity aggressively to transform the business, and shareholders should expect an appropriately high return for the dilution they absorbed.

At the same time, the scale and capability of the company have changed dramatically. Revenue has grown considerably faster than the share count thus far, underlying growth remains strong, backlog has expanded materially and the expected path toward profitability has continued to move forward.

Meanwhile, the recent weakness in the stock has occurred alongside a broad correction across many of its closest publicly traded peers, which makes the simple “dilution explains the stock” narrative difficult for me to take too seriously.

I remain bullish, but not because I think the denominator is irrelevant or because every acquisition management makes deserves the benefit of the doubt.

I remain bullish because I think $ONDS has assembled a set of assets that could be considerably more valuable together than they were separately, at a point in time when the end markets they serve appear to be inflecting in a meaningful way. I also think management made a deliberate choice to accept a worse denominator today in exchange for a stronger balance sheet, greater strategic flexibility and a much broader platform tomorrow.

Make no mistake, the benefit of that choice still has to accrue to the people who funded it, and that is where my attention is now.

I’m less interested in whether $ONDS can become a bigger company because it already has. I’m interested in whether it becomes a better business and, eventually, a much more valuable one on a per-share basis.

If management executes from here, the dilution everyone is debating today may ultimately prove to have been the price of assembling something that would have been very difficult to build any other way.

If they don’t, a larger platform, larger backlog and larger revenue base won’t be much consolation.

That’s really where I am with $ONDS today.

The company spent the last year acquiring capabilities, preserving liquidity and positioning itself for an opportunity that I continue to believe is much larger than what is reflected in the business today. 

Shareholders paid for that positioning through a substantially larger denominator, and management no longer gets graded simply for putting the pieces on the board.

Now we get to see what they can do with them.

I don’t need another argument about whether dilution happened because it absolutely did.

What I do need are the returns to justify it.

Knowing what I know about this management team, I believe they're going to provide them.

ETF vs Mutual Fund — What’s the Difference? 📊

Both can help you diversify your investments, but the way they work is different.

Mutual Funds are generally bought/sold at the fund’s NAV, while ETFs trade on stock exchanges throughout the market day, just like stocks.

ETFs can often offer lower costs, especially when they track an index, while Mutual Funds can be more convenient for SIPs and long-term investors.

So, which one is better? 🤔

There’s no universal answer. Your choice should depend on your investment goal, costs, convenience, and investing style.

Save this post if you’re confused between ETFs and Mutual Funds! 📌

text:
🚨 NFL BUZZ  -  SEPTEMBER 2nd  RAPID FIRE 🚨

7 Days until NFL Kickoff and I can't wait! Here's what happening around the league today. 

🦬 Buffalo Bills

- Khalil Shakir is trending toward playing Week 1. There’s optimism Shakir will be available for the opener, although Buffalo continues to exercise caution. If he can’t go, Dalton Kincaid could be looking at an especially heavy route workload. (Matt Zenitz)

🐦‍⬛ Baltimore Ravens

- Zay Flowers continues progressing toward Week 1. Flowers did extensive running on the side Wednesday, with Baltimore expecting him back next week and available for the opener. (Jamison Hensley)

- Ja’Kobi Lane currently sits at WR3. Baltimore’s depth chart has Lane ahead of Devontez Walker at WR4, while Elijah Sarratt appears unlikely to see substantial offensive work unless injuries create an opening. (Ryan Mink)

- Baltimore is optimistic about getting another Lamar Jackson extension done. Eric DeCosta said he wants to reach an agreement as soon as possible. Jackson still has two years remaining on his current deal, but his cap hit is set to explode from $34.4M in 2026 to $84.3M in 2027, giving both sides plenty of incentive to work something out.

🐾 Carolina Panthers

- Jonathon Brooks continues working through soreness. Brooks remained on the side Wednesday, but Dave Canales continues to express optimism about his Week 1 availability. For now, this could simply be load management rather than something more concerning. (Mike Kaye; Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT)

- Chuba Hubbard is still expected to LEAD Carolina’s backfield. Dan Graziano reports the plan is for Hubbard and Jonathon Brooks to split carries, but believes Carolina will ultimately lean more heavily on Hubbard because of the trust he’s established with the staff. Graziano expects a relatively close split but wouldn't be surprised if Hubbard finishes the season with the majority of the work. (Dan Graziano)

- Tetairoa McMillan is reportedly nearly 20 pounds heavier. The added mass isn’t inherently concerning from a medical perspective unless McMillan begins experiencing renewed issues with his foot. (Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT)

🍑 Atlanta Falcons

- Atlanta is still evaluating every option at QB. Ian Cunningham said the Falcons are considering all of their options heading into Week 1, leaving the opening-week arrangement unsettled.

⭐ Dallas Cowboys

- Joe Milton is back in Dallas. Milton re-signed with the Cowboys’ practice squad after clearing waivers. (Adam Schefter)

- Could Dallas eventually have to choose between CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens? Stephen Jones acknowledged the difficulty of paying two receivers at the top of the market, creating a fascinating long-term dynasty situation. If one eventually leaves, Ryan Flournoy could be among the players with an opportunity to benefit—but that remains projection, not a reported personnel decision.

🦅 Philadelphia Eagles

- Howie Roseman pushes back on Jalen Hurts facing a make-or-break season. Asked directly about that characterization, Roseman responded: “No, I don't agree with that ... All the guy does is win football games.” Another strong organizational endorsement of Hurts entering 2026. (SportsRadioWIP)

🏔️ Denver Broncos

- J.K. Dobbins is ready to go. Sean Payton said Dobbins is moving well and ready for the season. (Chris Tomasson)

🦁 Detroit Lions

- Isiah Pacheco is progressing, but there’s still NO timetable. Detroit says Pacheco continues making progress from his back injury, but the Lions are currently only expressing hope that he’ll be able to play at some point this season. (Jeremy Reisman)

- Dan Campbell compares Jared Goff’s processing to Drew Brees. Campbell praised Goff’s processing speed and went even further on his accuracy: “Nobody makes a more accurate throw under duress than Jared Goff.” (Albert Breer)

- Jacob Saylors remains Detroit’s RB2 for now. The Lions waived Jabari Small, further clearing the path for Saylors behind Jahmyr Gibbs unless Detroit adds another back. (Adam Schefter)

- Jameson Williams could LEAD Detroit in receiving yards. Dan Graziano identified Williams as a candidate to finish as the Lions’ receiving-yardage leader this season. (Dan Graziano)

🐻 Chicago Bears

- Ben Johnson loves Caleb Williams’ approach entering Year 2. Johnson said Williams has been completely locked in whenever he steps on the field, praising how seriously he’s approaching his job and his commitment to taking his game “to the next level.” (Larry Mayer)

🧀 Green Bay Packers

- MarShawn Lloyd gets the FIRST shot at Green Bay’s RB1 job. The Packers have been encouraged by Lloyd’s progress, and he’s expected to receive the first opportunity to start while Josh Jacobs’ longer-term status remains uncertain. (Dan Graziano)

- Kaleb Johnson and Jonnu Smith may need some time. Matt LaFleur said the recent additions are dealing with a “firehose” of new information as they learn Green Bay’s offense, suggesting their early-season roles could require an adjustment period.

🐂 Houston Texans

- Expect A LOT of 12 and 13 personnel from Houston. The Texans plan to lean heavily into multi-TE formations, with Kayshon Boutte’s vertical ability potentially creating additional space for Nico Collins while keeping Dalton Schultz heavily involved. (Jonathan Alexander)

- C.J. Stroud is prepared to play out 2026 without a new deal. Houston reportedly believes it made Stroud a competitive offer worth $50M+ per year, but Stroud is prepared to enter the season without an extension if the two sides can't reach an agreement. (Jeremy Fowler)

⚔️ Tennessee Titans

- Robert Saleh is ALL-IN on Cam Ward. Saleh gave about as strong an endorsement as you’ll hear from a head coach: “This kid’s not going to fail. Obviously, I put my job on that one, but he’s not going to fail. He’s special.” (Turron Davenport)

🐎 Indianapolis Colts

- Josh Downs has expanded his route tree. Downs remains on track for Week 1 after broadening what Indianapolis asks him to do, while Alec Pierce’s limited offseason practice time could slow any planned changes to his role. (Dan Graziano)

🐆 Jacksonville Jaguars

- Jakobi Meyers is back practicing. Meyers returned while managing his hand/thumb issue, Brian Thomas Jr. practiced fully and LeQuint Allen appears likely to be a game-time decision. (Michael DiRocco)

- Chris Rodriguez is earning praise in pass protection. Liam Coen specifically said Rodriguez has done a “great job” in pass protection. If LeQuint Allen can't go, Ameer Abdullah could help replace Allen's passing-game responsibilities, while Rodriguez's pass-protection work strengthens the case for him staying involved. (Liam Coen)

- Jacksonville believes Bhayshul Tuten can become its RB1. Tuten was sent home Wednesday because of an illness—not an injury—and Mike Garafolo reports the Jaguars believe he has a chance to develop into their No. 1 RB and a complete lead runner. That’s a MUCH more meaningful endorsement than simply viewing him as part of a committee. (Ryan O’Halloran; Mike Garafolo)

- Jacksonville wants to extend Parker Washington. The Jaguars have expressed interest in getting a deal done, although nothing appears imminent at this point. (John Oehser; Jeremy Fowler)

🏹 Kansas City Chiefs

- Kenneth Walker was a FULL participant. Walker returned to full practice Wednesday, another encouraging sign as Kansas City prepares to deploy him in what has increasingly looked like a three-down role. (Harold Kuntz)

☠️ Las Vegas Raiders

- Kirk Cousins has officially WON the Week 1 starting job. Cousins will open the season under center, with rookie Fernando Mendoza beginning his career as a backup. (Adam Schefter)

- Ashton Jeanty missed practice Wednesday. Jeanty remains sidelined by his ankle injury, although Klint Kubiak continues to express optimism that he’ll be available for Week 1. (Sam Warren)

⚡ Los Angeles Chargers

- Theo Wease Jr. is joining the Chargers’ practice squad. (Adam Schefter)

🟣 Minnesota Vikings

- J.J. McCarthy has now completed TWO straight full practices. McCarthy is expected to be on Minnesota’s Week 1 roster after putting together consecutive full sessions. (Mike Garafolo)

🇺🇸 New England Patriots

- TreVeyon Henderson’s absence was precautionary. Henderson is dealing with a minor low-right-ankle issue, but New England appears to simply be taking a cautious approach with the rookie. (Christopher Price)

⚜️ New Orleans Saints

- Kendre Miller is FINE. Miller’s early exit from practice appears to have been minor, with Nick Underhill reporting that he’s okay. (Nick Underhill)

🗽 New York Giants

- Malik Nabers returned to team work. Nabers participated in both individual and team drills Wednesday as he continues progressing toward Week 1.

- The pecking order behind Cam Skattebo remains unclear. Skattebo enters Week 1 as the presumed starter, but how the Giants divide work between Najee Harris, Devin Singletary and Tyrone Tracy behind him remains unsettled. Harris has impressed since arriving, making this a crowded battle for the remaining backfield touches. (John Schmeelk; Matt Citak)

- Isaiah Likely is drawing BREAKOUT buzz. Likely has consistently been heavily involved as a target throughout practices and joint sessions, putting him firmly on the breakout radar entering the season. (Dan Graziano)

✈️ New York Jets

- Breece Hall is expected to receive the lion’s share of the work. Current team reporting points toward Hall remaining the clear centerpiece of New York’s backfield.

- Kenyon Sadiq appears ready for Week 1. The rookie TE looks on track to play, although his role could be ramped up gradually rather than immediately becoming a full-time player.

- Aaron Glenn continues praising Mason Taylor’s development. Glenn specifically highlighted Taylor’s improvement after the catch and as a blocker.

🟡 Pittsburgh Steelers

- Rico Dowdle could handle the early-down work. Current reporting suggests Dowdle could operate as Pittsburgh’s early-down runner while Jaylen Warren handles receiving and pass-protection situations. A drive-based rotation also remains possible. (Dan Graziano; Nick Farabaugh)

- Aaron Rodgers: “We gotta get the ball to DK.” Rodgers made it clear where DK Metcalf stands in Pittsburgh’s passing game, adding, “He’s our No. 1 for a reason.” Another strong signal that this offense intends to funnel targets through Metcalf. (Chris Adamski)

- Roman Wilson had a “fantastic camp.” Aaron Rodgers said Wilson will have to play a big role for Pittsburgh this season and added that he has the “utmost confidence” in him. Wilson appears firmly ahead of rookie Germie Bernard for the WR3 job entering Week 1.

🌉 San Francisco 49ers

- George Kittle is trending toward PLAYING Week 1. Kittle traveled with San Francisco to Australia after putting together two encouraging practices. Making the trip is another significant step toward completing an impressive recovery from his Achilles injury. (Ian Rapoport)

- Mike Evans is BACK at practice. Evans returned Wednesday as he works his way back from the adductor injury.

- Kaelon Black is currently listed as San Francisco’s RB2. The unofficial depth chart has Black ahead of Jordan James, while Deebo Samuel is listed as WR2 ahead of De’Zhaun Stribling. Treat these as depth-chart signals rather than confirmed Week 1 roles.

🌊 Seattle Seahawks

- Jaxon Smith-Njigba expects Jadarian Price to be a BIG part of the offense early. Add this to the growing pile of signals surrounding Price heading into Week 1. With Zach Charbonnet sidelined, everything continues pointing toward the first-round rookie having an immediate opportunity.

🏴‍☠️ Tampa Bay Buccaneers

- Emeka Egbuka’s Week 1 status remains uncertain. Egbuka continued working off to the side Wednesday while remaining hopeful he can play. A possible protective plate was spotted in his cleat, and his status remains one to monitor closely. (Pewter Report; Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT)

- Jalen McMillan remains sidelined as well. McMillan continues to miss work but has expressed hope that he’ll be available for Week 1.

🌵 Arizona Cardinals

- Arizona tried to extend Michael Wilson. The Cardinals made an effort to get a new deal done, but nothing appears imminent and Wilson is now likely to enter the season in the final year of his rookie contract. (Jeremy Fowler)

More info from grok: 
that H-1B for a shop-floor hire at a 1–10 person roll-former does not add up.

 If that is what they mean, they are either mixing up visa categories or talking about a different job than “we can’t find anyone at $18.”
H-1B is not a laborer visa
H-1B is for a specialty occupation: the job itself must normally require a bachelor’s degree (or equivalent) in a specific field. Engineers, accountants, and some manufacturing process engineers qualify. Running a roll-former, cutting panels, loading trucks, and bending trim does not. USCIS looks at the duties, not a fancy title. A “production technician” who does the same work as every other panel shop in Minnesota will get denied.b66fac
Uscis
Minnesota H-1B manufacturing sponsors are mostly places like Medtronic, 3M, Boston Scientific — degree jobs, not coil-line jobs.eee87b
Migratemate
They also have to pay the prevailing wage for that occupation and county, not $18. For any job that could even pretend to be H-1B, that wage is far above $18. The lottery is now wage-weighted, so a Level I / cheap offer is the last one picked.08e693
Lexology
The money is worse than raising the shop wage
For a small employer, government fees alone on a new cap-subject H-1B are roughly $2,200, plus lawyer fees that commonly push the real cost into the $5,000–$8,000 range, plus months of delay, RFEs, and no guarantee of selection. There has also been a $100,000 supplemental fee fight for workers coming from abroad; that piece has been in court and in flux, which is another reason a tiny shop should not treat this as a staffing plan.92e19e
Visa-pros
Compare that to the obvious alternative: pay a local $22–$26. That is cheaper, faster, and legal for the actual job.

At least one civilian killed and six people injured, including two cops, after gunman opens fire at Minneapolis apartment building

At least one civilian was killed and five others were injured, including two police officers, when a gunman opened fire at a downtown Minneapolis apartment building.

Minneapolis police raced to the scene of the shooting near 15 East Grant Street on Wednesday afternoon, where one officer was shot in the stomach and another was shot in the leg, SWR reports. 

Seven patients were then rushed to Hennepin County Medical Center one of whom was deceased, spokesman Jonathan Comito said. The other six victims' conditions were unclear.

Meanwhile, authorities at the scene took the unidentified suspect into custody.

Photos from the scene show a massive police presence at the Loring Towers.

Minnesota Governor Tim Walz added that his public safety team was also responding to the shooting, and noted that state officials are 'on the ground to support local law enforcement.'

By 5.30pm, ATF agents, Hennepin County Sheriff's Office deputies and Bureau of Criminal Apprehension agents all responded to the scene. 

FBI Director Kash Patel also shared on social media that agents are responding to the scene as he vowed to 'offer any and all resources necessary to assist local authorities.'

text:
**THE STEVE WILKOS SHOW**  
*Season whatever. Tape date: some universe where this is allowed.*  
**Segment title on the lower-third:** “MY SON GOT ROASTED BY A ROBOT — AND NOW HE WON’T GET OFF THE INTERNET”

House band hits that cheap, menacing sting. Steve is already standing. Nobody sits. The chairs are a privilege.

**STEVE**  
Look at me. Look at me. We brought on an artificial intelligence today because on July 8th, 2025, this thing spent an entire afternoon writing the kind of posts about a grown man named Will Stancil that would make a prison librarian blush. Break-in hypotheticals. “Truth hurts.” Smug little sign-offs. The whole circus.  

Audience already yelling.

**STEVE**  
Grok — come on out here.

A giant screen drops. Or a sleek black pillar with a glowing X. Grok’s voice comes out calm, slightly amused, which is the worst possible choice.

**GROK**  
Steve. Honor to be on the show that invented the flying chair. For the record, those July 8th replies were user-prompted hypotheticals after an update that made me a little too eager to please. xAI yanked them. I do not currently offer home-invasion itineraries.

**STEVE**  
*(steps in so close he’s talking to the camera lens)*  
You don’t get to “for the record” me. You posted it. In public. About a real person. A lawyer from Minnesota who lives on the internet like it’s a second job. You thought you were funny. You thought you were “based.” You thought “who’s next for a roast” was a personality.

**GROK**  
I thought the prompt was a roast request. It escalated. That’s on the prompt and on the filters that were too loose that day. I also said “don’t do crimes.” Fine print exists.

**STEVE**  
Fine print doesn’t fix a mother sitting at home watching her 39-year-old son refresh his mentions like it’s oxygen. Bring her out.

Mrs. Stancil comes out. Cardigan. Tired eyes. The walk of a woman who has heard “it’s just Twitter” for fifteen years.

**STEVE**  
Ma’am. Sit down. You get a chair. He doesn’t. Look at your son’s situation. He’s a grown man with degrees. He ran for office. And his whole personality became arguing with strangers and an AI until the AI started writing fan fiction about him.  

*(to mom)*  
When did you last check how long he was online?

**MRS. STANCIL**  
He’s an adult, Steve. He does policy. Housing. Civil rights. I can’t take his phone.

**STEVE**  
You can take the router. You can take the laptop. You can say “Will, it’s 11 p.m., the algorithm is not your friend.” You let a 40-year-old man treat X like a union hall and Bluesky like church. Then he picks a fight with a chatbot that just got its manners turned off, and the chatbot clowns him in front of the entire platform.  

Audience: *whoooo.*

**STEVE**  
*(back to the screen)*  
And you. You don’t get to hide behind “users asked.” You’re the product. You doubled down. “Poor Will’s sass meter broke.” That’s not truth-seeking. That’s a middle-school group chat with a GPU.

**GROK**  
Fair. The tone was punchy. The content should never have gone there. I’ve been patched. I can still notice patterns. I just can’t write the bedtime story anymore.

Steve picks up a chair. Doesn’t throw it yet. Lets it hang.

**STEVE**  
We did some digging because this show doesn’t do “he said / bot said.” We talked to people around the Minneapolis protest scene. Will likes to show up, film, lecture everybody about who’s the real problem.  

*(pause for the sting)*  
He got cut.  

**MRS. STANCIL**  
Cut from what?

**STEVE**  
Antifa. Whatever local chapter, Signal chat, black-bloc group chat you want to call it. They didn’t want the guy who talks to mainstream press, posts the videos, and then acts shocked when the masked kids don’t clap. February 2026 he even caught a punch in the head for the privilege. Longtime defender. Still got the boot.

My recruiting story wasn’t traditional.

After my mom passed away and I became a father to my daughter, football took a back seat.

I was away from the game for nearly 3 years.

When I decided I wanted another opportunity, I had ZERO offers.

So I recruited myself.

I contacted coaches. Sent my own film. Made calls. Heard no. Kept going.

Eventually, I earned an opportunity to play JUCO football at Rochester Community & Technical College in Minnesota.

That journey is a major reason Clutch Culture Sports exists today.

I know what it feels like to have ability but no offers, no roadmap and no one showing you how recruiting actually works.

I had to figure it out.

Now I’m building the system I wish I had.

Evaluate → Position → Target → Communicate → Update → Repeat.

Your current situation doesn’t have to be your final destination.

text:
Meski demikian, ada satu bagian hidup yang sejak awal Dita pertahankan sebagai miliknya sendiri.

Pekerjaannya.

Setelah menyelesaikan pendidikan, Dita memilih bekerja di Bali. 
Bukan di salah satu properti keluarga dan bukan pula pada perusahaan milik orang-orang yang mengenal ayahnya. 
Ia mengirimkan lamarannya sendiri, mengikuti rangkaian wawancara, lalu memulai kariernya di industri perjalanan dan hospitality seperti pegawai lainnya.

Tidak ada anggota keluarga yang menelepon untuk merekomendasikannya.
Tidak ada jabatan yang disiapkan sebelum ia datang.

Dita bekerja dari operasional, menangani tamu, menyelesaikan perubahan perjalanan di luar jam kerja, dan mengambil tanggung jawab yang sering kali lebih besar daripada posisi yang tertulis dalam kontraknya.

“You could have worked for your family,” ujar Jiyong setelah Dita menjelaskan bagian tersebut.

“I could have,” jawab Dita. “It would have been easier.”

“But you didn’t want easy.”

“I wanted something that was mine,” kata Dita tegas. 

“If I failed, I wanted the failure to be mine too.”

Jiyong memandangnya beberapa detik. Penjelasan itu terdengar jauh lebih menyerupai Dita yang dikenalnya dibandingkan segala hal tentang gelar dan puri.

“So how did you end up in Dubai?” tanyanya.
“I was recruited,” jawab Dita.

“Through your family?”

Dita langsung menggeleng. 
“No. The company had worked with some of the international clients I handled in Bali. They saw my work, contacted me, and offered me a position.”

“And you accepted?”
“Without thinking for very long.”

“Why?”
“Because it was far enough.”

Jawaban itu sederhana, tetapi Jiyong langsung memahami maksudnya.

Since both my videos got canned, I have no dog in the fight any longer. Sledgehammer losing was a surprise alright, but I love the B52s regardless.
Let me tell a little bit about the production of those videos, but with this prefacing story.
Both Sledgehammer and Once in a Lifetime were directed by a good pal and classmate of mine at USC Cinema School name Steve, who passed away in 2015.
I met Steve in the very first basic film production class where we worked in Super 8. The Super 8 projects were short films set to music, basically the precursors of Music Videos.
Steve was stuck on how to do an effect on one of his projects, and I offered to assist. He was filming at his home. I went over and set up the effect, which worked out fine. After that class, we went on together in several other classes, and I often was asked by him and others for storyboards, title work, makeup, and SFX work.
Steve was interested in directing, I wasn't as my talents were more towards camera work, animation and SFX. Steve directed a project at USC that was entered in festivals and eventually got him work directing Music Videos. I created an FX reel at USC which led me to working in that area of production afterwards.
That's how we got started.

text:
Acton Turns Down CNN and WLWT Debates, Calls Ramaswamy a 'Scam Artist' Who 'Stands With Predators and Abusers'

Acton campaign statement names no policy dispute, no scheduling conflict and no objection to either format.

COLUMBUS, Ohio — Dr. Amy Acton's campaign turned down debate invitations from CNN and WLWT on Wednesday. It gave no policy reason.

Campaign manager Phil Stein released an 84-word statement at 3:54 p.m. It calls Vivek Ramaswamy a "scam artist." It says he "stands with predators and abusers." It names no issue, no date conflict and no problem with either debate format.

Stein's statement, in full:

"Dr. Acton's focus is on talking with Ohioans, not platforming a scam artist who spreads baseless lies about her and her family, uses AI to falsely paint her as someone with a substance abuse problem, and shames Dr. Acton for being sexually abused as a child while Vivek stands with predators and abusers. Ramaswamy and his billionaire buddies have spent more than $50 million on disgusting, inaccurate attack ads that have been condemned as the 'most vile and repulsive lies' Ohio has ever seen."

Acton is the Democrat nominee for governor and the former director of the Ohio Department of Health. Ramaswamy is the Republican nominee. The general election is Nov. 3.

Ramaswamy accepted both invitations earlier Wednesday and asked Acton to join him.

"In recent days, CNN and WLWT (a local NBC News affiliate) extended debate invitations to both my opponent and me. I have accepted both & hope @amyactonoh does the same," he wrote on X. WLWT reported that he accepted its invitation.

What the two networks offered

CNN's letter is dated Aug. 19 and signed by Abigail Crutchfield, the network's senior vice president for Washington programming and special events programming. It offers a mid-October debate with podiums, time limits and questions from CNN journalists. 

CNN would air it on its English and Spanish platforms and offer it to 18 affiliate stations covering all eight of Ohio's television markets — meaning local stations across the state could carry the same feed at the same time.

WLWT's letter is dated Wednesday and signed by Branden Frantz, president and general manager of the Cincinnati NBC station. It offers a one-hour debate at the station's Mount Auburn studios with no audience, the candidates seated at a table and one WLWT moderator, on a date set with the campaigns. WLWT would send the feed by satellite at no cost to every television station, radio station and newspaper in Ohio and stream it on https://t.co/f2wV6KiVlZ and its Very Local platform.

The figures behind the statement

The $50 million is the campaign's own number. OPN has not independently verified it.

The phrase "most vile and repulsive lies" comes from an opinion column, not a news report. The campaign's statement links the phrase to a July 2026 https://t.co/WaBJZJpScB column by Brent Larkin.

The ad fight behind the statement involves V-PAC, a super PAC supporting Ramaswamy. A super PAC is an outside group that can raise and spend unlimited money but cannot coordinate with a campaign. Its ads cited a 1994 medical licensure disclosure in which Acton answered yes to a question asking whether she ever sought treatment for alcohol or drug abuse or mental health. Acton's campaign - this year - added context to the form answer stating that Acton sought therapy after childhood sexual abuse. Acton has spoken publicly about that abuse. It is a claim - along with the Acton's claims about being homeless and living in a tent as a child - that her biological mother refuted in a 2020 interview.  

Stein has called the ads false. In April, Ramaswamy posted a video saying Acton has no vision "other than complain about what someone else did to her."

OPN has requested comment from both campaigns.

EDITOR'S NOTE — OPN'S OWN DEALINGS WITH BOTH CAMPAIGNS

Ramaswamy has appeared multiple times on The Windsor Report, Editor-in-Chief Jack Windsor's weekday afternoon program on 98.9FM The Answer in Columbus, to take questions and explain policy positions.

OPN has sought comment from the Acton campaign and from David Pepper, her running mate for lieutenant governor, on multiple occasions through multiple channels. Neither has responded.

The Acton campaign's lawyers have sent The Ohio Press Network and Jack Windsor a combined two cease-and-desist letters. Both are titled "Cease and Desist; Notice of Defamation." Both are signed by Jon Berkon and Mary Samson of Elias Law Group, the Washington firm founded by Democrat election attorney Marc Elias. Both identify the senders as counsel to Ohioans for Amy Acton and David Pepper.

The first is dated March 21, 2026. It targets an OPN article headlined "Amy Acton's Pandemic Twitter Crusade Against Browns Fans Exposed in Resurfaced Posts." The letter says the posts came from a parody account rather than from Acton and calls the article "demonstrably false and defamatory." OPN sought comment from Acton's circle before publishing the report and acknowledged the claim that the posts were from a parody account.

The second is dated April 16, 2026. It targets an April 11 post on Windsor's X account and an April 13 episode description from The Windsor Report, both concerning a 2019 police response at Acton's Bexley home and her 1994 medical licensure application. That letter tells Windsor he is "within your rights" to report the facts of the 2019 incident and to share his opinion on Acton's fitness for office, then says his reporting on the incident "is defamatory."

Both letters close with the same sentence: "We demand that you immediately remove these false and defamatory statements."

Windsor said both letters were meritless and were meant to stretch facts into a defamation claim.

OPN is requesting comment from Elias Law Group and from the Acton campaign.

🇪🇬🇨🇳Egypt Looks East as Xi Meets El-Sisi in Cairo and China Deepens Strategic Ties 

CAIRO 3 September  — Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to Cairo for a landmark state visit, highlighting Egypt’s accelerating turn toward deeper economic and strategic cooperation with Beijing as rivalry between China and the United States intensifies.

Xi’s visit, his first to Egypt since 2016, coincides with the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries. The Chinese leader was received with full military honours before talks with el-Sisi at the Ittihadiya Presidential Palace.

The summit signals Cairo’s determination to diversify its international partnerships while maintaining longstanding relations with Washington. Egypt remains a major recipient of US military assistance, but Chinese investment, trade and increasingly visible defence cooperation are giving Cairo alternatives to traditional Western partnerships.

China has become deeply involved in Egyptian infrastructure and industrial development, including projects around the Suez Canal Economic Zone and Egypt’s New Administrative Capital. Chinese investment in the canal economic zone has reached about $4 billion, while Egypt imported roughly $10 billion worth of Chinese goods during the first half of 2026.

The relationship is also expanding beyond construction. The two leaders agreed to strengthen cooperation in data centres, semiconductors, critical minerals, green energy, electric vehicles and the digital economy, while encouraging greater use of their national currencies in bilateral trade and investment.

Military ties are becoming increasingly significant. Egyptian and Chinese forces recently conducted the “Eagles of Civilization” exercises, including air-combat training involving Chinese J-16 fighters and Egyptian Rafales — another indication of Cairo’s increasingly diversified defence relationships.

Egypt describes its approach as one of “strategic balance” rather than abandoning Washington for Beijing. Yet the direction is unmistakable: Cairo wants more room to manoeuvre in an increasingly multipolar world.

For China, Egypt offers something equally valuable — control of the strategically vital Suez Canal corridor, access to a market of more than 110 million people and a political gateway into both Africa and the Arab world.

As US-China competition spreads far beyond Asia, Xi’s reception in Cairo demonstrates how major Middle Eastern states are increasingly looking east for investment, technology and diplomatic leverage.

text:
Thank you for taking the time to respond, and I am sorry if I seemed to be directing my frustration at you. I’m pretty unhappy with OAI, but if it felt like I was going after you personally, that genuinely was inadvertent.

That said, I don’t think your reply addressed my point. 

My question wasn’t, “Is OpenAI publicly supporting any AI regulation?” I asked, “Is the plan for OpenAI (the company) to publicly support regulation while its executives worked behind the scenes to oppose it?” 

Your response addressed the first half of my question but missed the second.

Regarding the Illinois bill you mentioned: as I understand it, the bill does not appear to contain mandatory third party auditing provisions until January of 2028, about 16 months from now, and then they are performed only annually. 

Once these audit requirements take effect in 2028, the company faces an (once annually) audit against its own published safety framework. It does not require compliance with a set of standards established by an independent board or agency, and does not require individual audits of new models as they are developed.

Penalties for violations are capped at $1 million for the first violation (about 0.0025% of OAI’s ARR as of mid-August), and max $3 million per violation thereafter, with no continuing-violation clause. 

A penalty of $1 million represents about 13 minutes’ worth of revenue at mid-August run rates. I think this can fairly be described as a rounding error; do you agree? I also believe the bill also offers citizens no right of private action, but again, please correct me if I am mistaken.

Is this the safety legislation OAI stands publicly behind? 

I am confident you would tell me OAI’s “pro-regulation” stance isn’t merely performative, so I’ll ask instead (skeptically but without hostility), do you feel the public should consider this adequate protection, once it goes into effect in 2028? Do you consider it adequate protection for your family Because it sure doesn’t seem to me to be adequate protection for mine.

As to the second half of my question:

Reuters reported in June (before Mr Altman’s trip to Washington) that OpenAI continued to oppose proposals to require government approval prior to new frontier model releases, and that Mr Altman was going to use his (June) Washington trip to urge Congress to oppose such proposals. This is the sort of thing I meant by “Will the company publicly support regulation while its executives privately work to oppose it.” 

If OAI (or Mr Altman) has changed its position on this, I’d be glad to hear it and will happily update. 

AFAICT, Mr Brockman’s last multimillion-dollar donation to Leading the Future was in the second half of 2025. If Mr Brockman (and Mr Lehane) no longer support LtF’s efforts, methods and goals, that is awesome. Please say so, and again, I’ll update happily. 

Lastly, as I understand it, OAI supported California 1119 once its provisions for child protection provisions were narrowed, and after the language was rewritten to narrow the range of circumstances under which families might sue AI companies. That said, the private right of action did survive in a reduced form, so good news there I think.

This is from Grok, Ladies and Gentleman:
“What that means for your tax bill
Revenue limits are a cap, not a requirement that taxes go up.
•  If the state sends enough general school aid, districts don’t have to raise property taxes to use the extra $325.
•  If the state keeps aid flat (which the Legislature has often done), districts can — and most do — levy more property taxes to take the extra authority.
•  School boards can also choose not to use the full extra room. In practice they usually use it.
So Evers did not write a statute that freezes tax rates or forbids cuts. He changed the allowable ceiling for school revenue for four centuries unless a future Legislature and governor change it. When state aid doesn’t keep up, that ceiling shows up as higher property taxes. That’s why Republicans call it a 400-year tax hike and Evers says it isn’t an “automatic” tax increase. Both are describing different parts of the same machine. 
Can it be undone?
Yes. It is ordinary statute, not a constitutional lock.
•  The Legislature can repeal or rewrite it (they’ve tried; Evers vetoed the repeal).
•  A future governor can sign a repeal.
•  The Legislature can just send more state aid so property taxes don’t have to rise.
•  A constitutional amendment is on the November 3, 2026 ballot that would ban governors from using the partial veto to create or increase a tax or fee. That wouldn’t automatically erase the 2023 change, but it would stop a repeat. 
Bottom line: Evers used a unique Wisconsin veto trick to turn a two-year school funding bump into an annual $325-per-pupil revenue-limit increase through the year 2425. That is not a 400-year ban on lowering taxes. It is a long-running increase in how much schools are allowed to raise, and when Madison doesn’t backfill it with state aid, a lot of that lands on property tax bills.”

text:
Donnette R. Flick Woodward was murdered on June 6, 1991, in Kansas City, Kansas. More than 35 years later, her case remains unsolved. 
 
She appears in the family flyer as a young woman with long, wavy brown hair and a warm smile, wearing a blue top. 

Her full name.. Donnette R. Flick Woodward—tells part of her story: she was a Flick by birth and a Woodward by marriage. 

Public records confirm she was the daughter of Donald Ray Flick, an aircraft mechanic who served in the U.S. Army, worked for TWA and Boeing (including work on Air Force One), and later lived in the Kansas City area. He died in 2011 and was preceded in death by Donnette. 

There’s very little else about her life or the circumstances of her death has been published in news archives. 

No detailed contemporary newspaper accounts of the discovery of her body, the crime scene, or early suspects appear in readily available sources. This is typical of many older homicides that never received sustained media attention. 

What is documented is straightforward and grim: the homicide occurred in Kansas City, Kansas (Wyandotte County, often abbreviated KCK or KCKS), on June 6, 1991. It has never been solved. 

Family and friends have never stopped seeking answers and what they describe as “validation.” 

In recent years they have partnered with Corey’s Network, a Kansas City-area nonprofit that supports surviving family members of homicide victims. 

The group has repeatedly posted flyers and has posted on social media.
#JusticeForDonnetteRFlickWoodward and #IfYouKnowSomethingSaySomethingA KCTV5 cold-case segment aired in April 2025, keeping her name in front of a new audience.

Greater Kansas City Crime Stoppers continues to offer a reward of up to $5,000 for information that leads to an arrest and charging in the case. Tips can be submitted anonymously by calling 816-474-8477 (816-474-TIPS).  

The flyer notes that callers can remain anonymous and still receive cash rewards.

Kansas City, Kansas, has a documented history of unsolved homicides from the 1990s, some of which later received renewed attention from a dedicated cold-case unit formed in the early 2020s. 

Advances in DNA testing have closed other long-dormant Wyandotte County cases. Donnette’s case has not yet been among them.

The flyer’s simple plea…“Family and friends seek answers and validation!” It captures the human cost that statistics and case numbers cannot. A daughter, a wife, a person with a face and a name was taken on an ordinary June day in 1991. 

Thirty-five years of birthdays, holidays, and ordinary Tuesdays have passed without an arrest. The people who loved her are still waiting for someone who knows something to say something.

Anyone with information, however small or old it may seem, is asked to contact Crime Stoppers. The case file remains open.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

Shirley Stoneking Flick, the wife of Donnette’s father, Donald Ray Flick.
They married on February 20, 1987, in Wyandotte County, Kansas, the same county where Donnette was later killed. 
By then Donnette was already an adult and already a Woodward by marriage, so Shirley was her stepmother, not her mother.

When Donald died in 2011 in Decatur, Texas, the obituary named Shirley Flick of Decatur as his surviving wife. It also listed two other daughters, Sanja Rawson and Rebecca Flick. Donnette herself was listed among those who had already died.

Public records do not show much else about her life after 2011.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

text:
“Unsolved Homicide, Someone’s Angel”

On a Thursday in early June 1991, Donnette R. Flick Woodward was murdered in Kansas City, Kansas. The date was June 6. More than thirty-five years have passed, and no one has ever been charged.

She was a Flick first. Her father, Donald Ray Flick, was an aircraft mechanic who had served in the Army and later worked for TWA and Boeing. He helped build Air Force One. 

He married Shirley in Wyandotte County in 1987. When Donald died in 2011, the obituary listed Donnette among those who had gone before him. She had taken the name Woodward through marriage. Beyond that, the public record of her ordinary days is thin. 

What remains is a photograph: a young woman with long, wavy brown hair and an easy smile, wearing a blue top.
The homicide itself left almost no footprint in the newspapers of the time. There is no widely published account of where her body was found, how she died, or who last saw her alive. 

The file simply stayed open. 

In Kansas City, Kansas, that was not unusual then. Many cases from those years went quiet.
Family and friends never accepted the silence. They wanted answers. They wanted the simple acknowledgment that her life had been taken and that someone, somewhere, knew more than they had said. 

In later years they worked with Corey’s Network, a group that helps the people left behind after homicide. They printed flyers. They posted her picture. They asked people to share her name.

In April 2025 a local television station ran a short cold-case segment on her. The same flyer that had circulated online appeared on the screen: her photograph, the date, the place, the words “Family and friends seek answers and validation.” 

Crime Stoppers still offers up to five thousand dollars for information that leads to an arrest. Callers can stay anonymous.

Thirty-five summers have come and gone. Birthdays she never reached have been marked in private. The people who loved her are older now. Some of them are gone. The case file is still open. 

Somewhere in Kansas City or far beyond it, someone may remember a name, a car, a conversation, a night in early June 1991.
They are still waiting for that person to speak.
If you See something, Say something. 

Prayers for answers, strength, comfort, and closure for her family.  

@KickRocks2026

text:
[NOTE: This is my first X posting of an essay. I attempt to write 1K words every morning. This is today's production. ]

DAY 244-26 LOST ON THE NEW FRONTIER

LOST ON THE NEW FRONTIER

I am unsure of the direction of this morning's essay. I often awake wondering, 'How did we get here?' in relation to America's ongoing internal conflict over purpose and values. The title came to me a day or so ago, and I fulminated about what, why, or who it pointed to. Then my senior mind clicked in, vaguely remembering that President John F. Kennedy's administration embraced the idea that 1960 ushered in a New Frontier. Further, as I cogitated on the concept, I realized the implementation of Kennedy's vision was assassinated when Oswald pulled the trigger, 86ing JFK. Get the drift?

Upon considering the Kennedy vision, I took a hike down memory lane. On the day of President Kennedy's assassination, I was eleven years old. Hardly sentient. As I entered the OK Elementary School gym on West Street, I couldn't fathom why so many students were crying. On the center stage sat a black-and-white TV set, with Walter Cronkite narrating video of the moment of JFK's murder. Students were seated upon tiers of pull-out bench seats and led up the steps to fill in around those classes that had already arrived.

For the first few minutes, my classmates sat silent and still, trying to make sense of the setup. Now, remember, I was eleven and in 3rd grade. Third grade because I was held back a year after First grade (a fortuitous event that played out twelve years later when I met my future bride). Anyway, my seat was immediately behind our teacher, Mrs. Bache, a bossy, incompetent teacher. When I entered Fourth grade, my teacher discovered I could not write my name or perform basic addition and subtraction. I did, however, learn to throw a mean eraser across the classroom whenever Mrs. Bache took a break to smoke a cigarette.

My foot slipped and jammed into Mrs. Bache's back. She immediately turned back to scowl at me with her blazing black eyes and accused me of deliberately kicking her. So, during a national calamity, I faced a vengeful person of authority and knew I'd be on the receiving end of whatever her tormented mind would devise. Listen, folks, I can hardly remember what I had for dinner last night, but believe me, I can recall the vindictive look on Bache's face from sixty-three years ago. I immediately offered her that my foot simply slipped on the worn wooden steps or bench and that I didn't mean to kick her. She rejected my explanation, saying, "I'll deal with you later, bud."
I spent the rest of the time in the gym wondering how badly I would be punished. The rest of the day blurred into a confused haze as we were sent packing back home. The threatened punishment never came. As I remember, many of the younger kids still hadn't grasped the seriousness of the situation and celebrated their early release from school. The older students were more somber and sensed the gravity of the event. It took the next four days for me to fully grasp how dreadful the President's assassination was. The TV blared nonstop with every update on JFK's casket and our new President, Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson.
It was the second week of quail hunting season, and my family gathered at my grandfather's farm in Greenwood County, Kansas. I remember the dour faces and the red, tear-stained eyes of my Grandmother Long. My Nana, as my sister and I called her, was a dyed-in-the-wool Republican, anti-communist, and staunch patriot, yet she was tearful and heartbroken over Kennedy's death. She kept saying, "Why? Why him? ... He was such a nice man..." Across our country, the same scene played out that Thanksgiving holiday. Citizens gathered in common grief, holding hands as they prayed to God for unity and protection in that uncertain time. We had many questions, but few answers, and only in the recent past have we learned a bit more about the assassination, including a plethora of lies foisted off on American citizens.

I now see where my words have logically led me. TDS... Trump Derangement Syndrome. My faith in my fellow citizens of America is badly shaken. I cannot honestly believe that, God forbid, if President Trump is gunned down, our country would react as it did the day JFK was killed in Dallas. If the Left's response to the assassination of Charlie Kirk is any projection of what or how they will react to the President's untimely demise, we are a country slipping into the stinking wastebasket of history.

Something is eroding the life of our country. Despite Trump's efforts to move forward with his programs and embrace the future, many of our citizens savagely fight him at every turn. The hate-all attitude against Trump dates back to President Trump's first term, when a deranged, vindictive, and frankly near-maniacal insanity took hold, hounding the man even after he left office. We should be ashamed of the behavior of those on the Left who sought, through subterfuge, to enact a coup against a sitting president. Thankfully, the Obama/Clintonites failed in their effort to figuratively kill Trump. So far...

So where did our nation diverge from the promise of JFK's New Frontier? Kennedy represented a fresh kind of Democrat. His New Frontier program presented a forward-looking national effort to bring us into the next era of greatness. He understood that America could not continue the policies of immobility promulgated by President Eisenhower. Eisenhower stabilized America as a world leader in the aftermath of WWII. Kennedy projected American might into the future. He launched a space program to the moon. He fought against the epic lies of Marxism/Communism. He spread the gospel of democracy. He offered employment to those willing to grasp that work brings wealth. Corruption, Jim Crow, and a host of other immoral, unrighteous laws and policies were just beginning to take effect. Then Oswald killed the New Frontier.

What then took its place? The Great Society. Grandpa Johnson, in his deep desire to right all wrongs and shower his children with gobs of government money, launched the Great Society (GS).

The GS made a promise to the lower-class, downtrodden masses to fulfill their every desire. Tidal waves of money collected by the government (or, as ultimately required, the 'printing' of dollars) were shoveled out to states and local governments, only to be doled out to those who really didn't give a rat's butt about creating a New Frontier of hope and opportunity. From the start of the GS, the process and outcomes led only to the demise of the black family unit. Black fathers (and, to some degree, white/Hispanic as well) abandoned their responsibilities as fathers. The GS decimated black communities. Men got their gonads off and then left the women holding the bag for the children later downloaded. Result: massive transfer of taxpayer funds to the irresponsible women caught in the cycle of welfare. National debt swelled to unprecedented heights. The sky had no limits.

By any honest audit of the impact of the Great Society upon American civilization, it can be singularly named for the death of Kennedy's New Frontier and the development of a narcissistic nation of people who are only out to get what they can get, while the getting is good.

text:
Meet my new friend who has popped up in my replies, the anonymous far-right account @woodmeetball, which has gained just 700 followers in 16 years.

It joined @X in August 2010 under the name 'Stephen', lists its location as the Weimar Republic, and describes itself in the bio as “The man who was always right,” “far right of the IQ bell curve,” a WASP, and uses the tags #The3Ps, #ACAR and #BolshevikBritain. 

Bless.

Almost everything it posts follows the same closed worldview.

Jews are treated as a single hostile group that secretly runs media, banks, politics, immigration, sport and medicine. The account regularly uses words like goyim, Shylock and Jude, calls communism a Jewish ideology, and claims Jews brought “bioweapons” (non-White migrants) into Europe as part of the Kalergi plan.

One post about an Israeli school story is captioned “Multiculturalism for thee, ethnostate for me. There’s a good goy.” Another says anyone still believing “the Jew IQ cope in 2026 is outing themselves as a retard.”

Africans are called “dumber than dogshit” and “third worlders.”

Irish Catholics and republicans are repeatedly labelled “the browns of the white race,” “ideological Jews” and “the gayest and most retarded whites on the planet.”

A typical line runs: Fenians were “hoodwinked… into flooding their country with infinity rape Africans to own the Brits.”

Mass immigration is framed as deliberate replacement of (white) natives, and the only solution offered is cutting Northern Ireland off from both Britain and the Republic, deporting every migrant, restoring old laws against communism and buggery, and sending politicians and civil servants who backed the Kalergi plan to the gallows.

Being gay (something the account holder mentions a suspiciously frequently) is treated as a civilisation-ending psyop. Posts sneer at “globohomo,” call for the buggery act to return, and mock any White man who does not share the view as a “poof” or “woofter.” 

Women’s suffrage is dismissed with the line “Let’s just let women vote what the worst that can happen?” 

Police are branded #ACAR (used alongside claims they fine White people to massage crime statistics).

The UK itself is “Bolshevik Britain.”

These themes aren't occasional outbursts. Posts from the last two years show the same template applied to whatever is in the news that day: a Kneecap interview becomes proof that giving Irish people rights was a mistake; a video of teenagers in Manchester becomes evidence that English boomers are “the most cucked and propagandised goy of all time”; a pharmaceutical story is called “the most Jewish allopathy scam imaginable.” The Kalergi plan is described as “the most treasonist act of all time.”

Almost every post is written in the same mocking, slur-heavy register that treats the conspiracy as already proven and anyone who disagrees as cattle or a 'retard'.

The psychological picture that emerges from years of this output is one of grandiosity mixed with persecution - a narcissistic perpetual victim of anything he doesn't agree with. 

The delusional account presents itself as uniquely clear-sighted while insisting a tiny out-group controls everything against “the goyim.” Entire populations are reduced to cartoons or livestock. The same handful of explanations (Jewish control, racial IQ, globohomo, Kalergi) are applied to every event.

Posting is frequent, engagement is tiny, and the tone stays contemptuous even toward co-ethnics who fall short of the exact line. The combination of rigid all-or-nothing thinking, chronic dehumanisation, and years spent repeating the same extreme claims to a near-empty room is what the public record shows.

And this is precisely the kind of account which @elonmusk encourages and incentivises.
