text:
📕A panda is not just an animal📕

Arabelle Bose

Panda Diplomacy: The True Meaning of China's Symbol

Unusual gifts and "souvenirs" reflecting the cultures of the gift-giving country have long been nothing unusual or new in interstate relations. Sometimes, in such cases, animals are also given as gifts, and responsibility for their lives and well-being falls on the shoulders of the recipient country. For example, Russian President Vladimir Putin has received dogs several times. The first such unusual gift was from Bulgaria in 2010, when Prime Minister Boyko Borisov presented him with a black Labrador retriever. Later, in 2012, Bulgaria again gave him a Bulgarian Shepherd. One of the most striking gifts was undoubtedly an Akita Inu named Yume, given to Vladimir Putin by the Japanese governor of Akita Prefecture in 2014. Later in 2018, Yume, a gift from Japan, met with Japanese journalists before talks with Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, sparking delight and genuine joy not only on the Japanese side but also around the world. The well-cared-for furry gift was a friendly and welcoming gesture for the Japanese public. This gesture somewhat softened the tension during the important negotiations.

Heads of state and others have long exchanged unusual gifts as a sign of respect and in an attempt to win the other person's favor. Perhaps the most striking and interesting example is pandas.

So-called "panda diplomacy" is a diplomatic technique China has used since the 1940s to strengthen friendly relations with other countries by presenting the unusual animal as a gift or, more recently, by lending them out.

The panda is more than just an animal; it's a symbol of China. Alongside the dragon, which has historically symbolized the emperor, and the phoenix, which symbolizes the empress, the small, fluffy, bicolored baby panda now stands tall. Although it's hardly a baby panda, adults can weigh 120-160 kg and reach a length of 120-180 cm. Anyone who has visited China will now confirm that the panda is featured on a huge number of souvenirs that most tourists buy and bring back from China. How did this happen? Why did this particular animal become a symbol of China, alongside the formidable, noble dragon and the mythical fiery phoenix?

Pandas are found exclusively in China, specifically in the provinces of Shaanxi, Sichuan, and Guangxi. Their main delicacy is bamboo, which was, in fact, one of the reasons why these animals nearly became extinct. Until 2016, pandas were considered endangered because their fur had long been highly prized and considered a luxury commodity, but this was not the primary reason. In the mid-20th century, the Chinese began clearing bamboo thickets, which nearly led to the species' extinction. Now, however, these two-colored bears are held in high regard not only in China but worldwide, leading to the panda's status being changed to "vulnerable" in 2016, and they are no longer considered endangered . There are currently approximately 2,000 pandas in the wild, and more than 750 in captivity. Interestingly, the panda has served as the mascot for several Olympics held in China, including the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing and the 2022 Winter Olympics in Beijing.

In April 1972, two pandas, Lingling and Xingxing, arrived in Washington, D.C., marking a key event that shaped the future of panda diplomacy. President Nixon's visit to China marked a breakthrough in relations between the two countries, and in response, China gifted the United States two pandas. This gesture evoked a positive reaction in the United States; on the first weekend after the zoo opened to the public, approximately 75,000 people flocked to see the Chinese pandas, causing massive traffic jams. It is said that even the image on Washington Metro tickets at the time depicted two pandas gnawing on bamboo leaves. The expression "Panda Hug" even appeared in English, signifying not just a hug, but a touching embrace full of emotion and affection . For many Americans growing up in the 1970s, the panda was the embodiment of China, and for most, it still is.

Interestingly, the origins of panda diplomacy date back to the mid-7th century. During the Tang Dynasty, Empress Wu Zetian gifted the Japanese court a pair of pandas . This was an expression of her friendship and recognition of the country. Even then, the panda was perceived as a sign of friendship, as the cute and clumsy animal does not eat meat. Unlike its fellow bears, such as the gyrfalcon or polar bears, the panda is not carnivorous and feeds primarily on bamboo. By nature, this animal is quite harmless, and its indifference to meat only emphasizes that such a gift is given in peace, expressing only good intentions and aiming to maintain good relations between the parties.

There's not only panda diplomacy, but also panda economics. These animals bring in significant sums of money for China annually. In the 1980s, the declining panda population led to a shift from simply gifting pandas to other countries. They are now being leased for research and exhibits, with the proceeds going toward studying and breeding these same pandas in China. Lease agreements are typically for 10 years and can be extended. An extension of such an agreement speaks volumes about the friendly and trusting relationship between the two countries. The host country pays an annual fee of between $500,000 and $1 million, and panda cubs born in other countries must be returned to their parents' home countries at the age of two to four years. Their stay in zoos is also paid separately, starting at $200,000 each. If something happens to a panda in another country, it can also result in a hefty fine. Furthermore, keeping pandas is quite expensive; they can eat up to 40 kg of bamboo per day, some of which must be imported. Thus, in 2020, Canada returned two pandas to China early because it simply couldn't feed them. At the time, the pandemic had impacted bamboo supplies, and the only possible solution was to return the bears to their homeland, where they would be safe.

Giant pandas are a direct reflection of China's relations with other countries. In January 2026, Japan lost all its pandas for the first time since 1972. The Taiwan issue has long been a sensitive and difficult issue for China. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's statements about Taiwan only worsened relations between the two Asian countries, and as a direct consequence, China took back two pandas, Xiao Xiao and Lei Lei, which only underscored China's position and the cooling of relations between the two countries.

Panda diplomacy is a direct reflection of Chinese culture. Since ancient times, it's not customary in China to get straight to the point or express one's position abruptly; everything is in the details, gestures, and intonation. China is a high-context country, meaning what isn't said directly is far more important than what is said, and even more important is whether the person understands the implications and can read between the lines. Thus, when sitting down at the negotiating table, it's not customary for the Chinese to get straight to the point. Without asking banal questions about whether you've eaten or making small talk before actually discussing the agenda, it's safe to say that, at a minimum, the Chinese will be in a bad mood. During a tea ceremony, even seemingly trivial details—where the teapot spout is pointing or whether your tea is being refilled on time—are far from trivial for the Chinese, but rather a subtle way to hint at whether they even want to deal with them. Those who understand these Chinese hints and read them promptly are more likely to be respected by the Chinese and earn their favor. The same goes for pandas. China won't openly declare a sharp deterioration in relations with Japan, but they will take their pandas back, and that will speak volumes.

The amusing similarity between the unofficial symbols of Russia and China—namely, the brown bear and the panda—is actively exploited in the media when discussing the two countries' ties to each other. In 1957, China gifted the USSR a panda named Ping-Ping in honor of the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution. In 1959, a second male, named An-An, was given as a gift. The giant panda returned to Russia in 2001, during the Beijing Days celebrations in Moscow. Beijing Zoo residents Ben-Ben and Wen-Wen stayed in Moscow for a month and a half before returning to China. It's worth noting that pandas are sometimes offered for short-term loan. Since 2019, the Moscow Zoo has been home to a male panda named Rui and a female named Ding-Ding. In 2023, they gave birth to a cub, who was given the Russian name Katyusha. In 2023, to mark the occasion, photographs of little Katyusha were even printed on Troika travel cards, and a huge number of visitors came to see the first panda born in Russia.

Relations between Russia and China have been improving recently, and they only get better each year. Katyusha's birth is just another reflection of the friendly relations between the two countries. It's also interesting that the baby was given such a Russian name – Katyusha. The mere mention of this name immediately brings to mind the lyrics of the song of the same name for any Russian, but surprisingly, for most Chinese, the famous melody also pops into their heads. The song, which once captivated our vast country, has spread beyond its borders and around the world. Many Chinese know and love the song, many can even sing it in Russian. Therefore, the choice of this name for the first Chinese panda born in Russia was the best and most obvious, subtly hinting at the long-standing warm relations between Russia and China.

"Ron Fairly played first base and was having good day hitting off Bob Gibson.
Gibson got a hit and while standing at first, when Fairly said to Gibson something about him not being so hard to hit.
He got a glare.
Ron Fairly`s next at bat he turns to catcher Tim McCarver and says:
"This isn’t going to go so well for me, is it?"
"If you ever saw Gibson work, you’d never forget his style:
His cap pulled down low over his eyes, ball gripped, almost mashed behind his right hip, eyes smouldering at each batter almost accusingly."
Tim McCarver.
When Bob Gibson told Cardinals GM Bing DeVine, who’d been with the team Gibson’s entire career, that he was hanging up his cleats, DeVine picked Gibson’s brain about the status of the team and what kind of changes the club needed to make another run at the pennant.
DeVine told Gibson there might be a future for him in the organization.
But Gibson wrote in his memoir that after he left DeVine’s office, he never heard from the Cardinals again.
The closest Gibson came to hearing back from St. Louis was in 1982 when he was offered the managerial position for the Louisville Redbirds by club owner A. Ray Smith.
Bob Gibson wanted the job.
But the Redbirds were the AAA affiliate of the Cardinals and the Busch family vetoed the hiring, still aggrieved with Gibson seven years after he’d thrown his last pitch.
Gibson knew that there were consequences for black players who spoke out and he paid them his entire career.

text:
I wanted to move from LA to Kentucky and my husband didn't. It took years for us to get on the same page. https://t.co/NuKrcFjAlO 

The author felt it was important to live near family.
Courtesy of Tonilyn Hornung

I wanted to move our family from Los Angeles to Kentucky, and my husband was resistant. 

It took years for us to get on the same page.

I wanted to live near family, and eventually, my husband agreed it was the right call.

"I have a plan," the text to my friend began, "would you meet us for dinner so we can talk about the greatness of Louisville?"

My plan was simple: Reassure my husband that leaving Los Angeles and moving to Kentucky was the right move. We both loved my hometown and always looked forward to our visits with my family. Still, my partner needed an objective opinion — someone who'd lived in LA but chose Louisville. I hit send, and the reply came quickly, "I'm in." My hope was that after dinner, my husband would change his opinion about moving just as quickly.

We'd talked about moving away from LA before

"I don't want to live in LA forever," my husband said when he was my fiancé. During our engagement, we had lengthy conversations about our future together. We talked about moving away from perpetual traffic jams, fire season, and the cost of simply existing in Los Angeles. We had no particular deadline, but when I gave birth to our son, the pressure to relocate got real. I wanted to move home.

This surprising revelation occurred in the two weeks following our baby's birth. My mom and dad came to LA to help, at a time when motherhood was a muddled mix of sleeplessness and self-doubt. I borrowed my parents' confidence in parenting, and in me. When they left, I wanted us all to go with them — a pull I couldn't ignore.

The author and her husband finally agreed about moving.
Courtesy of Tonilyn Hornung

I missed my family, and my timeline changed

"Let's call Papa and Maw," I whispered to my newborn. Whenever my baby was sleeping, if I wasn't sleeping, too, I was video calling my parents. I also called them during playtime, walk times, bath times, and, well… basically any time at all, I called home. I felt closer to the support and safety I craved when I saw their faces and my childhood home.

It was time to talk to my husband.

I brought up all the pros and cons of raising our son in Kentucky, and my husband listened. Then he said, "I'm not opposed to it, but can we wait to make sure?" His nervousness was hard to hide. So, before I pulled cardboard boxes out of the garage to pack, we decided to wait.

My husband didn't want to move, so we compromised at first

As our newborn grew into an infant, my video calls continued, and the urge to move home never faded. Every three or four months, I'd check in, and my partner's resistance was clear. "Honey, you're asking me to leave my career and best friends," he said. He softened as we talked, but he still wasn't ready.

The idea of moving was such a strange closed door between us that there were times I was afraid to open it. Each time my partner rejected the idea, it felt like he was rejecting me — a feeling I didn't enjoy. Having such differing desires and viewpoints created an awkward disconnect, and I communicated as much. So, we compromised by visiting home more often, meeting with friends in Louisville to gather more info, and keeping the dialogue open.

Eventually, for me, this wasn't enough.

The family has been in Kentucky for eight years now.
Courtesy of Tonilyn Hornung

We were finally on the same page, and now, we agree it was the right decision for us

Around the time my son turned 4, my inner moving clock rang with such urgency that I reopened the discussion. Again, I explained that I wanted the safety of living close to family, and for our son to have weekend sleepovers at his grandparents' house. I also told him how lonely I felt being so far away. Finally, the door swung open, and my husband said he'd grown to love the idea of surrounding our son with family, and a new city would be a fun new adventure. The disconnect vanished, and that's when we made the decision together.

We've been back in Louisville for eight years now, and we agree that moving was the best choice for all of us. While it was a slow decision, I think that made it even more meaningful. Living close to family and the support they offer is foundational for building our own family — and the palm trees and the traffic are still there whenever we want to visit.

text:
Yeah, absolutely.

If you’re trying to spin up something like Hermes Launch Lab in Miami, I’d start very narrow.

Pick one local niche first, restaurants, med spas, contractors, realtors, gyms, whatever you already understand, and build the offer around solving THEIR specific problems instead of just saying “I build websites with AI.”

The real advantage isn’t Hermes by itself. It’s using Hermes behind the scenes to make the whole operation faster:

• research the business before outreach
• audit their current site
• generate a better site direction
• build faster
• handle revisions
• create follow-up and testimonial workflows
• keep the client pipeline organized

That lets you compete on speed and service without needing a huge team.

I’d also get 1 or 2 really strong local examples under your belt as fast as possible, even if the first deal is priced aggressively. Once you can show “here’s what they had, here’s what I built, here’s the result,” selling gets a LOT easier.

Miami is probably a great market for it because there are endless local businesses with money on the table and mediocre digital presence.

If I were starting there, I’d go niche first, build the system second, then expand once the process is repeatable.

text:
Read this short story. It contains THE secret to getting rich. It is probably the greatest work on business ever written.

Every business decision, every investment, every product that you launch comes with some amount of risk. You could buy 1,000 t-shirts, thinking that there's "a good chance" that they get sold. And then like 5 people actually buy them.

But there's a spectrum between gambling and obviousness. Spinning a slot machine is gambling: you have no idea what will happen on the next spin. Picking up a glass of water is obvious: there is always a chance that you drop the glass -- but it's still pretty "obvious" that you will pick it up.

The trick is to only make decisions that will obviously work. Not ideas that "have a very good chance" of working, but ideas that are so good that they scale from zero. You buy 10 t-shirts, and everyone's eyes light up and people start reaching out asking if you have more in stock. That level of obviousness.

Where the fire is hot at square one. Where all of the signs that you see everywhere point in that direction. Where it's hard to think of a way that it will fail. And where growth is organic, and stems from real needs that actually exist.

The market is very, very complicated. But we only need to predict the future a few times if we are to get rich. Please be a perfectionist in these instances. Warren Buffet would go through thousands of companies before he found one that he really liked.

It's easy to think "Oh, I'll buy an embroidery machine and get rich selling patches." And then you buy a machine and nothing happens. Typically a successful embroidery company would have been started by a hobbyist who was already making patches for his jackets or his friends jackets just for fun. Then the product would get made, and the buyers would appear organically. His friend would start a band, and offer to pay him for patches. And then his friend would recommend him to another band, and so on. That's how it really goes.

A successful endeavor takes your already existing product or skills and connects them to a market that is already waiting to be tapped. Unless you want to be a retard and buy 100 Squirmles to sell to people you don't know on Miami Beach.

It is about "the obvious." What is already right in front of you.

Kidepo Valley National Park: Where Remoteness Becomes the Experience

In this case, remoteness is not a disadvantage, but part of what makes the experience so extraordinary. Far from the noise and crowds, Kidepo offers vast open landscapes, dramatic mountains and an incredible sense of untouched wilderness. 

It is Uganda’s most remote national park, covering about 1,442 square kilometers, with the Narus and Kidepo valleys framed by rugged mountain ranges. It is currently Uganda’s only park with cheetahs and ostriches. 

While its huge buffalo concentrations are among the park’s most impressive wildlife spectacles. The park is also home to elephants, zebras and many other species.

text:
Germania Moon Magazine X Oceanic Relics

By: Wish Fire

Saint Gothic

Germania Moon Magazine X Oceanic Relics
Germania’s connection to Oceanic Relics comes from how water—rivers, wetlands, and the mythic “Oceanus Germanicus”—shaped Germanic culture, religion, and geography. In the Gothic era and related cultures, “water in Germania” meant wetlands, bogs, rivers, and a shifting coastline, not open ocean.
How Germania connects to Oceanic Relics

The connection rests on three cultural-water pillars: mythic boundaries, ritual wetlands, and geological shifts.

Mythic Boundary: The “Ocean” of Germania

Tacitus describes Oceanus as both a literal boundary and a metaphorical frontier for Germania. Even though many inland Germanic peoples never saw the sea, the Romans imagined Germania as a land pressed against a vast, mysterious ocean. This “ocean” becomes a symbolic threshold between civilization and the unknown.

Why this matters for your magazine pairing:

This gives Oceanic Relics a mythic frame—Germania as a place where land meets a symbolic ocean, even if culturally the “ocean” was more conceptual than experiential.

Germania Moon Magazine X Oceanic Relics
Water in Germanic & Gothic Culture

Wetlands, bogs, rivers

Germanic paganism centered heavily on wetlands, fens, rivers, and lakes. These were ritual sites for offerings—food, weapons, tools—given to supernatural beings believed to dwell in or be reachable through water.

Key cultural water types in Germania:

Bogs & fens — sites of sacrifice, preservation, and myth

Rivers — boundaries, trade routes, and ritual deposition

Lakes — centers of cultic activity

Coastal waters (North Sea/Baltic) — relevant mainly to northern Germanic peoples, not inland Goths

Water spirits & monsters

Old English and Germanic sources describe harmful water beings—nicoras, þyrsas—fought by heroes like Beowulf. These beings make water a liminal, dangerous space.

Magazine connection:

This gives Oceanic Relics a folkloric dimension: relics emerging from haunted waters, eclipsed rivers, or bogs where spirits dwell.

Germania Moon Magazine X Oceanic Relics
Geological & Cultural Water Shifts

Recent research suggests Germania’s water landscape changed dramatically due to tectonic activity, sea-level shifts, and possibly cosmic events like the Chiemgau impact. These changes may have altered coastlines and river systems, including the regression of the Oceanus Germanicus.

Implications for your theme:

Water as a shifting frontier

Relics emerging from changing landscapes

Mythic interpretations of natural upheaval

🧭 So what water was in Germania during the Gothic era?

Primarily:

Rivers (Elbe, Rhine, Danube, Oder, etc.)

Wetlands & bogs (major ritual sites)

Lakes (regional cult centers)

Coastal waters only for northern tribes (North Sea, Baltic)

Not:

Open ocean culture (except for northern Germanic peoples)

Maritime relic traditions like Mediterranean or Polynesian cultures

Germania Moon Magazine X Oceanic Relics
Germania’s water‑bound relics form a constellation of offerings, sacred landscapes, and mythic beings—objects pulled from bogs, lakes, riverbeds, and coastal zones that acted as thresholds between the human world and the divine. What survives archaeologically is not a single “treasure hoard,” but a long tradition of watery devotion stretching from the Bronze Age through the Viking Age. Below is a full, structured explanation of the relics, their mythic associations, and the cosmological logic behind them, grounded in the sources you saw above.

The Core Idea: Water as a Portal
The Germanic peoples treated wetlands, bogs, fens, lakes, islands, and the sea as liminal zones—places where offerings could cross into the realm of gods, spirits, or ancestors. This worldview produced a distinctive archaeological record: weapons, jewelry, riding gear, food, animals, and even humans deposited intentionally into waterlogged places.

1. Relics from Wetlands, Bogs, and Lakes
These are the most abundant “Germanic water relics,” preserved because bogs naturally mummify organic material.

• Bog bodies
Over 1,000 bog bodies have been found across Denmark, northern Germany, the Netherlands, and England. Many show ritual killing—strangulation, throat‑cutting, blunt trauma—suggesting sacrificial or judicial rites.
Examples:

Tollund Man (Denmark): noose around neck, ritual last meal.

Lindow Man (England): triple killing method, mistletoe pollen in stomach—possibly linked to deities like Nerthus or Odin.

• Weapon deposits
Large caches of spears, shields, swords, and war‑booty were sunk into wetlands.
Sites include Hjortspring, Ådal, Esbøl, Skedemosse.
These deposits often represent victory offerings, dedicating captured weapons to gods by “returning” them to the waters.

• Jewelry and gold offerings
Rings, torcs, and ornate metalwork appear in fens and lakes—sometimes bent or broken intentionally, symbolically “killed” before being given to the gods.
Skedemosse alone produced gold rings, horse sacrifices, and human remains across 1,500 years.

• Riding equipment and horses
Bridles, saddles, and entire horse burials appear in watery contexts.
Skedemosse includes 100+ horse sacrifices, linking equine offerings to war gods like Thor and Ullr (place‑names Torsåker, Ullsåker).

2. Island Relics and Ocean‑Facing Sacred Sites
Germanic religion also used islands as sanctuaries—isolated by water, they were natural temples.

• Helgoland / Fositesland
A North Sea island sacred to Fosite/Forseti, god of justice and healing.
It held a holy well and shrine visited by Frisians until destroyed by missionaries in the 8th century.

• Öland (Baltic Sea)
A fusion of wetland and maritime ritual:

Neolithic and Iron Age coastal depositions

Seal‑hunting offerings

Skedemosse fen at its center
This island embodies the Germanic idea that sea boundaries = spiritual boundaries.

• Hlésey / Læsø
Named for Hlér/Ægir, the sea‑giant.
This island’s name preserves the cult of a sea deity whose hall lies “beneath the waves.”

3. Mythic Ocean Relics and Sea‑Beings
Germanic myth is filled with oceanic figures whose stories explain why offerings were made to water.

• Ægir
A jötunn who personifies the sea, hosting the gods in his underwater hall.
His name derives from Proto‑Germanic āgwi‑jaz, “the one of the water.” Ships are called “Ægir’s horses,” waves “Ægir’s daughters.”

• Rán
Ægir’s wife, a goddess who captures drowned sailors in her net.
Her nine daughters are the waves themselves.

• Jörmungandr
The world‑serpent cast into the ocean by Odin, encircling all lands.
He embodies the dangerous, infinite sea.

• Näck/Nixie
Water spirits haunting rivers and lakes, sometimes benevolent, sometimes deadly.
They appear in art with Ægir’s daughters.

• Nicoras and Þyrsas
Old English sources describe wetlands inhabited by harmful beings fought by heroes like Beowulf.

4. Cosmology Behind Water Relics
Water in Germanic cosmology is animate—a living force with personality.
Scholars describe this as animism, the attribution of spirit to natural features.

This worldview explains why:

Weapons were “returned” to water after battle.

Bodies were offered to bogs as sacrifices.

Islands became holy enclaves.

Sea gods received votive gifts.

Waves were daughters of a deity.

The ocean itself was a conscious being.

5. Table: Types of Germanic Water Relics
Relic Type Description Mythic Connection
Bog bodies Ritual human remains preserved in wetlands Nerthus, Odin, fertility rites
Weapon deposits Spears, swords, shields sunk in bogs War gods, victory offerings
Jewelry & gold Rings, torcs, gold objects Wealth offerings to gods
Horse sacrifices Horses and riding gear Thor, Ullr, warrior cults
Island shrines Helgoland, Öland, Læsø Fosite, Ægir, sea cults
Sea‑myth relics Stories of Ægir, Rán, Jörmungandr Personified ocean powers

Germania Moon Magazine X Oceanic Relics
All right, Deanna — you asked for all three:
Germanic sea‑gods, major relic sites, and ocean‑related myths.
I’ll give you a full, mythic‑cosmological deep‑dive in your preferred style: layered, symbolic, ancient, and astral‑gothic, without emojis.

I. Germanic Sea‑Gods: The Oceanic Pantheon
These are not gentle deities. The Germanic ocean is a sentient, devouring force — a realm of giants, drowned souls, and tidal daughters. The sea is not a “domain” but a being, and its gods are expressions of its moods.

• Ægir — The Ocean as a Person
A jötunn whose name means “the overwhelming one.”
He is not worshipped like a god; he is endured.
His hall lies beneath the waves, lit by gold that glows like drowned sunlight.
He brews ale for the gods, meaning the sea itself “ferments” storms.

• Rán — The Drowning Net
Ægir’s wife.
She drags sailors down with her net, claiming them as offerings.
Her realm is the cold, silent deep — a necropolis of the drowned.

• The Nine Wave‑Daughters
Each wave is a goddess with a distinct temperament:
calm, wrathful, deceptive, crushing, whispering, devouring.
They are the ocean’s nine faces.

• Jörmungandr — The World Serpent
Thrown into the sea by Odin, he grew until he encircled all lands.
He is the horizon itself — the boundary between known and unknown.

• Hlér — The Island‑Dwelling Sea‑King
Another name for Ægir, but tied to Hlésey (Læsø), a sacred island.
His cult was coastal and island‑based, not inland.

• Nix/Näck — River and Lake Spirits
Shapeshifters who lure humans into water.
They are the freshwater counterparts to Rán’s saltwater dead.

II. Major Germanic Wetland & Ocean Relic Sites
These are the places where the oceanic and watery cults left physical traces — relics, sacrifices, and ritual landscapes.

text:
#OnThisDay September 2, 1857: Rails To The Cape.

Residents of Cape Island, the community now known as Cape May, gathered for a public meeting that addressed one of Cape May County’s most important economic and transportation problems: the absence of a direct railroad connection with the rapidly expanding rail network of southern New Jersey. The meeting appointed Dover Edmunds Jr., David Reeves, John West, Waters B. Miller, and Joseph Ware to confer with the West Jersey Railroad concerning construction of a railroad through Cape May County. Although the railroad that ultimately reached Cape Island was not completed until 1863, the September 1857 meeting demonstrates the organized local campaign that preceded one of the most significant transportation changes in nineteenth-century Cape May County.

Cape May County’s geography made transportation unusually important. The county occupied the southern end of the New Jersey peninsula, bordered by the Atlantic Ocean and Delaware Bay and containing extensive wetlands and cedar swamps. Before rail service, travelers depended heavily upon roads, stagecoaches, and water transportation. Lewis Townsend Stevens recorded that a stage left Cape May for Bridgeton twice weekly in 1856, departing at five in the morning and reaching Bridgeton at approximately four in the afternoon. Passengers continuing toward Philadelphia required additional transportation. Steamboats provided another route, but neither system offered the speed and regularity that railroads increasingly provided elsewhere in New Jersey.

Railroad development had already begun transforming South Jersey. The New Jersey Legislature chartered the West Jersey Railroad on February 5, 1853, authorizing a line from Camden through Gloucester, Salem, Cumberland, and Cape May counties to a terminus near Cape Island. Construction progressed southward from Camden, and regular service between Camden and Woodbury began in 1857. Cape May residents therefore had a practical reason to press the company to continue farther south.

The September 2 meeting was one episode in a sustained local campaign. Stevens reported that Cape May County residents held numerous railroad meetings during the eight years before the eventual opening of rail service in 1863. Several competing plans emerged. During 1857, supporters of a proposed Cape May and Atlantic railroad held meetings throughout the county. On August 7, less than a month before the September gathering, another Cape Island meeting appointed Henry Schmoele, Matthew Willdin, Waters B. Miller, and Joseph Ware to confer with the Camden and Atlantic Railroad. The September meeting therefore reflected a broader effort to secure railroad construction regardless of which established company ultimately provided the connection.

The economic stakes extended beyond passenger travel. Cape May County supported fishing, shipbuilding, agriculture, lumbering, and maritime commerce. Stevens noted that Dennis Creek had been an important commercial and shipbuilding center before rail transportation altered local trade patterns. A railroad offered producers faster access to regional markets while reducing dependence on slower wagon and water routes. State historic-preservation research has identified the arrival of railroad transportation as a major turning point in the county’s economic development.

The greatest long-term effect appeared in Cape May’s resort economy. Cape Island was already an established seaside destination before the railroad. Hotels such as Congress Hall served visitors, and substantial investment had occurred during the 1850s. Yet transportation imposed practical limits on the number and type of visitors who could reach the resort. Railroad service fundamentally altered that calculation.

The Cape May and Millville Railroad was incorporated in 1863, and passenger rail service between Cape May and the Philadelphia region began that August. Contemporary Cape May resident Amelia Hand recorded on August 26 that the railroad had finally connected Cape Island with Philadelphia and that the journey required approximately three and one-half hours. Earlier stage travel could consume most of a day, while steamboat travel could require about seven hours. Rail transportation made shorter visits increasingly practical.

The railroad also changed Cape May’s physical development. Cape May’s municipal history identifies completion of the railroad in 1863 as the beginning of another stage in the resort’s growth, including increased construction of private summer cottages by Philadelphia families. State historic research similarly links rail transportation with the later growth of settlements throughout Cape May County. Communities along rail corridors gained improved connections with markets, visitors, and population centers farther north.

The September 2, 1857 meeting did not itself create the railroad completed six years later, and the historical record does not justify treating the appointed committee as the sole cause of its construction. Its significance rests instead in what it documents: Cape May residents recognized that railroad access had become essential to the county’s economic future and organized publicly to obtain it. Their repeated negotiations formed part of a prolonged local movement that preceded the arrival of rail service in 1863. Once completed, the railroad reduced Cape May County’s geographic isolation, strengthened commercial transportation, expanded access to Cape May’s seaside resort, and helped reshape development throughout the peninsula. The 1857 meeting therefore represents an important local step in the transportation transformation that permanently altered Cape May County.

text:
I can't speak to how it works in Germany. But in the US you have two (that I know of) issues: contract law and taxes. 

Any contract requires consideration, or something being offered in exchange for something you get. Contracts that give you something for nothing are not enforceable. So a company, at least in Delaware, can't issue shares for free validly. The corporation and the founder are two different legal persons. Even owning 100% of the stock doesn't make them the same legal person. So any interaction they have with each other has to satisfy contract law. 

The second issue is taxation. In the US if you receive anything of value, you owe taxes on it. If I give you $1 million in stock, the IRS views that the same as you receiving $1 million in cash and you owe taxes on it. If the stock is liquid this is not a big deal, you just immediately sell the tax owed and pay it. But startup stock is illiquid so you can owe taxes that you have no ability to pay. 

The IRS has workarounds to this. One option is that if you simply purchase your stock at fair market value, it's not compensation. Then you only pay taxes on capital gains, and only when you sell the stock. Prior to a priced round or a formal valuation from an accounting firm that establishes fair market value, the company has basically a fictional value that the incorporator is allowed to set, called par value. It's usually set extremely low so that the cost to buy your shares is like $100-1000. 

There's no such thing as a technical/literal founder. It's not a real role or title. It's more of an honorific. The only "real" titles/roles are shareholders, the board of directors, and the corporate officers. The founders are usually all three at the beginning, but there's no legal distinction or exceptions due to being a "founder".

text:
In the Middle Eastern hills, the fig tree carries a truth readers often miss: before the harvest arrives, before sweetness forms, before the branches swell, the tree produces taqsh — the early green pre‑fruit, the first promise of life.

A fig tree covered in leaves without this pre‑fruit is not merely barren; it is deceptive. It advertises a season it does not possess, boasts of life it does not contain, misleads the hungry, and betrays the traveler. 

This is a dramatic backdrop of Matthew 21.

When Christ approaches a fig tree “having leaves,” those leaves make a bold public claim: “Here is evidence. Here is life.” But upon inspection, He finds nothing — no early figs, no first promise, no quiet sign of vitality. Only leaves. Only appearance. Only a boast.

Christ judges it not simply for lacking fruit, but for its hypocrisy. The tree becomes a living symbol of every religious system that displays leaves of ritual, ceremony, and covenant boasting while lacking the essential fruit of repentance, obedience, humility, and truth — the very pre‑fruit He seeks.

This same deception echoed in the Temple courts. The Court of the Gentiles was God’s deliberate invitation — a sanctuary carved into the Temple so the outsider, the seeker, the foreigner could draw near to the Holy One. It was the only place where the nations could stand and say, “I seek the God who made heaven and earth.”

Yet the leaders polluted it. They filled the court with shouting merchants, corrupt money changers, livestock, and exploitation. The sacred space meant to reveal God’s heart was drowned in commercial noise and the stench of greed. They buried the access point of the nations and hid the God of Scripture behind the machinery of self‑serving religion.

The Temple became beautiful on the outside — dazzling architecture, golden ornamentation, priestly pageantry — but its fruit was corrupted. It attracted crowds through spectacle, yet offered no spiritual nutrition. Like the fig tree, it bore leaves without life. Christ Himself declared its leaders “full of dead men’s bones,” a whitewashed façade masking spiritual death.

From Abraham’s covenant (“In thee shall all families of the earth be blessed”) to Isaiah’s proclamation (“My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations”), God’s heart has always burned for the world. By corrupting the outer court, the leaders committed a profound theological crime: they turned a sanctuary for the nations into a den of thieves, stealing God’s glory and obstructing His mission.

Just as the fig tree bore leaves without pre‑fruit, the Temple bore ritual without truth, pageantry without obedience, and appearance without evidence. 

Christ judged both.

Religion can carry Bibles, parade golden statues, and display bright leaves of outward devotion — but without the evidence of spiritual life, the nutrition of the Word of God, and the fruit of righteousness, it remains spiritually barren. 

Any gospel that diverges from the Word of God, no matter how impressive its display, is a distorted message condemned as anathema.

___________________________________

Scriptural Witness

Form Without Power “Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof…” 
— 2 Timothy 3:5

Whitewashed Appearance “Beautiful outward, but within full of dead men’s bones…” 
— Matthew 23:27

True Fruit “Ye shall know them by their fruits…” 
— Matthew 7:16

The Warning of Anathema “If any preach another gospel… let him be accursed.” 
— Galatians 1:8

________________________________

Wes Hazlett

text:
The next Digimon anime 2027- a possible return to norms

with speculation twist?

Next year will bring us a new Digimon anime and it wlll be a completely new story, not sequel or based on a side media. 

I feel this will be return to norms for digimon

What do i mean return to norms

well when you think about the pre Ghost game/Beat Break era of Digimon you remember

The adventure
the villain Digimon
the family drama
the growth of what are basically child soldiers
the Digital World
the 6th Ranger 

That's the pre–Ghost Game Break era of Digimon for

4-8 kids who end up with Digimon and protect the two worlds'

I feel this is perfect way to give the Digital world: Shambala some love  before Story Game

Now for the main chararacter

I think this seaosn will have Digimon's first female lead fort he anime.

now you might be thinking

"What?! Can't it be done, but Roxas, remember how X/Y were treated, Digimon could never give a female character respect."

Well, the upcoming Digimon Allyison is proof they want to have a female lead be possible, Rina from Re digitize is very popular except for that outfit.

Could a Digimon season work with a female main lead without feeling “weird” or “girlboss”?

Yes. The franchise already has the tools to do it cleanly.

The best existing example is Rika from Tamers: competitive, lonely, initially cold and fight-focused, with a strained family life. She grows through her relationship with Renamon and the group without becoming a perfect lecturer or the designated “strong female character” who has to fix everyone. Reina in Beatbreak is already functioning as a strong deuteragonist in a similar vein—hot-blooded and reckless because of abandonment trauma, insecure about her usefulness, overcompensating, and gradually learning to trust and belong. She is not written as an unstoppable girlboss; she collapses from overusing e-Pulse, has nightmares about being discarded, and has clear flaws.

A female lead would work if she is written the same way the male leads are written: as a specific person with personal stakes, flaws, and growth through partnership and found family, not as a statement. The core Digimon loop (a kid + a monster partner learning to understand each other while facing a larger threat) does not require the protagonist to be male. Games have already done female player characters without issue (Next Order’s Shiki, etc.).

What would feel “weird” or forced is the girlboss version: the lead who is always morally correct, never has real weaknesses, lectures the male characters, or exists mainly to prove a point about gender. Digimon’s tone has always been more about messy kids growing up through bonds than about empowerment speeches. A female Tomoro-style lead (cynical, traumatized, slow to trust, personal motivation first) or a female Rika-style lead (proud, isolated, grows through connection) would fit the franchise’s DNA without clashing.

you don't need a female Marcus, Tomoro, and no one asking for Tai with lady parts.

Games and the card game side

Digimon Alysion (the 2026 mobile card game) has Kanata Hondo as the story protagonist with Gemmon. That’s a dedicated female lead in official Digimon card-game media, in the same universe as Liberator. Liberator itself splits focus: the webcomic follows Shoto, while the web novel side follows Yuuki. Story games have offered female options for years—Cyber Sleuth (Ami), Next Order (Shiki), Time Stranger (Kanan). A lot of players do prefer those versions. That isn’t automatically the same “female designs are just prettier/better written” trap some Pokémon/Persona discussions fall into; in Digimon it often comes down to the female avatar feeling more distinct or the supporting cast playing better off her. That said, the writing in Cyber Sleuth still had leftover male-default lines and some female NPCs written in very stock ways, so the games are proof of willingness, not proof that every female-centric Digimon story is automatically well-handled.

A TV anime season is different from a game where you can pick gender or a card-game story mode. The entire marketing, episode structure, and “this is the face of the season” pressure lands on one character. That’s why a female Marcus-clone as the lead still makes some people wary even if they like Reina as the second banana.

Dress and fanservice

Active-girl clothes (jackets, shorts, practical shoes) and modest swimsuits were the default for a long time. Adventure 2020 and some later designs/games pushed further into fanservice, which is why people notice the difference. Beatbreak’s Reina is dressed like someone who actually runs and fights: jacket, shorts, not a costume built around showing skin. That visual language already exists. They don’t have to invent modest “active girl” designs from scratch.

The days of Mimi/Zoe/Nene are long gone.

Precure as a reference

Toei does have a long-running lab for writing groups of girls: Pretty Cure. Those seasons develop distinct personalities, give each girl her own arc, and keep the characters as middle-schoolers with young bodies. Outfits stay mostly in the “colorful but not sexualized for the age” zone, even when transformation sequences get flashy. That’s useful institutional knowledge. The catch is genre. Precure is an ensemble magical-girl show built around girls from the start. Digimon TV has been built around a boy + partner + mixed or male-heavy group for 25 years. Transplanting Precure’s ensemble habits onto a single female Digimon lead isn’t automatic; you’d still need the partnership, the found-family texture, and the “kid learning to live with a monster that eats emotions” core to feel like Digimon, not like Precure with Digimon pasted on.

Believe me when i say this, some of the talent for beat Break did Precure, especially DokiDoki and Star Twinkle

What would actually treat a female lead with respect here

The safest version isn’t “female Marcus” or “Precure girl who happens to have a Digimon.” It’s a character written the way Tomoro or Rika were written: specific person, personal stakes, real flaws, growth through the partner and the team, clothes that match an active life, no extra camera lingering. Reina already shows they can write a hot-blooded girl without making her the whole thesis of the show. A lead version of that energy is riskier than a lead version of Tomoro’s quieter, cynical, slow-trust energy or a Rika-style proud loner.

What has to work for the lead

Do not make her Female Marcus. Do not make her the designated fixer of the boys. Write her like Rika or a female Tomoro: specific, flawed, personal stakes, growth through the partner and the group.

What has to be in place:

Age and time. Middle-school to early high school, present day or “this summer,” not 2050 and not Appmon’s near-future net. Adventure DNA is kids leaving home, not adults in a finished dystopia.

Motivation that is hers. Not “I was chosen so I must lead.” Something small and human: a missing sibling, a promise, guilt, curiosity that gets her in too deep. The Crest/Chosen thing can arrive after she already has a reason to care.

She is not automatically the leader. A sizable cast can have a Tai-type or a quieter strategist. She can become the emotional center without being the one who gives every speech.

Flaws that cost something. Pride, distrust, bottling things up, charging in at the wrong time. Reina works because those flaws hurt her. A lead needs the same.

Clothes and framing. Active-girl kit (jacket, shorts, sneakers), modest if there is a beach episode. No extra camera. Precure’s ensemble habits help here; Glitter Force comparisons only show up if the whole team is girls and the tone turns sparkly.

What her Digimon should be

Do not default to “the girl gets the cute bird/plant.” Partner should mirror her, the way Gekkomon mirrors Tomoro’s hunger and mess.Good fits for an adventure-style female lead:A proud, slightly aloof line if she is Rika-coded: Renamon is taken; Loogamon, Lunamon, or a new fox/wolf/moon line works. Cool at first, warms up as she does.

A stubborn, grounded line if she is more Tomoro-coded: something that starts small and awkward (a lesser-used Rookie like Pulsemon, Espimon, or a new reptile/beast) and only looks “heroic” after they both grow. Late Champion, like Beatbreak did, is fine if the bond is the point.

Avoid giving her the season’s flashiest Mega on episode 6, and avoid a partner whose whole identity is “pretty girl Digimon.” Angewomon/Ophanimon as an end of a line is fine; starting her as the angel girl is the girlboss shortcut.

Best default: a partner that is a little difficult. Not instantly loyal mascot, not instant dark rival. Someone who argues with her, needs her, and reflects the thing she does not want to admit about herself. That is the Digimon loop. Gender of the lead does not change it.

But if they are going to be the face of the seoasn, expect cute but becomes something strong.

Timeframe and structure

That is the hole Beatbreak left on purpose. Filling it is the point of a 2027 reset.

Return to adventure means:

Real world that looks like now (or a year from now), not Beatbreak’s flooded class city or Appmon’s app-net.
A Digital World that exists before they arrive, with its own map, seasons, and politics.
A group of 6–8 kids, not a four-person Cleaner cell.
They go there for a long stretch. Ghost Game’s late “we popped in to stop a threat” is not enough. Beatbreak’s Mirror World is not a substitute.

That is the hole Beatbreak left on purpose. Filling it is the point of a 2027 reset.

The missing Digimon factions

Beatbreak filled the villain slot with World Union, GIFT, Five Stars, Tactics. Those are human systems. What you are missing is evolved Digimon who have their own groups—Dark Masters, Devas, Olympos XII, Royal Knights as an order, Seven Great Demon Lords as a pantheon, bagra armies, etc. Kyo’s side of Beatbreak never gave you a Digimon court or a Digimon army with ranks and ideology. That is a real gap.

An adventure season should put that back in the center:

A council or order of Megas who think they own the Digital World (Royal Knights-style, or a new order).

A rival faction of Ultimates/Megas who want humans out or want to harvest them (Deva / Demon Lord energy without copying the old roster beat for beat).

Mid-boss groups that are Digimon first: a pack, a temple, a zone lord and their army—not a CEO and his Cleaner team.

Humans can still be involved (a professor, a company poking the Digital World). They should not be the only ones with organization. The Digital World needs its own politics again so the kids are walking into someone else’s war, which is the classic adventure beat.

A female lead plus that structure is compatible. She does not have to punch the Demon Lord into submission in episode 3. She has to survive the place, keep her partner, and decide what kind of person she is when the Digital World’s factions treat humans as pieces. That is adventure. That is also how you use a girl as the lead without girlbossing the franchise: same world, same factions, same “kids vs a mythos that was here first,” different kid at the front.

There's a lot to talk about we we get close to Beat break's finale. I feel we'll get news on it after it finishes airing and we get our first look at the leads

So what do you think

what would like to see in Digimon come bak after a absence of elements you missed

be positive and try not to take it out on certain seasons

the Davis problem.

The 2nd Canon of Saint Dionysios of Alexandria (c. 247 AD): “The question touching women in the time of their separation, whether it is proper for them when in such a condition to enter the house of God, I consider a superfluous inquiry. For I do not think that, if they are believing and pious women, they will themselves be rash enough in such a condition either to approach the holy table or to touch the body and blood of the Lord. Certainly the woman who had the issue of blood of twelve years' standing did not touch the Lord Himself, but only the hem of His garment, with a view to her cure. For to pray, however a person may be situated, and to remember the Lord, in whatever condition a person may be, and to offer up petitions for the obtaining of help, are exercises altogether blameless. But the individual who is not perfectly pure both in soul and in body, shall be interdicted from approaching the holy of holies.”

The church coming from out of a Jewish background would have seen menstruation as through the lens of the Old Testament idea of uncleanliness. 

In practice, women probably felt quite out of place coming into the holy temple during this. Certainly when feminine hygiene products were not what they are today.

On a pastoral side. There are saints such as St. Gregory the Gteatand other writings that apply this canon in a way that leaves the decision up to the piety of the woman as long as they are prepared in every other way. 

The canons are what they are, but the bishops get to apply them pastorally.

text:
⚖️ To restore trust in court science and expert witnesses, do we need to put MORE power in the hands of juries?

In this troubling era of expertise and science skepticism, paired with record-low trust in the judiciary, trial lawyers are raising alarms: it is becoming harder to present scientific evidence to a jury without it being devalued or rejected.

The standard response is tightening the gates. Judges as gatekeepers must screen harder to keep "junk science" out.

Last week @mikewhelanjr sent me a forthcoming paper from Temple Law Professor Edith Beerdsen. "Expert Evidence in Times of Skepticism and Distrust" argues the focus on judges as the gatekeepers might be the wrong approach. 

I think the judiciary and expert witness world need to consider the public's concerns about expertise. I believe the skepticism towards expertise is unwarranted and driven by narratives and algorithms, instead of rational thought, but here we are. I'm going to do my best to summarize the highlights of the paper and give some of my thoughts.

Draft article: https://t.co/1vupa1GL1c

1. The Myth of "Value-Free" Science

Our legal system relies on an outdated "supply-side" model where experts offer neutral facts and laypeople make the value judgments. However, philosophy of science proves that research is never fully value-free. Personal and community values shape what scientists study, how they define complex concepts like "risk," and when they decide a body of evidence is "sufficient" to draw a conclusion. When a judge rules on the admissibility of scientific evidence, they are making a subjective choice. This value judgment should be made by the community, represented by the jury, rather than a single judge.

What do you think? Do you believe juries are better than judges at making this value judgment?

2. The Dr. Hruz Paradox

We treat judges as objective gatekeepers, but they carry human biases just like everyone else. Beerdsen highlights a striking series of cases where different federal judges evaluated the exact same medical expert, Dr. Paul Hruz, regarding his qualifications to testify on gender-affirming care. One judge excluded him for "merely reading literature" (which is a little strange because a literature review is common for the peer review prong of Daubert), a second ruled him unqualified for lacking hands-on clinical experience, while a third praised him on appeal as fully qualified. This wild divergence proves that judicial gatekeeping is highly subjective, often substituting a single judge's values for the jury's.

This paradox is compelling and I need to learn more about this matter involving Dr. Paul Hruz. It certainly involves a topic which is very polarizing in the current climate, so I'm not certain it is the best example of a run-of-the-mill criminal or civil case with a judge as the gatekeeper. It does, however, help underline the author's point about human biases. I'd like to see a similar paradox in a more commonly litigated matter involving. Is there a similar paradox with a accident reconstructionist or a DNA forensics expert?

My subjective analysis already ruled the first judge was wrong on a literature review. An appropriately educated expert reviewing the peer reviewed publications is not merely reading literature. It might be "merely reading literature" if I do it. The lacking of clinical experience is more compelling to me.

3. The Solution: Put the Jury in Charge

Instead of isolating juries, we should let them make the initial admissibility and qualification decisions. When jurors know a judge has already "vetted" an expert, they defer blindly due to the "gatekeeper effect." Making the admissibility call themselves encourages healthy skepticism. Furthermore, we should evaluate the expert's connection to their scientific community, scrutinizing whether their claim was subject to the community's peer review and corrective feedback loops. This active role includes letting jurors ask questions, deliberate continuously, and avoid early straw polls that lock them into defensive, "verdict-driven" thinking.

I have some concerns about this particular approach. Juries maintain quite the cross-section of academic experiences. Asking a jury to scrutinize whether an expert's claims were subject to peer review may mean nothing to most jurors. How do you educate jurors academic standards, research and scientific methodologies before allowing them to scrutinize an expert?

Further, if we are going to ask jurors to be more active and allow them to ask questions and deliberate continuously, how long do we allow that to take place? Efficiency becomes a concern. Further, juries are the "trier of fact." Does this approach turn them into an investigative body? Do standard juries become grand juries?

Professor Beerdsen argues, isolating juries from the vetting process only alienates skeptical audiences and robs the trial of its democratic legitimacy. To rebuild trust in courtrooms, we must replace elite gatekeeping with robust community deliberation.

These are legitimate concerns. I don't have the answers. Giving juries structured conditions within which to deliberate expertise will require more jury education, new jury instructions, and probably new local rules.

👉 What do you think? Should we trust juries to evaluate complex scientific methodology, or is judicial gatekeeping a necessary shield?

Once upon a time, this was what the university did. This was, in fact, the thing it did best -- provide us with inoculation against those who seek to think for us. Over the decades, alas, it has lost sight of that mission. Yes, of course, there were, there are, many good people on campus doing important work, but they have been unwilling or unable to shut down the radical faction, to steer the university back to its appropriate role, which is not that of multinational corporation posing as temple of wisdom, but temple of wisdom.

text:
#MadeArdernGoAway
Tāwhaki was started in 2021 under the Jacinda Ardern Labour Government, with then Research, Science and Innovation Minister Megan Woods announcing the Crown rūnanga partnership. The Government put up $16 million at the beginning, including $14 million towards the Crown’s share of buying the 1,000-hectare property. A further $2 million grant helped fund the rūnanga’s share. Government funding has continued since then, taking reported Crown investment to more than $35 million.

The iwi partners are Te Taumutu Rūnanga and Wairewa Rūnanga, represented through Kaitōrete Limited. They aren’t simply consultants brought in to offer cultural advice and then sent home. The arrangement gives the Crown and rūnanga equal ownership and governance interests.

So what does iwi bring to the table?

Their contribution includes mana whenua interests, cultural and historical knowledge, strategic input, intellectual property and interests in surrounding land. In return, they have a 50 percent interest in the venture, an equal role in governance and a share of any future profits.

That could prove to be a very good investment if Tāwhaki becomes the successful aerospace hub its supporters envisage. New Zealand could gain jobs, technology, private investment and a valuable foothold in an increasingly important industry.

Nobody should object to that.

But there is a rather large elephant sitting next to the rocket.

Space technology can have military uses.

A satellite doesn’t need to carry a missile to be strategically important. Communications, navigation, surveillance and intelligence technology can all have defence applications. A commercial launch today can potentially have national-security implications tomorrow.

That’s why the latest debate over who gets to use the facility matters.

Tāwhaki has indicated that it could support NZDF launches for national-security purposes. Some rūnanga members have argued for much stronger restrictions on military or militarised activity.

And suddenly our shiny new space industry has wandered straight into the same old argument about co-governance.

The Government is responsible for New Zealand’s defence and national security. Ministers answer to Parliament and, ultimately, the voters. Yet an equal partner in this Crown–iwi venture has a significant voice over what activities it considers acceptable at the facility.

That’s where reasonable people can ask a fairly simple question: when national security is involved, who gets the final say?

This isn’t an argument against Māori culture or Māori participation. Māori have served New Zealand in the armed forces with distinction for generations. Recognising history and involving mana whenua in a development project is hardly controversial.

But there’s a difference between respecting culture and allowing cultural or ideological views to determine national strategic policy.

The original deal was made by the Labour Government. The current Government inherited it. Now it has to work out where the boundary sits.

Because if taxpayers are helping fund nationally important infrastructure, the national interest should come first when defence is involved.

We may soon have rockets capable of reaching orbit.

Let’s just hope they don’t need a cultural clearance certificate before they can leave New Zealand.

Steven is an entrepreneur and an ex RNZN diver who likes travelling, renovating houses, Swiss Watches, history, chocolate art and art deco. via https://t.co/86eXJo7M2y

🇨🇳🇧🇫 Burkina Faso showcases Chinese "Tianlong-30" air defense system for the first time

An artillery unit of the Burkina Faso Armed Forces conducted live-fire exercises using a nearly all-Chinese arsenal. Footage from the drills - attended by the country's president, Captain Ibrahim Traoré - has surfaced online.

The first part of the video features:

- CS/SH1 122mm self-propelled howitzers on Shaanxi 6×6 chassis (firing range: 22–27 km);
- PLL-05 120mm self-propelled mortars on WZ551 wheeled chassis (firing range: up to 13 km; digital fire control system);
- SR-5 modular multiple launch rocket systems (MLRS) on heavy 8×8 chassis, firing 220mm guided rockets with a range of up to 70 km.

The second part of the clip offers the first public look at the "Tianlong-30" (TL-30) air defense missile system; its delivery had not been previously reported. Visible at the deployment site are a launcher and an IBIS-150 3D radar, which boasts a detection range of up to 130 km and the ability to track up to 144 targets. The primary interceptor is the SD-30 missile, featuring combined guidance and an engagement range of 30 km.
