Trump said the reply would be hard. Monday night, outbound of Hormuz near Khasab, two VLCCs took projectiles: Saudi-operated Sidr(Bahri) and Sinokor’s Senegal Prosperity. UKMTO logged three unknown projectiles, no casualties, no spill. Iran claimed mines. CENTCOM called that false. At 12:00 ET on 1 September, US forces began striking IRGC targets for attacks on shipping and on American troops.

This is a coastal campaign. Local reports and a US official put blasts on the Hormuz–Oman belt: Bandar Abbas, Qeshm, Chabahar and Konarak, Jask, Sirik, Minab. CENTCOM named only “IRGC targets.” The geography is the strategy, radar, boats, anti-ship batteries, mine-rockets. The aim is to keep a residual outbound corridor, which had crawled back toward half of pre-war volumes in the lull, from being closed by cheap munitions. Attrition of the strait toolkit. Not a march on Tehran.

A strike on the mine battery is a warning. A strike on the whole south coast is a doctrine.

Doctrine this time: punish the shooters, leave the export island in the photograph. Imagery from 29 August still shows dozens of Iranian tankers idle off Kharg, the terminal that has historically moved most of Iran’s crude. Tuesday’s list does not put Kharg in CENTCOM’s sentence. Hitting coastal kit tries to reopen a lane without taking the last large official barrel off the water in one night. Seizing Kharg would be a different war presence over a loaded island, midterm oil that looks like 1973. That is not the noon package.

Tehran’s first answer is already on the tape: projectiles on tankers, missiles toward Jordan and the UAE after Larak, IRGC language of punishment. In Bishkek, Pezeshkian offered a return to the June memorandum if Washington returns first. The next menu is the one they have used all year, more shots at merchants, more drones at Gulf bases, more mine claims whether UKMTO confirms them or not. A full close of the residual lane still moves Brent. Using it every night is what thickens the US list.

Oil moved before the CENTCOM post and kept moving after it. Monday’s tanker reports lifted Brent back through $90. Tuesday screens sat near $92-94. The diesel crack had already printed through $100 a barrel on the same logic: not only crude, the fuel that runs trucks. Two VLCCs hit on the way out puts the half-recovery back on a war-risk invoice. If the south-coast strikes degrade launchers faster than Iran can reseed, the spike can fade. If another pair of hulls is hit this week, $92 is a floor.

The next US direction is more of the same belt until it isn’t. Repeats on mobile batteries, boats and coastal ISR, the summer pattern of “additional strikes after the latest ship.” What changes the map is a shift from IRGC tools to Iranian oil infrastructure. Kharg as an air target would tell Beijing and New Delhi the last official Iranian barrel is in play. Holding the island would mean a garrison this administration has spent six months trying not to own. Midterms are in November. Bessent is running the economic track in parallel.

Kharg is not a raid. It is a decision to take Iran’s remaining official export off the board and to stay there.

Kharg is a political file, not a raid. Idle hulls already show the tap is half-closed. Hitting it from the air would end official exports without a flag. Occupying it would mean a garrison in a midterm year. That is why noon’s list stopped at the coast. CENTCOM answered the belt that feeds Hormuz, not the island that feeds the budget. More nights like 1 September stay limited. Kharg is the choice to end those barrels in public and to own what follows.

text:
Good Wednesday morning, Central Alabama!

Dangerous heat is the biggest weather story for the next several days. A Heat Advisory is in effect for all of Central Alabama from 11 a.m. today through 8 p.m. Saturday. Afternoon temperatures will climb into the mid and upper 90s, and the humidity could push the heat index as high as 105 to 107 degrees. Warm nights will offer little relief and can add to the strain as the week continues.

A strong ridge of high pressure remains parked over the Southeast. The sinking air beneath that ridge is limiting rain, allowing temperatures to rise quickly, and keeping the humidity in place. If you work or spend time outside, drink water regularly, take frequent breaks in the shade or air conditioning, and move strenuous activity away from the hottest part of the afternoon when possible. Please check on older neighbors and never leave children or pets in a parked vehicle.

Today will be partly cloudy, hot, and humid with an isolated afternoon shower or thunderstorm possible. Highs will reach the mid to upper 90s. Most communities will remain dry, but any storm that develops could briefly produce heavy rain, gusty wind, and frequent lightning. Tonight will stay warm, with lows mainly in the lower to middle 70s.

Thursday and Friday will bring more of the same—hot afternoons, warm nights, and only limited relief from isolated storms. Rain chances increase somewhat across the southern half of Central Alabama late Thursday through the weekend, but coverage will remain uneven. Organized severe weather is not expected. Temperatures should ease only slightly early next week, with highs still in the lower to middle 90s.

Tropical Update
The National Hurricane Center has issued its final advisory on Tropical Depression Edouard, which is now inland over southeastern Texas. Edouard will not bring direct impacts to Central Alabama. No additional tropical cyclone formation is expected across the Atlantic basin during the next seven days.

Stay cool, take care of one another, and have a good Wednesday!

Steve Cochran

text:
Farmer mental health matters. Farming comes with plenty of pressure, from unpredictable weather and markets to long days and the weight of keeping a farm going. Having someone to talk to about these things can make a real difference. 

Arkansas farmer Matt Miles knows the importance of those conversations. Listen in as he shares his thoughts on looking out for one another and making it easier to talk about mental health.

text:
I’ve been up most of the night, I don’t feel well today, but I am still alive! My stomach hurts. I get stomach and back pain as well. My groin area is so sore and it makes it hard to walk. I also feel dehydrated, I don’t want to drink water, because puking is no fun. I do get hydration bags for my IV while receiving TPN. I have a pic with three lines, which is great. I’m on the IV pole 18 hours a day, so that I stop losing weight. I was below 100 pounds  recently, but I’ve gained weight and I believe I’m at 106 now. I’m useless today, but have lots to do, so I have to hope that things are improving. 

I was in school before my stomach became paralyzed. I had to work on essays and finals from my hospital bed. I enjoyed going to school and I was pretty good at it! 

These days we have setup a home studio. We plan to record mom, she wants this, and I’ve been trying to get her to do this for years. I was even planning a launch party! I’m so happy my parents are working so well together & that they’re including me, which has been my dream. 

A few years ago, I flew to Kauai from Portland, Oregon, and I had a proposal for my parents. I wanted to remake their original song that they wrote when I was a baby. Mom couldn’t let me do this. She said to Dad, right in front of me, “… our song, you aren’t gonna give her our song”, it hurt. I was trying to show them respect and honor them, but mom didn’t see it that way.

I’ve been fighting to stay alive ever since I was told that I have ovarian cancer.  I’ve traveled, I’ve worked with many different gyn oncs, and I tried chemotherapy and whatever else they were recommending. I had a debulking surgery in 2017, and again in 2018, the treatment wasn’t working at that time. The IV chemo (red devil is what they called it) worked well for awhile, then the world had to deal with staying indoors, and I had yet another recurrence. 

Blood was pouring into the toilet. I found out my ovarian cancer was now in my colon. 

The gyn onc put me on a pill version of chemotherapy, and it worked well and fast; thank God! But, then I ended living at the hospital for a couple of months. I was able to get drains and I stopped needing the paracentesis to drain liquid from my stomach, I was grateful! I still am. Without my hard working biliary drain, my pain would be excruciating. I create so much liquid that needs to be drained every day. I was off the chemo when I was inpatient. My doctor said no more chemotherapy for you, because of my drains and infections. I saw him again recently and no chemo is being offered and he wants me to just enjoy my days. He told me to go on hospice a year ago. If I had listened to him, then I wouldn’t be here today. It all seems too heavy, but I’m thankful for my family and friends and I hope our lives turn out better than expected. Love, Sayla

On the bright side, they generously gave me 1000 “points” that expire in a year, because apparently making my planned trip to Madrid worse off wasn’t quite enough of a gift.

We need legislation that requires the rental companies to hold your vehicle at the rental location until your scheduled rental date/time.  And if they do not have your vehicle?  Well then they should have to refund half the full rental price, on top of giving you a comparable vehicle for use.

Without holding these companies accountable, they will go on functioning with impunity.

Heck, in July, I had a rental with @thriftycars at the Portland Oregon airport, and I rented a Nissan Rogue (mid-size SUV) and they tried to pan off a Buick Encore (compact SUV) as the "same class" vehicle, which it is NOT.

text:
Scientists discover a massive heat anomaly deep inside Mars | Caltech, ScienceDaily

Summary: Mars has a hidden temperature divide, with its southern interior potentially hundreds of degrees hotter than the north and partially molten. The discovery could help explain several long-standing Martian mysteries, including unusual magnetism, seismic behavior, and clues to the planet’s ancient water history.

---

Researchers have uncovered a major temperature imbalance deep inside Mars, with the planet's southern interior appearing significantly hotter than its northern half.

Gravity measurements suggest that the interior beneath Mars's southern hemisphere is about 200 to 400 degrees Celsius warmer than the north and may be partially molten. The finding offers a new window into the Red Planet's geologic history, including periods when Mars may have had environments capable of supporting life.

The study was led by Caltech alumnus Alexander Berne (PhD '26), now a postdoctoral associate at the University of Arizona. The results were published August 27 in Nature.

Mapping Mars From Gravity

While completing his graduate work at Caltech, Berne developed a model that uses subtle variations in gravity to estimate the internal structure of a planetary body. He and his colleagues later applied that approach to Mars.

The researchers analyzed decades of observations from three Mars missions: Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Odyssey, and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. By tracking extremely small changes in the spacecrafts' velocities, the team was able to reconstruct the gravitational field surrounding Mars.

The Sun's gravitational pull on Mars changes over the course of the planet's seasons because Mars travels along a slightly elliptical orbit and rotates on a tilted axis. The researchers used a method known as tidal tomography to study how these gravitational signatures change over time and to build a model of the planet's interior.

"Scientists usually assume that the interiors of planetary bodies are generally spherically symmetric, but this is not necessarily true," Berne says. "As we get more gravity data, we can determine the three-dimensional intricacies of a planet's interior structure. These inferences in turn give us a blueprint for designing future missions and scientific exploration of these worlds. Understanding the interior structure of planetary bodies helps us unravel the processes that shaped their formation and evolution."

A Deep North-South Divide

Mars has long been known to look very different across its two hemispheres. The southern surface is dominated by tall mountains and heavily cratered terrain, while the northern hemisphere consists largely of broad, low-lying plains.

The new results show that this contrast may extend far below the surface. Researchers were surprised to find that Mars is also thermally uneven inside, with the southern interior hundreds of degrees hotter than the north.

That hidden heat could help explain several other puzzling features of Mars.

Scientists have detected unusual magnetic signatures in iron-rich minerals in the southern hemisphere. A hotter southern mantle could indicate that Mars once had a magnetic field strong enough to produce differences in magnetism between the two hemispheres.

NASA's InSight mission also previously found that seismic waves lose energy more quickly in the south. Higher temperatures in the region could help account for that behavior.

Clues to Mars's Watery Past

"The dichotomy that we see between north and south is important to understand because it gives information about processes that may have influenced the hydrology of Mars, including the formation of basins that may have held water," says Amirhossein Bagheri, a postdoctoral scholar at Caltech and co-author on the paper. Bagheri is also a former member of the InSight team.

Understanding the temperature difference could therefore provide new clues about how Mars evolved and how its landscape developed during periods when liquid water may have existed on the surface.

Researchers do not yet know what caused the thermal anomaly. Several possibilities remain under consideration.

One hypothesis is that a giant impact released heat from the north. Another suggests that spontaneous convection may once have occurred within the southern Martian mantle. A third possibility is that thick geological structures in the south trapped heat and prevented it from escaping efficiently.

text:
A phone call on the drive home from a routine leg scan completely erased a first-round NFL destiny.
In the winter of 2008, Boston College linebacker Mark Herzlich was arguably the most terrifying defensive weapon in college football. He was a consensus All-American, the ACC Defensive Player of the Year, and a projected locks-in first-round draft pick. When an intrusive ache flared up in his leg, he scheduled a quick MRI assuming it was a minor nerve irritation or a deep bone bruise. By the time his car hit the highway after the appointment, his phone rang with an urgent, chilling directive: book an immediate slot with an oncologist.
Ewing’s sarcoma. A rare, hyper-aggressive form of bone cancer was eating away at his left femur.
The medical staff didn't offer a clean compromise. They presented a brutal, binary ultimatum. Option one was a standard surgery to remove the malignant segment of the bone and replace it with a cadaver graft—a choice with high survival odds that would immediately permanently terminate his football career. Option two bypassed immediate removal for aggressive, experimental chemoradiation. It carried an unstable 40% to 50% survival rate, but it left the microscopic dream of gridiron contact on the table.
Herzlich willfully weaponized the gamble, choosing the path that risked his life just to salvage his game.
What followed was a hellish, agonizing grind through 168 days of system-destroying chemotherapy and fifty separate rounds of localized radiation. On July 23, 2009, surgeons sliced into his thigh to hammer a permanent 13-inch titanium rod down the center of his femur, structurally reinforcing a bone ravaged by cancer. He was just 21 years old, forced to watch his senior season vanish from a sterile hospital bed while his peers prepared for professional stardom.
He didn't survive through grand delusions of grandeur. He survived by forcing himself to become the most disciplined patient in the ward, managing the chaos by conquering small, unglamorous hourly goals.
Against all medical logic, he won.
Exactly sixteen months after his diagnosis, Herzlich walked back out onto the field for Boston College's 2010 season opener. The toxic treatment had permanently sapped his elite speed and natural explosiveness, but he anchored the defense anyway, starting all 13 games.
Yet, the NFL is an unforgiving business.
When the 2011 NFL Draft arrived, the league evaluated his medical charts with the same cold, clinical detachment as his initial surgeons. All 32 franchises passed on him through seven rounds, terrified of the long-term structural liability of a reconstructed leg. But New York Giants head coach Tom Coughlin refused to let him slip away. Coughlin, a former Boston College coach who had founded a prominent cancer charity decades earlier after losing a player to leukemia, recognized the rare composition of Herzlich’s character and signed him as an undrafted free agent.
Herzlich didn't just fill space; he earned a roster spot on pure merit, starting two games as a rookie before an ankle injury sidelined him.
The team's championship run kept moving without a hitch. In February 2012, just twenty-seven months removed from the radiation treatments meant to bury his athletic career for good, Mark Herzlich hoisted the Lombardi Trophy at Super Bowl XLVI. Legacy isn't built on the clean, unblemished paths; it's forged in the terrifying spaces where a man looks a terminal diagnosis in the eye and demands his future back.

A divided nation. A deadly plot. A man caught between two worlds.

Will Manley is a rising star in the U.S. Government’s clandestine services—an undercover agent tasked with stopping a domestic terror group bent on reshaping America. But as he immerses himself in their radical ideology, he faces a battle more personal than he ever anticipated: a choice between his government career and the legacy of his Native American roots.

At the heart of the struggle is Elias McArdle, a brilliant and ruthless former U.S. Army commander. Meanwhile, Lenape elder Rebecca Hurney offers a path of healing through ancient wisdom—but time is running out. 🇺🇸🇺🇦 Bessent just blamed Ukraine for the fuel prices hitting Americans, and the diesel shortage has a stranger source closer to home

Larry Johnson joined as the Treasury Secretary offered a new explanation for the pump. 

On camera, Bessent said upward pressure on prices comes partly from Kyiv's strikes on Russian refineries:

"Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets"

Larry's diesel research points somewhere Bessent didn't.

American refineries are producing plenty, but substantial volumes are being shipped abroad, to Israel and to the US military according to his sources, which he can't independently confirm.

If true, the squeeze on farmers and truckers is partly a paper shortage of Washington's own making:

"the United States is creating its own shortage"

The global shortage is real, and Russia made it worse by halting its own diesel exports, though two Americans just back from driving Vladivostok to Moscow report fuel everywhere and no crisis.

The bigger picture came from two summits.

At the G20 in North Carolina, China reportedly refused to sign a declaration that Hormuz must be open.

At the SCO in Bishkek, India joined Russia and China in calling the strait Iran's business.

Larry calls the new world multimodal, many neurons firing at once, and for the next two weeks those neurons meet in Vladivostok and Delhi with no American in the room.

@Kenny_Wallace @KWallaceShow 
NO ARRESTS HAVE BEEN MADE YET — PLEASE KEEP SHARING!

A heartbreaking theft has hit one of NASCAR’s most respected veterans, and the racing community is rallying around Dave Marcis after his Arden, North Carolina, home was burglarized over the weekend.

Marcis was out of town when deputies responded to the break-in. According to the Buncombe County Sheriff’s Office incident report, the case is classified as felony breaking and entering at a residence. Investigators reported that no force was used to enter the home, and high-value items were stolen.

Among the reported stolen property are guns, jewelry, Rolex watches, knives and personal NASCAR memorabilia—including knives honoring past Winston Cup championship drivers.

But the loss goes far beyond the dollar value.

Former NASCAR driver Robert Pressley, who lives in the Arden area, had breakfast with Marcis Tuesday morning and learned more about what was taken.

“It’s all personal stuff,” Pressley said, noting that some of the watches were gifts given to Marcis and his late wife, Helen, who passed away just eight months ago.

That timing makes the theft particularly painful.

Some of the stolen items represent memories shared by Dave and Helen, while other pieces document decades of Marcis' life in NASCAR.

And there may be another reason the thieves will have difficulty turning the memorabilia into money.

Many of the items reportedly have Marcis' name on them.

“You’ve got so much stuff with his name on it, it’s going to be hard to get rid of it,” Pressley said.

For those who know Marcis, that's hardly surprising. His connection to the Western North Carolina racing community runs incredibly deep.

Pressley said Marcis has maintained a race shop in the Arden area for approximately 55 years. Their families' racing histories are intertwined as well.

“My dad and him raced together,” Pressley explained. “Then me and him raced together back in the ‘80s, ‘90s and up to 2000s when we both retired.”

Pressley described Marcis as someone who is “loved by everybody” while also calling him tougher than anyone they had ever raced against.

Another member of the racing community, Darrell Payne, emphasized just how much Marcis has meant to others over the years.

“If you needed to know something or you just needed someone to have your back, even as an official, it was Dave Marcis. Dave was there,” Payne said.

Payne also pointed out what makes this theft especially devastating:

“A lot of the stuff that they stole is irreplaceable.”

That's the part that should resonate with every racing fan.

A Rolex can have a monetary value. A firearm can be replaced. But a personalized piece of NASCAR history, a gift from a loved one, or an item connected to decades of memories cannot simply be purchased again.

The Buncombe County Sheriff’s Office investigation remains ongoing, and no arrests have been made.

Anyone with information about the break-in, the stolen property or anything suspicious surrounding the incident is asked to contact the Buncombe County Sheriff’s Office.

Racing fans, please SHARE this story.

Someone may see one of these items offered for sale, recognize Dave Marcis' name on a piece of memorabilia, or know something that could help investigators.

Let's help bring these pieces of Dave and Helen Marcis' memories back home.

15 Essential Media, Publishing & Broadcasting Stories for Industry Leaders

Welcome to today's Press Monitor review of Indian print media. Here are the 15 most impactful stories shaping the media, publishing, and broadcasting landscape, tracked by Press Monitor's comprehensive media monitoring across Indian publications. This press review highlights key developments that demand your attention.

1. Penguin India Memoir Dispute
Maintaining that there was no external pressure behind its decision to not publish Sonia Gandhi's memoir, Penguin Random House India on Monday said there was an impasse over ‘a particular issue’ during discussions on the ‘Belonging: A Journey of Love’. The publisher didn’t disclose the contentious issue, citing ‘agreement and author confidentiality’. The fresh clarification comes amid a controversy over the India publication of the Congress leader's much anticipated memoir following an announcement by the US-based Alfred A Knopf, an imprint of Penguin Random House, that the book would be released worldwide on November 10. Several Congress leaders have raised issues of governmental pressure and freedom of expression. Former Rajasthan chief minister Ashok Gehlot alleged that pressure was put on Penguin India to remove sections relating to PM Narendra Modi, the RSS and China’s occupation of Indian territory during the Modi regime. In its latest statement, PRHI specifically rejected suggestions that the decision was driven by outside intervention. ‘We feel it is important for us to correct certain misrepresentations regarding the forthcoming memoir ‘Belonging’. This is a book that we at Penguin Random House India, were really keen on publishing as it was a hard-won acquisition,’ Pallavi Narayan, spokesperson of PRHI, said. ‘Since the content of the book is confidential and under embargo, there was no external pressure whatsoever,’ the publisher said. PRHI said the manuscript had gone through its ‘normal editorial process’ during which several points were raised and deliberated upon with the author's representatives. ‘On some, they agreed to changes and on others, we accepted the author's position. Unfortunately, and ultimately, an understanding could not be reached on a particular issue,’ it said. The author's team subsequently informed the publisher that they did not wish to proceed with the publication, PRHI said, adding that it respected their decision. ‘Since we are bound by an agreement, and author confidentiality is paramount to us, we will not divulge details of what led to the impasse,’ the publisher said. As publishers, it was its ‘responsibility and duty’ to critically assess a manuscript, ask questions, make recommendations and exercise its independent editorial judgement, Penguin India said. ‘We did just that with Belonging as well,’ it said. Monday's statement reiterates Penguin’s earlier position that it remained willing and keen to publish the memoir and that editorial scrutiny, including factchecking and recommendations, was part of its normal publishing process. The controversy intensified in political circles and on social media after reports that PRHI had backed out of publishing the memoir following disagreements over editorial changes, with the publishing house facing criticism from netizens as well as opposition leaders. Former Madhya Pradesh chief minister Kamal Nath had also questioned whether the publisher's position was influenced by pressure from elsewhere. The memoir, in which the reclusive Gandhi is expected to write about her childhood in post-war Italy, her marriage into the Nehru-Gandhi family, the assassination of her husband Rajiv Gandhi and her entry into politics, has attracted considerable attention ahead of its international publication. PRHI is the Indian subsidiary and operating company of global publishing group Penguin Random House. —PTI
Why it matters: The controversy over Sonia Gandhi's memoir 'Belonging' underscores the delicate balance between editorial integrity and external pressures in publishing.
Key detail: Penguin Random House India denied external pressure, citing an impasse over a 'particular issue' during the editorial process.

Source: Asian Age, with cross-coverage from Indian Express, Telegraph, Tribune, Free Press Journal, Hindustan Times.
Next step: Industry watchers should monitor freedom of expression debates and publisher-author relationships.

2. Times of India Social Impact Summit Honours ESG & CSR
A front-page report in Times of India says: The Times of India Social Impact Summit, in partnership with Malabar Gold & Diamonds, The Responsible Jeweller, and the Reliance Foundation, is honouring those who have achieved excellence in the domains of ESG and CSR. This event will bring together innovators and leaders from Non-profit, Corporate and Government organisations driving real change across the nation.
Why it matters: Recognition of ESG and CSR excellence sets benchmarks for corporate responsibility.
Key detail: The summit, in partnership with Malabar Gold & Diamonds and Reliance Foundation, brought together non-profits, corporates, and government.

Source: Times of India, Economic Times.
Next step: Companies can benchmark their own ESG initiatives against those honoured.

3. Indian Express: 'Not an Industry, It's a Mission'
"A front-page report in New Indian Express says that the publication is more than just a business; it’s a dedicated mission. This statement reflects the core values of the organization, highlighting its commitment to journalistic integrity and impactful storytelling."
Why it matters: A reaffirmation of journalistic mission over commercial motives.
Key detail: The statement reflects Indian Express's commitment to integrity and impactful storytelling.

Source: New Indian Express, Morning Standard.
Next step: Reflect on the role of media as a mission-driven entity.

4. U.S. Treasury Blocks Media from G20 Finance Summit
A front-page report in Morning Standard says the U.S. Treasury Department is preventing certain journalists from covering a finance meeting among the world's most powerful countries. Reporters from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and Bloomberg News were denied credentials to the Group of 20 finance ministers' meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, according to the Times. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told the Associated Press the decision 'has nothing to do with point of view.' The Times called the exclusion 'a blatant attempt to evade public scrutiny,' noting the summit's significance for global economic issues including Iran sanctions and inflation. Jim Tankersley, Berlin bureau chief of The Times, was allowed to attend.
Why it matters: Restrictions on press access at a major global finance meeting raise transparency concerns.
Key detail: Reporters from NYT, WSJ, and Bloomberg denied credentials; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the decision was not about viewpoint.

Source: Morning Standard.
Next step: Media rights organisations may challenge access restrictions.

5. Subhash Chandra Clarifies Rs 6,250 Crore Settlement
A front-page report in Economic Times says Subhash Chandra of Essel Group is facing public backlash due to a personal insolvency process approved by the National Company Law Tribunal. The tribunal approved a repayment plan of six hundred and twenty-five crore rupees, while admitted claims against personal guarantees stood at twenty-two thousand crores. In an interview, Chandra clarified that claims from Indian banks are only fifty-three thousand one lakh rupees, and he expects principal creditors to fully repay the amount while denying allegations of using associate companies to swing the vote.
Why it matters: The Essel Group founder addresses personal insolvency and repayment plan controversy.
Key detail: NCLT approved a Rs 625 crore plan against claims of Rs 22,000 crore; Chandra says bank claims are only Rs 53,100 crore.

Source: Economic Times.
Next step: Creditors and investors will watch the repayment process closely.

6. Microdrama Market Consolidation: Retention Over Acquisition
A front-page report in Economic Times says India’s microdrama market is set for an overhaul, with the next phase of growth hinging on retention, engagement and sustainable monetisation rather than user acquisition, according to industry executives.
Why it matters: India's microdrama sector shifts focus to sustainable monetisation.
Key detail: Industry executives highlight the next phase hinges on engagement and retention, not just user acquisition.

Source: Economic Times.
Next step: Content creators should adapt strategies for long-term viewer loyalty.

7. Big Players Enter Microdrama Space: Yash Raj Films, Sun TV
A front-page report in Mint says mainstream entertainment players such as Yash Raj Films and Sun TV Network have recently announced an entry into microdrama creation even as early entrants such as Pocket FM have exited the space.
Why it matters: Mainstream entertainment giants enter microdrama creation, signalling market validation.
Key detail: Yash Raj Films and Sun TV Network announced entry, while early entrant Pocket FM exited.

Source: Mint.
Next step: Competitors must innovate to capture market share.

8. SIT to Probe Messi Match Fraud in Kerala
A front-page report in The Hindu says Kerala Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan has ordered a special investigation team to probe suspected tax fraud and corruption involving the previous LDF government's plan to bring Lionel Messi and the Argentina team to Kochi in August 2025. The inquiry focuses on a suspected GST evasion of Rs 22.68 crore linked to foreign remittances made by a sponsoring news broadcasting company.
Why it matters: Alleged GST evasion and corruption in the 2025 Messi match event.
Key detail: SIT probes suspected tax fraud of Rs 22.68 crore linked to foreign remittances by a sponsoring news broadcaster.

Source: The Hindu.
Next step: Legal proceedings will clarify the extent of financial irregularities.

9. Ahmedabad Media Delegation Visits PIB Jammu
A front-page report in State Times says journalists from Ahmedabad visited the Press Information Bureau (PIB) in Jammu as part of a media outreach programme aimed at providing journalists first-hand exposure to developmental, infrastructure and research initiatives in Jammu & Kashmir. The delegation interacted with PIB Jammu Director Neha Jalali and visited IT Jammu, IIT and NHAI projects.
Why it matters: Media outreach programme fosters understanding of developmental initiatives in J&K.
Key detail: Journalists visited PIB, IIT Jammu, and NHAI projects.

Source: State Times.
Next step: Such exchanges can strengthen regional media capacity.

10. Dish TV Sets 38th AGM for Sept 29, 2026
A front-page report in Business Standard says that Dish TV India Limited will hold its thirty-eighth Annual General Meeting on September 29, 2026, via Video Conferencing. The company has appointed National Securities Depository Limited as the authorized agency for facilitating remote e-Voting and e-Voting during the meeting.
Why it matters: Corporate governance matters for shareholders.
Key detail: AGM to be held via video conferencing; e-voting facilitated by NSDL.

Source: Business Standard.
Next step: Shareholders should participate in the AGM.

11. Festive Shopper Upgrades Drive Brands to Center Stage
A front-page report in The Times of India says festive season upgrades spur brands to prioritize multi-medium visibility. The article emphasizes securing brand presence across print, experiential, influencer channels during high-traffic windows as shoppers transition from wishlists to purchases.
Why it matters: Festive season spurs brands to invest in multi-medium visibility.
Key detail: Brands prioritise print, experiential, and influencer channels during high-traffic windows.

Source: Times of India.
Next step: Marketers should plan cross-channel campaigns for upcoming festivals.

12. Focus Bharat Marks 11th Anniversary with Media Conclave
A front-page report in First India says Focus Bharat celebrated its 11th anniversary with a felicitation ceremony and media conclave at Hotel Clarks Amer in Jaipur. Chief guest Dr Jagdeesh Chandra welcomed the event and felicitated BJP leader Promila Rajput for her achievements.
Why it matters: Celebrating a milestone in regional journalism.
Key detail: Felicitation ceremony and media conclave in Jaipur; BJP leader Promila Rajput honoured.

Source: First India.
Next step: Regional media outlets can draw inspiration from this longevity.

13. Deccan Chronicle Expands Offices Across Multiple Cities
A front-page report in Deccan Chronicle says the newspaper has established various office locations across India, including Hyderabad, Vijayawada, Visakhapatnam, Rajahmundry, Anantapur, Karimnagar, Nellore, Chennai, Coimbatore, and Venkatachalam, making it accessible to a wide readership.
Why it matters: Geographic expansion increases readership reach.
Key detail: Offices in Hyderabad, Vijayawada, Chennai, Coimbatore, and more.

Source: Deccan Chronicle.
Next step: Competitors may consider similar expansion strategies.

14. MP Power Company Invites E-Tender for Airtime Services
A front-page report in Hindustan Times says that M.P. Paschim Kshetra Vidyut Vitaran Company Limited is inviting e-tenders for the supply of airtime services and existing 800 MHz wireless radio sets working under City Circle, Indore. The tender is valid from 1st October 2026 to 30th September 2028.
Why it matters: Government procurement for communication infrastructure.
Key detail: Tender for supply of airtime services and 800 MHz radio sets in Indore, valid from Oct 2026 to Sep 2028.

Source: Hindustan Times.
Next step: Bidders should review tender documents.

15. Tribune Launches Social Media Update for Breaking News
A front-page report in Tribune says that the Tribune's Facebook and Twitter page are now offering breaking news and special stories.
Why it matters: Traditional newspapers adapt to digital distribution.
Key detail: Tribune's Facebook and Twitter pages now offer breaking news and special stories.

Source: Tribune.
Next step: Readers can follow Tribune on social media for real-time updates.

text:
The market is underestimating Celsius underlying earnings power - $CELH 

In Q1 2026, net margin was 14.1%, or 14.5% after adjusting for a $4.4m one-off, up roughly 1pp yoy. Q2 reported net margin fell to 6.8%, but adding back the $80.9m after-tax distributor termination charge lifts normalized net income to approximately $120m, implying a 14.6% net margin, also up about 1pp yoy. On this basis, normalized H1 net margin was approximately 14.5%.

So what should we assume for H2? Based on management commentary on the Q2 earnings call, a 14% net margin seems reasonable, essentially assuming CELH sustains the level of profitability already achieved in H1.

Now make the revenue assumption deliberately boring: zero H2 growth versus H1. That gets FY26 revenue to roughly $3.2b. At a ~14% normalized net margin, CELH would generate around $450m of normalized consolidated net income. Against a $7.7b market cap, that implies just 17x normalized earnings.

To be fair, we also need to adjust for the PepsiCo partnership economics, since CELH has preferred stock outstanding. The preferred carries a 5% contractual dividend and is also treated as a participating security under the two-class method, meaning a portion of residual earnings is allocated to preferred holders based on their participation rights. Based on H1, I’m assuming roughly $85–90m of total FY26 preferred claims (19-20% of net income). This leaves roughly $360m attributable to common shareholders, which equates to ~21x forward earnings.

Notably, the preferred structure is currently a drag on earnings available to common shareholders. However, this drag should shrink as a percentage of earnings as the company scales, because the fixed preferred dividend becomes less meaningful relative to a growing earnings base.

Now here is what the market  Is missing. Celsius' margin structure is still immature

Monster provides some perspective, with roughly 56% gross margins and ~23% net margins in Q2 2026. CELH does not need to get anywhere close to that for our investment case.

CELH is currently running at around 48% gross margins, while management has repeatedly discussed a path back toward the low 50s. The margin bridge is fairly tangible: (1) integration benefits as Alani and Rockstar fully roll onto CELH’s purchasing, freight and inventory network, including the benefit from working through higher-cost legacy inventory; (2) structural supply-chain savings from the second North Carolina line, vertical integration, direct sourcing and broader network optimization; and (3) revenue growth management, including price-pack architecture, channel and mix optimization, and better returns on trade and promotional spend. Management has indicated that these initiatives should build through the back half of 2026, with a substantially larger opportunity in 2027 and 2028.

If gross margin moves from ~48% to 51–52%, that alone adds roughly ~2.5-3% percentage points to the bottom line after tax. Then there is operating leverage. In Q2, SG&A dollars were essentially flat yoy while revenue grew 11%, taking SG&A to 29% of revenue from 32%.

Put those together and I don’t think going from ~14% to a ~18–20% normalized net margin over the next three years is particularly aggressive. That still leaves CELH well below Monster-like economics. Let us use ~19% as the base case.

Now assume 10% annual revenue growth from a ~$3.2bn FY26 base. That gets you to roughly $4.26b of revenue by FY29. At a 19% net margin, Celsius would generate close to $810m of normalized consolidated net income, or roughly $690m attributable to common shareholders after allowing for the Pepsi preferred economics.

At 25x earnings, that would imply an equity value of roughly $17.25b, versus around $7.7b today, or approximately 125% upside. Even at 20x, the implied value would be around $13.8b, or roughly 80% upside.

Actually, with no margin expansion and a flat 14% net margin, the stock still offers roughly 64% upside by 2029 at a 25x multiple.

Now imagine Celsius grows above 10%, which seems entirely plausible, and on top of that commands a higher multiple. That is the magical setup.

Heads, I don’t lose much. Tails, I can double my money in the base case and potentially triple it if things get spicy

Weird how you never hear about any of this in the news...... TRUMP DOES THE UNTHINKABLE...
I've never heard anything negative about the man until he announced he was running for president.

• He's never even tried alcohol or tobacco. He doesn't do drugs. 

• His work ethic is beyond unparalleled as a hardworking businessman. 

• He's one of the most generous celebrities in the world with a heart filled with more gold than his $100 million New York penthouse.

Since the media has failed so miserably at reporting the truth about Trump, I decided to put together some of the acts of kindness he's committed over three decades which has gone virtually unnoticed or fallen on deaf ears. 

• In 1986, Trump prevented the foreclosure of Annabell Hill's family farm after her husband committed suicide. Trump personally phoned down to the auction to stop the sale of her home and offered the widow money. Trump decided to take action after he saw Hill's pleas for help in news reports. 

• In 1988, a commercial airline refused to fly Andrew Ten, a sick Orthodox Jewish child with a rare illness. The boy had to travel with an elaborate life-support system. Trump contacted the grief-stricken parents after hearing this and didn't hesitate to send his own plane to take the child from Los Angeles to New York so he could get his treatment. 

• In 1991, 200 Marines who served in Operation Desert Storm spent time at Camp Lejune in North Carolina before they were scheduled to return home to their families. However, the Marines were told that a mistake had been made and an aircraft would not be able to take them home on their scheduled departure date. When Trump got wind of this, he sent his plane to make two trips from North Carolina to Miami to safely return the Gulf War Marines to their loved ones. 

• In 1995, a motorist stopped to help Trump after the limo he was traveling in got a flat tire. Trump asked the Good Samaritan how he could repay him for his help. All the man asked for was a bouquet of flowers for his wife. A few weeks later Trump sent the flowers with a note that read: We've paid off your mortgage. 

• In 1996, Trump filed a lawsuit against the city of Palm Beach , Florida, accusing the town of discriminating against his Mar-a-Lago resort club because it allowed Jews and blacks. Abraham Foxman, who as the Anti-Defamation League Director at the time, said Trump put the light on Palm Beach not on the beauty and the glitter, but on its seamier side of discrimination. Foxman also noted that Trump's charge had a trickle-down effect because other clubs followed his lead and began admitting Jews and blacks. 

• In 2000, Maury Povich featured a little girl named Megan who struggled with Brittle Bone Disease on his show and Trump happened to be watching. Trump said the little girl's story and positive attitude touched his heart. So he contacted Maury and gifted the little girl and her family with a very generous check. 

• In 2008, after Jennifer Hudson's family members were tragically murdered in Chicago , Trump put the Oscar-winning actress and her family up at his Windy City hotel for free. In addition to that, Trump's security took extra measures to ensure Hudson and her family members were safe during such a difficult time. 

• In 2013, New York bus driver Darnell Barton spotted a woman close to the edge of a bridge staring at the traffic below as he drove by. He stopped the bus, got out and put his arm around the woman and saved her life by convincing her to not jump. When Trump heard about this story, he sent the hero bus driver a check simply because he believed his good deed deserved to be rewarded.

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Mint has announced that the “2026 President Donald J. Trump $1 Coin” is officially in circulation, giving Americans a historic new way to mark the exact location of a putt they’re about to miss.

Within minutes, golfers reportedly began hoarding the coins after learning they could purchase a ball marker for one dollar instead of paying $34.99 in the pro shop.

“It’s a beautiful coin. Incredible coin. Other ball markers are tiny. Weak. You put mine down, everybody knows you’re away,” Trump said in an entirely made-up statement.

The coin features Trump’s likeness on one side and, according to early clubhouse reports, an understanding that anything inside six feet is good.

“I marked my ball four feet from the hole,” said local golfer Bill Henderson. “When I came back, the coin was two feet away and my scorecard said birdie.”

Trump dismissed concerns about the coin’s tendency to move closer to the cup.

“It was a perfect placement. The original placement was very unfair. Everybody saw it.”

Early reviews suggest the marker performs exceptionally well on the right side of the green, although golfers using it on the left report being told they’re putting from the wrong tees.

One foursome experienced a 45-minute delay after the coin refused to recognize the results of a closest-to-the-pin contest.

“I was closer. Much closer. They measured his ball, then they stopped measuring. Very suspicious.”

The Mint’s fictional announcement warned golfers that the coin remains worth exactly one dollar, regardless of claims made at the beverage cart.

Trump disagreed.

“It’s worth at least twenty. Maybe fifty. A guy at the turn offered me a hot dog for it. That tells you everything.”

Meanwhile, Democratic Congressman Chip Spendwell welcomed the coin, saying he was collecting them to fund a $4 million study into whether miniature-golf windmills contribute to climate change.

“People think those blades turn themselves,” Spendwell said. “We need answers. And a fact-finding trip to a course in Hawaii.”

Trump immediately responded in another imaginary statement: “Four million to study miniature golf? I could study it for three million. And I’d get a free replay.”

At press time, a golfer who three-putted while using the coin had blamed the previous administration.

text:
EXCLUSIVE: US Mysteriously Waives Sanctions Against Iran’s Bloodthirsty State Broadcaster, Again, Even as Network Puts Bounties on Trump Family’s Heads | Adam Kredo, Washington Free Beacon

The State Department quietly waived mandatory sanctions on Iran's radical state broadcaster at two pivotal junctures this year, enabling the broadcaster to air the forced confessions of anti-regime protesters in January and, just this month, encourage and support assassination plots against President Donald Trump, his cabinet members, and his 20-year-old son Barron, according to nonpublic notifications transmitted to Congress and obtained by the Washington Free Beacon.

The Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) is the hardline regime's chief propaganda organ, responsible for blasting Tehran's virulent brand of radicalism to a domestic audience and supporters across the globe, including inside the United States. The IRIB has become instrumental to the regime's survival in the past year, since nationwide protests inside Iran threatened the mullahs' hold on power in the lead-up to the U.S.-led war. In recent weeks, the IRIB—which oversees a wide network of media including newspapers, websites, and social media channels—has been responsible for publishing a series of disturbing death threats against Trump, his wife Melania, and their son Barron. This includes an Aug. 23 video, since taken down, purporting to document both Melania and Barron's movements as part of an assassination scheme that the Secret Service says it is actively monitoring.

But during this time, the State Department waived longstanding sanctions on the IRIB, permitting it to freely operate and access satellite services that are pivotal to its existence, the Free Beacon has learned. Crippling financial sanctions and taking steps to block the IRIB's technical operations would make it hard for the regime mouthpiece to broadcast outside Iran, and would undermine its internal broadcasting and publishing operations as well.

In 1999 and 2003, the United States and its allies bombed state television in Belgrade and Baghdad, effectively shutting down state media for a time. The United States is not believed to have targeted Iranian state broadcasting in its current campaign.

The White House and State Department would not comment on the reasons for the waivers. Sources familiar with the situation suggested the waivers may be a naive effort—dating back to the Obama administration—to coax Iran towards a lasting agreement. The U.S. intelligence services, which rely heavily on the Israelis for intelligence about Iran, may also appreciate the ability to gauge the regime's thinking by following state media.

The most recent iteration of the IRIB waiver was signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio on July 2 and transmitted privately to Congress a week later, according to a copy of the notification reviewed by the Free Beacon. An almost identical version was approved by Rubio on January 6 and transmitted to Congress shortly thereafter. Both documents maintain that it is "vital to the national security of the United States" to waive sanctions on the IRIB and allow it to conduct financial transactions for the provision of "ground connectivity" and telecommunications services. Without these waivers, the IRIB's capabilities would be crippled by sanctions.

The July waiver was approved just over two months before the Trump administration unveiled Operation Economic Outcast, a vast and multi-pronged campaign to crush Iran's financial networks through sanctions on the regime and its international enablers. That effort, however, could be undermined by an active IRIB waiver that continues to relieve pressure on one of the regime’s most powerful state organs.

While versions of the IRIB waivers issued throughout this year have been approved multiple times since 2013 across successive U.S. administrations, both Republican and Democrat, the timing of the two most recent iterations is fuelling calls for the Trump administration to carefully reassess whether the policy actually remains "vital to U.S. national security interests"—particularly at a time when the IRIB is airing credible death threats against the president and his family.

"This is basically an autopilot waiver unless someone intervenes," a former U.S. official with knowledge of IRIB sanctions told the Free Beacon, speaking only on background about the sensitive matter. "Once upon a time, someone told someone this was important to keep going. Has anyone asked whether that's still true today?"

The IRIB controls radio, television, and news outlets across Iran and is the chief distributor of the regime's radical anti-America, antisemitic, and pro-terror agitprop. The waiver essentially allows the IRIB to engage in financial transactions that, by and large, would otherwise be prohibited by America's heavy sanctions regime, which specifically include the state broadcaster.

The waivers excuse the broadcaster from an array of American sanctions it's been subjected to since 2013. These include mandatory congressional sanctions and executive orders linked to the IRIB's role as a regime propaganda outlet. Congress determined that the IRIB had contributed to human-rights abuses by broadcasting forced confessions and sham trials, and in 2013, the Treasury Department sanctioned the IRIB under an executive order, finding that it restricted the free flow of information, censored media, and jammed foreign broadcasts.

Sanctions waivers for the IRIB have long been controversial. They stem from a secret 2013 deal between the Obama administration and the Iranian regime, which the Free Beacon reported on when it became public. The first Trump administration also came under scrutiny from its GOP allies, as well as Iranian dissidents, for approving the IRIB waiver in 2018, when Iranian protesters were again being violently suppressed by the regime. The Biden administration, too, landed in hot water for bypassing sanctions on the IRIB in 2024, at a time when Tehran's press was celebrating Hamas's Oct. 7 terror spree.

Still, the most recent approval of this policy by the State Department remains somewhat of a mystery amid the military conflict with Iran. The IRIB and its radical networks have helped sustain the hardline regime's morale throughout the war, and they continue to foment terror across the globe. Earlier this year, at the height of Iran's anti-regime protest movement, the IRIB televised nearly 100 coerced confessions from dissidents who were often tortured beforehand.

Both the White House and State Department have repeatedly expressed concerns over the IRIB's death threats against Trump's family and his senior officials, and vowed harsh reprisals for any assassination attempts. In March, the Justice Department successfully convicted an Iranian operative who traveled to the United States as part of a murder-for-hire plot against Trump.

The State Department would not provide a response to multiple Free Beacon inquiries about the IRIB waiver, the reason for granting it, or what will happen next time it comes up for renewal in the coming months. The White House also did not respond to similar questions, with both declining to provide a policy rationale for approving the waiver in both January and July. It is possible, however, that the July version was issued as a potential olive branch to Tehran as the Trump administration was working to enact a ceasefire that is now in tatters.

The IRIB's now-viral Aug. 23 video publicized locations associated with Barron Trump and offered a $10 million bounty on his head. The Secret Service confirmed earlier in the week that it is aware of the threat. Barron is no longer physically attending classes on New York University's Greenwich Village campus and is believed to be pursuing his undergraduate studies in Washington, under greater security.

"The U.S. Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees," Secret Service spokesman Nate Herring said in a statement. "Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence."

Other recent IRIB videos, including several published in the wake of the late Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei's death, purported to document Trump's own movements and urged jihadist sympathizers outside Iran to exact retribution for Khamenei's killing.

Given the expanding—and credible—threats posed by the IRIB's radical networks, regional observers are recommending the Trump administration finally penalize the state broadcaster for attempting to recruit and reward would-be assassins.

"The U.S. should rescind the sanctions waiver that allows satellite broadcast service for IRIB. IRIB is not just a state news network. It is an arm of Iran's security and intelligence services, which weaponize IRIB against the Iranian people and the U.S. and its allies," said Jason Brodsky, policy director at the advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran. "The broadcasting of bounty videos calling for the killings of President Trump and his family counts as incitement."

Tehran, Brodsky added, "may be trying to recruit radicalized individuals who have access to the United States to carry out these kinds of terror plots. The Iranian regime followed this playbook in 2022 when the author Salman Rushdie was almost stabbed to death in New York by an individual motivated by Islamic Republic fatwas and bounties."

text:
MARKET UPDATE — WEDNESDAY, 2 SEPTEMBER 2026

Oil is now writing the world's monetary policy.

A second wave of US strikes on Iran in three days pushed Brent to $97 a barrel and European gas to a three-year high. Government borrowing costs hit multi-decade peaks from Tokyo to London to Washington. Then, almost unnoticed, America's jobs engine coughed — leaving central banks trapped between prices that won't fall and a workforce that's weakening.

🟢 The one chain that explains everything today

🔸 War in the Gulf → oil and gas up → inflation up → bond yields up → rate-hike bets up → shares down.

💡 In plain English: when energy costs more, everything that is made, grown or moved costs more. Central banks fight rising prices by raising interest rates. Higher rates make borrowing dearer for governments, companies and households — and make shares look less attractive next to safe bonds paying nearly 5%.

Every story below is a link in that chain.

🟢 The bond market is the story

🔸 The US 10-year Treasury yield touched 4.8182% — its highest since November 2023. 

🔸 The 30-year sat near 5.28%, close to its highest since 2007. 

🔸 Japan's 10-year hit 3.01% — a level not seen in roughly three decades. Its 30-year is the highest since 1996. 

🔸 Germany's 10-year rose to 3.39%, the highest since 2011. UK gilts hit a post-2008 high for a second day. France's 10-year is at 4.26%, with its gap over Germany near the widest since Mario Draghi saved the euro in 2012.

💡 What a "yield" is: the interest a government pays to borrow. When investors get nervous about inflation or debt, they demand more interest — so yields rise and the price of existing bonds falls. This is happening everywhere at once, which is what makes it serious.

🔸 Why it matters: 
Evercore's Julian Emanuel notes that since the bull market began in October 2022, a 10-year yield at or above 4.75% has been "noxious to stocks." We are above it.

🔸 The counter-argument: 
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent insists high yields signal strength, not distress — "The world is awash in debt… the only way out is to grow our way out." He blames a temporary energy shock plus a boom in AI investment, and expects AI productivity gains to prove "extremely disinflationary" later. He also admitted a plan to cut the deficit is "weeks or even months away." Markets are voting the other way.

🟢 The Fed is being cornered

🔸 Traders now price a ~70% chance the Fed raises rates on 16 September — up from around 37–40% a week ago. (Estimates across desks ranged 66–70% through the session.) 

🔸 A majority now expect another hike after that before year-end. 

🔸 Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has said the Fed will "have work to do" if inflation doesn't fall. 
Governor Michael Barr echoed it: if inflation doesn't cool quickly, it's time to raise.

💡 Why this is unusual: 
for two years the debate was how fast the Fed would cut. It is now about how hard it must hike — a complete reversal, driven almost entirely by energy.

🔸 Then came the twist. August's ADP private payrolls came in at just 38,000 jobs, below the 47,000 expected and July's 44,000. The official July report showed the economy actually lost 23,000 jobs.

💡 The trap: the Fed may have to raise rates into a slowing jobs market — tightening the screws on an economy already tiring. That is the textbook definition of a policy squeeze, and it is why Friday's official jobs report (8:30am ET) matters more than usual.

🔸 The calendar that will decide September: 
jobs report Friday → CPI inflation 11 September → Fed decision 16 September → Bank of Japan 18 September. The ECB is expected to hike next week.

🟢 Energy: the engine of the whole problem

🔸 Brent spiked to $97.04 and WTI to $92.29 — five-week highs — before fading back to roughly $94–95 and $89–90 as the session wore on. That round trip tells you how twitchy this market is. 

🔸 European gas (Dutch TTF) broke €75/MWh for the first time since early 2023 — up about 25% this month. 

🔸 EU gas storage is only 63% full heading into winter, the lowest in over a decade. Germany has warned it may miss its 70% legal target.

💡 Why gas matters as much as oil: 
Europe heats homes and generates power with it. Eurozone inflation already accelerated to 3.3% in August, with energy prices up 14.3%. That is why European bonds are being hit hardest.

🔸 The real-world bite: 
Ryanair — Europe's largest airline and among its best-hedged, with 80% of fuel locked in — is cutting winter capacity to limit exposure to jet fuel near $140 a barrel, saving €70–100m. It warned that weaker rivals may not survive, meaning "a material increase in short-haul airfares across Europe" next year. 

🔸 Veteran commodities analyst Jeff Currie made the key point: "Nobody on the planet consumes crude oil except refineries." The pain is in diesel, petrol and jet fuel — and those markets look far worse than crude. 

🔸 US petrol has stayed above $4 a gallon, up nearly 30% year-on-year. Diesel is closing on its record $5.80. The diesel "crack spread" — refiners' profit per barrel — has hit $100. 

🔸 Brown University estimates Americans have paid $51.9bn extra for petrol and $43.1bn extra for diesel since the war began — about $725 per household.

🔸 Politics enters: with midterms under three months away and voters telling pollsters they're worse off, Trump summoned Marathon, Phillips 66, Chevron, Valero, PBF and Delek to the White House. The problem: US refineries have run at 95%+ utilisation for 12 straight weeks — the longest streak since 2000. There is no spare capacity to squeeze. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve is down to 286m barrels against roughly 730m capacity.

💡 Translation: the White House has run out of levers. The only real fix is ending the war.

🟢 Geopolitics: no off-ramp visible

🔸 US strikes on Iranian air-defence, radar, minelaying and communications sites killed 18 people, including four at a wedding in Kuhestak. Iran retaliated against US bases in Jordan, plus targets in Bahrain and Kuwait. 

🔸 Trump: he "couldn't care less" if Iran returns to talks, and Iran "will be hit again at a much harder and higher level." Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei promised "unforgettable lessons."

🔸 Hormuz is choking. Only four commodity vessels transited on Tuesday, against a 10-day average of about 13. The IRGC says two oil tankers struck sea mines and were disabled. Two Filipino crew were killed aboard a Saudi Bahri vessel. 

🔸 Energy Secretary Chris Wright claimed 17m barrels crossed Hormuz on Monday, near the pre-war 20m. Goldman Sachs says that figure is "heavily debated" — and the shipping data does not support it.

🔸 Why this won't resolve quickly: 
RBC BlueBay's Mike Bell — "The perception that this is all going to be over by Christmas is fading fast." Goldman's Rich Privorotsky notes that previous oil spikes were met with diplomacy; this time the US escalated while oil was rising and during market hours. No one is trying to cool prices. 

🔸 Iran isn't isolated: 
China, Russia and India backed it at this week's Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit. And an FT investigation revealed Russia has been secretly helping Iran build supersonic ramjet cruise missiles (programme "C430L") capable of threatening US warships — a strategic technology transfer, not just spare parts.

🟢 Shares: resilient, but the floor is being tested

🔸 US futures were roughly flat-to-firmer after the ADP miss — S&P 500 futures ~7,650 (+0.1%), Dow futures ~52,964 (+0.3%), Nasdaq futures ~29,107 (−0.1%) — after the S&P fell more than 1% already this week. 

🔸 Overseas was uglier: Nikkei −3%, Kospi −3.8%, STOXX 600 −0.3%. Japan and South Korea import nearly all their oil. 

🔸 The level to watch: BTIG's Jonathan Krinsky says 7,600 is the S&P's key support, and his base case is that it fails, taking the index back to 7,200–7,300 — roughly 7–8% below the record high.

💡 Support level: a price where buyers have stepped in before. Break it, and sellers often gain the upper hand.

🔸 The bull case is earnings. With 97% of the S&P reported, companies are pacing for 52% profit growth, more than double the 23.1% expected in June (a striking figure, single-sourced to FactSet via Barron's — treat with care). But earnings season is over. As Barron's puts it: great profits are now old news, and September is a macro month.

🔸 How to hedge it: 
Evercore screened for "negative beta" stocks — shares that rise when the index falls — and found 115, the most since the dot-com bust. The list skews to energy, utilities, staples and insurers (insurers earn more on their bond portfolios as yields rise): CF Industries, APA, LyondellBasell, Occidental, ConocoPhillips. Energy trader John Arnold's crude 50% tech / 50% energy portfolio is up 37% year-to-date — a barbell that owns both the AI boom and the war.

🟢 Company movers

🔸 GitLab +20% premarket — earnings and guidance beat on AI-linked demand. 

🔸 Dell +8–9% — big beat, exiting the quarter with a $95bn AI-server backlog. That single number is the clearest evidence yet that AI capital spending is still accelerating. 

🔸 MongoDB −14% despite strong earnings — disappointment over its multi-cloud database growth. 

🔸 Credo −9% and Palo Alto −2% despite beats. (Palo Alto is still up 97% in 2026.) When good results get sold, positioning is stretched. 

🔸 Chevron committed $7bn to Venezuelan heavy oil, doubling output there to 600,000 bpd over five years — a Trump administration win and a quiet, long-term answer to Gulf supply risk. 

🔸 Shein fell a second day post-IPO to about HK$46–47. Swissquote's Ipek Ozkardeskaya: its customers are so price-sensitive that "even a small increase in prices could lead to a significant drop in sales volumes." A tariff-and-inflation casualty in real time. 

🔸 After the bell: Broadcom — consensus $29.2bn revenue. Alongside HPE and Snowflake, it is tonight's read on whether the AI trade still has legs.

🟢 Currencies, gold and crypto

🔸 The dollar index rose to ~99.75–99.87, a two-week high. Higher oil helps the dollar because America produces its own energy; Europe and Japan must buy it. 

🔸 The yen firmed to ~159.6–159.9 after BoJ Governor Ueda said consecutive rate hikes are possible. Markets price a high chance of a move to 1.25% on 18 September. 

🔸 The New Zealand dollar fell 1% even though the RBNZ raised rates — because it warned of mounting risks to growth. A reminder that hikes born of fear don't support a currency. 

🔸 Schroders expects the euro at $1.10 by year-end, on the view the ECB is nearly done hiking while the Fed is only starting. 

🔸 Gold fell 0.6% to ~$4,302 — a three-week low. Silver −1% to $63.59.

💡 Why gold fell on a war day: 
gold pays no interest. When bonds offer nearly 5% and the dollar strengthens, holding gold costs you more. Geopolitics alone isn't enough.

🔸 Bitcoin −0.6% to ~$76,950; ether −1% to ~$2,395. Crypto is trading as a high-risk tech asset, not as digital gold. Rising real yields drain liquidity from the assets furthest out on the risk curve — and that is exactly where crypto sits.

🟢 The grown-ups aren't in the room

The G-20 finance ministers' meeting in Asheville ended without a consensus statement — China wouldn't sign. Instead: a row over inviting Russia's finance minister to the group photo, US ministers mocking Canada's military, and a renamed Great Lake.

💡 Why a trader should care: the last time global bond markets strained this badly, coordinated policy calmed them. This week's summit showed that coordination isn't available. Markets are being asked to price a debt-and-energy shock with no adult supervision. That is a genuine risk premium, and it is showing up in yields.

🟢 What It Means

🔸 September is a macro month, not an earnings month. Every large move from here is tied to a date: Friday's jobs report, CPI on the 11th, the Fed on the 16th, the BoJ on the 18th. 

🔸 Oil is the master variable. Goldman's Privorotsky: 
"Oil sits at the centre of everything. If energy keeps rising, the Fed reaction function gets dragged with it and sustained upside becomes much harder."

🔸 The risk is two-sided and violent. Saxo's Ole Hansen calls it "binary" — a credible peace signal could send oil tumbling $5 in a session; further escalation could push Brent beyond $100 (Capital Economics). 

🔸 Watch 4.75–4.85% on the 10-year and 7,600 on the S&P. Those are the two lines that decide whether this is a wobble or a correction. 

🔸 The bull market isn't over — it's on hold. AI capital spending is still real (Dell's $95bn backlog says so). Corporate profits are exceptional. What's changed is the price of money. When bonds pay 5% risk-free, equities must work harder to justify themselves.

💭 Thought for the Day

"A smooth sea never made a skilled sailor." — Franklin D. Roosevelt

Every generation of investors is handed one market that teaches it more than a decade of calm ever could. Panics are loud; patience is quiet — and it is patience that compounds. The chart that frightens you today becomes the entry point you wish you'd taken. Read carefully, size sensibly, and let the storm do the work of separating you from the crowd.

Sources: MarketWatch, The Wall Street Journal, Financial Times, Barron's, Reuters, Al Jazeera, TradingView, CME FedWatch, FactSet, EIA, Kpler.

USS Abraham Lincoln arrives in Thailand after 286 days at sea
——
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier arrived at a port in eastern Thailand on Wednesday, following deployment in West Asia that kept the vessel at sea for more than 250 days.

Associated Press journalists observed the Lincoln, which carries around 5,000 service members, entering Laem Chabang port in Chonburi province shortly after the USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. destroyer passed through the area.

The extended deployment has raised concerns after reports of worsening mental health among crew members and shortages of supplies, including food and hygiene items.

The crew was not immediately available to reporters. The carrier's hull appeared to require maintenance, with prominent patches of what looked like rust visible, particularly near the waterline and along the edge of the flight deck where fighter jets and helicopters were stationed.

Asked about the ship's condition, Lincoln commanding officer Capt. Dan Keeler said that “it is normal for a long deployment and we’re not going to make further comments.”

Keeler also offered a brief response when asked about US President Donald Trump's description of the record-setting deployment as “not nearly long enough.”

“So, the president speaks for himself,” he said. “That is what I think about that.”

“Abraham Lincoln’s visit to Laem Chabang is a clear demonstration of our enduring commitment to our allies and partners in Thailand, and we are all very excited to make Thailand the first port visit on our historic deployment,” Keeler said previously in a prepared statement.

The USS George Washington, which is normally based in Asia, replaced the Lincoln in West Asia in August.

text:
I debated whether or not to post this picture because I never want something like this to be about me. But the more I thought about it, the more I realized that if posting it puts a few more eyeballs on Cases For A Cause and the incredible work they’re doing, then it’s absolutely worth sharing.

A few weeks ago, I was fortunate enough to receive the Servant’s Heart Award at the CIADA Convention. I was humbled just to be nominated, much less selected, but what made the award especially meaningful was the opportunity that came with it: $10,000 to donate to the charity of my choice. I didn’t have to think very long about where I wanted that money to go. I chose Cases For A Cause.

If you aren’t familiar with them, you should be. Cases For A Cause works with children in foster care and was built around a simple idea that hit me right in the heart: no child should have to carry their belongings from place to place in a trash bag. Through their Carry The Cause program, they provide children with personalized, full-size suitcases filled to help meet their needs and give them something that belongs to THEM. Their work has grown to include meeting other needs for children in foster care, creating special experiences and memories, providing shoes, and working with families, social workers and community leaders to fill gaps where help is needed. 

This past Sunday in Salisbury, I finally got the chance to see my friend Alex Hiatt and officially present Cases For A Cause with the BIG check. Alex and the people surrounding this organization are doing the kind of work that doesn’t always make headlines, but absolutely changes lives. They’re helping kids during some of the most uncertain and vulnerable moments they will ever experience and reminding them that they matter.

I’m incredibly thankful to Greenville Auto Auction for sponsoring the Servant’s Heart Award and for making the $10,000 charitable gift possible. I’m thankful to everyone who voted for me and believed I was worthy of receiving it. But most of all, I’m thankful for people like Alex and organizations like Cases For A Cause that roll up their sleeves every single day and do the work in our communities.

Awards are nice but being able to take something I was blessed to receive and turn it into an opportunity to help somebody else is the part that matters.

Thank you, Alex, for what you do. Thank you to everyone involved with Cases For A Cause. And thank you for reminding all of us that you don’t have to change the entire world at once. Sometimes you start by changing the world for one child, one family and one suitcase at a time. ❤️

Oh…and good morning! ☀️

text:
The AM Brief, Wednesday August 19, 2026 Part 3

Good Morning,

It’s noon in Miami and here is a recap of events that caught my eye. Part 3

     Redfin reports that U.S. homebuyer demand fell to a record low 966,752 active participants in July 2026, a 2.5% decline from June. With 1,462,921 homes for sale, sellers now outnumber buyers by 51.3% nationally. Miami faces the country's widest imbalance, with a 154% surplus of sellers (18,437 sellers vs. 7,258 buyers). Persistently high mortgage rates, hovering in the mid to high 6% range, continue to suppress affordability and buyer activity. While the seller surplus provides significant negotiating leverage for those still in the market, Redfin clarifies that this "buyer’s market" does not equate to affordability, as elevated financing costs keep many potential purchasers sidelined.

     U.S. home prices remained essentially stagnant in July, rising only 0.27% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. Market stability is being propped up by affluent purchasers, including high income professionals, who are driving demand for higher end properties and preventing a broader price correction. Despite flat monthly performance, prices climbed 3.4% year over year, marking the fastest annual pace in 12 months. While national prices are resilient, some regions, specifically parts of the East Coast, Midwest, and Texas have experienced localized price dips. While wealthy buyers support overall stability, the "luxury threshold" (90th percentile) actually declined 2.7% annually as of July, suggesting price softening at the very top end of the market. Inventory levels are rising, but the volume of active listings remains insufficient to force significant downward pressure on national home values.

    Miami’s cost of living now surpasses New York City’s, driven by housing costs roughly 5% higher and average annual home insurance premiums of $8,292, four times the New York average. Despite this, developers and high net worth individuals continue to favor Florida. The primary incentive is the absence of state income tax, which contrasts sharply with New York’s aggressive tax environment, where combined federal, state, and city effective top marginal rates can reach between 50% and 55%. While Florida offers significant annual tax savings, the "sticker shock" of mandatory insurance and housing expenses is increasingly forcing middle income residents to relocate or seek rentals.

Sources : The Capitalist (8-18), Forbes Daily (8-19)

Thank you for reading
Live your best life,
AL Maulini

text:
It’s a good question, and I can give you my honest take fwiw. Might be long but off the cuff here. 
First, start with the macro. The 10yr is pushing 4.8% near multi year highs. That matters when you’re asking the market to capitalize cash flows years into the future. This drives higher discount rates in many acquisitions models to pull down terminal cash flow.  
High beta names get hit the hardest, and even more so those that are trying ti break towards EBITDA and FCF+. And when short is 40%+ best believe you’re gonna get smoked in this “wind” 😉.
For $ONDS specifically, to put broad not until tide changes when fundamentals overpower the capital structure. And by structure I am talking largely the warrants and corresponding hedged. They have the stock by the balls, and despite all the things you mentioned.. YoY, raised guidance, etc., the structure has not shown any real cracks. 
On the dilution, yes and catalyst is proof that the capital raised is creating more value than the dilution destroyed. We as bulls know this is happening and it seems like it is going to take for it to be so overly obvious in reported numbers for the market to catch on. But also, the number of shares out has grown substantially. I agree in things to generally accretive but that takes time.  It takes time for the market to absorb this shit. It played perfectly into the hedge. They get all this volatility and create a very very lucrative market to run their arb. Do you notice any trends in Fridays? Yeah that’s “them”. 
We can be frustrated at them or the deals made, but for $1.5B they are going to  return well above that. Guy walks into a bar offers you 1.5billy… oh you need growth capital? 
Now I am of the opinion a major program of record (Ultra?) or 9+ fig contacts would blow “them” up. In time the fundamentals will be too overpowering. When who knows. I would have thought by now, my naive ass. Eric and business are doing the right things. Also doesn’t help govts are moving so damn slow it’s embarrassing. 
Anyway to simplify, you need the warrant related short hedge to unwind, dilution fears to fade, backlog to convert into revenue, margins/EBITDA to inflect, and eventually a friendlier macro backdrop and the stock will be much much higher. The setup can change fast. 
I took “notes” of the CEOs public addressing of the shorts, and just waiting for that to materialize.
