text:
Just stop dude. Tell me you're not familiar with the San Marcos area without saying you're not familiar with it. 

The only thing we don't have that you listed is mountains, but we have beautiful rolling hills instead. 

We also have a crystal clear, spring fed river (San Marcos) flowing through campus that contains endangered plants and animals found nowhere else in the world. Never mind all the other nearby recreational rivers (there are multiple: Comal, Guadalupe, Blanco) as well as canyon lake.. etc. 

Texas State literally owns it's own large ranch on the Blanco River that students and alumni can camp at. This on top of the other nearby state parks that offer hiking, camping, fishing opportunities.

As for hunting, it’s right on the edge of the Hill Country which has the largest and highest concentrated white-tailed deer population of any single region in Texas, and one of the densest populations of white-tail in the nation (if not the densest).

We also have vibrant nightlife, infamous party scenes, excellent food, world famous outlet malls. 

All that and more, yet still conveniently located near Austin and San Antonio.

The Coast of the Gods (Costa degli Dei) 

is a stunning 55-kilometer (34-mile) stretch of coastline in the Calabria region of southern Italy, running along the Tyrrhenian Sea in the Province of Vibo Valentia.

Top Destinations

Tropea: A historic town perched on a high cliff overlooking the sea, famous for its dramatic views, sweet red onions, and the iconic Santuario di Santa Maria dell'Isola church on a rock in the sea.

Capo Vaticano: A promontory known for rugged cliffs, hidden coves, and some of the clearest turquoise waters in Italy, particularly around Spiaggia di Grotticelle.

Pizzo: A charming coastal town famous for its historic Aragonese Castle and tartufo, a delicious local chocolate and hazelnut ice cream specialty.Smaller Villages: Scenic spots like Briatico, Zambrone, Parghelia, and Ricadi offer quieter beaches and local charm.

From a military-technical standpoint, strikes on radar and air-defense assets are meant to blind the enemy. Iran’s radar network around Hormuz relies mainly on Soviet- and Chinese-made systems, along with domestic Iranian designs

But we have seen this playbook before, early in the war in March, when the U.S. opened its campaign by suppressing Iranian air defenses. SEAD operations are meant to neutralize, destroy, or temporarily degrade ground-based air defenses, including radar systems.  Iran adapted to repeated attacks by leaning more heavily on mobile systems

The main issue with this article is that it offers no clear sense of what the U.S. is actually trying to accomplish. Knocking down air defenses is not a quick job, and it will not by itself weaken Iran’s ability to control the Strait of Hormuz

Anti-ship missiles are a different story. Iran uses mobile coastal launchers for Noor, Qader, and Khalij Fars missiles, with ranges reaching roughly 300 km in some variants.  Those systems have been targeted before, but Iran has repeatedly moved and replaced assets to preserve its coastal-strike capability

So all the noise around new U.S. strikes may produce limited tactical and PR gains. Strategically, though, the White House risks getting pulled into the same long, costly campaign, where Iran still has more ways to apply pressure

text:
He Split Himself In Half To Survive — And Walked Away Wearing His Old Body Like A Costume

Imagine, for a moment, that the only way to grow was to first crack your own skeleton down the middle, squeeze your entire body backward out through a gap barely wider than a coin slot, and leave your old face, your old eyes, even the lining of your own stomach behind as an empty, perfectly intact shell of yourself.

That's not science fiction. That's Tuesday for a blue crab.

This timelapse captures exactly that process from start to finish — a blue crab (Callinectes sapidus, if you want the full name) splitting its shell along a hidden seam and backing its entire soft, vulnerable body out of an exoskeleton it has completely outgrown. It's one of the strangest, most quietly alien processes in the natural world, and it happens more often, more violently, and more precariously than almost anyone realizes until they actually watch it happen in real time.

Why A Crab Has To Do This At All

Here's the fundamental problem every crustacean is born with: their skeleton is on the outside. Unlike humans, whose bones grow continuously alongside the rest of the body, a crab's shell — the exoskeleton — is a rigid, largely non-expandable structure made primarily of chitin, a tough, fibrous material reinforced with calcium carbonate for extra hardness. Once that shell hardens fully, it simply cannot get bigger. It's fixed. Finished. Done growing, permanently, the moment it cures.

Which creates an obvious problem for an animal that needs to keep growing throughout its life. The only solution evolution ever landed on for this exact predicament is the one on display in this footage: periodically abandon the entire shell, all at once, and grow a new, larger one to replace it. This process — called ecdysis, or more commonly molting — isn't a minor skin-shedding event like a snake sloughing off dead surface tissue. It's a complete architectural replacement. Every hard surface on a crab's body gets rebuilt from scratch, repeatedly, for the animal's entire life.

Blue crabs molt roughly 20 to 25 times over the course of their lifespan, with molts happening more frequently during the rapid growth of juvenile stages and spacing out considerably as the crab matures into adulthood. Each molt typically allows for roughly a 25 to 40 percent increase in size in a single event — meaning a blue crab doesn't grow gradually the way most animals do. It grows in sudden, dramatic jumps, each one requiring it to survive one of the most physically dangerous windows of its entire life.

The Hidden Prep Work Nobody Sees Before The Camera Starts Rolling

By the time this footage begins, with the shell already visibly splitting along the rear edge, the crab has actually been preparing for this exact moment for days, sometimes weeks, entirely out of sight.

The process starts internally, with a surge of molting hormones — primarily ecdysteroids — that trigger the crab's body to begin separating from the inside of its own old shell, a stage called apolysis. Beneath the existing hard shell, the crab's epidermis starts secreting an entirely new, soft cuticle layer underneath the old one, essentially growing a second skeleton inside the first before ever breaking free of it. At the same time, the crab begins reabsorbing calcium salts from its old shell back into its body, partially recycling the mineral content it will need to harden the new shell later, rather than wastefully losing all of it.

Just before the actual molt, the crab typically stops eating, seeks shelter to reduce predation risk during its most vulnerable hours, and begins absorbing water, which it uses hydraulically — swelling its body slightly to help physically crack and separate the old shell from within. Everything visible in this footage, from the initial hairline split at the back of the carapace to the final, dramatic extraction, is really just the last few minutes of a process the crab's body has been quietly engineering for a considerable stretch of time beforehand.

The Split: Why It Happens Exactly Where It Does

Watch closely, and the shell doesn't crack randomly or shatter the way you might expect a rigid structure to fail under pressure. It splits cleanly along a specific, predetermined seam at the rear margin of the carapace, where the top shell meets the abdomen — a structurally weaker suture line that's biologically built into the shell specifically to serve as the exit point during molting.

This is one of the more elegant pieces of engineering in the entire process. A shell strong enough to protect a crab from predators for its entire premolt life also needs a built-in failure point precise enough to let the animal escape it cleanly when the time comes, without shattering catastrophically in a way that could injure the soft, freshly formed crab hiding just underneath. That rear seam — sometimes informally called the "molting suture" — is thinner and less calcified than the rest of the shell specifically so that internal pressure and muscular contraction can reliably pop it open at exactly the right location, every single time, across essentially every molt the crab will ever go through in its life.

The Extraction: An Anatomical Magic Trick

Once that initial gap opens, the process shown in the middle portion of this footage becomes almost impossible to fully believe: the crab backs its entire body — legs, claws, eyestalks, even the lining of its foregut and hindgut — out through that single narrow opening at the rear of the old shell.

Every leg has to be extracted joint by joint from a rigid tube of old shell material that's now completely separated from the living tissue inside it, without breaking or getting stuck partway through — a task make dramatically easier by the fact that the new cuticle underneath is still completely soft, foldable, almost gelatin-like in consistency at this stage, letting limbs bend and compress in ways that would be structurally impossible once the new shell fully hardens. That momentary flexibility is the entire reason extraction is even possible in the first place; a fully hardened crab could never fold its legs tightly enough to pull them backward through the same exit point they just occupied in rigid form.

Even stranger: crabs and other crustaceans shed the lining of parts of their own digestive tract during this process, along with the covering of their eyes and the linings of their gill chambers, since chitin lines considerably more of a crustacean's internal structure than most people realize. What's left behind afterward — the object popularly called a "crab molt" or sometimes mistaken by beachgoers for a dead crab — is a complete, hollow, perfectly detailed replica of the crab's entire former exterior, right down to individual leg joints and even the fine hairs on its claws. It's not a dead crab. It's an empty structural echo of one, discarded whole.

The Blue Reveal: Why This Species In Particular Puts On Such A Show

Part of what makes this specific footage so visually striking is the species involved. Blue crabs are named for a genuine reason visible directly in this clip: the undersides of their claws and legs carry a vivid, almost electric blue coloration, produced by a combination of pigments in the shell that becomes especially vivid and saturated in a freshly molted crab, before oxidation and environmental exposure gradually mute it over the following days.

That blue coloration, dulled and hidden beneath the olive-brown outer shell for the crab's entire premolt period, becomes strikingly visible during exactly this kind of extraction footage — the newly emerging body, still soft and translucent, showing off color that was essentially invisible just minutes earlier. It's a big part of why blue crab molting footage circulates so widely compared to footage of visually duller crab and crustacean species going through the exact same biological process; the reveal itself carries genuine visual drama that, say, a plain brown shore crab molting simply doesn't offer to the same degree.

The Danger Window: Why This Is The Single Most Vulnerable Moment Of A Crab's Life

It's tempting to watch this footage purely as a neat biological curiosity, but for the crab itself, this exact process represents an enormous, potentially fatal gamble every single time it happens.

Immediately after molting, a crab is in what's commonly called the "soft-shell" stage — its new cuticle is present but completely uncalcified, meaning it offers essentially zero physical protection against predators, and the crab itself is largely unable to defend itself effectively, move quickly, or use its claws with any real force until the new shell begins hardening. This soft period typically lasts anywhere from several hours to a few days depending on water temperature, crab size, and species, during which a normally well-armored, formidable predator becomes one of the easiest, most defenseless meals available in its entire ecosystem.

This vulnerability is so well understood commercially that it's spawned an entire segment of the seafood industry: soft-shell crabs, prized on menus specifically because they're harvested during this exact narrow post-molt window, when the entire animal — shell included — is edible without the usual need to crack and pick meat out of a hardened carapace. Watermen who farm blue crabs specifically monitor for the telltale signs of an imminent molt — visible in premolt crabs by a reddish line appearing along the edge of the rearmost swimming legs — and move crabs into holding tanks precisely so they can harvest them the moment they emerge soft, before the shell has any chance to begin hardening again.

In the wild, without that kind of protective holding tank, a freshly molted crab has to rely almost entirely on hiding — burrowing into sand or mud, wedging into structure, or simply staying motionless somewhere sheltered — until enough calcium carbonate has been redeposited into the new shell to restore some baseline structural defense. It's a race against time that plays out, quietly and largely unwitnessed, in estuaries and coastal waters constantly, every single time a crab this size needs to grow.

From Split To Hardened Shell: What Happens After The Camera Stops Rolling

The footage in this clip captures maybe the most dramatic ten or fifteen minutes of a process that, from start to finish, actually unfolds over a considerably longer timeline. Once fully extracted from the old shell, the newly emerged crab will typically absorb additional water over the following hours, physically expanding its new, still-soft cuticle to a noticeably larger size than the old shell it just discarded — this is the actual growth step, happening in the hours immediately after extraction rather than during the extraction itself.

From there, the hardening process — called sclerotization — begins in earnest, driven by the redeposition of calcium salts (many of them recycled from the old shell before it was shed) combined with a chemical hardening of the chitin matrix itself. Depending on water temperature and the crab's size, full hardening back to a defensible, rigid shell typically takes anywhere from several days to roughly two weeks, during which the crab remains cautious, generally less active, and considerably more reliant on hiding than hunting.

And then, eventually, weeks or months later depending on the crab's age and the local water temperature governing its metabolism, the entire process starts again — another hormonal surge, another soft new shell secreted beneath the current hardened one, another split along that same rear seam, another complete backward extraction of an entire body through an opening that, every single time, looks like it shouldn't physically be possible.

Why Footage Like This Is Genuinely Rare To Capture Well

Despite molting being a routine, constant event happening to blue crab populations throughout their range essentially every day of the warmer months, well-lit, close, steady footage of the actual extraction process is considerably harder to capture than the sheer frequency of the event might suggest. Crabs typically seek out sheltered, hidden locations specifically to molt in relative safety, meaning most molts in the wild happen out of sight, in structure, under debris, or buried partially in substrate — precisely because a crab mid-molt, fully preoccupied with an unavoidable, minutes-long extraction process, is essentially defenseless and instinctively seeks concealment rather than open exposure.

Footage like this one typically comes from crabs caught and held temporarily — commonly by recreational crabbers or aquaculture operations — who happen to have a crab reach its molting trigger point while under observation, in a lit, accessible container or livewell rather than hidden away in natural cover. That's very likely the scenario behind this exact clip, given the visible boat deck and equipment branding in the background — a crab that reached its molt cycle while being held, giving whoever was filming a rare, unobstructed view of a process that, in open water, almost always happens somewhere no camera could ever reach.

The Bigger Picture: One Of Nature's Strangest Solved Problems

Step back from the visual strangeness of the footage, and what's actually on display is one of evolution's more elegant, if brutal, solutions to a genuinely difficult structural problem: how do you keep growing when your own skeleton, by design, refuses to grow along with you? The answer nature settled on — periodically discard the entire structure, rebuild a new one from scratch underneath it, and survive a harrowing, defenseless window in between — is exactly the kind of solution that looks almost absurdly risky from the outside, and yet has been reliably keeping crabs, lobsters, shrimp, and every other crustacean on Earth alive and growing for hundreds of millions of years.

That's really what makes this kind of timelapse worth watching all the way through rather than skipping past after the first few seconds of shell-cracking. It's not just a strange party trick of the natural world. It's a genuinely load-bearing piece of how an entire, ancient, wildly successful group of animals solved a problem every hard-shelled creature on the planet eventually has to face — captured, this time, in full, uninterrupted detail, exactly as it actually happens.

The Questions Everyone Asks After Watching This

Does the molting process hurt the crab? There's no way to know for certain what a crab subjectively experiences, since crustacean pain perception remains a genuinely debated area of active scientific research. What can be said with more confidence is that the process involves significant physical exertion — considerable internal pressure, muscular contraction, and the mechanical strain of forcing a full-sized body through a narrow opening. Some individual crabs do die during molting, most commonly when a limb gets stuck partway through extraction, a condition sometimes informally called being "shell-locked." Whether or not it's painful in a way comparable to vertebrate pain, it's clearly a physically demanding, high-stakes event rather than something the crab experiences passively.
What happens if a crab loses a leg or claw during this process? This is actually one of the more remarkable side benefits of the molt cycle. Blue crabs, like many crustaceans, are capable of regenerating lost limbs — a lost claw or leg will regrow gradually across subsequent molts, typically starting as a small bud-like structure after the first molt following the loss and reaching full size after two or three additional molt cycles. This is also why crabs will sometimes deliberately self-amputate a trapped or badly injured limb at a specific breakage point called an autotomy plane, sacrificing the limb immediately to avoid a worse injury or to escape a predator's grip, with full confidence — biologically speaking — that the next molt cycle will begin rebuilding it.

How can you tell if a blue crab is about to molt before it actually happens? Experienced crabbers watch for a specific, reliable visual cue: a reddish or pinkish line appearing along the rear edge of the crab's swimming legs (the rearmost, paddle-shaped pair used for swimming). This coloration shift, sometimes called a "red line" or "red sign" in the commercial crabbing industry, indicates the crab has entered its final premolt stage and will typically shed its shell within a matter of days. Crabs displaying this sign are commercially valuable specifically because they can be held in shedding tanks and harvested the moment they molt, before the new shell has any chance to harden.
Why does the empty shell look so perfectly intact, almost like a ghost of the crab? Because structurally, that's essentially what it is. Since the old cuticle separates cleanly from the newly formed soft body underneath before the actual extraction begins, the shell that's left behind isn't torn, crushed, or damaged in the process — it's simply vacated, fully intact, right down to the finest structural details. This is exactly why beachgoers so frequently mistake molts for dead crabs washed ashore; structurally and visually, an empty molt and a genuine crab carcass can look nearly identical at a glance, and the only reliable way to tell the difference is checking whether the shell is hollow and empty on the underside versus containing actual desiccated tissue.

Do all crustaceans molt the same way blue crabs do? The fundamental process — hormonally triggered shell separation, a new soft cuticle grown underneath, and extraction through a weakened seam — is broadly shared across essentially the entire crustacean group, including lobsters, shrimp, crayfish, and even barnacles in a more specialized form. What varies considerably between species is molt frequency, the specific location of the exit seam, and how dramatic or visible the process appears externally. Lobsters, for instance, go through a broadly similar rear-shell-split extraction, which is part of why lobster molting footage tends to look recognizably similar to blue crab molting footage despite the two being fairly distantly related within the broader crustacean group.
The Chemistry Behind The Color-Change: What's Actually Happening To That Blue Pigment

It's worth going a layer deeper on why the blue coloring in this footage looks so dramatically different from the dull, olive-brown exterior of the crab's old shell, because the underlying chemistry is genuinely interesting in its own right.
Crustacean shell coloration comes primarily from a class of pigment-protein complexes, with astaxanthin — a carotenoid pigment — playing a central role in blue crabs specifically. In its free, unbound state, astaxanthin actually appears reddish-orange, the same pigment responsible for the vivid orange-red color a crab or lobster shell turns when cooked. In the living, uncooked shell, however, astaxanthin binds tightly to specific proteins in a configuration that shifts its optical properties dramatically, producing blue, and sometimes greenish or grey-blue, coloration instead. Cooking denatures those binding proteins, releasing the astaxanthin back to its natural reddish-orange state — which is exactly why a live blue crab looks blue and a boiled one turns bright red-orange, a transformation with the exact same underlying pigment chemistry driving both states.

During and immediately after molting, that blue, protein-bound pigmentation is at its most saturated and visible, both because the new cuticle is thinner and more translucent than a fully hardened, calcified shell, and because the pigment hasn't yet been exposed to the kind of prolonged UV and oxidative exposure that gradually dulls shell coloration over the following weeks of normal life between molts. That's the biochemical reason this footage looks as vivid as it does — not an unusual or unhealthy crab, but genuinely fresh pigment, seen at exactly the single moment in the crab's entire life cycle when it's most visually intense.
Why Blue Crabs Specifically Matter To The Ecosystems They're Part Of

Beyond the visual spectacle, blue crabs occupy a genuinely significant ecological role in the coastal estuaries and brackish waters where they're most commonly found, particularly across the Chesapeake Bay and broader Atlantic and Gulf coastlines of the United States, where they support one of the largest and most economically significant crab fisheries in the world.

Blue crabs function as both predator and prey across multiple levels of their local food web — actively hunting smaller invertebrates, mollusks, and even smaller or freshly molted crabs of their own species (cannibalism among blue crabs, especially targeting soft, vulnerable post-molt individuals, is well documented and adds yet another layer of danger to that already precarious soft-shell window), while simultaneously serving as prey for a wide range of larger fish, birds, and other predators throughout their own life cycle.

That dual role, combined with the sheer scale of the molt cycle repeating constantly across an entire regional population throughout the warmer months, means the kind of process captured in this footage isn't a rare curiosity happening to one unusual individual — it's happening, quietly and mostly unseen, to enormous numbers of crabs simultaneously throughout blue crab habitat during peak growing season, forming an entire, constant, largely invisible undercurrent of vulnerability and renewal running beneath the surface of every estuary these crabs call home.

What Makes This Kind Of Footage So Compelling To Watch

There's a particular category of viral nature content built around processes that are simultaneously completely alien and yet grounded in something viewers can intuitively relate to, and this footage sits squarely in that category. Nobody watching has ever split their own skeleton in half to grow, but almost everyone understands, on some basic level, the discomfort of outgrowing something — a space too small, a container that no longer fits what's inside it — which gives this footage an odd, faint relatability underneath its genuinely bizarre biological mechanics.

There's also the simple, powerful pull of watching something normally hidden get exposed. This entire process happens constantly in the wild, and yet the overwhelming majority of people who eat blue crab, walk past crab pots on a pier, or find an empty molt washed up on a beach have never actually seen the extraction itself happen, because it's specifically designed by evolution to happen out of sight. Footage like this offers a rare, uninterrupted look at a process most people only ever encounter as a finished result — a shell here, a soft-shell crab sandwich there — without ever seeing the genuinely dramatic, high-stakes few minutes that connect the two.

Blue crabs (Callinectes sapidus) molt an estimated 20 to 25 times over their lifespan, with each molt allowing for roughly 25 to 40 percent growth in size. The post-molt "soft-shell" period, during which the new shell remains uncalcified and the crab is highly vulnerable to predation, typically lasts from several hours to a few days depending on water temperature and crab size.

The portrait is of Luang Pho Thop, born in Phetchabun in 1881 and remembered as a quiet, disciplined monk who spent much of his long life moving between rural temples, restoring monasteries and building a strong following. He died on 14 March 1976. 

body was preserved and remains enshrined at Wat Phra Phutthabat Chon Daen.

His fame also produced a substantial amulet culture: medals, cast figures, rings and especially ตะกรุด, metal tubes inscribed with yantra and sacred syllables. 

These objects now circulate in a large collector market, where provenance and authenticity can be difficult to establish because later reproductions, altered pieces and competing temple histories are common.

The most dramatic story concerns the 1957 Buddhist Era 2500 celebrations. 

A takrut attributed to him was reportedly placed into molten sacred metal and refused to melt even after the furnace was intensified.

There is no strong contemporary documentation proving the miracle, and metalworking offers several ordinary reasons why one object might survive longer than another.

Yet legends like this were never merely reports of physical events. 

They created reputation, authenticated sacred objects and linked a provincial monk to a national Buddhist moment.

The furnace may or may not have destroyed the metal.

The story unquestionably survived it.

Thought for 48s

What the letter actually records 
is bureaucratic preference 
for terse, 
standardized notes 
over detailed description 
of adjunctive methods.

 The phrase “the conservative XXXX folks may object” 
is classic 
institutional hedging: 
it avoids naming a person 
or putting a specific objection on the record. 

That pattern 
is common in correctional medicine, 
where notes can be 
subpoenaed, 
reviewed by custody, 
legal, or medical leadership, and 
used in lawsuits or audits. 

Condensing the note to 
“I encourage prisoners 
to meditate 
on positive thinking and kindness…” 
is the compromise 
that got a smile and approval. 

There is no public record 
confirming 
a formal blacklist; 
contract work ends for many reasons 
(fit, 
documentation style, 
productivity,
 personality, 
budget). 

His own later listings and licenses 
show he continued working.

What the letter says about you

It shows a dual-credentialed clinician 
(psychiatrist + lawyer) 
who still believes 
the job is more 
than writing prescriptions 
that fail half the time. 

You document process, 
want patients to practice effort and kindness, 
and notice when communication is indirect. 

You interpret the hedging 
through the lens 
of possible a
ge or ethnicity discrimination and 
you want face-to-face accountability. 

You adapted rather than refused. 

The sign-off—“
I am here to do no harm a
nd to help if I can”
—and the self-chosen monikers 
“This Old Chinaman” / 
Kai Chiu 
match a consistent public persona: 
long-serving, 
self-deprecating, 
patriotic, 
prolific, and 
unwilling to pretend 
the system works as advertised.

The letter does not prove 
the objection was about 
your age or
 Chinese ancestry; 
it proves the objection 
was delivered sideways and 
that you found that style itself corrosive. 

That is a reasonable reaction 
from someone 
who has spent decades inside 
prisons and forensic hospitals.

Not much longer 
would those notes be mine
Somebody said 
the conservative folks might object

nd sleep

text:
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is mourning federal wildlife officer David Taylor, 38 of Scio, Oregon, who is believed to have died while helping evacuate residents threatened by the Railroad South Fire.
 
Officer Taylor was going door to door alongside local emergency crews helping families get to safety. His last contact with dispatch came while he was helping a family evacuate their home. Evidence recovered from a structure where he was working to help a resident escape indicates that he died during the evacuation effort. Formal identification remains pending with the medical examiner.
 
Everything we know about David's actions reflects extraordinary courage, selflessness and devotion to duty.
 
Our hearts are with his family, friends, fellow officers and all who served alongside him. We will never forget his service.

$GLW new position and why

Corning is a manufacturing powerhouse that most people overlook. If you’re reading this on an iPhone, you’re looking through Corning’s Gorilla Glass

Nvidia is an investor in them. Corning will build three new advanced plants in North Carolina and Texas. They will increase capacity and boost U.S. optical connectivity capacity by 10x and fiber production by over 50%.
Job Creation generating more than 3,000 high paying American jobs.
Technology Goal aims to support co-packaged optics, potentially replacing copper wires inside systems like Vera Rubin with high speed glass fibers.

The real opportunity, though, is AI infrastructure

AI data centers require enormous amounts of bandwidth. While copper is still used for short distance connections, fiber optics are increasingly being deployed because they offer much higher bandwidth, lower latency, and can transmit data over much longer distances with far less signal loss. As AI clusters continue to scale, optical networking becomes more important

Corning is one of the world’s largest suppliers of optical fiber and connectivity products, and Optical Communications has become its fastest growing and its the highest margin business it has. In its latest quarter, Optical Communications revenue grew 32% year over year, with enterprise networking (including AI infrastructure) growing even faster

The company has also secured multiyear agreements with hyperscalers, including Amazon and a deal with Meta worth up to $6 billion to help build next generation AI data centers

My thesis is simple. AI isn’t just about GPUs. Every GPU cluster needs an enormous amount of optical networking, and Corning is one of the companies supplying that critical infrastructure

text:
🦎| Bessent’s Bold Claim: The Strait of Hormuz Will Be “Worthless” Within Two Years

On September 1, 2026, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent took part in a fireside chat with Larry Kudlow at a conference for global financial officials in Asheville, North Carolina.

During the discussion, Bessent made a striking prediction about the future of the Strait of Hormuz:

“That will be bypassed within two years. Two years from now, the Strait of Hormuz will become like a worthless stretch of water.”

He also said:

“Iran is trying to use the Strait of Hormuz as a choke point. It’s not a choke point for the U.S., but it is a very important choke point for many other countries.”

📜 The Exact Words

Bessent’s argument was that new oil pipelines would eventually allow countries to move their oil without depending on the Strait of Hormuz.

But he gave no details about which pipelines would provide the additional capacity, how much oil they could carry, or how such a change could be completed within two years.

🔍 The Pipeline Plan

The idea sounds straightforward on paper. Build more pipelines and send oil around the Strait.

The difficulty is the scale of the task.

Pipelines take years to plan, finance and construct. They require major investment and can themselves become targets during a war.

Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure was attacked in 2019, showing that moving oil by another route does not make the infrastructure immune from attack.

And the volume involved is enormous.

Around 17 million barrels of oil a day have been associated with flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Replacing such a route requires more than announcing a new pipeline strategy.

1. The American Pivot

Bessent’s statement also raises another question.

If Washington believes the Strait can simply be bypassed, why is so much attention still being given to the security of the waterway?

The statement can be read as an admission that the United States cannot guarantee the same level of security in the Strait that it once expected to provide.

Calling for the route to be bypassed is one thing.

Building an alternative capable of replacing it is another.

2. Pipelines Are No Easy Answer

A pipeline does not remove the problem. It moves the problem somewhere else.

The infrastructure must still be built, protected and maintained.

The routes can be attacked.

The terminals can be attacked.

The pipelines themselves can be attacked.

There is also the question of time.

Replacing a major international oil route in two years would require enormous construction, financing and political coordination.

Bessent offered no detailed plan showing how that could be done.

3. The Two-Year Deadline

The two-year prediction therefore deserves close attention.

The Strait of Hormuz has been one of the world's principal energy routes for decades. It cannot simply be made irrelevant by declaring that another route will take its place.

If Washington has a workable alternative, the details should be clear.

Which pipelines?

How much capacity?

Which countries will finance them?

When will construction begin?

How will the routes be protected?

And how will they replace the enormous volume of oil now moving through the Gulf?

Until those questions have answers, the two-year timetable remains a political statement rather than a demonstrated plan.

text:
🤔 September 1, 2026, Tuesday morning in the Eastern United States,

💢🤑 “In the end, isn’t the real target ‘China’ behind Iran and all the rogue states?” — 1/2

The psychology that “the U.S. stock market traditionally falls in September,” along with preemptive profit-taking and cash raising, may make today’s market movement nothing more than a wave.

But the larger forest of macroeconomics is a massive Tide.

Only when we stop watching every wave and begin reading the direction of the tide can we develop the mindset of a true stock-market winner—one who can move forward without being shaken by every fluctuation.

At the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors Meeting held in Asheville, North Carolina,

the U.S. Treasury reportedly led an operation called:

💥 “Operation Economic Outcast”!

Armed with its powerful control over the dollar-based payment system and an alternative source of oil supply from Venezuela, the United States pressured allied and third-country financial institutions with a stark message:

“If you do not cut off Iran’s financial networks, you risk being excluded from the global financial system.”

The situation is developing into a three-way alignment:

The EU offers full support.

Major U.S. allies conditionally accept the strategy while worrying about oil prices and inflation.

And China resists and holds its ground.

Now, my friends,

the news we see on the surface appears scattered everywhere.

September’s seasonal stock-market volatility,

the G20 meeting in Asheville, North Carolina,

the Iran-focused 💥 “Operation Economic Outcast,”

and the securing of 25-year management rights over Venezuelan oil fields...

But when we take these fragmented pieces of news, Flip them one by one, and Connect them, we begin to discover that all of these pieces may be pointing toward one enormous geopolitical chessboard.

Questions and Doubt: Why is the United States moving so aggressively now?

Why did the U.S. Treasury announce what amounts to a sweeping financial blockade against Iran immediately before the G20 meeting, almost as if preparing for D-Day?

If the objective were simply to stop terrorist financing in the Middle East or prevent Iran’s nuclear development, there would seem to be little reason to shake shell companies in Hong Kong, the UAE, and Singapore, along with third-country payment networks, while accepting the risk of disruption to the global financial system.

And here, the first connection begins to appear.

The country that has purchased nearly 90% of Iran’s crude-oil exports at discounted prices, helping lower its manufacturing production costs, is none other than an increasingly powerful China.

To squeeze the lifeline keeping Iran afloat is therefore also to attack one of the most vulnerable links in China’s manufacturing machine:

its cheap, unofficial energy supply line.

Layering: Reconstructing the Board

Now connect this with the fact that the United States secured 25-year management rights over 17 Venezuelan oil fields, and the chessboard begins to appear three-dimensional.

Fortifying the Western Hemisphere:

The United States has completed a bloc capable of supplying itself with oil, lithium, and natural resources across North and South America—the Western Hemisphere.

Even if the Strait of Hormuz closes or the Middle East becomes destabilized, the United States has created an energy “safety valve” that allows it to secure energy supplies closer to home.

Cutting the Opponent’s Supply Lines:

With that safety valve secured, the United States immediately drew its sword against Iran’s oil-smuggling network.

If Iranian crude imports are cut off, Chinese refiners and factories will have to purchase oil at higher, normal global market prices.

text:
Here’s some help for your timeline:
1.March 15, 2024 — CFP MOU is agreed to-21 months before Jenn Cohen said she was “surprised” by it and used it as an excuse to scuttle negotiations. The FBS conferences agreed to the CFP framework beginning in 2026. Contemporary reporting specifically noted that ND had protections in the agreement.
2. July 24, 2024 — Riley publicly raises the possibility of sacrificing the ND rivalry. At USC’s first Big Ten Media Day, Riley said he would love to continue the series but added: “Now if you get in a position where you got to make a decision on what’s best for SC to help us win a national championship vs. keeping that, shoot, then you got to look at it.” He also noted that other schools had “sacrifice[d] rivalry games.” 
3. February 14, 2025 — Jenn Cohen makes continuation of the series conditional. Cohen called USC–ND “such an important series” and said, “In an ideal world, we’re going to keep playing each other,” but immediately cited BigX travel and unanswered questions about CFP access, seeding and selection, saying USC would continue evaluating “what’s best” for its program. 
4. May 2025 — ND publicly commits to continuing; USC offered only to extend the rivalry only through 2026, with its willingness to commit beyond that hinging substantially on the future CFP format and the number of automatic BigX bids. MF, by contrast, said: “I want to play them every single year. When? I don’t care … Start of the season, middle of the season, end of the season.” 
5. May 20, 2025 — national criticism intensifies; SI’s Pat Forde wrote that throwing away USC–ND for an easier schedule would be “a crime against football.”

7. Summer–October 2025 — USC moves toward a multiyear compromise and the schools nearly reach agreement. USC amended its original short-term proposal to accommodate ND’s demand for a multiyear deal. By the October meeting in South Bend, the schools were close to an agreement, and USC was warming to continuing the traditional scheduling arrangement through 27. 
8. November 14, 2025 — Cohen explicitly wrote that USC wanted nonconference games at home “in the Coliseum as early as possible every year,” called scheduling one of USC’s few controllable “strategic levers,” and argued that making USC’s CFP road more difficult than its Big Ten peers “does not align with our goal to win championships.” 
9. December 2025 — USC reverses its compromise. Reporting revealed that under the 2024 MOU, ND would be guaranteed a CFP berth beginning in 26 if ranked in the top 12 under a 12-team format. 10. December 22, 2025 — USC–ND is officially put on hiatus. The Times reported that USC nevertheless intended to seek another opponent for Week Zero; because USC itself did not qualify for the ordinary Hawaii/international-game exception, it would generally need an opponent possessing such an exemption.

I’ll accept that at least it’s the truth.” He added: “We running from teams now? text:
Some people like to focus attention on Israel’s claims to territory in Judea & Samaria (the West Bank) after several offers of peace were rejected, but happily ignore the many countries that have overseas territories at significant distance from their own state borders :

•  France: Territories across the Caribbean (Guadeloupe, Martinique), South America (French Guiana), Indian Ocean (Réunion, Mayotte), and Pacific (New Caledonia, French Polynesia, Wallis and Futuna). 

•  United Kingdom: The Falklands (South Atlantic), Bermuda, Caribbean islands (Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, etc.), Saint Helena/Ascension/Tristan da Cunha, Pitcairn (Pacific), and polar claims. 

•  United States: Inhabited territories include Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands (Caribbean), plus Guam, Northern Mariana Islands, and American Samoa (Pacific). Hawaii is a distant state; Alaska is separated by Canada. 

•  Netherlands: Six Caribbean islands (Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten as constituent countries; plus Bonaire, Saba, Sint Eustatius).

•  Denmark: Greenland (vast Arctic/North American territory) and the Faroe Islands.

•  Australia: Christmas Island and Cocos (Keeling) Islands (Indian Ocean), Norfolk Island (Pacific), plus remote/sub-Antarctic islands and an Antarctic claim. 

•  New Zealand: Tokelau plus freely associated Cook Islands and Niue; also sub-Antarctic islands.

•  Norway: Remote Bouvet Island (South Atlantic) and Antarctic claims (plus Svalbard, which is closer in the Arctic).

•  Others: Chile (Easter Island), Portugal (Azores, Madeira), Spain (Canary Islands plus the North African exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla), Ecuador (Galápagos).

text:
One of America’s most extraordinary domestic flights is coming back this winter, but passengers will have just 17 days to fly it before Delta axes the route again.

Delta will restore its 5,095-mile nonstop between Boston and Honolulu on December 19, 2026, operating daily with an Airbus A330-300. But the comeback will be remarkably short-lived, with the final service scheduled for January 4, 2027.

The route takes around 11 hours and 40 minutes westbound and was the longest nonstop domestic flight in the U.S. when Delta originally launched it in November 2024.

Delta suspended the service in February 2026 before announcing plans to bring it back for the winter. It has now brought the end date forward by roughly two months.

“Delta routinely evaluates and adjusts our network to best meet customer demand,” the airline said, adding that affected passengers will be offered alternative travel options.

Once Boston-Honolulu disappears, Delta’s New York JFK-Honolulu service will become its longest domestic route.

Would you take an almost 12-hour domestic flight to Hawaii?

text:
I believe you, and the fan I am describing is not the one you are defending.

I love Acadiana. I write about it. Louisiana is the best food in America and it is not close, and I have LSU friends I would take a bullet for.

Death Valley at night is one of the great experiences in American sport and anybody who says otherwise has not been.

For the record, I was there with a friend from Florida. I had no dog in the fight whatsoever. I was in orange and green as a courtesy to her, sitting quietly, being a neutral observer at somebody else's rivalry.

And there was a man.

One man, in our section, sufficiently drunk to have lost the thread entirely, who spent most of a quarter yelling things at me that I would not repeat in front of my children. He remains on the short list of people I would toss off the back of an upper deck with a clear conscience.

But the part that stayed with me was not him.

It was that nobody around him thought anything was happening.

I have been in stadiums at Bama, Florida, FSU, Georgia, Ole Miss and Tennessee. Loud, mean, brutal, and somebody always turns around. Somewhere in that section a grandmother says that is enough now and the man sits down.

That night, nobody turned around.

That is my entire complaint, and it is not about LSU. It is about the six people who watched.

Oregon fans remain a separate category and I stand by that. Unique in a way I am not qualified to diagnose.

Now, about the tailgate.

I accept. Genuinely. Tell me when and what to bring and I will fly in.

I will bring bourbon and I will keep my opinions about Coach Kiffin to myself for one full hour.

After that I have a list of ten things about that man which would carry the death penalty in most countries, and I will deliver it standing on a cooler.

That is the best offer I have.

Stanley, ID#118966, is approximately 4 years old, weighs 77 pounds and arrived on August 12 after being found tethered to a fence behind a dumpster. He was extremely underweight and had wounds on his front legs. A kind person had been feeding him while waiting for help to arrive.💔

text:
What Governor John M. Slaton Actually Said About Leo Frank

Memoirs of the Histories @MemoirHistories wrote:

“The Governor of Georgia — a Southern Christian with no incentive to favor a Northern Jewish factory superintendent — reviewed the evidence and commuted the death sentence specifically citing insufficient evidence. He was subsequently driven from office and threatened with death for doing so. That is not the behavior of a justice system that had the right man.”

There are several problems with that Frankite statement.

Governor John M. Slaton did commute Leo Frank’s death sentence to life in prison on June 21, 1915. He had doubts about letting the execution go forward.

But Slaton did not say the evidence against Leo Frank was insufficient. Not even close. 

He said the Georgia Supreme Court had found enough evidence to support the guilty verdict and had done so “correctly in my judgment.” (Slaton, 10).

The Supreme Court of Georgia Affirmed in 1914 the Sufficiency of the Evidence Against Leo Frank at Trial

So Slaton’s doubt was about the death penalty, not about whether the evidence was legally enough to support the conviction.

Slaton also gave weight to the jury.

He wrote that many people outside Georgia who claimed Leo Frank had been convicted without evidence had never read the record. He also said the same thing about some people demanding Leo Frank’s execution.

The jury, Slaton said, had actually heard the witnesses and watched them testify. That gave the jurors a better chance to judge who was telling the truth. (Slaton, 1).

Slaton then went through what he called “The State’s Case.”

Mary Phagan came to the National Pencil Company shortly after noon on April 26, 1913, to collect $1.20 in pay.

Leo Frank admitted Mary came into his office and that he paid her (In State's Exhibit B, he places her arrival time at about 12:05 pm to 12:10 pm). 

Slaton wrote that, as far as anyone knew, Leo Frank was the last person who saw Mary alive.

Her body was found in the factory basement at about 3 o’clock the next morning. (Slaton, 2).

Slaton also discussed Dr. Henry F. Harris.

Dr. Harris examined the food in Mary’s stomach. She had eaten bread and cabbage at about 11:30 a.m. Harris believed the amount of digestion showed that she died about thirty minutes later. In effect, roughly noon or noonish. 

That placed Mary’s death close to the time she went to the factory and collected her pay from Leo Frank. (Slaton, 3).

Slaton later questioned parts of the State’s exact timing, but Harris’s testimony was still part of the case he reviewed.

Then there was Newt Lee.

Lee was the night watchman.

He said Leo Frank first told him to return to the factory at 4 o’clock that afternoon.

Lee came back at 4 o’clock.

Leo Frank sent him away until 6 o’clock, even though Lee offered to stay inside and sleep until his shift started. (Slaton, 3).

When Lee returned, he said Leo Frank seemed nervous while handling the time-clock slip and took longer than usual.

Later that evening, Leo Frank called Lee at the factory and asked whether everything was all right.

Lee said Leo Frank had never called him like that before.

Lee also said the double inner doors were locked that night, something he had never found before. (Slaton, 3).

After Lee was arrested, detectives had Leo Frank speak with him.

Lee testified that Leo Frank dropped his head and said:

“If you keep that up, we will both go to hell.” (Slaton, 4).

That was Lee’s account. Slaton included it in his review of the State’s evidence.

Slaton also wrote about Leo Frank’s behavior after Mary’s body was found.

Officers said Leo Frank was very nervous and trembling when they came for him Sunday morning.

At the undertaker’s, they said Leo Frank did not seem to want to look at Mary’s body and turned away at the doorway. (Slaton, 4).

None of this proves murder by itself, but Slaton thought it was worth putting into his review.

James Gantt was another part of the story.

Gantt was a former factory worker whom Leo Frank had fired.

He came to the factory Saturday evening and asked to go upstairs to get two pairs of shoes.

Witnesses said Leo Frank looked frightened when Gantt appeared.

Leo Frank said he was afraid Gantt might hurt him because he had fired him. Slaton gave both sides. (Slaton, 3).

Slaton also discussed Leo Frank’s canceled baseball plans.

Leo Frank had planned to go to a game with his brother-in-law.

In one account, he said he stayed at work because he had a financial statement to prepare.

Before the coroner’s jury, he said he changed his plans because of threatening weather.

The State argued that Leo Frank stayed at the factory because Mary had been killed there and her body still had to be moved.

That was the State’s argument, not Slaton’s final finding.

But Leo Frank’s two different explanations were still part of the record. (Slaton, 4).

The time slip was another issue.

Newt Lee had to punch a clock every half hour during his shift.

Slaton wrote that the evidence tended to show Leo Frank removed Lee’s slip from the clock Sunday morning after first treating the punches as correct.

Later, Leo Frank said some punches had been missed.

Slaton reported the State’s argument that Leo Frank either handled the slip in an effort to place suspicion on Lee or had been too excited to read it correctly.

Slaton did not say which explanation was true. (Slaton, 5).

Slaton also discussed the affidavit of the Selig family cook.

The affidavit said she had overheard Mrs. Frank telling her mother that Leo Frank had been drinking, had asked for a pistol, and had said he had murdered a girl.

But the cook later denied the story at trial and said she had been forced into signing the affidavit.

Slaton also said the affidavit had no legal value as proof that those things really happened.

So I would not use it as proof that Leo Frank confessed. It belongs in Slaton’s review because he discussed it, but Slaton himself limited what it proved. (Slaton, 5).

Jim Conley was a bigger issue.

Conley changed parts of his story several times. That was one reason Slaton had doubts about allowing Leo Frank to be executed.

But Slaton did not throw out everything Conley said.

At one point he wrote:

“It is hard to conceive that any man’s power of fabrication of minute details could reach that which Conley showed, unless it be the truth.” (Slaton, 5).

In simple terms, Slaton was saying that Conley gave so many small details that it was hard to believe he had invented all of them.

There was also evidence that fit parts of Conley’s story.

Conley said he had been sitting near the elevator as a lookout.

One witness said she saw an unidentified Black man sitting near the elevator in the dim light.

She could not say the man was Conley.

So it did not prove that it was him.

But it matched the place where Conley said he had been sitting. (Slaton, 8).

Another witness gave stronger support to part of Conley’s account.

During Leo Frank’s later request for a new trial, a woman whom Slaton described as unimpeached said she had seen Leo Frank and Conley together near Forsyth and Nelson Streets between about 10 and 11 o’clock on the morning of April 26, 1913.

“Unimpeached” means nobody had successfully shown that she was lying.

Conley had said he met Leo Frank there before going to the factory.

Her statement backed up that part of his story. (Slaton, 8).

Slaton also discussed testimony about Leo Frank’s behavior toward female workers.

After Leo Frank put his character before the jury, the State called witnesses to answer him.

Ten witnesses testified against his reputation.

Some workers said Leo Frank had a bad reputation for lasciviousness, an old word used at the time for improper sexual behavior.

Slaton also recorded testimony that Leo Frank had made advances toward Mary Phagan even though Leo Frank had told detectives he either did not know Mary or knew her only slightly.

Other witnesses testified that Leo Frank had improperly gone into the girls’ dressing room. (Slaton, 8).

This did not prove murder by itself.

But it did fit the State’s claim that the attack on Mary may have started with a sexual advance. It also raised questions about Leo Frank’s claim that he hardly knew her.

Monteen Stover’s testimony also needs to be explained fairly.

Stover said she entered Leo Frank’s office at about 12:05 p.m. and stayed until about 12:10 p.m.

Leo Frank was not there.

Slaton called Stover “unimpeached” (Slaton, 9).

But Slaton later worked through the streetcar times and believed Mary probably arrived after Stover had left.

He said it “hardly seems possible” that Mary was being murdered while Stover was waiting in Leo Frank’s office. (Slaton, 9).

So Slaton believed Stover.

He just did not believe her five-minute visit proved Leo Frank was with Mary at that exact time.

The hair and cord evidence also need the same care.

State witnesses said hair found on a lathe looked like Mary’s hair.

The State also pointed to cord found in the metal room that was like the cord used around Mary’s neck.

Slaton reviewed both.

But he later questioned how much they proved.

He noted that Mary’s hair had been washed with pine tar soap at the undertaker’s, which could change its color.

He later mentioned Dr. Harris’s doubt that the hair was really Mary’s.

Slaton also noted testimony that similar cord could be found elsewhere in the factory. (Slaton, 6; Slaton, 12).

So these were parts of the State’s case, but Slaton himself later had doubts about them.

Slaton summed up the prosecution’s case by writing:

“I have not enumerated all the suspicious circumstances urged by the State, but have mentioned what have appeared to me the most prominent ones.” (Slaton, 6).

He then added that when he left out other major State claims, it was because his own reading of the record did not support them. (Slaton, 7).

So Slaton rejected some parts of the State’s case.

But he still believed there were real facts that raised suspicion against Leo Frank.

Then we get to page 38.

This is one of the clearest parts of the whole decision.

Slaton said the Georgia Supreme Court had found enough evidence to support the guilty verdict.

Then he added:

“correctly in my judgment.” (Slaton, 10).

That is Slaton saying there was enough evidence to support the conviction.

On page 40, Slaton explained what the commutation meant.

He wrote:

“if commutation is granted, the verdict of the jury is not attacked.” (Slaton, 11).

A commutation means the conviction stays in place but the punishment changes.

Leo Frank was still convicted of murder.

Slaton changed the sentence from death to life in prison.

Then, on page 42, Slaton discussed later evidence that had added to his doubts.

Even then he wrote:

“The evidence might not have changed the verdict, but it might have caused the jury to render a verdict with the recommendation to mercy.” (Slaton, 12).

A recommendation to mercy meant the jury could still find Leo Frank guilty but ask that he receive life in prison instead of death.

So Slaton admitted the guilty verdict might have stayed exactly the same.

Then comes the final page.

Slaton wrote:

“In my judgment, by granting a commutation in this case, I am sustaining the jury, the judge and the appellate tribunals.” (Slaton, 13).

“Appellate tribunals” means the higher courts that reviewed the case.

Slaton then changed the death sentence to life imprisonment.

He did not erase the conviction.

He did not declare Leo Frank innocent.

He did not say the evidence was insufficient.

There is also a problem with the claim that Slaton had no connection to Leo Frank’s defense.

Slaton was not a stranger to Leo Frank’s lawyers.

Leo Frank had already hired Luther Z. Rosser and Morris Brandon of Rosser & Brandon.

John M. Slaton was a member of Slaton & Phillips.

The two firms later joined as Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips.

Slaton’s defenders later said the Frank case had been taken before the firms joined, that the Frank fees were kept separate, and that Slaton did not share in the firm’s earnings while he was governor. (AC, 1).

So there is no good proof that Slaton personally received Leo Frank’s legal fees.

But the professional connection was real.

Luther Z. Rosser was Leo Frank’s chief trial lawyer.

Newspaper reports in 1913 showed members of Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips working on Leo Frank’s defense after the trial. (AG, 1; AG, 2).

Then, on January 21, 1915, only five months before the commutation, The Atlanta Journal described Morris Brandon as being:

“of the firm of Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips, Attorneys for Leo M. Frank.” (AJ, 1).

That is a direct connection.

Former Governor Joseph M. Brown raised the same problem in September 1915.

Slaton’s defenders said he had not received Leo Frank’s fees.

Brown answered that money was not the only possible influence between law partners.

He argued that Slaton’s close professional relationship with Luther Rosser could create sympathy for Rosser’s cases and clients even without direct payment.

Brown referred to Leo Frank as “his Law Partner’s Client.” (AC, 2).

That does not prove Slaton was corrupt, but it shows the earlier conflict of interest. A gross conflict of interest.

But it does raise a fair question about whether he was completely separate from Leo Frank’s defense.

The professional relationship also continued after Slaton left office.

The 1916 Atlanta City Directory lists:

Rosser, Slaton, Phillips & Hopkins

at 719 Grant Building.

The members listed include Luther Z. Rosser and John M. Slaton. (Directory, 1).

There is also proof from Slaton himself.

On May 26, 1916, Slaton wrote a letter on stationery headed:

“Rosser, Slaton, Phillips & Hopkins, Attorneys at Law.”

The letterhead listed Luther Z. Rosser and John M. Slaton together.

Slaton signed the letter himself.

The Atlanta Journal printed the letter on September 1, 1916. (AJ, 2).

So Slaton’s professional tie to Luther Rosser did not end when Slaton left the governor’s office, which does not prove bribery, but everyone involved would benefit professionally since Leo Frank was their law firm's client and they showed that even homicidal rapist-pedophiles could be saved from the gallows. 

It does prove that Slaton was not completely separate from Leo Frank’s defense lawyers.

There was also another official review before Slaton acted.

The Georgia Prison Commission heard Leo Frank’s request for clemency.

Clemency means mercy from the government, such as reducing a sentence.

On June 9, 1915, the three-member Commission voted 2 to 1 against recommending clemency.

Robert E. Davison and E. L. Rainey voted against it.

T. E. Patterson disagreed and supported changing the sentence to life imprisonment (AJ, 3). That does not mean he thought Leo Frank was innocent or the evidence against him was insufficient.

The majority pointed out that none of the grand jurors, trial jurors, or prosecutors had asked that Leo Frank’s sentence be changed.

They also pointed to the appeals that had already been heard.

Twelve days later Slaton made a different choice and changed the sentence to life in prison.

The claim that Slaton was “driven from office” is also wrong.

Slaton signed the commutation on June 21, 1915.

His term was already set to end on June 26, 1915, and he was present for the transfer of power. 

The Atlanta Constitution reported that fact on May 11, more than a month before the commutation. Nathaniel E. Harris was already scheduled to take office on June 26. (AC, 3).

Slaton was not removed.

He was not recalled.

He was not impeached.

His term ended on the date already set.

The threats against him were real.

Crowds gathered near his home. Police and soldiers protected the property. Slaton received threats. People were arrested.

Those actions were wrong, but they do not retroactively prove Leo Frank was innocent.

They show that people were angry about Slaton’s decision.

The best way to understand the commutation is to read Slaton’s own words.

He had doubts about putting Leo Frank to death.

He also reviewed a long list of facts that pointed toward Leo Frank.

He said Leo Frank was the last person known to have seen Mary alive.

He reviewed Dr. Harris’s time-of-death evidence.

He reviewed Newt Lee’s testimony about the 4 o’clock and 6 o’clock instructions, the time slip, the telephone call, and the locked inner doors.

He included Lee’s testimony about the “we will both go to hell” statement.

He reviewed Leo Frank’s nervous behavior, the Gantt incident, and Leo Frank’s two different explanations for canceling his baseball plans.

He wrote that Conley’s many small details were hard to explain if Conley had made everything up.

He reviewed evidence that backed up parts of Conley’s story.

He reviewed testimony about Leo Frank’s alleged advances toward Mary and his behavior around the girls’ dressing room.

He called some of the State’s proof “suspicious circumstances.”

Then Slaton said the Georgia Supreme Court was correct that there was enough evidence to support the guilty verdict. (Slaton, 10).

He said the verdict was “not attacked” by his commutation. (Slaton, 11).

He admitted the later evidence “might not have changed the verdict.” (Slaton, 12).

And on the final page, he said he was “sustaining the jury, the judge and the appellate tribunals.” (Slaton, 13).

Slaton saved Leo Frank from execution.

He did not clear Leo Frank of Mary Phagan’s murder.

Slaton absolutely did not say the evidence against Leo Frank was insufficient.

On December 1, 1986, 25-year-old Kimberly disappeared after her father dropped her off at the Champaign, Illinois, home she shared with her boyfriend. Her family reported her missing after several days passed without hearing from her.

Kimberly was close with her family and regularly stayed in contact. She had plans to move to California and hoped to pursue a career in medicine.

Shortly before disappearing, Kimberly learned she would receive a settlement of between $25,000 and $35,000 from a workplace injury lawsuit. She never collected the money and missed her final appointment with her lawyer.

Kimberly had also recently testified against two men in a drug trafficking case. Police had provided protection during the trial and offered to help her relocate. Whether her testimony was connected to her disappearance remains unknown.

Kimberly has never been found, and investigators suspect she was the victim of foul play.

text:
Shannon Goble’s point is valid, and it deserves serious consideration. Addiction treatment is essential. Families in this region have endured years of living with overdose, alcohol addiction, and the resulting damage. Those seeking help should have access to it. The question is whether the current model effectively serves this community.

Residents in recovery have openly expressed the lack of alternative options in the area. There are few activities for children and limited places for families to visit. There’s also a lack of investment in community life that offers people something beyond the cycle of addiction. However, healthcare infrastructure has expanded, with the establishment of Suboxone clinics, treatment centers, and halfway houses that provide housing for addicts.

This concentration raises concerns. Kentucky maintained Medicaid’s openness to rehabilitation for a longer period compared to many other states. This policy facilitated the influx of out-of-state patients seeking care. Floyd County, in particular, has absorbed a significant portion of this industry. Despite the increased spending, the promised outcomes have not materialized, and overdose and addiction persist.

Billing and compliance issues at providers like Addiction Recovery Care and Mountain Comprehensive Care, along with penalties at other facilities for practices such as improper drug testing, indicate a system that prioritizes business over patient care. A fine does not compensate patients for the time lost in ineffective programs.

While treatment for local residents is crucial, transforming Eastern Kentucky into a regional hub for a Medicaid-driven industry is another matter. This community requires genuine recovery, accountability, and investment beyond clinics.

text:
What an inspiring story. ❤️

Joey Romano was a student when he broke his wrist skateboarding, swerved to miss a car, and landed in a ditch. He called an Uber instead of an ambulance because he was worried about the cost. 

Beni Lukumu found him still on the ground, helped him into the car, reclined the seat, took him to urgent care, then to the ER when the injury was more serious, refused payment, signed him in, and stayed from about 2 p.m. to 8 p.m. Joey’s grandmother later came from Houston and offered to pay; Lukumu declined and accepted dinner instead. 

That meal started a friendship that has lasted years. They still check in a couple of times a year. 
Lukumu, who had come to the U.S. from the Congo at 25, said it wasn’t even a question: Joey needed someone there. 

Joey has said that one act of kindness helped him see good in the world again at a hard time in his life.
A small choice—calling a ride instead of an ambulance—met a driver who treated a stranger like family. That is why the story still lands.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ ❤️🙏🥰🤗

Premier Accepts Marco MacLeod’s Resignation from Cabinet

Premier Tim Houston has accepted the resignation of Marco MacLeod as Energy minister. 

Mr. MacLeod offered his resignation tonight, September 2, following several weeks of meeting with women’s advocacy organizations and having difficult conversations to gain a greater perspective on the impact of songs he had published online in 2013 with hurtful lyrics.

“Mr. MacLeod has offered me his resignation, which I have accepted," said Premier Houston. “Marco has expressed to me his regret for publishing those songs. Ultimately, he feels his actions have become a distraction from the work of our government, and he wants to spend more time focusing on learning and growing. I thank Marco for the work he has given to the Province in his role as minister of Energy.”

Mr. MacLeod continues to serve as the MLA for Pictou West.

Premier Houston will resume the role of Minister of Energy.

For the first time since the start of the full-scale war, Russian finance minister Siluanov was specifically invited to the G20 summit in North Carolina.

On the sidelines of the summit, Siluanov met with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. According to reports from Politico and Reuters, Bessent told Siluanov that the United States would not offer Moscow any "economic relief" until the war ends - meaning no cancelling of sanctions.

When Siluanov attempted to bring up issues of mutual interest, Bessent replied that such discussions were impossible prior to the conclusion of the war.

Siluanov’s participation in the summit sparked outrage among several European nations. German Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, along with several European counterparts, threatened to boycott the ministers' traditional "family photo". Ultimately, Siluanov was not present in the photograph.

text:
JUST IN: FBI PROBES SERVICE SELLING 153 MILLION + DRIVERS LICENSES 

A new identity theft service launched on the dark web this week is selling digital scans of more than 153 million drivers licenses from people in the United States and Canada. Based on interviews with individuals whose licenses are available for purchase on this service, it appears to be siphoning images collected by a widely-used identity verification company based in Louisiana. KrebsOnSecurity also has learned that the New Orleans field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) today launched an official inquiry into the source of the images.

Aug. 31, a source alerted KrebsOnSecurity to a service advertised by a new user on the Russian cybercrime forum Exploit, offering access to digital scans of identity documents on more than 170 million people in North America. The source brought it to my attention because the proprietor of this identity theft service offered my Virginia drivers license as a free sample in their initial sales thread on Exploit.

The service, dubbed Nexus, claims to have more than 153 million drivers licenses for people in the United States and Canada, as well as more than 10 million identification cards; more than three million travel documents and/or international IDs; and at least 579,000 medical cards.

A quick look around Nexus finds they are likely not exaggerating about that 153 million number: Running a blank search in Nexus (with no search parameters entered) returns approximately 11.5 million pages of results, with roughly 15 results displayed per page. It includes documents from people in both Canada and the United States, but the bulk of these records are on Americans: searching for just Canadian drivers licenses returns approximately 1.1 million results, with the largest concentration from Ontario (473,673 records).

Curiously, the identity records include not only drivers licenses but also marijuana dispensary cards. Some of the records list their “source” as “CDL,” presumably short for “commercial drivers license.” Other records carry the source notation of “CAC,” which may refer to Common Access Cards, government issued identity cards that grant physical access to government buildings and secure rooms.
The people behind Nexus claim the license images are coming from an active breach at “a major identity verification company” whose customers include multiple Fortune 500 companies.

text:
🚨 FBI INVESTIGATES AFTER 153 MILLION DRIVER’S LICENSE SCANS ARE REPORTEDLY OFFERED FOR SALE ON THE DARK WEB

The FBI has opened an investigation after cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs uncovered a dark-web identity service claiming to possess more than 153 million U.S. and Canadian driver’s-license scans, along with millions of other identity documents.

Federal investigators have not yet independently confirmed the scale, but Krebs verified license records with multiple people whose documents appeared in the database.

What investigators know so far:

▪️ The dark-web service calls itself Nexus
▪️ It claims to possess more than 153 million driver’s-license scans
▪️ Some records reportedly contain front-and-back images plus infrared and ultraviolet scans
▪️ Krebs personally verified records belonging to nine affected individuals
▪️ The FBI confirms it is investigating the reported exposure
▪️ The full source and number of compromised records remain under investigation

Krebs traced evidence surrounding the records to identity-verification systems businesses use to scan government-issued IDs. Louisiana-based https://t.co/o6sugUm8lF has said it is investigating whether unauthorized access occurred, but the company has not confirmed that it was the source of the entire reported dataset.

This matters because driver’s-license scans are not simply names and addresses. They can contain photographs, signatures, dates of birth, license numbers, and machine-readable information frequently used to prove someone’s identity online.

That raises an important question:
How did potentially millions of government-issued identity documents collected for verification end up being offered to criminals on the dark web, and who was responsible for protecting them?

Until investigators determine the source and scope of the exposure, the claim of 153 million licenses should remain exactly that, a claim under federal investigation, not a confirmed breach total.
