DETAILED SUMMARY
FAKE SR. LUCY? OUR LADY OF FATIMA REVEALED: 
Kokx News founder Stephen Kokx speaks with Dr. Peter Chojnowski about his efforts to expose the "fake" Sr. Lucy of Our Lady of Fatima.

00:00–01:24 INTRODUCTION AND GUEST CONTEXT

Host Stephen Kokx welcomes longtime traditional Catholic commentator Dr. Peter Chojnowski (rendered as “Honki” in the auto-transcript) to discuss Sister Lucy Truth, the project Chojnowski founded in 2017. Kokx notes Chojnowski’s decades of involvement with Fatima questions and asks how the work began—whether by a sudden interior prompting or by simply noticing photographic anomalies. Chojnowski replies that Fatima had already been part of his life for many years. 

01:24–02:55 BACKGROUND WITH THE FATIMA CENTER AND BLUE ARMY

Chojnowski explains that he worked with Fr. Nicholas Gruner at the Fatima Center from 2000 onward, traveling internationally to lecture on the apparitions, the Third Secret, and especially the Miracle of the Sun. He also wrote for Catholic Family News, then associated with Gruner. His personal connection dated to the 1970s Blue Army and the fact that his birthday falls on October 13. Fatima, he says, was “in my bloodstream.” The new project grew out of that long immersion rather than a sudden revelation. 

02:55–07:45 THE PROBLEM: PRE-1967 VERSUS POST-1967 PHOTOGRAPHS

In 2017 Chojnowski examined articles by Dr. Marian Horvat on Tradition in Action that compared photographs of Sister Lúcia dos Santos before and after 1967. The contrast shocked him. Despite years of speaking about Fatima, he had never closely studied adult photographs of the seer beyond her childhood images. Profiles from 1946 at Fátima looked markedly different from the woman who appeared with Pope Paul VI in 1967. Chin, nose, eyebrows, and forehead structures appeared inconsistent. A colleague at Catholic Family News, Cornelia Ferreira, urged a strictly forensic, scientific investigation rather than a theological one: the question was ontological—whether the two women were the same person.

Chojnowski assembled photographs from official shrine publications, videos, and handwriting samples from memoirs and later letters. He hired specialists who were not selected for Catholic affiliation. The first facial-recognition analysis, obtained through a private investigator in late June 2018, indicated two different individuals. That result launched the systematic collection of expert reports.

07:45–12:11 THE EXPERTS: FORENSIC ARTISTS, SURGEONS, AND FACIAL RECOGNITION

Among the consultants was Lois Gibson, holder of a Guinness World Record for the largest number of successful criminal identifications through forensic art (more than 1,600). Gibson produced three reports: two addressing whether the pre- and post-1967 women were the same person, and a third asking whether the 1967 figure was the same woman who appeared from 1982 until her death in 2005. She concluded it was “impossible” that they were the same person, citing radically different facial structures. Her earlier dental training in fitting dentures reinforced the judgment about jaw and chin differences. She further stated that a single impostor occupied the role from 1967 through 2005.

Plastic surgeons and maxillofacial surgeons reached the same conclusion, pointing to skeletal features that aging, lighting, or dental work could not explain. Experts treated age as a variable and still found the discrepancies decisive. The investigation therefore framed the case as one continuous substitution rather than a series of different stand-ins.

12:11–14:43 PRESENTATION TO THE OHIO STATE CORONERS ASSOCIATION, MAY 2025

On 9 May 2025 Chojnowski presented the accumulated evidence for one hour to the annual conference of the Ohio State Coroners Association in Columbus. More than one hundred coroners and investigators attended. Using photographs, video, and a step-by-step breakdown of visual identification methods, he argued that two distinct women had been presented to the public as Sister Lúcia. At the close he asked for a show of hands. No one believed they were the same person; the room indicated unanimous agreement that they were two different people. Chojnowski described the reception as the first time a professional identification body had examined the material and found it convincing.

14:43–18:21 LETTER FROM HIGHLAND COUNTY CORONER DR. JEFFREY BERRY

A follow-up letter from Dr. Jeffrey Berry, Highland County Coroner, thanked Chojnowski and called the presentation methodical. Berry wrote that the photographs demonstrated “a clear fraud”: the pre-1960 visionary had been replaced by an impostor in 1967, immediately after the Council and in the Paul VI era. He stated that 100 percent of the more than one hundred coroners and investigators present agreed the women were different. Berry added that the case could involve not only fraud but possible murder and that the scientific letters from recognized experts would aid future legal identifications of the deceased. Chojnowski found the written confirmation heartening and offered to present the same material to any state coroners’ association.

18:21–21:53 NEXT STAGE: IDENTIFYING THE REAL SISTER LÚCIA AND THE IMPOSTOR

The investigation now seeks two answers: what happened to the original Sister Lúcia and who the substitute was. Discovering the impostor’s identity may reveal motive. A linguist at the University of Coimbra analyzed video recordings of the later “Sister Lucy.” The accent was located in Viseu, a city in northern Portugal well north of both Fátima and Coimbra. The speech pattern was described as urban or suburban rather than highly educated or rural. The woman is a native Portuguese speaker; bringing in an outsider would have been culturally implausible. Most observers assume she must already have been a religious, because she lived the enclosed Carmelite life for decades. How a person could abandon her own identity and assume another’s remains an open question. Photographs from the 1967 event show a woman who appears no older than forty, although the real Lúcia would have been about sixty.

21:53–25:14 NATIVE PORTUGUESE SPEAKER AND THE DIFFICULTY OF THE SUBSTITUTION

The tapes confirm fluent, native Portuguese. Chojnowski notes that simply recruiting a poor woman off the street and paying her family would still require her to live a complete lie inside a convent for the rest of her life—an extraordinary demand. The 1967 images already display a public, outgoing manner that contrasts with the reserved character known from earlier photographs and writings of the authentic seer.

25:14–31:10 CARLOS EVARISTO INTERVIEWS AND CONTRADICTIONS WITH THE ORIGINAL MESSAGE

Portuguese researcher Carlos Evaristo interviewed the later “Sister Lucy” on 11 October 1992 and again on 11 October 1993—the anniversary of the opening of Vatican II. In the recorded 1993 conversation she stated that the conversion of Russia did not mean conversion to the Catholic Faith but a conversion allowing every person to follow his or her own religion, language that aligns with post-conciliar religious liberty. She also claimed the Third Secret was intended only for the Pope, not for the world—the opposite of what the original Lúcia had said. Evaristo himself later went to the Portuguese police, questioning whether the woman was authentic; he was directed to a Dr. Zugabe who assured him everything was in order.

Fr. Gruner, who died in 2015 before the Sister Lucy Truth investigation began, had speculated in print that the 1993 interview subject might not be genuine, yet he never fully endorsed a 1967 substitution. Chojnowski is certain that if Gruner had seen the later forensic reports he would have accepted the impostor thesis. Fr. Paul Kramer, a former collaborator of Gruner’s, has already stated that a fake Sister Lucy was inserted.

31:10–33:11 IMPACT ON THE FATIMA COMMUNITY

In spring 2024 the Fatima Center’s Fatima Crusader acknowledged a substitute from 1967 onward but treated the fact as secondary to the message itself. Chojnowski disagrees: authentic teaching can come only from the authentic seer. Everything that cannot be traced to the pre-1960 Lúcia must be regarded as fraudulent or at least suspect. He has repeatedly asked for any photograph or eyewitness account showing the two women together or any priest who met the “real” Lúcia while the public figure was appearing with popes; none has been produced. Everyone who met “Sister Lucy” after 1960 assumed she was the original visionary.

33:11–35:13 THE AUTHENTIC SISTER LÚCIA AND THE 2000 THIRD SECRET DOCUMENT

The only writings and images that can be accepted without reservation belong to the period before approximately 1960. A court-approved handwriting expert examined later letters and declared them clever forgeries. The same expert, however, judged the vision text released by the Vatican in 2000 to be authentic handwriting of the original Lúcia. That finding is consistent with the long-standing view that the published vision lacks Our Lady’s own explanation of its meaning—unlike the first secret (the vision of hell), which was accompanied by an interpretation. Cardinal Ratzinger supplied an official commentary in 2000, but the words of the Virgin herself remain missing. Some researchers, including the late Fr. Hesse, questioned whether the language of “corpses” even fits a purely visionary account.

35:13–39:07 THE VISION OF HELL, THE MISSING EXPLANATION, AND THE LARGER CRISIS

The pattern of an unexplained vision plus a Vatican interpretation fits the broader “Fourth Secret” hypothesis that an accompanying text has never been released. Chojnowski places the substitution inside the larger post-1958 crisis: irregularities surrounding the 1958 conclave, the “color revolution” of Vatican II, and the failure to consecrate Russia in the manner requested. The last known apparition to the real Sister Lúcia occurred in 1929; the approaching centenary recalls the century that elapsed between the request to King Louis XIV and the French Revolution. The scale of the deception—selecting a woman who did not even resemble the original seer—suggests the stakes were extremely high.

39:07–43:08 WHY REPLACE HER? THE 1969 LETTER AND PAUL VI’S 1967 APPEARANCE

If the original Lúcia had been willing to endorse the post-1960 changes, no substitution would have been necessary. The fact that one occurred implies she would not have cooperated. A 1969 letter attributed to her, written as the new Mass was being introduced, insists that whoever is not with the Pope is not with God and praises Paul VI. The handwriting expert declared that letter fraudulent. Video of the 13 May 1967 ceremony shows the later woman raising Paul VI’s hand like a victorious athlete and urging the crowd to cheer him—an outgoing, promotional gesture alien to the known character of the real seer. The substitute proved comfortable in public, mixed easily with crowds, and consistently promoted the Vatican’s preferred narrative.

43:08–47:11 COMMUNION IN THE HAND AND THE JOHN PAUL II NARRATIVE

An eyewitness who visited the Coimbra Carmel during the lifetime of the later “Sister Lucy” reported seeing her receive Communion in the hand at a Novus Ordo Mass, an action that scandalized him. She appeared affable, frequently kissed and held John Paul II’s hand, and kept a letter from him on her deathbed. The 2000 Vatican interpretation of the Third Secret centered the 1981 assassination attempt on John Paul II, turning a 1960-era warning into a prophecy about an event two decades later. 🏛️ THE PHILOSOPHY DIVIDEND: 
The Ninety-Minute Rule 🤜 

🎖️ THE INSTITUTIONS THAT NEVER LEFT ▸ ▸ ▸ 📖 Post 4 OF 10 
The exact screen-time limit Peter Thiel and Snap's own CEO impose on their own kids. West Point had zero philosophy courses until a cheating scandal forced the issue. The Naval Academy's ethics requirement has the identical origin story.

Post 3 showed a pattern in executives who chose philosophy voluntarily, in peacetime, with no one forcing the question. This chapter goes somewhere the stakes are non-negotiable: institutions that train people to make life-and-death decisions, and the founders who built the products now shaping a generation's attention.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE SCANDAL THAT TAUGHT WEST POINT PHILOSOPHY

West Point's curriculum has always leaned toward engineering, mathematics, and the hard sciences — that's not in dispute. What is genuinely surprising is how recently, and how reluctantly, philosophy entered it at all.

✅ ESTABLISHED FACT: before 1976, West Point offered no formal courses in philosophy. That year, a cheating scandal made national headlines, and an outside blue-ribbon commission reviewing the Academy's entire curriculum recommended — among other changes — expanding philosophy offerings specifically to address ethics. The Academy complied. Every cadet at West Point is now required to take a philosophy course built around ethics, and cadets can major in philosophy directly, with the program's own description stating plainly that philosophical inquiry has "immense practical importance" for officers who will one day command at the highest levels.

The Naval Academy's story runs on a nearly identical track. 📊 STRONG EVIDENCE: its "Ethics and Moral Reasoning for the Naval Leader" course was written into the core curriculum following a December 1992 cheating scandal involving members of the electrical engineering department's Class of 1994. The Naval Academy teaches the course to sophomores specifically, on the reasoning that midshipmen should confront these questions before their commitments deepen, rather than waiting until commissioning is imminent.

🔍 WHAT THE EVIDENCE SHOWS: neither institution added serious ethics or philosophy training proactively, as part of an educational ideal. Both added it reactively, after an integrity failure exposed a real gap in how their students were being formed. That's a less flattering origin story than "the military always valued the humanities" — and a more useful one, because it means the requirement survived on demonstrated necessity rather than tradition alone. Today, West Point's core curriculum runs a full multi-year sequence: history, literature, and psychology in the first year of the sequence, followed by political science, philosophy, and economics, on top of an engineering-heavy STEM core — not instead of it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE BUILDERS WHO WON'T LET THEIR OWN KIDS NEAR IT

A different kind of high-stakes decision shows the same pattern from an unexpected angle: the people who built the technology now competing for a generation's attention are, disproportionately, the ones limiting their own children's access to it.

📊 STRONG EVIDENCE: Peter Thiel, an early Facebook investor and board member, has said publicly that he limits his own children to ninety minutes of screen time per week. Snap CEO Evan Spiegel has said he holds his own child to that identical ninety-minutes-per-week limit — on a platform he personally runs. Steve Jobs told a New York Times reporter in 2010 that his own children had never used the iPad his company had just released, saying plainly, "we limit how much technology our kids use at home." Bill Gates did not permit his children to have cell phones until age fourteen.

💡 The honest conclusion: these are not people opposed to technology — they built the industry. What they're modeling, in their own homes, is closer to what this series has been arguing about the humanities all along: a deliberate choice to protect the kind of unhurried, undistracted judgment that heavy technology use crowds out, made by the people with the clearest possible view of what that technology actually does to attention.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Put the two findings next to each other and a pattern emerges that neither institution stated outright, but both acted on: when the stakes are genuinely high — a command decision under fire, a child's developing attention — the people closest to those stakes consistently choose more humanities and less unmediated technology, not less. It's civilian higher education, operating at a comfortable remove from those stakes, that drifted the other way.

🕸️ Post 5 goes back to that civilian drift directly — who benefited from it, and who's already trying to reverse it.

text:
Ireland Has Been Invaded — But What Does an Invasion Mean?

There are certain words which nations learn to use carefully. War is one. Occupation is another. And perhaps the most evocative of them all is invasion.

An invasion, in the conventional understanding, is not difficult to recognise. There are soldiers at the frontier, aircraft overhead, tanks upon roads that yesterday belonged to somebody else. There are uniforms and maps and, sooner or later, graves.

Russia invaded Ukraine in precisely this familiar and terrible sense. Russian forces crossed an internationally recognised frontier. Missiles struck Ukrainian cities. Towns were occupied. Millions were displaced.

But Ireland presents us with a quite different and considerably more awkward question.

Can a country undergo something that its citizens experience as an invasion without a foreign army ever crossing its frontier?

Can demographic change become so rapid, and government policy so detached from public consent, that people begin to believe something fundamental about their country is being altered without their permission?

And if Irish people are asking that question, is the proper response really to call them names—or to answer them?

Ukraine itself has become the scene of difficult arguments about language, religion, political opposition and national identity during wartime. The Ukrainian authorities maintain that exceptional measures are necessary to defend the State against Russian aggression and influence. Critics argue that some restrictions have gone too far.

These are complicated matters. War has always had an unfortunate habit of turning complicated matters into slogans.

The same is true of those who have left Ukraine.

Not every Ukrainian arriving in Western Europe has come from a trench outside Kharkiv. Ukraine is a very large country and substantial parts of it are geographically far removed from the fighting. 

Some people have unquestionably escaped immediate and genuine danger. Others may have left for the mixture of economic, familial and personal reasons for which human beings have migrated since antiquity.

Ireland was entitled—and, in the case of people genuinely requiring protection, morally right—to offer sanctuary.

But there is a curious modern notion that compassion requires the suspension of curiosity.

It does not.

Sanctuary and accountability are perfectly capable of occupying the same room.

Ireland, after all, is not merely an administrative territory with a tax code attached to it. It is an old nation with an ancient language, a distinctive culture and a history in which sovereignty was purchased at an extraordinarily high price.

Generations struggled to preserve the Irish language and Irish identity. 

Men and women fought a War of Independence. Irishmen subsequently fought one another in a Civil War over the political settlement that followed it, my own family included.

It is therefore hardly unreasonable for their descendants to ask what obligations the sovereign Irish State owes to the Irish people when immigration occurs on a scale capable of producing substantial demographic and social change.

Nor is it unreasonable to ask who is paying for it.

And that brings me to a telephone call.

Earlier today, I telephoned the director of an Irish college seeking information concerning student finance and the expenditure of public money. I anticipated the rather mundane ritual familiar to every journalist: a question asked, an answer given where possible, perhaps a courteous refusal where it was not.

Instead, after approximately ten minutes, the conversation was brought to an end before I had been afforded a reasonable opportunity to put several questions which I considered matters of legitimate public interest.

My use of a withheld telephone number also became an issue.

This was peculiar. Journalists, politicians, businesspeople and millions of perfectly ordinary citizens withhold telephone numbers for entirely legitimate reasons. Privacy is not evidence of dishonesty.

More significant was the invocation of #GDPR.

I had asked for no student's name. I had requested no address, PPS number, bank details or other identifying information. I was asking about policy, procedures, numbers and public money.

Data-protection law exists for the admirable purpose of protecting people's personal information. It ought not to become a velvet curtain which descends whenever an institution is confronted with an inconvenient question.

And there are questions.

I understand that approximately 200 former students associated with the College may have received support under the PLC Bursary for Displaced Persons (Ukraine) Scheme.

Is that number correct?

How much public money was involved?

What payments were made to qualifying students? What funding, if any, was received by the institution in connection with those students? What checks were undertaken to establish eligibility?

And what mechanisms exist to identify and report suspected abuse?

Those questions acquired considerably greater importance after I was contacted by a person whom I can only describe as a whistleblower.

The source alleges that addresses in County Mayo may have been used in connection with applications for Irish pensions by relatives of Ukrainian students. 

I have further been told that some of those concerned may subsequently have returned to Ukraine; that some recipients may not reside at the addresses declared to the authorities; and that correspondence relating to State payments is allegedly collected on behalf of people who are elsewhere.

There is a further, very specific claim which requires investigation.

My source tells me that there is, in effect, a period of approximately twelve weeks between arrival or application and certain pension arrangements becoming payable, after which money and associated entitlements can allegedly continue to be paid through bank accounts even where a recipient subsequently unknowingly returns to Ukraine.

Is that true?

I do not presently know.

And that is precisely the point.

These are allegations, not findings of fact. I publish them here as questions requiring answers, not conclusions requiring applause.

If the twelve-week claim is nonsense, the responsible State authorities should say so.

If Irish pensions cannot lawfully be obtained in the circumstances described to me, they should explain the eligibility requirements.

If a Ukrainian obtains a pension and returns permanently to Ukraine, say what those requirements are and how they are enforced.

If checks exist, tell the taxpayer what they are.

And if payments have been obtained improperly, then somebody ought to explain how it happened.

I have accordingly sought comment from the Department of Social Protection, Student Universal Support Ireland and the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.

For behind these individual allegations lies the considerably larger matter of money.

Ireland has committed enormous public resources in responding to displacement from #Ukraine. Whatever one's opinion of that policy, there is one elementary proposition which should unite government and opposition alike:

Public money belongs to the Irish public.

It is not a slush fund for @MichealMartinTD, @HMcEntee  or any government to fund @ZelenskyyUa's war machine.

A “fifth column” is a group operating within a country that secretly seeks to undermine it, traditionally on behalf of, or in sympathy with, an external power or enemy.

If Ireland's governing political establishment is to be described as a pro-Ukrainian fifth column, however, the question requiring an answer is this: whose interests is it actually serving—Ireland's, Ukraine's, or somebody else's?

An individual belonging to such a group is known as a “fifth columnist.”

And from this side of the Atlantic, it seems to me that the Irish Government has surrendered far too much of Ireland's hard-won independence without a single shot being fired. If that perception is even partly justified, it should be ringing alarm bells throughout the country.

Ask yourself why the Government under Micheal Martin is neglecting the needs of its own citizens while committing hundreds of millions of euro to Ukraine and spending billions accommodating and supporting Ukrainians in Ireland.¹ 

Then ask your public representatives the same question: where do the interests of the Irish people come in?

My #whistleblower uses a much harsher description, referring to those whom the source alleges are exploiting Ireland's generosity as “vultures.” 

The allegation is serious; the question for Government is whether there is evidence of such abuse and, if so, what it is doing about it.

The nations wealth does not belong to ministers. It does not belong to civil servants. It does not belong to colleges. 

And it most certainly does not become the property of Ukrainians merely because the Government has established programmes intended to assist them.

Entitlement must depend upon law and eligibility, not Ukrainian nationality or political fashion.

So who cancelled accountability?

Every euro obtained improperly is a euro unavailable to somebody legitimately entitled to it: an Irish pensioner, a person with a disability, an Irish family struggling with housing costs—or, for that matter, a person genuinely dependent upon Irish protection.

And so we arrive again at that troublesome word: invasion.

Are Ukrainians landing at Dublin Airport an invading army?

Of course not.

There are no Ukrainian tanks rolling through Westport. There are no Ukrainian soldiers occupying government buildings in Dublin. To pretend otherwise would turn a serious argument into a caricature.

But that does not dispose of the real question.

At what point does demographic change, encouraged and financed by the State, become a legitimate matter of sovereignty, cultural continuity, public expenditure and democratic consent?

There is a temptation in modern politics to answer such questions by attacking the person who asks them. Call him xenophobic, racist, extremist, conspiratorial—and with luck nobody will notice that the original question remains sitting patiently in the corner.

Ireland should be more confident than that.

The Irish language survived attempts at suppression and centuries of decline. Irish culture survived conquest. Irish national consciousness survived incorporation into a considerably more powerful neighbouring state.

A country possessing that history ought to be capable of discussing immigration without hatred and national identity without embarrassment.

I confess that I once regarded much of the rhetoric about “population replacement” as the feverish product of the internet. 

I remain deeply wary of it, particularly when a complicated demographic question is transformed into a conspiracy supposedly orchestrated by some shadowy hand.

But Ireland's small population makes rapid demographic change a legitimate subject for serious examination.

How many people can the country accommodate?

What effect does immigration have upon housing, schools, medical services and welfare expenditure?

How much is being spent?

What safeguards protect the taxpayer?

How many recipients remain resident in Ireland?

And above all: who decided what level of change the Irish people were prepared to accept?

Those questions are not answered by producing another cheque.

Nor are they answered by moral indignation.

There is anger in Ireland. Some of it may be based upon misunderstanding or misinformation; some may prove entirely justified. 

The Irish Government's responsibility is therefore not to dismiss it but to establish the facts.

If Ukrainian relatives are being awarded Irish pensions after satisfying precisely the same statutory conditions as everybody else, publish those conditions and explain them.

If my whistleblower's allegations are wrong, establish that too.

Journalism should demand nothing less.

The Irish fought a War of Independence because sovereignty meant something. They endured a Civil War because the terms of that sovereignty mattered enough to divide families and former comrades, my own included.

A century later, nobody is proposing another battlefield.

But the descendants of those generations are entitled to ask whether sovereignty means merely possessing a flag and a parliament—or whether it still includes the right of a people to determine, democratically and transparently, the future character of their own country.

Ireland has not surrendered to a foreign army.

Across this side of the pond, one of my favourite phrases comes from the Preamble to the Constitution of the United States: “We the People.” 

How fascinating, then, to discover that the same great democratic principle finds its own distinctly Irish expression in Article 6 of Bunreacht na hÉireann, which declares:

“All powers of government, legislative, executive and judicial, derive, under God, from the people…”

There, in a few remarkable words, lies a principle that governments occasionally need reminding of: the people do not derive their authority from the State; the State derives its authority from the people.

But has the Irish State surrendered too much control over immigration, public expenditure and demographic change without adequately consulting the people in whose name it governs?

And who exactly are those people? 

Bunreacht na hÉireann answers that question in words which have stood since 1937: 

“We, the people of Éire.”

Article 6 goes further. 

The powers of government derive from the people. Government therefore governs in their name—not the other way around.

How long before a @MichealMartinTD or a @HMcEntee seeks to erase “the People” from Ireland’s constitutional conversation to make way for what one Ukrainian organisation calls the “Future of Ukrainian Nation” in Ireland? 

These are not my words, but the name chosen by Future of Ukrainian Nation (FOUN), based in County Kerry. 

The question Ireland must surely ask is unsettlingly simple: whose national future is Micheal Martin's Government elected to protect?

That is the question.

And rather than condemning those who ask it, perhaps somebody in Mr. Martin's government ought finally to answer it.

¹ Note: Official figures presented to the Oireachtas Committee of Public Accounts show expenditure on Ukraine accommodation of €1.165 billion in 2024, a provisional €719 million in 2025, and €607 million provided for 2026. In December 2025, the Government also announced an additional €125 million financial-support package for Ukraine.

AI Overview
Samuel Nicholas was not Catholic. He was born to a prominent Quaker family in Philadelphia and was raised in the Religious Society of Friends.
Background and Faith
Quaker upbringing: He was a member of the Arch Street Meeting House community.
Disownment: He was disowned ("read out of meeting") by the Philadelphia Quaker community in 1776 because he joined and raised troops for the Continental Marines during the American Revolutionary War, which violated the Quaker peace testimony.
Burial: Despite being expelled from the congregation for taking up arms, he was buried in Quaker fashion at the Arch Street Meeting House grounds.

For this morning's update I used a strict approximately 10-hour cutoff: 20:00 CEST yesterday to 06:00 CEST today.
The most consequential stories are not really about price.
They are about regulation, enforcement, market structure, tokenization and the gradual collision between decentralized infrastructure and conventional financial law.
𝗨.𝗦. 𝗖𝗥𝗬𝗣𝗧𝗢 𝗟𝗔𝗪 - 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗬 𝗔𝗖𝗧 𝗜𝗦 𝗕𝗔𝗖𝗞
At 22:38 Zurich time last night, https://t.co/4LWDuBMDKL reported that SEC Chair Paul Atkins expects the CLARITY Act to move forward in the U.S. Senate within roughly two weeks.
The key date is 15 September, when the Senate is scheduled to hold a cloture vote.

That is important language: a cloture vote is not final passage. It is a procedural vote on moving the legislation forward.

The bill matters because it attempts to create something U.S. crypto regulation has lacked for years: a more explicit division of responsibility between the SEC and CFTC, together with registration, disclosure and other market-structure rules.

If it advances, arguments over whether crypto needs regulation increasingly become arguments over exactly which regulator gets which part of it.

That is progress of a sort.

𝗡𝗘𝗪 𝗝𝗘𝗥𝗦𝗘𝗬 𝗪𝗔𝗡𝗧𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗨𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗠𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗥𝗧
One of the more interesting legal cases overnight has almost nothing to do with Bitcoin - but quite a lot to do with the future architecture of crypto markets.
New Jersey has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to resolve whether states can regulate sports-event contracts offered by federally regulated prediction markets.
Different federal appeals courts have reached different conclusions.
At the centre of the dispute is a deceptively simple question:
If an event contract trades on a CFTC-regulated market, is it federally regulated derivatives trading - or can a state still treat the activity as gambling?
That distinction matters far beyond Kalshi.
Prediction markets are rapidly becoming one of the places where derivatives law, gambling law, blockchain infrastructure and political-event trading collide.
A Supreme Court ruling could finally draw a national line.

Probably the most relevant overnight story from an AML/sanctions perspective:

The U.S. Department of Justice says crypto seizures connected with fundraising for Hamas have reached more than $560,000.

According to CoinDesk, FBI agents also took control of domains and servers, including https://t.co/cjJuYTrSJ1, in an effort to intercept donations allegedly intended for the Al-Qassam Brigades.

This is a useful reminder of both sides of the crypto-financial-crime debate.

Crypto can provide rapid, cross-border transfer infrastructure.
But public blockchains also create transaction trails that investigators can follow, cluster and ultimately connect with wallets, exchanges, domains and infrastructure.
For compliance teams, screening the name is only half the job. Wallet attribution, transactional exposure and counterparty-chain analysis increasingly matter just as much.

Kraken parent Payward has reportedly pushed its planned U.S. IPO back to the second quarter of 2027 at the earliest.
The company confidentially filed a draft S-1 in November 2025 but had already delayed listing plans as market conditions became less attractive.
That is interesting because crypto adoption and crypto-equity valuations are not necessarily the same trade.
An exchange can grow, regulation can improve and institutional adoption can deepen while the public-equity window remains unattractive.
Crypto may trade 24/7.
IPO committees, apparently, still prefer patience.

Solana is around $100.55 this morning, but the more interesting SOL story is happening below the price chart.
SGP-0002 has passed with 67% support.
The proposal doubles Solana's annual disinflation rate from 15% to 30%, while leaving terminal inflation at 1.5%.
That would reduce the estimated journey to terminal inflation from around 5.7 years to about 2.8 years.

SOL Strategies CEO Michael Hubbard argues the change is premature and unlikely by itself to have a measurable effect on SOL's price.

What I find interesting is the broader issue:

Changing token issuance is effectively monetary policy.

Except here the "central bank meeting" is a validator governance vote visible onchain.

Stablecoins are increasingly difficult to describe simply as "another category of cryptocurrency".

They are becoming payment rails, settlement assets, trading collateral and treasury instruments.

Which means the interesting questions increasingly concern reserves, redemption, custody, insolvency segregation, AML, sanctions and regulatory perimeter - not whether a stablecoin trades at $0.9999 or $1.0001 before breakfast.

Ondo Finance has asked U.S. regulators to accommodate perpetual futures tied to individual stocks under the existing security-futures framework.

Its Panama-based offshore affiliate reportedly processed around $8 billion in cumulative volume by 14 August.

The SEC and CFTC are now considering precisely the sort of questions that become unavoidable as securities, derivatives and blockchain infrastructure converge.

Is a stock perpetual a security future?

How should margin work?

Which market-data rules apply?

What happens when price formation and execution occur onchain?

Tokenization is moving past the comparatively easy question of "Can we put a representation of a security on a blockchain?"

The harder question is now:

Can we rebuild the market around it?

One theme ties several of this morning's stories together.

Blockchain is gradually becoming less visible.

That sounds strange, but it may be a sign of maturity.

OpenSea adding another chain is increasingly an infrastructure decision.

Ondo arguing about security futures is capital-markets law.

RLUSD growth is payments and liquidity.

Solana inflation is monetary governance.

The DOJ tracing wallet flows is financial-crime investigation.

The technology is still there.

But the interesting questions are increasingly legal, economic and institutional rather than "What is a blockchain?"

My read this morning:

The price action is almost the least interesting thing happening.

Bitcoin is basically flat. ETH is slightly weaker. A handful of altcoins are running. A handful of speculative tokens are falling.
But underneath that, something much larger continues.
Crypto is slowly moving from fighting for permission to exist toward fighting over the rules under which it becomes part of ordinary financial infrastructure.

Who regulates a token?

Who regulates a perpetual?

Who regulates a prediction market?

Who can freeze a stablecoin?

How do you screen a permissionless wallet?

How should a blockchain record ownership?

And what exactly happens when "onchain" stops being a separate financial sector and simply becomes another way financial markets work?

Those are much more interesting questions than whether Bitcoin moves 0.23% before breakfast.

text:
Michelangelo Antonioni on Actors and Acting:

"The film actor need not understand, but simply be. One might reason that in order to be, it is necessary to understand. That's not so. If it were, then the most intelligent actor would also be the best actor. Reality often  indicates the opposite.  

When an actor is intelligent, his efforts to be a good actor are three times as great, for he wishes to deepen his understanding, to take every  thing into account, to include subtleties, and in doing so he trespasses on  ground which is not his-in fact, he creates obstacles for himself.  

His reflections on the character he is playing, which according to popular theory should bring him closer to an exact characterization, end up by thwarting his efforts and depriving him of naturalness. 

The film actor should arrive for shooting in a state of virginity. The more intuitive his work, the more spontaneous it will be. The film actor should work not on the psychological level but on the  imaginative one. And the imagination reveals itself spontaneously-it  has no intermediaries upon which one can lean for support.  

It is not possible to have a real collaboration between actor and director. They work on two entirely different levels. The director owes no  explanations to the actor except those of a very general nature about the  people in the film. It is dangerous to discuss details. Sometimes the actor and director necessarily become enemies. The director must not compromise himself by revealing his intentions. The actor is a kind of Trojan horse in the citadel of the director.

I prefer to get results by a hidden method; that is, to stimulate in the actor certain of his innate qualities of whose existence he is himself unaware-to excite not his intelligence but his instinct-to give not justifications but illuminations. One can almost trick an actor by demanding one thing and obtaining another. The director must know how to demand, and how to distinguish what is good and bad, useful and superfluous, in everything the actor offers."

("Reflections on the Film Actor", Antonioni, Film Culture, 1961)

text:
Sargon was not the name given him at birth, but the throne name he chose for himself, meaning, as noted, "Legitimate King." It is a Semitic, not Sumerian, name, and so it is generally accepted that he was a Semite, but there is no way to know if this is true. Nothing certain is known of Sargon's birth or younger years. In fact, although his name was among the most famous in antiquity, he was unknown to the modern world until the 19th century, when his inscriptions and autobiography were discovered among the many texts of the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh. The Legend of Sargon of Akkad reads, in part:

My mother was a changeling, my father I knew not,
The brother of my father loved the hills,
My home was in the highlands, where the herbs grow.
My mother conceived me in secret, she gave birth to me in concealment.
She set me in a basket of rushes,
She sealed the lid with tar.
She cast me into the river, but it did not rise over me,
The water carried me to Akki, the drawer of water.
He lifted me out as he dipped his jar into the river,
He took me as his son, he raised me,
He made me his gardener.(Bauer, 95)
Akki adopted the boy and raised him as his own son. Sargon rose in stature at court to become the king's cupbearer. Scholar Susan Wise Bauer notes that, "ancient cupbearers were not merely butlers. The Sumerian inscriptions do not describe the cupbearer's duties, but in Assyria, not too long afterwards, the cupbearer was second only to the king" (97).

In his capacity as cupbearer, Sargon had the king's trust, but this was put to the test when a neighboring king, Lugalzagesi of Umma, embarked on a military campaign of conquest in the region. Ancient Mesopotamia (like ancient Greece) was dotted with many small city-states, all of which fought one another over fertile territory and water.

Lugalzagesi of Umma (reign circa 2358-2334 BCE) marched his army through the region of Sumer and conquered the city-states one by one, uniting all of them under his authority as the king Eannatum of Lagash had before him. He seems to have earlier agreed to leave Kish alone, but after conquering Uruk, he decided to move on Kish.

Bauer writes how, "Ur-Zababa, learning that the army of the conqueror was approaching his city, grew so frightened that he 'sprinkled his legs'"(97), a line from the literary work Sargon and Ur-Zababa. Ur-Zababa had grown suspicious of Sargon and, although there seems to be no evidence that the cupbearer had given him cause, decided to send him to Lugalzagesi, ostensibly with an offer of peace, to get rid of him.

Whether Ur-Zababa actually included in the message anything about terms and conditions is not known; what is known, at least according to Sargon and Ur-Zababa, is that the message asked Lugalzagesi to kill Sargon upon receiving it. For whatever reason, Lugalzagesi refused to comply and instead invited Sargon to join him. Together, they marched on Kish and took the city easily. Ur-Zababa escaped and went into hiding.

Precisely what happened next is unclear owing to the many legends that grew up around Sargon's life and reign over the centuries. It is possible that he had an affair with Lugalzagesi's wife at this point or that he was sent on a mission, which he turned into the first engagement of his own conquest of the region. Whatever happened between him and Lugalzagesi, they were as quickly antagonists as they had been allies.

Sargon marched on Uruk and took it. Lugalzagesi marched his army from Kish to meet Sargon in battle and was defeated. Sargon then put him in chains, tied a rope around his neck, and took him to the city of Nippur, sacred to the god Enlil, upon whom Lugalzagesi had relied, and forced him to march in humiliation through Enlil's gate. Sargon chose for himself the goddess Ishtar (Inanna) for his divine protector and, with both Ur-Zababa and Lugalzagesi out of the way, proclaimed himself king of Kish and swiftly subdued the region of Sumer.

The Akkadian Empire
Forming an empire is one thing, but keeping it operating is quite another. Still, in administration, Sargon proved himself as capable as he was in military conquest. In order to maintain his presence throughout his empire, Sargon strategically placed his best and most trusted men and women in positions of power in the various cities. The "Citizens of Akkad," as a later Babylonian text calls them, were the governors, clergy, and administrators in over 65 different cities.

One of his inscriptions reads: "From the sea above to the sea below, the sons of Akkad held the chiefdoms of his cities," and Bauer notes how, "In this kingdom, the Sumerians rapidly found themselves living as foreigners in their own cities...When Sargon took over a city, it became an Akkadian stronghold, staffed with Akkadian officials and garrisoned with Akkadian troops" (99). Sargon's placement of trusted officials drew the various regions more closely under his control.

Sargon cleverly placed his daughter, Enheduanna, as high priestess at Ur and, through her, seems to have been able to manipulate religious, political, and cultural affairs from afar. Enheduanna is recognized today as the world's first author known by name, and, from what is known of her life, she seems to have been a very capable and powerful administrator in addition to her literary talents. This arrangement worked so well that Sargon's grandson, Naram-Sin, would appoint his daughter to the same position.

The stability provided by this empire gave rise to the construction of roads, improved irrigation, a wider sphere of influence in trade, as well as developments in arts and sciences. The Akkadian Empire created the first postal system, where clay tablets inscribed in cuneiform Akkadian script were wrapped in outer clay envelopes marked with the name and address of the recipient and the seal of the sender. These letters could not be opened except by the person they were intended for because there was no way to open the clay envelope, save by breaking it, thus ensuring privacy in correspondence.

Sargon also standardized weights and measures for use in trade and daily commerce, initiated a system of taxation which was fair to all social classes, and engaged in numerous building projects such as the restoration of Babylon (which, according to some sources, he founded – though this claim has been repeatedly challenged). He also created, trained, and equipped a full-time army – centered in the city of Akkad – where, as an inscription reads, 5400 soldiers "ate bread daily" with the king. While this does not seem to be the kind of professional army later created by the Assyrian king Tilgath Pileser III (as it seems it was neither year-round nor kept in a near-constant state of mobilization), it was a great advance over the armies of the past, filled by unwilling conscripts.

Even with these improvements to the lives of the citizens of Mesopotamia, the people still rebelled against Akkadian rule. Throughout his life, Sargon would continually put down uprisings as city-states asserted their autonomy and rose against the empire. As the centuries passed, however, whatever difficulties the people had with Sargon's rule were forgotten, and all that was remembered were his heroic feats and the 'golden age' of the Akkadians. For the next 3,000 years, the Sumerians, Babylonians, Assyrians, and others would tell tales of Sargon of Akkad and his glorious victories, citing Sargon's own words from his purported autobiography:

In my old age of 55, all the lands revolted against me, and they besieged me in Agade but the old lion still had teeth and claws, I went forth to battle and defeated them: I knocked them over and destroyed their vast army. Now, any king who wants to call himself my equal, wherever I went, let him go!

According to the Sumerian king list, Sargon reigned for 56 years and died in old age of natural causes. If he had seemed larger than life to his people during his reign, he assumed an almost god-like status in death. Kriwaczek writes:

Up until now, civilization based itself upon the belief that humanity was created by gods for their own purposes. The cities, the repositories of civilization, were divine foundations, having started, we guess, as sacred pilgrimage centres. Each city was the creation and home of a particular god. It is as if 'real life' was the one lived by the gods in the divine realm while what went on down here on earth was a largely irrelevant sideshow.The age of Sargon and Naram-Sin altered all that, switched the focus to the human world, and introduced a new conception of the meaning of the universe: one that made people rather than gods the principal subjects of the Mesopotamian story. Humanity was now in control. Men - and women - became rulers of their own destiny. To be sure, people were still pious, still presented sacrifices to the temples, offered the libations, performed the rites, invoked the gods' names at every opportunity. But the piety of the age now had a quite different flavour.(119)

Legend & Legacy
The legends which grew up around Sargon and his dynasty were still being written, copied, and performed publicly in the last days of the Assyrian Empire (612 BCE), and the famous copper head of Sargon (found at Nineveh in 1931, making clear his importance to the Assyrians) is one of the most instantly recognizable works of Mesopotamian art. The story of the baby set forth in a basket on the river, who is found by nobility and grows up to be a great leader of his people, was used to great effect by the Hebrew scribe who borrowed it to write the biblical book of Exodus and the story of the hero Moses.

Sargon's story is the tale of the hero who rises from obscure beginnings to save his people. Whether he was seen as this kind of savior by those who lived under his reign is doubtful, considering the number of rebellions he had to put down, but to those who came after him, those who lived under the occupation of the Gutians (described by scholar Samuel Noah Kramer as demoralizing, destructive, and "a ruthless, barbaric hoarde"), he and his dynasty represented the glorious age of hero-kings which was now gone.

The tales of Sargon are thought to have inspired the Sumerians to rise up and throw off the oppressive Gutian rule circa 2050 BCE. Under the Sumerian kings Utu-Hegal and Ur-Nammu, the Gutians were challenged and, under Ur-Nammu's successor, Shulgi of Ur, were driven from Sumer, which allowed for the flourishing of the so-called Sumerian Renaissance of the Ur III period (circa 2112 to circa 2004 BCE). The two greatest Sumerian kings of the Ur III period, Ur-Nammu (reign circa 2112-2094 BCE) and Shulgi of Ur (reign 2094 to circa 2046 BCE), both patterned their public images after those of Sargon and Naram-Sin.

Conclusion
After Sargon's death, the empire passed to his son Rimush, who was forced to endure what his father had and put down the rebellions challenging his legitimacy. Rimush reigned for nine years and, when he died, the kingship passed to Sargon's other son, Manishtusu, who ruled for the next 15 years.

Though both sons ruled well, the height of the Akkadian Empire was realized under Sargon's grandson, Naram-Sin. During his reign, the empire grew and flourished beyond the boundaries even Sargon had attained. After his death, his son Shar-Kali-Sharri became ruler, and, at this time, the empire began to unravel as city-states broke away to form their own independent kingdoms.

Shar-Kali-Sarri waged almost continual war against the Elamites, the Amorites, and the invading Gutians while trying to hold the empire together, but it could no longer be maintained. The Gutian invasion has been most commonly credited with the collapse of the Akkadian Empire and the Mesopotamian dark age that ensued, and this was certainly the view of later scribes in ancient Mesopotamia who portrayed the Gutians as destroyers of civilization.

Recent studies, however, suggest that it was most likely climate change that caused a famine and, perhaps, disruption in trade, weakening the empire to the point where the type of invasions and rebellions that were easily met and put down in the past could no longer be managed as effectively.

Famine is alluded to in a later work of Mesopotamian naru literature, The Curse of Agade, which tells of the destruction of Akkad by the will of the gods. Whether famine, invasion, the wrath of the gods, or all three, the city of Akkad fell, the great kings were gone, and the empire passed into the legends which would be told, retold, written, and copied until the stories of what once was became all that was left of the Akkadian Empire of Sargon the Great.

Hey Americans! Escape Debt By Going To War With Iran!

Today in dystopia, war pundits have begun suggesting that the US could recruit sufficient troops for a ground invasion of Iran by offering young Americans debt forgiveness in exchange for enlisting.

I guess it was only a matter of time.

In an article titled “The war with Iran will not be won through airstrikes, so what’s left?”, the Jerusalem Post’s AJ Jaff writes the following:

“Recruitment numbers are running below what a ground invasion of Iran would require. Estimates for a successful ground campaign against Iran’s 31 provincial commands and its Mosaic Defense Doctrine run between 750 thousand and 1.5 million American troops. The current active US Army stands at roughly 452 thousand. The math does not work, obviously.

“Based on American history, however, there is a path forward. Not conscription or a draft in a world war-era sense, but enlistment through a ‘debt forgiveness program.’

“The average American aged 18 to 34 carries more than $40 thousand in non-mortgage debt across student loans, credit card balances, auto loans, and personal loans, with some estimates go as high as $100 thousand.

“This is the cohort the Pentagon needs. A federally administered debt-forgiveness enlistment program that fully discharges student loan, credit card, and loan balances after 24 or 36 months of service, and extends the GI Bill, would produce voluntary enlistment at scale.”

“This is not theoretical.

“It is the American state doing what the American state has always done when it needed staff it could not otherwise generate. World War II offered the GI Bill. Vietnam offered college deferments. The post 9/11 wars offered signing bonuses and citizenship pathways. The Iran war will need to offer debt relief. The economics of the indebted American 20-and 30-something make this the most efficient conversion mechanism available to the Pentagon and the Trump administration.

“The moral reading on this is uncomfortable. But states generate the soldiers they need through the incentives that work on the population they have.”

In a Twitter essay on the same subject published earlier this month, AJ Jaff used more blunt language:

“When the choice is decades chained to $45,000+ in debt, or a few years of service that erases it and hands you a clean start, a huge share of desperate young people will take the offer. Not because they ‘support the war’. Because the debt was engineered into a cage, and service is the ONLY door out.”

The Jerusalem Post says that Jaff is a Canadian who currently serves as the head of security for an unnamed “multinational organization,” describing him in his author bio as “a retired officer of the Canadian Armed Forces and a recognized expert in international security, crisis management, and geopolitical risk.” 

There isn’t much publicly available information about Jaff apart from this, and yet here he is being amplified by one of Israel’s largest English-language newspapers. So we can expect we’ll be seeing this idea pop up again elsewhere. 

It’s just everything ugly about the US empire all rolled up in one neat little package, isn’t it? Struggling American citizens strapped with mountains of bills because they live in a dystopia which plunges people into debt for the privilege of living on the planet they were born on, desperately enlisting to go kill people in an imperialist war of aggression overseas in the hope of one day getting their heads above water financially.

It just might be the most American idea anyone has ever had.

[Title: SHE IS A WONDER]  

[Verse 1] 
Who is the most dangerous woman in all the world?  Not the one with an army. Not the one with a throne. Not the one with kingdoms she can call her own.  She's the woman who lost her fear of losing, because Christ became greater than everything here.  You can't buy her. You can't flatter her. You can't frighten her back into line.  Her life is hid with Christ in God.  So what do you offer a woman like that?  Money?  It burns.  Power?  It passes.  A crown?  She knows another King.  

[Hook] 
SHE IS A WONDER.  WHO IS SHE  that looketh forth as the morning?  FAIR AS THE MOON.  CLEAR AS THE SUN.  TERRIBLE—>  TERRIBLE AS AN ARMY WITH BANNERS.  SHE IS A WONDER.  Not because the woman is great—>  BUT BECAUSE SHE KNOWS WHAT CHRIST IS WORTH.  

[Verse 2] 
She came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon.  She sought wisdom when other men thought they already possessed it.  But now she has read what Jesus said,  “The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it...”  And why?  “Behold, a greater than Solomon is here.”  Greater than wisdom. Greater than kings. Greater than every crown this world can bring.  So she doesn't play footsies with theological kings.  She has watched them measure one another with rulers God never gave them.  Everybody crowned. Everybody certain. Everybody talking.  Brother—>  she has one question.  [Silence]  WHO IS CHRIST TO THEE?  

[Hook] 
SHE IS A WONDER.  FAIR AS THE MOON.  CLEAR AS THE SUN.  TERRIBLE—>  TERRIBLE AS AN ARMY WITH BANNERS.  But whose banners?  “We will rejoice in thy salvation,  and in the name of our God  WE WILL SET UP OUR BANNERS.”  Banner after banner after banner—>  not bearing her name.  She knows whose Name goes on the banner.  

[Bridge] 
Some already tried to undress her.  Pull apart her words. Search her history. Measure her flesh. Tell the world what they think they found.  Brother— > “All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.”  She already stood there.  Naked. Opened. Known.  Before the Father and before the Lord Jesus Christ.  So put down your magnifying glass.  Because while you were trying to strip her bare—>  the Word was waiting to strip you.  King—>  take off your crown.  Scholar—>  put down your wisdom.  Preacher—>  leave your pulpit.  Rich man—>  leave your gold.  Queen—>  leave your title too.  Everybody naked.  Everybody opened.  Nobody gets a costume before the Father.  Now answer— > WHO IS CHRIST TO THEE?  

[Breakdown] 
That's why she's dangerous.  Not because she can destroy you.  Because the world's leverage cannot own her.  Threaten the flesh?  “This mortal must put on immortality.”  Offer her the world?  It passeth away.  Offer her glory?  She knows where glory belongs.  Offer her wisdom?  She found the One greater than Solomon.  Tell her to fear man?  “The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?”  There goes your leverage.  

[Final Hook]
WHO IS SHE  that looketh forth as the morning?  FAIR AS THE MOON!  CLEAR AS THE SUN!  TERRIBLE AS AN ARMY WITH BANNERS!  SHE IS A WONDER.  But look beyond the woman.  Look beyond the Queen.  Look beyond the banners.  A GREATER THAN SOLOMON IS HERE.  Not the Queen—> CHRIST.  Not the woman—>  CHRIST.  Not the wonder—>  CHRIST.  And in the name of our God  WE WILL SET UP OUR BANNERS.  So kings, keep your crowns.  Armies, keep the names of men.  She already knows the Name she marches under.  JESUS CHRIST.  

[Outro] 
Who is the most dangerous woman in the world?  The one the world cannot purchase.  The one fear cannot shepherd.  The one who knows her life is hid with Christ in God.  Fair as the moon.  Clear as the sun.  Terrible as an army with banners.  She is a wonder.  But Christ is her Wonder.

text:
My view is that five first-round picks sounds extremely harsh, and it is already at the highest level of punishment we have seen in NBA history. The Timberwolves were also initially stripped of five first-round picks in the Joe Smith salary-cap circumvention case.

But I still think the Clippers got off too lightly.

The Joe Smith case was straightforward. Smith himself signed below-market contracts to help Minnesota preserve cap space, with a secret agreement that would eventually lead to a deal worth as much as $86 million over seven years. Once it was exposed, the NBA voided his contract, stripped his Bird rights, and Smith became a free agent.

The Kawhi Leonard situation is different. His contract has already been in effect for years. He has been paid and has played under it. The NBA has now determined that Leonard violated the rules through the actions of his uncle Dennis Robertson, who was acting on his behalf. Yet Leonard was fined only $700,000, received no suspension, his contract remains valid, and he can still play and be traded.

That is where this starts to feel absurd to me. If this is how the rule works in practice, should players simply stop negotiating these benefits themselves and have family members do it instead? Your uncle, aunt, cousin — whoever. As long as the third-party income is not written directly into the NBA contract, what exactly is stopping this from becoming another recruiting tool?

What makes this even more frustrating is that teams around the league are cutting payroll, breaking up rosters, moving assets and sacrificing talent because of the luxury tax and the second apron. They are trying to stay competitive while operating within the rules.

But if third-party payments can be used this way, why would this stop with superstars? A team could theoretically pay a player $8 million on the books and then find another way for him or his family to receive millions more outside the salary cap. If that becomes an effective way to compete for players, then what is the point of having a salary cap in the first place?

This is why third-party payments are so problematic. NBA maximum salaries are defined by the CBA based on a player's years of service and eligibility. Once a player qualifies for a certain maximum, there is a limit to what teams can officially offer him. But if one team can also create millions of dollars in additional income for the player or his family outside the contract, that obviously gives him another reason to sign there or stay there.

If Kawhi did nothing wrong, why was he fined $700,000? If the Clippers did nothing wrong, why was Steve Ballmer suspended, why was the team fined $30 million, and why were five first-round picks taken away?

If the NBA itself has concluded that rules were violated, then how is this fair to every other team that follows the salary cap, luxury-tax and second-apron rules?

I also do not believe other NBA teams are unaware that third-party arrangements can exist. The real question is not whether teams know about them. It is whether they are willing to use them in a way that violates the rules.

If the teams that follow the rules are ultimately the ones being punished competitively, then who exactly is the NBA salary cap supposed to restrict?

text:
In Tennessee I watched a coach punt on fourth and one from midfield, and I heard a sound come out of ninety thousand people that I had heard once before, in a factory, when a machine had failed.

The ball traveled eighteen yards. The other team caught it. The stadium began breathing again.

Behind me a man in overalls spoke to no one and to everyone. He said, "You cannot punt there. You cannot punt there. You cannot punt there." He said it three times. He was not asking the coach. He was informing the universe.

His wife said, without looking, "Bill."

He said, "Not there, Denise."

I asked Denise later what her husband did for a living. She said, "Installs windows."

He installs windows. From sixty rows up and one hundred yards out, on fourth and one, he had known the correct call, and the coach had not, and the coach makes eleven million dollars, and Bill makes considerably less, and Bill was right. The next drive the other team scored.

Bill did not say I told you so. He did not need to. The whole section had already looked at him. He was the mayor of the section for the rest of the game. Strangers offered him beer. A child asked to sit on his shoulders. He was, briefly, everything a man of his station could ever hope to be.

At the end of the game Denise handed me a fried pie and said, "He was in the marines."

I said that made sense.

She said, "He was a cook."

Bill was a cook in the marines and knew more football than the coach and this is the most Tennessee sentence I have ever been told.

In my land, a lord does not receive advice from the sixty-third row.

Here every man in the sixty-third row is briefly a lord, on any Saturday, whenever the coach punts on fourth and one, which he never should, ever, Bill.

text:
Calvinism does not have a mystery problem. It has a sin problem.
James 4:17: if you know the good you ought to do and you do not do it, that is sin. That is God’s standard for us.
Now apply their own system without the word games.
God knows how to regenerate. On their confession He does not regenerate all. He “passes over.” He withholds the only thing that, in their system, can raise the dead. That is a known good not done. By the standard He gave creatures, that is sin.
“Creator creature distinction” does not save this. That is just Rules For Thee But Not For Me with a seminary accent. If “good” means one thing when a man leaves a drowning child and another thing when God leaves a man without the only grace that can save him, you are no longer talking about the same God. You are protecting a system.
They will quote “I will have mercy on whom I will.” That is lazy eisegesis. That is the Texas Sharpshooter. Paint the bullseye after you fire the verse.
Read the scene. Exodus 33. Israel has just built a calf. They think mercy is their ethnic property. God tells those stiff necked covenant people that mercy is His to give. He can bring in the people they wanted fenced out. Paul puts the same line in Romans 9 because the fight on the table is Gentiles in the mercy of God, not a prenatal damnation list. Romans 9 is not even a book Paul wrote. He wrote one letter. The chapter cut is late scaffolding. Rip 9:15 out, ignore 9:24, ignore 9:30–33, ignore chapter 10’s “whoever,” ignore chapter 11’s branches that can be grafted back if they do not stay in unbelief, and you can make the sentence mean TULIP. That is not exegesis. That is target practice on a barn wall.
While we are here, drop the other Sharpshooter texts too. “The end from the beginning” is not God meticulously decreeing every rape and every “voluntary” rejection. “My thoughts are not your thoughts” is a rebuke of paganized Israel, not a permission slip to say God did not mean what He said. That last move is the serpent’s move. “Did God really say?” becomes “this is what God really meant.”
Here is Calvinism in a nutshell.
God gives them the nature, the desires, and the preconditions so they will reject Him. They then “voluntarily,” with no other option available, reject what was never even offered to them.
That is a programmer loading impossible feed and speed into a CNC, watching the machine break the tool exactly as programmed, then smashing the machine and blaming it for voluntarily breaking the tool because “it is in the nature of the machine.”
The machine did what it was set to do.
In every version of this system Adam’s fall reaches all and God’s regeneration reaches some. Some is smaller than all. They will say that is decree, not weakness. Fine. Then say it plainly: the damage is allowed a wider census than the cure, and the same God authored the nature that made the damage certain.
If God authors all, He authored that nature. He authored the “voluntary” choice. He authored the passing over. Then He judges the output of the program He loaded.
You cannot make that consistent without the Unholy Trinity of Reformed Doctrine.
You beg the question. You assume exhaustive decree and classical pagan omniscience first, then hunt verses to dress the assumption.
You special plead. “Voluntary” means one thing for us and another thing for the man whose every desire was assigned before he existed. “Good” means one thing in James 4:17 and another thing in WCF 3. “Authors whatsoever comes to pass” and “not the author of sin” get to sit in the same sentence.
You violate A and Not A. God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, yet He does not author evil. The offer is sincere, yet the only means is withheld. Mercy is His character, yet passing over a known rescue is not a failure to do good. Compatibilism does not resolve this. It moves the contradiction one link down the chain and slaps “mystery” on the weld.
That is why there is no consistent Calvinism.

text:
Here is what your other thread said. Electricity is the binding constraint for the AI build-out. Data-center load is driving multi-year power shortages, interconnection queues, and a race for firm (24/7) generation. Nuclear, gas turbines, grid equipment, and on-site power are the immediate winners; large-scale fusion remains mostly private and years away from commercial electricity.

These are publicly traded companies with direct, current exposure. Rankings emphasize growth in generation, equipment orders, contracted load, and earnings/cash-flow visibility rather than short-term stock momentum. Scores are subjective assessments of company expansion potential and ability to generate/grow income (earnings + dividends/cash returns) as of late 2026. This is not investment advice—valuations, regulation, execution, and policy can change quickly.

1. GE Vernova (GEV)
Gas turbines, grid equipment, and electrification for data centers and utilities. Record backlogs (gas equipment well over 100 GW under contract/slot reservations) and exploding data-center orders make it the clearest “picks-and-shovels” play. High-margin service revenue follows every turbine sold.
Company growth: 94 | Income generating: 82
2. Constellation Energy (CEG)
Largest U.S. nuclear operator. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Meta and others) have signed long-term nuclear PPAs for carbon-free baseload. Post-Calpine scale and restart projects add capacity. Nuclear scarcity plus contracted demand supports premium pricing.
Company growth: 91 | Income generating: 86

3. Vistra (VST)
Large independent power producer with nuclear + gas fleet and long-term contracts (Meta, Amazon). Strong Texas/ERCOT and PJM exposure plus retail operations. Mix of merchant upside and contracted cash flow.
Company growth: 90 | Income generating: 84
4. Eaton (ETN)
Electrical equipment, power distribution, and data-center infrastructure. Data-center orders have surged (often 60–85%+ growth in relevant segments) with multi-year backlogs. Essential for connecting new load to the grid.
Company growth: 88 | Income generating: 83

5. NextEra Energy (NEE)
Largest U.S. renewable developer plus regulated Florida utility. Massive pipeline of new generation (including gas and storage) aimed at data-center load; long dividend-growth history. Scale and development capability are hard to replicate.
Company growth: 85 | Income generating: 88
6. American Electric Power (AEP)
Regulated utility with heavy transmission exposure and one of the largest contracted data-center pipelines. Capital plans have been raised repeatedly; load growth in Texas, mid-Atlantic, and Southwest is heavily data-center driven.
Company growth: 84 | Income generating: 85

7. Bloom Energy (BE)
Solid-oxide fuel cells for behind-the-meter / on-site power. Fast deployment versus multi-year grid interconnects; large Oracle campus deal and rising product revenue. Higher-risk, higher-growth profile than traditional utilities.
Company growth: 89 | Income generating: 72
8. Talen Energy (TLN)
Independent power producer with nuclear assets and expanding data-center offtake (Amazon and others). High projected earnings growth from contracted nuclear plus gas. More volatile than regulated names but closer to the demand curve.
Company growth: 87 | Income generating: 78

9. Vertiv (VRT)
Thermal management, power systems, and cooling for high-density AI racks. Direct beneficiary of rising rack power density (100–300+ kW). Strong order growth tied to hyperscale build-outs.
Company growth: 86 | Income generating: 80
10. Quanta Services (PWR)
Transmission, distribution, and data-center electrical construction. The physical build-out of lines, substations, and interconnects is a multi-year bottleneck. Recurring infrastructure spending plus data-center work.
Company growth: 83 | Income generating: 81

Notes on fusion and “Quantum Fusion”
Commercial fusion electricity is not yet here. Leading developers (Commonwealth Fusion Systems, Helion, others) remain private. A few public vehicles exist or are forming (e.g., General Fusion via SPAC, TAE/Trump Media merger still pending), but they are pre-revenue and high-risk. Established names above already participate in adjacent nuclear, grid, and high-temperature-superconductor supply chains.
Utilities and IPPs with nuclear or large contracted load generally offer the better combination of growth and visible income. Equipment and construction names offer faster top-line expansion but more cyclical or lower current yields. Diversify across generation, equipment, and regulated infrastructure rather than concentrating in any single name. Always check latest filings, offtake contracts, and regulatory developments before investing.

text:
A bomb is the last item on the nuclear shopping list. Before it come the facilities, enriched material, trained personnel, legal permissions. The Saudi agreement addresses these prerequisites, would not giving Riyadh a weapon, but would establish a negotiated route toward that capability.

The public language has been categorical, ie no enrichment, but the agreement reads quite differently. It prohibits enrichment during an initial study period, after which American companies and their foreign suppliers could build and operate a Saudi facility enriching uranium to 5%. A subsequent bilateral decision could raise that level to nearly 20%. Congress must pass judgment on the framework now (although it will receive no additional vote when the more consequential threshold is considered later).

20% sounds safely removed from the roughly 90% used in nuclear weapons, but uranium enrichment is nonlinear. By the time material reaches 20%, most of the work needed to reach weapons-grade concentration is done. The remaining 80% is a shorter road. 

Saudi Arabia could therefore acquire some of the leverage associated with a weapon without ever assembling one. And Mohammed bin Salman’s declaration that the kingdom would pursue a bomb if Iran obtained one gives that latent capability an unusually clear political context.

The arrangement would also alter the diplomatic climate of the region. Washington spent years treating Iranian enrichment to 20% as a serious proliferation threat. A Saudi pathway to the same threshold would give Tehran a ready accusation of unequal treatment. Turkey, Egypt and other governments would have reason to ask why they should permanently surrender an option granted to Riyadh. An exception offered to one capital soon arrives in another as a precedent - something seen again and again in nuclear diplomacy. 

No Saudi bomb need ever be built for the regional balance to change.

🇺🇸 🇦🇺 ANZUS just turned 75, but what Pete Hegseth and Richard Marles discussed today may be more important than the anniversary itself.

The U.S. and Australia agreed to accelerate cooperation on AUKUS and American force posture in Australia, and that posture is increasingly central to Washington's strategy for deterring China.

Australia offers something extraordinarily valuable in a potential Western Pacific conflict: strategic depth.

Guam and other major U.S. facilities closer to China could face enormous missile pressure in a war over Taiwan.

Australia sits much farther away, while still providing the ports, airfields, logistics, maintenance and infrastructure needed to project American power north into the Indo-Pacific.

That architecture is already being built. From 2027, HMAS Stirling in Western Australia is expected to host rotations of up to four U.S. nuclear-powered submarines and one British submarine.

American personnel are already there preparing the base. U.S. bombers, fighters and ISR aircraft are rotating through Australian bases. Marines operate from Darwin. Logistics, pre-positioning, cyber and space cooperation are expanding.

AUKUS adds nuclear-powered submarines, autonomous undersea systems, AI, hypersonics and other advanced technologies to the equation.

And Marles revealed today that Washington and Canberra are discussing further expansions of U.S. force posture beyond what has already been announced.

There is an interesting historical symmetry here: Marles noted today that around one million American servicemen used Australia as a base from which to project power north during the Second World War. He then added: That history “feels very pertinent today.” https://t.co/OkmviMRdqA
