text:
Rashee Rice | WR | KC: 2026 projection

Entering his fourth-year in the NFL, Rashee Rice steps into the 2026 season firmly entrenched as the primary target in the Kansas City offense. Last year offered a clear window into his ceiling, as he commanded a 29 percent target share and averaged 18.76 PPR points per game across eight appearances while playing on a 74.9 percent snap share. The underlying opportunity was elite, highlighted by 9.75 opportunities per game and 2.75 red-zone opportunities per game. That usage profile is now fortified by a significant offseason shift in the wide receiver room. Rice inherits a massive share of position room work now vacant at 38.5 percent, alongside 31.9 percent of team targets now vacant. The offense itself remains a high-end environment for wide receiver production, operating at 61.6 plays per game with a 4.0 pass rate over expected and a market-implied team points per game of 24.8. Patrick Mahomes needs a primary read, and Rice has already shown he can command volume at an elite rate. Recent games cement that alpha status. Late last season, Rice reeled off heavy target totals, including nine targets against Denver, twelve targets against Indianapolis, and another twelve targets against Dallas resulting in 29.4 PPR points. Even in quieter outings like the eight-target game against Houston, the baseline involvement stayed intact. Projections peg his volume at 7.96 targets per game with 2.8 red-zone opportunities per game, maintaining his status as a core offensive centerpiece. Yet, fantasy managers must weigh the risks tied to a medium confidence sample built primarily on one useful season of heavy usage. While his role as the projected starter and WR1 is secure, efficiency can fluctuate in any passing attack, and maintaining a nearly 30 percent target share over a full season is a demanding threshold. The schedule strength index sits at 0.971, indicating a slightly tougher than average overall slate of opponents against his position, which could occasionally test his efficiency. Even so, the sheer volume of vacated work and the quality of the surrounding offense provide a sturdy floor for a player entering his prime with true WR1 expectations.

What to watch:
• Monitor how the massive 38.5 percent share of vacated position room work translates into early-season target distribution.
• Watch his red-zone utilization to see if he converts his 2.8 projected red-zone opportunities per game into high-value touchdowns.
• Track his snap share to ensure it stays above the 74.9 percent mark he posted last season.
• Evaluate how he handles the tougher defensive matchups on the schedule given the 0.971 strength index.

text:
Why clean somebody's house for five dollars a day when two paintings bring fifty. That was Mary Ann Carroll's arithmetic, and she fed seven children on it, driving a 1964 Buick loaded with wet boards around a state where no gallery would hang her. Carroll is the one woman on the Hall of Fame list of twenty-six, and the woman who taught seven of the men on that list is not on it at all. Her name is in here, and you can carry it out with you.

An art room in a Fort Pierce high school in the early 1950s had no paint in it. Seven of the boys who sat in that room grew up into the Florida Highwaymen, whose roughly two hundred thousand paintings are known around the world for their color.

The teacher was named Zanobia Jefferson.

She taught them with pastels, because the school had no paints in it. Lincoln Park Academy was funded poorly and unequally against the white schools of the county, and she was not going to sit waiting on a delivery.

She had arrived in 1950 with her husband Robert, both of them hired at Lincoln Park, the school the county set aside for its Black children. She was brought in to teach science, and the building had no art department in it at all.

She built one.

The school had been open forty-four years by then and had spent every one of them short. It began in 1906 in an old school supply building on North Eighth Street, which is the kind of joke the record makes without meaning to.

In 1923 it ran eight grades with five teachers, and not one of the five had schooling past the twelfth grade. The county's own account of those years says teaching materials were scarce.

That is how a school system writes down that it sent nothing.

Florida at that point had no four-year high school for Black students anywhere south of Palatka. The families of Fort Pierce raised two thousand six hundred dollars out of their own pockets so their children would not have to stop at the eighth grade.

A four-classroom building went up in 1925 at a cost of ten thousand dollars. When new textbooks and furniture finally arrived in 1946, the local record marked it as almost unheard of for a Black school, which tells you plainly what the other years had been.

Into that walked a woman who had held a scholarship to the Art Institute of Chicago from the sixth grade through high school. She had gone on to Fisk University from 1944 to 1948, where no major in art was offered yet, and where one of her teachers was Aaron Douglas.

Douglas had put the Harlem Renaissance on walls before Fisk brought him in to build its art program, and she sat in his classroom.

So Jefferson knew precisely what a real art education looked like, and precisely what her students in Fort Pierce were not being handed. She started with what she had.

Pastels, a room with no paint, and boys who expected to spend their lives in the citrus groves and the packing houses.

One of them was Alfred Hair. The teachers liked him because he was personable and hungry to do well, and she could see what was already in his hands.

He was not serious about it at first. He had other things to do on Saturdays.

His mother asked her to take those Saturdays, and she said yes. She spent her weekends on a boy who had not yet decided he wanted them.

The town those Saturdays sat inside was split by the railroad tracks. The Klan marched in Fort Pierce.

Jefferson watched movies from the balcony and could not try clothes on in the white-owned stores downtown. She went about her business and kept teaching.

Then A. E. Backus, the white landscape painter who lived at the end of Avenue C, came to Lincoln Park and offered his services as an art teacher. The counselor who took the message called Jefferson, and Jefferson gave him a name.

She gave him Alfred.

Nobody wrote down the year. The accounts run from 1954 to 1958, and one version has her taking the boy across town herself on a school trip, which she also did with as many as a hundred students at a time.

The most consequential introduction in the history of Florida painting has no agreed date, because at the time nobody considered a Black teacher's decision a fact worth recording.

Jefferson was handing her best student to a white man on the other side of town, because that studio held everything her room did not.

Paint, canvas, instruction, and customers.

Backus had all four, and he kept his doors open to everyone, which in that county came close to defiance. He loved jazz, he was friendly with Zora Neale Hurston through her last Fort Pierce years, and he gave the teenage Alfred Hair a job stretching canvases.

Hair was the only one of them who ever received formal lessons from Backus. That one true fact has been doing enormous work ever since, because it is the fact everybody repeats and the only one most people ever hear.

By the time Hair graduated in 1961 he had done the arithmetic. Backus could sell a single painting for three hundred and fifty dollars, and Hair could sell ten for thirty-five apiece.

So he stopped painting like Backus and started painting like a man with a quota.

Upson board, a wallboard sold for construction work, tacked in a long row across a frame on the wall of a converted patio. His widow, Doretha Hair Truesdell, could still point out the line on that wall decades later.

They would tack the board all the way across, she said, and paint the sky all the way across, and then come back down through it. Twenty boards going at once, sometimes thirty paintings in a day.

He invented a way of dragging a palette knife that the others called fast grass. Frames were cut from crown molding and brushed with gold to look older than they were.

The oil was often still wet when the paintings went into the trunk, which is why those frames were built deep enough to keep the wet faces apart.

Then out onto U.S. 1 and A1A, to motels and banks and doctors' offices and anyone who would open a door. Hair kept a fleet of cars for his salesmen to borrow and drove a pink Cadillac himself.

He told people he would be a millionaire by thirty-five. He was moving around fifty paintings a week.

Jefferson was in her classroom on Avenue I through every year of it, teaching the next ones. The record of whose hands were actually on those boards is thinner than the record of whose names went on the front.

Several dozen paintings from 1966 and 1967 are signed Freddy, and for forty years nobody could say who Freddy was. Collectors traded theories.

The answer, when it came out in 2010, was that Doretha Hair painted the backgrounds and her husband came behind her and did the detail. Freddy was the two of them, and she is not one of the twenty-six.

Jefferson is one uncredited woman in this story and Doretha Hair is the second, and the group has not even been given a name yet.

Mary Ann Carroll never sat in Jefferson's classroom, but she grew up in the same Lincoln Park neighborhood and made the same calculation. She was sixteen when she saw Harold Newton painting in a yard, and eighteen when she sold her first one.

Why clean somebody's house for five dollars a day, she said, when she could paint two paintings a day and make fifty. She raised seven children on that answer, alone, taking night classes at Means Court School and driving a 1964 Buick Electra loaded with wet boards around the state.

Jefferson was on a teacher's salary at Lincoln Park through all of those years.

Al Black could not paint at all when he started. He was the salesman, the best one they ever had, working on something like a thirty-five percent commission and actively discouraged from picking up a brush himself.

His opening line at a stranger's door survives, word for word, because he was still saying it forty years later. Good morning, sir, my name is Al Black, I have some oil paintings, I want to know if you all would be interested if it wouldn't take up too much of you all's time.

That is a Black man on a white stranger's porch in the middle of the 1960s, opening with a promise not to take up too much of anybody's time.

He learned to paint by accident, and by damage. The wet paintings rubbed against each other in his car all day, so he taught himself to touch up the scratches, and repairing other men's skies is how he became a painter.

Jefferson kept teaching through all of it. Her former students were running an art industry out of backyards on Avenue D, and not one gallery in South Florida would take a single canvas.

On the night of August 9, 1970, Alfred Hair was shot and killed at Eddie's Place, a bar on Avenue D where the men gathered to settle up the day's sales. The next morning the Fort Pierce News Tribune carried it on the front page.

He was twenty-nine years old.

The versions of what started it have never fully agreed, and the fact at the center of them has never moved. Some of the painters put down their brushes and did not pick them up again.

The market cooled through the seventies and collapsed in the eighties, as tastes turned and Disney World reshaped what Florida was supposed to look like. Al Black had nothing left to sell.

Harold Newton, the most gifted of all of them, had a stroke that took his hands out of the work. He died on June 27, 1994, at fifty-nine.

Within a year of his death, a dealer named Jim Fitch published an article that gave the group a name.

He called them the Highwaymen, after the roads they had been pushed onto because no gallery would hang a Black man's work. Newton, who had been on that highway longer than anyone, never heard the word applied to him.

Jefferson disapproved of the name and said so at once. She had watched that highway get chosen for those boys by every door that closed, and she was not going to applaud it as a brand.

She went to every exhibition they held. She hung their paintings in her own house and answered every invitation to come and talk about them.

Al Black was not at those exhibitions. He had arrived at the Central Florida Reception Center in 1996, in the same stretch of months those first articles were running, on fraud and drug charges.

A nurse there carried one of those newspaper stories to Dr. Diane Rechtine, the prison's medical director. Rechtine called the patient into her office and asked him straight out whether he was that Al Black.

Doc, he told her, if you'll just let me paint, I'll show you.

They let him paint. He put Florida on the concrete walls of the place, ninety murals at that facility alone, thirty-five more at Zephyrhills, a handful at Tomoka, six at Hillsborough, well over a hundred in total before he walked out in 2006.

He said it made him feel like he was not tied down. He put three birds in the sky of almost every one of them.

Jefferson was retired in Fort Pierce through those same years, in her seventies, still turning up whenever her former students had a show.

He painted all of those walls as an inmate, which made every one of them the property of the state. Hillsborough Correctional later closed, and the state sold the site, one hundred thirty-five acres and roughly a hundred thirty-four thousand square feet of buildings, to a developer for three and a half million dollars.

Six Al Black landscapes were inside it, behind bolted doors, in the dust.

In 2004, two years before he walked out, Florida inducted twenty-six of these artists into the Florida Artists Hall of Fame, twenty-five men and one woman. At least seven of the twenty-six had learned their first lessons in an art room with no paint in it.

Her name was not on the list.

By then Jefferson had been teaching more than forty years. When Fort Pierce integrated, Black teachers and principals across the region lost their jobs, and she was among those who kept working, moving on to Fort Pierce Central until she retired in the nineties.

She was a sculptor and a painter in her own right. She stopped painting around 1983, the year Robert died.

The Smithsonian's own account of the Highwaymen has outlived her. It says the artists apart from Alfred Hair were not traditionally trained, and her name does not appear anywhere on the page.

One of that museum's object labels goes further and calls the whole group self-taught.

The director of the Backus Museum in Fort Pierce names that outright as a myth. It is well documented that several of them were her students.

The encyclopedia entry that millions of people read carries her name as a link to a page nobody has ever written. Click it and you are invited to go write her yourself.

There is a twenty-foot obelisk on Avenue D honoring the Highwaymen, faced with mosaic copies of their own paintings. The commission for it went to a white artist from Miami, which NPR reported in 2012 as a sore point in the neighborhood.

The work has always been worth having, and the hands have always been priced under it.

In 2003, thirty-three years after her husband was killed, Doretha Hair was still raising money to fix his grave. Alfred Hair's paintings were selling for thousands of dollars by then.

The grave is covered by a mosaic today, out at Pine Grove Cemetery, where Black and white burials were once kept apart. It is a stop on the walking trail now.

Jefferson is on that trail too. Marker number four, standing out front of the school that never had the paint.

So here is the errand, and it is a small one.

The next time this story comes past you with the white painter's name in it, add one clause before you pass it on. Not instead of Backus, beside him, where she has been the whole time.

Zanobia Jefferson died on January 2, 2016, at eighty-nine.

Four years before that, at eighty-three, a reporter asked her about the day she sent Alfred Hair across town. "I never knew, or had any idea," she said, "the far-reaching effects of that trip."

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXcAK
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

text:
September 3, 2015 —

『IS〈Infinite Stratos〉2: Love and Purge』 was released for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Vita in Japan!

🎉 Celebrating its 11th anniversary in 2026!

Based on Izuru Yumizuru's popular light novel series Infinite Stratos, this romantic adventure game follows the events of the “World Purge” story.

Several days after the World Purge incident, Ichika Orimura and the heroines of IS Academy find themselves facing another mysterious crisis.

Houki, Cecilia, Rin, Charlotte, Laura, Kanade, and Tatenashi begin training with a simulated World Purge system.

But during the training, an unknown program hacks into the system!

The heroines become trapped inside a virtual world and, even worse, lose their memories—including their memories of Ichika.

Ichika must dive into the virtual world to save them.

But each heroine is now living inside a completely different fairy-tale world!

📖 The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
🌹 Rapunzel
🧜‍♀️ The Little Mermaid
🌈 The Wizard of Oz
The heroines have forgotten who they really are and now live as characters within these stories.
Can Ichika restore their memories and bring everyone back to the real world?
The game features several unique systems.

💗 Brave Heart System

Your choices affect Ichika's “Brave Heart” parameter.

Make the right choices, strengthen your relationship with the heroine, and aim for the True Ending!

There is also a special:

💆 Communication Mode

where Ichika interacts with the heroines through his massage skills.

Successful communication increases the Brave Heart parameter and brings you closer to the True Ending.

And if you manage to save all of the heroines…

💗 A special Harem Route awaits!

The game also features an original opening theme, “Overflowing,” performed by Minami Kuribayashi.

The ending theme, “Sleeping Lover,” is performed by the main heroines Houki, Cecilia, Rin, Charlotte, and Laura.

With its combination of romantic adventure, virtual reality, fairy-tale worlds, familiar characters, and original story content, Love and Purge offers an experience that fans of Infinite Stratos couldn't get from the anime alone.

11 years later, it's a fascinating snapshot of the PS3/PS Vita era of anime-based visual adventures.

Which Infinite Stratos heroine was your favorite? ✨

text:
Once upon a time in the quiet coastal town of Eldridge Bay, where the sea whispered secrets to the cliffs and the wind carried the scent of salt and pine, there lived a young cartographer named Elara Voss.

Elara spent her days bent over parchment in a cluttered attic room above her grandmother’s bookstore. Maps of forgotten places covered every surface—coastlines that no longer matched the tides, mountain ranges that had shifted in old stories, islands that sailors swore existed only in dreams. Her grandmother, Mira, had taught her that every map held two truths: the one drawn in ink and the one hidden in the spaces between the lines.

One foggy morning, a sealed letter arrived with no return address. Inside was a single sheet of yellowed paper and a small brass key. The paper contained coordinates written in a hand that trembled: 47°12'N, 122°18'W, and beneath them the words “Where the tide forgets its name.” The key was cold and ornate, shaped like a tiny compass rose.

Elara packed a satchel with her finest pens, a waterproof journal, dried fruit, and the old brass sextant her grandfather had left her. She told Mira only that she was chasing a rumor of an uncharted cove. Mira simply nodded, pressed a warm loaf of bread into her hands, and said, “Bring back the story, not just the map.”

She hired a small fishing boat from old Captain Reed, a man whose face was mapped with wrinkles like depth contours. They sailed north under a sky the color of wet slate. For three days the sea was restless. On the fourth morning the fog parted like a curtain, revealing a narrow inlet guarded by twin pillars of black rock. The water inside was unnaturally still, reflecting the cliffs so perfectly that the boat seemed to float in a second sky.

Elara rowed the dinghy ashore alone. The beach was black sand mixed with fragments of white shell that formed strange patterns underfoot. At the base of the taller cliff she found a door—not carved, but grown from the rock itself, sealed with iron bands green with age. The brass key fit perfectly.

Beyond the door a staircase spiraled downward into cool darkness. Bioluminescent moss lit the way in soft blue-green. The air smelled of salt, ink, and something older—like paper left in rain. At the bottom stretched a vast cavern. In its center stood a circular stone table, and upon the table lay a single unfinished map.

The parchment was larger than any she had ever seen. Coastlines curved in elegant, living lines that seemed to shift when she looked away. Rivers pulsed faintly as if carrying real water. In the margins, notes written in many hands chronicled centuries of voyages, some ending in discovery, others in silence. At the very center a blank space waited, outlined in silver ink that refused to dry.

As Elara touched the blank region, the cavern filled with low voices—sailors long gone, explorers who had stood where she stood. They spoke of a place that moved with the tides of memory, a sanctuary that appeared only to those who mapped with honesty rather than conquest. The blank space began to fill itself under her fingertips. Mountains rose. Forests darkened. A small bay took shape, and within it a town that looked remarkably like Eldridge Bay, yet older, quieter, and somehow more true.

She worked for what felt like hours, or days. Time loosened. When the last line settled, the map glowed once and then lay still. The voices faded. In their place a soft light revealed a second door at the far end of the cavern—this one open, leading upward into daylight that did not match the sky she had left behind.

Elara rolled the completed map carefully and stepped through. She emerged on a high ridge overlooking a valley she had never drawn yet somehow recognized. Below, people moved with unhurried purpose. Children chased paper boats along a stream. An elderly woman who looked like Mira, only younger, waved from a doorway. The air tasted of possibility.

She spent a season in that valley, learning its paths, naming its stars, recording its stories in her journal. She taught the children how to read the wind in the grass and how to leave blank spaces on their own maps so wonder could still enter. When the season turned and the first frost silvered the leaves, she knew it was time to return.

The cavern accepted her again. The stone table was empty now. The map she had completed rested in her satchel, lighter than it should have been. Climbing back to the black-sand beach, she found Captain Reed’s boat waiting as though no time had passed. He asked no questions. They sailed home under stars that seemed closer than before.

Mira was waiting in the bookstore doorway. Elara unrolled the map across the largest table. The old woman traced the new coastlines with a finger that did not shake. “You didn’t just find a place,” she said. “You reminded it that it was allowed to exist.”

In the years that followed, Elara became the quiet chronicler of Eldridge Bay and the lands beyond ordinary charts. Travelers came seeking directions to places that could not be reached by ordinary roads. She would study their faces, then draw a single careful line and leave the rest open. Some returned with stories. Others never returned, and that, too, became part of the map.

One autumn evening, when the fog rolled in thick from the sea, a child appeared at the bookstore with a brass key shaped like a compass rose and a scrap of paper bearing new coordinates. Elara smiled, packed her satchel once more, and stepped into the mist, ready to follow wherever the tide forgot its name next.

The years layered themselves like transparent sheets of vellum. Elara’s hair silvered at the temples. Her hands remained steady. The attic filled with more maps—some finished, many deliberately incomplete. She taught apprentices the difference between accuracy and truth. Accuracy measured distances; truth measured longing.

On her seventieth birthday the sea sent an unusually calm morning. She walked alone to the old black-sand inlet, though no boat was needed this time. The twin pillars of rock stood exactly as they had. The door of living stone opened at the touch of her own weathered key. Down the spiral stairs the bioluminescent moss still glowed. The circular table waited, empty except for a single fresh sheet of parchment and a quill that wrote in silver.

Elara sat. She did not draw coastlines or mountains. Instead she wrote names—Mira’s, Captain Reed’s, the children who had grown and the ones still growing, the sailors whose voices had guided her, the quiet valley that had taught her to leave space. When the parchment was full she rolled it gently and placed it at the center of the table. The cavern exhaled, a long soft sound like the turning of a page.

She climbed back into daylight that felt both familiar and new. On the beach a younger woman waited—one of her former apprentices, now a cartographer in her own right, holding a small brass key. They did not speak at first. The younger woman simply offered her arm, and together they walked the path home as the tide began its slow, remembering return.

In the bookstore that evening the lamps were lit against the gathering dark. Maps covered the walls and tables and floor. Somewhere in the middle of it all, a blank space waited patiently for the next hand willing to fill it with care. Outside, the sea kept its secrets and shared them freely with anyone who listened long enough. And the story, like every true map, continued beyond the edge of the page, open to whatever came next.

text:
Pathum Thani Police Probe Officers’ Treatment of Couple Helping Drug User

Pathum Thani police have ordered a three-day investigation after a couple said officers at Lat Lum Kaeo Police Station were asleep and berated them when they sought help for a woman who had used drugs.

The couple found three women staying in a temple pavilion at about 2 am. Muang Pathum Thani police found methamphetamine pills, crystal methamphetamine and drug paraphernalia, arrested one woman and handed another to social services. The third was released because no drugs were found on her.

The couple offered to take the third woman to Lat Lum Kaeo Police Station so officers could contact her family. They said several officers were asleep and, when awakened, asked why they had brought her there and suggested they could be accused of unlawful detention. Video recorded outside shows an officer yelling at the couple not to post the footage and threatening legal action.

The officers’ response appeared inconsistent with government policy to identify drug users and refer them for screening and treatment. Provincial police chief Pol Maj Gen Peerapol Chotikasathien ordered the station superintendent to identify any officers who neglected their duties or spoke inappropriately, saying those responsible would face disciplinary action.

The ting most people miss about Abram (later named Abraham) is that he wasn't from Canaan. He was from Ur. This would have made him in all likelihood ethnically Kassite (possible relatives of the Hurrians) or Hurrian proper, Akkadian (unlikely), or even possibly Sumerian. This will be important later,

The Jews claim Abraham lived in the 20th century BC through the 18th century BC, but we know from the account of the Battle of Siddim (which will be important again later) that a Hittite king named Tudḫaliya (Tidal/Tudal in the Hebrew rendering) was involved, which means that the battle could not have taken place any earlier than the 15th century BC.

Abram (as he was still called at the time) is traditionally placed in his 70s during the Battle of Siddim. We know from Genesis chapter 11 that Abram's father, Terah, took his family from Ur to the city of Haran, in the Mitanni Empire, and that Terah died in Haran. Haran, a city ruled by a late Sintashta (Indo-aryan or Indo-Iranian) warrior nobility, with kings named things like "Artadhāman" ("His Abode is Ṛta"), "Citrarata" ("Whose Chariot is Radiant"), and "Priyamazdha" (Whose Wisdom is Dear"), is where Abram spent his formative years. this was the culture he grew up in. Mitanni was a majority Hurrian society which had been conquered by late Sintashta (Indo-Aryan or Indo-Iranian) nomadic warriors roughly 200 years before abram was born.

Abram, per Genesis chapter 12, didn't leave Haran until he was 75 years old, first going to Egypt, and then to Canaan. The Battle of Siddim takes place in Genesis chapter 14, where we are introduced to the Hittite king Tudḫaliya and the most controversial figurre in the Old Testament, a "priest of the most high God", Malkî-ṣed̠eq, or Melchisedech ("Righteousness is My King"). Theophoric names are common in Canaan at the time, but "ṣed̠eq" (righteousness) was not the name of any known god of the Canaanites, save for the Phoenicians, but they won't be an influential power for another two centuries at the time of this battle, being the rulers of a minor city-state under the rule of Egypt at the time.

Melchisedech is interesting for a few reasons. First is that he's a monotheist, which is highly unusual at this point in Levantine history. The oldest form of monotheism documented outside the Bible in this region is Atenism in Egypt, but Akhenaten its founder won't live for another century. Abram hasn't yet fathered the patriarchs of the Israelites yet, so archaic Israelite religion doesn't yet exist, so where does this ancient strain of monotheism come from? The literal Aryans. This was the time period in which the branch of Indo-European religion which would become Zoroastrianism was founded, and the same time in which the Indo-Aryan oral tradition which would later become the Vedas was positing that the gods were mere aspects of a supreme God.

The other interesting thing about Melchisedech is his connection to Christ. The Jewish priesthood traces back only as far as Aaron, essentially placing the founding of Israelite monotheism in the 13th-11th centuries, a few centuries after Abram and Melchisedech. Christ's eternal priesthood, and therefore the priesthoods of the Catholic and Orthodox churches, derives of course from His own authority as God Himself, but also from that of Melchisedech, as stated in Psalm 110:4 and quoted in Hebrews 7:17, "Thou art a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedech.".

While the "Salem" Melchisedech is king of is often equated with Jerusalem, the more likely candidate is a Palestinian town named Salim, about 5 days travel from Damascus, the southern most Mitanni held city at the time, by horse. Keep in mind that border regions at the time where generally thought of as being roughly 5 days in either direction from the closest city you controlled to your neighbor. This would have put Salim/Salem in the sphere of influence of the Hittites, the Mitanni, and the Egyptians, and made Salim fairly well disputed territory.

Abram also builds the second recorded altar in the Old Testament, after Noah built his following the receding of the Flood. Interestingly, Canaanite altars for personal use were almost universally for the offering of incense, and were always built into the courtyards of homes, while personal altars for actual *sacrifice* were a near universal feature of Indo-European homes, settled or nomadic. Abram, after the Battle of Siddim, speaks with a late Sintashta (Aryan) priest, and builds an altar of sacrifice in the manner of his Aryan homeland. This is the first act of true worship we see Abram offer to God.

Later, in Genesis chapter 23, we see the death of Sarah (earlier Sarai), and Abram, now named Abraham, needs to bury her. After the required period of grief, Abraham goes... to the Hittites, an Indo-European people. Saying that he was a sojourner among them, he asked permission to bury his wife among them. The Hittites respond that he is "a prince of God among us: bury thy dead in our principal sepulchres". This is odd, given that in ancient Indo-European cultures, such honors are not given to religious and cultural outsiders. We know from the Vedas and the Avesta that the status of "arya", that is, ethnic and religious kinship, is dependent on someone performing the proper rites and sacrifices. To be held in such esteem by the Hittites, Abraham's faith would have had to be not only recognizable, but familiar to his hosts. We can conclude, therefore, that Abraham was practicing some manner of Indo-European religion at the time. During this period, the various Indo-European cultures would not have diverged so much that they would not be able to find at least some familiar elements within each other's religious practices, while unrelated cultures would have seemed alien.

 Sarah died in Hebron, but her grave "Looked towards Mamre, this is Hebron in the land of Canaan". One cannot build a grave which looks toward, the land it is in, so Abraham must have travelled back towards his home in Haran (now firmly in Hittite territory with the collapse of the already shrinking Mitanni Empire into a small regional kingdom), and buried his wife among familiar people instead of alien Semites.

Abraham was an ethnic Hurrian who followed an early form of Indo-Iranian monotheism, making him Aryan by the standards of the literal historical Aryans. text:
I think the criticism here is missing the actual context.

These were people who lost their lives suddenly and tragically in the floods. Kala Bhairava is traditionally associated with protection from and liberation in the context of akal mrityu, untimely death. 

So performing a Kala Bhairava-related ritual for those who died suddenly is not inherently some attempt to declare Shiva or Kala Bhairava as an “independent supreme authority.” It is a ritual being performed in a particular context for a particular purpose.

And regarding the argument that this is “not Vedic”, Kala Bhairava worship belongs primarily to the Puranic and Agamic traditions, rather than being a practice found directly in the four Vedas. But “not directly Vedic” does not automatically mean “invented” or “concocted.” 

A huge amount of contemporary Hindu temple worship, deity rituals, festivals and traditions developed through the Puranas, Agamas, Tantras and other established Hindu traditions alongside the Vedic foundation. 

We should also be careful before calling someone a “so-called yogi or swami.” Just as there can be fake lawyers, fake doctors, fake politicians, fake officers and fake spiritual teachers, the existence of fraudulent people in a profession doesn't make the entire profession fraudulent.

I have personally seen many things Sadhguru has done and spoken about for human wellbeing, spiritual awareness and raising human consciousness.

 You may disagree with his philosophy or particular practices, just as people may disagree with ISKCON's approach, but that doesn't automatically make everything he does “concoction.”

Different Hindu traditions emphasize different paths, practices and philosophical frameworks. Vaishnava traditions may place Krishna at the center; Shaiva traditions place Shiva at the center; Shakta traditions place Devi at the center. 
There are deep philosophical differences between these traditions, and they can certainly be debated. But disagreement doesn't require dismissing another tradition as fake or spiritually illegitimate.

What matters here is also what was actually done. From what was announced, the Kala Bhairava Karma was being performed for people who lost their lives in the Nepal floods, and it was being offered without charging the families for the ritual. There was also humanitarian assistance being provided.

So instead of asking, “Does this fit my particular theological framework?”, perhaps we should first ask: 
Was help being given? 
Was a traditional ritual being performed for the deceased? 
Was anyone being exploited or charged for it?

We can disagree on theology without disrespecting another Hindu tradition or the people who are grieving.

After seeing your post, I also watched a video on YouTube where Sadhguru speaks about Krishna. He clearly says that Krishna is the complete incarnation of the Divine. So he is not saying that Shiva alone is the Supreme or dismissing Krishna's supremacy.

The statement that he is presenting Shiva as some “independent supreme authority” is your interpretation, not necessarily what he himself is claiming.

Spiritual traditions don't become false simply because they aren't identical to our own. 🙏🏽

And let’s not forget the beautiful traditional verse
Shivaya Vishnu-rupaya, Shiva-rupaya Vishnave;
Shivasya hridayam Vishnur, Vishnos cha hridayam Shivah.

And Aithareya Upanishad...

We are Hindus 
We are Sanatani's 
We love Our Dharma

text:
Thursday, September 3, 2026
 
 The Broken Alabaster: Poured Out for the Master
 
 Scripture Reading: IICorinthians 4:10-11 (“King James Version”)

10. Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body.

11. For we which live are always delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh.

Key Verse: John 7:38 (“King James Version”)

38. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.

Note to reader: All verses quoted are from "King James Version."

The core passage, John 7:38, is proclaimed by Jesus during the Great Day of the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot). During this feast, the High Priest carried a golden pitcher of water from the Pool of Siloam to the temple altar, recalling the water from the rock in the wilderness. Against this backdrop, Jesus announces that true spiritual irrigation—the Holy Spirit—flows not from ritual structures, but out of the innermost being (koilia) of the believer.

The complementary narrative from Matthew 26:6–13 features Mary of Bethany breaking her alabaster box of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and pouring it on His head.

Core Theological Themes

The Anti-Self-Realization Principle: Modern spiritual trends emphasize personal fulfillment and self-actualization. Chambers sharply contrasts this with the Gospel: Christ calls the believer to a process of spiritual depletion for His glory.

The "Squeezed Grape" Metaphor: Jehovah does not preserve the believer as a whole, admired specimen. The life of Christ must be crushed like grapes in a winepress so that the sweet wine of the Spirit can flow to others.

The Economy of Holy Waste: The world—and often worldly minded disciples (Matthew 26:8)—evaluates spiritual devotion by functional efficiency and cost. Christ evaluates devotion by total surrender, deeming acts of pure sacrifice as "a good work" (kalon ergon).

The Crushing Before the Flowing

We spend much of our lives guarding our alabaster boxes. We polish the exterior of our talents, our reputations, and our spiritual blessings, keeping them intact for display. But the Lord Jesus Christ has no interest in static beauty. He seeks a vessel that is willing to be shattered.

Consider the vintage of the Kingdom. A grape remains useless to the thirsty traveler as long as it preserves its shape upon the vine. It must be plucked, placed in the press, and crushed until every drop of its life passes out. True spiritual power is never born of self-preservation; it is the child of sacrifice.

The Joy of Holy Abandonment

When Mary entered the house in Bethany, she did not measure her offering by drops. She broke the box. The fragrance filled the room, and immediately the voices of calculation arose: "To what purpose is this waste?" (Matthew 26:8).

Let the world call your devotion waste! When you abandon your life completely to Christ, calculating neither cost nor return, the Master is crowned with joy. He does not ask you to store up His blessings as stagnant pools, but to let Him pour them out through you until hundreds are refreshed by the overflow.

Voices of Inspiration

Pastor Charles Spurgeon: The Prince of Preachers

"If Christ be anything, He must be everything. Oh, to be eaten up for Christ! To have our whole nature consumed by the flaming fire of love to Him!"

Pastor Spurgeon urges us to remember that Mary’s ointment was not wasted because it landed on the head of the Savior. Whatever is surrendered to Jesus is placed in the only secure vault in the universe. If you pour your life out at His feet, you haven't lost it; you have given it its eternal purpose.

Pastor Oswald Chambers: The Refiner’s Flame

"God can achieve His purpose through the total ruin of a human life."

Chambers reminds us that spiritual success cannot be measured by human metrics, credentials, or visible achievements. The true test of a Christian life is simple: Is Jesus Christ getting His way in you, or are you still holding onto your own spiritual self-realization?

Pastor William Branham: The Deep Calling Unto Deep

"You must be willing to lay everything on the altar until there is nothing left of yourself, only Christ living in you."

A vessel must be entirely empty before the power of the Holy Spirit can fill it without obstruction. When self is thoroughly crucified, the "rivers of living water" flow unrestricted from the inner sanctuary of the believer.

Scriptural Array for Meditation

John 12:24"Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit."

Philippians 2:17"Yea, and if I be offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I joy, and rejoice with you all."

Romans 12:1"I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service."

Daily Practical Application

1. Morning Surrender And Relinquishment

Begin your morning by handing your agenda over to Jehovah before the day begins. Pray: "Lord, I break my plans at Your feet today. Use me, spend me, or set me aside as it pleases You."Intentionally release your right to an uninterrupted schedule.

2. Welcoming the Midday Crushing 

When interruptions, criticisms, delays, or uncomfortable circumstances cross your path, reframe your response. View these moments not as annoying hazards, but as the crushing press of Jehovah designed to extract the sweetness of Christ’s patience and character from your life.

3. Practicing Anonymous Ministry

 Perform at least one deliberate act of extravagant service or encouragement today without seeking recognition, praise, or acknowledgment from others. Let it be a private poured-out offering reserved strictly for the eyes of the Master.

Questions And Answers

Q1: Why did the disciples consider Mary’s act of devotion to be a "waste?"

The disciples viewed the situation through human economics and functional utility. The ointment was valued at three hundred pence—nearly a full year's wages. They saw an immediate material problem (poverty) and believed the money should meet that functional need. They failed to recognize that worship directly offered to the Son of Jehovah transcends all temporal utility.

Q2: What does it mean that Jesus's teaching is "anti-self-realization?"

Modern culture teaches individuals to discover, build, and express their personal identity for self-actualization. Jesus teaches the opposite: "He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it" (Matthew 10:39). His goal is not to refine our natural ego, but to crucify it so that the resurrection life of Christ may take its place.

Q3: How can a believer know if living water is flowing out of them?

The evidence of living water flowing is not personal self-satisfaction or visible success, but the spiritual refreshment of those around you. When people leave your presence drawn closer to Christ, refreshed in spirit, or conviction-led toward holiness, the rivers are flowing.

Prayer 🙏: Shatter My Alabaster Box
 
My merciful,omnipotent, and sovereign Heavenly Father, I come before You acknowledging how easily I fall into the trap of self-preservation.  Forgives us of our transgressions Jesus Christ.  I confess that I spend so much of my life guarding my alabaster boxes—protecting my pride, curating my reputation, and polishing the exterior of my talents and spiritual blessings just to keep them safe, intact, and on display for others to admire.

Forgive me for clinging to static beauty and safe religion. I recognize today that You do not seek a polished ornament to sit on a shelf; You seek a vessel willing to be broken at Your feet. Lord Jesus, I yield my life to You. Break through my need for control, my desire for approval, and my fear of being poured out.

Shatter my alabaster box, Lord. Let whatever fragrance is stored within my heart be spilled entirely for Your glory and the blessing of those around me. I hold nothing back. Consume my life, crush my self-reliance, and let the living waters of Your Holy Spirit flow through my brokenness today.  I love You son much, Abba Father, and I offer myself to You through Yeshua HaMashiach, my Lord, Master, and Savior. Amen.

Adapted from Oswald Chambers, "My Ultimate for His Highest.  The classic daily devotional."

Your ignorance reflects your lack of education. This is not surprising. 

1947–49 was not a one-way expulsion. The UN partition plan of November 1947 proposed two states. Jewish leadership accepted it. Arab leadership and the surrounding states rejected it and immediately launched attacks on Jewish communities. Civil war started the next day. 

When Israel declared independence in May 1948, five Arab armies invaded with the explicit aim of preventing a Jewish state. Palestinian displacement (flight + expulsion + fear after massacres like Deir Yassin + some Arab evacuation orders) happened inside that war. 

At the same time, roughly 800,000–850,000 Jews were driven out of or fled Arab countries; most were absorbed by Israel. That parallel displacement is almost always omitted in the Nakba-only framing. 

1967 was not an unprovoked land grab. Egypt closed the Straits of Tiran (a recognized casus belli [cause for war]), expelled UN peacekeepers from Sinai, massed troops, and broadcast annihilation rhetoric. 

Soviet intelligence fed Syria a false report of an imminent Israeli attack. Israel struck first, but after those steps. Jordan joined despite Israeli warnings. The result was occupation of the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai, and Golan. That occupation is real and has produced settlements, checkpoints, and restrictions. It did not appear in a vacuum after “peaceful coexistence.” Arab states issued the Khartoum “three noes” (no peace, no recognition, no negotiation) immediately afterward. 

Hamas is not just “resistance that appeared 40 years later.” It was founded in 1987 during the First Intifada, yes. Its 1988 charter is not a document about ending occupation of 1967 lines. 

It calls for the destruction of Israel, frames the conflict as a religious duty of jihad, cites antisemitic tropes, and rejects negotiations. Hamas has spent decades attacking civilians (suicide bombings, rockets, October 7) while also providing social services that built popularity. Gaza is not “occupied” in the same way as the West Bank: Israel removed every settlement and soldier in 2005. Hamas won the 2006 election, then seized Gaza by force in 2007 and turned it into a launch pad. 

October 7 was launched from territory Israel had already left. 
Polls matter here. Large shares of Palestinians (often majorities in the West Bank, substantial minorities in Gaza) have described the October 7 attack as “correct.” Support for Hamas has fluctuated with events but has been high enough, repeatedly, that the “Gazans supported Hamas’s attacks” claim is not invented. That does not mean every civilian in Gaza is a combatant or “deserves” anything. It does mean treating the population as having zero agency or political preference is also one-sided. 

Jewish historical connection is not a 19th-century colonial invention. There was a continuous Jewish presence in the land for centuries after the Roman exile, documented archaeologically and in contemporary sources. Zionism was a modern nationalist movement responding to persecution, but it was not landing on empty or exclusively Arab soil. Both peoples have deep claims. Pretending only one side has a “homeland” being “slowly taken” erases that.

None of this makes the occupation painless, settlements uncontroversial, or Palestinian civilian deaths acceptable. 

It does mean your ignorant version—“Israel started taking the land in 1948, occupied everything in 1967, then Hamas merely fought back decades later”—leaves out the wars Arab states started.

The rejection of partition and later peace offers, the Jewish refugees. 

Hamas’s actual ideology, and the 2005 Gaza withdrawal. 

Both narratives that start the clock only at their preferred atrocity are incomplete. The conflict is a long chain of rejection, terror, occupation, and retaliation, not a morality play with one original aggressor.

text:
Happy Birthday, Alan Ladd.

A major box office draw in the 1940s and early 50s, the diminutive Ladd was the star of both classic noirs and and Westerns, while his screen partnership with the 4 ft 11 Veronica Lake made him one of Hollywood’s most popular leading men. Born in Arkansas, on September 3, 1913, he was given a long-term contract with Universal in 1933, but the studio eventually decided he was too short, and dropped him after six months. One night, Ladd was playing the roles of a father and son on the radio when his performance was heard by the agent Sue Carol. Impressed by his talent and his looks, she signed the actor and enthusiastically promoted him. Ladd's first notable role was in the 1939 film “Rulers of the Sea”. He tested unsuccessfully for the lead in “Golden Boy” (1939), but soon won other parts. Paramount had owned the rights to “A Gun for Sale”, a novel by Graham Greene, since 1936, but waited until 1941 before filming it, changing the title to “This Gun for Hire”. Director Frank Tuttle was struggling to find a new actor to play the role of Raven, a hit man with a conscience. Ladd auditioned successfully, and Paramount signed him to a long-term contract in 1941. According to author David Thomson: ‘Once Ladd had acquired an unsmiling hardness, he was transformed from an extra to a phenomenon. His calm, slender ferocity make it clear that he was the first American actor to show the killer as a cold angel,’ while his rapport with the entrancing Veronica Lake captured the public imagination. His next film was “The Glass Key” (1942), again with Lake. Now a star, he had a cameo spoofing his tough guy image in “Star Spangled Rhythm” which featured most of Paramount's stars, and then appeared in “China” (1943) with Loretta Young. Young did not like working with Ladd: “I don't remember hearing him laugh, or ever seeing him laugh. He wouldn't look at me. I think he was very conscious of his looks. He would not look beyond a certain point in the camera because he didn't think he looked good... Jimmy Cagney was not tall but somehow Jimmy was at terms with himself. I don't think Alan Ladd ever came to terms with himself.” After Ladd’s war service, Paramount commissioned Raymond Chandler to write an original screenplay for him titled “The Blue Dahlia” and the film was released to great acclaim. It was followed by “O.S.S” and “Two Years Before the Mast”. The latter was a blockbuster, earning over $4 million. In 1947, Ladd was ranked among the top 10 most popular stars in the U.S. His next role was in the 1949 version of “The Great Gatsby”, but it was not a success. In February 1950, Paramount announced that Ladd would star in a film version of the novel “Shane”. “Shane”, an iconic Western in which he played the silent, courageous title character, was a huge hit. Ladd went freelance, but his instinct for choosing material was poor: George Stevens offered him the role of Jett Rink in “Giant” (1956), which he turned down because it was not the lead; James Dean took the part, and the film became one of the successes of the decade. Ladd retired from acting in 1963. On November 2, 1962, he was found lying unconscious with a bullet wound near his heart. After coming round he said he thought he had heard a prowler, grabbed a gun, and tripped over, accidentally shooting himself. In truth, Ladd was a depressive with an increasing dependence on alcohol. Nor did he ever get over his lack of height, which was 4 ft 6. In his memoirs, actor/producer John Houseman wrote of Ladd: "Since he himself was extremely short, he had only one standard by which he judged his fellow players: their height.” On January 29, 1964, Ladd was found dead on his bed after an accidental overdose of alcohol, anti-depressants and barbiturates. He was only 50.

Greeting Mayor Randy Westlund 

Thank you for asking. 

Kratom, nor its semi synthetic derivative 7OH should be banned. 

Strict regulation while preserving access is essential. 

Kratom and 7-Hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) helps millions of people for pain relief and harm reduction. 7OH while more potent than Kratom also offers therapeutic benefit for moderate to severe pain when utilized responsibly. Too many chronic pain patients have been abandoned, force tapered or have barriers to accessing pain care or any care at all. 

Cuts to Medicare and Medicaid leave people without being able to access or afford acute or chronic care services and when they can they’re still left with high deductibles or copay’s that prevent them from seeking services. Those with other health insurance plans face the same dilemma. Affordability or not being able to establish care.

I began taking Kratom regularly on Mother’s Day of 2019. It became my life preserver. In April of 2024, I began using micro doses, minute servings of 7OH for analgesia. 

I didn’t have any medical care for 10 years until approximately 6 weeks ago. I suffer with incurable illnesses, rare diseases and disabilities that limit my ability.  I have Major depression and anxiety disorders. Managing chronic illness can be difficult day after day. One of my conditions is Complex Regional Pain Syndrome, also known as the suicide disease due to its unrelenting and debilitating nature. 

Small therapeutic servings of 7OH helped me greatly. I was able to increase my limited weight bearing capabilities and enjoy time with my grandchildren. 

Due to my husband and I both having poor health, we moved in with our Son and his family just 9 months ago. 

While I’m not well, I’ve done much better and have been able to take my 2 year old granddaughter out to play a couple of times a day. 

I lived off a day bed prior. 
I’m able to smile.
Laughter finds me,
And living isn’t so hard to bear.

September is suicide prevention and awareness month. It’s also chronic pain awareness month. 

I’m a multi attempt suicide survivor. I live in pain every day, but now I’ve been able to cope with it, and feel the joy of the Lord and my grandchildren. I’m able to contribute again. 

Please keep Kratom alkaloids and derivative legal. Safe guards and oversight will go a long way in ensuring adults retain the right to choose and save their own lives.

Regulation and education not prohibition. 

Feel welcome to contact me if you have any questions. 

Respectfully, Twinkle VanFleet, Patient Advocate and Community Manager- 14th Ave Baptist Church, Elk Grove, California.

Actress #LizaSoberano is taking on a prestigious new role beyond acting as she joins the jury for the Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary at the upcoming Venice Film Festival.

In a social media post on Thursday, Soberano shared the news alongside an exclusive report from international entertainment news website Variety.

“Honored to be joining the jury for the Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary at the Venice Film Festival. Grateful to be part of a celebration of powerful storytelling and the filmmakers who bring important stories to light,” she captioned the post.

According to the report, the prize was founded by the Golden Globes and Artemis Rising Foundation, with support from Think-Film Impact Production. It honors a documentary feature film in the festival’s official selection, whether in or out of competition, that exemplifies the power of documentary filmmaking to illuminate important social issues through compelling storytelling.

“I’ve always believed that film has the power to do more than entertain—it can challenge injustice, offer safety, inspire hope and remind us of our shared humanity,” Soberano said.

“Documentary filmmaking is where some of the most courageous and unforgettable storytelling is happening today. I’m honored to serve on this jury, because celebrating documentary filmmakers isn’t only about recognizing extraordinary talent; it’s where the future of cinema is heading,” she added.

Soberano, who moved from California to the Philippines as a child, built a stellar career in the country before crossing over to Hollywood, making her international film debut in Focus Features’ “Lisa Frankenstein” in 2024.

She is also set to lend her voice to DreamWorks Animation’s upcoming film “Forgotten Island,” which is scheduled for release in September.

Beyond her creative work, Soberano is an active ambassador for Save the Children Philippines and an advocate for women and children’s rights, the protection of children from online sexual exploitation, and mental health.

(✍️ Kiko Escuadro 📸 Liza Soberano / Instagram)

My ABC Wide World of Sports story: I was coming home from visiting my favorite aunt in San Diego. Mom worked for Eastern Airlines at the time, so I got first class both ways flying standby. (Loved that perk, BTW.) They were showing the same episode of WWoS that I'd watched on the way out, a surfing contest in Hawaii.

Of course I talked with the guy next to me on the way home. He found me very amusing because I was young, in college, and super-liberal, and he was about ten years older and a wealthy businessman already. He told me which surfer he thought would win. "Nah," I said. "It's going to be a different one." I remembered the winner from the flight out.

"Twenty bucks says you're wrong," he told me. I told him I didn't really bet much, he kept pushing, finally, I shrugged and said okay.

My surfer wins, businessman looks surprised and starts to get his wallet out. I stop him, tell him the truth, he laughs when he finds out I hustled him.

Upshot of that trip: My dad wasn't home when we landed, The businessman passed by the phone booth where I was waiting, asked if I had a ride home. When I said no, Dad was out, he offered a ride in his limo. Nice guy. I accepted. A free limo ride was better than a hustled twenty, if you ask me.

text:
🌹Pope Saint Gregory the Great, Ora pro nobis🌹

Feast Day - Sept 3
Pope Saint Gregory I, also known as the Great, was the Pope of the Catholic Church between 590 and 604 AD.

Gregory was born around 540 in Rome. The exact date of his birth is unknown. Although the Western Roman Empire had collapsed long before his birth, many ancient Roman families still commanded great wealth and influence in the city. Gregory was born into one such family. His great-great-grandfather was Pope Felix III who reigned from 483 to 492. (Astute readers may suspect this to be a scandal, but this was at a time before the clergy took vows of celibacy.)

His father was named Gordianus, and he was a senator and a Prefect of Rome. Gordianus also held a position in the Church with the title of Regionarius, but there are no records from the time which describe the post. Gregory's mother was Silvia, also from a noble family. Silvia's sister (Gregory's aunt), Pateria are both recognized as saints in the Catholic and Orthodox churches. Gregory had a brother, but nothing is recorded, neither his name or his fate.

Gregory's family was very wealthy and owned estates on the island of Sicily which provided income.

When Gregory was just two years old in 542, the Plague of Justinian swept through the region. This plague was caused by a now-extinct strain of Yersinia Pestis, more commonly known as the Black Death. The plague was the most severe outbreak of deadly disease the world had ever known and remained the worst such incident until the Black Death in the 14th century. About a third of the population in Italy was wiped out by the disease.
In addition to disease, the barbarian Ostrogoths sacked Rome in 546. The Franks attempted an invasion in 554. Both of these incursions were short lived. It is unclear how these massive events impacted Gregory's development as a child, but it is thought his family retreated to Sicily during part of that time. Peace followed in Italy after these upheavals.

Gregory was well educated and excelled in all his studies. He also became an expert in law. He excelled so much he became the Prefect of Rome, just as his father had been. Gregory was only 33 years old.

After Gregory's father had died, Gregory had the family villa in Rome converted into a monastery. Today the monastery still stands as the San Gregorio Magno al Celio. This famous monastery fell into ruin in the following centuries but was restored during the 17th and 18th centuries.

As a monk, Gregory was hard and strict. When a monk on his deathbed confessed to stealing three pieces of gold, Gregory ordered he be left to die alone. After the poor monk had died, Gregory ordered his body thrown on a dung heap along with the three coins. Then, in a turn of heart, Gregory offered 30 Masses for the deceased monk.

Pope Pelagius II, who reigned from 579 to 590, chose Gregory to serve as an ambassador to the imperial court in Constantinople.

The Pope had a problem with the Lombards invading from the west. Gregory was ordered to request military aid from the emperor. But the emperor felt there were greater threats to the east, and he refused Gregory's request.

In 590, Pope Pelagius II died, and Gregory was proclaimed pope by acclamation. This was not something Gregory wanted, but he accepted the burden nevertheless.

Gregory made clear he preferred the monastic life in a series of writings praising it. He also referred to himself as a servant of God. The habit remains in practice to this day and many clergy still refer to themselves as servants.

Pope Gregory was famous for the emphasis he put on missionary work. He sent many people out to bring many to Jesus and into the Church. Anglo-Saxon Britain was, at that time, still on the frontier of Christendom. It was Pope Gregory who dispatched St. Augustine (of Canterbury) to Kent in 597 (not to be confused with St. Augustine of Hippo).

text:
Trump's face is now on money, with $1 coins going into circulation. Trump is the first living president to be on a circulating coin in 100 years. In addition to the president's portrait, the U.S. Mint said the coins commemorate the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, with inscriptions "1776 ~ 2026," "LIBERTY" and "IN GOD WE  TRUST."

The rolls of $1 coins (25 to a roll) go for $61. A bag of 100 coins goes for $154.50, according to the Mint's website. The coins can be used as legal tender.

"These coins are also in circulation, so check your pocket change. Collect them today!" the U.S. Mint wrote in a social media post Wednesday.

The coins are not real gold, but feature a gold-colored finish made of manganese brass. They were produced at the Philadelphia Mint, according to the Mint. It's not clear how many coins were produced.

The Mint said 250,000 of the coins have a special "July 4th" markings, which were randomly included in the rolls and bags, and were struck on July Fourth at the Philadelphia Mint, according to the Mint's website.

The last and only time a living president was featured on hard currency struck by  the U.S. Mint was a century ago for the U.S. Sesquicentennial. The silver half-dollar coin featured then-President Calvin Coolidge silhouetted behind the bust of President George Washington. At the time, the Mint produced a million of the coins with 860,000 of them ultimately returned and melted due to low demand.

The legality of the Trump coin's production has come into question after Treasury  Secretary Scott Bessent failed to have the coin reviewed by the bipartisan Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, an 11-person body established by Congress to advise the secretary on designs of hard currency, according to members of the committee.

The Treasury pushed back on the criticism, saying that it offered the committee "multiple reasonable opportunities to review proposed designs" but that  it declined.

"Accordingly, the Mint’s statutory obligation to seek CCAC review has been fulfilled," U.S. Treasurer Brandon Beach wrote in a statement in March, adding that Bessent has "sole discretion on final  design selection."

There is currently a household order limit of two items that will remain in place until 2 p.m. ET on Sept. 3, according to the U.S. Mint.

In the fifth book of Eusebius, there is a fragment taken out of the writings of Apollonius, in which, among other things, he reproaches Montanus with being the first that dissolved marriage, and laid down laws for fasting. He does not say, that Montanus absolutely prohibited marriage or certain kinds of food. -It is enough if he lay a religious obligation on the consciences, and command men to worship God by observing those things; for the prohibition of things that are indifferent, whether it be general or special, is always a DIABOLICAL TYRANNY. That this is true in regard to certain kinds of food will appear more clearly from the next clause, 

“Which God created.” It is proper to observe the reason, that, in the use of various kinds of food, we ought to be satisfied with the liberty which God has granted to us; because He created them for this purpose. -It yields inconceivable joy to all the godly, when they know that all the kinds of food which they eat are put into their hands by the Lord, so that the use of them is pure and lawful. 
What insolence is it in men to take away what God bestows! 
Did they create food? 
Can they make void the creation of God? 
Let it always be remembered by us, that he who created the food, gave us also the free use of it, which it is vain for men to attempt to hinder. 

“To be received with Thanksgiving” God created food to be received; that is, that we may enjoy it. This end can ever be set aside by human authority. He adds, with thanksgiving; because we can never render to God any recompense for his kindness but a testimony of gratitude. 
-And thus he holds up to greater abhorrence those wicked lawgivers who, by new and hasty enactments, hinder the sacrifice of praise which God especially requires us to offer to him. Now, there can be no thanksgiving without sobriety and temperance; for the kindness of God is not truly acknowledged by him who wickedly abuses it.”
(John Calvin at 1Timothy chapter 4)
