𝐌𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐟𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐞𝐧𝐫𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐆𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐉𝐞𝐰𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐬𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐌𝐨𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐣𝐞𝐰𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐌𝐲𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐮 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐨𝐭 𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐝. Everyone paid twelve instalments, twelve months and every payment tracked on an instalment card that the jeweller personally signed but he vanished, The culprit, Mohan Lal, proprietor of Mohan Jewels at Vivekanandanagar,

This case from Mysuru is not an isolated incident. It is a pattern that repeats itself across India, in small cities and large ones, every single year.

The concept is straightforward. A jeweller offers you a monthly instalment plan typically 11 to 15 months. You pay a fixed amount each month. At the end of the tenure, the jeweller adds a bonus of one or two months and lets you buy gold jewellery worth the full accumulated amount but is not regulated by RBI. It is not regulated by SEBI. If the jeweller closes the shop and leaves, consumer money is gone.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐦𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐬𝐤 𝐛𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐫𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐠𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐬𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞.

1. Ask to see the GST, every legitimate jeweller selling goods must have one. If they cannot produce it, stop immediately.

2. Is the jeweller a member of a recognized trade body, GJEPC, IBJA, or a state jewellers' association? Membership does not guarantee integrity, but its absence removes one layer of accountability.

3. Get the scheme terms in writing, not just on the instalment card, but on a printed document with the jeweller's name, GST number, address, and signature. If they resist, walk away.

4. What exactly happens if you miss a payment? What exactly happens if you want to withdraw before maturity?

5. Never pay in cash. Always pay through a traceable digital channel — Google Pay, NEFT, bank transfer

6. Always photograph your instalment card after each entry. If the jeweller signs it, photograph that signature. Your phone's camera is your most important protection in this transaction.

7. Ask for a receipt for every payment. If they say the instalment card is your receipt, that is acceptable, but insist it carries jeweller's GST number, store's full address, date of each payment.

If your goal is eventually buying jewellery, a scheme from @Mia_by_Tanishq, @Malabartweets, @KalyanJewellers , or another large listed chain carries significantly lower risk than one from a small neighbourhood jeweller. These companies are publicly accountable, audited, and cannot simply disappear.

At @OrvanyaIndia , we are building consumer education around exactly these kinds of decisions, not just jewellery exchange, but the broader question of how Indian consumers can engage with the jewellery industry with genuine knowledge and genuine protection.

Because gold is not just a purchase in India. For most families, it is savings, security, and trust accumulated over years

What Is Europe Preparing For? Gold Moves to London While Britain Rearms

Sometimes the most interesting geopolitical stories are not found in a dramatic speech, a leaked document or a sudden military deployment. They appear when several seemingly unrelated decisions begin moving in the same direction, and that may be what we are seeing in Europe right now.

The Netherlands has quietly changed where it keeps a significant portion of its national gold reserves. Between March and August 2026, the Dutch central bank shifted approximately 86 metric tons of gold from North America toward London, reducing the share stored in New York and increasing the amount held at the Bank of England.[1] At almost the same time, Britain has been accelerating one of the largest military drone expansions in its history, committing more than £5 billion over four years toward drones and autonomous military systems while also linking British production directly with Ukrainian battlefield knowledge and Ukrainian manufacturers.[2][3]

Those two developments are not proof of some secret coordinated plan, and there is no public evidence that the Netherlands moved its gold because Britain is expanding drone production or because either government possesses secret knowledge that a European war is imminent. Still, when several major governments begin changing how they think about financial reserves, military production, domestic manufacturing and crisis readiness at roughly the same time, it is fair to ask whether they are simply reacting independently to the same worsening security environment.

That leads to a more useful question than simply asking whether there is a conspiracy: what exactly are European governments preparing for, and are they seeing risks that the public still tends to underestimate?

What Did the Netherlands Actually Do?

The Dutch central bank, De Nederlandsche Bank, has been unusually straightforward about why it rearranged its gold reserves. It says that increasing geopolitical unrest requires greater crisis preparedness and that gold stored in London can be accessed and traded more easily during an emergency.[1]

Before the move, approximately 31.3 percent of Dutch gold was stored in New York, 19.7 percent in Ottawa and 18.1 percent in London. After the restructuring, London’s share jumped to 32.1 percent, while New York and Ottawa were each reduced to 18.5 percent. The Netherlands itself continues to hold roughly 30.8 percent of its reserves domestically.[1]

The total amount of Dutch gold did not change, which is an important distinction. This was not the Netherlands abandoning the dollar or suddenly buying gold because it expected financial collapse. It already owned the gold. What changed was the judgment about where an emergency reserve should physically and financially sit.

The Dutch central bank specifically described gold as protection against “extreme systemic risks” and said increasing the London allocation would make the reserve more immediately usable during a serious crisis.[1] Central bankers are generally careful with their language, so when a central bank says it is rearranging billions of euros worth of national reserves in order to improve crisis preparedness, that deserves attention even if the explanation remains practical rather than dramatic.

Why London?

There is a very straightforward explanation for choosing London, and it should not be dismissed merely because it sounds less exciting than a geopolitical theory.

London remains one of the world’s dominant markets for wholesale physical gold. The Bank of England stores roughly 400,000 gold bars for Britain, foreign central banks and other approved institutions, and gold already sitting inside its vaults can effectively change ownership through accounting records without requiring tons of metal to be physically transported across borders.[4]

That makes London extremely useful during a financial emergency because it offers liquidity, established infrastructure and immediate access to one of the world’s deepest bullion markets. The Dutch central bank has openly said this is one of the reasons for the move. Gold held in New York and Ottawa can certainly be valuable and secure, but gold held in London is much easier to mobilize quickly within the global bullion system.[1]

The practical explanation is therefore strong, but it raises another question that is harder to ignore. Why has immediate crisis liquidity become important enough to justify rearranging 86 tons of sovereign gold now? Europe already has plenty of publicly visible reasons to be nervous, so perhaps the more interesting issue is not whether a secret exists, but whether governments are beginning to take those visible risks more seriously than the general public does.

Maybe They Do Not Know Something We Do Not

Governments do receive classified intelligence, but national security planning is not built only around secrets. It is also built around risks that are already visible to everyone.

Russia’s war against Ukraine continues. Drone and missile technology is advancing extremely quickly. China is increasing pressure on Taiwan. Shipping lanes, energy networks and financial infrastructure have all become more vulnerable to disruption, while cyberwarfare can hit communications and banking systems without an army ever crossing a border.

European governments have also spent the past several years discovering that economic interdependence does not automatically prevent conflict. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine shattered many of the assumptions that shaped European policy after the Cold War, while sanctions, energy disruptions and supply-chain problems demonstrated how quickly economic systems can become part of a geopolitical confrontation.

That means European governments may not be sitting on a secret report predicting catastrophe. They may simply have reached a more cautious conclusion about the same information available to everyone else.

Individuals usually prepare for what they think is likely. Governments are supposed to prepare for what would be catastrophic if they guessed wrong. If there is only a modest chance of a severe European security crisis, an ordinary citizen may reasonably ignore it. A central bank responsible for national reserves and a defense ministry responsible for national survival cannot afford to do the same.

That brings Britain into the picture.

Britain Is Doing More Than Buying a Few Drones

Britain’s military drone expansion has moved well beyond experimentation. In June 2026, the British government announced more than £5 billion in drone and autonomous-systems investment over four years, describing it as the largest drone investment in the history of the UK Armed Forces.[2]

That follows years of planning shaped directly by the war in Ukraine. Britain’s Defence Drone Strategy explicitly says the UK wants an industrial base capable of scaling production during wartime and that military procurement must adapt at the speed at which drone warfare changes on the battlefield.[5]

The key point is that Britain is no longer thinking only about buying equipment. It is thinking about manufacturing capacity, production speed, industrial resilience and the ability to replace losses during a prolonged conflict. That is a much broader strategic shift than simply adding another weapons program to the defense budget.

The relationship with Ukraine makes the development even more interesting. In 2025, London and Kyiv reached an agreement allowing Ukrainian battlefield technology and data to feed directly into British production lines, with the British government saying the arrangement would allow UK manufacturers to develop military equipment using information generated directly from Ukraine’s front lines.[6]

Ukraine has become one of the world’s most important laboratories for modern drone warfare, while Britain has industrial capacity, engineering expertise, capital, aerospace companies and access to Western markets. Ukraine brings something Britain cannot manufacture on its own: years of current combat experience against another major military power. Combining those two advantages makes strategic sense whether one believes a wider war is coming or simply believes modern warfare has permanently changed.

Ukrainian Drone Manufacturing Is Also Moving Into Britain

The relationship is becoming physical rather than theoretical. In February 2026, one of Ukraine’s major drone manufacturers opened a production facility in Suffolk, with the British government saying the factory could create as many as 500 jobs while manufacturing drones that support Ukraine’s military.[3]

Britain has simultaneously increased drone deliveries to Ukraine dramatically. In April it announced plans to provide at least 120,000 drones, including reconnaissance, long-range strike, logistics and maritime systems. By June, Britain announced a package that included 150,000 Ukrainian-produced drones along with hundreds of air-defense missiles and radar systems.[7][8]

At some point, this begins to look like more than wartime aid. Britain is helping Ukraine survive today while also building domestic expertise, production capacity and industrial relationships that could matter long after the current war ends.

That does not mean Britain expects a war next year. It does suggest that Britain no longer views Ukraine as an isolated conflict whose lessons can be filed away and forgotten.

Does the Dutch Gold Move Toward Britain Mean Something Bigger?

Possibly, but probably not in the most dramatic sense.

There is no evidence that the Netherlands chose London because it believes Britain is somehow safer than the United States in every possible future crisis. Britain would itself be deeply involved in almost any major NATO conflict involving Europe, so the move is more logically understood in financial terms.

London gives the Netherlands something extremely valuable during uncertainty: speed, liquidity and proximity to one of the world’s major financial centers.

If Europe faced a serious banking disruption, war, sanctions emergency or breakdown in normal financial markets, gold stored in London could potentially be pledged, sold or exchanged more quickly than reserves sitting elsewhere. The Netherlands may therefore be reducing concentration risk while placing more of its emergency reserve somewhere that can be mobilized rapidly.

That is sensible risk management, but the decision to diversify still tells us something. Countries usually diversify when they believe concentration creates vulnerability. The Netherlands apparently believes the geopolitical environment has deteriorated enough that its old allocation is no longer ideal.

That is the signal worth watching. The most important question may not be why the gold went specifically to Britain, but why the government decided that the location of its gold suddenly mattered more than it did before.

Is Britain Quietly Becoming a Strategic Hub Again?

Britain occupies an unusual position in Europe. It is no longer part of the European Union, yet it remains one of NATO’s strongest military powers. It possesses nuclear weapons, major intelligence capabilities, a large defense industry, deep Atlantic connections and one of the world’s most important financial centers.

London is already one of the principal repositories for sovereign gold, while Britain is also expanding drone manufacturing, autonomous systems and other technologies shaped by the lessons of Ukraine. Britain’s national security strategy specifically identifies Ukraine’s experience with drones, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare and communications as lessons the British military intends to absorb.[9]

None of this proves that Britain is consciously positioning itself as some kind of military and financial fortress for Europe, but the ingredients are interesting. European money already moves through London, sovereign gold is increasingly being concentrated there, Ukrainian battlefield knowledge is entering British factories, and British military production is expanding at the same time.

It is therefore reasonable to ask whether Britain sees an opportunity in the breakdown of the old European security order. The UK may believe that the post-Cold War period is ending and that countries able to manufacture weapons, finance security and connect real battlefield experience with industrial production will become far more strategically important.

If that is the case, this would not be a temporary reaction to Ukraine. It would be a long-term repositioning of Britain’s role in Europe.

Could This Simply Be Europe Finally Waking Up?

There is also a much simpler explanation tying these developments together: Europe may simply be waking up to a world that is more dangerous than it believed ten years ago.

For decades, much of Europe operated under assumptions that now look less certain. Russia was expected to become increasingly integrated with Europe economically. Large conventional wars inside Europe seemed unlikely. The United States would always provide overwhelming military protection, and global financial systems were expected to remain broadly stable regardless of political disagreement.

Several of those assumptions have been badly shaken. Russia invaded Ukraine, Western governments froze Russian sovereign assets, energy supplies became political weapons, supply chains became security concerns, and drone warfare demonstrated that relatively cheap weapons can strike infrastructure far behind the traditional battlefield.

Against that background, the Dutch central bank rearranging gold for easier crisis access and Britain building drone factories do not necessarily require a hidden explanation. They may simply be different governments reacting to the same underlying change in the world.

The Netherlands improves access to its emergency reserves. Britain expands weapons manufacturing. Germany increases defense spending. Ukraine pushes drone technology forward at wartime speed. Taiwan orders tens of thousands of attack drones. European governments increase ammunition production and reconsider how much military manufacturing they need at home.

These developments may not be parts of one secret plan. They may be separate responses to the same conclusion: the world has become less predictable, and depending on the assumptions of the last thirty years is becoming increasingly risky.

What Would Make This More Concerning?

One gold transfer does not signal an approaching war, and one drone factory does not either. Even billions in defense spending can be explained by long-term modernization rather than an expectation that conflict is imminent.

The more useful approach is to watch whether additional signals begin pointing in the same direction.

If more European central banks start relocating significant reserves geographically closer to Europe, that would be noteworthy. If governments simultaneously increase strategic stockpiles of fuel, food, medicines and critical materials, the preparedness argument would become stronger.

Britain’s defense contracts also deserve watching. If drone and missile production continues expanding far beyond the quantities required to support Ukraine, particularly through long-term contracts designed primarily to equip the British military, that would suggest the government expects the industrial buildup to outlast the current war.

Civil-defense spending may eventually provide an even clearer signal. Large new investments in shelters, emergency communications, backup electrical infrastructure, reserve medical systems and civilian preparedness would tell us a great deal about how European governments assess future risk.

The question should therefore not be whether one unusual development proves something sinister. It should be whether more pieces keep appearing on the same side of the board.

So What Do They Know?

Probably much of the same thing the rest of us know.

Russia has shown that major war in Europe is possible. Ukraine has demonstrated that drones and relatively inexpensive autonomous weapons can radically alter battlefield economics. China and Taiwan are preparing for the possibility of conflict in Asia. Economic sanctions have shown that financial reserves and international payment systems can themselves become geopolitical weapons, while critical infrastructure has increasingly become part of the battlefield.

European governments undoubtedly possess intelligence unavailable to the public, but we do not need classified information to explain why they are preparing more seriously.

Perhaps the surprising part is not that governments are changing their behavior. Perhaps it is that ordinary people still find those changes surprising.

Something Is Clearly Changing

It would be irresponsible to claim that the Netherlands moving gold to London and Britain building drones proves European governments know a major war is coming. There simply is not evidence for that conclusion.

It would be equally shortsighted to dismiss every development as routine and therefore ignore the broader pattern.

The Netherlands did not move 86 tonnes of gold because absolutely nothing had changed. Its own central bank explicitly cited increasing geopolitical unrest and crisis preparedness.[1] Britain is not investing more than £5 billion in drones because nothing has changed either. Its government has openly said that Ukraine and the requirements of modern warfare are reshaping its military thinking.[2][5]

Ukraine’s battlefield knowledge is being connected directly with British industry because governments believe those lessons matter beyond Ukraine itself.[6] Taken together, these facts do not tell us that war is inevitable, but they do suggest that European governments increasingly believe the possibility of a far more dangerous world deserves serious preparation.

That may ultimately be the least dramatic and most important answer to the question, “What do they know that we don’t?”

Perhaps there is no great hidden secret. Perhaps governments have simply begun planning around risks that much of the public still prefers to treat as distant possibilities.

The gold is being repositioned, the factories are expanding, military doctrine is changing and governments are placing greater emphasis on resilience. Each development has a perfectly logical explanation on its own, but taken together they leave a question worth continuing to ask:

What exactly is Europe getting ready for?

Footnotes

[1] De Nederlandsche Bank, September 2, 2026 — “DNB improves tradability of gold reserves.” The Dutch central bank says it shifted approximately 86 tonnes of gold from reserves held in the United States and Canada toward London between March and August 2026 because of increasing geopolitical unrest and a desire to improve crisis preparedness. London’s share of Dutch reserves rose from 18.1% to 32.1%, while New York’s fell from 31.3% to 18.5%.

[2] UK Ministry of Defence, June 29, 2026 — UK drone transformation. The British government announced more than £5 billion for drones and autonomous military systems over four years, describing it as the largest drone investment in the history of the UK Armed Forces.

[3] UK Ministry of Defence, February 26, 2026 — Ukrainian drone manufacturing in Britain. Ukrainian manufacturer Ukrspecsystems opened a new drone production facility in Suffolk that the British government says could create up to 500 jobs while supporting Ukrainian military production.

[4] Bank of England — Gold custody and the London gold market. The Bank says it stores around 400,000 gold bars for Britain, foreign central banks and other approved customers. Its position gives central banks direct access to London’s highly liquid physical gold market.

[5] UK Defence Drone Strategy. Britain’s strategy was developed using lessons from Ukraine and calls for a resilient industrial base capable of scaling drone production in wartime, faster procurement and rapid adaptation as battlefield technology changes.

[6] UK Government, June 23, 2025 — UK-Ukraine battlefield technology partnership. Britain and Ukraine agreed to feed Ukrainian frontline technology and data into UK production lines so British companies can rapidly develop and manufacture military equipment informed directly by combat experience.

[7] UK Ministry of Defence, April 15, 2026 — UK drone package for Ukraine. Britain announced plans to provide at least 120,000 drones during 2026, including long-range strike, intelligence, reconnaissance, logistics and maritime systems.

[8] UK Ministry of Defence, June 18, 2026 — 150,000-drone package. Britain subsequently announced a £752 million package that includes 150,000 Ukrainian-produced drones along with more than 350 air-defense missiles and radar systems.

[9] UK National Security Strategy 2025. The British government says it is incorporating Ukraine’s experience with land warfare, drones, artificial intelligence, disrupted navigation systems and secure satellite communications into its own approach to warfighting.

The Reichskonkordat ("Concordat between the Holy See and the German Reich"[1]) is a treaty negotiated between the Vatican and the emergent Nazi Germany. It was signed on 20 July 1933 by Cardinal Secretary of State Eugenio Pacelli, who later became Pope Pius XII, on behalf of Pope Pius XI; and by Vice Chancellor Franz von Papen on behalf of President Paul von Hindenburg and the German government. It was ratified on 10 September 1933 and it remains in force. The treaty guarantees the rights of the Catholic Church in Germany. When bishops take office, Article 16 states that they are required to take an oath of loyalty to the Governor or President of the German Reich established according to the constitution. The treaty also requires all clergy to abstain from working in and for political parties. Breaches of the agreement by the Nazis began soon after it was signed, and escalated throughout their rule. The Church protested, including in the 1937 Mit brennender Sorge encyclical of Pope Pius XI. The Nazis planned to eliminate the Church's influence by restricting its organizations to purely religious activities.[2]

The Reichskonkordat is the most controversial of several concordats that the Vatican negotiated during the pontificate of Pius XI. It is frequently discussed in works that deal with the rise of Adolf Hitler in the early 1930s and the Holocaust. The concordat was described by the Nazis as giving moral legitimacy to the Nazi regime after Hitler had acquired quasi-dictatorial powers through the Enabling Act of 1933, an Act itself facilitated through the support of the Catholic Centre Party.

The treaty places constraints on the political activity of German clergy of the Catholic Church. With passage of the 1935 Nuremberg Laws, for example, a policy of nonintervention was followed. The majority of the German church hierarchy regarded the treaty as a symbol of peace between church and state.[3] From a Catholic Church perspective, it has been argued that the Concordat prevented even greater evils being unleashed against the Church.[4] Though some German bishops were unenthusiastic, and the Allies at the end of World War II felt it inappropriate, Pope Pius XII successfully argued to keep the concordat in force. It is still in force.

Führer Directive No. 30 (German: Weisung Nr. 30) was a May 1941 directive issued by German dictator Adolf Hitler during World War II. It ordered German support for Iraqi Arab nationalists, who were fighting the British.

Background
Führer Directive No. 30 dealt with German intervention in support of Arab nationalists in the Kingdom of Iraq. During the 1930s, representatives of Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy attempted to gain favor with various Iraqi nationalists and promised support against the British. On 1 April 1941, Rashid Ali and members of the pro-Axis "Golden Square" staged a coup d'etat against the pro-British government of Regent Abd al-Ilah. On 2 May, after tensions mounted on both sides, the British launched pre-emptive air strikes against Iraqi forces and the Anglo-Iraqi War began. Rashid Ali immediately requested that the Germans make good on the earlier promises of assistance.[1]

The ratlines (German: Rattenlinien) were systems of escape routes used by Nazis and their collaborators to flee Europe from 1945 onwards in the aftermath of World War II. Two primary routes developed independently with their operators eventually collaborating, the first transferring through Spain and the second through Rome and Genoa. Some escapees settled at these locations or used them to flee elsewhere, with the majority settling in Argentina or other South American countries such as Brazil, Chile, and Paraguay.

The ratlines were supported by some clergy of the Catholic Church, such as Austrian bishop Alois Hudal and Croatian priest Krunoslav Draganović, as well as some outlets of the International Committee of the Red Cross. The Nazis paid Argentine officials (starting c. 1943) to shield their agents, bolstering the rise of Juan Perón, whose regime set up additional ratlines through Scandinavia and Switzerland.

A number of significant Nazis and their collaborators escaped, including Ustaše leader Ante Pavelić, as well as Schutzstaffel (SS) officers Adolf Eichmann and Josef Mengele, both perpetrators of the Holocaust. Starting in 1945, the United States utilized the ratlines to aid the escape of some Soviet defectors and informants, as well as Gestapo leader Klaus Barbie (who had traded intel with the U.S. Army while being held in Austria). Decades later, the ratlines remain a subject of investigation[b] and cultural interest.

Francoist Spain
The origins of the first ratlines are connected to various developments in Vatican-Argentina relations before and during World War II.[11] As early as 1942, the Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Luigi Maglione – evidently at the behest of Pope Pius XII – contacted an ambassador of Argentina regarding that country's willingness to accept European Catholic immigrants in a timely manner, allowing them to live and work.[12] Anton Weber, a German priest who headed the Roman branch of Saint Raphael's Society [de], travelled to Portugal with the intention to travel to Argentina, seemingly to lay the groundwork for Catholic immigration.[12]

Some Catholic leaders decided to work with the Nazis in an attempt to fight against their common enemy of Bolshevism. By 1944, ratline activity which was centered in Francoist Spain was conducted in an attempt to facilitate the escape of Nazis.[13] Among the primary organizers were Charles Lescat, a French member of Action Française – an organization suppressed by Pope Pius XI and rehabilitated by Pope Pius XII – and Pierre Daye, a Belgian with contacts in the Spanish government.[14] Lescat and Daye were the first to flee from Europe with the assistance of the Argentinian cardinal Antonio Caggiano.[14]

By 1946, hundreds of war criminals were living in Spain, as well as thousands of former Nazis and fascists.[15] According to U.S. Secretary of State James F. Byrnes, Vatican cooperation in turning over these "asylum-seekers" was "negligible".[15] Unlike the Vatican emigration operation in Italy which centered on Vatican City, the Spanish ratlines – though fostered by the Vatican – were relatively independent of the Vatican Emigration Bureau's hierarchy.[16]

Croatian Franciscans
A small but influential network of Croatian Franciscan priests led by Father Krunoslav Draganović organised a highly sophisticated ratline with headquarters at the San Girolamo degli Illirici Seminary College in Rome, with links from Austria and an embarkation point in Genoa. The ratline initially focused on aiding members of the Croatian Ustaše including its leader, Ante Pavelić.[25]

A number of priests participated, included Father Vilim Cecelja (former Deputy Military Vicar to the Ustaše),[26] who founded a branch of the Croatian Red Cross in Austria (which the ICRC only supported in an unofficial capacity). He used his Red Cross and U.S. papers to travel freely around Salzburg, where many Ustashe and Nazi refugees remained, providing Red Cross identities to numerous individuals who lacked identification. In October 1945, Cecelja was arrested by the CIC for his Ustaše ties.[27] Father Dominik Mandić (an official Vatican representative at San Girolamo and treasurer of the Franciscans) used his Italian secret police connections to ensure that the Franciscans' identity cards would be considered sufficiently official to issue them Italian identity cards.[28] Finally, Draganović would phone Monsignor Karlo Petranović in Genoa with the number of required berths on ships to South America.[29]

The Draganović ratline was an open secret among the intelligence and diplomatic communities in Rome. As early as August 1945, Allied commanders in Rome were asking questions about the use of San Girolamo as a "haven" for Ustaše.[30] A U.S. State Department report of 12 July 1946 listed nine war criminals, including Albanians and Montenegrins as well as Croats, plus others "not actually sheltered" at San Girolamo Seminary who "enjoy Church support and protection".[31]

In February 1947, CIC Special Agent Robert Clayton Mudd reported ten members of Pavelić's Ustaše cabinet living either in San Girolamo or in the Vatican itself. Mudd had infiltrated an agent into the seminary and confirmed that it was "honeycombed with cells of Ustashe operatives" guarded by "armed youths". Mudd reported a car protected under diplomatic immunity transported unidentified people between the Vatican and the seminary.[32] Additionally, by mid-1947, British intelligence was aware that Petranović mainly helped war criminals.[29]

Argentine haven
See also: Argentina during World War II and Operation Bolívar
The Nazis had a presence in Argentina before the war, peaking with 2,110 members in 1935.[37] In June 1941, Germany sent 83 boxes of documents from its embassy in Tokyo, Japan, via the MS Nana Maru to Buenos Aires.[38][3] Customs agents impounded the boxes, which were searched by Argentina's foreign ministry. Five boxes contained Nazi propaganda hidden amid material labeled as "scientific, literary and cultural",[6] while the others housed mostly children's books, magazines and war photographs. A month later, Argentine officials raided the secret offices of the banned Nazi Party (disguised as German labor organizations). Perhaps 5,000 seized memberships from the German Labor Front and the German trade union association were stored by the Supreme Court of Argentina.[3]

In 1940, Hitler's Secret Cabinet Council dispatched an agent to Credit Suisse in Zurich to set up and manage a Swiss bank account for Nazi Germany. Eventually, at least four accounts were maintained by the German Foreign Office under pseudonyms, in addition to some held by the German Red Cross and one that was used for the economic arm of the SS.[39] German-Argentine millionaire Ludwig Freude, who oversaw Buenos Aires's German Overseas Bank (a subsidiary of Deutsche Bank), made contact with Swiss banks; by 1941, Nazi supporters in Argentina held as many as 890 accounts.[6][40][1][41] In May 1943, SS functionary Walter Schellenberg secured a secret agreement with the Argentine military that excluded Nazis from arrest in Argentina and established a diplomatic pouch exchange system between the two regimes. The Argentine nationalists conducted a coup d'état that June, opening a way for Juan Perón's rise to power.[42] Meanwhile, German wealth derived from looting Holocaust victims was placed in a Reichsbank account under the false name of Max Heiliger.[43] By 1944, this was worth millions of Reichsmarks, in addition to shipments to the Reich Chancellery headquarters of Martin Bormann.[44] SS officer Otto Skorzeny facilitated the international transfer of wealth from the account, reportedly depositing it in the name of Perón's future wife, Eva.[44] According to The New York Times, the U.S. State Department reported in 1945 that "the personal fortunes of Nazi officials" were delivered to Buenos Aires via diplomatic pouch, with Nazi higher-up Hermann Göring possessing over US$20 million and a U-boat loaded with Nazi loot.[45]

After Germany's surrender on 8 May 1945, the captain of U-530, then operating in the northern Atlantic Ocean, opted to surrender to the Argentine Navy in Mar del Plata, Buenos Aires Province, which occurred on 10 July.[46] He was unable to explain why the voyage had taken two months nor the absence of usual documents. The Navy reported that no officers were aboard, while the police purportedly reported that Adolf Hitler and perhaps Eva Braun had been seen disembarking from a submarine.[46] The captured U-boat and its crew were sent to North America, which did not discourage the U-977 from surrendering in Buenos Aires in mid-August in hopes of being sheltered.[47][c]

On 18 January 1946, Bishop Antonio Caggiano, leader of the Argentine chapter of Catholic Action, flew to Rome to be consecrated as cardinal by Pius XII. Both Caggiano and French cardinal Eugène Tisserant heavily interceded in helping Lescat and Daye and their associates emigrate from Spain to Argentina.[49][14] In early 1946, Caggiano implored the Argentine consul in Rome to stamp the passports of three confirmed French war criminals (and five other Frenchmen) with Argentine tourist visas, regardless of missing return tickets and health certificates.[50] The first documented case of a French war criminal arriving in Buenos Aires was Émile Dewoitine on 28 May 1946, after sailing first class on the same ship with Caggiano.[51][d]

Role of U.S. intelligence
Although the CIC arrested Father Vilim Cecelja (who provided some Ustaše with false identities) in October 1945,[27] the U.S. agency reportedly helped some of the Croatian nationalists flee from Europe. The CIC is also estimated to have aided the escapes of perhaps 70 Soviet defectors and informants to South America, as well as Klaus Barbie,[5] whom the Austria-based 430th CIC began protecting in April 1947.[93] The regional CIC director established a local ratline as early as 1945. In November 1947, ex-SS officer Karl Hass, who had assisted Hudal in helping Nazis flee Europe, was brought to Austria to aid the CIC in the anti-Soviet matter.[94]

After rumors circulated that Barbie had been employed by the 66th CIC in Germany, the French demanded Barbie's extradition in 1950; the 66th was until then unaware that he was being sheltered by the 430th.[93][5] Barbie gave the CIC access to knowledge about the French occupation zone in Germany, the Communist Party of Germany, and former SS officers.[95] Meanwhile, he learned about the Austria-based Document Disposal Unit (DDU), a U.S. State Department intelligence unit led by CIA director Allen Dulles and staffed with Office of Strategic Services (OSS) men, also sometimes operating as War Department or OSS entities.[93][96] Fearing that France may have fallen to communism and wanted to extract CIC intel from Barbie,[95] the State Department claimed that he could not be found in the U.S. Zone of Austria, and by 1951, facilitated his escape via Draganović's route through Rome.[93][96] This ratline was reinforced by the DDU, which aimed to eliminate French and British control. Barbie settled in Bolivia and spent 33 years there before his arrest.[93][96] In the early 1980s, a former CIC official claimed that "Barbie was the only Nazi we took out [of Europe]."[5]

The 430th reported in 1950 that in mid-1947, the Army instructed them to begin using Draganović's Roman network to evacuate some people out of Austria, supported by a U.S. official at the International Refugee Organization (IRO). The directive applied to:[97]

visitors who had been in the custody of the 430th CIC and completely processed in accordance with current directives and requirements, and whose continued residence in Austria constituted a security threat as well as a source of possible embarrassment to the Commanding General of [the U.S. Forces in Austria], since the Soviet Command had become aware [of] their presence in [the] US Zone of Austria and in some instances had requested the return of these persons to Soviet custody. ... [Draganović] handled all phases of the operation after the defectees arrived in Rome, such as the procurement of IRO Italian and South American documents, visas, stamps, arrangements for disposition, land or sea, and notification of resettlement committees in foreign lands.

According to the CIC, Draganović charged fees for his role in the escapes: US$500 per child, US$1,000 per adult, US$1,400 for a very important person and over US$1,500 for individuals older than 60.[5] After June 1951, the 430th was no longer responsible for aiding ratline escapees, which the CIA was then slated to perform.[98] Former SS officer Tscherim Soobzokov was enlisted as a CIA spy early in the Cold War to gain intel from Soviet-aligned contacts in the Middle East; he moved to the U.S. and later worked for the FBI.[99][j]

Pope Benedict XVI[a] (born Joseph Alois Ratzinger;[b] 16 April 1927 – 31 December 2022) was the head of the Catholic Church and sovereign of Vatican City from 2005 until his resignation in 2013. Following his resignation, he chose to be known as "pope emeritus", a title he held until his death on 31 December 2022.[1][2]

Ordained as a priest in 1951 in Bavaria, Ratzinger embarked on an academic career and established himself as a highly regarded theologian by the late 1950s. He was appointed a full professor in 1958 when aged 31. After a long career as a professor of theology at several German universities, he was appointed Archbishop of Munich and Freising and created a cardinal by Pope Paul VI in 1977, an unusual promotion for someone who had only been ordained to the episcopate less than a month prior and not having much pastoral experience. In 1981, he was appointed Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, one of the most important dicasteries of the Roman Curia. In 2002, he also became Dean of the College of Cardinals. Before becoming pope, he had been "a major figure on the Vatican stage for a quarter of a century"; he had had an influence "second to none when it came to setting church priorities and directions" as one of John Paul II's closest confidants.[3] Following the death of John Paul II on 2 April 2005, a conclave elected Ratzinger as his successor on 19 April; he chose Benedict XVI as his papal name in honour of Benedict XV and Benedict of Nursia.

Wartime and ordination
Ratzinger's family, especially his father, bitterly resented the Nazis, and his father's opposition to National Socialism resulted in demotions and harassment of the family.[21] Following his 14th birthday in 1941, Ratzinger was conscripted into the Hitler Youth—as membership was required by law for all 14-year-old German boys after March 1939[22]—but was an unenthusiastic member who refused to attend meetings, according to his brother.[23] In 1941, one of Ratzinger's cousins, a 14-year-old boy with Down syndrome, was taken away by the Nazi regime and murdered during the Aktion T4 campaign of Nazi eugenics.[24] In 1943, while still in seminary, he was drafted into the German anti-aircraft corps as Luftwaffenhelfer.[23] Ratzinger then trained in the German infantry.[25] As the Allied front drew closer to his post in 1945, he deserted back to his family's home in Traunstein after his unit had ceased to exist, just as American troops established a headquarters in the Ratzinger household.[26] As a German soldier, he was interned in US prisoner of war camps, first in Neu-Ulm, then at Fliegerhorst ("military airfield") Bad Aibling (shortly to be repurposed as Bad Aibling Station) where he was at the time of Victory in Europe Day, and released on 19 June 1945.[27][26]

Ratzinger and his brother Georg entered Saint Michael Seminary in Traunstein in November 1945, later studying at the Ducal Georgianum (Herzogliches Georgianum) of the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. They were both ordained in Freising on 29 June 1951 by Cardinal Michael von Faulhaber of Munich – the same man Ratzinger had met as a child. He recalled: "At the moment the elderly Archbishop laid his hands on me, a little bird – perhaps a lark – flew up from the altar in the high cathedral and trilled a little joyful song".[28] He celebrated his first Mass later that summer in Traunstein, at St. Oswald's Church.[29]

Ratzinger's 1953 dissertation, earning him a Doctor of Theology degree from the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, was on Augustine of Hippo: it was titled The People and the House of God in Augustine's Doctrine of the Church. His habilitation (which qualified him for a professorship) was on Bonaventure.[30] It was completed in 1957 and he became a professor at Freising College in 1958.[31]

Capitalizing on the Premium Hospitality & Cruise Line Networks
Target Audience: Agribusiness CEOs, International Sales Directors, and Luxury Foodservice Procurement Officers.

1/5 🛳️ If your entire Hass export strategy is reliant on retail supermarkets, you are overlooking one of the highest-margin sectors in the world: the premium hospitality and cruise line network.
While supermarkets squeeze your margins with fixed seasonal pricing, the luxury cruise and resort sectors will pay a massive premium for guaranteed, elite-tier supply continuity. Here is how to break into this exclusive B2B pipeline. 👇

2/5 The Zero-Defect Ripening Mandate:
Executive chefs at 5-star mega-resorts and luxury cruise lines operate on hyper-precise event menus. They cannot afford the operational drag of cutting open an avocado only to find internal graying or stringy fibers.
To win this business, you must bypass raw green-skin shipping and offer pre-conditioned, uniform Stage 3 (Breaking/Turning) or Stage 4 (Firm-Ripe) fruit. This requires a seamless partnership with specialized regional ripening centers near their major port hubs (like Miami, Barcelona, or Singapore).

3/5 Logistics via Marine Hotel Suppliers:
Cruise lines do not buy directly from individual farms; they procure via specialized Marine Hotel Suppliersand cruise-line chandlers (e.g., Sysco Marine, World Fuel Services, or specialized regional provisioners).
Your marketing strategy must target the Category Procurement Directors of these provisioning firms. Prove to them that your packing house has custom palletizing protocols designed to survive the tight 4-hour loading windows at international cruise terminals.

4/5 Sizing and Presentation Standards:
Unlike retail buyers who look for medium pre-packs, luxury hospitality demands aesthetic consistency.
• For Banquets/Buffets: High demand for large, uniform Sizes 12–14 to maximize yield per piece.
• For Plated Fine Dining: Precise Sizes 20–22 to control strict plate-cost portions.
Your sorting lines must be calibrated to sort not just for weight, but for flawless pear-shaped geometry with zero neck curvature.

5/5 The Ultimate Pitch: Food Safety & Traceability:
A single foodborne illness outbreak on a cruise ship can trigger a multi-million dollar liability nightmare.
To even be considered by corporate hospitality buyers, your operations must back up their supply with elite-level compliance: GlobalG.A.P., IFS Food, or SQF Level 3 Certification. Lead with your food safety data, and the premium margins will follow.
Have you ever explored the marine hospitality sector for your export volumes? Let’s talk numbers in the replies.

text:
Two days later, I received a message from our ground floor reception desk stating that Christian was standing in the main lobby of Summit Crest Group, demanding an audience with the Chief Executive Officer.

At that point, he still could not accept that the woman he had treated like an inferior dependent was the powerful executive ruling the entire organization.

I decided to grant him a five-minute meeting in my office.

When Christian stepped into my suite on the top floor of the tower, he stared in total disbelief at the panoramic glass windows, the private boardroom, and the architectural models of our commercial projects across Miami, Nashville, and Atlanta.

Then his eyes met mine as I sat behind my desk.

His face fell completely.

“So it was all completely true,” Christian muttered weakly.

“I never once lied to you about who I was as a human being,” I stated calmly. “I simply chose not to disclose the exact size of my bank accounts.”

“Why would you keep something like that from your own husband?” he asked softly.

“Because when I first met you seven years ago, I truly believed you were an honest man,” I explained sincerely. “You were deeply in debt back then, but you shared your limited meals with me. You rode in my beat-up truck when I was still building this business from scratch, and I fell in love with that humble man.”

Christian sat down in the leather chair without waiting for an invitation.

“Valerie, that same humble man is still standing right here in front of you,” Christian pleaded desperately.

“No, that man died the moment you started believing the world owed you luxury for simply existing,” I corrected him.

He rubbed his shaking hands together anxiously.

“Paige deceived me about everything, Valerie,” Christian claimed mournfully.

“And you deceived me for seven long years,” I pointed out directly.

“She told me her father was ready to invest millions into my firm, and she swore the baby was mine,” Christian whispered quietly. “She made me feel like…”

“Like a real man?” I finished his sentence for him.

He lowered his head, unable to meet my eyes.

I was repeating the exact words he had spat at me on the porch the night he threw me out into the rain.

“Valerie, we can easily rebuild our marriage from scratch,” Christian begged eagerly. “Now that I know who you truly are, I can help you manage this entire corporation. I know sales, I know high-net-worth people, and we can become an unstoppable power couple.”

I let out a short, quiet laugh at his absurd offer.

“That response is precisely what I needed to hear to know you haven’t learned a single thing,” I said calmly.

“What do you mean by that?” he asked in confusion.

“You are not asking to reconcile with your wife,” I revealed clearly. “You are simply begging to regain access to the Buckhead estate, the luxury car, the social standing, and my private fortune.”

Christian stood up abruptly from the chair.

“I care deeply about our marriage, Valerie!” Christian shouted defensively.

“Then name one single quality you miss about me that has nothing to do with my money or what I can purchase for you,” I challenged him directly.

He opened his mouth to speak, but no words came out.

That dead silence was my official divorce.

Our legal separation proceedings moved forward rapidly that same month. Under state law, our premarital agreement was rock solid, and because the Buckhead residence belonged entirely to a corporate entity, Christian had no legal standing to claim it as marital property.

I fail to see where Israel is the problem. Arab and Palestinian leaders rejected every major formal two-state offer while launching or sustaining waves of attacks on Jewish and Israeli civilians. Egypt, Jordan, the UAE, Bahrain, and Morocco signed peace or normalization agreements with Israel and honor them; peace holds. If Israel wanted to eradicate a people or place it would have happened. It has not.

Rejected offers  
1937 Peel Commission: British partition into small Jewish state and larger Arab state. Arab Higher Committee and Mufti Haj Amin al-Husseini rejected any Jewish state. Jews accepted in principle.  
1947 UN Partition Plan Res 181: Jewish and Arab states. Arab leadership rejected it and launched war. Jews accepted.  
1967 post-Six-Day War: Israel offered land-for-peace under UN 242. Arab League Khartoum replied with three no’s: no peace, no recognition, no negotiation.  
2000 Camp David: Clinton and Barak offered Palestinian state on roughly 91-95 percent of West Bank plus all Gaza, land swaps, shared Jerusalem arrangements. Arafat rejected with no counter-offer. Second Intifada followed.  
2000-2001 Clinton Parameters and Taba: refined offer near 97 percent with swaps. Arafat effectively rejected.  
2005 Gaza Disengagement: Sharon unilaterally withdrew all settlers and forces from Gaza and some northern West Bank settlements. PA under Abbas took control. Hamas later seized Gaza; rockets and rejectionism continued.  
2008 Olmert offer: roughly 93-94 percent of West Bank with 1:1 land swaps, all Gaza, shared Jerusalem holy basin, limited refugee return. Abbas did not accept.  
2020 Trump Peace to Prosperity: Palestinian state with land swaps, $50B economic package, security conditions. Abbas and PA rejected it outright.  
Oslo 1993 created the PA and a process; final-status talks collapsed amid violence and rejections. Bush Roadmap and Kerry talks stalled without signed deals.

Key attacks  
1920 Nebi Musa riots: Arab mobs kill Jews in Jerusalem.  
1921 Jaffa riots: dozens of Jews killed.  
1929 Hebron and Safed massacres: 133-plus Jews slaughtered; Jewish communities erased in Hebron.  
1936-1939 Arab Revolt: hundreds of Jews killed in attacks on settlements, roads, and civilians.  
1947-1949: after rejecting partition, civil war attacks plus invasion by Arab states; thousands of Jews killed.  
1950s: fedayeen raids from Gaza/Egypt and Jordan kill hundreds of Israeli civilians.  
1960s-1970s PLO terrorism including airplane hijackings and bombings. 1972 Munich Olympics: Black September takes Israeli athletes hostage; 11 murdered. Ma’alot school massacre 1974. Coastal Road bus massacre 1978.  
First Intifada 1987-1993: stabbings, shootings, Molotovs; roughly 200 Israelis killed.  
Second Intifada 2000-2005: suicide bombings and shootings; over 1,000 Israelis killed.  
Post-2005 Gaza: thousands of rockets and mortars from Hamas and Islamic Jihad; major rounds 2008-09, 2012, 2014, 2021. Knife and car-ramming waves from 2015.

text:
Taiwan Is Trying to Learn Ukraine’s Lessons Before the Shooting Starts

Taiwan’s latest defense push deserves more attention than it is getting, because it shows just how seriously Taipei is taking the possibility that China may eventually turn years of military pressure into something far more dangerous. Taiwan is no longer simply buying a few expensive American weapons and hoping the United States will come to the rescue. Increasingly, it appears to be trying to build the kind of layered, drone-heavy, missile-heavy and difficult-to-destroy defense that Ukraine was forced to invent after Russia invaded.

The enormous difference is timing. Ukraine had to learn many of these lessons while Russian missiles were already falling and Russian troops were crossing its borders. Taiwan has the benefit of watching that war unfold from a distance and asking what Ukraine wishes it had possessed on February 23, 2022. Taiwan is now trying to build some of those capabilities before its own February 24 ever arrives.

That makes the Taiwan Strait one of the most important military races in the world today. China is trying to develop enough capability and confidence to isolate or defeat Taiwan before outside help can meaningfully intervene. Taiwan is trying to make itself so dangerous, so resilient and so expensive to attack that Beijing never becomes confident enough to try.

The unsettling question is simple: which side gets what it wants first?

Taiwan Is Starting to Buy Weapons That Look Very Familiar

Taiwan’s cabinet has proposed another NT$145.7 billion, or roughly $4.6 billion, in additional defense spending for 2026. Among the systems included are more than 600 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones, more than 40,000 coastal attack drones and more than 100 suicide drone boats, along with additional domestically produced missiles and other equipment.[1]

Those numbers are worth stopping over for a moment. Forty thousand attack drones are not a demonstration project, and more than one hundred explosive unmanned boats are not simply an experiment to see whether the technology works. Taiwan appears to be trying to create mass, and mass is one of the great lessons emerging from Ukraine.

The spending also comes after Taiwan’s parliament approved a separate six-year drone-focused plan worth roughly NT$240 billion. Taiwan’s planned defense budget for 2027 is expected to exceed NT$1 trillion for the first time, while President Lai Ching-te has increasingly emphasized domestic weapons production, unmanned systems and artificial intelligence as parts of the island’s future defense.[1][2]

This does not mean Taiwan is abandoning fighter aircraft, ships or traditional weapons. It means something more subtle may be happening. Taiwan increasingly seems to understand that it cannot simply build a smaller mirror image of the Chinese military and expect to win a contest of numbers.

China will have more ships.

China will have more aircraft.

China will have more missiles.

China will have more soldiers.

Taiwan’s job is therefore not necessarily to match those numbers. Its job is to make China pay an unacceptable price for trying to use them.

Ukraine has provided a remarkably useful demonstration of how that can be done.

Ukraine Changed the Economics of Warfare

One of the great lessons from Ukraine has been that inexpensive weapons can destroy extremely expensive ones if they are available in sufficient numbers and used intelligently. Small drones costing hundreds or thousands of dollars have destroyed tanks, artillery systems, air-defense equipment and even strategic aircraft worth millions or billions. Ukraine’s unmanned boats and missiles have also helped deny Russia the level of freedom in the Black Sea that might have been expected from the overwhelming difference between the two countries’ conventional navies.[3][4]

That does not mean drones have replaced every other weapon on the battlefield. What Ukraine has demonstrated is that the economics of warfare have changed. A defender may not need a million-dollar interceptor every time the attacker sends something cheap. It may not need another enormous warship to threaten an enormous enemy warship. Cheap, disposable and mass-produced systems can force expensive military platforms to operate much more cautiously.

Taiwan could potentially exploit that lesson even more dramatically because China faces a geographic problem Russia did not face when it invaded Ukraine.

Russia could drive across a land border.

China has to cross the Taiwan Strait.

One Hundred Miles of Water Changes Everything

Any large Chinese invasion would require moving enormous amounts of men and equipment across roughly 100 miles of water. Soldiers, armored vehicles, ammunition, fuel, food, communications equipment and engineering units would somehow have to make that journey and then get ashore in sufficient numbers to sustain an invasion.

That creates an extraordinary period of vulnerability.

A tank sitting aboard a landing ship is not yet a battlefield weapon. A soldier packed aboard a transport is not yet fighting on Taiwanese soil. Fuel inside a supply vessel is useless to a Chinese armored unit if the ship carrying it never reaches the beach.

Taiwan increasingly appears to be building around that reality. Missiles, sea mines, coastal drones, unmanned boats, mobile launchers and other distributed weapons could potentially make the Taiwan Strait and the approaches to the island extraordinarily dangerous.

The strategically located Penghu Islands offer a good example. Sitting in the Taiwan Strait roughly 50 kilometers from Taiwan’s main island, Penghu could become a major obstacle for Chinese forces approaching Taiwan. Taipei has strengthened the islands with Hsiung Feng III anti-ship missiles, drone forces and expanded military exercises, while civilians there have participated in emergency and civil-defense preparations.[5]

The goal is not necessarily to sink every Chinese ship. It is to make the crossing uncertain enough that Chinese planners can never comfortably calculate how many ships, troops and supplies will actually make it through.

That is a very Ukrainian way of looking at warfare.

China’s Pressure Is Growing at the Same Time

Unfortunately for Taiwan, its preparations are not happening in a vacuum. Chinese military pressure around the island has been increasing dramatically.

According to CSIS, Chinese military aircraft carried out a record 3,764 incursions into Taiwan’s de facto air-defense identification zone during 2025, an increase of 22.4 percent over 2024. Chinese naval activity has also remained at much higher levels than only a few years ago.[6]

The trend becomes even more striking when China’s coast guard is included. A separate CSIS analysis found that between 2020 and 2025, the daily average number of distinct Chinese coast guard vessels entering waters near Taiwan increased by more than 500 percent, while incursions into Taiwan’s second maritime security ring more than quadrupled.[7]

Taiwan’s own 2026 defense report describes China as becoming increasingly assertive and unpredictable while improving its ability to control the air and sea around the island. Chinese forces now conduct military activity near Taiwan almost every day and routinely practice operations connected to blockades, joint strikes and maritime control.[8]

That matters because repeated exercises do more than send political messages. They allow Chinese pilots, ship crews, missile units, commanders and logistics systems to practice operating around Taiwan again and again.

There is another danger as well. When large Chinese exercises become routine, it becomes increasingly difficult to distinguish another exercise from the beginning of something real.

An invasion does not necessarily have to begin with Beijing announcing that the invasion has begun.

Taiwan Is Learning From Ukraine — But So Is China

There is a dangerous tendency to talk about the lessons of Ukraine as though Taiwan is the only country studying them.

China is watching too.

Taiwan’s latest defense assessment says Beijing has been studying drone swarms, ammunition consumption and problems coordinating allied forces that have emerged from recent wars, including Russia’s war against Ukraine.[8]

China has every reason to examine Russia’s failures carefully. Moscow expected Ukraine to collapse quickly, failed to eliminate Ukrainian political leadership and command structures, underestimated Ukrainian resistance and eventually became trapped in a long war of attrition.

Beijing would presumably want to avoid exactly that outcome.

That means a future Chinese attack could place enormous importance on the opening hours and days. Cyberattacks, electronic warfare, missile strikes, attacks on communications, air-defense suppression and attempts to disrupt Taiwan’s command structure could all be used to weaken the island before major landing operations even begin.

China may also conclude that an immediate amphibious invasion is unnecessary. A blockade or maritime quarantine could pressure Taiwan economically while forcing Taipei, Washington and other governments to decide how far they are prepared to escalate in order to break it.

This is therefore not simply China preparing an invasion while Taiwan prepares to stop it. Both militaries are studying the same modern wars and trying to make sure they are the ones who learned the correct lessons.

Taiwan Has One Advantage Ukraine Never Had

Taiwan possesses something Ukraine did not have before Russia invaded: Ukraine itself as a warning.

Taiwan can study what happens when ammunition stockpiles are inadequate. It can watch what happens when electrical infrastructure comes under sustained missile attack. It can study how command systems survive, how communications networks are dispersed, how civilians are mobilized and how drones can be manufactured and modified at wartime speed.

Perhaps most importantly, Taiwan can examine all of the things Ukraine wishes it had done earlier.

Build ammunition stockpiles before the war.

Build drone factories before the war.

Disperse military assets before the war.

Strengthen civilian preparedness before the war.

Create redundant communications before the war.

Build domestic weapons production before supply lines are threatened.

Taiwanese defense planners have been discussing asymmetric defense for years, and early assessments after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine already pointed to lessons involving missiles, mines, territorial defense and other systems intended to make an invasion extremely difficult.[9] What is different now is that Taiwan appears to be moving toward those capabilities at substantially greater scale.

Forty thousand coastal attack drones suggests the lesson is moving beyond theory.

Taiwan Does Not Have to Be Stronger Than China

This may be the most important part of the entire equation.

Taiwan does not necessarily have to build a military capable of defeating China in a traditional head-to-head war. Given the enormous difference in population, industrial capacity and military spending, that may be impossible.

What Taiwan needs is something different.

It needs to convince Chinese leaders that attacking the island could become a disaster.

Beijing has to consider not only whether China could eventually defeat Taiwan, but how many ships might be sunk doing it, how many aircraft might be lost, how many troops might die crossing the Strait, how much economic damage a war would cause and what happens if the opening attack fails to produce the rapid collapse Chinese planners expected.

Those questions matter enormously because amphibious warfare is already among the most difficult military operations possible. Adding tens of thousands of drones, mobile anti-ship missiles, mines, unmanned boats, dispersed defenders and hardened infrastructure makes the calculation considerably uglier.

The objective is deterrence through uncertainty.

China does not need to believe Taiwan can conquer China.

China needs to believe Taiwan might ruin China's invasion.

But China Has an Objective Too

China is trying to solve exactly that problem before Taiwan can make it unsolvable.

Its expanding air and naval activity around the island gives Chinese forces more experience operating in the region. China’s coast guard increases Beijing’s ability to apply pressure below the level of outright war, while repeated blockade-style exercises improve its ability to isolate Taiwan.[7][8]

From Beijing’s perspective, there may therefore be a window.

If China believes Taiwan is rapidly becoming more difficult to invade, domestic drone manufacturing is expanding, American weapons continue arriving and regional alliances are strengthening, Chinese leaders could eventually conclude that waiting makes their military problem worse rather than better.

That does not mean an invasion is inevitable or even likely in the immediate future. It does mean the strategic competition contains an uncomfortable timing problem.

Taiwan wants time because every additional year potentially gives it more drones, missiles, hardened facilities, trained reservists and domestic weapons production.

China also wants time because every additional year potentially gives it more ships, missiles, aircraft, amphibious capabilities and experience operating around Taiwan.

At some point, however, one side may decide time is helping the other side more.

That is where this becomes dangerous.

So Who Gets There First?

This may eventually become the central question surrounding Taiwan.

Does China develop enough confidence in its ability to blockade, isolate or invade Taiwan before the island completes its transformation into a far more heavily armed and resilient target?

Or does Taiwan build enough missiles, drones, mines, unmanned boats, dispersed defenses and domestic manufacturing capacity that Beijing looks across the Strait and concludes that the price has become unacceptable?

Ukraine demonstrated what can happen when a supposedly weaker country survives the first blow and then learns how to fight a much larger opponent while the war is already underway.

Taiwan is attempting something even more ambitious.

It is trying to absorb those lessons before the first missile is launched.

China is increasing the pressure while Taiwan is increasing the defenses, and both sides are studying the same wars for clues about what comes next. That makes the Taiwan Strait more than a military standoff. It has become a race between two competing ideas of victory.

China wants to become powerful enough that resistance appears hopeless.

Taiwan wants to become dangerous enough that invasion appears foolish.

Neither side has achieved that objective yet.

The question that may ultimately decide whether there is a war is which one gets there first.

Footnotes

[1] Reuters, September 3, 2026 — Taiwan proposes additional $4.6 billion in 2026 defense spending. The proposal includes more than 600 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones, more than 40,000 coastal attack drones and more than 100 suicide drone boats. Reuters also reports that Taiwan's parliament approved a separate six-year NT$240 billion drone-focused spending program in August.

[2] Reuters, September 2, 2026 — Taiwan's defense spending set to exceed NT$1 trillion. President Lai Ching-te said Taiwan's defense budget for the coming year would exceed NT$1 trillion for the first time and emphasized self-reliance, domestic military industries, artificial intelligence and unmanned systems.

[3] CSIS — “How Ukraine’s Operation Spider’s Web Redefines Asymmetric Warfare.” CSIS argues that Ukraine demonstrated how inexpensive FPV drones and creative logistics can destroy exceptionally valuable military platforms and alter traditional cost calculations in warfare.

[4] CSIS — Maritime lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war. Analysis of the Black Sea conflict notes that Ukraine, despite possessing little conventional naval power, used unmanned surface vessels, missiles and asymmetric tactics to inflict heavy losses and limit the freedom of Russia's much larger Black Sea Fleet.

[5] Reuters, August 28, 2026 — Penghu Islands preparations. Reuters reports that Taiwan has deployed long-range Hsiung Feng III missiles and drone forces on Penghu, while conducting military and civil-defense preparations for scenarios including blockade and invasion.

[6] CSIS ChinaPower — Chinese military activity around Taiwan in 2025. CSIS reports a record 3,764 PLA aircraft incursions into Taiwan's de facto ADIZ during 2025, up 22.4 percent from 2024, alongside persistently elevated Chinese naval activity.

[7] CSIS, May 5, 2026 — “The Geometry of Coercion.” Between January 2020 and December 2025, CSIS found that the daily average of distinct Chinese coast guard vessels entering Taiwan's nearby waters increased by more than 500 percent, while incursions into Taiwan's second maritime security ring more than quadrupled.

[8] Reuters, August 31, 2026 — Taiwan's annual defense report. Taiwan described China's behavior as increasingly assertive and unpredictable and said Beijing is studying drone swarms, ammunition consumption and allied-coordination problems from recent wars. The report also highlighted Chinese practice of blockade and maritime-control operations around Taiwan.

[9] CSIS — “Ukraine and Taiwan: Parallels and Early Lessons Learned.” Early analysis following Russia's full-scale invasion emphasized Ukraine's demonstration of the value of asymmetric capabilities and discussed Taiwan's need for systems including surface-to-surface missiles, mines and other weapons intended to make invasion and occupation extremely difficult.

Namibia’s tourism sector faces the challenge of ensuring that its economic benefits reach local communities, young people, and small businesses while protecting the country’s fragile natural and cultural resources.

These were the concerns raised during the public consultation and validation workshop on the draft revision of Namibia’s National Policy on Sustainable Tourism Development, held in Swakopmund.

Environment, Forestry, and Tourism Ministry Executive Director Sikongo Haihambo said the policy review is an opportunity to address gaps in the current tourism framework and ensure the sector responds to changing realities and future challenges.

Haihambo said the revised policy must create an environment where Namibians, particularly young people and small and emerging businesses, can participate meaningfully in the tourism value chain.

The policy is also expected to address the need for tourism development to benefit communities across all regions, rather than concentrating economic opportunities in established destinations.

Erongo and Kunene are considered strategically important to the country’s tourism industry, with attractions including the Namib Desert, Skeleton Coast, Brandberg, Swakopmund and Walvis Bay.

Haihambo said these areas offer opportunities for marine and coastal tourism, adventure tourism, cultural and heritage tourism, community-based tourism, conferences, events, and desert experiences.

However, he cautioned that tourism development must not come at the expense of the fragile desert and coastal ecosystems that sustain the industry.

He said unlocking the full potential of tourism will require coordinated planning, investment and stronger collaboration between government, the private sector, local authorities and communities.

He therefore called on stakeholders participating in the consultation to openly identify gaps and practical challenges in the draft policy and provide recommendations that can make it more effective.

Nutmeg (Myristica fragrans) is an evergreen tropical tree famous for producing two valuable spices: nutmeg, which comes from the seed, and mace, the reddish covering surrounding the seed.

Unlike ordinary crops that are harvested for only one product, a mature nutmeg tree provides an opportunity to generate value from both nutmeg and mace.

🌰 𝗡𝗨𝗧𝗠𝗘𝗚 & 𝗠𝗔𝗖𝗘 – 𝗧𝗪𝗢 𝗩𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗘 𝗦𝗣𝗜𝗖𝗘𝗦

Nutmeg is widely recognized as a culinary spice. The dried seed is ground and used in:

🍰 Baking and confectionery
🍛 Curries and spice blends
🥤 Beverages
🍲 Traditional and specialty foods

The red aril surrounding the seed is known as mace and is also dried and marketed as a valuable spice.

Nutmeg and its derivatives are also used in essential oils, perfumes, soaps, cosmetics and other processed products, creating opportunities for value addition.

🌱 𝗡𝗨𝗧𝗠𝗘𝗚 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗗𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦

Nutmeg is a warm, humid tropical crop and performs best where there is adequate moisture throughout the year.

🌡️ Temperature: Approximately 20–35°C
💧 Rainfall: Around 1,500–2,500mm annually
📍 Altitude: Up to approximately 1,200m above sea level
🌱 Soil: Deep, fertile and well-drained soils
🧪 Soil pH: Approximately 5.5–7.0

The crop does not perform well under frost, prolonged drought or waterlogged conditions. Good drainage and reliable moisture are therefore important when establishing a nutmeg orchard.

📍 𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘 𝗖𝗔𝗡 𝗡𝗨𝗧𝗠𝗘𝗚 𝗕𝗘 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪𝗡 𝗜𝗡 𝗞𝗘𝗡𝗬𝗔?

Suitable areas may include warm and humid parts of:

📍 Coastal Kenya – Kilifi, Kwale and Lamu
📍 Western Kenya – Kakamega, Bungoma and Vihiga
📍 Lake Region – suitable warm and humid areas
📍 Lower elevations of Central & Eastern Kenya where adequate moisture or irrigation is available

The exact suitability of a farm depends on rainfall, temperature, soil type, drainage, altitude and water availability.

🌳 𝗡𝗨𝗧𝗠𝗘𝗚 𝗙𝗔𝗥𝗠𝗜𝗡𝗚 & 𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚

Because nutmeg develops into a sizeable evergreen tree, farmers should provide adequate space for canopy development.

📏 A spacing of approximately 8m × 8m can be considered, depending on site conditions and farm management.

During the early years, suitable farmers may intercrop nutmeg with crops such as bananas, pineapples and other compatible shade-tolerant crops, helping make productive use of the available land while the trees are still young.

Mulching and adequate moisture are particularly important during dry periods.

⏳ 𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗡 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗡𝗨𝗧𝗠𝗘𝗚 𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗥𝗧 𝗙𝗥𝗨𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚?

Nutmeg is a long-term investment crop. Farmers should not expect immediate returns.

🌱 Production generally begins around 6–8 years after planting, depending on planting material and growing conditions.

The major advantage is longevity: once established and properly managed, nutmeg trees can remain productive for many decades.

🌰 𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗩𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 & 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗖𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗜𝗡𝗚

When mature, the nutmeg fruit splits open, revealing the seed surrounded by the red mace.

The mace is separated and dried, while the nutmeg seed is also carefully dried before storage, processing or grinding.

This creates two separate products from the same fruit — nutmeg and mace.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

It was a Tuesday morning in Paris, the third of September, 1783, and the room at the Hôtel d’York was quiet in the way rooms are quiet when something long in coming is about to be finished. Benjamin Franklin was seventy-seven, worn by gout and by years of court and committee, yet still the most recognizable American in Europe. John Adams had come from the Netherlands, all New England rectitude and barely contained fire. John Jay, lately of Spain, sat with the lawyer’s reserve of a man who had learned not to trust every smile offered in a foreign capital. Across from them was David Hartley, member of Parliament, old acquaintance of Franklin’s, sent to put the King’s name to what the King had never wanted to admit.

They signed.

The first article still has the ring of a door closing forever. His Britannic Majesty acknowledged the United States—New Hampshire, Massachusetts Bay, Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia—to be free, sovereign, and independent states. He relinquished, for himself and for his heirs, every claim to their government and their soil. A monarch who had called them rebels now treated with them as a nation.

What followed on the map was almost as remarkable as the words. Britain yielded the country east of the Mississippi, south of the Great Lakes, north of the Florida line. Franklin had wanted Canada and did not get it. What they did get was a continent in outline—room enough, if they could keep it. Fishing rights off Newfoundland and in the Gulf of St. Lawrence were written down. The Mississippi was to remain free to both peoples. Debts were to be honored. Congress would “earnestly recommend” that the states restore what had been taken from Loyalists, a phrase that would prove easier to sign than to enforce. British armies were to withdraw “with all convenient speed.” The last of them would leave New York on a cold November morning two months later, the Union Jack coming down a greased flagpole at the Battery while a sailor named Van Arsdale climbed with cleats to put the American colors in its place.

The path to that table had been anything but simple. France had been the indispensable ally, and the treaty of 1778 forbade a separate peace. Jay, who had spent fruitless months in Madrid, did not believe the Comte de Vergennes meant the new republic to have much more than a strip of seaboard hemmed by the mountains. So the Americans, against the letter if not quite the spirit of the alliance, dealt directly with Britain. The preliminary articles of November 30, 1782, were kept close until France and Spain settled their own accounts the same September day at Versailles. When the seals were affixed, the United States was not a client. It was a country.

Eight years of war had come down to ink and wax in a rented room. Winter at Valley Forge, the long retreats, the sudden glory at Saratoga and Yorktown, the borrowed money and the borrowed time—all of it gathered into a document that began, as so many of their great papers did, in the name of the most Holy and undivided Trinity, and ended with four signatures and the date. The greatest empire on earth had been made to write the independence of a people who had claimed the old English liberties and then refused to stop at the water’s edge.

The paper remains. So does the nation it named.
