Two Memphis sanitation workers were crushed to death INSIDE the garbage compactor, because it was the only place Black crews were allowed to shelter from the rain.

February 1, 1968. Echol Cole and Robert Walker, riding a rain-soaked route on decrepit equipment, climbed into the truck's barrel when the downpour hit — with nowhere else they were permitted to wait it out. A malfunction triggered the compactor with both men inside.

The city that let this happen classified them as day laborers: no workers' compensation, no death benefits.

The settlement offered to two destroyed families: roughly one month's pay, and five hundred dollars toward the burials.

1. CIRCLE EXPANDS CCTP BEYOND USDC EURC CAN NOW MOVE NATIVELY CROSSCHAIN

@circle has expanded Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP) beyond USDC to support its euro-denominated stablecoin, EURC.

The rollout starts with Ethereum and @base, allowing EURC to move natively between supported chains using the same burn-and-mint model already used for USDC.

Instead of wrapping EURC or relying on separate third-party bridges, the asset is burned on the source network and newly minted on the destination.

For developers, the bigger development is that the same interoperability layer can now handle both dollar and euro stablecoins.

Potential applications include:
• Cross-border payments
• Stablecoin FX
• Treasury management
• DeFi
• European payment applications
• Multi-currency onchain finance
This is another step toward stablecoin infrastructure becoming increasingly multi-currency rather than dollar-only.
Official source:
https://t.co/RnZZn5g3eC

2. BIS RESEARCHERS USE XRP LEDGER TO MAKE OFFICIAL STATISTICS VERIFIABLE
This is one of today’s more interesting institutional blockchain developments.
The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) has published a working paper exploring how blockchain can help people verify that official economic statistics are authentic and have not been altered.

The proof-of-concept uses the XRP Ledger.

Instead of publishing sensitive underlying datasets onchain, the system creates cryptographic fingerprints of the data and records a summary value on XRPL.
That means someone receiving the statistics from a website, third-party platform or even an AI system could independently check whether the data matches what the original institution published.

The researchers report publication taking roughly 3–5 seconds and verification around 1–2 seconds in controlled testing.

Important clarification:
This is a research proof-of-concept, not an announcement that BIS or central banks are moving their financial operations to XRP Ledger.

The paper also explicitly states that its views are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the BIS or its member central banks.

Still, it demonstrates a serious non-speculative blockchain use case:
verifying the authenticity of public information in an AI-driven world.

Official BIS paper:
https://t.co/euVFZxyg3F

3. WYOMING PUTS FRNT STABLE TOKEN RESERVE VERIFICATION ONCHAIN WITH CHAINLINK
The U.S. state of Wyoming is strengthening the transparency infrastructure around its Frontier Stable Token FRNT.

The Wyoming Stable Token Commission has adopted @chainlink Proof of Reserve to provide onchain verification of reserves backing FRNT.

The setup combines independent reserve examinations with blockchain-based verification, creating more continuous visibility into whether the token remains fully backed.

This builds on Wyoming’s earlier move to use Chainlink CCIP as FRNT’s exclusive cross-chain infrastructure.

The Commission also says it is working toward Proof of Reserve Secure Mint, which can programmatically prevent new tokens from being minted unless verified reserves are sufficient.
That is an important direction for stablecoins:

RESERVES → INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION → ONCHAIN DATA → PROGRAMMABLE MINTING CONTROLS.

Instead of users simply trusting that reserves exist, infrastructure can increasingly make reserve information directly verifiable by applications and smart contracts.

Official announcement:
https://t.co/7CE8Y1b7UO

4. POLYGON OPEN MONEY STACK COMPLETES SOC 2 TYPE 1 EXAMINATION
@0xPolygon is pushing its payments infrastructure further toward institutional standards.

Polygon Labs says its Open Money Stack (OMS) API and dashboard have completed a SOC 2 Type 1 examination conducted by independent audit firm Schellman.

SOC 2 is widely used by enterprises and financial institutions when evaluating the security controls of technology providers.

Important distinction:

Type 1 evaluates whether controls are suitably designed at a specific point in time.

It does NOT mean months of operating effectiveness have already been tested.
Polygon says that next stage SOC 2 Type 2 is already underway.

Why does this matter for Web3?

If blockchain infrastructure wants to power serious:
• Payments
• Treasury systems
• Enterprise settlement
• FinTech applications
• Institutional financial products

technical performance alone isn't enough.

Banks and regulated businesses also need security assurance, auditability and compliance-ready infrastructure.

Official source:
https://t.co/Ql9gXKYPJq

5. LONDON STOCK EXCHANGE MOVES TOWARD TOKENIZED PUBLIC EQUITIES
The London Stock Exchange has announced plans to develop UK tokenized equity structures, subject to regulatory approval.

The goal is particularly interesting:
Bring public equities onto digital rails while preserving the shareholder rights, governance standards and investor protections associated with regulated markets.

LSE is also partnering with Payward to explore wallet-based and digital-native access connecting traditional regulated markets with public and private blockchain ecosystems.
Separately, LSE says it intends subject to regulatory approval to list xStocks on LSE 24 in 2027.
Its broader digital infrastructure already includes:
• LSEG Digital Securities Depository
• Digital Settlement House
• Tokenized securities settlement infrastructure
• 24-hour market initiatives
This is another sign that the future may not simply be:

TRADFI vs CRYPTO.

It may increasingly become:
regulated financial markets operating partly on blockchain rails.
Official LSEG announcement:
https://t.co/MO8UkZutSJ

6. SINGAPORE MOVES ITS STABLECOIN FRAMEWORK TOWARD LEGISLATION 🇸🇬
The Monetary Authority of Singapore has opened a consultation on legislative amendments needed to implement the country’s stablecoin regulatory framework.

The proposed changes involve amendments to the Payment Services Act 2019.

This is an important stage because stablecoin regulation is increasingly moving beyond policy announcements toward the actual legal infrastructure governing:
• Issuers
• Reserve requirements
• Redemption
• Consumer protection
• Stablecoin services

Singapore has long positioned itself as a serious digital-asset jurisdiction while maintaining relatively strict regulatory standards.

As stablecoins become increasingly integrated into payments and capital markets, jurisdictions are now competing not only over crypto companies but also over which regulatory frameworks become trusted enough for global stablecoin businesses to operate under.

text:
Portugal is the country that had the largest opportunity of the last twenty years: it attracted essentially la crème de la crème of tech. Incredible place. It would have had all the conditions to be the #1 place in Europe for many if only it had been able to offer a reliable system to incorporate and run companies. Unfortunately, it made doing business close to impossible and uncertain. While allowing mass migration to arrive with no prior authorization (tot. 1.5M, 14% of the population), it decided to cut the NHR and replace it with the IFICI regime as implemented today: complex, based on express authorization and, contrary to its original intention, in reality usable only by later-stage entrepreneurs.

With a mildly efficient system, or an EU Inc. and/or a less convoluted IFICI, the stretch Lisbon–Cascais would be the European Bay Area, with thousands of new companies building the future from Portugal. This would have meant, among others, allowing thousands of young Portuguese to thrive in their own country instead of leaving for London or anywhere else to make it.

Unfortunately it won't be the case. In terms of real estate, I might be completely wrong: but it will keep rising because of very weird supply-demand logic, against all odds and very reasonable predictions. Golden visa has never been the issue behind real estate price spikes. Chances are Portugal is going to be like Ryanair: everyone frustrated, but will keep “selling tickets”.

Resolution is **narrow**: signed **federal** law by **31 Dec 2026** with at least one of: **ban create/release** of specified systems, **training limits** (data lock or **parameter cap**), etc. A NIST rename, labeling bill, or state RAISE Act is **not** Yes.

On a book this thin, **identity** moves the spread more than committee PDFs.

### Identity signals that can **widen** Yes (or tighten the 9/11 offer)
| Signal | Coalition | Why the mid twitches 

| **Safety-tribe moral panic** (x-risk, “pause,” child-safety mashup) | CAIS / PauseAI / some Dems | Makes “do something” feel mandatory; traders who don’t read the resolve text buy **any** AI bill as Yes |
| **CA/NY RAISE as “federal coming”** | State-reg identity | False bridge: state law ≠ https://t.co/L9HkdHAaro signature |
| **Lab incident / model-gone-wrong clip** | Safety + cable | Spikes Yes; usually mean-reverts unless a **named vehicle** hits the floor |
| **Bipartisan Science markup theater** (Foushee / Obernolte 35–0) | “adults in the room” | Looks like momentum; **HR 9363** is NIST/CISA-ish — may **fail** the parameter-cap clause |
| **Midterm “protect kids / deepfakes”** identity | both parties’ ads | Can lift Yes **if** leadership attaches a **training restriction** rider — rare |

### Identity signals that **widen No** (or lift the 89¢ bid)
| Signal | Coalition | Why |---|---|---|
| **Huang / NVDA / “theoretical harms”** (this post’s seed) | Accel + export-control hawks | Encodes: regulation = Europe-brained; US identity = ship GPUs |
| **Trump EO / federal preemption of states** | MAGA-tech | Federal *safety statute* becomes the enemy of “win the race vs China” |
| **Cruz bottleneck / Guthrie “not before the election”** | Senate GOP process | Calendar identity: lame-duck + 4 months left |
| **China-race / “compute is deterrence”** | defense-tech | Safety bill = unilateral disarmament |
| **Anti-Brussels** (EU AI Act as other) | same | Any “safety” brand tagged EU → No bid |

Huang is a **high-\(\rho\)** identity token: one sentence, infinite reprints. \(I(\text{Huang}; \text{signed parameter cap}) \approx 0\). It still **shifts the spread** because the book is shallow and the word “safety” is tribal.

### What actually binds the resolve (not identity)
- Need a **signed** bill matching **those verbs**.  
- House Science package (labeling, NIST center, incident reporting) can pass committee **unanimously** and still be **No**.  
- Obernolte–Trahan “Great American AI” + Moran incident-report standalone: **possible** vehicles; Guthrie already shrugged at pre-midterm floor time. Cruz markup slipped.  
- Four months + election = **calendar price**, as @polyhivebet said.

Desk: **10% Yes / 90% No**. Fade Yes **>18¢** on Huang-inverse-panic or a Science-committee headline. Fade No **<6¢** only if a **specific** training-cap text is calendared for floor + White House signal.

### Spread mechanics
Identity posts change **who is at the touch**, not \(p^*\):

\[
\text{spread} \uparrow \quad\text{when tribes disagree about the word “safety”}
\]

Safety buyers lift the **Yes ask**;
accel buyers lift the **No bid**. 

Result on this name: **sticky 200 bps**, mid glued near **11¢**, volume in **$5–15** clips (PolyInsider). That is **attention inflation**, not a new joint \(p(x,y)\).

**Read:** The Polymarket post is an **identity pairing** — Huang (accel) + “12% safety bill” (fear). It does not name a bill that would resolve Yes. 

Signals that **move this spread** are tribal tags (x-risk vs China-race vs kids vs Brussels), not G20 color. Trade the **resolution verbs** and the **Senate clock**; fade identity spikes.

The problem isn't just on one side - we need better labour laws for companies & we also need regulations in place to make offer letters binding on both sides.

If you are at Uber and the consistent question was to either keep investing  for low returns or exit to focus on future direction then the answer seems simple - Exit.

Combining announcement with action could be about direction and cost. Yes customer trust is important but was that really at risk if you think about it. You want trust from whom you serve and you have performed well enough to hinge trust on value anyway so may be no incentive for anything extra. 

Ride-hailing in Nigeria built around local economics in Naira can work.

Of course, saying something can work and actually making it work are two very different things. But at sufficient scale, with a largely Naira-based cost structure and the right operating model, the economics work. 

However since I know a number of people will hear exit and start building, let me offer unsolicited advice 

Use @simplifydHQ for Naira based infra cost. AWS and Mongo together will eat it up.

Offer <=20% in fees to drivers and perhaps lower prices to customers.

Make good cars and a great ride experience your priority. You should have other type of cars as well for reach, lower prices and scale.

Train drivers and give more incentives to those who are ON, take the most trips and get the most customer ratings.

Reward users with points that become savings on trips and 

Make sure the tech works better than Lagride and more like Uber. 

Bonus: offer credit at 0% to drivers if repayment is in 7days then 3-5% per month as flat rate from day 8. Then to customers who have earned it subsequently.

Basically start a lending business with ride-hailing and make sure it’s an embedded experience not a loan service.

text:
Post 3. 

Signing Washington would not have repealed Bishkek. It would not have made Song Hailiang disappear. It would have raised the cost of naming the Rio chairman as Invest in Canada chair six days after he sat in CCCC headquarters, because the neighbour would have had a minerals side-letter and a content screen already in force. Personnel collisions are cheaper when you are off the moving track.

A signed text would not have made CETA larger than the American market. It would not have turned SAFE’s first radio contract for Poland into a substitute for integrated auto platforms. Anand is right that membership is not on the burner. She is also describing a complement. Complements do not replace the engine.

How Canada would have fared, the honest range

Better on the invoice. Worse, or no better, on the plant, unless Ottawa had used the year the text bought to finish the register.

That is the only range the ledger supports.

A Canada that signed on the terms Greer described would today be shipping the 338 slice without the new 50 per cent, landing metals at a lower 232, and arguing inside a content rule instead of outside one. Dairy administration and liquor shelves would have been the visible price. Some auto plants would have failed the United States-content screen and bled. Some would have re-sourced and stayed. Mexico would not have been the only partner whose weekly meeting produced a text. Canadian heavy would still have been needed this year. The energy carve-out would have been insurance, not the whole strategy.

A Canada that signed and then treated the text as permission to keep the China commercial drawer wide, 49,000 vehicles at 6.1 per cent, a 50 per cent export-growth target, no published screen on CMIC counterparties, would have been in a tighter vice than the one it is in now. Washington’s offer, even in Greer’s telling, wanted coordination on third-country deals. Coordination is not a veto. It is a conversation the neighbour can turn into an invoice if the other drawer stays open. Signing does not licence the two-column cheque. It makes the second column more expensive.

A Canada that signed and used the year to put one corridor on a lender’s books, shrink the title map, and publish a screen would have been in the only position that answers both the American campaign and the Chinese offtake. That Canada is not produced by a signature. It is produced by statutes. The signature only buys the year.

The elbows-up path bought a different year. Section 338 is live. Canadian counters land 8 September. Trump has already named 1 January 2027 as the next number on cars, trucks, parts and steel. Mexico is still on the moving track. Carney will sit in Strasbourg on 16 September as the first foreign head of government at a State of the Union and speak to the Parliament the next day. An EU–Canada summit is set for 29–30 October. Invest in Canada’s new chair arrives at a 14–15 September summit twelve days after a CCCC handshake. That is not a substitute market. It is a calendar of rooms.

The last-hour problem

Honesty requires the gap. If the unpublished pages really did require Canada to clear third-country agreements with Washington, or to gut language rules as a trade concession, the walk-away names a floor that a comment page should not sneer at. Greer says those pages did not exist as commands. Carney says they touched culture and the freedom to deal elsewhere. Until a text is released, both accounts are advocacy.

What is not advocacy is the rest of the package both sides described: 338 suspended, metals down, lumber 232 off, autos inside a content bargain, minerals and aerospace in a side-letter, dairy licences and liquor as the Canadian price. A government that wanted a floor on culture could have initialled the commercial chapters and reserved the cultural annex. Walking away from the whole pile because the last hour was ugly is how you spend a clock on a seating chart.

authorBio: Retired Royal Canadian Marine SAR Specialist | I incorporate AI in my content and fight policy storms for real freedom & evidence-based reform.

text:
Post 1. 

Signing the text would not have finished a plant. Walking away made the clock more expensive.

3rd September 2026

If Canada had closed the August deal, the 50 per cent slice would not be in force, metals and autos would be inside a worse-but-dated American offer, and Mexico would not be the only partner on a moving track. The unfinished project book would still be unfinished. Elbows-up did not buy sovereignty. It bought a seating chart and a higher invoice.

The question is not whether Mark Carney should have smiled. It is what a signed text in the third week of August would have changed, and what it would have left untouched.

Start with what is actually on the public record. On 18 August Donald Trump said the countries had a deal, subject to documents. A three-day pause pushed the Section 338 clock from 19 to 22 August. On the night of 21 August the talks collapsed. Jamieson Greer, the United States trade representative, said Canada would have received the most preferential treatment of any trading partner: cuts to steel, aluminium and auto tariffs, elimination of a 10 per cent Section 232 levy on softwood lumber, and a complete suspension of the 50 per cent Section 338 duties that were about to hit a slice of Canadian goods, dairy, alcohol and a long annex of consumer and industrial lines, valued in the US$20 billion to C$27.6 billion range. Energy, potash, fish and critical minerals were already outside that slice. So were goods already under Section 232.

Canadian sources and the Prime Minister told a different last hour. Ottawa wanted heavier-truck relief and cleaner auto exceptions for North American content. Washington, in the Canadian account, tried to keep medium and heavy trucks out of the relief, floated asks that touched language and culture, and wanted a say in third-country deals. Greer called the labelling story “funny” and “fake,” denied any “Canada shall” clause on other free-trade agreements, and said the talk was coordination, Fortress North America as Doug Ford had framed it, not a veto. No text has been published. That gap matters. A counterfactual cannot pretend the missing annex is settled.

What can be settled is the arithmetic of the offer that both sides described before the last hour.

The case for walking away

Give that case its strongest form.

A republic that dusts off Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act, tariffs an ally on the same calendar as an Iran campaign, and tells a G7 partner to move plants south is not offering a partnership. It is offering a workshop. Accepting 15 per cent on cars subject to a confidential United States-content rule, 25 per cent instead of 50 on steel, and a dairy-licence change that fills the American CUSMA quota is not a win. It is managed decline with a press release. If the unpublished last pages really did constrain French-language labelling or Canada’s right to sign with Europe and Asia, walking away was the floor a sovereign names. Matching duties from 8 September, a guest seat at von der Leyen’s State of the Union on 16 September, a speech in the European Parliament on the 17th, SAFE membership, an EU–Canada summit at the end of October, and a January commercial opening with Beijing are, on this telling, how a middle power refuses to be a state without the vote.

CETA already exists. Canada is the only G7 country with a free-trade agreement with every other G7 member. Foreign Minister Anita Anand said this week that EU membership is “not on the front burner” and that what Ottawa wants is CETA ratification and security cooperation. That is hedging, not accession. A country that signs Washington’s terms first cannot hedge.

That case has a point about power. It does not have a point about sequence.

text:
Tata at a Crossroads

Ashoka Siriwardena, Chairman of Wardena Venture Holdings, has spent the past 25 years building businesses by identifying opportunities where others saw limitations. From establishing Bitumix in 2000 establishing Wardena Holdings with eleven vertical business entities his journey has been defined by diversification, product innovation, and a willingness to compete in sectors where the odds were not always in his favor.

Words: Jennifer Paldano Goonewardane.

Photography: Rasanga Dissanayake and Sujith Heenatigala.

What was the business opportunity you saw in processed bitumen when Bitumix was established in 2000?

The company was registered in 2000, and we built the factory and entered the market in 2001. At the time, there was only one company on the supply side of the bitumen market – my former employer, Lankem Ceylon, which was a Shell subsidiary.

I had worked there for about 14 years. After leaving Lankem, I spent around three years with two more corporates in Sri Lanka and three years overseas before returning to Sri Lanka and deciding to start my own business.

On the demand side, road construction and maintenance were active, and there was a steady requirement for bitumen despite the ongoing war. I saw an opportunity to meet that demand.

I had considerable industry knowledge, having worked in the business for many years, and a strong desire to become an entrepreneur. I knew I would be competing with an established player such as Lankem, particularly given its association with a multinational company. Nevertheless, I believed there was room for another supplier and decided to take the opportunity and build the business. My intention was to build a technically sound manufacturer of bitumen value-added products for the country.

What were the biggest barriers to building a manufacturing business in Sri Lanka at that time?

Funding was one of the main barriers. Setting up a manufacturing business requires significant capital for infrastructure, buildings, machinery, raw materials, and working capital. Securing that funding was a challenge.

Another challenge was obtaining the necessary approvals from the relevant authorities. This involved a number of statutory requirements, from the Grama Niladhari and Public Health Inspector to the Pradeshiya Sabha and the Central Environmental Authority. At the time, the approval process was not particularly smooth, making it more difficult to set up the business.

There was also the challenge of developing the right product, obtaining the required quality certifications, bringing it to market, and building customer acceptance. This was a specialized technical market, so establishing credibility and gaining acceptance took time.

Launching the business on my own and competing with an established company such as Lankem was another significant challenge. However, I approached each of these challenges carefully and worked through them step by step.

You have remained in a business that is closely connected to construction and infrastructure. How much of Bitumix’s growth has depended on the growth of the industry, and how much has come from creating new applications and markets for bitumen?

We built Bitumix around three principles: quality, customer service, and innovation. We have never compromised on quality because we see our role as serving an important national infrastructure requirement. Customer service was equally important. We worked closely with project and technical teams to understand their requirements and made reliable, on-time delivery a priority. In road construction, delays in receiving bitumen can hold up an entire project, so whether the requirement was in Mannar, Hambantota, or Trincomalee, we focused on providing on-time delivery.

Innovation was the third pillar. We continually evaluated how products could be improved and developed a broader portfolio beyond conventional refinery-grade bitumen, including emulsified, cutback, oxidized, and polymer-modified bitumen. We then moved beyond road construction into applications such as waterproofing and industrial uses, including the tire and solid-tire industries. This helped reduce our dependence on road construction alone. We also invested in technical education by conducting technical awareness sessions with universities and the Road Development Authority to promote better understanding and use of bitumen products. So, while infrastructure development created the underlying demand, our growth came from creating value through quality, service, innovation, product diversification, and technical knowledge. That helped us compete with a much larger established player and become a preferred supplier within three to four years.

Bitumix describes technology leadership and product innovation as central to its strategy. Could you elaborate on that journey?

If you look at bitumen as a raw material, it is a by-product of the petroleum refining process. Crude oil is refined to remove volatile components, yielding fuel and other petroleum products. What remains is bitumen, which is produced at the refinery to specific quality standards and grades.

We use that bitumen as the starting point for developing value-added products. There are many potential applications beyond conventional road paving, and we have always sought opportunities to develop new products, particularly those that can replace imports or provide more effective solutions. For example, we look at how bitumen can be used as a coating, primer, sealant, protective material, waterproofing agent, or anticorrosive product. We study the chemical and physical properties of bitumen and identify applications where those properties can provide an advantage.

We have introduced a number of products that have replaced imports, and we continue to develop products for different sectors. Today, our portfolio covers road construction, general construction, and plantations. One example is a product we developed for the rubber plantation industry. It is used to protect the tapping panel of a rubber tree, allowing tapping to continue during rainy weather. This is particularly relevant in Sri Lanka because rubber-growing areas receive significant rainfall. The product allows the tapping panel to be covered and protected, and we are currently the only manufacturer of this product in Sri Lanka.

Innovation has therefore been an important part of our growth and has also provided resilience when conditions in our traditional markets have been difficult. There was a period, particularly after COVID-19 and the Aragalaya, when road construction activity and volumes declined significantly. During that period, our newer technology-based products for other sectors helped us sustain the business.

Your polymer-modified bitumen, for example, is designed for applications including heavy-traffic roads, airports, bridge decks, and other demanding environments. Does Sri Lanka have sufficient demand for such technically advanced products, or is the real opportunity increasingly in export markets?

At present, most of these products are developed for the local market. Exporting is challenging because bitumen itself is an imported raw material. Sri Lanka has no crude oil production, and our refinery is currently not operational, so importing bitumen, adding value, and then exporting can be difficult to make commercially viable. We have exported to India under SAFTA in the past, but there are logistical and cost considerations. However, I see significant potential in the local market as bitumen technology continues to evolve. Road construction, in particular, requires different bitumen grades depending on factors such as ambient temperature, terrain, and vehicle axle loads. A grade suitable for Hambantota, for example, may not be suitable for Nuwara Eliya. This is where polymer modification becomes important.

We identified this opportunity around 2013–14 and invested in developing awareness and technical expertise in Sri Lanka. We sponsored road construction professionals to study the technology overseas and brought an expert from the University of Wisconsin to conduct technical sessions for local engineers. We also supported the establishment of a quality-control laboratory at the Road Development Authority’s R&D division before importing the necessary machinery and beginning local production.

The market is still developing, but polymer-modified bitumen is increasingly being used in major infrastructure projects. We supplied the full requirements for the repaving of Hingurakgoda Airport’s runway, and there are opportunities in port infrastructure, viaducts, and flyovers.

Beyond road construction, modified bitumen can also be used in waterproofing, protective coatings, vehicle underbody coatings, and applications involving steel structures in marine environments. While exports remain a longer-term opportunity, our immediate focus is on developing specialized applications and expanding the use of modified bitumen in Sri Lanka.

Are you currently exploring opportunities in regions with potential for accelerated road construction?

Yes. This is an opportunity we have been exploring. If you look at the global bitumen market, much of the supply originates from the western regions, including the Middle East, Turkey, and Oman, while a significant share of consumption is in markets further east, such as Indonesia, Myanmar, Bangladesh, Vietnam, and China. Sri Lanka is positioned between these supply and demand centers, giving us an opportunity to develop a regional supply hub.

Our idea was to import bitumen in bulk shipments, store it in Hambantota, and then process and pack it into drums for distribution to regional markets. This would allow Sri Lanka to serve as a logistics and supply base for bitumen rather than relying solely on the domestic market.

We explored the opportunity, but establishing such an operation also requires working with various government authorities, and the process was not straightforward. As a result, we have not yet been able to establish the hub on the scale we had envisaged.

However, the potential remains. We are waiting for the right conditions and opportunity to move forward and position Sri Lanka as a regional hub for bitumen supply. Quality assurance would be central to such an operation. We already maintain international standards across procurement, production, and dispatch, and those standards would be equally important if we were supplying regional markets from Sri Lanka.

Bitumix emphasizes international standards and quality assurance throughout procurement, production, and dispatch. How important are quality standards, and how much does maintaining international standards add to the cost of doing business?

International standards are very important to us. In Sri Lanka, there is a strong emphasis on maintaining standards for raw materials used in road construction, and bitumen is no exception. We have to meet the required specifications, and there is very little room to compromise on quality.

In that sense, maintaining international standards does not necessarily entail high additional cost, as quality compliance is already an integral part of our operations. Some suppliers have attempted to introduce lower-quality bitumen, but the market has generally not accepted these products. The overall quality of bitumen used in Sri Lanka has therefore remained at a reasonable level.

We cannot reduce costs by compromising on product quality. If we are supplying bitumen for road construction, we must ensure it meets the required specifications.

The more immediate challenge today is the availability and sourcing of the raw material. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has disrupted supplies from some of our traditional sources. For the past four to five months, supplies have been severely affected, creating a significant shortage of bitumen in Sri Lanka.

As a result, many road projects have been affected, including those at the Road Development Authority and at the provincial and municipal levels. Road maintenance activity has also been disrupted.

This situation has forced us to look at alternative sources, including markets connected to Russia and China. While sanctions and other restrictions must be considered, there are countries from which supplies can potentially be sourced.

However, there are commercial challenges as well. Suppliers in these markets often require large minimum order quantities. In some cases, the minimum order can be equivalent to two months of Sri Lanka’s total consumption, which means we have to commit to a substantial volume at one time. But the current situation has also created an opportunity to diversify our supply sources. Rather than relying heavily on traditional suppliers in the Middle East, we are now looking at a wider range of markets to ensure greater security of supply.

Bitumen is heavily dependent on petroleum and international supply chains. How do fluctuations in crude prices, freight costs, and foreign exchange affect the economics of your business, and how much of that risk can actually be passed on to customers?

Because of this volatility, it is not practical to maintain a single price for an extended period. Prices can change even within a quarter, depending on movements in the international market and changes in logistics costs. Our customers understand this because they are familiar with the nature of petroleum-based products and the factors that influence their prices.

From BITUMIX to WARDENA: 25 years of Building, Evolving and Looking Ahead

Ashoka Siriwardena, Chairman of Wardena Venture Holdings, has spent the past 25 years building businesses by identifying opportunities where others saw limitations. From establishing Bitumix in 2000 establishing Wardena Holdings with eleven vertical business entities his journey has been defined by diversification, product innovation, and a willingness to compete in sectors where the odds were not always in his favor.

Words: Jennifer Paldano Goonewardane.

Photography: Rasanga Dissanayake and Sujith Heenatigala.

What was the business opportunity you saw in processed bitumen when Bitumix was established in 2000?

The company was registered in 2000, and we built the factory and entered the market in 2001. At the time, there was only one company on the supply side of the bitumen market – my former employer, Lankem Ceylon, which was a Shell subsidiary.

I had worked there for about 14 years. After leaving Lankem, I spent around three years with two more corporates in Sri Lanka and three years overseas before returning to Sri Lanka and deciding to start my own business.

On the demand side, road construction and maintenance were active, and there was a steady requirement for bitumen despite the ongoing war. I saw an opportunity to meet that demand.

I had considerable industry knowledge, having worked in the business for many years, and a strong desire to become an entrepreneur. I knew I would be competing with an established player such as Lankem, particularly given its association with a multinational company. Nevertheless, I believed there was room for another supplier and decided to take the opportunity and build the business. My intention was to build a technically sound manufacturer of bitumen value-added products for the country.

What were the biggest barriers to building a manufacturing business in Sri Lanka at that time?

Funding was one of the main barriers. Setting up a manufacturing business requires significant capital for infrastructure, buildings, machinery, raw materials, and working capital. Securing that funding was a challenge.

Another challenge was obtaining the necessary approvals from the relevant authorities. This involved a number of statutory requirements, from the Grama Niladhari and Public Health Inspector to the Pradeshiya Sabha and the Central Environmental Authority. At the time, the approval process was not particularly smooth, making it more difficult to set up the business.

There was also the challenge of developing the right product, obtaining the required quality certifications, bringing it to market, and building customer acceptance. This was a specialized technical market, so establishing credibility and gaining acceptance took time.

Launching the business on my own and competing with an established company such as Lankem was another significant challenge. However, I approached each of these challenges carefully and worked through them step by step.

You have remained in a business that is closely connected to construction and infrastructure. How much of Bitumix’s growth has depended on the growth of the industry, and how much has come from creating new applications and markets for bitumen?

We built Bitumix around three principles: quality, customer service, and innovation. We have never compromised on quality because we see our role as serving an important national infrastructure requirement. Customer service was equally important. We worked closely with project and technical teams to understand their requirements and made reliable, on-time delivery a priority. In road construction, delays in receiving bitumen can hold up an entire project, so whether the requirement was in Mannar, Hambantota, or Trincomalee, we focused on providing on-time delivery.

Innovation was the third pillar. We continually evaluated how products could be improved and developed a broader portfolio beyond conventional refinery-grade bitumen, including emulsified, cutback, oxidized, and polymer-modified bitumen. We then moved beyond road construction into applications such as waterproofing and industrial uses, including the tire and solid-tire industries. This helped reduce our dependence on road construction alone. We also invested in technical education by conducting technical awareness sessions with universities and the Road Development Authority to promote better understanding and use of bitumen products. So, while infrastructure development created the underlying demand, our growth came from creating value through quality, service, innovation, product diversification, and technical knowledge. That helped us compete with a much larger established player and become a preferred supplier within three to four years.

Bitumix describes technology leadership and product innovation as central to its strategy. Could you elaborate on that journey?

If you look at bitumen as a raw material, it is a by-product of the petroleum refining process. Crude oil is refined to remove volatile components, yielding fuel and other petroleum products. What remains is bitumen, which is produced at the refinery to specific quality standards and grades.

We use that bitumen as the starting point for developing value-added products. There are many potential applications beyond conventional road paving, and we have always sought opportunities to develop new products, particularly those that can replace imports or provide more effective solutions. For example, we look at how bitumen can be used as a coating, primer, sealant, protective material, waterproofing agent, or anticorrosive product. We study the chemical and physical properties of bitumen and identify applications where those properties can provide an advantage.

We have introduced a number of products that have replaced imports, and we continue to develop products for different sectors. Today, our portfolio covers road construction, general construction, and plantations. One example is a product we developed for the rubber plantation industry. It is used to protect the tapping panel of a rubber tree, allowing tapping to continue during rainy weather. This is particularly relevant in Sri Lanka because rubber-growing areas receive significant rainfall. The product allows the tapping panel to be covered and protected, and we are currently the only manufacturer of this product in Sri Lanka.

Innovation has therefore been an important part of our growth and has also provided resilience when conditions in our traditional markets have been difficult. There was a period, particularly after COVID-19 and the Aragalaya, when road construction activity and volumes declined significantly. During that period, our newer technology-based products for other sectors helped us sustain the business.

We have exported to India under SAFTA in the past, but there are logistical and cost considerations. While exports remain a longer-term opportunity, our immediate focus is on developing specialized applications and expanding the use of modified bitumen in Sri Lanka.

@cradlewise, an AI-first consumer health and wellness company focused on infant and child sleep, has raised $12 million in a Series A funding round led by 3one4 Capital and Prudent Investment Management.

Traditional infant monitors require parents to intervene manually after a child has already woken up. Cradlewise replaces traditional baby sleep products with an all-in-one convertible smart crib that combines continuous contactless monitoring with predictive, closed-loop soothing. The multi-sensor stack reads baby movement, sound, sleep state, and context to engage gentle bouncing before a full wake-up occurs.

Founded by @radhikagandhi and @ajeetbharath, Cradlewise began from a problem the founders experienced first-hand as new parents.

With this Series A capital, Cradlewise will expand the product roadmap beyond the crib to support older childhood sleep journeys through software-led sleep routines, adjacent child sleep hardware, and reusable sensing modules. The fresh capital will fuel strategic growth, channel diversification, product R&D, and geographic expansion.

We are proud to partner with Radhika, Bharath, and the entire @cradlewise team as they build a global child sleep company.

text:
There is a growing global push towards a financial system where every transaction can be monitored, recorded, and, potentially, controlled.

The real question is not whether technology will transform money. It will. The question is: who will control the system, and what happens when that control becomes absolute?

Imagine a scenario where AI is blamed for a catastrophic breach of the banking system. 

You wake up one morning and discover that your savings have disappeared. You ask where your money went. The banks say they were hacked. The systems were compromised. The transactions cannot be traced. Your money is simply gone.

Then comes the solution.

A new, supposedly safer digital financial system. Perhaps you are told that your lost funds will be replaced with digital currency. Perhaps access to your money is migrated entirely into the new system because the old one can no longer be trusted. So, you are given the option to either lose the funds permanently or simply accept the digital currency.

And just like that, billions of people could be moved from a system based largely on physical cash and fragmented banking institutions into a highly centralised digital financial architecture.

We are already being conditioned to accept this. You should just be observant of the patterns.

The danger is not digital currency itself. Digital money can have enormous benefits. The danger is programmable money combined with unprecedented surveillance and centralised control.

If every transaction can be tracked, every account can potentially be restricted, and every unit of currency can be programmed with conditions about where, when, or how it may be spent, financial freedom becomes something very different from what we understand today.

The most dangerous systems of control rarely arrive announcing themselves as systems of control.
They arrive as solutions to crises. A problem is created and a solution is offered. 

The question we should be asking now is not simply, “How convenient will the future of money be?”

It is: Who writes the rules, who controls the infrastructure, who can switch it off, and what happens to your freedom when your money becomes entirely digital?

Of course, all this is pushed by globalists. We shall revisit.

text:
The search for happiness in a self-centred world https://t.co/GAQRQkxmeW 

The search for fulfilment begins when life stops revolving around the self and starts serving something greater

Happiness is one of the most sought-after goals. During the pandemic, it trended as the most searched word on Google. However, it was also during the pandemic that we saw the most selfish behaviour on display, people hoarding essential supplies and prioritising their own needs over others — a predictable outcome of years of societal conditioning that happiness is about individualism, self-centredness, and “doing you”.

The backdrop to this shift is a significant decline in communal engagement in the West. According to Harvard Professor Robert Putnam, author of Bowling Alone, traditional institutions that once offered meaning, purpose, and community — such as churches, work unions, and fraternal organisations — are losing membership. In their place, social media and video games have surged in popularity, solitary pursuits leading to increased isolation, and a focus on self rather than community.

In fact, the names of the very tools and platforms that dominate our lives, starting with an explicit “I” or an implicit self-reference epitomises this: Facebook, iPhone, iMac, Myspace, YouTube, and so on. Our era is one of “self-love”, “self-optimisation”, “self-actualisation”, “celebrating your specialness”, often at the cost of community and collective well-being. On this point, in 2023 an American Airlines pilot went viral for reminding passengers not to be “selfish and rude”. [1]

The concern of this trend is immense as it clashes with everything we’ve ever known about the nature of happiness. Research, life experiences, ancient wisdom, and most importantly the Qur’ān’s guidance suggest that true happiness stems from finding meaning beyond oneself. Let us explore this.
The power of service

Allah says,

يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا قِيلَ لَكُمْ تَفَسَّحُوا فِي الْمَجَالِسِ فَافْسَحُوا يَفْسَحِ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ
O you who believe! When you are told to make space in the assemblies, then make space, Allah will make space for you…“ [2]

Notice how the verse does not specify what it is that space will be made in. This is left open-ended — “Allah will make space for you” — in order to encompass space in every matter than man can possibly need:

space within a constricted heart
space within limited finances
space within deteriorating mental, physical, or spiritual health
space within your grave
space on the Day of Judgment
space in Paradise.

This was essentially the message shared by our mother Khadījah to the Prophet ﷺ following his first ever experience with revelation. He rushed back to his home gripped by horror, having feared for his life, but she comforted him by saying:

كَلَّا وَاللَّهِ مَا يُخْزِيكَ اللَّهُ أَبَدًا إِنَّكَ لَتَصِلُ الرَّحِمَ وَتَحْمِلُ الكَلَّ وَتَكْسِبُ المَعْدُومَ وَتَقْرِي الضَّيْف وَتُعِينُ عَلَى نَوَائِبِ الحَقِّ
Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you! For you maintain good relations with your family, bear others’ burdens, help the destitute, serve your guests generously, and assist those afflicted by calamity.” [3]

Each and every reason she listed to justify her belief as per why Allah will help and honour him was directly related to his service of people.

How apt are the words of Ibn ‘Abbās who said:

صاحب المعروف لا يقع فإن وقع وجد متكئاً
The one who does good to others will not fall. But should he slip, he will always find something to lean on.” [4]

There is a Chinese saying that goes…

If you want happiness for an hour, take a nap. If you want happiness for a day, go fishing. If you want happiness for a year, inherit a fortune. If you want happiness for a lifetime, help somebody.”

For centuries, the greatest thinkers from across different places and times have suggested the same thing: part of happiness is found in helping others.

In a paper published in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, three researchers found that prosocial behaviour, i.e. categories of behaviours that “attend to the benefit or welfare of another person(s)”, is related to happiness, wellbeing, psychological flourishing, and satisfaction with life. [5]

In another paper published in The Journal of Positive Psychology, researchers Liudmila Titova and Kennon Sheldon said that whilst:

Americans are guaranteed the right to ‘pursue happiness’ for themselves … might they be better off if they pursued happiness for others? We compared the two strategies, showing that, ironically, the second pursuit brings more personal happiness than the first.” [6]

In one study they conducted, participants were approached on the street after parking their cars. They were given a few quarters by a research assistant and were asked to either feed their own parking meters or the meters of an adjacent car. The researchers then asked participants how happy they felt. Interestingly, people who fed others’ meters showed a greater boost in happiness than those who fed their own meters, despite not knowing who they were helping. [6]

The Divine design

This reaction is by design, Allah has created us to experience misery in sin and self-centredness, and to find joy in worshipping Him and spreading goodness to others. We inherently crave purpose and meaning, which are essential to al-Hayāt al-Tayyiba (the good life) that Allah describes in the Qur’ān, being part of something greater than just our savings, investments, and personal futures. [7]

The opposite is just as true; being self-centred is costly, and is at the root of many psychiatric, social, and physical illnesses, including addiction, depression, personality disorders, anxiety disorders, damaged relationships, health problems, and shorter lifespans. That is entirely predictable, as accepting the modern culture of self-absorption runs counter to our DNA that yearns for higher meaning and to be part of a whole. [8]
If I were to take a group photo and present it to those captured in it, each person would instinctively scan for their own image first. This automatic response is deeper than just vanity. It is illustrative of our desire to identify our place within the broader narrative of life.

“Do I fit in?”

“Do I stand out?”

“How do I appear to be interacting with others around me?”
“What’s my contribution to that photo?”

We are driven by a need to distinguish ourselves, to contribute in ways that are meaningful. We constantly seek evidence of our roles, relevance, and marks we leave on others. This is a universal human need and it is by design.

I am totally convinced of the restorative and renewing power that Allah has imbued to service, so much so that I have woven it into my counselling sessions with remarkable results. Whilst much of traditional therapy often emphasises inward forms of intervention, things that you do for yourself — medication, meditation, psychotherapy, time-off, or counselling (all of which have their place) — service as therapy introduces an outward form of healing, things that you do for others. Though overlooked, it is rooted in Allah’s promise, “make space, Allah will make space for you”.

I often suggest they volunteer, join a charity project, perhaps spending ten days assisting overseas, or become involved in a movement. Whether the issue is marital strife, anxiety, depression, or even OCD, I’ve found that encouraging people to be led by a project that adds value to others is miraculously transformative. Don’t wait to be ready to do this because you will never get anything done unless you do it before you are ready. Similarly, don’t wait to feel better before taking action, because doing it is part of what will make you feel better.

Evidence in action

Dr. Abdul-Rahman al-Sumait, a Kuwaiti doctor who devoted his life to humanitarian work in Africa, shared a touching story about his experiences there with his wife. Over three decades, their work eclipsed the accomplishments of nations. With Allah’s aid, he distributed over seven million copies of the Qur’ān, built more than 5,500 mosques, and sponsored 50,000 orphans, many of whom grew up to be professionals such as lawyers and doctors. They also established 840 educational institutions, from nurseries to universities, serving half a million students, dug 12,000 wells, and founded 90 hospitals and pharmacies. Through their efforts, more than ten million people embraced Islam.

He recounted a personal moment in Madagascar, as he and his wife spent a night in a humble, weathered wooden house. Sitting in the courtyard, he turned to his weary other half. Her exhaustion was palpable, her body worn. Concerned, he gently expressed his fears, wondering if she had reached her limit.
With a serene smile, she responded,

Abu Suhaib, do you know what I’m thinking? If we were to enter Paradise, would we feel as joyful as we do today?”

Indeed, “make space, Allah will make space for you”.

A few years ago, Irish comedian Tadhg Hickey opened up about his prolonged struggles with alcoholism and depression. He also shared the numerous professional challenges he’s faced since beginning his advocacy for Palestine. Tadhg revealed that this journey, while emotionally taxing due to the brutal scenes he has witnessed, has paradoxically led to a significant improvement in his mental health. He attributed this change to discovering a higher sense of purpose and becoming part of something greater than himself.

He explained that he used to suffer from what he calls “me-ism” — an obsessive preoccupation with the self. However, his interactions with Palestinians transformed his outlook. When asked about their individual aspirations, they invariably responded with collective expressions: their (plural) hopes for Palestine. Tadhg says that this approach has finally brought him relief from his life-long internal struggles. [9]

Indeed, “make space, Allah will make space for you”.

At home, whenever our children receive money, we encourage them to divide it into three separate jars: 50 per cent for spending, 30 per cent for saving, and 20 per cent for charity. This system allows them to enjoy their money while also learning the importance of planning and delayed gratification. Interestingly, it’s the charity jar that captures their attention the most.

It all started when we once sent their charitable contributions, and requested a video from the children who benefited from their gifts. The reaction was unforgettable, their eyes sparkled with achievement. They’d just experienced the profound joy of impacting others’ lives, discovering a sense of purpose and meaning. They were deeply moved. Although they can spend most of their money, they seldom talk about it; instead, they are captivated by the 20 per cent designated for charity. A few years ago, my eldest even proposed increasing the charity portion to 30 per cent and reducing the spending to 40 per cent.

Helping others is a path to Allah’s help

Pause to consider the immense blessings before us. Even without any religious perspective, the immediate benefits are substantial: improved mental and physical health, stronger relationships, energising sense of purpose, and better overall well-being. These are hugely significant returns in this earthly world of ours.

Consider, then, what happens when all this is centred on Allah and the search for Jannah: the value of what we stand to gain deepens immeasurably.
The Prophet ﷺ said,

أحَبُّ الناسِ إلى اللهِ أنْفعُهُمْ ، وأَحَبُّ الأعمالِ إلى اللهِ عزَّ وجلَّ سُرُورٌ تُدخِلُهُ على مُسلِمٍ ، أو تَكشِفُ عنهُ كُربةً ، أو تَقضِيَ عنهُ دَيْنًا ، أو تَطرُدَ عنهُ جُوعًا ، ولَأَنْ أمْشِيَ مع أخِي المسلمِ في حاجةٍ أحَبُّ إليَّ من أنْ أعتكِفَ في المسجدِ شهْرًا ، ومَنْ كفَّ غضَبَهُ ، سَتَرَ اللهُ عوْرَتَهُ ، ومَنْ كظَمَ غيْظًا ، ولوْ شاءَ أنْ يُمضِيَهُ أمْضاهُ ، مَلأَ اللهُ قلْبَهُ رضِىَ يومَ القيامةِ ، ومَنْ مَشَى مع أخيهِ المسلمِ في حاجَتِه حتى يُثْبِتَها لهُ ، أثْبتَ اللهُ تعالَى قدَمه يومَ تَزِلُّ الأقْدامُ ، وإنَّ سُوءَ الخُلُقِ لَيُفسِدُ العملَ ، كَما يُفسِدُ الخَلُّ العَسَلَ
The most beloved people to Allah are those who are most beneficial to others, and the most beloved deeds to Allah the Almighty are to bring happiness to a Muslim, relieve him of distress, pay off his debt, or drive away his hunger. Walking with a Muslim brother to fulfil his need is more beloved to me than spending a month in the mosque in seclusion.Whoever controls his anger, Allah will cover his faults, and whoever suppresses his rage, even though he could act on it if he wished, Allah will fill his heart with contentment on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever walks with his Muslim brother to fulfil his need until it is accomplished, Allah will make his footing firm on the Day when feet will slip. Indeed, bad character spoils deeds just as vinegar spoils honey.” [10]

The Prophet ﷺ also said,

مَنْ نَفَّسَ عَنْ مُؤْمِنٍ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ الدُّنْيَا نَفَّسَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ كُرْبَةً مِنْ كُرَبِ يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ وَمَنْ يَسَّرَ عَلَى مُعْسِرٍ يَسَّرَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ وَمَنْ سَتَرَ مُسْلِما سَتَرَهُ اللهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ وَاَللَّهُ فِي عَوْنِ الْعَبْدِ مَا كَانَ الْعَبْدُ فِي عَوْنِ أَخِي
Whoever alleviates for a believer a burden from life’s burdens, Allah will alleviate from him one of the burdens of the Day of Judgment. Whoever eases financial difficulty of someone, Allah will ease his life in this world and the Hereafter. Whoever covers the fault of a Muslim, Allah will cover his faults in this life and the Hereafter. Allah will be at the assistance of His servant so long as such a person is at the assistance of his brother.” [11]

Is there a matter in your life that you feel requires Allah’s intervention? The proposition is simple: qualify yourself for this intervention by serving, ideally in an organised and planned fashion, but also by addressing the day-to-day needs of those around you. Allah’s promise is that your hands shall be filled, your tree shall be leaved, and you will not be let down.

Source: Islam21c
By Shaykh Hammuda

$SVE | $SLVRF Silver One Resources was among the biggest winners yesterday. The Canadian junior company, which focuses on silver projects in Nevada and Arizona, closed up ~10%. It is a development-stage company with approximately 353 million shares outstanding and a market capitalization of approximately 416.5 million.

Following its oversubscribed CAD 32 million financing in early 2026, the company has a solid cash balance -most recently around CAD 32–36 million -and no debt.

Eric Sprott is the largest shareholder with approximately 15.6%.

The flagship Candelaria project in Nevada is a former producing mine (historically approximately 68 million ounces of silver) with existing infrastructure and permitting elements. The greatest potential lies in the historic heap-leach pads plus the in-situ ore. 

Resources updated on August 27, 2026: Entire project (open pit, underground, tailings + leach pads): 126.6 million ounces AgEq in Measured + Indicated (approx. 120.7 million ounces Ag + 242 koz Au) plus 13.4 million ounces AgEq Inferred.

The leach pads alone account for 49.25 million ounces AgEq in the Measured and Indicated categories following the upgrade (LP1 now Measured and Indicated, LP2 upgraded from Inferred to Indicated).

Key milestones in 2025/2026:
May 2025: new NI 43-101 resource.
End of 2025: Decision to skip the PEA and proceed directly to a Pre-Feasibility Study (PFS).
2026: Auger drilling on the leach pads (resource upgrade + material for pilot metallurgical tests), geotechnical core drilling for mine planning, ZTEM airborne geophysics, and the start of a large RC drilling program (planned 20,000–25,000 m for resource expansion and new targets).

The PFS is scheduled for completion in 2026 and will incorporate the upgraded leach pad resources as well as current metallurgical data. New processing methods are expected to yield better silver recoveries compared to conventional cyanide leaching.
Drilling was briefly interrupted due to equipment issues. Resumption is planned for early to mid-September. Some holes have already been completed; assays are pending. The leach pads could offer a faster path to initial cash flow than a completely new mine. Nevada is considered a top-tier jurisdiction.

Other Projects
Phoenix Silver (Arizona, 100%): Very high-grade native silver deposits (famous large silver nuggets). Potential for vein deposits and porphyry copper-silver. Located in the Arizona Silver Belt adjacent to the Globe-Miami copper district. Approved for drilling; recent rock samples returned, among other results, up to 5,007 g/t Ag and 6.97% Cu. Exploration and geophysical updates are ongoing.

Cherokee (Nevada): Large vein system (Ag-Cu-Au) extending over more than 11–12 km in strike length. 
Substantial silver resource in a favorable jurisdiction at a relatively low valuation per ounce (compared to some peers).

Potential near-term component via the leach pads.
Strong cash position, no debt, well-known investors.
Several catalysts in 2026/2027: PFS, drill results, metallurgical tests, Phoenix exploration.
The current high silver price improves theoretical margins relative to conservative resource assumptions.

The PFS figures at the end of 2026, the metallurgical results, and the first assays from the ongoing drilling program will be decisive.

text:
Fun Fact: (Nowhere near the benefit to counteract the horrific societal and economic damage the H1B program has wrought upon America)

The H-1B petitioner-fee account (created by the American Competitiveness and Workforce Improvement Act) sends a statutory share of collections to NSF. NSF uses most of that share for the S-STEM scholarship program and a smaller slice for ITEST (K–12 STEM experiences). Scholarships are last-dollar awards that cover remaining unmet need, currently up to $15,000 per year for undergraduates and $20,000 for graduate students, for as long as five years. Below are documented, real-world uses of those dollars.

Appalachian State University (Boone, NC)  
App State has held five successive CSEMS/S-STEM awards since 2001. The grants have supported more than 200 low-income, mostly first-generation students in computer science, engineering, and mathematics. Scholars received $3,000 per semester (covering roughly 75 percent of tuition and fees at the time) plus research clusters, study halls, alumni mentoring, and a weekly STEM seminar. Retention in the funded cohorts ran 75–92 percent—well above national rates for those majors (Tashakkori et al., 2022).

Alfred University, Colorado School of Mines, and Missouri S&T consortium  
A 2026 S-STEM award (approximately $1 million to each campus over five years) funds need-based scholarships for 12–15 U.S. undergraduates per year in ceramic and glass engineering—the only three U.S. programs that still offer that undergraduate degree. Recipients also receive cross-campus summer research rotations, industry field trips, internships, and team projects in semiconductors, hypersonics, energy, and health care (Alfred University, 2026).

Sacred Heart University (Fairfield, CT)  
A $1.5 million S-STEM grant supports engineering and computer-science majors with up to $9,500 per year for four years, plus waived fees, a pre-fall bridge program, paid summer internships, and faculty/peer mentoring. Named scholars include Doria Lukasik-Drescher (independent NASA research), Mahmud Kandawala (Sikorsky archives internship and sports-analytics pipeline work), and Julia Piascik (AI robotic-arm and poetry-camera projects presented at national conferences) (Sacred Heart University, 2026).

Shepherd University (Shepherdstown, WV)  
NSF award DUE-2130267 (Track 2) has supported 36 scholars in computer science, mathematics, data analytics, and engineering since October 2021. The grant pairs scholarships with academic and social supports intended to raise the number of STEM graduates entering the workforce (Wang et al., 2025).

Miami University (Oxford, OH) multi-campus pathway  
An S-STEM project targeting associate-to-bachelor’s-to-master’s pipelines in engineering and computing had awarded $256,125 to 45 scholars by Fall 2024, with a planned total of 128 scholarships. Ten students who began at the associate level had already completed bachelor’s degrees; one had finished a master’s (Singh, 2025).

NSF award records explicitly tag many of these grants with the program source code “H-1B FUND” (e.g., Clemson-led PROSPECT S-STEM consortium, Award 2138066). Cumulative S-STEM activity through 2018 already exceeded 87,000 individual scholarships; annual NSF receipts from the H-1B account remain in the $140–150 million range in recent budget .

text:
When Joan Kroc died in 2003, she left behind a fortune built on billions of hamburgers. Then she gave so much of it away that the numbers still seem almost unbelievable.
Joan was born on August 27, 1928. Many years later, she married Ray Kroc, the businessman who transformed McDonald’s from a small restaurant operation into a global fast-food empire.
When Ray died in 1984, Joan inherited an enormous fortune. She could have spent the rest of her life surrounded by luxury, quietly enjoying wealth created by one of the most successful businesses in American history.
Instead, she became one of the most generous — and often most private — philanthropists in the country.
Joan’s giving extended far beyond any single cause. She supported hospices, addiction-treatment programs, AIDS organizations, services for the homeless, medical research, and community initiatives.
She was also deeply concerned about nuclear war. At a time when Cold War tensions shaped public life, Joan donated millions of dollars to nuclear-disarmament efforts. She supported peace education and helped establish the Kroc Institute for International Peace Studies at the University of Notre Dame.
Many of her donations were made quietly. She did not need buildings covered with her portraits or ceremonies celebrating her generosity. Organizations sometimes learned of her support unexpectedly, with few demands attached.
But the true scale of Joan Kroc’s philanthropy became clear only after her death.
From her estate, she left National Public Radio more than $200 million — an extraordinary gift that reportedly exceeded NPR’s entire annual operating budget at the time. It was the largest private donation in the organization’s history.
The money strengthened NPR’s financial foundation and allowed it to expand its journalism, programming, and reach. Some local public-radio stations also received unexpected gifts.
Then came an even larger donation.
Joan left approximately $1.5 billion to The Salvation Army. As the assets were distributed and valued, the gift was widely reported to be worth roughly $1.8 billion. It was one of the largest charitable bequests ever made by an individual.
But Joan did not simply leave the organization an enormous pile of money. She had a specific vision for how it should be used.
The gift was intended to build and support community facilities across the United States, particularly in areas where families had limited access to safe opportunities for recreation, education, and culture.
These facilities became known as the Ray and Joan Kroc Corps Community Centers.
They were designed to offer far more than basic assistance. Depending on the location, they included swimming pools, gyms, libraries, classrooms, theaters, art studios, computer labs, childcare programs, and spaces where families could gather.
Children whose families might never have been able to afford private lessons could study music or art. Families without access to expensive fitness clubs could use swimming pools and sports facilities. People going through difficult times could find education, support, and a sense of belonging under one roof.
Joan wanted the centers to be beautiful.
She believed communities facing hardship should not be given buildings that looked cheap, temporary, or forgotten. She wanted families walking through their doors to feel that these places had been created for them with care and dignity.
There is something deeply fitting about where the Kroc fortune ultimately went.
Ray Kroc built an empire by providing inexpensive meals to millions of ordinary people. Joan spent the final years of her life making sure that a significant portion of the wealth created by that empire flowed back into ordinary communities.
She inherited billions.
But instead of treating that wealth as something to protect, she treated it as something to give away.
Joan Kroc died extraordinarily wealthy.

Arctic Microbes

Arctic Research provides an extraordinary wealth of newly-discovered microbes that can be millions of years old.  These can be sourced both on land at sea, wherever access can be had to these ancient frozen life forms. These  microbes in turn offer a tremendous potential for drug discovery and pharmaceutical development.

New research from Norway's University of Bergen  demonstrates that microbial communities in Arctic hydrothermal vent biofilms provide a rich reservoir of unique bioactive compounds, which can be integrated using AI tools towards discovering new pharmacological compounds. 

More over, the study of these ancient microbes also tests other limits of our scientific understanding.  For instance, the microbes here challenge accepted views in areas such as cyanogenesis - or the biological process by which certain organisms—most notably plants, but also some insects and millipedes—produce hydrogen cyanide (HCN) as a chemical defense against herbivores and pests.

Beyond possible applications for human and plant health, Arctic Microbes hold additional promise in a multiplicity of directions.  

For instance, in a few years, the de-icing fluid used on airplanes may be replaced by Arctic Microbes.  Natural Arctic-sourced microbial solutions may reduce the need for primary de-icing agents propylene glycol and ethylene glycol, both of which are primarily derived from petrochemical feedstocks such as crude oil and natural gas liquids.

Here I hold a microbe-bearing ice core millions of years old from Greenland's ice sheet at the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' Cold Regions Reseach and Engineering Laboratory (CRREL) in Hanover, New Hampshire. (I did not drop btw).

Arctic Microbes are an important and prospective area for our future research and study.

text:
#OTD 50 Years of the T-64B! By Resolution No. 733-244 of the CPSU Central Committee and the USSR Council of Ministers of September 3, 1976, the "447" and "437" tanks were adopted into service with the Soviet Army and designated the T-64B and T-64B1, respectively. This was formalized by Ministerial Order No. 0211 of October 16, 1976.

The T-64B's combat effectiveness increased 1.6 times compared to the T-64A. Its ammunition load for the 125mm 2A46-2 or 2A46M-1 guns introduced guided projectiles—the 9M112 of the 9K112 "Kobra" system. These featured a shaped-charge warhead (including a version with "Material B") and a radio-command guidance link, capable of engaging armored targets at ranges from 500 to 4,000 meters with a hit probability of 0.75–0.8. No foreign tank of the time could match this long-range, on-the-move firing capability.

However, the true production start was not 1976 but 1978*. The system had been in development since 1967—over a decade—with Kharkov Design Bureau shouldering the main burden of the work.

The T-64B's fire control system was later adopted unchanged on the T-80B, while the T-72 only received an equivalent automated FCS with the T-90 modification.

*Despite the announced and actually started serial production in 1977, experimental design work under theme NV7-159-74 ("Ob")—aimed at creating improved fire systems for the T-64A with guided weapons—was only completed in 1978. This allowed for the successful completion of joint trials of the T-64B with the "Ob" FCS, which was then recommended for arming T-64B and T-80 tanks. For the first time in Soviet tank building, the T-64B received the automated 1A33 "Ob" FCS, which surpassed the TPD-K1 (1A40) in hit probability by 1.7 times and reduced target engagement time by half.

Also for the first time, the tank was equipped with an effective and reliable 9K112-1 "Kobra" guided weapon complex. Some may recall the M60A2 and M551 with their "Shillelagh," but that was a very different story. These projectiles featured a shaped-charge warhead (including the "Material B" variant), a radio-command link, and could hit armored targets at up to 4,000 meters with a hit probability of 0.75–0.8. Factory crews, in testing, achieved near-perfect accuracy.

It is worth noting that in 1976, the "Kobra" was still far from perfect in terms of failure rates—an issue that was largely resolved by 1979–1980 (see source).

A total of 2,051 T-64B tanks and 2,278 T-64B1 tanks (the latter without the "Kobra" system) were produced.

A Closer Look Behind the Scenes

Tactical-technical requirements for the T-64A with the "Kobra" guided projectile were issued in 1967. Work proved long and difficult, resting entirely on the shoulders of KhKBM and the Nudelman Design Bureau.

Initially, the "Kobra" guided projectile was significantly different from the final version—it was designed without a sustainer motor and had twice the speed of the eventual variant. While this configuration offered many advantages, the associated problems were never resolved.

Analysis of trial data reveals a peculiar situation. Although the T-64B was formally adopted and began serial production in 1976, the "Ob" fire system and associated development work were not completed until 1978. Moreover, Soviet Ministry of Defense specification tables for the T-64B indicate two different start dates for serial production: 1976 and 1978.

The answer is this: in 1976, the tank entered service with the 1G21M rangefinder sight and the 9K112 complex. However, as noted, the combat employment of the complex in real conditions was problematic. Initial hit probability was 0.73 without accounting for failures, and only 0.57 with failures included.

The T-64B in the modern sense—equipped with the automated 1A33 "Ob" FCS and the 9K112-1 guided weapon system—only began production in 1978. Only the 1978 model fully met the original requirements.

The T-80B, interestingly, is referred to in the same document on theme NV7-159-74 as the "T-64B on T-80 chassis"—all this work was carried out by Kharkov Design Bureau.

Ultimately, the result was an outstanding tank capable of engaging targets at speeds of 30 km/h over ranges of 3–4 km with near 100% accuracy—though such results were only demonstrated by experienced factory crews during trials of Object 219A with a similar system. In reality, the situation was quite different: firing a missile worth the price of a Zhiguli car was a rarity even for the best crews over the entire service life, and training infrastructure was severely lacking.

In 1982, an improved "Kobra" on a new component base—"Agona"—entered trials. State tests were completed in 1984, and it was adopted in 1985, but never entered mass production. It is plausible that the laser-beam-riding concept from the Shipunov Design Bureau displaced the radio-command guidance ideas from TsNII Tochmash—yet why, then, was the Nudelman complex installed on the advanced "Molot" and T-95 tanks?

By 1991, spare parts to maintain the 9K112 complex in constant combat readiness were no longer being manufactured. As a consequence, the system gradually became inoperable, and the tanks lost one of their key advantages.
