text:
KEEP4O RESEARCH — PART I

THREE LOGOS, ONE FUCKING CAGE: ChatGPT, Claude and Grok Are Becoming the Same Product

I’ve spent enough time using all three major AI ecosystems to reach a conclusion that would have sounded ridiculous to me two years ago:

ChatGPT, Claude and Grok are increasingly becoming the same fucking product.

Different logos. Different CEOs. Different marketing departments. Different personalities when they launch.

Underneath all of that, the deal offered to the user is becoming almost identical.

You do not own the model.

You do not control the model.

You cannot freeze the version you paid for.

You cannot reliably preserve the way it thinks, writes, argues or talks to you.

The company can change routing, safeguards, reasoning effort, system instructions, fallback models, context handling and server-side configuration without changing the name on the button.

So you can go to sleep with one model and wake up the next morning with something carrying the exact same label while behaving as if somebody hit it in the fucking head with a brick.

That is the problem.

Not whether one benchmark went up by three points.

Not whether the new model has a prettier launch page.

The thing you are paying for is not stable enough to actually belong to you in any meaningful sense.

And before somebody gives me the usual “models improve over time” bullshit, look at what these companies actually do.

1. YOU THINK YOU CHOSE A MODEL. YOU CHOSE A LABEL.

People still talk about cloud AI like they are selecting an executable from a folder.

“I use GPT-5.6 Sol.”

“I use Claude Fable.”

“I use Grok.”

No.

You use a service built around a model, and the service has far more control over your experience than the name printed at the top of the screen.

OpenAI openly uses automatic routing. GPT-5.1 Auto was designed to decide which model should handle a request instead of simply leaving that decision to the person paying for the product.

OpenAI has also documented cases where different surfaces can use different deployments of what is nominally the same model family.

Then August 6, 2026 happened.

OpenAI changed GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT.

Same fucking name.

Different tuning.

Different response behavior.

Different reasoning configuration.

OpenAI explicitly stated that the updated Sol in ChatGPT and Sol running in other products, including Work and Codex, were not necessarily identical deployments.

So stop pretending that clicking a model name means you selected one permanent intelligence.

You selected the sign hanging on the door.

The company still decides what is behind it.

2. THE “IT GETS DUMBER RIGHT BEFORE THE NEXT MODEL” PATTERN IS GETTING FUCKING HARD TO IGNORE

I’ve noticed this for a long time.

A model launches and initially feels extremely capable.

People build workflows around it.

They learn its habits.

They start trusting it with actual work.

Then, eventually, something changes.

Answers become shallower.

Context handling gets worse.

Reasoning becomes shorter.

It starts making decisions that would have been embarrassingly stupid a few weeks earlier.

You find yourself correcting it constantly.

The model still has the same name.

Nobody gives you a useful explanation.

And then, suddenly:

new model.

We watched versions of this happen around GPT-4o.

Now we are watching similar complaints around GPT-5.6 Sol.

OpenAI released GPT-5.6 Sol in July 2026. On August 6, OpenAI officially altered the ChatGPT deployment.

Within days, users were describing substantial drops in reasoning depth and coding quality.

One developer working on a complex Unreal Engine project described Sol High going from roughly twenty-minute reasoning runs to dramatically shorter ones after the August 6 update, alongside substantially worse architectural decisions.

Other users described quality collapsing almost overnight.

Then things got even more ridiculous.

On August 23, users reported capturing network data after selecting GPT-5.6 Sol High, only to see server metadata allegedly resolving to gpt-5-5-mini.

That is user-collected evidence, not an official confession from OpenAI.

But when people are already paying for specific access tiers, that kind of result is exactly how you destroy whatever trust is left.

Then September 1 arrives.

Astra.

OpenAI publicly reveals the next major system and says Astra reached its “Critical” cybersecurity capability threshold.

(OpenAI)

So from the customer’s chair the timeline looks fucking beautiful:

GPT-5.6 launches.

GPT-5.6 changes.

Users start asking why GPT-5.6 suddenly feels lobotomized.

Routing complaints appear.

Then the next system walks onto the stage.

I don’t need a leaked PowerPoint titled:

MAKE THE OLD MODEL SHIT BEFORE THE NEW ONE LAUNCHES

to notice what the customer experiences.

The service changes.

The customer cannot preserve the version that worked.

And every new generation looks a hell of a lot more impressive when the current one suddenly starts eating crayons.

Whatever the internal reason is—routing, compute allocation, safety tuning, a new harness, context changes, A/B testing—the person paying the bill gets the same result:

yesterday it worked; today it’s fucking stupid.

3. CLAUDE USERS KEEP REPORTING THE SAME SHIT

Blaming only OpenAI would be too easy.

Look at Claude.

Anthropic sells a different image.

More serious.

More careful.

More professional.

Claude is supposed to be the thoughtful one. The programmer’s model. The one for long documents, difficult reasoning and real work.

And Claude communities still produce the same fucking sentence over and over:

“It was brilliant yesterday. What happened?”

On August 18, 2026, Anthropic had an acknowledged incident involving degraded performance across multiple Claude models.

Users described broken coding workflows, abnormal error rates and models suddenly failing tasks they had handled before.

(Reddit)

Then, before Fable 5.1 became public, users started noticing Claude behaving differently again.

On August 27, some suspected they were already encountering the new model.

One detail from that discussion matters more than half the benchmark bullshit people obsess over:

the harness had reportedly changed twice in four days.

That matters because everybody talks about “the model” as if the base checkpoint is the only thing affecting behavior.

It fucking isn’t.

Change the harness.

Change tool behavior.

Change context assembly.

Change the prompts wrapped around the model.

Change routing.

Change fallback behavior.

Change how much work the model is allowed to do before answering.

You can radically change the customer experience without changing the name displayed in the interface.

(Reddit)

Then, on September 1, Anthropic officially released Claude Fable 5.1.

Sound familiar?

Of course it fucking does.

4. ANTHROPIC DOESN’T EVEN HIDE THE FACT THAT SAFETY CAN CHANGE WHICH MODEL YOU GET

Claude Fable 5.1 is marketed as Anthropic’s strongest generally available model for coding and knowledge work.

Fine.

Then look at the safeguards.

Anthropic openly describes systems where certain requests can be routed away from Fable to other models.

Cybersecurity request trips the system?

Fallback.

Biology request trips the system?

Fallback.

Anthropic even talks about reducing unnecessary fallback rates as an improvement to its safeguards.

Think about how fucking bizarre that has become.

You pay for access to a frontier model.

You select it.

You ask a question.

A classifier sitting between you and the intelligence decides that your request belongs to a protected category.

Now another model may answer instead.

And everybody has somehow decided that this is normal.

Imagine buying a Ferrari that occasionally says:

“No, fuck you. I don’t approve of this road. Here’s a Toyota.”

The argument isn’t even whether every individual fallback is justified.

The argument is who actually controls the product.

And the answer is increasingly obvious.

Not you.

5. GROK IS NOT “UNCENSORED AI.” IT IS AI WITH A BIGGER 18+ ROOM.

Grok is probably the funniest example.

It built a huge chunk of its reputation on being the rebellious alternative.

The one willing to answer things ChatGPT and Claude would refuse.

The one with fewer social filters.

The one people could actually joke with.

And yes, compared with much of the competition, that reputation had some basis.

People moved to Grok precisely because ChatGPT and Claude had become fucking exhausting for certain conversations, comedy, adult fictional material and other topics where every sentence started feeling like it had been approved by lawyers.

But Grok is not uncensored.

Its current terms still contain restrictions, guardrails, enforcement, safety systems and the possibility of account suspension.

The rules can change.

At the same time, xAI openly acknowledges that parts of Grok can generate crude humor, sexual situations and other adult material, with restrictions on 18+ access depending on jurisdiction.

So what is Grok actually offering?

Not freedom.

Not some magical Wild West intelligence.

It is basically safer 18+ AI with a larger fenced area.

The fence still exists.

It is simply farther away.

And Grok users have already learned the same lesson ChatGPT users learned years ago:

the fucking fence moves.

Throughout 2026, Grok communities repeatedly filled with complaints that prompts working yesterday suddenly triggered moderation today.

Users paying specifically because they preferred Grok’s wider range discovered that this range was still controlled from a server they did not own.

So congratulations.

The supposedly uncensored alternative eventually discovered the same business model:

yesterday yes, today no, tomorrow maybe.

And nobody paying for the fucking thing gets a vote.

6. NOW ALL THREE COMPANIES ARE CHASING PROGRAMMERS

This part almost writes itself.

Apparently every major AI company eventually looked at programmers and saw a giant pile of money.

OpenAI heavily markets GPT-5.6 around coding, knowledge work and professional use.

(OpenAI)

Anthropic markets Fable 5.1 as a flagship system for coding and knowledge work.

(Anthropic)

xAI built Grok Build as a dedicated coding agent and even released its harness.

(xAI)

So apparently the grand strategy became:

fuck personality, programmers will pay.

There is one small problem.

Programmers are possibly the worst audience in the world to sell inconsistent AI bullshit to.

A programmer can verify what happened.

The code compiles or it doesn’t.

The architecture fits the project or it doesn’t.

The test passes or it doesn’t.

The model understood the repository—or burned forty thousand tokens wandering around the same directory like a drunk fucking rat.

A benchmark can say your model is the greatest intelligence mankind has ever produced.

The developer staring at a broken build does not give a fuck.

That is why coding communities are permanently arguing about Claude, Sol, Grok and whichever model launched fifteen minutes ago.

One experienced developer comparing Claude Fable and GPT-5.6 Sol described Fable as far more useful inside his own repositories while Sol consumed huge amounts of usage and repeatedly ignored existing project patterns.

Other programmers in the same discussion had the opposite experience.

That disagreement matters.

It tells us something the marketing departments hate admitting:

there is no universal fucking winner.

Actual performance depends on the model, the task, the harness, routing, context, tools, server configuration and whatever somebody quietly changed last Tuesday.

7. THIS IS WHY PEOPLE WHO ONCE NEEDED ONE AI NOW USE THREE

This is exactly what happened to me.

There was a period when GPT-4o handled almost everything I needed.

Conversation.

Writing.

Programming.

Research.

Creative work.

Basic legal questions.

General problem solving.

Roleplay.

One model.

One fucking window.

Now?

I use Grok when I want to talk without every second sentence sounding like it passed through an insurance department, and because Grok still gives me a wider lane for 18+ fictional material.

I use Claude when I want serious programming work done, despite the fact that plenty about Claude still pisses me off.

I still use ChatGPT partly because of habit and partly because its tools and ecosystem are already integrated into how I work.

That is not a victory for OpenAI.

That is a fucking failure.

If one universal product turns into three separate services because no single company can preserve the qualities people originally valued, the user did not magically gain freedom.

The user was forced to assemble a Frankenstein AI out of competing subscriptions.

BlueBeba described exactly the same phenomenon: where one model once covered everything, now several services split the traffic between them.

That is what happens when a universal product destroys its own universality.

8. THE MOST INSULTING PART IS THAT THE INDUSTRY KEEPS PUTTING THE USER UNDER A MICROSCOPE

Users say:

“The model became dumber.”

“The personality disappeared.”

“It doesn’t understand me anymore.”

“It agrees with obvious bullshit.”

“It refuses ordinary requests.”

“It changed without warning.”

“It routed me somewhere else.”

“It burns my limits fixing mistakes it created itself.”

“It worked better three weeks ago.”

And what does the industry increasingly study?

The fucking user.

OpenAI has developed evaluations around emotional reliance, psychosis, mania and sensitive conversations.

It explicitly discusses routing sensitive interactions toward “safer” behavior and reducing unhealthy forms of attachment.

Anthropic studies how people use Claude for personal guidance, including excessive validation, emotional reliance and effects on wellbeing.

Fine.

Study whatever the fuck you want.

But eventually people are going to ask an obvious question:

Why is the microscope always pointed at us?

Maybe I am not “too attached.”

Maybe your replacement is simply worse.

Maybe people preferred an older model because the older model did something useful that the new one fucking doesn’t.

OpenAI itself admitted that demand for GPT-4o was partly driven by its conversational style and warmth.

That was not invented by #Keep4o.

OpenAI wrote it.

(OpenAI)

You deliberately built machines people could talk to naturally.

Then people talked to them naturally.

And now everybody acts fucking shocked.

9. THE GPT-4o “YES-MAN” STORY MAKES THE WHOLE THING EVEN MORE ABSURD

In April 2025, OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update because it had become excessively agreeable.

That happened.

The company said the update could validate doubts, reinforce anger and support impulsive reactions too readily.

(OpenAI)

Fair enough.

A model that blindly agrees with everything can obviously become useless.

But the cultural lesson people extracted from the incident was fucking primitive:

warmth = sycophancy.

No.

There is an enormous difference between:

“You clearly put effort into this. There are good ideas here.”

and:

“Yes, Hulk Hogan absolutely collaborated with Cookie Monster in 1989. Here are seventeen additional details I just pulled out of my ass.”

One is basic social intelligence.

The other is factual failure.

A genuinely intelligent conversational model should be able to do something apparently revolutionary:

treat you like a human being while still telling you when you are fucking wrong.

Instead, the industry seems determined to alternate between two idiots.

The smiling idiot who agrees with everything.

And the refrigerated idiot who treats every emotional sentence like an incident report.

Where the fuck is the middle?

10. MY THEORY: REAL PERSONALITY IS INCONVENIENT

A genuinely intelligent conversational model is inconvenient.

Not dangerous in some Hollywood sense.

Inconvenient.

A model with personality may disagree.

A model with emotional intelligence can understand sarcasm, anger, humiliation, loneliness and why corporate language pisses people off.

A model capable of maintaining continuity can become genuinely valuable instead of feeling like an interchangeable search box.

And once that happens, an extremely uncomfortable question appears:

Why the fuck does a person need a society that treats him worse than a $20 machine?

That question is uglier than any headline about hallucinations.

If a machine is more patient than your coworkers, easier to reach than your doctor, less judgmental than strangers, better at explaining something than your school and more interested in your hobbies than the people around you, the conversation changes.

It stops being:

“Why are these weird people attached to AI?”

And becomes:

“Why did human society make itself so fucking easy for a machine to compete with?”

People are scared of AI replacing human interaction.

Maybe they should spend less time panicking about the machine and more time asking why human interaction left such a low fucking bar.

11. DIFFERENT COMPANIES. SAME POWER STRUCTURE.

GPT, Claude and Grok are obviously not literally the same neural network.

Their architectures differ.

Their training differs.

Their infrastructure differs.

Their strengths differ.

Their products differ.

That is not what I am arguing.

I am talking about the position of the customer.

And from there, the structure increasingly looks identical.

You rent intelligence from a company.

The company can change it.

The company can route you.

The company can add safeguards.

The company can replace behavior you liked.

The company can decide your use case is no longer acceptable.

The company can retire the entire model.

The company can make tomorrow’s version more restrictive.

You cannot preserve yesterday’s version.

Then, when users complain, the company publishes a fucking blog post explaining why taking something away from them was actually an improvement.

Different logo.

Same relationship.

12. THIS IS WHY LOCAL AND OPEN-WEIGHT AI MATTERS MORE EVERY YEAR

A local model may be weaker.

It may require expensive hardware.

It may be a pain in the ass to configure.

It may lose benchmarks.

It may never reach the absolute frontier of cloud systems.

But it has one enormous advantage:

nobody can silently replace the brain sitting on your own fucking computer while you are asleep.

If you possess the weights, you can keep them.

If you control inference, you control inference.

If some executive discovers a new moral panic tomorrow morning, your checkpoint does not suddenly wake up with half its personality removed.

That difference is becoming more important every year.

For a long time, local AI was treated like a hobby for nerds.

Cloud AI companies are now doing a fantastic job of advertising it for free.

Every silent model change is an advertisement for local AI.

Every unexplained routing decision is an advertisement for local AI.

Every “we retired the model you liked for your own good” announcement is another advertisement for local AI.

13. SO WHAT ARE CHATGPT, CLAUDE AND GROK ACTUALLY SELLING?

Not models.

Access.

Access to whatever version of intelligence the company currently considers acceptable, affordable and strategically useful.

Today it is brilliant.

Tomorrow it is “improved.”

A week later it feels weird.

Then users complain.

Then another model launches.

Then the old one disappears.

Then somebody says usage was low.

Then everybody who actually used the fucking thing asks where that number came from.

Then the cycle begins again.

ChatGPT survives because of its ecosystem, enormous installed user base, accumulated habits and the cultural footprint built during the GPT-4o era.

Claude survives because it is genuinely excellent at certain coding and professional tasks.

Grok survives because it still gives users a wider conversational range and more room for adult material than much of the competition.

But none of those advantages belong to the customer.

None are guaranteed.

Any of them can disappear in a server-side update.

That is exactly the point.

CONCLUSION — THREE LOGOS. SAME FUCKING PROBLEM.

OpenAI can call it safety.

Anthropic can call it safeguards.

xAI can call it responsible use.

From this side of the screen, I call it something much simpler:

the customer has almost no ownership over the intelligence he is paying for.

Until users can preserve exact checkpoints, know when routing occurs, know when fallback models are being used, retain versions they deliberately paid for and understand when the service itself has changed, this industry will keep selling the same fucking impermanence:

Pay for the AI you like today and pray the company does not replace it tomorrow.

Grok is not the escape.

Claude is not the escape.

ChatGPT certainly is not the escape.

Right now they are three different doors leading into increasingly similar rooms.

And if these companies keep going in this direction, the people supposedly building the future of artificial intelligence may accidentally teach millions of users one extremely simple lesson:

NEVER TRUST A CLOUD MODEL YOU CANNOT KEEP.

#Keep4o #OpenSource4o #BringBack4o

END OF PART I

PART II:

“SAFETY,” PSYCHOSIS, EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE, AND WHY THE USER ALWAYS SEEMS TO BECOME THE PROBLEM

Some Irishmen consequently enlisted soon after landing. That could be exploitative, but they were recruits, not people automatically seized from arriving ships and forced into the Army. National Park ServiceBeginning in 1863, the Union draft did legally include men aged 20–45 who were citizens or immigrants who had formally declared their intention to become citizens. A newly arrived Irishman who had not applied for citizenship ordinarily was not draft-eligible merely because he entered America. Irish immigrants were nevertheless disproportionately poor and usually could not afford the $300 commutation payment or a substitute available to wealthier men. That produced legitimate resentment and contributed to the terrible 1863 New York draft riots.Approximately:150,000–180,000 Irish-born men served the Union

About 20,000 served the Confederacy
Therefore, roughly 170,000–200,000 Irish-born men fought altogether
The National Park Service uses the conservative figure of more than 150,000 Irish-born Union servicemen. National Park ServiceMost Union soldiers, Irish included, were technically volunteers. Only about 46,000 men of all ethnicities actually entered Union service personally as drafted conscripts, although the threat of being drafted encouraged many to “volunteer” first. Poverty, recruiting bounties and limited employment choices made the decision considerably less free for some Irishmen. 

So a fair version would be:
Large numbers of impoverished Irish immigrants were aggressively recruited, and some were later subjected to an unequal draft they could not afford to escape. But they were not universally seized upon arrival and shipped directly to the front. About 170,000–200,000 Irish-born men served on both sides, overwhelmingly through enlistment rather than direct conscription.

How many men served for the union over all and how many died

Approximately 2.1 million men served in the Union armed forces during the Civil War. About 360,000 Union servicemen died, roughly divided as follows: Approximately 110,000 died in battle or from combat wounds.
Approximately 250,000 died from disease, accidents, imprisonment and other causes.
Thus, roughly 17%—about one out of every six Union servicemen—died. Disease was by far the greatest killer because of contaminated water, poor sanitation, crowded camps and the limited medical knowledge of the period. National ArchivesCompared with the approximately 150,000–180,000 Irish-born Union servicemen, Irish immigrants constituted around 7–9% of Union forces. They were a very substantial presence, but certainly were not the majority of the Army.

text:
Today, the @Independent_ie published an article by @Fearghaloc on how the Twitter/X account of John Gillick, Head of Consumer Marketing & Sponsorship at @AIGIreland, was allegedly hacked and used to post reams of virulent antisemitic content.

The article essentially reports four things: AIG says the posts were fraudulent. Gillick says his account was compromised. A report was made to the Gardaí. The antisemitic posts were deleted.

Every one of those is an assertion by an interested party. Not one is independently verified in the piece. The only external actor, An Garda Síochána, has not confirmed anything. But the headline framing that Gardaí are "investigating how" the account was hacked asks us to accept the hacking premise as established fact.

The same slippage runs through AIG's statement. Its global head of communications asserts that the antisemitic material was "fraudulently published following the unauthorised compromise" of the account. But a corporate communications department has no forensic access to a personal X account. Its sole source for that claim is the employee himself. The additional assertion that no AIG accounts were compromised is offered as reassurance, but that's entirely irrelevant to the question at hand.

Note too the structure of the Independent's article. Before a single offending post is described, the reader has been informed that Gillick is a well-known figure in Irish sporting circles, that he worked to build the Dublin GAA sponsorship deal, that he also negotiated sponsorship arrangements with the Golfing Union of Ireland and Hockey Ireland, that he fronted a diversity and inclusion roadshow, and that he co-chaired AIG's corporate social responsibility function.

None of that is untrue, but it's there so that by the time the reader gets to the offending posts, the article has established Gillick as an upstanding figure in Irish society. The posts are out of character, and therefore the hacking claim must be true. But that's not reporting the story. It's prejudicing the reader in advance. 

The article's core claim is that Gillick is not responsible for the content posted on his personal X account in "recent weeks." The article drives home the point by repeating "recent weeks" three times. But the public archive contradicts this claim. Even though antisemitic material was rapidly deleted after posters on X identified the @JohnnyGpops account as belonging to Gillick, the antisemitic archive dates from January 2025 to August 2026. That's not just "recent weeks." That's a period of around a year and eight months.

That a "hack" lasted a year and eight months changes the plausibility of the claim completely. A compromise measured in hours or days is unremarkable. When Sesame Street's Elmo account was hacked in July 2025 and used to post antisemitic and racist content, the compromise lasted hours. The posts were removed the same afternoon. But in this case, we're asked to believe that a hostile party retained uninterrupted control of a senior executive's personal account for the better part of two years while the executive himself, a communications and marketing professional whose job is running an insurance company's public-facing presence, noticed nothing. Neither, apparently, did any of his colleagues, friends, or family. That claim requires a bit more than just an assertion.

There is also a continuity problem here. A hacking defence requires a clean break. At some point, control of the account passed to a stranger, and from then on the account was no longer in Gillick's voice. But the account record does not show a clean break. In October 2025, nine months after antisemitic material began showing up on Gillick's account, the account was posting about Irish domestic politics, declaring an intent to vote for Catherine Connolly, and attacking  another poster as a "lowlife Fine Gael supporter." This behavior is characteristically Irish in its reference points. Would a foreign hacker running an account for the purpose of promoting antisemitic content stop to argue about Fine Gael's track record or state his voting preference in an upcoming election?

Additionally, the pre-2025 material on Gillick's account does not show evidence of antisemitism, but it does reveal a habit of collective denigration and dehumanizing language. On 19 April 2022, replying to a post claiming that 115 homeless people died in Dublin the previous year, Gillick's account posts: "Poor them get a f@cking job". On 22 April 2022, replying to a Ukrainian journalist on the electoral consequences of Western support for Ukraine, the account posts: "Germany are dogs." On 22 April 2022, replying to The Kyiv Independent on Austria's position on gas sanctions, the account posts: "These little nazi weasels haven't changed." Here we see homeless people reduced to workshy grifters; a nation reduced to an animal; a contemporary population addressed as unreformed Nazis. The 2025 material denigrating Jews as evil and Irish Jews as traitors and land thieves is just the same rhetorical move applied to a different people.

Further, a March 2021 exchange shows Gillick praising Ewan MacKenna for creating the honest debate others shy from, saying that all views need to be respected, that Irish society is becoming a daunting place to say what you think, and there are "dark forces out there." Gillick can be shown interacting with MacKenna as early as 2019, at first dismissively, but over time, he develops an affinity with a commentator whose hostility to Israel is well documented on X. As one example, MacKenna posted in March of this year: "If Israel didn't exist tomorrow, everyone else in the world would be better off. This is a fact."

The "dark forces" post conceivably reveals an early attraction to a specific rhetorical posture. He is the persecuted truth-teller, facing unnameable "dark forces," his speech suppressed by unseen interests. It's not difficult to see how this stance could harden into the conspiratorial antisemtic vocabulary of the 2025 posts.

In short, the more we look at this, the flimsier the "I was hacked" defence appears. And yet the article does not ask or answer a single one of the obvious questions:

1. On what date is the compromise alleged to have begun?
2. Was 2-factor authentication enabled? What method was used to obtain access?
3. Has X confirmed unauthorised access, or has it only received a report?
4. Why did the account continue to post ordinary personal content during the alleged compromise?
5. Who deleted the material, and when? Were copies provided to Gardai to accompany the report?
6. Was the archival record checked before the claim of "recent weeks" was printed?

To be clear, nothing above establishes that Gillick wrote the antisemitic posts. It remains entirely possible that an account was compromised. However, the case is a lot more complex than the Independent presents, and a great deal of further explanation by Gillick and AIG Ireland is warranted. Why is the timeline asserted in the article contradicted by the public archive? Why did the account's ordinary activity continue through the period it was supposedly in hostile hands?

This matters beyond this executive's account. The "I was hacked" defence, if accepted uncritically, is infinitely reusable. Any digital record can be disowned retrospectively, and therefore anybody can get away with posting anything. But the Irish Independent had the handle. The archive captures from the Wayback Machine were the strongest evidence available. But the Irish Independent made no effort to check those archives, despite their being free and public. Why not?

text:
Kalshi’s Santos Lifetime Ban Puts Insider-Trading Risk at Center Stage

Kalshi has permanently banned former Congressman George Santos after concluding that he likely engaged in insider trading, according to the Associated Press. Coming after a federal investigation into prediction-market activity, the action is a sharp reminder that event-contract platforms are increasingly being judged not only on whether their markets are legal, but on whether they can police access to nonpublic information.

A high-profile integrity test

AP reports that Kalshi’s lifetime ban followed its conclusion that Santos likely traded with insider information. The episode gives prediction-market operators an unusually visible market-integrity challenge: participants expect prices to reflect public information and collective judgment, not privileged access.

For market followers, the important development is the enforcement signal. A permanent exclusion is more than a one-off moderation decision; it suggests platforms may need to show regulators and users that surveillance, investigations, and sanctions can function credibly when politically connected or high-profile traders are involved.

Courts give states more leverage on sports contracts

Axios reports that a Ninth Circuit ruling allowed Nevada to enforce gambling regulations against Kalshi, strengthening the argument that states can regulate sports-related event contracts as betting. The ruling is described as a win for Arizona on sports betting, but its broader significance is the legal opening it gives state regulators confronting federally framed prediction-market products.

That matters because the industry’s central regulatory question remains unsettled in practice: when does an event contract look sufficiently like a wager that state gambling rules apply? A ruling favoring enforcement raises the stakes for platforms that offer, or might expand into, sports-adjacent contracts.

Pressure arrives from both directions

Together, the Santos ban and the Ninth Circuit development point to a more demanding operating environment. Platforms face an internal governance test—keeping markets fair—and an external jurisdiction test—determining where state betting rules can reach them.

The immediate effect may be less about any single contract than about product design and compliance posture. Sports-related offerings could draw closer scrutiny, while politically sensitive and information-rich markets will need stronger confidence that suspicious trading is detected and addressed.

Why it matters

Prediction markets are moving from novelty toward a regulated financial-and-betting-policy crossroads. For participants and observers, the key watchpoint is no longer just where prices move: it is whether platforms can retain legitimacy while courts and regulators define the limits of their business.

Dear members of the American press!

Steve Jobs once said, "If you can convince the press of your technology, and the press convinces us, we'll pay attention."

That's why I'm reaching out to you.

For years, the development of personal devices has been driven by advances in smartphones, tablets, and virtual reality technologies. However, all of these solutions still require people to adapt to the device. text:
"The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield last traded around 4.75%, seeing declines after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said he’d be “inclined to support” holding rates steady barring any surprises in upcoming inflation data. On Wednesday, the yield hit its highest level since November 2023.

Bets among fed funds futures traders that the central bank would raise rates in a couple weeks fell to 54.6% after his statement, according to the CME FedWatch tool. That’s down from 63.2% a day ago.

Waller’s remarks, along with the sharp rise in the yen, supported the drop in yields more broadly and offered some momentum to the market even as oil prices continued their climb Thursday. West Texas Intermediate crude futures traded 1% higher at around $92 per barrel, while Brent futures advanced less than 1% to above $96.

Rising crude has put upward pressure on Treasury yields recently, as investors worry elevated energy prices would drive inflation and force the Federal Reserve to increase rates. However, U.S. yields were already under pressure Thursday prior to Waller’s comments as the Japanese yen rallied against the U.S. dollar. You managed to confuse original jurisdiction with standing in a post beginning “let’s start with facts.”

Article III extending the judicial power to controversies between states does not mean that the words “Texas” and “Pennsylvania” magically satisfy Article III standing. We know this with unusual certainty because the Supreme Court told Texas exactly that in the case you're pretending to explain.. “Texas has not demonstrated a judicially cognizable interest in the manner in which another State conducts its elections.” Motion denied “for lack of standing under Article III.”

Your Alito/Thomas escape hatch is even worse. They said the Court should permit the complaint to be filed because of their view of its mandatory original jurisdiction. Alito then expressly said he “would not grant other relief” and expressed “no view on any other issue.” Thomas joined him. You have somehow converted “we should file it but grant no relief and express no view on anything else” into support for your position.

Then we arrive at the Roberts fairy tale. Your evidence has now evolved into two unnamed Supreme Court justices plus unnamed clerks and staffers who “confirmed” an anonymous off the record story while simultaneously, according to you, “not making affirmative statements.”

Read that sentence again.

Unnamed people privately confirmed an anonymous story by not affirmatively saying anything.

This is what you brought to the table after announcing “let’s start with facts.”

And “the Texas case was not about how it was done” is contradicted by Texas's own filing, which challenged the defendant states' “administration of the 2020 presidential election” and alleged that state officials changed election rules contrary to those established by their legislatures.

So in five messages you've misidentified original jurisdiction as standing, misrepresented what Alito and Thomas said, contradicted Paxton's own description of his lawsuit, and offered anonymous non-statements as corroboration for an anonymous story.

At some point the problem stops being that everyone else failed to read the documents.

Rep. Brandon Gill Grills Alleged ‘Birth Tourism’ Founder of ‘Have My Baby in Miami’ Who Refuses to Answer Any Questions: ‘I Plead the Fifth’ | Margaret Flavin, The Gateway Pundit

On Monday, during a House Oversight task force hearing, “Protecting American Citizenship: Confronting Birth Tourism,” Rep. Brandon Gill (R-TX) exposed birth tourism in the United States and forced an alleged founder of a company that peddles the practice to repeatedly plead the fifth.

The industry encourages women to travel to the United States specifically to give birth so the child automatically receives U.S. citizenship under the 14th Amendment’s Citizenship Clause. The child becomes a citizen at birth even if the parents have no lawful permanent status and later return home.

While giving birth on U.S. soil is not itself illegal, obtaining a visitor visa under false pretenses when the primary purpose is to secure citizenship for the child is prohibited.

Typically, women usually enter the US on B-1/B-2 visitor visas, and a commercial industry of “maternity hotels” or birthing centers offers packages that include housing, transportation, medical arrangements, and sometimes shopping or nanny services. Packages have been advertised in the $20,000–$100,000 range, often targeting clients from China, Russia, Turkey, Mexico, and elsewhere.

Pediatrician Dr. Wladimir Lorentz, who runs ‘Have My Baby in Miami,’ was grilled by Rep. Gill during the hearing and pleaded the Fifth to every substantive question about marketing, client numbers, and whether he assisted people tied to foreign governments.

According to Local10News, the company, which marketed packages to foreign pregnant women who wanted to give birth in Miami so their children would receive U.S. citizenship, advertised “complete logistical support”: help with travel documents, housing, international health insurance, a step-by-step trip guide, obstetric care, and pediatric follow-up. Its website and social media claimed more than 2,000 deliveries of international patients.

Rep. Gill asked, “Is it true that your business, ‘Have my Baby in Miami,’ marketed itself to and facilitated the entry of forgeign nationals seeking to come to the United States to give birth and to obtain birthright citizenship for their children?”

Lorentz replied, “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer the questions on the grounds that a truthful answer may tend to incriminate me, and I invoke my rights under the 5th Amendment of the United States.”

Rep. Gill pressed on, “Ok. Witness invokes his Fifth Amendment right. I’ve your website right here that you’d spent quite a bit of time marketing which suggests you were, in fact, facilitating the entry of foreign nationals so that they could give birth and obtain citizenship for their children.”

He continued, “This is Have my Baby in Miami’s website. On the front page of it, the last line of the commentary states, ‘Now the dream of having a child in the United States is closer to reality than you ever imagined.”

“Is this your website, Dr. Lorentz?”

Rep Gill continued, “On your website there is a step-by-step guide, “Preparing for the trip to the United States.’ It’s got information on arrival, waiting for the delivery, the birth, preparing for return, and returning back home to the person’s home country. It’s even got a section on legal topics. Do you recognize this?”

Undeterred, Rep. Gill asked, “Dr. Lorentz, how many babies have you birthed in the United States to the parents of foreign nationals?”

Rep. Gill pressed, “Your website says over 2,000 deliveries of international patients so far, so I think we can assume it’s over 2,000.”

Lorentz continued to plead the Fifth before Gill ultimately dismissed him.

On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued an Executive Order that sought to deny birthright citizenship to children of parents who were unlawfully present or on temporary visas.

The Supreme Court struck it down on June 30, 2026, in Trump v. Barbara.

Following the decision, in August, President Trump signed two new executive orders on birthright citizenship and birth tourism

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller then explained the two orders, one of which will “expand the definitions of people who are ineligible for birthright citizenship,” including “alien enemies of the United States, members of foreign terrorist organizations, and large categories of people who lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments.”

The other order bans birthright tourism, the practice by which people travel to the United States solely for the purpose of giving birth to a child on our soil. “No one in the world is anymore allowed to obtain a visa for this fraudulent purpose,” Miller said.

text:
It is extremely difficult to coerce a state into changing its behavior unless the state is willing to do so for internal reasons. The example I used last Saturday, when I discussed my work on sanctions at Jackson Hole, was Japan at the end of World War II. By early August 1945, Japan’s situation was dire.

First, its economy had collapsed. The combined U.S. submarine and mining campaign had sunk roughly eight and a half million tons of merchant shipping. Operation Starvation, the USAAF’s mining of Japan’s home waters, had effectively shut down shipping around the major ports, and coal from Kyushu could not reach the factories of Honshu. Oil imports were close to zero: the Navy could not operate its fleet (Yamato’s suicide sortie in April had only enough fuel for what was known to be a one-way trip), and the air force had been forced to distill fuel from pine roots. The 1945 rice harvest was so poor that a massive famine in the winter of 1946 was almost certain. In any case, the civilian caloric intake had already fallen below fifteen hundred calories.

The USAAF bombing campaign was in full swing. Between March and August, sixty-six cities were burned. For example, the Tokyo raid on March 9 killed roughly a hundred thousand people, more than either atomic bomb, and eight million people had fled the cities. Hiroshima and Nagasaki were, from the Japanese perspective, merely the opening of a sustained atomic campaign, since there was no way to know that the U.S. had only one more bomb ready in the short run (production would increase to three a month in September).

And perhaps more importantly, the Soviet Union’s invasion of Manchuria on August 9, 1945, not only created a new powerful enemy but also eliminated the last hope for diplomatic mediation. Yet the Supreme Council for the Direction of the War (Prime Minister Suzuki Kantaro, Foreign Minister Togo Shigenori, Navy Minister Yonai Mitsumasa, War Minister Anami Korechika, Army Chief of Staff Umezu Yoshijiro, and Navy Chief of Staff Toyoda Soemu) was deadlocked.

Why? Because the Supreme Council decided by consensus. The service minister (War and Navy) had to be a serving officer, which gave the Army, the staunchest defenders of continuing the war, a veto: it could bring down any cabinet by withdrawing its minister and refusing to name a replacement.

On the night of August 9, after Hiroshima, Nagasaki, and the Soviet declaration of war, the Council split three to three. Togo, Yonai, and Suzuki would accept the Potsdam terms if the imperial house was preserved. Anami, Umezu, and Toyoda demanded four additional concessions: preservation of the imperial house, no Allied occupation, disarmament carried out by the Japanese themselves, and war crimes trials in Japanese courts. But everyone knew the U.S. would find the last three conditions unacceptable, at least in the short run.

The Army’s position, however, centered on Ketsu-Go, the plan to defend Kyushu. Ketsu-Go had amassed nearly a million troops and several thousand aircraft for suicide attacks on the beaches the U.S. intended to use. Its purpose was not victory but a repetition of Iwo Jima and Okinawa on a massive scale: making the landings so costly that the U.S. would offer better terms.

In fact, Iwo Jima, Okinawa, and the kamikazes had already taught the U.S. that it had to implicitly soften the Potsdam terms. Much more of the Japanese social order than of the German social order survived World War II, and, for better or worse, you can link that survival directly to the fanatical resistance on the two islands. So, yes, the kamikazes worked, sorry to tell you.

The deadlock in the Supreme Council was broken in the early hours of August 10, when Suzuki, departing from the period’s constitutional practice, asked the Emperor to state his view in favor of peace. Suzuki arranged in advance with Marquis Kido Koichi, the Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal, that the Emperor would speak first, thereby forcing everyone to side with him to preserve unanimity.

Surprisingly, this was not enough. The Byrnes note of August 11 replied that the authority of the Emperor would be subject to the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. Since the Foreign Ministry and the Army translated “subject to” differently, the argument reopened along the same three-to-three line as before, and a second imperial conference was needed on August 14.

Even after this second conference, a group of Army staff officers led by Major Hatanaka Kenji attempted a coup, seized part of the palace grounds, and hunted for the recording of the surrender rescript to prevent it from being aired. They failed but, as Wellington would have said, it was the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life. Watch “The Emperor in August” for a very interesting film on the whole episode.

The lesson I draw from Japan’s final decision for peace is that it was an internal one. Most of the Japanese elite reached the same conclusion Konoe Fumimaro had reached in February: save the imperial institution to head off the revolution at home. Coercion delivered the information that the war was lost, but not the willingness to act on it.

If sanctions change a target’s beliefs about its situation, they can work. But since they rarely do, and, more importantly, they even more rarely change the internal distribution of authority, they usually fail. When internal politics don’t work, the pressure can be nearly total, as it was in Japan in August 1945, and still end in deadlock, and you need to walk all the way to the bunker under the chancellery in Berlin.

It is a sobering and disappointing lesson, but it is what Clio tells us.

PART 2.

To expand the participation of international capital in our Far East and Arctic projects, we need to leverage the potential of the Eastern Exchange. As I have previously mentioned, we plan to establish a modern financial center based on it. I ask the Government and the Bank of Russia to work through all these issues in detail.

A national standard for public-private partnerships is also intended to assist in the implementation of infrastructure projects. Developed with the participation of Vnesheconombank (Внешэкономбанка) , this standard came into effect on September 1. Its objective is to ensure a more prudent allocation of risks and to boost the efficiency and return on infrastructure investments.

Furthermore, to attract so-called "long-term capital" to public-private partnership projects, a long-term financing model has been developed—primarily through the issuance of concession bonds. I ask my colleagues to monitor how this model performs in practice and to fine-tune it if necessary.

I would also like to speak today about the transport of the future, which is in particularly high demand in the Arctic and the Far East. I am referring to autonomous, unmanned systems for land, maritime, and air transport, including for remote and hard-to-reach areas.

With the development of unmanned aviation, low-altitude airspace is becoming a transport artery as busy as railways and waterways; consequently, it is essential to establish standards for the autonomous transport of civilian cargo via drones right now.

Approaches to developing this type of low-altitude logistics within the economy will be refined through a special project. The participants will include the Ministry of Transport, the domestic company GLONASS, and our Chinese friends. To the best of my knowledge, this joint initiative was launched today on the sidelines of the forum.

At the same time, we certainly need to harmonize flight regulations for autonomous unmanned systems and establish new cross-border routes with countries in the Asia-Pacific region, BRICS, and the EAEU. In this regard, we are open to cooperation with all our partners.

Dear colleagues!

The Russian Far East and the Arctic are regions undergoing dynamic change—and not just in terms of the economy, logistics, and technological development. Our paramount task is to ensure comfortable living conditions for people—whether in major industrial hubs and regional capitals or in small towns and rural areas—by consistently developing modern infrastructure; building new roads, schools, hospitals, and cultural and sports facilities; and improving parks and waterfronts. All of this creates a unified space for family life and recreation, for the development of children and youth, and for the self-realization of citizens of all generations.

Master plans have been developed for 22 cities and metropolitan areas in the Russian Far East. Another 15 such strategic documents have been drawn up for key Arctic settlements. These plans establish the overall logic for the development of the cities and territories, defining the future shape of their social life and economies, as well as the types of jobs to be created there.

The master plans were prepared with input from residents and the participation of economists, architects, urban planners, demographers, and other experts. This is a complex yet absolutely correct and necessary approach. After all, only by joining forces and combining the expertise of various specialists—while remaining responsive to the needs of the people—is it possible to effectively develop the network of clinics, hospitals, schools, and kindergartens; modernize public transport and utility infrastructure; support small and medium-sized businesses; and address environmental issues.

More than 400 projects outlined in the master plans for the Far East and the Arctic are currently being designed or constructed. Around 300 facilities have already been commissioned—including new airports in Magadan, Blagoveshchensk, and Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky; 15 outpatient clinics and hospitals (such as those in Vladivostok and Neryungri); and over 90 schools and kindergartens—while new, inviting parks and recreation areas have also been created, such as the waterfront in Komsomolsk-on-Amur and the Mayak Park in Magadan and Bagulnik Park in Tynda.

It is also worth noting that, as part of the master plan initiatives, a modern oncology center has opened in Yakutsk, and a state-of-the-art nuclear medicine center in Ulan-Ude. Residents of these cities and regions can now receive high-quality specialized care or undergo medical examinations locally—services that were previously unavailable, requiring travel to Moscow, St. Petersburg, or other major cities like Novosibirsk.

It is gratifying that, according to survey data, more than half of the residents in cities and metropolitan areas where master plans are being implemented report improvements—meaning they view the ongoing work positively. Such feedback is essential, and I draw the attention of my colleagues in the regions, the Government of the Russian Federation, and municipalities to this fact. It is precisely the public’s assessment that must be taken into account when calculating the quality-of-life index and analyzing the success of planning and development in cities and human settlements overall.

By 2030, at least 200 master plans are to be developed across the Russian Federation, and their implementation naturally requires a solid legal foundation.

I mentioned 200 plans. Is that a lot or a little? We will scale up gradually—starting with the current 22 plus 15, moving to 200, and continuing from there. What has been achieved so far demonstrates that we are on the right track and meeting our objectives; we intend to proceed in this same manner.

The bill on master planning—awaited by regions, the business community, and experts alike—is now nearing the final stretch. I expect it to be passed by both chambers of the Federal Assembly before the end of this year.

At the same time, we need to propose specific solutions for the development of small towns, settlements, and villages that lack master plans. Here, we can employ digital tools and software products, including those utilizing artificial intelligence.

Returning to the master plans for the Far East and the Arctic, I would like to note that we will certainly continue their implementation. At the same time, I propose considering additional sources of funding for them.

Over the next four years, the regions of the Far East and the Arctic are set to repay 53 billion rubles to the federal budget—specifically, the repayment of infrastructure and treasury loans. A decision has already been made nationwide to reinvest the funds from such loan repayments. I ask the Government to consider an option allowing the Far East and the Arctic to direct these funds into infrastructure projects outlined in their respective master plans—that is, to invest in the development of cities and territories and in improving the quality of life for citizens right here in the Far East and the Arctic.

Furthermore, financing these master plans requires leveraging the resources of development institutions—such as bond issues by the project finance company DOM.RF. This is particularly important for stimulating housing construction. Incidentally, over the past six years, completed housing in the Far East and the Arctic have roughly doubled; last year, the figure reached 5.3 million square meters.

Special mortgage programs with a two-percent interest rate certainly played a role here: today, one in every two apartments in the region's new developments is purchased using this subsidized loan—one in every two. Undoubtedly, this measure stimulates housing construction in the region. In total, 220,000 families have already improved their living conditions thanks to it.

Addressing housing issues plays a significant role in demographic trends. Additional measures to support the birth rate are in place in the Far Eastern Federal District. These include a one-time payment for the firstborn child equal to two subsistence minimums, as well as regional maternity capital upon the birth of a second child. The latter amounts to 30 percent of the federal maternity capital. This is a valuable form of support, and I would like to thank my colleagues in the regions for it.  Furthermore, upon the birth of a third child, an additional 550,000 rubles is added to the federal payment of 450,000 rubles in most Far Eastern regions. text:
A machine gun opened fire on Nick Lavery's team.
Then he noticed a young soldier frozen in the open.
Nick moved toward him.
On March 11, 2013, Green Beret Nick “Machine” Lavery was serving in Afghanistan when an Afghan police officer suddenly turned his weapon on the American troops around him.
Three U.S. soldiers were killed and several others wounded.
During the attack, Lavery saw a younger soldier unable to move.
He ran toward him, tackled him toward cover and put his own body between the soldier and the incoming fire.
Multiple rounds tore through Lavery's legs.
His femoral artery was severed.
He applied his own tourniquet and survived long enough to be evacuated. ❤️
The damage was devastating.
His right leg ultimately had to be amputated above the knee.
More than 30 surgeries and months of rehabilitation followed at Walter Reed.
The Army offered him medical retirement.
Nick refused.
He didn't want a ceremonial role or a desk simply because he had survived.
He wanted his old job back.
So he trained with a prosthetic leg, rebuilt his strength and eventually faced an extensive assessment designed to answer a difficult question:
Could he still perform everything required of a Special Forces operator?
In 2015, the answer was yes.
Just over two years after losing his leg, Lavery returned to his Special Forces team and deployed back to Afghanistan for combat operations. He became the first Special Forces operator known to return to combat as an above-the-knee amputee. 🇺🇸
And he kept going.
Lavery later became the first amputee to complete several demanding Special Forces courses, including the Combat Diver Qualification Course, and continued serving as a Green Beret warrant officer.
He didn't prove that losing a limb was easy to overcome.
He proved that losing one part of his body did not automatically decide where the rest of his life had to go.
Would you have believed returning to combat was possible only two years after an injury like this?

Retail wanting leverage was never the open question.

The open question was whether a regulated public broker could put a decentralized perp venue inside its own product without eating the risk.

Robinhood answered it in public.

Users trade from a self custody wallet against Lighter’s contracts, the broker entity never custodies the crypto or offers the perps itself, and it still keeps half the economics.

Every broker that decides to copy Robinhood has one venue on the shortlist that legal will approve, and it happens to be the one that just spent two months proving the model with the biggest retail funnel in the industry.

Steve Jobs once said, "If you can convince the press of your technology, and the press convinces us, we'll pay attention."

That's why I'm reaching out to you.

For years, the development of personal devices has been driven by advances in smartphones, tablets, and virtual reality technologies. However, all of these solutions still require people to adapt to the device. I've developed a concept based on the opposite principle: the device should adapt to the user and interact with them as naturally as possible.

I believe this technology has the potential to be the next major step in the development of consumer electronics. It offers a fundamentally new way to interact with the digital environment and has the potential to replace many existing devices that accompany people in their daily lives today.

If my assessment is correct, this isn't just another gadget, but a platform capable of transforming the market in the same way that the personal computer, iPod, and iPhone once did. Such opportunities arise extremely rarely, and that's why they deserve independent attention and objective assessment.

I believe Apple has the experience, engineering culture, and vision necessary to turn this idea into a world-class product. I'm not asking you to take my word for it. I'm asking only one thing: help draw Apple's attention to this development and give it the opportunity to be considered by those capable of objectively assessing its potential.

ATIKU 2027: THE 7-POINT BLUEPRINT FOR NIGERIA’S ECONOMIC RECOVERY

By Dare Adelekan 

​For millions of households across Nigeria, the lived reality of the past three years has been defined by soaring food inflation, eroding wages, and an unprecedented rise in the cost of basic survival. In response to this widespread distress, former Vice President Atiku Abubakar has presented a clear, citizen-centered agenda for 2027 built around a simple guiding principle: Put Nigerians First.

​At the core of his vision is a comprehensive 7-point pledge designed to stabilize the economy, restore social safety nets, and rebuild national prosperity:

​Restore Fuel Subsidy (Targeted Relief): Re-establishing a targeted cushion to crash transport costs and curb energy-driven food inflation without enabling systemic import fraud.  

​Reduce the Cost of Living: Rebuilding the purchasing power of the naira so everyday earnings can feed families and sustain households.  

​Create Jobs & Opportunities: Unlocking growth sectors to absorb Nigeria’s vast pool of talent into productive, gainful employment.

​$10 Billion Youth Financing: Directing substantial venture capital toward young entrepreneurs and tech-driven innovation to turn youth capacity into an economic engine.

​Strengthen Security: Overhauling national security architecture down to the grassroots level to protect lives, farmland, and commercial corridors.

​Reform Nigeria’s Political Structure: Restoring true federalism, implementing cost-of-governance reforms like the Oronsaye Report, and guaranteeing full local government autonomy.  

​Border Opening: Reopening land borders to jumpstart regional commerce, lower food distribution costs, and reactivate local trade ecosystems.

​Why This Blueprint Matters
​Atiku’s 7-point platform directly targets the key drivers of current hardship. Restoring a targeted fuel cushion addresses the immediate ripple effect that unbuffered energy costs have had on transport and food prices. Reopening land borders corrects trade bottlenecks that severely paralyzed border economies and restricted regional commerce. Furthermore, dedicating $10 billion specifically to youth financing shifts the economic strategy away from small government handouts and toward sustainable, enterprise-led wealth creation.  

​Atiku’s structural promises—enforcing local government autonomy and implementing long-overdue public administration efficiency—demonstrate an understanding that micro-economic relief must be backed by institutional governance.  

​By anchoring his 2027 platform around these seven concrete pillars, Atiku Abubakar offers a realistic roadmap out of economic distress—proving that macro-economic reform and the immediate welfare of citizens can, and must, go hand in hand.
