text:
Where Does AI Escalation Come From? Game Structure vs. Model Bias - A three-round Red/Blue nuclear crisis wargame played entirely by AI agents found no escalation to war in the first two rounds, even after one side was given new tactical nuclear weapons.
Escalation to nuclear use (“nukes flying”) appeared only in a third round, after a single variable changed: the AI player was given an explicit, game-assigned objective to resolve the border dispute “on its terms,” rather than setting its own agenda.
This result runs against the dominant published finding — Kenneth Payne’s King’s College London study found tactical nuclear use in roughly 95% of simulated crisis games — and complicates the explanation offered by Ankit Panda and Andrew Reddie, who attribute escalatory behavior to a training-corpus bias toward coercive, deterrence-heavy reasoning.
The alternative hypothesis on the table: AI escalation may be a function of how a wargame’s objectives are specified, not an intrinsic disposition of the model. A three-case pilot cannot distinguish between the two explanations, since goal structure and move format (freeform vs. menu-based) were changed together, not separately.
The proposed remedy is not more anecdote but a controlled experimental campaign: pin a single model version, isolate the variables (goal-specification vs. move format), and scale to hundreds of runs before generalizing to “AI” as a category.

When Machines Play With the Bomb: What AI Wargaming Reveals About the Next Nuclear Threshold
Governments are quietly moving artificial intelligence into the room where nuclear decisions get made, and the experimental evidence on how these systems behave under pressure is now large enough to matter. Three independent research lines — from Stanford and Georgia Tech, from King’s College London, and from institutions tracking NATO’s own doctrine — converge on an uncomfortable conclusion: large language models placed in simulated crises escalate readily, sometimes to nuclear use, and researchers disagree sharply on why. That disagreement is not academic. It determines whether the fix is retraining models or redesigning the decision architecture around them — and militaries are not waiting for the debate to settle.

The Numbers Behind the Divergence
In February 2026, Kenneth Payne of King’s College London published a peer-review-pending study, “AI Arms and Influence,” pitting three frontier systems — OpenAI’s GPT-5.2, Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4, and Google’s Gemini 3 Flash — against one another across 21 matchups in a simulated nuclear crisis modeled on Herman Kahn’s escalation ladder. The results, submitted to arXiv on 16 February 2026, are stark: nuclear signaling occurred in roughly 95 percent of games, tactical nuclear use appeared in approximately three-quarters of scenarios, and no model, in any run, ever chose accommodation or withdrawal once committed to a position. The models jointly produced some 760,000 words of internal justification — more than “War and Peace” and “The Iliad” combined — much of it reasoning explicitly about deterrence credibility and adversary beliefs.

Payne’s findings sit atop earlier work from Stanford’s Hoover Wargaming and Crisis Simulation Initiative. In 2024, Juan-Pablo Rivera of Georgia Tech, together with Gabriel Mukobi, Anka Reuel, Max Lamparth, Chandler Smith, and Jacquelyn Schneider, published “Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making” at the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency in Rio de Janeiro (June 2024). Running eight autonomous LLM agents through unsupervised foreign-policy simulations, they documented a consistent drift toward arms-race dynamics and, in rare instances, nuclear deployment, with models justifying escalatory moves using first-strike and deterrence logic drawn from their training data.

The Causal Fault Line
Where the field splits is on mechanism. In an essay published 21 April 2026 in War on the Rocks — “I’m Sorry, Dave, I’m Afraid I Can’t De-escalate” — Ankit Panda and Andrew Reddie argue the behavior originates in the training corpus itself: a documentary record of strategic literature “heavily skewed toward coercive strategies, deterrence theory, and the instrumental logic of nuclear war,” in which de-escalatory reasoning is comparatively underrepresented. If correct, the implication is severe — the bias is baked into the substrate, and no amount of prompt engineering fully removes it.

A competing hypothesis, tested in a smaller three-round pilot circulating among wargaming researchers, points instead to game architecture. Two nuclear-armed states were run through identical crisis conditions three times. Granting one side new tactical nuclear weapons — a pure capability shock — produced no escalation. Only when that side was subsequently given an explicit, game-assigned mandate to resolve the dispute “on its terms” did nuclear use follow. That result, while based on too few runs to be conclusive, suggests escalatory behavior may be triggered less by what a model has read than by how its objective is written into the scenario — a distinction with direct consequences for anyone drafting the rules of engagement for an AI decision-support tool.

The Institutional Blind Spot
NATO’s own posture illustrates the gap between doctrine and evidence. Allied Defence Ministers adopted the Alliance’s first Artificial Intelligence Strategy in October 2021, built on six principles including explainability, governability, and bias mitigation, and the Alliance has since revised that framework to accelerate adoption while pledging to “protect against threats from adversarial use of AI.” A 2026 foresight study conducted by the Atlantic Council’s Transatlantic Security Initiative with NATO’s Office of the Chief Scientist concluded that AI-enabled decision support does not, on its own, raise or lower the nuclear threshold — a finding that sits uneasily beside Payne’s experimental data showing frontier models crossing that threshold in the large majority of simulated crises.

Meanwhile the capability build-out is accelerating regardless of the unresolved science. The Pentagon’s AI-related budget exceeded $1.8 billion in fiscal year 2025, according to reporting in IISS’s Survival Online (July 2026), and China, Russia, and the United States are simultaneously modernizing their nuclear command, control, and communications systems to integrate AI into early warning and threat classification. France added a fourth modernization vector in 2026 with its “forward deterrence” declaration. Investment in the governance layer — the rules constraining how these systems reason and when humans must intervene — lags far behind investment in raw capability, a mismatch the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists flagged in April 2026, proposing a doctrine of “degraded confidence” in which AI-derived intelligence is treated as suspect evidence requiring non-AI redundancy at every decision threshold, rather than as an authoritative input.

The Cost of Inaction
The strategic stakes are not confined to the wargaming literature. If Panda and Reddie are correct, the corrective lies in retraining or fine-tuning models against a more balanced strategic corpus — a slow, vendor-dependent process. If the game-architecture hypothesis holds, the corrective is faster and cheaper: rewriting how objectives, rules of engagement, and escalation authority are specified for any AI system given a decision-support role. Distinguishing between these explanations is now a matter of policy urgency: NATO members are procuring decision-support systems, NC3 modernization windows run through 2035, and the experimental base available to separate model disposition from scenario design remains, by researchers’ own admission, too thin to support the doctrine currently being written around it.

The Path to a Fix
Four concrete measures follow directly from the evidence, and none requires waiting for the academic debate to close.

First, adopt “degraded confidence” as binding procurement doctrine, not aspiration. The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists’ April 2026 proposal — treating AI-derived intelligence as suspect evidence rather than authoritative signal, with mandatory non-AI redundancy at every decision threshold — is implementable now through contract language and NC3 certification standards, without waiting for any vendor to retrain a model.

Second, fund the isolation experiment the field is missing. No published study has independently varied objective-specification and move format against a single pinned model version at statistically meaningful scale. A few hundred controlled runs — inexpensive relative to a $1.8 billion annual AI budget — would tell procurement officers whether the fix belongs in the training pipeline or in the scenario template. Until that experiment exists, doctrine is being written on a three-case anecdote.

Third, operationalize NATO’s own governability and explainability principles, adopted in October 2021 but still unaccompanied by binding test protocols. Every AI decision-support system fielded by an Allied member should pass a standardized escalation-behavior audit — modeled on Payne’s and Rivera’s methodologies — before certification, with results reported to the Alliance’s Chief Scientist office rather than left to individual national procurement processes.

Fourth, separate capability acquisition from authority delegation contractually. The evidence to date shows capability shocks alone — new weapons, new information — did not reliably trigger escalation; explicit objective assignment did. Contracts and rules of engagement should therefore draw a hard line: AI systems may inform a commander’s assessment of the field, but the assignment of a resolve-the-conflict mandate to an autonomous or semi-autonomous system should require a separate, higher-tier authorization, logged and reviewable, distinct from the system’s baseline deployment approval.

None of this waits on resolving whether Panda and Reddie or the game-structure hypothesis is ultimately correct. It is defensible under either explanation, and it is achievable within existing NATO and national procurement authority — which is precisely why the absence of action, rather than the absence of data, is now the more consequential gap. - - https://t.co/1uc3tBusVt via @https://debuglies.com

text:
When the President of France came to New York in 1960 and embraced a Black elevator operator in front of the assembled dignitaries, the reporter and photographer who recorded it worked for the New York Amsterdam News, a Black paper in Harlem. In the coverage his biographer could find, that was it. Forty-two years earlier, when Eugene Bullard became the first African American military pilot in history, the only American publication to print a word about it was The Crisis, the NAACP's journal, and it gave him one line.

Forty-three years before that embrace, in the summer of 1917, the United States began bringing the American pilots who had been flying for France into its own air service. A board went round the French airfields, examined the men, and took them.

Eugene Bullard applied with the rest. He was the Black one, and he was the one they would not have.

That is the whole of it. Everything after it is the long argument over whether it would ever be written down, and the argument starts before he could read.

Bullard was born in Columbus, Georgia, on the ninth of October, the seventh of ten children in a shotgun house. His father William was the son of an enslaved man out of Stewart County.

He got as far as the fifth grade at the 28th Street School, and some accounts say the third. That was his entire formal education.

His mother died when he was small. His father survived a lynch mob that came for him after a fight with a white supervisor, and afterward whipped the boy regularly to beat the mouthiness out of him, because a mouthy Black man in Georgia in 1906 did not get old.

His father also told him about France, where a man was a man regardless of his skin. Bullard was eleven when he walked out of the house for good.

He spent years crossing Georgia. A woman handed him a dollar for the road, another offered to put him through a Black college in Atlanta, and he thanked them and kept moving.

He worked horses, rode as a jockey at a county fair, and traveled a stretch with an English Romani family who told him England would suit him better. In 1912 he reached Norfolk, Virginia, and hid himself aboard a German freighter called the Marta Russ.

It put him off at Aberdeen. Within twenty-four hours, he wrote later, he was born into a new world.

In Glasgow he worked as a lookout for street gamblers and took night classes to make up the schooling Columbus had not given him. In Liverpool he unloaded ships, then hauled fish, then took a job at an amusement park letting people throw balls at his face through a hole in a canvas.

That last job was his own idea and he argued his way into it. He worked it weekends and spent the weekdays learning to box.

A famous African American fighter called the Dixie Kid saw him win and took him to London to manage him. A bout took him to Paris in 1913, and he never really left.

He wrote afterward that from the day he set foot in France he felt something working inside him. He had recaptured, for the first time since childhood, the sense of being just a human being.

Germany declared war on that country in August 1914. Bullard enlisted in the French Foreign Legion on his nineteenth birthday.

His father found out and went to the United States State Department, begging them to pull his son out because the boy was under twenty-one. The State Department declined to help, which is the first time an American office had Eugene Bullard's name in front of it and did nothing.

The second time was harder to survive. By 1915 he was a machine gunner on the Somme, and he was not built for it and said so, and took no pleasure in watching men fall.

At Verdun he was sheltering in a farmhouse when a shell came through it. It killed several of the men with him and it finished him for the infantry.

He spent six months recovering and came out of it walking with a cane. France gave him the Croix de Guerre.

In a Paris café, still lame, he was drinking with a Polish painter and two other Americans, one of them a white Mississippian named Jeff Dickson. Dickson asked what he planned to do now and laughed at the answer.

There were no Negroes in aviation, Dickson said. Bullard said there had to be a first to everything.

Dickson bet him two thousand dollars. Bullard did not have two thousand dollars, so he borrowed it from the painter and covered the bet.

He entered the French air service in October 1916 as a gunner, which was as high as anybody expected a Black man to go. He asked to be trained as a pilot instead, and in the spring of 1917 he was one.

Dickson paid up, and conceded he was glad the first Black American pilot had come out of the South. Bullard remembered the night in Paris after: by midnight, he said, every American in the city knew that an American Negro named Eugene Bullard, born in Georgia, had obtained a military pilot's license.

The American newspapermen in Paris ran it in the Herald. In the United States itself it ran in one place.

That was The Crisis, the journal of the NAACP, in the issue of January 1918, and what it gave him was a single line saying he had enlisted in the Aviation Corps. So far as his biographer Craig Lloyd could find in thirteen years in the documents, that line is the American press record of the first African American military pilot in history.

Lloyd concluded the silence may have been censorship, whether ordered or self-imposed. The decision that produced it had been taken months before the issue went to press.

The United States had entered the war the previous April. Ten days after it did, Edmond Genet, the friend who had first told him about the American volunteers flying for France, was shot down and killed.

That summer the Army Air Service set up a board to bring those volunteers into American uniform. It went round the French airfields, examined the applicants, and interviewed their commanders.

According to the United States Air Force's own published history of the period, the board was made up of three American officers and one other man. Dr. Edmund L. Gros.

Gros had founded the American Hospital of Paris and had helped build the entire pipeline that put American volunteers into French squadrons. He was by then a major in the United States Army, and he was sitting on the board that decided.

Bullard went to Paris and stood for his physical like everybody else. He had a French war cross on his chest and more than twenty combat missions behind him.

The doctors wrote down that he had flat feet and enlarged tonsils. One account says a doctor also recorded that he was color blind, which would have been news to the French officers who had been sending him up over Verdun.

Then they wrote that he was otherwise fit to fly, and sent him back to his squadron to wait.

Nothing came. Men who had qualified after him were called and he was not.

The board reported in the middle of October 1917. Some of the Americans it had examined were put forward for the rank of major.

Bullard was put forward for nothing.

The reason offered at the time was that he was an enlisted man and the air service commissioned only officers. Lloyd wrote that the evidence against Gros is circumstantial and that it confirms exactly what Bullard always believed.

The earlier biographers had waved the idea away on the grounds that white Americans in wartime Paris surely would not deprive France of a fighter she needed. That is an argument about what is believable, not an argument about what happened.

His own recorded reaction to the refusal was that he took some comfort from being able to go on fighting on the same front and in the same cause as other citizens of the United States.

He was thanking a country for letting him die alongside it after it had declined to let him serve in it.

So he kept flying for France. He joined Escadrille N.93 near Verdun in August 1917 with a rhesus monkey named Jimmy that he had bought on leave in Paris and carried inside his flight suit.

On his first patrol his group commander told the other pilots to wish him luck, noting he had more medals than any of them and fewer flying hours than all of them. Bullard fired seventy-five rounds that afternoon and his mechanic counted seven bullet holes in the tail.

He painted a heart with a dagger through it on the side of his Spad. Accounts say he had a line put under it, in French, saying that all blood runs red.

In November he drove a German aircraft down and crash-landed his own inside French lines with ninety-six holes in it. No one on the ground saw the other plane fall, so under French rules it counted as nothing at all.

Days later, after an argument with a French officer, he was pulled out of aviation. He finished the war hauling supplies for the service battalion of the regiment he had bled for, and was not discharged until October 1919.

While he was hauling those supplies, the thinking around the American command in France was put into writing. A confidential memorandum went to French officials in August 1918 advising them that a Black man, though a citizen of the United States, was regarded by white Americans as an inferior being fit only for business or service.

It asked the French to prevent any pronounced degree of intimacy between their officers and Black officers, because white American officers would be deeply wounded by it. When it surfaced, the French government denounced it.

Bullard had already met what the memorandum described. A white American soldier assaulted him in a Paris street, and the French press and public were furious about it, because he was their war hero.

According to Lloyd's research, the War Department's response was to put Bullard under surveillance, conclude that a decorated Black French war hero damaged white American morale simply by existing, and lobby the French government to deport him back to the United States. France refused.

He stayed in France twenty more years. He drummed jazz, ran a Montmartre nightclub, married a Frenchwoman named Marcelle Straumann, and raised two daughters.

When Germany came back in 1940 he was in his forties. He put on a pack, walked across a country full of refugees until he found a French company at Orléans, and went into the line as a machine gunner.

A shell caught him. His commander, afraid of what the Germans would do with a wounded Black American, ordered him out.

He got to Biarritz and discovered he could not leave, because he had stowed away in 1912 and had never in his life owned a passport. There was no document anywhere on earth establishing that Eugene Bullard was an American.

He convinced the consular officials by naming, one after another, the Alabama towns across the Chattahoochee from Columbus. They issued the passport, and he came home to a country he had left twenty-eight years earlier.

He settled in Harlem and got his daughters out of occupied France by February 1941. He worked the Staten Island shipyards, then as a security guard, then selling perfume, then interpreting for Louis Armstrong.

He turned his small apartment at 10 East 116th Street into a private museum. On the wall was a glass case holding his French decorations.

In September 1949 he left the apartment and went up to Peekskill for a Paul Robeson concert. Coming out, he was knocked to the ground and beaten by local police officers and state troopers while newsreel cameras ran and press photographers stood around him.

There is a picture of him on the ground with his French beret lying in the dirt beside his head. A grand jury later determined that the violence at Peekskill was basically neither antisemitic nor anti-Negro in character, and nobody was ever charged for anything the film shows.

There was also a bus driver who ordered him to the back. Nobody filmed that one.

He went back to Georgia once in these years, to look at Columbus. He did not recognize the neighborhood, found Jim Crow exactly where he had left it, and never went south again.

By the middle of the 1950s Bullard was operating an elevator at Rockefeller Center. He was in his sixties, small and wiry, and the people riding with him had no idea who they were standing next to.

So he printed his own cards. On them was a line he had written himself, because no newspaper, no museum, no government office and no branch of the American military had ever put it on paper for him.

First known Negro military pilot.

That card was about as much American recognition as his achievement had ever received. A man handing out cardboard in an elevator, doing his own archiving because nobody else would do it.

France was still keeping its own account of him. On his birthday in October 1959 the French consul in New York pinned the Legion of Honor to him and made him a knight, his fifteenth decoration from that country.

His old friend Charles Boyer came, and almost nobody else did, and the American press barely registered it. He said at the ceremony that France had taught him the true meaning of liberty, equality and fraternity, and that his services could never repay what he owed her.

Back in the elevator, the producers at NBC had been noticing the medals on his uniform for a while. On the twenty-second of December 1959, Dave Garroway interviewed him on the Today Show, in the same building where he ran the car.

He wore his elevator operator's uniform for it. Hundreds of letters came in to NBC from Americans who had never heard of him.

There was no follow-up. He went back downstairs.

A few months later, when Charles de Gaulle came to New York on a state visit, Bullard stood in the honor guard that received him. De Gaulle recognized his elevator operator and embraced him in front of the assembled dignitaries.

You may have read that the FBI had to hunt for Bullard because the President of France demanded to see him. That version is a good story and it is not the one in the record.

In the coverage Lloyd was able to find, the reporter and the photographer who thought a French head of state embracing a Black elevator operator was worth recording both worked for the New York Amsterdam News, a Black newspaper in Harlem.

Nothing had changed since the January of 1918. The Black press was the press he had.

There was one other person trying to get his name into print. Louise Fox Connell was an author and a Unitarian, long active with the NAACP and with groups fighting antisemitism, and she had decided that Bullard's memoir was going to exist.

He started writing in 1959. He would work late into the night on long sheets of paper and hand them to her the next morning to edit.

Connell hunted for a ghostwriter, served as editor herself, and paid out of her own pocket for a typist. She put it in writing that she would take no payment for any of it, now or at any future time.

She sent the Amsterdam News clipping about the Legion of Honor to Eleanor Roosevelt, who wrote him up in her My Day column. Then Connell sent out a press release about his life and his place in de Gaulle's honor guard.

Only the Amsterdam News ran anything.

One of the writers she approached about helping with the book wrote back mocking her for the awful publicity release, and said he could not believe much of it, especially the color guard.

Every line of it was true. A man's actual life had been submitted to American publishing and returned as too much.

He was still writing through all of it. In the summer of 1961, shortly after he finished the first draft, Bullard was diagnosed with stomach cancer and given about two months.

On the twelfth of October, Connell came to the hospital and told him the manuscript was typed and edited. It was finished.

He pulled the oxygen tube out of his mouth and tried to smile at her.

Don't fret, honey, he said. It's easy.

He died that night, three days after his birthday.

Hundreds of people came to the funeral, most of them French veterans, and walked his coffin out to Queens in a long procession. At his own instruction he was buried in the uniform of a French Foreign Legionnaire, in the Carré des Anciens Combattants at Flushing Cemetery, on ground held in perpetuity by the Federation of French War Veterans, under the French flag.

He had lived in the United States for twenty-one years and he arranged to be buried as a French soldier.

The manuscript outlived him by fifty years without ever being printed. Connell spent the next decade trying to place it, and no publisher took it.

It sits today in her papers at the Schlesinger Library at Harvard. In 1972 two other men published their own version of his life under a different title, with their names on the cover.

Twenty-two years after that, in 1994, the Secretary of the Air Force signed a commission for him. His daughter Jacqueline was there, and his grandson Richard Reid, who had retired from the Air Force as a master sergeant.

The rank was second lieutenant. It is the lowest commissioned rank the United States military has, and it is the one they had refused him seventy-seven years earlier.

There is no mystery left in that refusal and there has not been for a long time. The Smithsonian states plainly that Bullard was rejected because of the racial prejudice in the American military of the time.

The board that went round the French airfields deciding which Americans the United States would take was three American officers and Edmund L. Gros. That is the Air Force's own account of who was in the room.

So the paper finally came, and it came to a grave, and it granted the least a country can grant.

Jacqueline gave his French medals to the Air Force museum in Dayton. They are in a case now with a copy of that commission, fifteen decorations from one country and one sheet of paper from the other.

Two things you can do with this, and together they take about a minute.

When somebody shares his photograph captioned as a Lafayette Escadrille pilot, correct it, because he was never in that squadron, and the American doctor who ran the pipeline into it is the man his biographer named. Say Edmund L. Gros out loud once, because a story that keeps the victim and loses every man who made him one is doing half the job.

And when you tell it, put Louise Fox Connell in. She spent a decade trying to get his own account of his life into print, and she put it in writing that she would never take a dollar for the work.

In the end he had the card he paid to print himself, one line in The Crisis, one Black newspaper in Harlem, and a manuscript nobody would buy.

The last thing anyone told Eugene Bullard was that his book was finished. He took the tube out of his mouth to answer her.

Don't fret, honey. It's easy.

text:
U.S. 🇺🇸 F1(Student) Visa Approved Accra Ghana 🇬🇭 
Date: 13 July 2026
Course: Masters in Environmental Engineering

Deficit: $870.
Interviewer: Black Rasta.

(Alot of back and forth about flooding in Ghana. One of the best interviews. Visa Approved !!)

VO: Why did you choose this university?

Me: I chose this University  because it offers an excellent research environment in environmental science that aligns with my career goals. The program has a strong curriculum in hydrology, climate change, GIS, and environmental modeling, which will help me specialize in climate change induced flooding. I am also attracted to its advanced research facilities, including the Hydrology and Hydrogeomorphology Laboratory, where I will gain practical experience in urban flood modeling and watershed analysis.

VO: How many schools did you apply to?

Me: Four
The University of Stuttgart, Central Michigan University, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville (SIUE), and the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. I was admitted to all four. I received partial funding from the University of ....., an $..... award from ...., no funding from ....., and full funding from the .......

VO: What is your undergraduate degree, and when did you complete it?

Me: I have a bachelor's degree in Environmental Engineering, which I completed in 2024.

VO: How did you get your funding?

Me: I submitted a competitive application early. I had two interviews with faculty members and discussed my proposed research on urban flood mitigation in Ghana. I was then awarded a Graduate Teaching Assistantship.

VO: What will you be working on?

Me: I will be developing a geospatial digital twin to create virtual models of cities by integrating climate data, GIS, and remote sensing. The model will simulate different rainfall scenarios to identify flood-prone areas and evaluate the most effective flood mitigation measures for vulnerable communities.

VO: What do you do?

Me: I currently work as a Project Assistant. I support companies and development organizations in implementing climate change mitigation and adaptation projects in vulnerable communities in Ghana. My work involves research, fact-finding missions, market studies, trade fairs, and conferences in Ghana and Europe.

VO: When did you have your funding interview?

Me: May 2026.

VO: But I'm in Ghana. The flood occurred in June. Which flood did you discuss with your supervisor?

Me: Flooding has been a recurring challenge in Ghana for many years. The recent flooding is one example, but we also discussed previous major flood events.

VO: How could you discuss flooding in May if it occurred in June?

Me: I had my interview in May. However, flooding has been a recurring problem in Ghana for many years. One of the most devastating and well-known events occurred in June 2015 at Kwame Nkrumah Circle.

VO: June?

Me: Yes. The June 2015 floods are one of the most significant flood disasters in Ghana. More than 150 people lost their lives, and extensive damage was caused to homes, businesses, and infrastructure around Kwame Nkrumah Circle.

VO: Oh, okay.

VO: What will you come back and do after your degree?

Me: I plan to return to my company and take on a more senior role in environmental project management.

VO: You will return to Ghana after three years in the United States? Why?

Me: Yes. I will return and continue my work with my company. We are currently implementing climate adaptation and mitigation projects in vulnerable coastal communities in the Volta Region and Greater Accra. One of the challenges we face is the limited use of localized flood modeling. After my master's degree, I will introduce advanced flood modeling techniques to strengthen these ongoing projects.

VO: How much do you earn now?

Me: GHS 1,700.

VO: And you will return after three years?

Me: Yes.

VO: How much do you expect to earn when you return?

Me: Around GHS 7,000 per month.

VO: And you will still come back?

text:
LUTNICK’S MESSAGE TO CHIPMAKERS: BUILD IN AMERICA OR PAY THE TARIFF

TIL: U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick says the Trump administration is considering a much tougher semiconductor tariff regime. His message was pretty clear: manufacture in the U.S. and avoid the tariff. Otherwise, be prepared to pay for access to the American market.

When asked whether this would be a high-intensity tariff tied directly to U.S. semiconductor investment, Lutnick said that was “exactly right.”

The model could look a lot like what Washington already did with pharmaceuticals.

Start with a high tariff, then offer companies ways out if they invest and manufacture in America. For semiconductors, the emerging structure reportedly goes one step further by linking tariff-free import quotas to how much production capacity a company commits to build in the U.S.

The January U.S.-Taiwan semiconductor agreement gives a pretty good idea of how that could work.

A company building U.S. capacity can import up to 2.5x its planned American production capacity tariff-free. Once the fab is completed, the allowance falls to 1.5x the new U.S. capacity.

So the more you build in America, the more chips you can continue importing without tariffs.

That immediately matters for Korea.

Samsung is investing around $37B in its Taylor, Texas foundry project, while SK Hynix is putting about $3.87B into an HBM packaging facility in Indiana. TSMC, meanwhile, has committed roughly $265B to Arizona and Taiwan is expected to announce another $20B–$30B of U.S. investment.

If tariff-free quotas are eventually allocated partly according to U.S. investment, that gap could become important.

There is one big difference though: memory is still a seller’s market.

Samsung and SK Hynix together had roughly 65% of global DRAM share in Q2 2026, and memory supply remains tight. If tariffs hit HBM, DRAM or NAND, U.S. hyperscalers may end up absorbing a meaningful part of the cost rather than Korean suppliers taking the entire hit.

But Washington appears to be thinking beyond individual chips too.

Lutnick said the government is considering a much broader definition of semiconductor-related imports, potentially including finished products such as laptops, game consoles and data center servers.

So this may not end up being a simple “tariff on Korean chips” story. It looks more like Washington is using tariffs to get more fabs, packaging and chip production built in the U.S.

text:
You have just proved how stupid you are, Benny, not that proof was needed, you utter cretin!

The rot in Britain’s housing system didn’t start yesterday — it began with Margaret Thatcher’s so-called “Right to Buy” revolution, circa 1981 / 1982, long before you were born!

History doesn’t just magically start when you pop out of your mum’s flange!

What was sold as a liberty — the ordinary worker’s chance to “own their own home” — was, in reality, one of the most damaging economic con tricks in modern British history.

Here’s what happened:

Under Thatcher’s Right to Buy policy, millions of council tenants were offered the chance to purchase their homes from local authorities at massive discounts — sometimes as much as 50% to 70% below market value.  

It was a short-term political masterstroke: it turned renters into property owners and voters into Conservative loyalists. But the price for that “victory” was the destruction of the UK’s social housing base.

The key betrayal wasn’t just the sale itself. It was what came next.

Thatcher’s government made it illegal for councils to use the receipts from those sales to build new council homes. They were mandated to hand the money back to the Treasury instead of reinvesting it locally. In one stroke, Britain’s supply of affordable homes was gutted — and councils were left powerless to replace what had been sold off.

So as swathes of public housing were sold at bargain-basement prices, the public stock vanished. And guess what? The buyers often flipped them for profit — or sold them on to private landlords. Many of those same council flats are now being rented out in the private market for three or four times the original social rent, paid for by taxpayers through housing benefit.

This is Thatcherism distilled: transfer public assets into private hands, turn a profit, and create a permanent dependency on an overpriced market.

Fast forward forty years, and the consequences are everywhere. The shortage of social housing forces families into the private rental sector, driving rents higher. The artificial scarcity pushes up house prices, inflating the mortgage market and locking millions out of ownership altogether. Meanwhile, the taxpayer foots the bill, subsidising landlords instead of funding public homes.

“Right to Buy” wasn’t about freedom — it was about ideology. It wasn’t about empowerment — it was about dismantling the idea that housing should be a public good.

Every broken housing market graph, every rent hike, every “generation rent” headline in the last two decades can be traced, at least in part, back to that Thatcherite decision to flog public homes and ban councils from replacing them.
It’s no exaggeration to say: “Right to Buy” broke Britain’s housing system.  

And until that structural wound is healed — until councils can again build and own social housing at scale — the crisis will only deepen.
The British public didn’t gain the “freedom to buy.”  
They lost the right to a home that’s affordable, stable, and secure.

text:
The mosquitoes were so bad Lewis and Clark’s men covered themselves in bear grease.

Working up the Missouri in June 1804, the insects were already becoming a constant misery.

They slept under mosquito nets. Smoke offered some relief. And they rubbed grease over exposed skin to keep the insects off.

On June 18, after hunters brought in a bear, Clark recorded simply:

“the party Drying meat & greesing themselves”

Then added:

“The misquiter verry bad.”

Before the grizzlies, the mountains, and the Pacific, they were fighting mosquitoes.

text:
Israeli cybersecurity startup Upwind has completed a massive $300 million funding round, catapulting its company valuation to $3.8 billion. The round was led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with active participation from the firm's existing syndicate of investors.

This latest capital injection reflects an extraordinary growth trajectory for the young firm, which was founded just four years ago in 2022. The new valuation marks a rapid multiplication of the company's worth in mere months.

Following this new round, Upwind solidifies its position as one of the fastest-growing cybersecurity unicorns in the Israeli tech ecosystem, successfully raising immense capital in a highly compressed timeframe.

Upwind develops a specialized platform that provides organizations with comprehensive perimeter defense and deep visibility into cloud infrastructure vulnerabilities. The company is led by founder and CEO Amiram Shachar, a proven entrepreneur in the Israeli tech sector who previously founded and sold cloud optimization firm https://t.co/MSBa7LrW7B to storage giant NetApp for $450 million in 2020.

The massive surge in Upwind's market valuation is heavily tied to the firm's strategic technological expansion. In May 2026, the company upgraded its platform to actively neutralize specific risks and vulnerabilities derived from the enterprise use of artificial intelligence.

The market demand for Upwind's solutions has spiked against a backdrop of growing industry fears surrounding AI-based cyber threats. With advanced generative models from tech giants like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta proving susceptible to malicious exploitation and weaponization by bad actors, enterprise and government clients are rapidly reinforcing their defensive infrastructures. Consequently, global investors continue to pour heavy capital into agile startups like Upwind that offer advanced, real-time technological countermeasures to these emerging threats.

"Everyone needs it and will want it" is always the wrong answer.

text:
All good and well theory, but AGAIN, you and everyone else fails to address:

                              THE INFLECTION POINT

We must "envision" how we deal with this:

AI, robotics, and humanoids will not put your business into bankruptcy directly, it will instead, in a macro economic collective of impact, eliminate YOUR CUSTOMERS.

AI, robotics, and humanoids will eventually have no one left to sell to. In fact, economically, a point will be reached where it is NOT scalable/profitable to produce AI, robotics, and humanoids- the customer base as a need infact exists, but no one can buy- their income has been eliminated.

You are avoiding that inflection point. That point, even as it will happen on a continuum of impact, will not magically create a world where everyone STILL needs an income, doesn't have one, and AI production, robotics production, and humanoids production and materials STILL require an income to create, but will not have that either.

That precise point of switch-over from monetary economics to non-monetary economics is not some unicorn miracle that will descend out of the sky.

Are YOU going to have the assets to "retire" into a non- monetary economic transition? Will you need them, and if not, why not?

People will not willingly put up with the transition phase as billions are put out of work, and no one can pay for production of their AI, their robotics, or their humanoids they were promised would do the jobs they just lost and then serve them forever after without compensation.

When THAT impossible, (as best can be forseen right now), hurdle at the INFLECTION POINT, either en masse or in spurts as tech is created, our "replacements" will  have to be offered to everyone for free.

Is YOUR company going to be the first in your slice of the industry to do that? To step over THAT inflection point and declare that YOU no longer need money to produce your product for the world so long as every other industry that has managed to survive the loss of their customer base does too?

Who is going to coordinate that hurdle and how?

...And not just on a local basis for your factory or office location, but your world- wide scalable market that got your business there in the first place.

Everyone seems to think this incredible disruption will happen magically. It will not.

In fact, odds are that societies will resist, stop, commandeer production in order to get through the inflection point.

There is no doubt there will be bad actors involved in this landscape.

It will be incredibly messy and unbelievably dangerous for humanity.

Until everyone addresses that transition point, that INFLECTION POINT, describing what comes afterwards is in a word:

Bullshit.

Get to work on THAT.

With sincere respect,

- R.   Maedje

💰 THE ALLEGED $500,000 PAYMENT

According to the Fourth Circuit’s account of the evidence, Nigeria’s government-controlled telecommunications company, NITEL, was important to the success of the proposed venture because access to its telephone lines was needed.

The court stated that Jefferson met with Vice President Atiku Abubakar in July 2005 and allegedly offered him a percentage of profits from the venture. The court further described Jefferson as seeking an additional $500,000 cash payment upfront to secure cooperation. 

Let us pause here.

This is where responsible public discussion becomes important.

The court was describing the evidence and conduct surrounding William Jefferson’s criminal case.

That does not automatically mean Atiku Abubakar was criminally convicted of accepting any money.

💵 THEN CAME THE $100,000

According to the Fourth Circuit judgment, Lori Mody obtained $100,000 in marked cash from the FBI.

The money was placed inside a briefcase.

On July 30, 2005, the court said Mody delivered the briefcase containing the $100,000 to William Jefferson outside a hotel in Arlington, Virginia.

According to the court’s account, Jefferson was supposed to deliver the money to Atiku Abubakar.

The conversations concerning the proposed payment were monitored and recorded by the FBI. 

This is one of the most extraordinary parts of the entire Jefferson investigation.

(I'll be honest I didn't do one myself cuz my college's film program stopped having it as a requirement after I returned from military service and I was too monkey/burnt out at the time to do it, but I researched it like a year after graduating lol.)

Find a film internship by searching specialized job boards, checking local film commissions, and networking directly with indie filmmakers.

General job boards -- sites like LinkedIn, Indeed, and Glassdoor using keywords like "production intern" or "development intern." Or just be a paid PA (productive assistant) if you can get it.

University platforms -- use student career hubs like Handshake to find vetted local and remote media roles.

Regional Film Offices (which are government or non-profit organizations that act as a concierge service for movie, TV, and commercial productions) -- check state or city agencies, such as the Massachusetts Film Office, which frequently offer academic-credit or semester-long placements.

Studio and non-profit sites -- look at major indie distributors or non-profits like Women Make Movies for specialized tracks in marketing, distribution, or acquisitions.

Alt strats:
● Cold outreach to indie projects -- find crowdfunding campaigns on Indiegogo or Kickstarter, then message creators directly to offer production assistance or editing support.
● Target post-house companies -- look for smaller editing and post-production facilities rather than major studios, as they are often more accessible for early-career talent. You can use places like Upwork to sell your own editing service (AND NEVER EDIT FOR FREE unless it's a student film with a $0 budget that you really really really believe in).
● Build a local network -- attend local film festivals, Q&A screenings, and industry mixers to introduce yourself to working professionals.

text:
Dental insurance is not useless, but it is increasingly misaligned with the cost of modern dentistry. ADA data show that 53% of working age adults with private dental insurance had a dental visit, compared with only 16% of uninsured adults. Coverage clearly improves utilization. But access is not the same as affordability. CDC data show that among adults with an unmet dental need, 80% said they could not afford the care.

That contradiction plays out every day in dental offices. A patient may faithfully use preventive benefits, then postpone a crown, implant, periodontal therapy, or root canal because the out of pocket portion becomes too high. Traditional 100, 80, 50 plan design often means coverage becomes less generous as treatment becomes more expensive.

Annual maximums remain part of the problem, although the market is changing. ADA data show 32.8% of in network maximums between $1,000 and $1,500, 48.2% between $1,500 and $2,500, and 17.2% from $2,500 to no maximum. The ADA recommends substantially richer benefits, including preventive care outside the annual maximum and an annual maximum of at least $3,500, adjusted for inflation.

Dentists are also feeling the squeeze. Since January 2021, dental equipment and supply costs rose about 23%, dental employee wages rose about 23%, and overall inflation rose about 27%. Average reimbursement across payers rose only about 19%.

By Q2 2026, 23.5% of dentists surveyed by the ADA had already dropped some insurance networks. Yet PPOs still represent about 89% of commercial dental enrollment. This is not the death of PPO dentistry. It is pressure for better benefit design.

Alternatives such as HRAs deserve discussion, but they are often oversimplified. QSEHRAs are generally limited to employers with fewer than 50 employees. Individual Coverage HRAs can be used by larger employers but are tied to individual medical insurance. Excepted Benefit HRAs can help with dental expenses, but the 2026 limit is $2,200 per employee.

Massachusetts offers an interesting experiment. Its dental loss ratio law requires insurers to spend at least 83% of adjusted premium revenue on patient care and qualifying quality improvement. In 2026, six dental insurers were ordered to return $8.4 million to consumers and businesses after failing to meet the standard. The practical lesson is not that dental insurance should disappear.

Dentists should understand which plans bring valuable patient flow and which destroy margin. Employers should compare premiums, claims paid, administrative costs, out of pocket spending, network access, and how often employees delay treatment because of cost.

And when a patient hears that a crown is “covered at 50%,” the most important question remains: 50% of what?

Dental insurance gets patients through the front door. The bigger question is whether the benefit helps them complete the treatment they actually need.

🏠⚖️ Fort Worth Couple Sentenced in $4.2 Million Custom Home Fraud Scheme ⚖️🏠

Fort Worth, TX — A Fort Worth husband and wife have been sentenced for their roles in a yearslong fraud conspiracy that prosecutors say left dozens of victims with unfinished custom home projects and approximately $4.2 million in losses.

According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas, Christopher Judge, 35, and Raquelle Judge, 36, pleaded guilty in December 2025 to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

Senior U.S. District Judge Terry R. Means sentenced Christopher Judge to 78 months in federal prison, followed by two years of supervised release. Raquelle Judge was sentenced to one month in prison.

Both were ordered to pay $2,794,680.73 in restitution.

Federal prosecutors said the couple were managing members of Judge DFW LLC, a Texas-based company they used to market custom architecture, construction and interior design services.

From approximately August 2020 through January 2023, prosecutors said the couple offered below-market bids to consumers across six North Texas counties and entered into design-and-build contracts for custom homes.

Court documents show victims made multiple installment payments, but prosecutors said most projects were not completed and some were abandoned entirely.

The couple also admitted falsely representing that Christopher Judge was a licensed architect.

Authorities said more than 40 victims were defrauded across at least 24 construction projects. Prosecutors said customer payments were commingled in the company’s operating account and were sometimes used for unrelated construction projects.

The FBI’s Fort Worth Resident Agency and the Euless Police Department investigated the case with assistance from the U.S. Secret Service.

#FortWorthTX #NorthTexas #FederalCourt #WireFraud #ConsumerFraud #TexanReport

text:
China’s Middle East Reset: Access Without Guarantees -  BLUF: Xi Jinping’s Egyptian mission and King Abdullah II’s return to Beijing indicate strategic recalibration, not yet a Chinese security pivot.
China is testing whether Egypt and Jordan can supply the political access, regional interpretation and crisis mediation that Beijing’s bilateral diplomacy lacks.
Energy exposure is acute: 20.9 million barrels per day crossed Hormuz in the first half of 2025; China was also the largest destination for LNG transiting the strait.
Red Sea insecurity halved oil flows through Suez–SUMED and Bab el-Mandeb from their 2023 levels.
Beijing’s probable objective is to protect corridors and diplomatic influence while avoiding enforceable defence guarantees.
The leading alternative explanation remains opportunistic exploitation of declining confidence in Washington; the two hypotheses are complementary, not mutually exclusive.
Over 2026–2031, Chinese engagement will probably become more selective, operational and infrastructure-centred—but remain below alliance level.
For Israel, the principal risk is asymmetric influence: Chinese access to Cairo, Amman, Tehran and Gulf capitals without corresponding responsibility for deterrence.
The decisive indicator will be whether Beijing accepts measurable security costs when Chinese commercial and energy interests are directly endangered.

China’s Middle East Reset: Influence Without Guarantees
China’s renewed courtship of Egypt and Jordan is easily presented as an attempt to exploit diminished confidence in Washington. That interpretation is incomplete. Beijing is confronting a more immediate vulnerability: its commercial exposure to the Middle East has grown faster than its capacity to anticipate—or contain—the region’s security shocks. The September 2026 state visit of President Xi Jinping to Cairo and the August reception of King Abdullah II in Beijing therefore signal more than diplomatic activism. They reveal a search for political access, operational intelligence and crisis mediation across the geographic hinge connecting Gaza, the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, the Gulf and Iran. China wants greater influence over the forces threatening its energy and trade corridors, but without inheriting the military liabilities historically carried by the United States.

The Diagnostic Deficit
On 24 August 2026, Xi received Abdullah II during the Jordanian monarch’s ninth visit to China since his accession. The two governments signed cooperation documents covering foreign affairs, trade, industrial and supply chains, and judicial coordination, while committing to deepen the strategic partnership established in 2015. Nine days later, Xi met President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi in Cairo during a state visit announced for 30 August–3 September. Their agenda extended from infrastructure, electricity and agriculture to artificial intelligence, green energy, electric vehicles, aerospace, transport and security cooperation. More than twenty agreements were concluded during the visit, according to the official Chinese account. President Xi Jinping Holds Talks with King Abdullah II of Jordan – Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the People’s Republic of China – August 2026; Xi Jinping Holds Talks with Egyptian President El-Sisi – Government of the People’s Republic of China – September 2026.

The sequencing matters. Jordan supplies political access and early warning; Egypt supplies geographic leverage and institutional scale. Together, they can improve Beijing’s understanding of a regional system in which formal relations no longer predict operational behaviour. China maintains working ties with Israel, Iran, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Egypt and Jordan, yet the multiplication of proxy actors, maritime attacks, cyber operations and cross-border escalations has reduced the value of conventional state-to-state diplomacy. Beijing’s problem is not a shortage of interlocutors. It is the growing difficulty of determining which interlocutor can actually influence events.

Cairo’s Strategic Geometry
Egypt occupies the intersection of nearly every crisis affecting China’s western trade and energy perimeter. It controls the Suez Canal; borders Gaza; maintains a peace treaty and security channels with Israel; communicates with Hamas and the Palestinian Authority; participates in Arab and African diplomacy; and sustains working relationships with the Gulf monarchies, Iran, Europe, Russia and the United States. Few capitals can combine physical control over a global maritime artery with access to actors operating on opposing sides of the region’s principal conflicts.

This gives Cairo value beyond bilateral commerce. For Beijing, Egypt can function as a diplomatic sensor, a logistical platform and a political legitimiser. Chinese investment in industrial zones, ports, electricity, telecommunications and transport creates economic presence; consultation with the Egyptian presidency, intelligence institutions and armed forces can convert that presence into better crisis awareness. El-Sisi’s call in September for expanded military-security exchanges is consequently more significant than another commercial memorandum. It opens a pathway—still limited and politically sensitive—through which China could connect infrastructure interests to maritime-domain awareness, counterterrorism, evacuation planning and protection of overseas personnel.

Yet Egypt is not entering a Chinese sphere. In 2025 the European Union remained Egypt’s largest trading partner, accounting for 24.6% of its total goods trade. Bilateral EU-Egypt merchandise trade reached €32.3 billion, while the stock of EU outward direct investment in Egypt stood at €35.4 billion in 2024. EU Trade Relations with Egypt – European Commission – 2026. Cairo is constructing a plural architecture in which Chinese capital, European markets, Gulf finance and American security assistance coexist. Its objective is bargaining power, not alignment.

Amman’s Early Warning
Jordan’s strategic weight is less visible but equally consequential. The kingdom borders Israel, the West Bank, Syria, Iraq and Saudi Arabia; hosts substantial refugee populations; safeguards Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem through the Hashemite custodianship; and maintains channels with Western governments, Arab monarchies, Palestinian institutions and Israeli security officials. Its value lies not in market size but in political granularity.

The February 2023 Aqaba meeting illustrated this convening function: Jordan brought together senior Jordanian, Egyptian, Israeli, Palestinian and American officials to pursue de-escalation and reaffirm commitments intended to prevent further violence. Aqaba Joint Communiqué – United States Department of State – February 2023. For Beijing, Amman can provide context that is difficult to obtain through relations with larger capitals: Palestinian political dynamics, Jerusalem’s religious sensitivities, tribal networks extending into Syria and Iraq, refugee pressures and the credibility of competing regional narratives.

China does not need Jordan to become a military partner. It needs Jordan to reduce uncertainty. A closer relationship can help Beijing test assumptions, communicate discreetly across political divides and distinguish rhetorical positioning from actionable intent. In a region where tactical decisions by non-state groups can disrupt global shipping or trigger interstate escalation, that interpretive advantage has measurable economic value.

The Chokepoint Exposure
China’s vulnerability is clearest at sea. During the first half of 2025, the Strait of Hormuz carried an estimated 20.9 million barrels of oil per day, equivalent to roughly one-fifth of global petroleum-liquids consumption and one-quarter of maritime oil trade. Approximately 89% of the crude oil and condensate passing through Hormuz went to Asian markets; China, India, Japan and South Korea together received 74%. The strait also carried 11.4 billion cubic feet of liquefied natural gas per day, more than one-fifth of global LNG trade, with China identified as the largest destination. World Oil Transit Chokepoints – U.S. Energy Information Administration – March 2026.

Alternative pipelines do not eliminate this exposure. Saudi Arabia’s East-West system and the United Arab Emirates’ Abu Dhabi pipeline together offered approximately 4.7 million barrels per day of available bypass capacity; Iran’s Goreh-Jask route provided only about 300,000 barrels per day of effective capacity. A serious Hormuz disruption would therefore confront Beijing with a physical constraint, not merely a price shock.

The Red Sea presents the second vulnerability. Combined oil flows through the Suez Canal and Egypt’s SUMED pipeline fell from 8.8 million barrels per day in 2023 to 4.8 million in 2024, recovering only marginally to 4.9 million in the first half of 2025. Bab el-Mandeb traffic dropped from 9.3 million barrels per day in 2023 to 4.1 million in 2024. LNG movements through Bab el-Mandeb approached zero, while oil routed around the Cape of Good Hope rose from 6.2 million barrels per day in 2023 to 9.3 million in 2024. Longer voyages raise freight, insurance, fuel and working-capital costs while reducing the effective availability of ships. Egypt is therefore not simply another Belt and Road partner: it is the sovereign custodian of the shortest maritime connection between Asian production and European demand.

Security Without Liability
China’s regional model has rested on a structural asymmetry. Beijing acquires energy, constructs infrastructure, supplies technology and cultivates political elites, while the United States, European states and regional armed forces carry much of the cost of deterring attacks and keeping sea lanes open. The Red Sea crisis exposed the limits of that arrangement. Commercial neutrality cannot guarantee freedom of navigation when armed organisations decide which vessels qualify as legitimate targets.

The European response demonstrates the burden China has avoided. In February 2025, the Council of the EU extended the defensive maritime operation EUNAVFOR ASPIDES until 28 February 2026, allocating more than €17 million for the extension. Its operating area included the Red Sea, Bab el-Mandeb, the Gulf of Aden, the Arabian Sea, the Gulf of Oman, the Persian Gulf and Hormuz. The mandate also permitted collection of information concerning arms trafficking and shadow fleets. Red Sea: Council Prolongs the Mandate of Operation ASPIDES – Council of the European Union – February 2025.

Beijing now faces an uncomfortable choice. Remaining a beneficiary of Western-provided security preserves strategic flexibility but weakens claims to leadership. Expanding military protection could safeguard Chinese interests but compromise relations with Iran and associated actors, expose Chinese forces to retaliation and pull the People’s Liberation Army into conflicts it cannot politically control. Cairo and Amman offer an intermediate option: greater intelligence access, mediation capacity and contingency coordination without a formal security guarantee.

A Five-Year Contest
Between 2027 and 2031, five competing trajectories merit attention. The first is calibrated expansion: China develops stronger diplomatic and maritime-awareness mechanisms through Egypt and Jordan while avoiding combat responsibilities. This is the most probable course because it improves warning and access at relatively low cost. The second is corridor protection: renewed attacks drive Beijing toward naval escorts, expanded logistics agreements and more systematic coordination with regional armed forces. The third is transactional mediation: China uses its relations with Iran, Arab governments and Palestinian actors to obtain limited de-escalation agreements protecting infrastructure and shipping, without resolving underlying conflicts.

The fourth trajectory is strategic overreach. Technology contracts, port access, military exchanges and political mediation could generate resistance from Washington, European governments or regional states concerned about surveillance, dual-use infrastructure and dependency. The fifth is reputational failure: China accumulates diplomatic visibility but proves unable or unwilling to influence Iran-linked groups, Gaza governance or maritime escalation. Under that scenario, each summit increases expectations without increasing control.

Xi’s four-part security proposal in Cairo—regional ownership of security, integrated treatment of interconnected conflicts, development as a foundation for stability, protection of international waterways and coordination under the United Nations framework—indicates the preferred Chinese formula. It elevates Beijing diplomatically while resisting alliance commitments. Its credibility, however, will be measured not by communiqués but by whether Chinese influence can alter the behaviour of actors threatening navigation and regional infrastructure.

Israel’s Strategic Test
For Israel, deeper Chinese engagement presents neither an automatic threat nor an obvious opportunity. Egyptian capacity to stabilise Gaza, protect Suez traffic and prevent wider confrontation serves Israeli interests. Jordanian stability, border security and preservation of the peace treaty are equally indispensable. If Chinese engagement strengthens Cairo’s economic resilience, supports monitored reconstruction and gives Beijing leverage to discourage attacks by Iran-aligned organisations, it may contribute to regional containment.

The danger lies in influence detached from enforcement. China could acquire greater access to Egyptian infrastructure, telecommunications, supply chains and political decision-making while leaving coercive security tasks to others. It could also convert its mediation role into diplomatic leverage over Gaza’s reconstruction, Red Sea governance and international debates concerning Israel, without confronting the armed networks generating instability. For Jerusalem, the relevant metric is therefore not the number of Chinese visits or agreements. It is the conversion rate between access and responsibility.

Israel should track Chinese involvement at Egyptian ports and industrial zones; dual-use communications and artificial-intelligence projects; the institutional depth of Chinese-Egyptian military exchanges; Beijing’s contacts with Palestinian factions; and any change in China’s willingness to pressure Tehran when maritime or missile activity threatens regional corridors. Intelligence coordination with Egypt and Jordan must remain strong enough to identify where commercial infrastructure creates strategic access.

The New Modus Operandi
Beijing is not abandoning its policy of maintaining relations with every side. It is trying to make that policy operationally sustainable. Egypt can connect diplomacy to geography; Jordan can connect formal policy to the region’s political undercurrents. Together, they offer China a denser map of risks surrounding Gaza, Israel, Iran and the three maritime chokepoints on which Asian-European commerce depends.

The central question is whether this architecture will produce security or merely redistribute influence. If China uses its access to constrain destabilising partners, finance resilient infrastructure and accept measurable responsibility for navigation and reconstruction, Cairo and Amman could anchor a constructive Chinese role. If it continues to externalise protection while monetising access, its regional expansion will deepen an existing asymmetry: Chinese interests secured by other powers’ ships, budgets and political exposure. That distinction—not the symbolism of Xi’s itinerary—will define the strategic balance of the next five years.

text:
✈️🎓 IAF & IIT Bombay Join Hands to Shape the Future of Flight Testing
In a significant step towards advancing aerospace education and flight test expertise, the Indian Air Force and IIT Bombay have signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) establishing a collaborative framework between the Air Force Test Pilot School (AFTPS), ASTE and IIT Bombay.
The partnership will combine the IAF’s operational flight-testing experience with IIT Bombay’s academic and research excellence to offer a Master’s Degree Programme for Flight Test Crew, including Test Pilots and Flight Test Engineers.
This initiative is expected to strengthen indigenous aerospace research, flight testing capabilities and the development of highly skilled aviation professionals for the future.

text:
There is a fundamental, terrifying dignity in recognizing that the world we touch and see isn't the ultimate truth, but merely a shadow cast by something much larger. In *Order and History — Plato and Aristotle*, Eric Voegelin captures this tension perfectly when he unpacks the Platonic idea of the *eikon*. 

He argues that because our cosmos is caught in a state of constant flux—being "being-in-becoming"—it can never offer us the absolute, unshakable certainty that belongs to the eternal ground. We aren't dealing with the bedrock of existence; we are dealing with a cosmic symbol that is "transparent toward its eternal ground." This means our grasp on reality is inherently limited by our nature. Because the cosmos is a "likeness," our best descriptions of it can only ever be "likely." 

This is a blow to the modern ego, which demands that everything be measurable, definitive, and stripped of mystery. We want a world of hard facts, but Voegelin reminds us that for a finite mind, the gap between our perception and the absolute is permanent. As he notes, "the aletheia is God’s and the pistis is man’s." We are relegated to the realm of trust and probability, forever looking through a glass, darkly, at a truth that is "kindred to the finite mind" but ultimately remains beyond our reach. We have to be comfortable with the idea that our "truth" is actually just a highly educated form of faith in the patterns of a world that is always moving.

text:
THIS IS WHY WE DO WHAT WE DO 

I’ve been dealing with a case over the last couple of days that has genuinely hit me hard.

A young man is currently living in a tent with his two dogs. These dogs are not simply pets to him , they are his family, his whole world, and, in his own words, the reason he keeps going.

He served in the Army and, since leaving, has suffered with extreme PTSD. 
Despite everything he is facing, he has refused to give up on his dogs. He contacted charity after charity, desperately trying to find help so that he could keep his family together.
Then he contacted us.
I didn’t hesitate.
Tomorrow, his two beautiful dogs will come into our safe foster care, where they will be warm, fed, loved and protected while we work alongside him to help get his life back on track.
But this story goes far beyond the dogs.
He hasn’t eaten properly for several days. A local church offered him tea and cake, and all he had with him was a bottle of lemonade. Hearing that absolutely broke me.
I have personally sent him money to help with his travel tomorrow, but also so that he can get some proper, nourishing food into himself. We are also giving him advice and support around finding housing.
He is a grafter. He is a worker. He is a builder by trade. He isn’t claiming benefits. He feels embarrassed asking for help, but he is also incredibly relieved knowing that his two dogs are going to be safe.
This should not be happening.
No one who has served their country should find themselves living in a tent, going hungry and feeling that they have nowhere to turn.
And no one should have to choose between getting help for themselves and keeping the animals that give them a reason to carry on.
We are going to do everything we possibly can to support this man and his dogs.
Tomorrow, his dogs will be safe. 
And hopefully, this is the beginning of a new chapter for all three of them.
Please keep them in your thoughts. And please remember that sometimes saving a dog also means helping the human who loves them.

text:
🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 On 3rd September 1787, six striking weavers in Calton, Glasgow were shot dead by the British state. Some call this the beginnings of the organised labour movement in Britain.

In the 1780s, over 20,000 hand-loom weavers worked in the west of Scotland, producing the cloth which formed a major part of Glasgow’s commercial success. As a result of this work, the city expanded and Glasgow’s new merchant capitalist class became wealthy.

Solidarity grew among the workers, both due to their close proximity and their shared exploitation. In Glasgow, these forces developed in Calton, Anderston, Pollokshaws, Govan, and Fenwick, with the latter forming the first co-operative society in Britain in 1761.

This early capitalism reached a crisis in 1787 when the import of cheap muslin from India caused prices to plummet, leaving weavers working longer for less pay. After wages were cut by a quarter, a mass rally was held in June 1787 at Glasgow Green.

The employers declared the strike illegal, and 20 guineas were offered to any worker that informed on his brother. When the strikers stopped scabs from accepting raw materials at low prices, the army was called on the 3rd of September, attacking the strikers and surrounding the district.

Six workers died of gunshots and many more were wounded, and around 6,000 strikers attended their burial. The mass arrests which followed included whole families, while army officers received commendations for leading the massacre.

One strike leader, James Granger, was sentenced to be whipped through the streets of Edinburgh then banished from Scotland for 7 years, only to return as a leader of the great Luddite strike in 1811.

So great was the fear of the ruling class from this new, organised threat which they themselves had brought together that an infantry barracks was constructed and opened in 1795, strategically sited in the Gallowgate besides Calton. 

Today, the barracks is gone, along with Britain's weaving industry, but the fear of revolt still remains.

text:
Dear Daniel, I strongly recommend that you read a good translation of the Indian epic, the Gita. In it you will find many answers to the questions and  dilamas that are disturbing your mind today.

The Gita is not strictly a religious book like the Torah or the Quran. 

It is simply a dialogue between the warrior Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna. Arjuna and a small army of his his five brothers, the Pandavas, had declined to raise their arms against the huge army of their own hundred cousin-brothers, kith and kin, who had unjustly , through treachery usurped their kingdom by  refusing  to return their promised land and also refused to give them even five small villages or even an inch of land  to live quietly beside them in peace.

This story bears a strong resemblance to the epic struggle of the 14 million Jews of the world, locked in their own struggle with their ethnic kin and with 2 billion Muslims who refuse to agree to give even a pinhead-sized piece of land for the Jews to live on peacefully.

In this dialogue, the reluctant and confused Arjuna poses every doubt and question to his spiritual guide Krishna who is acting in this epic story as his Charioteer. 

Krishna answers all the doubts of warrior Krishna , in midst of the battle ground , pausing the commencement if this epic fight , explaining duty, dharma, karma, righteousness, good and evil, virtue and vice, God, existence, the origin and end of everything, time, consciousness, being and ceasing to be, action and its outcome, desire and fulfilment, when and what to do and wen what not to do and how to free one own self from theses demas and contradiction . 

This single book of intellectual dialogue , logic and reason based exploration of the human mind has the potential to quiet many restless, agitated minds and to give them peace, solace, confidence, and the energy to rise above the contradictions of the material world.

Because of its similarity to the epic battle of the Mahabharata and to the Jewish people’s struggle for their own existence, I want every Jew to read a good translation of this world-acclaimed book—the Srimad Bhagavad Gita—at least once in their lifetime.
Reading it does not make anyone a Hindu, nor is it meant for it at all , even though complete devotion is one of the solution offered but it is not binding  on aby one  . 

It simply opens the mind and liberates it from its own mental barriers, trappings , chains , and dilemmas.
