text:
Thursday Soybean Report
September 3, 2026

The soybean market is experiencing moderate profit-taking this Thursday, backing off slightly after climbing to fresh multi month highs near the $12.85 mark. Bulls are catching their breath following a powerful late August rally driven by aggressive Chinese buying, continuous export flash announcements, and policy momentum surrounding domestic renewable fuel mandates. 

While harvest activity is beginning to expand across southern growing regions, tight spot pipeline supplies and firm domestic processing margins continue to provide a high structural floor.

Futures & Market News
CBOT soybean futures are trading 14 to 16 cents lower in today’s session, reflecting short term long liquidation and profit-taking across the broader grain complex.

September 2026 (U) is trading at $12.75 4/8, down 15 2/8 cents. November 2026 (X) sits at $12.85 4/8, down 16 2/8 cents. January 2027 (F) is trading at $12.98 2/8, down 14 6/8 cents.

Key Driver: Today's pullback follows a robust early-week surge that carried futures above $13.00 intraday. The complex received a major macro boost from expanded renewable fuel exemptions and biofuel mandate expectations, alongside persistent private flash sales to China (including 202,000 MT confirmed earlier this week). 

However, with September harvest expanding and the high stakes September WASDE report scheduled for next week, commodity funds are locking in gains.

USDA Soybean News: Crop Progress & Export Activity

National Crop Quality: Monday afternoon's USDA Crop Progress report showed national soybean condition ratings holding near 61% Good-to-Excellent, down 8 points from last year's pace as late August dryness trimmed topsoil moisture across Western Belt states.

Crop Maturity: Pod dropping and leaf discoloration are accelerating rapidly across the Midwest, with over 15% of the national crop dropping leaves, signaling the transition into widespread harvest operations over the next two weeks.

Flash Sales Continuation: Daily export activity remains a core support pillar. Private exporters reported another flash sale of 202,000 MT to China for 2026/27 delivery, demonstrating that international end-users are actively booking U.S. origin despite the recent price rally.

Commitments of Traders: Managed Money
Managed money funds expanded their net-long stance significantly over the past two weeks, shifting from a defensive short position into a strong long configuration (estimated at over +150,000 contracts).

November futures are testing interim technical support around the $12.80 line. A close below this level opens the door toward former resistance at $12.50, while major overhead resistance sits firmly at $13.10 to $13.20.

Crop & Weather Update
Weather conditions across the Corn Belt remain predominantly dry and warm, allowing mature fields to dry down quickly for harvest.

While late August dryness restricted pod-fill potential on late-planted fields in peripheral regions, it has created ideal early harvesting conditions across the Delta and southern Midwest. Field notes indicate strong local variability, aligning closely with final Crop Tour estimates that projected a national crop of 4.572 billion bushels on a 53.3 bpa yield.

Biofuel & 45Z Industry News
Domestic processors continue to run aggressive crush schedules, supported by robust soybean meal demand and strong soy oil values.

The regulatory narrative remains exceptionally supportive as biofuel policy developments reinforce domestic feedstock demand. Facilities are prioritizing domestic soy oil accumulation in preparation for the Section 45Z tax credit implementation, keeping local basis values historically firm ahead of peak harvest receipts.

Regional Cash Bids (Nebraska & Iowa)
Country cash bids have adjusted lower alongside today's board correction, though spot processor basis remains narrow as crushers look to keep pipelines filled ahead of heavy combine movement.

Lincoln, NE (Crush): Spot Delivery at $12.45
Sioux City, IA (Crush): Spot Delivery at $12.41
Norfolk, NE (Crush): Spot Delivery at $12.49
O’Neill/Ainsworth, NE: Spot Delivery at $11.99

Summary & Strategies
Summary: The market is undergoing a brief breather after pushing past $13.00 earlier in the week. Driven by expanding Chinese export bookings, strong biofuel demand mandates, and late season crop deterioration, November futures are holding well above their summer baselines.

Strategies:

Commercials: Use board pullbacks to lock in end-product oil and meal coverage while domestic crush spreads remain strong.
Producers: November beans trading near $12.85 offer a prime pricing opportunity. For unhedged new-crop bushels, consider scaling in forward sales or setting price floors to mitigate seasonal combine pressure as harvest accelerates through September.

Since Monday Open: November Beans are down 2 4/8.

$AVGO is down roughly 5.3% despite reporting another quarter of exceptional AI growth.

Broadcom delivered:

• Adjusted EPS of $3.32 vs. $3.22 expected
• Revenue of $29.59B vs. $29.24B expected
• AI semiconductor revenue of $16.7B, up 221% YoY
• Next-quarter revenue guidance of approximately $34.8B
Those are strong numbers.
So why is the stock falling?
Because the market expected more.

Broadcom entered earnings with an enormous valuation and extremely optimistic assumptions around custom AI chips. Guidance came in only slightly above consensus—not high enough to satisfy investors positioned for another major upside surprise.

The chart reflects that disappointment:

• Opened near $351.84
• Reached $362.07 early
• Reversed toward $347.65
• Session low sits at $342.50

My key levels:

• $342.50: immediate support
• $350: first level bulls need to reclaim
• $362: major intraday resistance
• Below $342: downside momentum could accelerate

The long-term AI thesis remains powerful. Broadcom continues to benefit from custom accelerators and high-speed networking demand.
But today offers a useful reminder:
A company can beat Wall Street estimates and still miss the expectations embedded in its stock price.
Is this a buying opportunity—or evidence that AI valuations have moved too far ahead of fundamentals?

- Khartoum 1967: The Arab League summit’s “no peace, no recognition, no negotiation” is a matter of public record.

- Camp David / Clinton Parameters (2000): Dennis Ross, who led the U.S. team, and President Clinton have described Barak’s acceptance and Arafat’s refusal — President Clinton has framed that refusal as a reversal and a betrayal. Palestinian negotiators later confirmed they did not accept the package as presented.

- Olmert 2008: Olmert has described the maps and terms publicly; Abbas has said he did not accept them. Condoleezza Rice and other participants recorded the same outcome.

- Gaza 2005: The disengagement from Gaza is a matter of Israeli government decision and implementation; subsequent Hamas rule, massive rocket fire, and the massacres of October 7 are documented.

Wilf’s framing matches the thesis she has developed in 'The War of Return' (with Adi Schwartz) — the core obstacle has been Palestinian rejection of Jewish sovereignty itself, institutionalized through the “right of return” demand that would end Israel as a Jewish-majority state, rather than a dispute only over 1967 lines or settlements.

But wait, there's more.
Planetary Digital Twin Network (PDTN)
Executive Summary
PDTN proposes transforming the existing Starlink satellite constellation into a global, continuously operating Earth and Space monitoring system.
By leveraging hardware already deployed in orbit and future advances in onboard AI computing, PDTN would create a real-time digital model of Earth’s atmosphere, gravity field, magnetosphere, and space-weather environment.
Unlike traditional scientific satellite missions that depend on a small number of highly specialized spacecraft, PDTN would utilize the scale, redundancy, and global coverage of thousands of satellites already serving a communications mission.
The core premise is simple: every Starlink satellite is already collecting information into a continuously updated planetary model.
The Opportunity
Current weather, gravity, and space-weather monitoring systems rely on numerous independent satellite programs, many of which are expensive, aging and limited in coverage.
Starlink represents a fundamentally different architecture.
· Thousands of satellites are distributed globally
· Continuous communication with earth
· Precision inter-satellite laser link
· Onboard system and power system exposed to the space environment
· Frequent hardware refresh cycles
The constellation already forms the framework of a planetary-scale sensor network. PDTN seeks to unlock that capability through network. PDTN seeks to unlock that capability through software, data integration and future orbital computing resources.
Atmospheric Monitoring
Every radiant transmission between Starlink satellites and ground terminal passes through Earth’s atmosphere.
Small changes in signal properties can reveal information about:
· Water vapor
· Rain and storm systems
· Air density
· Temperature gradients
· Pressure variations
· Atmospheric turbulence
With millions of communication paths active daily, PDTN could generate a highly detailed three-dimensional atmospheric model with global coverage, including remote oceans and polar regions.
The result would be a continuously refreshed atmospheric dataset capable of supplementing conventional weather observation systems.
Gravity Mapping
Starlink satellites communicate using highly precise laser links. Minute variations in satellite separation caused by Earth’s uneven gravitational field can provide information about
· Groundwater movement
· Ice sheet mass changes
· Ocean circulation
· Seasonal mass redistribution
· Geological process
Rather than relying on a handful of dedicated gravity satellites, PDTN could collect gravity-related observations across a much larger constellation, increasing geographic coverage and observation frequency.
Magnetosphere and Space Weather
Every Starlink satellite operates within Earth’s magnetic environment and is directly exposed to solar activity.
Telemetry already generated by constellation can contribute to monitoring:
· Solar storms
· Radiation flux
· Charged particle activity
· Geomagnetic disturbances
· Spacecraft charging effects
The constellation’s global distribution offers an opportunity to monitor space weather continuously rather than from a limited number of dedicated observation points.
Orbital Computing
The primary new capability envisioned by PDTN is the deployment of advanced orbital computing resources.

· Instead of transmitting all raw observations to Earth, future orbital computing systems would:
· Aggregate data across the constellation
· Process observations in near real time.
· Identify patterns and anomalies
· Generate predictive models
· Reduce communication bandwidth requirements.
As orbital computing power increases, the constellation could evolve into a self-organizing scientific platform capable of generating a continuously updated digital representation of Earth and near-Earth space.
Self-Calibrating Intelligence
Traditional scientific missions depend upon highly specialized instruments designed for maximum precision.
PDTN embraces a different philosophy; use large numbers of moderately sensitive measurements combined with advanced algorithms and artificial intelligence.
With thousands of satellites collecting observations simultaneously, software can compensate for the limitations of individual sensors through statistical averaging, pattern recognition and continuous calibrations.
The result is an organic sensing network whose accuracy improves as the constellation grows.
Strategic Benefits
PDTN offers several advantages:
· Global coverage
· Continuous operation
· High redundancy
· Frequent hardware replacement
· Reduced dependence on aging scientific satellites
· Lower marginal cost than dedicated monitoring constellations
· Near-real-time environmental awareness
· Enhanced resilience during natural disasters and space-weather events
Long-Term Vision
PDTN represents more than a scientific mission.
It is a pathway toward a continuously updated digital twin of Earth and its surrounding space environment.
By integrating atmospheric sensing, gravity monitoring, magnetospheric observation, space-weather analysis and orbital computing into a single distributed architecture, Starlink could evolve beyond communications infrastructure and become a planetary intelligence platform.
The vision if straightforward; Transform a communications constellation into a living model of Earth – continuously sensing, learning, and updating in real time.
Planetary Digital Twin Network (PDTN)
One Constellation. One Planet. Continuous Awareness.

text:
Robert M. Pirsig, 1991. A standalone reading of the sequel to Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance.

Lila: An Inquiry into Morals is not a second road trip with better scenery. It is an attempt to turn the earlier book’s live question — what is Quality? — into a full metaphysics, and then to see whether that metaphysics can survive contact with a person who is coming apart.
Pirsig later put the difference cleanly: Zen is a skeleton of a philosophy inside a full-bodied novel; Lila is a skeleton of a novel inside a full-bodied philosophy. He privately ranked Lila higher. Readers generally did not. Zen became a vernacular classic. Lila was a 1992 Pulitzer fiction finalist, spent a few weeks on the bestseller list, and then settled into the status of the difficult sequel.
That reception is not an accident. The book is colder, more schematic, and morally more uncomfortable than Zen. It is also, if you care about the actual argument, the more important of the two.
The story, stripped down
Phaedrus — Pirsig’s thin disguise for himself — is sailing his boat south from the Great Lakes toward New York and, eventually, Florida, racing winter ice. He is living on the proceeds of a famous book and trying to finish another one, assembled on thousands of index slips. Isolation is the plan. Isolation does not happen.
In a Kingston bar he meets Lila Blewitt, a drifting, sexually blunt, already-fraying woman who has just been discarded by a man. One night of drinking, dancing, and sex puts her on the boat. The next morning Richard Rigel, a lawyer-sailor who knew Lila in Rochester and who has already decided that Zen licensed the moral collapse of the 1960s, asks the question that organizes the whole book: Does Lila have Quality?
Phaedrus says yes.
The rest of the voyage is the cost of that answer. They sail down the Hudson. He thinks. She does not follow the thinking. Flashbacks open the source of the slips: a Bozeman colleague named Dusenberry, a peyote ceremony among Native Americans, and the realization that anthropology, as practiced, cannot admit value as a primary fact. In Manhattan the city appears as “the Giant,” a social superorganism that eats biological bodies. Lila unravels. A street connection named Jamie comes aboard; there is a half-formed scheme involving the boat; Lila attacks him, convinced he has killed her “baby.” She returns catatonic, cradling a doll fished from the river. They flee to Sandy Hook. Rigel reappears and offers to take her back to Rochester. She goes with him, claiming Phaedrus is trying to kill her. Her long obsession, it turns out, was Rigel all along.
Phaedrus is left with the doll. He treats it as the idol of her private religion, holds an inner dialogue with it, and leaves it for the tide. The book’s last moral judgment is that the unguarded yes to Rigel was the only moral act of the trip. Everyone gets the Quality they already valued: Lila gets Rigel, Rigel gets righteousness, Phaedrus gets Dynamic freedom. It is not a tragedy and not a reconciliation. It is an accounting.
Lila is not a muse. Pirsig rewrote her repeatedly because a compliant foil would not hold the book. She is biologically vivid, socially wrecked, intellectually almost absent, and dynamically ferocious — breaking patterns faster than new ones can latch. The doll is her static latch: a baby, a god, a self she can hold when every public pattern has rejected her. She is, in the book’s language, a culture of one.
What Zen left unfinished
Zen established Quality as the primary empirical reality: the event from which subjects and objects are later deduced, not a property of either. It split Quality into Classic and Romantic. That split explained a certain kind of cultural war — technicians versus aesthetes — but it did not explain disagreement about Quality itself. If Quality is one and prior to thought, why do people fight over it?
Lila’s first cut is different and more basic: Dynamic Quality versus static quality. Classic/Romantic is not the same distinction. Conflating them is the most common way to misread the sequel.
The Metaphysics of Quality
Pirsig’s claim is blunt. Quality, value, and morality are the same thing. A thing does not create value; value creates a thing. If something has no value, it cannot exist. The universe is therefore a moral order, not a valueless machine onto which morals are later painted. Subject-object metaphysics is the enemy because it parks values on the “subjective” side and then treats them as unreal.
Dynamic Quality is the pre-intellectual cutting edge of experience: always new, never fully nameable, the surprise that weakens old patterns. It is the source of growth, art, mysticism, and evolution. It is also dangerous. Without a latch, it looks like chaos or madness.
Static quality is any pattern that can repeat, be remembered, be taught. It is what lets an organism last. Without it there is no memory, no law, no language, no self that persists overnight.
The working formula is simple: without Dynamic Quality a pattern cannot grow; without static quality it cannot last. Evolution is the migration of static patterns toward Dynamic Quality. A new better pattern appears at the Dynamic edge; it then “latches” into a static form so the gain is not lost. The latch can later become a prison. That ratchet — invention, then conservation, then resistance to the next invention — is the engine of the book.
Four static levels
Everything that can be put in an encyclopedia falls into four discrete levels. They are not a smooth continuum. They operate at the same time, often against each other. Higher levels emerge from lower ones and then fight them for freedom.
1. Inorganic — physics, chemistry, gravity: patterns that beat chaos.
2. Biological — life against death, hunger, sex, disease, the law of the jungle.
3. Social — law, manners, cities, celebrity, families, “the Giant.” Social patterns sit on biological bodies and use them.
4. Intellectual — ideas, science, philosophy, the demand for truth. Built on social patterns, then turned against them.
Phaedrus’s later mapping is useful: objects roughly equal inorganic plus biological patterns; subjects roughly equal social plus intellectual patterns. They are parallel evolutionary levels, not two substances. That is how he tries to dissolve the mind-matter problem without collapsing one into the other.
Five moral codes
This is the book’s real invention. There is not one morality. There are five, stacked:
1. Inorganic over chaos
2. Biological over inorganic — a doctor killing a germ is moral
3. Social over biological — law, prisons, taboos against theft and rape
4. Intellectual over social — Galileo against the Church; an idea killing a custom is more moral than a custom killing an idea
5. Dynamic over all static patterns — freedom from domination by any latch, without requiring the destruction of the patterns themselves
The order of precedence is:
Dynamic > Intellectual > Social > Biological > Inorganic
Immorality is a lower pattern dominating a higher one. Society persecuting Galileo is immoral. A criminal fighting society is not the same case as Galileo fighting society, even though both look like rebellion. Subject-object liberalism, Pirsig says, could not tell them apart because it only saw “individual versus society.” The Metaphysics of Quality claims it can: one fight is biological against social, the other intellectual against social.
That elegance is also the danger. The same rule can be made to sound like dressed-up Social Darwinism — a village may kill brigands because a village is “higher.” Some of Pirsig’s examples are crude. The system marks the yard lines; it does not, despite the tone of certainty, pick every winner.
How the story tests the system
The philosophy says Quality precedes subjects and objects. The plot makes you feel what that costs when two people share a berth and never share a world.
Rigel is static social Quality as a person: family, reputation, the duty to expose the affair that wrecked a marriage. He is not a cartoon. He is right that Lila destroys social patterns. He is wrong that this exhausts her Quality.
Phaedrus is intellectual static patterns as a person. Fame has not cured isolation. He does not love Lila so much as use her as the problem that forces the metaphysics to become moral. His own history of institutionalization keeps him from treating her breakdown as a simple chemical error. His weakness is that he analyzes intimacy instead of inhabiting it.
Lila is the exam. The refined answer is not a simple yes. Biologically she has Quality. Socially she does not. Intellectually she is almost blank. Dynamically she is the thing to watch. Insanity, in this frame, is not falsehood first. It is nonconformity to surrounding static patterns. A lone person cannot be insane; insanity is a relationship. The mystic and the lunatic look similar from the outside because both have left public static patterns. The difference, Pirsig says, is that the lunatic has locked onto a private static pattern of his own, while the mystic has abandoned static patterns for Dynamic Quality. Lila lives in the dangerous zone between those two. The doll is her attempt to latch.
The book’s most honest sentence about her is not the sorting. It is the reversal: it isn’t that Lila has Quality; Quality has Lila. The yes to Rigel is treated as Dynamic judgment — recognition before the slips could intervene. After that, everyone retreats into their static pattern.
That is why the characterization remains a wound. The philosophy is working as designed when it sorts her by levels. The novel is failing as a novel when a person becomes primarily a sorting. Pirsig knows this in flashes and still does it. Any honest reading has to hold both facts.
The cultural diagnosis
The historical chapters are the most durable part of the book after the five codes.
Until the end of the Victorian era, American public life was dominated by social patterns: manners, respectability, the family as moral unit. After World War I, intellectual patterns took the wheel — science, expertise, the idea that society should be redesigned from above. Fascism is read as a social-pattern revolt against intellect. The 1960s hippie movement is read as an attempted Dynamic revolt against both social and intellectual patterns. It failed, in this account, because it could not tell Dynamic Quality from biological Quality. Free love and drugs looked like liberation and often collapsed into the lower level they thought they had escaped. They had no static latch.
Celebrity is to the social level what sex is to the biological: it looks Dynamic and is not. It is the organizing lure of social patterns. New York is the Giant made visible.
The Native American material is the origin myth of the slips, not reliable ethnography. Pirsig’s claim is that Plains Indian value-language treats Good as a noun, the center of experience, rather than an adjective stuck onto objects. American culture, he argues, is a tense fusion of European static order and Native Dynamic freedom — which is why Americans can preach equality and status in the same breath. The anthropology critique has a real point: value-blind “objectivity” will miss what a culture actually is. The Lakota-as-Dynamic / European-as-static contrast is too clean and now dated. Treat Dusenberry and the peyote night as the scene that generated the system, not as a field report.
What the book actually does
Zen asked what Quality is and showed a mind broken and remade by the question. Lila asks: if Quality is the primary reality, what is morality?
It gives a usable grammar for conflicts that ordinary ethics fumbles:
• biology versus society (sex, crime, public health, family)
• intellect versus society (Victorian collapse, scientific amoralism, the 1960s)
• Dynamic Quality versus every latch (art, mysticism, revolution, insanity)
The sanity argument continues Zen’s electroshock story at the level of theory. Lila’s breakdown is the cost of being Dynamic without a supporting Giant. “Good is a noun” is the one-sentence reduction: goodness is not a property you assign to objects after the fact. It is the thing the objects are made of. Ultimate Quality still isn’t a noun either — Pirsig admits that — but if the metaphysics has to collapse into one sentence, that is the sentence.
What it does not do
It does not replace Zen. The motorcycle was an image that could hold the thought. The boat never quite becomes that. Third-person distance makes the philosophy less intimate and, for many readers, less persuasive.
It does not convince academic philosophy. Pirsig complained that seriously thinking people did not understand him and offered a prize to anyone who could prove the metaphysics wrong. That is devotion, not method. The system can absorb counterexamples by redescribing them as the wrong level of Quality. That unfalsifiability is a genuine weakness.
It does not escape the problem it set itself. Zen’s power was that Quality precedes definition. Lila defines a system around the undefinable. Critics who call this self-defeating are not being pedantic. Once Quality is taxonomized into four static levels plus a Dynamic remainder, the book is doing category-and-instance work of the kind it claimed to leave behind. Dynamic Quality then functions as a mystical leftover that cannot be cross-examined.
The New York Review of Books attack still has teeth: Quality cannot do all the moral work claimed because it cannot be specified; Phaedrus does not obviously embody Quality in the narrative; the Lila-as-test-case is asserted more than dramatized; the evolutionary-moral rule has a Social Darwinist odor in its cruder examples.
Lila herself remains the book’s moral problem. She is the question made flesh. That is philosophically coherent and novelistically insufficient. Do not flatten her into “the biological woman.” Also do not pretend the portrait is adequate as a life.
How to read it now
Read Lila after Zen, not instead of it. Zen is the experience of Quality. Lila is the attempt to make that experience legally binding on morals, culture, sanity, and evolution. The attempt is half-success, half-trap, which is more interesting than a clean success would have been.
The parts that still work are the distinction between Dynamic and static, the four-level stack as a way to stop flattening every conflict into “individual versus society,” and the warning that liberation without a latch collapses downward. The parts that do not work are the pretense that the taxonomy is exhaustive, the dated anthropology, and the habit of treating a woman in breakdown as the proving ground for a system.
Pirsig’s last move is the one that still cuts. The only moral act on the trip was not the metaphysics. It was the moment before the metaphysics, when he refused to let social contempt settle the question of another person’s Quality. The book is most alive there, and most in trouble everywhere it tries to make that moment into a chart.

text:
one of my favorite cold email angles ever was generating the customer before I had the client.

this works stupidly well in boring old economy markets where 1 transaction can pay for the entire engagement. lenders, brokers, equipment companies, whatever.

when u lead w a sample, the positive replies become ample.

instead of emailing a lender saying “we generate leads,” go generate the lead first.

I talk to so many borrowers now that I always have at least 10+ introductions I can make in real time, so when I send this campaign out, its not a lie, it's just manifesting as bait to reel them in and make cold-email easier.

I generate demand for funding offers at all times, then I find the supply side that wants to pay for it so it's always a moving vehicle their jumping into rather then building a car from scratch just for this specific lender.

do this:

1. pick a 2 sided market where one side needs something expensive + the other side gets paid to provide it

borrowers + lenders. companies + equipment dealers. buyers + business brokers. shippers + freight companies.

2. run the first cold email campaign to the demand side

find a handful of ppl actively looking for the thing. take the calls. qualify what they need, the timing, budget + whether they actually want an intro.

tell em u work w a network of providers + will find the right fit.

3. take the real opportunity to the supply side

the lender email is stupid simple:

“{{firstName}}, got a borrower in Florida looking for $X for {{use}}. they fit {{2-3 real facts}}. can I send him your way?”

that email gets a hell of a lot more interest than “we help lenders book more calls.”

4. when they say yes, dont just throw the lead over

say:

“great. I built a good relationship w them, so lets take 10 mins first to make sure this actually fits your box. free tomorrow for a call? here's my booking link bud”

now the alignment call is booked because u brought something they already want.

5. give em the opportunity if it fits, then show them where it came from

“this is 1 of the borrowers we're generating through a channel you're likely not using. we can continue to push these borrowers around your exact credit box + create 10-40 unique borrower conversations over the next 90 days.”

then define the borrower, transaction size, geography, use of funds, qualification rules, handoff + exactly what happens when an opp gets rejected.

important: the opp has to be real.

if u already placed it, say that. send the redacted profile as a sample + explain that the same campaign is producing more. dont pretend somebody is still available when they arent. small old economy markets remember every lie.

a bunch of lenders will ask if they have to pay. some will leave the second they hear theres a fee. perfect. the ones who stay understand what a qualified borrower is worth.

Ive acquired 12+ lenders as clients like this + built an ecosystem around this exact idea. our internal partner gets first dibs on the deals. everybody else pays for access to the demand we create.

u can keep leading w your garbage offer + asking strangers to believe a promise.

or u can create the first piece of value, put it in front of them + let the sample sell the machine behind it.

this is for the dogs, if you are scared of being loud, making a lot of noise, breaking shit and have the stress tolerance of child, go back to generating 1 lead per 20,000 emails sent.

the ones you piss off, do they remember you, yes if you are an idiot, with our email flow + how we start the call - they walk away with a potential free intro either way so they get what they came in for.

our education email flow that leads them into the call will also announce that if there is a fit and they want more then just the one, we will discuss an engagement and our average engagement is between 20-60K with a long row of case studies and mechanism decks below it.

the difference between "hey we can do x y z" and "hey I have x ready right now do you want it" is night and day.

Whiskey Jug Genie by Sultonna Nadine is a lighthearted and charming paranormal fantasy that mixes magic, humor, and a touch of romance for pure escapist fun.

When quiet London apothecary shop owner Martin buys an old whiskey jug on vacation, he has no idea he’s about to release Bubba, a genie who’s been trapped inside for 200 years and is thoroughly out of touch with the modern world. Chaos, spells, cultural clashes, and plenty of laughs ensue as the unlikely pair (along with a very annoyed cat) try to navigate the mess. Set against the backdrop of contemporary London with elements of white magic and everyday wonder, the story balances humorous situations with warmer moments. Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

• September 1, 2026 — Draft State rules would make parents prove status for children’s passports under Trump’s revived birthright order; not final, challenged.

• September 1, 2026 — Whistleblower says a rushed ballot portal could reject tens of thousands after one error; unadjudicated, with USPS previously rebuked.

• August 31, 2026 — State proposed $4M for right-wing European media and $25M for conservative civic groups before elections; recipients undisclosed, illegality unproven.

• August 31, 2026 — Judge dismissed with prejudice DOJ’s suit forcing California to bar transgender girls from girls’ sports, finding no clear Title IX condition; appeal possible.

• August 31, 2026 — Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned amid reported Hegseth tensions after the Army chief’s removal; no official reason.

• August 30, 2026 — Administration deported an Afghan protected from return to Afghanistan to Central African Republic; legality unresolved.

• August 30, 2026 — Venezuela announced a 25-year U.S. oil deal for 17 fields; Trump claims majority control, Venezuela retains ownership. Corruption unproven.

• August 30, 2026 — Trump demanded FCC punishment of NBC’s Kristen Welker over coverage; no action or ruling.

• August 29, 2026 — DHS claimed, without public evidence, up to 250,000 noncitizens on four states’ rolls; experts say illegal voting is rare and the method error-prone.

• August 28, 2026 — Judge kept Trump’s hush-money case in state court, calling Daniels concealment private conduct; 34 convictions remain on appeal.

• August 28, 2026 — Trump renewed birthright limits after earlier blocks; judge denied immediate relief procedurally, case ongoing.

• August 27, 2026 — After court blocked Trump renaming, allies sought Kennedy Center branding and DOJ raised demolition/replacement; Trump denied a tear-down plan.

• August 27, 2026 — Judge barred Pentagon retaliation against Anthropic, finding First Amendment, due-process and arbitrary-action violations.

• August 27, 2026 — Judge temporarily blocked Trump mail-ballot rules as likely unconstitutional, citing no fraud evidence and high disenfranchisement risk.

• August 2026 — Appeals court blocked DOJ subpoenas to Letitia James’ office because the acting U.S. attorney was unlawfully appointed.

• August 2026 — Pentagon fired the Stars and Stripes editor, raising concern over political control of military journalism.

• August 2026 — Administration eased career-worker firings through suitability/ranking rules; unions allege political patronage. Case pending.

• July 2026 — Wild-horse removals/sales surged; some may have entered the slaughter pipeline. BLM denies knowingly selling for slaughter.

• February 6, 2026 — White House deleted Trump’s post depicting the Obamas as primates after backlash, blaming staff.

• February 2026 — Trump expanded lower-tariff Argentine beef imports; U.S. ranchers and GOP lawmakers said it favored foreign producers.

• 2025–2026 — ICE raids and violent operations terrorized families and communities.

• 2025–2026 — Public-health and vaccine policy were driven into political extremism over science and trust.

• 2025–2026 — Administration investigated people who investigated, sued, criticized or defeated Trump.

• 2025–2026 — Favored prosecutors were installed without Senate confirmation; courts rejected several amid loyalty concerns.

• 2025–2026 — Press attacks, journalist subpoenas and punishment threats targeted truth-tellers.

• November 2025 — Judge dismissed the Comey/James cases because the Trump-backed prosecutor was unlawfully appointed; dismissals without prejudice.

• August 5, 2025 — RFK Jr.’s HHS cut nearly $500M from 22 mRNA projects; experts warned of weaker pandemic readiness.

• March 2025 — Government wrongfully deported Kilmar Ábrego García despite legal protection, then was ordered to return him.

• March 2025 — Trump used the Alien Enemies Act for gang removals, triggering due-process litigation.

• February 27, 2025 — Bondi gave influencers mostly public “Epstein Files” after saying a client list was on her desk; DOJ later said none existed.

• February 22, 2025 — Trump/Hegseth removed the Joint Chiefs chair, Navy chief and military lawyers in an unprecedented shake-up; politicization alleged.

text:
Einat Wilf’s point in the Oxford Union debate is that Israel repeatedly and genuinely sought a two-state peace, while Palestinian and broader Arab leadership consistently rejected a Jewish state (in any borders) and answered concessions with war and terror.

The debate took place at the Oxford Union on 18 June 2026. The motion was “This House Believes Israel Never Truly Wanted Peace with Palestine.” The motion passed 208–129. 

Wilf spoke for the opposition. She argued the opposite: Israel wanted peace “too much,” made offer after offer, absorbed attacks, and will not dissolve the only Jewish state to prove its good faith. 

Wilf walked through a sequence of historic decisions:

- Jews accepted the 1947 UN Partition Plan (a Jewish state on limited, largely arid, non-contiguous land; most of the fertile area assigned to an Arab state). Arab states and Palestinian militias rejected it and went to war. Refugees resulted from that war, not from a prior Israeli “land grab.”

- After 1967, Israel offered peace. The Arab response was the Khartoum “Three No’s”: no peace, no recognition, no negotiation.

- Israel entered Oslo in 1993. In 2000 the Second Intifada followed, with suicide bombings that killed more than 1,000 Israelis.

- In December 2000 the Clinton Parameters (all of Gaza, ~96% of the West Bank plus swaps, East Jerusalem as Palestinian capital, international force in the West Bank) were accepted by Israel under Ehud Barak and rejected by Yasser Arafat.

- In 2008 Ehud Olmert offered a near-total West Bank withdrawal with land swaps, a Gaza link, East Jerusalem as capital, and international trusteeship over the Old City including the Temple Mount. Mahmoud Abbas walked away.

- In 2005 Israel withdrew every settlement and soldier from Gaza. Hamas later used the territory, work permits, and medical access as cover for the 7 October 2023 massacre.

She closed by flipping the question: when did Palestinian Arabs ever accept peace with the Jewish state? Peace is desired, she said, but not at the price of the state’s existence.

The Heinousness of Homosexuality: 

"To the question of how heinous this sin is, the Westminster Larger Catechism Question 150 offers a simple answer: 

Q.150. Are all transgressions of the law of God equally heinous in themselves, and in the sight of God? A. All transgressions of the law of God are not equally heinous; but some sins in themselves, and by reason of several aggravations, are more heinous in the sight of God than others.

Larger Catechism Question 151 sheds more light on what makes some sins more heinous. Three key points demonstrate this sin’s seriousness without going into detail.

First, the heinousness of sin arises “from the circumstances [of the sin]…if in public, or in the presence of others, who are thereby likely to be provoked or defiled.” Public announcements of private sins are commonly avoided for obvious reasons. 

This problem is further compounded by the fact that a minister’s [church officer's] public reputation will be damaged. The churches’ reputation will be sullied as well. People will know him less as a minister of the gospel (who certainly sins) and more readily known as the-pastor-who-struggles-with-homosexuality.

Secondly, the heinousness of sin arises from the “persons offending…if they be of riper age, greater experience or grace, eminent for profession, gifts, place, office, guides to others, and whose example is likely to be followed by others.” 

As pastors of many years with worldwide recognition and influence, some of their private-sins-turned-public-testimonies are worse than if they were never a pastor. Paul insists that church leaders “be above reproach” (1 Timothy 3:2). Unfortunately, many in the church seem to think an admitted homosexual porn addict is close enough. 

Lastly, the heinousness of sin arises from “the nature and quality of the offense.” It is a sexual sin. And sexual sins are especially wicked, according to the Apostle Paul.

Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body. What? Know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? (1 Corinthians 6:18ff).

But homosexuality is not merely a sexual sin like other sexual sins. While desiring the opposite sex is acceptable within marriage, desiring the same sex is never acceptable. Allberry correctly acknowledges this.

"I think you’re right to suggest that there’s not an exact symmetry between same-sex temptation and opposite-sex feelings because there are godly ways of expressing heterosexual sexual desires. There are not godly ways of expressing homosexual sexual desires. So in that sense, there’s a distinction between the two." 
 
Because of the absolute prohibition on homosexual intercourse, this sin is more heinous than struggling with adultery. Heterosexual intercourse is allowable under certain conditions. Homosexual intercourse is never permissible, a qualitative difference.

When a public church officer declares his lust toward men from the rooftops, it amplifies the sin’s heinousness. This point should be obvious, just as if your church treasurer announced that he was “money-attracted and have been my entire life. By that I mean that I have lustful, glamorous and deep emotional attractions to money…”

Thus, the issue of God being anti-gay is doubly essential. Since homosexuality is more heinous than many other sexual sins, it should be treated as a more serious sin in the church—something that should not be lightly talked about or ignored when discovered by church officers."

text:
Let me get this straight. Your argument is that seeing things is satanic.

Then take it up with God, because He is the one who kept doing it. He put a rainbow in the sky as a sign. He lit a bush on fire and told Moses to come look. He led two million people through the desert with a visible pillar of cloud and fire. He told Moses to build a bronze serpent and said anyone who looks at it lives. He gave Israel a tabernacle with gold, embroidery, and carved cherubim, then gave Solomon a temple so ornate it made a visiting queen go weak in the knees. If beauty and visible signs are the serpent's playbook, God has been running it since Exodus.

Then the Incarnation happens and your argument really falls apart. God became visible. That is the whole event. John opens his letter by saying what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what our hands have touched. Jesus told Thomas to look at His hands. He said if you have seen me you have seen the Father. He fed five thousand, walked on water, and raised Lazarus in front of a crowd, and He said if you don't believe me, believe the works. The signs were the argument.

Your own citations do not say what you need them to say. Genesis 3 is not condemning Eve's eyeballs, it's condemning her disobeying a direct command. The tree was fine. God made the tree. And 1 John says the lust of the eyes, not the use of them. Lust is disordered desire. If the mere act of looking were sin, the beatific vision is a problem, since Scripture's promise for heaven is that we will see Him face to face.

The Matthew 4 one is the most self-inflicted. Satan showed Jesus the kingdoms of the world and offered him political power over all of them. Jesus refused. Rome offers you a crucifix, a poor man nailed to wood, which is the exact opposite pitch. Satan said take the glory and skip the cross. The Church says take the cross. You have those backwards.

Also, and I say this gently, you made this argument using a book. That is a physical object you look at with your eyes. By your own logic, reading is the fall of man.

The real difference here isn't eyes versus no eyes, it's whether God works through matter. Catholics say yes, because He made matter, called it good, and then took some on permanently. The serious Protestant version of this objection is about the second commandment and whether images become idols in practice. That's a real debate. This post isn't having it.

text:
In 1998, Warren Buffett gave a 1-hour masterclass on how to never lose money investing.

Here are the 22 most valuable lessons from his lecture:

1. You only have to get rich once. If you have $100 million and can make 10% unleveraged or 20% leveraged, the difference between $110 million and $120 million at year-end means nothing to your life, your family, or anything. But the downside, especially with other people's money, is disgrace, humiliation, and facing the friends whose money you lost. The equation never makes sense.

2. To make money they did not need, they risked money they did have and needed. That is just plain foolish, Buffett says, regardless of your IQ. If you hand him a gun with a million chambers and one bullet and offer him any sum to put it to his temple and pull once, he will not do it. There is nothing on the upside that justifies the downside. People do this financially all the time without thinking.

3. The smartest people in finance went broke, and that is the most fascinating story Buffett knows. Long-term Capital Management had 16 people with possibly the highest average IQ of any business in the country, 350 to 400 combined years of experience, and most of their own net worth in the firm. They still went bankrupt. Buffett says if he ever wrote a book, it would be called why smart people do dumb things.

4. Beta and sigmas tell you nothing about the real risk of going broke. The LTCM team relied heavily on mathematics and believed a six- or seven-sigma event could not touch them. They were wrong. History does not tell you the probabilities of future financial events. The real risk is not volatility. It is a permanent, irreversible blind spot in something crucial, often caused by knowing a great deal about something else.

5. Invest only in businesses you can understand. That one rule narrows the field by about 90%, and that is fine. Buffett can understand Coca-Cola. he cannot value an internet company, and he says if a student handed him a valuation of one on a final exam, he would flunk them. People thought Enron was incredible because it had a good track record, but almost nobody understood how it made money. That was the signal to avoid it.

6. You want a business that is a castle with a wide moat around it. Inside the castle, you want an honest, able, hard-working duke. The moat can be low cost, like Geico in auto insurance, or brand, or patents, or location. But a wonderful castle will always be attacked, so the job of every manager Buffett owns is one thing: widen the moat. Throw crocodiles and sharks into it to keep competitors out.

7. Moats change slowly and invisibly, but they change. Thirty years ago, Kodak's moat was as wide as Coca-Cola's. They had share of mind; the little yellow box meant best in everyone's head. Then they let Fuji into the Olympics and narrowed their own moat. Coca-Cola's moat, by contrast, is wider now than 30 years ago. Every time infrastructure gets built in a country that is not yet profitable, the moat widens a little. You cannot see it day by day, but in 10 years, the difference is enormous.

8. Share of mind beats share of market. When you say Disney, every person in the room has something in their head. Say Universal Pictures or 20th Century Fox, and you have nothing. A mother with two kids will pick the $17.95 Disney video over the $16.95 alternative because she knows it will be fine and does not want to preview ten videos to decide. That little bit of certainty in the customer's mind is worth a fortune.

9. The best businesses have pricing power and require little capital. see's candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 when Buffett bought it for $25 million. The entire thesis was whether the price could go to $2.25 without hurting sales. It could, because nobody wants to hand their valentine a box of candy and say, "This year I took the low bid." Today, See's makes $60 million on the same formulas and still takes almost no capital. Compare that to GM, which had to reinvest every dollar into better factories and whose stock barely moved over 50 years.

10. The best businesses earn a royalty on other people's capital. Coca-Cola sells a formula and collects a royalty on every drink. American Express takes a few percent of every dollar you spend. You put up the capital, they take a cut. Low capital intensity is one of the most underrated qualities in a business and one of the surest paths to durable wealth.

11. Define your circle of competence and stay inside it. The size of the circle does not matter. Staying inside, it does. If you know which 30 companies out of thousands you actually understand, you are fine. Buffett understood H.H. brown shoes and Frank Rooney, so he closed that deal in five minutes. If you do not know enough to understand a business instantly, you will not understand it in a month either.

12. Ignore the macro entirely. Buffett has never bought or skipped a business because of a feeling about interest rates, the economy, or any macro forecast. If Alan Greenspan and Bob Rubin both whispered exactly what they would do for the next 12 months, it would not change what he pays for anything. You want to focus on what is important and knowable. The macro is important but not knowable, so you ignore it.

13. Inactivity is the strategy, not a flaw. Wall Street makes money on activity. You make money on inactivity. A broker is like a doctor paid by how often he changes your pills. If everyone in a room trades their portfolio with everyone else every day, they all end up broke, and the intermediary keeps the money. Buffett looks for one good idea a year and rides it to its full potential. He measures Berkshire by how little turnover there is, like a church where the same people fill the seats every Sunday.

14. If you understand businesses, diversification is a mistake. For the 99% who will not evaluate businesses, Buffett recommends a low-cost index fund and extreme diversification. But if you bring real intensity to evaluating companies, owning more than six is a terrible idea. Very few people got rich on their seventh best idea. A lot of people got rich on their best one. Buffett keeps about half his money in what he likes best.

15. Buffett's biggest mistakes are mistakes of omission, not commission. The times he understood a business well enough to act and instead sat there sucking his thumb. He passed on healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan and on Fannie Mae in the mid-eighties, each a multi-billion-dollar miss. Accounting never captures these. The $2,000 he put into a Sinclair service station as a young man, money he lost, has an opportunity cost of about $6 billion today.

16. Focus on what will happen, not when. Coca-Cola went public in 1919 at $40 a share and dropped to $19 within a year. There was always a reason not to buy: the great depression, world war, sugar rationing, thermonuclear weapons. But one share bought then and reinvested would be worth about $5 million. If you are right about the business, you will make a lot of money. The timing is the tricky part, so do not focus on it.

17. When hiring, look for integrity, intelligence, and energy. But if the person lacks the first one, you actually want them dumb and lazy. Because a person with intelligence and energy but no integrity will destroy you. Buffett borrowed this from Pete Kiewit. The trait everyone screens for last is the one that matters most.

18. Here is a thought experiment Buffett gives students. Imagine you could own 10% of one classmate for the rest of their life. You would not pick the highest IQ or the best grades. You would pick the person you respond to best, the one who is generous, honest, gives credit to others, and has leadership qualities. Now imagine you also had to short one classmate. You would pick the egotistical, greedy, slightly dishonest one. The qualities that decide both are not talent. They are character.

19. Every quality on the admirable side is achievable, and every quality on the repellent side is removable. The things that make you want to own 10% of someone are not the ability to throw a football or run fast; they are behavior, temperament, and character, all of which anyone can choose. Buffett's point: you already own 100% of yourself, so you might as well become the person worth betting on.

20. The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken. Buffett sees people in their forties and fifties trapped by self-destructive patterns they can no longer change. At a young age, you can choose any habits you want. Ben Franklin and Ben Graham both did exactly this, looking at people they admired and simply deciding to behave like them. There was nothing impossible about it.

21. Take a job you would take if you were already independently wealthy. Buffett told a 28-year-old at Harvard who wanted a consulting job "to look good on his resume" that it was like saving up sex for your old age. There comes a time to just start doing what you love. Buffett offered to work for Ben Graham for free, was told he was overpriced, and kept pestering him for years. Take the job you would jump out of bed for. You cannot miss.

22. You won the ovarian lottery, and that should shape how you think. Buffett imagines a genie 24 hours before your birth letting you design the world's rules, with one catch: you do not know which of 5.8 billion balls you will draw. Born here or in Afghanistan, with an IQ of 130 or 70, male or female, able-bodied or not. If you could put your ball back and draw one of 100 random others, most people would not, because they are already in the luckiest 1%. Buffett knows he is perfectly wired for a market economy that pays him like crazy, while an equally good citizen leading scout troops and teaching Sunday school is not, purely by luck.

text:
COLORADO: A TALE OF TWO FUTURES

In November, Colorado voters will be presented with two very different paths.

One accelerates us down the road we are already traveling, a path of higher costs, higher taxes, more government spending and a business climate increasingly less competitive with our neighbors. The other offers Colorado an opportunity to correct its course.

Imagine looking back from the year 2032.

FUTURE 1: Colorado’s $2.7 Billion Mistake - In 2026, voters approved Initiative 195.

They were promised $2.7 billion a year in new revenue for schools, health care and childcare, while most Coloradans received modest tax cuts.  

But people changed their behavior.  Entrepreneurs moved before selling businesses. Investors delayed capital gains. Companies placed their next facility, jobs or headquarters in lower-tax states. Many businesses never formally “left” Colorado. They simply made their next investment somewhere else.

Rural families felt it too. Farmers selling land and owners retiring from family businesses discovered that one major lifetime transaction could push them into the highest tax brackets. Pass-through businesses paid higher taxes on income retained for equipment, inventory and payroll.

Eventually, revenues fell short of projections. But the spending commitments remained. Lawmakers drained reserves, delayed infrastructure, increased fees and began looking for new taxpayers to fill the gap. 

Colorado didn’t collapse. The damage was quieter: businesses that never arrived, jobs created elsewhere, investment lost and a tax base increasingly dependent on volatile income. 

Colorado wagered $2.7 billion that taxpayers and capital would stand still. They didn’t.

FUTURE 2: Colorado's Course Correction

Now imagine a different 2032.

Voters rejected Initiative 195 and approved Initiative 232, sending a clear message: Keep income-tax rates capped. Make government live within reasonable limits.

This time, lawmakers listened. Instead of asking how to raise more money, they asked where existing dollars were going. Duplicative programs were consolidated. Improper payments were recovered. Waste, fraud and abuse became continuing targets of oversight. Agencies were expected to demonstrate results. Lawmakers also rediscovered the difference between a priority and a wish list. Schools, roads, public safety and assistance for the truly vulnerable came first.

Then Colorado attacked another driver of unaffordability: excessive regulation. Permitting became faster and more predictable. Barriers to housing, energy development and business growth were reduced. Small businesses spent less time navigating bureaucracy and more time hiring and investing. Slowly, Colorado’s trajectory changed. Entrepreneurs stayed. Employers expanded. Investment returned. Jobs followed.

By 2032, Colorado was once again competing with surrounding states not only for businesses, but for families looking for an affordable place to live. The comeback didn’t happen because government found another source of money. It happened because government learned to do better with what it already had.

The Choice Is Ours

One future asks taxpayers to accommodate a more expensive government. The other asks government to adjust to the realities facing taxpayers. We can accelerate down Colorado’s increasingly unaffordable path. Or we can change direction.

I urge you to reject Initiative 195 and support Initiative 232.
  
The future isn’t written yet. Colorado voters get to write it.

#PreserveTABOR 
#NoOn195
#YesOn232

text:
California's TFAIA and New York's RAISE Act both include whistleblower provisions for AI workers. Which better protects the people building frontier AI?

Neither, categorically. It depends. Our new comparative guide breaks it down.

What the guide finds:
📌  New York offers broader substantive coverage: contractors and former  employees are explicitly protected, and any worker can report a  "substantial and specific danger to public health or safety".

📌  California offers a more worker-friendly burden of proof: a  "contributing factor" test shifts the burden to the employer to prove it  would have acted the same way anyway.

📌  California bars the contractual mechanisms e.g. NDAs, pre-dispute  arbitration, equity-linked offboarding that have historically kept  disclosures out of view. New York does not.

📌  Both states still have gaps. Neither defines clear response obligations  for authorities, and neither expressly covers equity in remedies.

The guide also sets out targeted recommendations for legislators and workers in both states.

text:
If Ottawa walked away from a trade deal to buy time before Alberta votes... then Albertans have a problem.

Ottawa wants to use oil and gas as leverage... but we know two things:

1. We have to keep our people employed.
2. Ottawa still needs that revenue.

Choosing to hit a "self destruct" button may help accelerate meeting our governments green objectives by collapsing the oil and gas industry - that is likely the silver lining that will be on offer, and the direction Alberta and the rest of Canada will be steered in - but it's also going to cripple Canada economically.

There is no getting around it. The world runs on oil. International shipping, continental logistics, aviation, almost everything that you need depends on oil to get it to you.

Our government had spent the past decade attempting to kill the oil and gas industry in Canada - and now, when we need to pivot to international markets, we can't because we are at least a decade behind having the internal pipeline infrastructure to deep water ports in BC for export to make that pivot, and no political will to it. 

This kind of short sightedness has been a consistent problem with our political and policy development apparatus. Wonderful visions of "tomorrow" and not focused in the here and now.

Nobody is asking (yet) what happens if the oil and gas industry pulls out of oil production in Alberta?  What happens if that is stopped, and instead we have to rely on international oil imports into eastern refineries from outside the country to maintain our internal oil and gas supply chains?

Well, it would firmly put power back in Eastern hands.  Something Montreal power brokers especially would heartily want. 

"Uppity Westerners! No diesel or gas for you! Buy the Chinese EVs or freeze and starve." 

The East, of course, would not suffer any interruptions at all for diesel and gasoline.

Would that happen? I'm not sure... all I can say with any certainty, is that Eastern Canada is unusually preoccupied with the Alberta referendum results if they have enough bearing on trade talks to justify walking out.

History demonstrates when the East is that interested in Alberta oil and gas, that's usually not good for the west. 

They're not saying what they really want or what the objective really is.

(And don't tell me it's about just "sticking it to Trump."  None of us out west are stupid when it comes to major industries in our Province)

I'm also suspicious of the known ties the East has with "progressive" Democrats in the USA, especially California with its radical economy wrecking environmental policies.

Ottawa purposefully locking itself into a highly emotional diplomatic stance with the Republican Party led administration in the USA is a real concern, and is going to be a factor when Alberta goes to a referendum in October.

If the Democrats want to stick it to the Republicans... they can stop using their influence in Canada's government and our economy as the bat to beat them with ahead of midterm elections.
