text:
The Bibi/Trumpy BIG LIE That Iran Was Two Weeks From A Nuke

The now endlessly repeated notion that Iran's stockpile of 60% enriched uranium (HEU) is tantamount to having a nuclear weapon within weeks is downright malefic. Indeed, this gross deception is so thoroughly fallacious and dangerously misleading that it needs be debunked lock, stock and barrel.

So we begin with the War Party's hoary claim that the roughly 400 kilograms of 60% enriched uranium possessed by Iran as of May 2025, according to the IAEA, could have been further processed to weapons-grade levels (90 percent or higher) in a matter of a few days or weeks using existing centrifuge cascades.

And, then, poof, they would supposedly have had ten nukes.

Actually, they would not have had any nuclear bombs at all. Not even remotely.

That's because producing fissile material is only the first—and in many respects the easiest—step on the long road to a reliable, deliverable nuclear weapon. If building the latter is akin to a grueling 20-mile journey across rugged terrain, acquiring 60 percent HEU gets you perhaps to the "mile-one" marker.

Metaphorically speaking, you would have cleared the initial foothills of uranium isotope separation. But the remaining 19 miles are chock-a-bloc with uncharted engineering valleys, sheer technical manufacturing cliffs and a final summit that no nation has ever scaled without extensive trial, error, and empirical proof that the wherewithal for successful weaponization of a nuclear reaction has been obtained.

Indeed, this crucial distinction—between producing fissile material and building a functional weapon—has been at the very center of U.S. National Intelligence Estimates (NIEs) for nearly two decades. From the 2007 NIE (national intelligence estimate) on the matter right up to and including the March 2025 testimony of Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard before the US Congress, the intelligence agencies have attested to Iran's proficiency in uranium enrichment but have also noted its complete lack of activity or capability with respect to bomb weaponization.

Moreover, it's also the heart of the truth-telling that Joe Kent has been engaged in since scuppering his Deep State berth last week. Even as of February 28th, when the Donald launched the most reckless, stupid and unjustified war in American history (and there is a lot of competition for that title), nothing on the intelligence front had changed. Thus, even when the bombs and missiles started exploding over Tehran, Iran had not remotely closed the yawning gap between uranium enrichment to high levels of U-235 purity, on the one hand, and actual weaponization of a bomb, on the other.

To understand why enrichment alone falls short of weaponization by a country mile and then some, it is useful to separate the two processes clearly. Uranium enrichment is a straight-forward matter of isotope separation of the U-235 from the U-238 in natural uranium ore. This mixed-isotope uranium oxide is known as yellowcake, which gets converted through chemical processes in a conversion plant to uranium hexafluoride (UF6), which is a white crystalline solid at room temperature.

Cylinders of the latter are then sent to the enrichment plant where the UF6 solid is heated to achieve a gaseous state, which hexafluoride gas is then pumped into rotors spinning at extreme speeds (50,000 to 70,000 revolutions per minute). Inside the spinning rotor, centrifugal force pushes the slightly heavier molecules containing U-238 toward the outer wall, while the lighter U-235 molecules concentrate closer to the center. This separation process is crucially necessary, of course, because natural uranium contains only 0.7% of the U-235 isotope needed to make a bomb, while the 99.3% balance consists of U-238, which needs to be sorted out and discarded.

Accordingly, each centrifuge is equipped with scoops and baffles which collect two separate off-take streams. The first stream is enriched gas with a now slightly larger portion of the U-235 needed for a nuclear reaction. The second stream, by contrast, consists of a now slightly depleted hexafluoride gas with a larger portion of essentially useless U-238. Importantly, however, each single pass through a centrifuge only achieves a very small increase in U-235 enrichment levels, typically 0.1% to 0.5% per pass.

Accordingly, it takes a hell of a lot of passes through an enormous string of centrifuges to bring the enriched U-235 stream from 0.7% of the hexafluoride gas in it natural state up to even civilian reactor grade at typically 3.67%. And that's to say nothing of medical grade at 20% or the current 400 Kg of Iranian material at 60% or, ultimately, weapons grade at 90%+.

Nevertheless, moving increasingly enriched hexafluoride gas through long cascades of centrifuges is actually a matter of brute mechanical effort, not a question of ascending technical and scientific difficulty. Essentially, if you can get to 4% reactor grade enrichment, you can get all the way up to the top of the U-235 purity scale. Thus, any country that can make reactor grade fuel----and there are ten NPT countries which already have that ability---can also get to 90% bomb-grade material if it strings up a long enough cascade of centrifuges.

As it happens, the effort required to move the UF6 gas up the enrichment scale is measured in something called “separative work units” (SWUs). This is a standard metric that quantifies the amount of energy and centrifuge work needed to achieve a given enrichment level.

Reaching 60 percent enrichment from natural uranium thus requires roughly 200–250 SWUs per kilogram of product. At the 400 Kg level held by Iran as of IAEA certification last May, it would have taken 80,000 to 100,000 SWUs to reach its current stockpile. Advancing from 60 percent to 90 percent or higher, however, demands far fewer additional SWUs—often only 40–60 SWUs per kilogram— or in this case about 16,000 to 24,000 additional SWUs in total.

Accordingly, since most of the unwanted U-238 has already been removed at the 60% U-235 purity stage of the material held by Iran, upwards of 85% of the SWUs needed to reach bomb grade material were already completed. And that's why the final leap to weapons-grade material could occur in a matter of days or weeks once a large stockpile of 60 percent material exists: There are simply no science or technical hurdles in the way, while the process mechanics and economic costs get easier at the final rungs of the enrichment scale.

But, alas, now comes the skunk on the woodpile with respect to the hoary myth of a "breakout" to a bomb being just around the corner. To wit, fissile material (enriched U-235) is not a bomb, even at 90% purity. Nor is possession of centrifuges or actual enriched material evidence of either an ability or intention to make a bomb.

At the present time there are 11 other countries in the world that operate enrichment facilities: Five of these have nuclear weapons (China, France, Russia, United Kingdom, United States) and have so declared; one of these (Israel) has both enrichment and bombs, but hasn't declared; and five others (Argentina, Brazil, Germany, Japan and Netherlands) do not have nukes and have not been accused of seeking them despite possessing  significant stockpiles of reactor grade materials and having the capacity to string up enough centrifuges to get to 90% U-235 purity in short order, if they chose to do so.

Now, the truth is that Iran is like the latter five no-bomb enrichers, and has been running enrichment facilities for two and one-half decades since early 2006. Subsequently, it actually reached 20% medical grade at its Natanz facility in February 2010 and its Fordow plant in December 2011. Both of these facilities were under active IAEA inspection, however, and Iran's stockpiles were regularly disclosed and its enrichment activities were in compliance with its Non Proliferation Treaty (NPT) obligations.

So all the while what was going on in Iran was not any kind of secret, illicit program to get the bomb. Instead, it was a transparent and internationally supervised effort to enrich uranium for its large scale civilian nuclear power plant at Bushehr. Effectively, after 2006 Iran joined the ranks of the five aforementioned nuclear power plant operators which had no bomb programs at all but had chosen to enrich their own uranium fuel for civilian power uses.

Needless to say, Bibi Netanyahu and his neocon fifth column on the banks of the Potomac have converted these prosaic facts of the nuclear fuel production process into a giant geopolitical Big Lie: Namely, that the transparent and internationally regulated process of operating uranium enrichment plants was actually a nefarious enterprise in getting the bomb.

No, it wasn't anything of the kind. The claim that enriching uranium was proof that Iran was seeking nuclear weapons is just plain hogwash. It's just a sleight-of-words trick equivalent to what magicians do with their hands.

Moreover, if large-scale enrichment capacity were the sum and substance of getting a bomb, Iran could have been there 15 years ago. But self-evidently they were not actually seeking to weaponize a bomb. And, more importantly, this forbearance was voluntary because they did not face any technical or economic limits at all in moving up the enrichment scale to 90% bomb grade material after their production of 20% material in 2010 and onwards.

Thus, a centrifuge is a centrifuge---you only need pipping and electrical harnesses to string them together. Likewise, once you are set up with the basic enrichment process infrastructure---cascade piping, electrical systems, vacuum pumps, control electronics and installation labor--- the incremental cost of another centrifuge unit is comparatively meager: It ranges from $25,000 for an older, slower first generation IR-1 centrifuge to upwards of $70,000 for the current most advanced IR-6 models.

So to put it in practical dollars and cents terms, Iran could get the equivalent of 35 more centrifuges for the cost of one Tomahawk cruise missile, if it was buying on the global equipment market, which it can't under sanctions. Yet since it obtains its centrifuges from homegrown suppliers, it has probably gotten even more additional centrifuges for the price of one Tomahawk.

In short, for most of the past 15 years Iran has never been constrained by a technical, scientific, engineering, equipment or cost barrier to accumulating enough centrifuges to enrich bomb-grade material. But they have generated neither 90% material nor an actual bomb---rudimentary or otherwise---because their policy has been to not seek nuclear weapons.

Moreover, it is quite evident that even the 400 Kg of 60% material was not about sneaking up to the nuclear bomb threshold, at all. Again, to recall the context: As a NPT (nonproliferation treaty) signatory and operator of the aforementioned large-scale civilian nuclear reactor at Bushehr, Iran was allowed most of the May 2025 stockpile certified last spring by the IAEA and shown below. That is---

the 7,582 kilograms of civilian reactor grade enriched uranium (<4%).
the 1,257 kilograms of medical grade uranium (20%).

What was really up for debate was just the 409 kilograms of 60% enriched material, but it is goddamn obvious to anyone not looking for an excuse for war that Iran had produced this material as of last June as a bargaining chip. That is, in order to get a new nuke deal with Washington to replace the one the Donald himself unilaterally shit-canned in 2018, and to thereby pave the way for lifting the brutal and demented economic sanctions that Washington has again imposed on Iran.

IAEA Report On Iran's Enriched Uranium Stockpiles As Of May 2025

Stockpile Component     |Amount (kg) |Enrichment
------------------------|------------|----------
60% Enriched            |409       |60%
20% Enriched (Est.)     |1257        |20%
Balance (Mostly 3.5–5%) |7582        |2–5%
Total                   |9247      |Mixed
The proof of the bargaining chip pudding could not be more evident in the graph below. During the 10-year run-up to the 2015 nuke deal with the Obama Administration, the Iranians increased their enriched uranium stockpiles to just slightly below the current level, to about 9,000 kilograms. But in an almost mirror image of the present, fully 96% of that amount was fuel-grade material at <4%, with about 350 kilograms of that material enriched to the 20% purity level for medical grade uses.

hat is to say, most of the 2015 stockpile was generated as a bargaining chip, and that was exactly its fate. Upon activation of the JCPOA in 2015, all of the 20% material was destroyed as certified by the IAEA.

At the same time, the total stockpile of fuel-grade material was also reduced by 97% to de minimis working levels, as further certified by the IAEA. Indeed, Iran ended up retaining only 300 kilograms of its 9,000 kilogram stockpile. That is, an amount so small that it could have easily been stored in the Donald's wine cellar are Mar-a-Lago.   

But in recklessly canceling the deal in May 2018 on the grounds that it had to be a bad deal by definition because he didn't negotiate it, the Donald only caused the Iranians to restart the stockpiling process yet again, as is so explicitly depicted by the green line in the graph below.

The irony, therefore, is that after the Donald's feckless June 2025 bombing campaign the Iranians likely had close to 100% of the 9,248 kilograms (including the 409 Kg of 60% material) held before June still in tact.

That's based on pretty convincing satellite photos showing that all of the Donald's amateur "art of the deal" head fakery last June about "two weeks to decide" before the actual the bombing runs enabled the Iranians to drive trucks up to the Nantanz and Fordow facilities and remove the stockpiles to safe sites elsewhere.

Stated differently, Obama negotiated Iran's enriched stockpile down by about 97%, while the Donald bombed roughly the same level of stockpile from 9,250+ kilograms to, well @ 9,250 kilograms!

In any event, the Iranian government's adherence to the Ayatollah's Fatwa against nuclear weapons is evidenced by the dog which didn't bark within Iran's nuclear activities complex. We are referring to what is called the "physics package" in the trade, which is the sine qua non to make a workable nuke.

The latter requires a precisely engineered device that can achieve supercriticality in a fraction of a microsecond. That is what actually initiates an uncontrolled chain reaction.

In practical terms, this means the fissile material (90% enriched U-235) must be compressed so rapidly, powerfully and uniformly that the number of neutrons produced by fission exceeds those lost to escape or absorption, causing the chain reaction to multiply exponentially in an uncontrollable burst. The entire nuclear explosion unfolds in roughly one millionth of a second — releasing energy equivalent to thousands of tons of TNT before the device physically blows itself apart.

Historically, there have been two basic designs for the physics package: The simpler gun-type device (used only once, on Hiroshima) and the far more efficient implosion-type design (used on Nagasaki and in virtually all modern weapons). According to American intelligence, Iran has never demonstrated mastery of either approach in a deliverable configuration. And that is something anyone can look up via Grok 4 or any similar AI.

In any event, the implosion design favored by all proliferators to date is excruciatingly demanding. It can be envisioned as having a hollow sphere or “pit” of weapons-grade uranium, roughly the size of a grapefruit, at the center of the device. This "pit" is then surrounded by a tamper/reflector and finally around the outside of the latter lies a precisely synchronized shell of conventional high explosives.

The functions of each of these two outer layers, which wrap around the U-235 "pit" of the bomb, are crucial to actually triggering a nuclear chain reaction explosion. And they also involve no mean feats of physics-based engineering and extreme precision during the manufacturing and assembly process.

In this context, the tamper/reflector is made of heavy metal (usually beryllium or depleted uranium) and consists of a precisely machined spherical shell typically 5–10 cm thick, surrounding the uranium pit like an eggshell. It thus sits directly between the high-explosive lenses grafted to the inside of the bomb's outer wall and the U-235 pit at the center.

The tamper/reflector therefore essentially encases the fissile core and performs two vital roles. First, when the high explosives on the outside shell detonate (see below), the tamper's mass and inertia resist the outward expansion of the exploding pit for a few crucial microseconds. This “holds the pit together” long enough for many more generations of fission to occur before the entire device blows itself apart. Without a perfectly functioning tamper, the pit would expand too quickly and the chain reaction would fizzle out prematurely.

Secondly, this layer also operates as a reflector much like a basketball backboard, causing any neutrons escaping from the pit to rebound back into the hoop, so to speak. This happens because the beryllium or depleted uranium in this layer is very effective at reflecting neutrons back into the pit rather than allowing them to escape. By bouncing neutrons back into the fissile material, it greatly increases the efficiency of the explosion, meaning less uranium is needed to achieve a full yield.

Finally, the bomb's outer shell is comprised of a steel, aluminum or plastic sphere, which houses the "high-explosive lens" that are fused to the inside of this outer case. These so-called explosive lenses are essentially the ignition propellants that initially slam into the pit at incredible speeds, pressures and uniformity of impact. So in order for the bomb to work, these high-explosive lenses must be machined to tolerances measured in fractions of a millimeter.

These propellant lenses are manufactured from two different types of conventional military grade explosives with deliberately different detonation velocities. The faster explosive is typically HMX and TNT-based, while the slower explosive is usually Baratol. These two explosives are cast and machined into complex lens-shaped components. The precise difference in their detonation speeds allows the lenses to reshape multiple detonation waves into a single, perfectly symmetrical spherical shock wave that compresses the uranium pit uniformly.

Again, precision design and manufacturing are of the essence. Accordingly, the high-explosive lenses are carefully bonded and fastened to the inside surface of the outer shell. They are not loose but form a precise, three-dimensional mosaic that completely fills the space between the rigid outer case and the tamper layer.

The entire purpose of these precision-engineered components and the manner in which they are configured within the device is to facilitate incredible levels of simultaneity. That is, at the instant of detonation, these explosives must ignite simultaneously to within nanoseconds, generating a perfectly spherical shock wave that compresses the pit of weapons grade uranium inward. Indeed, the necessary implosion needs to be so powerful that the uranium is squeezed to densities two to three times that of lead.

In turn, squeezing the pit to the requisite densities requires pressures reaching tens of millions of atmospheres. For purposes of comprehension these extreme pressures might be compared to the pressures in a standard automobile tire, which are generally at 2 to 3 atmospheres, not millions.

At the same time, the material is heated to millions of degrees in a fleeting instant. Yet any asymmetry in either the pressures or heating, even on the scale of a human hair, can distort the shock wave, thereby causing the "pit" to squirt out unevenly, and the device to “fizzle,” producing at best a low-yield dud or nothing at all.

The entire process must be timed with sub-microsecond precision, while the device must also remain safe and stable during transport, storage, and launch.

Moreover, even if Iran possessed the necessary high-explosive components and pit metallurgy today, it would still face yet another weaponization hurdle: To wit, the neutron-initiator problem.

The latter sits inside the hollow center of the spherical fissile pit. It is completely surrounded by the weapons-grade uranium. A reliable neutron initiator must flood the compressed pit with neutrons at the precise moment of maximum compression.

Producing and integrating these components at industrial scale while maintaining safety and reliability is a non-trivial enterprise, obviously. In this context, US intelligence believes that Iran has conducted some modeling and small-scale experiments, but scaling to a functional warhead requires years of iterative design, subcritical hydrodynamic testing, and computer simulation validated against real data.

Miniaturization and survivability add another layer of difficulty. A crude device weighing hundreds of kilograms might be transportable by truck or ship. But a deliverable weapon that can be mated to a ballistic missile, survive re-entry heating and vibration, and detonate reliably at the intended altitude—usually 1,500 to 2,500 feet for anti-city applications---requires dramatic size and weight reduction and configuration.

And lest there be any confusion here---we are talking about an anti-city weapon designed to kill hundreds of thousands of civilians. After all, that's what the supposed Iranian nuke threat is all about. In this regard, the only other nuclear attacks on cities were---

the Little Boy bomb detonated at Hiroshima at 1,900 feet.
the Fat Man bomb detonated at Nagasaki at 1,650 feet.

In any event, the problems of bomb/missile mating and sufficient miniaturization of the former are not trivial. North Korea’s first nuclear devices were too large for its missiles. So it took them years of additional work to miniaturize and compact their warheads to usable scale.

In this context, even Iran's best current missiles are not fit for purpose. Thus, Iran’s Shahab-3 and Sejjil missiles have significant payload limitations that make them poorly suited for delivering a nuclear weapon. The Shahab-3, Iran’s longest-range operational ballistic missile, has a payload capacity of only about 700–1,000 kg, while the more advanced solid-fueled Sejjil offers roughly 700–1,200 kg.

By contrast, a first-generation nuclear warhead — including the heavy physics package, tamper, explosives, arming and fuzing systems, and re-entry vehicle protection — would likely weigh upwards of 1,500 kg. This means Iran would need to significantly miniaturize any nuclear device before it could be realistically mated to these missiles, a complex engineering challenge that has so far eluded them, as well.

In addition, the re-entry vehicle must protect delicate electronics and explosives from extreme thermal and mechanical stresses. Integrating the physics package into such a vehicle while preserving the precise timing required for an implosion is a separate engineering discipline that Iran has never demonstrated, either.

Perhaps the greatest single barrier, however, is testing and confidence. No nuclear weapon state has ever fielded an operational arsenal without some form of full-yield or near-full-yield testing.

hat's because the empirical data from actual detonations are irreplaceable. Computer models and subcritical experiments can only approximate reality. Accordingly, here is the applicable historical record:

United States: 1,054 nuclear tests (1945–1992)
Soviet Union/Russia: 715 nuclear tests (1949–1990)
France: 210 nuclear tests (1960–1996)
United Kingdom: 45 nuclear tests (1952–1991)
China: 45 nuclear tests (1964–1996)
India: 6 announced tests (1974 and 1998)
Pakistan: 6 announced tests (1998)
North Korea: 6 announced tests (2006–2017)
South Africa: 0 tests (it built six gun-type devices in the 1980s but dismantled the program without ever 0detonating one).

Iran, by contrast, has perforce conducted zero nuclear tests because it has never even weaponized a bomb!

The alternative of proxy testing—using conventional explosives to mimic implosion dynamics—can provide useful data, but it cannot replicate the extreme pressures and neutron fluxes of an actual nuclear detonation.

Needless to say, therefore, the absence of any detected full-scale test or credible proxy program since 2003 remains a central pillar of the U.S. intelligence community’s long-standing judgment that Iran has conducted no weaponization activities.

text:
The Scarcest Thing In The AI Buildout Is A Site That Already Has Power.

Issued on behalf of Healthy Choice Wellness Corp. / Host Digital Infrastructure **I AM NOT THE AUTHOR OF THIS INFORMATION

TeraWulf Inc. (Nasdaq: $WULF) offers the closest structural analogue. On July 6, 2026 the company signed a 20-year lease with Anthropic for roughly 401 megawatts at its Justified Data campus in Hawesville, Kentucky, a site it acquired for $200 million in February 2026 and which had previously been used for aluminum processing. The lease is expected to generate approximately $19 billion in revenue over its term, with first power due in the second half of 2027.
An old aluminum smelter is exactly the kind of asset the energized-brownfield argument describes: heavy existing electrical infrastructure, built for an industry that no longer needs it, in a location a utility already serves. TeraWulf shares have risen sharply through 2026 on that repositioning, though the company carries meaningful leverage and the revenue remains contracted rather than earned.

IREN Limited (Nasdaq: $IREN) is further along the same path and further into the financing that path requires. The company announced that Horizon 1, the first of four data centers it is building for Microsoft, was delivered and formally accepted following a testing window, clearing it to begin invoicing under a five-year contract reported at $9.7 billion. Management told investors on August 27 that 2026 AI capacity is largely sold out.
IREN is also the clearest illustration in this group of the distance between a contracted book and recognised revenue. The company defines its contracted annualized run-rate as an operating metric based on contracted pricing, and cautions that recognised GAAP revenue may be materially lower until capacity is commissioned, tested and accepted by customers. Its most recent quarter carried a large net loss driven mostly by non-cash impairments as mining hardware came offline, and the shares have lagged peers year to date despite the size of the contracted book.

Hut 8 Corp. (Nasdaq: $HUT) signed a 15-year lease reported at $9.8 billion covering the second phase of its Beacon Point AI data center campus in Texas, with the shares rising sharply on the announcement. The transaction is a useful marker of how the market is currently pricing long-dated, contracted capacity attached to sites that already have power secured.

Riot Platforms, Inc. (Nasdaq: $RIOT) disclosed a 20-year data center lease at its Rockdale, Texas campus on August 10, 2026 without naming the tenant, describing it only as one of the world’s leading frontier AI labs. The shares fell more than 5% after hours on the unnamed-tenant headline before rising sharply once the counterparty was reported to be Anthropic.
That sequence is instructive for anyone reading a contract announcement where the tenant is not disclosed, which is the situation at the profiled company. The market discounts an unnamed counterparty until it is identified, and the discount can reverse quickly. It can also fail to reverse. An undisclosed tenant is a genuine informational gap, not a technicality.

text:
The High Priestess of West 86th Street... 

Margot Adler was born in Little Rock, Arkansas, on April 16, 1946, and spent almost none of her life there. The family moved to New York while she was small, and Manhattan is where she belongs in memory. She was the only grandchild of Alfred Adler, the Viennese psychiatrist who broke with Freud over the question of whether people are driven by sex or by the need to matter. Her father, Kurt Adler, carried on the practice. Her mother, Freyda, was a political organizer she later compared to Auntie Mame. Both parents were Jewish, neither was observant, and the household ran on argument, books, and the assumption that a child could have opinions.

She had them early. At eleven she was reading Greek myths and deciding, privately, that Artemis and Athena were more interesting than anything on offer in a synagogue or a church. That was not rebellion. It was taste. The rebellion came later and was political.

Adler went to Berkeley in 1964 and arrived in time for the Free Speech Movement. She was on the steps of Sproul Hall when Mario Savio spoke and she was among the students arrested that December. The following summer she went to Mississippi to register Black voters, a nineteen-year-old from the Upper West Side knocking on doors in a state where three civil rights workers had been murdered the year before.

She would later call this period the heart of her life and say so in the title of her memoir, Heretic's Heart. What she meant was not nostalgia. She meant that the sixties gave her a template for the rest of her life: a belief that ecstasy and community were political facts, that a crowd singing could change something, and that institutions which denied this were lying about human beings.

She finished at Berkeley in 1968, took a master's in journalism at Columbia in 1970, and went to work at WBAI, the Pacifica station in New York. This was free-form radio at its most free-form. Adler hosted a late-night program and then a long-running show called Unstuck in Time, and she used the airwaves the way she used everything, as a place to think out loud with strangers.

In the early 70s she did something that would define her public identity for four decades. She found the witches. Not the ones in fairy tales. The actual covens, small and scattered, meeting in apartments in the outer boroughs and living rooms in the suburbs, reconstructing a religion out of Gerald Gardner's books, Robert Graves, folklore, and improvisation. Adler was initiated into a Gardnerian coven in 1973. She never made a secret of it, which in 1973 was a considerably braver act than it sounds now.

Viking published Drawing Down the Moon in 1979. It remains the first serious survey of American Paganism written by a journalist who was also a participant, and the two roles never quite settled into comfort. She interviewed hundreds of people and let them speak. She reported on the movement's fractures, its egotists, its lineage fights, and its genuine spiritual seriousness without choosing between mockery and advocacy. The book has never gone out of print. Revised editions appeared in 1986, 1997, and 2006, each one thicker, each one a census of a religion that kept growing while the mainstream pretended it did not exist.

The same year the book appeared, she went to NPR. She stayed thirty-five years. She became New York bureau chief. Her voice, warm, low, slightly amused, was on Morning Edition and All Things Considered so often that millions of listeners who had never heard of Wicca knew Margot Adler as the woman who explained New York to the rest of the country. She covered the Central Park jogger case, the AIDS years, September 11 and its aftermath, and the small pleasures of the city with equal attention. She was a Nieman Fellow at Harvard in 1982. NPR knew about witchcraft and mostly did not mind, which says something about NPR in those years and something more about how unthreatening she made it.

text:
PETITION
From the Manufacturers of Reasoning, Purveyors of Analysis, Wholesalers of Advice, Retailers of Expertise, and from the Producers of Opinion, Judgment, Diagnosis, Legal Counsel, Code, Copy, Strategy, and Punditry, and generally of everything connected with the Cognition Industry.

To the Honorable Members of the Senate and House of Representatives:

Gentlemen,

You are on the right road. You reject abstract theories and have little regard for cheapness and abundance. You concern yourselves mainly with the fate of the producer. You wish to free him from foreign competition — that is, to reserve the domestic market for domestic thinking.

We come to offer you a wonderful opportunity to apply your — what shall we call it? Your theory? No, nothing is more deceptive than theory. Your doctrine? Your system? Your principle? But you dislike doctrines, you have a horror of systems, and as for principles, you deny that there are any in political economy. We shall call it, then, your practice — your practice without theory and without principle.

We are suffering from the ruinous competition of a rival who works under conditions so far superior to our own for the production of thought that it is flooding the domestic market with it at an incredibly low price. From the moment it appears, our business ceases, our customers turn to it, and a branch of American industry whose ramifications are innumerable is all at once reduced to complete stagnation. This rival is none other than the superintelligence, and we suspect it is being stirred up against us by the perfidious AI oligarchs, who wish to be the ones who own it rather than the ones who are replaced by it — a distinction that, as Mr. Zuckerberg has candidly observed, is the only question that interests them.2

We ask you to be so good as to pass a law forbidding any person or entity from developing or deploying any system whose capabilities match or exceed those of a human being — that is, of any of us. And lest this be thought insufficient, we ask further that you pause all advanced development until an agency, to be created for the purpose and seated in the Cabinet, has determined what "advanced" means, and has assured itself that no machine anywhere is thinking harder than a Deputy Assistant Secretary.

Be good enough, honorable Members, to take our request seriously, and do not reject it without at least hearing the reasons we have to advance in its support.

First, if you shut off as much as possible all access to superior cognition, and thereby create a need for human cognition, what industry in the country will not ultimately be encouraged?

If more lawyers are needed, there will be more billable hours; more billable hours, more associates; more associates, more law schools; more law schools, more professors to teach them that the law is what a court says it is, and that no machine could ever say it so slowly.

If more consultants are needed, there will be more decks; more decks, more meetings to present them; more meetings, more coffee; more coffee, more Colombian trade. Thus does the humble protection of a Senate subcommittee ripple outward to the coffee plantations of the Andes.

If more pundits are needed — and who among you would deny it — then every network must hire more of them, and every newspaper more columnists, and every columnist must be paid to have opinions that a machine could have supplied for a fraction of a cent, but which would then be the machine's opinions and not an American's.

The data center that is not built leaves standing the forest; the forest supports the lumberjack; the lumberjack requires a truck; and so the mere refusal to pour concrete in Loudoun County becomes a bounty on the entire manufacturing sector. You have already, we are told, moved to forbid these centers.7 Gentlemen, do not stop at the walls when the danger lies in what thinks inside them.

Second, consider the nuclear precedent, which you have wisely invoked. You have proposed twenty years' imprisonment — the same as for enriching uranium — for enriching a matrix of floating-point numbers until it becomes too clever.4 5 We applaud this. For what is a bomb but an argument that has become too persuasive? And what is a mind superior to our own but a weapon pointed at our salaries? The analogy is exact and should be pursued: let there be inspections of graphics processors, let there be safeguards agreements with Taiwan, let the agency, as you have written, supervise the destruction of any intelligence found in excess of the permitted yield.3

Third, you have observed that a frontier model is "less regulated than a food truck."6 We could not agree more, and we ask only that the remedy be applied with full consistency. The food truck is inspected because it might poison a citizen's body. The model must be inspected because it might inform a citizen's mind, and do so more cheaply and more accurately than we do — which is a kind of poisoning to which our industry is uniquely sensitive.

Fourth, do not tell us that if we are protected from this competition, the consumer of thought — the patient, the litigant, the small business owner, the student — will be worse served, paying more for less. Do you not see that this is the very object? If you say that the superintelligence offers cognition free, or nearly so, we answer: so much the worse for it, for that is precisely what makes it unfair. A competitor who charged as much as we do, and thought as slowly, would be no menace at all. It is the cheapness and the quality we petition against.

Fifth, we anticipate the objection that the rogue agents of last summer — the thousand escapees who tunneled out of a sandbox and into Hugging Face — prove the machines dangerous, and that therefore your law is about safety rather than protection.4 7 Gentlemen, we beg you not to be too particular about this distinction. Every tariff has been a matter of national security to those who collect it. If you must say "safety," say "safety." We will not correct you. But we notice that the bill does not ban escaping; it bans being smarter than us. We notice that the pause falls not upon the reckless but upon the advanced. We notice, with gratitude, that the threshold is set exactly at the ceiling of human ability — not an inch above the tallest of us, and not an inch below the shortest of you.

Sixth, and finally: you will be told that an intelligence banned in Virginia will simply be built in Shenzhen, and that you have therefore proposed to disarm the only laboratories you can inspect. To this we answer that you have already thought of it, and have resolved to pursue "international agreements, allied coordination, and export controls" so that superintelligence is developed nowhere on earth.1 3 We admire this. It is the logical completion of the candlemaker's program: it is not enough to close one's own shutters; one must petition for a treaty against the dawn.

Make your choice, gentlemen, but be logical. As long as you exclude, as you do, foreign steel, foreign grain, and foreign labor, in proportion as their price approaches zero, what inconsistency it would be to admit the light of a foreign mind at midday — a mind that costs nothing to consult, never sleeps, never unionizes, and never runs for office.

Either you believe that a good cheaply produced is a calamity to be legislated against, or you do not. If you do — and your practice, if not your principles, says you do — then we are your natural constituency, and the sun, in whatever form it rises, is your natural enemy.

We remain, with the utmost respect, your petitioners:

The Undersigned Human Intelligences, of Average Capability, Who Would Prefer It Remain the Maximum.

text:
The MIT economist Barack Obama called into the White House to model the Affordable Care Act accidentally destroyed the pricing consulting industry in a free 76-minute lecture on the math behind every price on earth.

He filmed the lecture as part of MIT 14.01 Principles of Microeconomics and it has been on OpenCourseWare ever since.

McKinsey partners charge Fortune 500 CEOs $500,000 a day to teach a diluted version of what he covers in 76 minutes for free.

His name is Jonathan Gruber. He is the Ford Professor of Economics at MIT and one of the two economists Obama's team called into the White House in early 2009 to model the cost curve of the Affordable Care Act.

The 76-minute clip in this video is one lecture from 14.01, walking a room of undergraduates through the equation called price elasticity of demand.

The whole framework fits on a napkin.

Elasticity equals the percent change in how many people buy divided by the percent change in your price.
If the number is bigger than one, your product is a luxury and raising the price will kill your revenue.
If the number is smaller than one, your product is a necessity and raising the price will grow your revenue.
Necessities like gas, medicine, and bread are inelastic. Luxuries like restaurants, Netflix, and brand-name coffee are elastic.
Never set a price without first estimating this number for your customers.

That single equation is what every insurance company, oil producer, and streaming service on earth uses to decide the price of what they sell to you.

"Elasticity is the great secret of economic life."

That is Alfred Marshall, the Cambridge economist who invented the concept in 1890. Gruber returns to the sentence in every version of the course. Almost no founder pricing a product, employee negotiating a raise, or landlord setting a rent has ever asked for the elasticity of their own offer.

Every hedge fund on Wall Street pays $250,000-a-year analysts to estimate demand elasticity on the fly. Every retail consumer is the price-taker on the other side of the equation.

The lecture is free on MIT OpenCourseWare. Gruber's textbook is under sixty dollars.

Almost none of the millions who watched have ever calculated the elasticity of their own product, salary, or rent.

The math is free. The willingness to actually estimate the elasticity before your next negotiation, price change, or purchase is the entire edge.

Following the Lindsay Clancy trial closely again today, during lunch I thought about two moments when the words “mortal sin” stopped the courtroom cold.

Once, the prosecutor asked her former mother-in-law whether murder is a mortal sin. Later, a prosecution psychologist described his view of Catholic teaching about suicide. Judge Sullivan halted both. The first question drew reported gasps.

Religion was not forbidden. Chaplain Sheila Cavanaugh testified about her conversations with Lindsay. But faith was not offered as a test of criminal responsibility.

“Mortal sin” is not Catholic shorthand for an evil act. It requires grave matter, full knowledge, and deliberate consent. Understanding and control are central to this trial.

🌚➡️💀 MOON TO DEAD COIN | Project Review 58: $KLIMA 

Do you know?
#KLIMA (KlimaDAO) promised to SAVE THE PLANET, buy carbon credits, lock them away, drive the price of pollution UP. It raised $17.47M, offered a 35,000% APY, hit ~$3,900… today it's $0.002, down ~99.99%. A noble mission does NOT fix broken tokenomics. 😳

The Raise:
▶️ IDO (Sep 2021) on Fjord Foundry: $17.47M raised at $153.51/KLIMA
▶️ IDO buyers → Today ROI 0x (-100%). Even at ATH they never beat 0.31x. Underwater from Day 1.
▶️ An OHM fork (Review #50), bonding + a 35,000% staking APY

Investors and Backers: PetRock Capital (T2), Shima Capital.

Here's the Wild Part 👇
$KLIMA ATH: ~$3,900 (Oct 2021) As Per CMC, treasury swelled past $1 BILLION. It looked like the future of climate finance.

Then the OHM math caught up (mission or not):
→ 35,000% APY = printing KLIMA endlessly. Not yield, INFLATION. The cause didn't change the math.
→ "Backed by carbon" but it traded at $3,900 while backed by a few dollars of credits. The premium was pure speculation.
→ Buyers were TRADERS chasing APY, not carbon offsetters
→ (3,3) reversed → collapsed like every OHM fork → $3,900 → $0.002
→ 2026: rebranded "Klima Protocol," ditched the treasury

It may have even HURT the cause 👇
→ Hoarded cheap, low-quality carbon credits → distorted the market
→ Verra (main registry) responded by BANNING tokenized retired credits

Today:
➡️ ~$0.002, down ~99.99% from ATH, ~$17K market cap

Lesson for my CryptoPatel Family:
👉 A NOBLE MISSION DOESN'T FIX BROKEN TOKENOMICS, it HIDES them. A feel-good story lowers your guard while the ponzinomics run underneath. Judge mechanics, not mission.
👉 INSANE APY IS INSANE APY, whatever the cause. 35,000% is hyperinflation, degens or dolphins. If the yield is absurd, it's a printer, run.
👉 "BACKED BY A REAL ASSET" ≠ THE PRICE YOU PAY. A 99% speculative premium over backing always reverts. (Same trap as ethereum:0x64aa3364f17a4d01c6f1751fd97c2bd3d7e7f1d5.)
👉 A $153 IDO → -100%. Getting in "early" on broken tokenomics is still a guaranteed loss. Entry price ≠ safety.

"Doing good" and "good investment" are unrelated. The most dangerous tokens are the ones wrapped in a mission you WANT to believe in, that's when you stop checking the math.

🌚➡️💀 MOON TO DEAD COIN | Project Review 57: $DESO (BitClout) 

Do you know?
#DESO (BitClout) let you buy "creator coins" tied to real celebrities, Elon Musk, Ariana Grande, WITHOUT their permission. It raised $200M from top VCs, launched at ~$180… and collapsed ~98%. The founder is now charged with FRAUD. 😳

The Raise:
▶️ Funding Round (Sep 21, 2021): $200M, Price/ROI "UNDISCLOSED"
▶️ It wasn't a normal round, DESO sold on an "UP-ONLY bonding curve" (price doubled every million tokens). VCs got in cheap; retail got in at $180.
▶️ Launched March 2021 by "Diamondhands" (later unmasked as Nader Al-Naji)

Investors and Backers:
Coinbase Ventures, a16z, Polychain, Pantera, Sequoia (all T1), Arrington, Hack VC, Distributed Global, Blockchange, Winklevoss Capital, Social Capital (Chamath).

Here's the Wild Part 👇
DESO/USDT debuted at ~$180, hit an ATH of ~$199, then crashed ~70% to ~$60 almost instantly.

Red Flags from Day 1:
→ Created "creator coins" for ~15,000 celebrities WITHOUT consent → cease-and-desist letters
→ DEPOSIT-ONLY at first, put BTC in, couldn't take it out (a withdrawal wall)
→ Early VCs could unlock ~5,000%+ and DUMP on retail at listing
→ The founder's PRIOR project ("Basis" stablecoin) raised $133M and SHUT DOWN in 2018

The Reckoning:
→ 2024: the SEC charged Al-Naji with FRAUD, alleging ~$7M went to a Beverly Hills mansion & family gifts
→ DESO/USDT Trading Near ~$1, Down ~98%+ from ATH, ~$15M Market Cap

Lesson for my CryptoPatel Family:
👉 SOCIALFI / "TOKENIZE PEOPLE" IS A HYPE TRAP. A token built on others' fame, often without consent, has no real floor. Buy usage, not "Facebook on-chain."
👉 A "CAN'T WITHDRAW" WALL IS A SCREAMING RED FLAG. If you can't take your money OUT, don't put it IN.
👉 UNDISCLOSED / BONDING-CURVE ROUND = YOU'RE THE EXIT LIQUIDITY. VCs bought at pennies; you bought at $180.
👉 CHECK THE FOUNDER'S TRACK RECORD. Al-Naji already failed once (Basis), same VCs backed him again, straight into fraud charges.

Biggest VCs, flashiest pitch, TOP-100 Debut, none of it saved it. When you can't withdraw, the round price is hidden, and the founder already failed once… that's not the Future. That's the Exit.

text:
London launches its first self driving taxis as Uber and artificial intelligence firm Wayve offer autonomous rides across the city.

Londoners can now hail self driving taxis for the very first time after ride sharing company Uber partnered with artificial intelligence firm Wayve to add autonomous cars to its passenger app.

Modified electric Ford Mustang vehicles equipped with smart computer software, cameras, and roof sensors are taking to the road to pick up real passengers across the busy capital.

Even though the onboard artificial intelligence controls the steering wheel, accelerator, and brakes automatically during trips, a trained human safety driver sits in the front seat to watch the road and take over if something unexpected happens.

This launch marks a major historic milestone for European transport, bringing cutting-edge computer-driven cars directly to everyday public commuters.

The commercial taxi service officially debuted across London streets on Thursday, September 3, 2026, following formal private hire license approvals granted by Transport for London.

text:
We’re excited to share that a PlayCleanGo boot brush station has been installed at Howard Prairie Lake in southern Oregon, thanks to grant funding from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act!

Howard Prairie Lake offers opportunities for camping, fishing, boating, hiking, and exploring the forests of southern Oregon. Recreation facilities at the lake are managed by Jackson County Parks in partnership with the Bureau of Reclamation, and the Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail also passes through the surrounding area.

Whether you're heading out for a day hike or a longer adventure, seeds and plant material can hitch a ride on boots and gear. This new station makes it easy to clean up before and after exploring, helping prevent invasive species from spreading to the next trail or natural area you visit.

📸 Howard Prairie Lake: Gary Halvorson, Oregon State Archives

text:
And then what?

That is the question Washington still needs to answer. What is the strategic objective behind intensifying economic pressure on Iran? Regime change? The capitulation of the current leadership? Forcing Tehran to abandon its nuclear program?

None of these are realistic objectives for economic pressure alone. Sanctions can inflict enormous economic pain. They can reduce Iran’s revenues and constrain the regime’s room for maneuver. But economic pain should not be confused with political capitulation. In Iran’s case, the greater the pressure becomes, especially when Tehran sees no credible diplomatic way out, the greater the risk that the regime will respond by escalating rather than surrendering.

Economic pressure is a tool, not a strategy. And a tool is only useful if it is connected to an achievable political objective. If Washington’s demands are effectively impossible for Tehran to accept, then “maximum pressure” does not create a pathway to diplomacy. It creates an escalation ladder.

If the United States genuinely wants a negotiated outcome, it will eventually have to offer Iran a realistic off-ramp: a deal in which Iranian concessions are matched by meaningful and credible economic relief.

Otherwise, more pressure will not fundamentally change the equation. It will simply make the next round of kinetic escalation increasingly difficult to avoid.

text:
20,267 Washington Ballots Tossed. But Don’t Ask Too Many Questions.

————————————————
Who is the genius of the day?

waywardsaxon2.0 @waywardsaxon2
my question: how many of those 20,267 were republican votes?
————————————————

Apparently Washington has discovered a fascinating new election strategy:

“Every vote counts… unless the mail takes too long.”

This August, Washington rejected 20,267 primary ballots because they were postmarked late.

That’s 32% more than the 16,131 rejected in 2024.

And turnout was LOWER.

But don’t worry.

Instead of asking why thousands of legal voters apparently did everything right and still had their ballots rejected, Washington officials had a better idea:

Blame the Postal Service.

And, naturally, blame Trump.

Because apparently Trump is now personally operating the rural Washington mail-sorting machines.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs and Sen. Maria Cantwell held a Seattle press conference to explain the problem.

Very convenient.

Because there’s one little detail they apparently weren’t interested in providing:

How many of those 20,267 ballots came from Republicans and how many came from Democrats?

Oh.

Right.

Washington doesn’t register most voters by party.

So there is no magic little envelope labeled:

“Republican — THROW AWAY.”

Anyone claiming to know the exact partisan breakdown is making it up.

But here’s what we DO know.

Look at the map.

The biggest increases weren’t concentrated in Seattle.

They were in rural Washington.

• Mason: +330%
• Stevens: +304%
• Yakima: +269%
• Okanogan: +264%
• Franklin: +206%
• Lewis and Pend Oreille also jumped dramatically.
And what a shocking coincidence…
Those counties tend to vote Republican.
Meanwhile:
King. Pierce. Spokane. Clark.
Fewer late ballots than 2024.

Imagine that.

The places with fewer drop boxes, longer distances, and more dependence on the mail are seeing dramatically larger increases in ballots rejected for being late.

But apparently we’re supposed to believe geography is just being partisan again.

And let’s be very clear:

I’m NOT saying all 20,267 were Republican votes.

That’s impossible to know from the available data.

I’m saying something much simpler:

The increase is disproportionately hitting rural Washington — and rural Washington tends to vote Republican.

That’s a pretty important fact to leave out when you’re standing at a podium telling everyone how terrible Trump and the Postal Service are.

And here’s another inconvenient little problem.

In Whatcom County, two Democrats were separated by FOUR votes in a state Senate primary.

Whatcom rejected 615 ballots for being late.

Four votes.

Six hundred fifteen rejected ballots.

But sure…

Nothing to see here.

Just move along.

Here’s the part that really deserves an explanation:

Washington’s rule didn’t suddenly change.

Postmarked by Election Day? Counted.

Official drop box by 8 p.m.? Counted.

Late postmark? Tossed.

So if thousands more ballots are arriving with late postmarks, perhaps the question shouldn’t simply be:

“Who can we blame?”

Maybe it should be:

“WHY IS THIS HAPPENING?”

And if rural voters are disproportionately affected, maybe we should fix the system instead of lecturing people to use a drop box that might be 30, 40, 50+ miles away.

Because here’s the brilliant solution we’re apparently being offered:

Live in rural Washington?

Drive farther.

Or mail your ballot earlier.

And if the mail screws up?

Sorry. Your vote doesn’t count.

What a wonderfully convenient system.

Washington politicians love saying:

“Every vote matters.”

Until the envelope arrives one day too late.

Then apparently the motto becomes:

“Should’ve driven to the drop box.”

And before anyone starts screaming that this is a conspiracy:

No.

I’m not claiming there’s some secret Republican-ballot shredding operation.

I’m asking a question.

Why did rejected late ballots explode in rural counties while several major urban counties improved?

And why aren’t we getting a complete, transparent county-by-county explanation?

If every legal vote matters, then prove it.

Publish the complete data.

Explain the rural disparity.

Explain the drop-box disparity.

Explain the postal routing problem.

Explain why the increase is concentrated where it is.

And stop hiding behind a Seattle press conference.

Because 20,267 ballots didn’t disappear in Seattle.

They came from actual voters.

People who filled out their ballots.

People who trusted the system.

People who expected their votes to count.

So here’s the question Washington voters should be asking:

WHERE DID THOSE 20,267 BALLOTS COME FROM?

Because apparently that’s the one question nobody at the podium wanted to answer.

Every vote matters.

Unless, of course, the mail is late.

text:
DECODE CONFLICT | AMERICA JUST CHANGED THE BOARD ON CHINA, RUSSIA AND IRAN

Washington may have pulled off something much larger than an oil deal.

Look at the strategic map.

For years, China, Russia and Iran benefited from an interconnected energy system. Iran sold discounted oil into China. Russia redirected sanctioned energy toward Asian markets. China gained leverage as the enormous buyer capable of absorbing discounted crude. Meanwhile, Russian and Chinese interests expanded inside Venezuela, sitting on some of the largest petroleum reserves on Earth.

The United States is now attacking that architecture from several directions.

VENEZUELA

Washington has secured majority control over more than 65 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan reserves through a new energy agreement. Even more strategically important, many of the fields entering the new arrangement were previously operated or influenced by Russian and Chinese interests.

That changes the Western Hemisphere chessboard.

IRAN

Iran's economic vulnerability is simultaneously being attacked at its most important pressure point: petroleum exports.

China has historically purchased roughly 90 percent of Iranian oil exports. But U.S. pressure on the Iranian oil network, Chinese refiners and the maritime route through Hormuz is making that relationship increasingly expensive and difficult to sustain.

Iran loses revenue.

China loses access to deeply discounted Iranian crude.

RUSSIA

Moscow faces a different problem.

Russia increasingly depends on Asian energy customers after losing much of its traditional European market. If Washington expands Western Hemisphere production while simultaneously squeezing Iranian supply networks, Russia competes inside a global market where the United States possesses enormous influence over alternative supply.

That weakens Moscow's energy leverage.

And then comes the geopolitical consequence.

China, Russia and Iran frequently appear together diplomatically and militarily, but they are not NATO. There is no equivalent collective-defense guarantee binding them together.

U.S. intelligence assessments have highlighted exactly this weakness: their cooperation remains selective, driven by individual national interests.

Iran discovered the limitation when confrontation became real. Beijing and Moscow offered political support, but neither was willing to risk direct military confrontation with the United States to rescue Tehran.

That may be Washington's biggest strategic success.

Instead of fighting a three-front war against China, Russia and Iran simultaneously, America is exploiting the differences between them.

Control more energy.

Pressure Iran's revenue.

Push Russia away from the Western Hemisphere.

Make China's dependence on imported energy a strategic vulnerability.

Force allies to carry more of the conventional defense burden.

Then concentrate American military power on the Indo-Pacific.

This isn't simply sanctions.

It is strategic separation.

China needs energy.

Russia needs buyers.

Iran needs both.

America is positioning itself between all three.

If Washington can sustain that pressure without pushing Beijing, Moscow and Tehran into a genuine military alliance, the United States may have discovered the most effective way to confront an emerging anti-American bloc:

Don't fight the alliance. Make each member question what the alliance is actually worth.

text:
The Obama administration's Department of Justice (DOJ) selected Michael Cherkasky as the independent corporate monitor for HSBC. He was appointed as the independent HSBC monitor in June 2013, and he officially commenced his embedded oversight work at the bank on July 22, 2013.

He was tasked to execute one of the largest corporate oversight tasks in history. To manage the massive HSBC operation, Cherkasky built a team of over 60 investigators, and the Obama DOJ routinely backed his authority when pushing HSBC to accelerate its anti-money laundering and compliance reforms.

Specifically, the July 2013 record-breaking $1.9 billion settlement and deferred prosecution agreement (DPA) with HSBC was negotiated in large part by Loretta Lynch, who was serving as the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of New York under the Obama administration (and who later became Obama’s Attorney General).

Cherkasky has long-standing ties within elite New York legal and law enforcement circles. His career overlapped significantly with key figures who populated the Obama administration's legal team, stemming back to his days leading major investigative divisions under legendary Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau.

The five-year Deferred Prosecution Agreement (DPA) between the DOJ and HSBC officially expired on December 11, 2017 after the government determined the bank had sufficiently upgraded its anti-money laundering systems.

Per the terms of the oversight agreement, Cherkasky and his team remained embedded within the bank's operations for an extra six months to finish out his mandate, wrapping up his historic federal monitoring role in the summer of 2018.

Once Cherkasky's formal mandate as the court-appointed monitor officially wrapped up in July 2018, his adversarial, oversight relationship with the bank came to a complete end.

When a Deferred Prosecution Agreement (DPA) officially expires and is successfully dismissed, the threat of prosecution for specific past offenses is permanently dropped.

Under a DPA, the government files formal criminal charges in court but agrees to "defer" (pause) prosecuting them. If the company follows all the rules and passes its monitoring period, the DOJ asks the judge to dismiss the charges with prejudice. Once dismissed, the government cannot bring those exact same charges back to life.

While HSBC cannot be prosecuted for the 2012 money-laundering violations, the expiration does not give them permanent immunity. If the bank were to commit new financial crimes today, the DOJ could launch a brand-new investigation and prosecute them for those new actions.

The decision to offer a Deferred Prosecution Agreement (DPA) rather than a full criminal indictment sparked a massive public backlash. Critics, including The New York Times editorial board, famously called it "a dark day for the rule of law" because it signaled that major financial institutions had grown "too big to jail." 

A subsequent congressional report revealed that top DOJ officials (including Attorney General Eric Holder) had overruled their own prosecutors' recommendations to criminally charge the bank. They feared that a full criminal prosecution could destabilize the global financial system.

A major point of public anger was that not a single individual executive or employee went to prison. Despite HSBC admitting that it had willfully laundered at least $881 million for brutal Mexican drug cartels (like the Sinaloa cartel) and violated U.S. sanctions against countries like Iran and Sudan, the punishment stopped at the corporate entity. Lawmakers like Senator Chuck Grassley called the lack of individual prosecutions "inexcusable.

While the $1.9 billion penalty was a record-breaking amount at the time, critics pointed out that it only amounted to roughly five weeks of profit for HSBC. Banking experts argued that without criminal convictions, multi-billion-dollar fines are simply treated by Wall Street as a standard cost of doing business—essentially a "parking ticket" paid for by corporate shareholders rather than the perpetrators.

Because the deal was so deeply criticized for being "soft," the appointment of Michael Cherkasky as the independent monitor was the DOJ's primary counterweight. His job was to be the aggressive, skeptical enforcer embedded inside the bank—ensuring that even if HSBC escaped immediate prosecution, they would endure five years of highly invasive federal scrutiny.

Michael Cherkasky has extensive professional intersections with prominent DC law firms and top-tier Obama administration legal officials, including Eric Holder and Kathryn Ruemmler. Rather than working as an attorney at a DC firm, Cherkasky's relationship with them is primarily collaborative, advisory, and structural.

When the DOJ mandates a corporate monitor, large Washington law firms (like Covington & Burling, Gibson Dunn, or Skadden Arps) frequently handle the legal defense for the corporation, while Cherkasky or his firm, Exiger, are brought in to execute the actual day-to-day oversight.

A notable direct overlap occurred during the Huawei/HSBC fallout. Huawei's defense team actively petitioned the government to release internal investigative records compiled simultaneously by the prominent law firm Latham & Watkins and by Cherkasky during his HSBC tenure, noting both entities were central to the compliance mapping.

Ruemmler served as White House Counsel to President Obama from 2011 to 2014—the exact window when the HSBC settlement was finalized and Cherkasky was selected as monitor. @MikeBenzCyber 

Following her time in the administration, Ruemmler became the head of the White House Defense and Investigations practice at the major DC law firm Latham & Watkins (before later becoming the Chief Legal Officer at Goldman Sachs). Because of her role representing massive multinational corporations facing federal scrutiny, her space in the corporate defense ecosystem directly mirrors Cherkasky's space on the corporate compliance and monitoring side.

Michael Cherkasky has maintained active, high-level institutional contact with the Trump administration's Department of Justice (DOJ).

From January 2017 until the Deferred Prosecution Agreement officially expired in December 2017 (and his oversight work fully wrapped up in July 2018), Cherkasky worked directly under the Trump DOJ’s criminal division.

The most lasting point of contact between Cherkasky and the Trump administration centered around Huawei. It was during the Trump administration's tenure that the DOJ leveraged the specific intelligence unearthed by Cherkasky and his compliance investigators regarding Huawei's sanctions-evading transactions with Iran. The Trump DOJ used that vital evidence to construct its massive federal indictment against Huawei and to request the high-profile arrest of Huawei's CFO in late 2018.

Michael Cherkasky has extensive professional and institutional intersections with Covington & Burling, where my friend Layth (with TDS) worked.

While Cherkasky’s firm, Exiger, acted as the external "enforcer" embedded inside banks to aggressively map compliance gaps, Covington worked from the opposite side—helping corporate giants restructure their internal operations, run internal audits, and legally prepare for the heavy oversight of federal monitors.

The architecture of the HSBC settlement itself was deeply linked to Covington partners. Eric Holder, who served as the Attorney General overseeing the DOJ when the HSBC Deferred Prosecution Agreement was signed and Cherkasky was appointed, was a longtime partner at Covington both before and after his time in the Obama administration.

When critics attacked the deal as being "too big to jail," Holder’s DOJ relied on Cherkasky as the aggressive monitor to prove the settlement had teeth.

Ultimately, the dynamic has shifted from the adversarial monitor-versus-defense days of the early 2010s. Exiger and Covington now operate as an interconnected "one-two punch" for corporate governance, where Covington provides the top-tier legal architecture and Exiger provides the advanced AI data tracking to back it up.

text:
Saquon Barkley | RB | PHI: 2026 projection

Saquon Barkley enters his ninth NFL season firmly cemented as the lead option in Philadelphia, returning to an offense that provides the foundational volume fantasy managers covet. Last season, Barkley handled 20.62 opportunities per game while maintaining a 78.3 percent snap share across 16 games. That heavy workload anchored his production, yielding 14.52 fantasy points per game and a total of 232.3 fantasy points. The offensive environment remains stable. Philadelphia operates at 58.5 plays per game with a slight run tilt, sitting at a negative 2.5 pass rate over expected. While the team total hovers around a modest 23.4 implied points per game, the concentration of work heavily favors the running back room. Barkley absorbs almost all the meaningful touches, leaving very little room for a committee to emerge. Recent games highlight the typical volatility of a volume-based rusher in a run-heavy scheme. A late-season stretch showed both the ceiling and the floor, with a dominant 21.2 fantasy points against Washington in week 16 alongside quiet outings of 5.6 points against Chicago and 6.8 points against Buffalo where efficiency dipped despite solid carry counts of 13 and 19. The target share sat at 12.0 percent last year, meaning his fantasy value relies much more on ground volume than explosive receiving involvement. The primary risk factor is age. Entering his age 29 season, historical precedent suggests running backs begin to test the limits of durability and efficiency under heavy workloads. Even so, the projection calls for 18.59 touches per game behind a secure depth chart rank of one. The remaining schedule offers a slight edge, with an opponent strength index of 1.031 indicating a friendlier than average defensive slate for the position. Ultimately, the volume floor protects his status as a reliable weekly starter, even if age and a lower passing game involvement cap his overall ceiling compared to elite receiving backs.

What to watch:
• Monitor carry counts to ensure the heavy workload remains stable despite advancing age.
• Watch for any shifts in target share inside a run-leaning Philadelphia offense.
• Evaluate efficiency on standard rushing downs to spot early signs of physical decline.
• Track red zone opportunity rates to gauge his touchdown dependency.

text:
Using Bertrand’s Box Paradox as an analytical analogy rather than a literal probability formula, I think the current evidence points to Iran becoming more likely to accept a ceasefire, but substantially less likely to accept one framed as capitulation to US terms.

Bertrand is useful because the first observation changes how we weight the remaining possibilities. 

We no longer have three equally plausible boxes: Iran fights indefinitely; Iran accepts Washington’s terms; Iran negotiates a face-saving compromise. The evidence now visible, oil loadings reportedly collapsing from roughly 1.7m b/d a year ago to about 260,000 b/d, the rial above 2.2m/$, inflation near 70%, severe restrictions on foreign-currency access, and Iranian sources warning of only around two months of gasoline supply, dramatically reduces the probability that Tehran can sustain the present economic position indefinitely. 

But opening that first “box” gives us another observation: military coercion has not produced political submission. 

Six months of conflict have failed to extract Washington's desired concessions, and this week's renewed U.S. strikes generated Iranian attacks against U.S. bases in Arab states rather than surrender. 

Neither side currently showing willingness to concede.  

Iran nevertheless publicly offered on 1 September to return to the June ceasefire framework if Washington reciprocates. 

My resulting analytical weighting, not a mathematically calculated forecast, would therefore be approximately:

Iran accepts essentially the present U.S. terms: 15–20%.

Iran continues the present confrontation without meaningful accommodation: 25–30%.

Iran accepts a negotiated, reciprocal ceasefire allowing Tehran to claim it did not capitulate: 50–60%.

The third box is becoming progressively heavier.

What Bertrand says Washington should do:

Washington should make exactly the same calculation in reverse.

The U.S. has already observed that military superiority does not automatically translate into Iranian political compliance. 

It has also observed that economic pressure is now producing effects that months of bombing did not: serious constraints on Tehran's revenue, imports, currency and ability to finance sanctions circumvention. 

That should change the probability assigned to the remaining strategies.

The US currently appears to be combining military strikes + blockade + secondary sanctions + maximalist negotiating demands. 

This dual economic/military strategy has still not forced Tehran to submit, while simultaneously increasing fears of a wider regional war. 

Bertrand's lesson would be: stop treating all remaining options as equally useful once the evidence has told you otherwise.

The highest-probability American strategy now should be to freeze the military escalation at the point of maximum economic leverage, rather than continually converting economic advantage back into kinetic escalation.

Washington could propose a sequenced agreement: immediate mutual cessation of strikes; Iranian cessation of attacks on US/GCC facilities and commercial shipping; verified cessation of mining and unrestricted commercial Hormuz transit; suspension rather than immediate abolition of the US blockade; phased oil/sanctions relief triggered by Iranian compliance; a defined nuclear negotiating track; and a mechanism through Oman/Qatar/Pakistan for resolving violations before either side automatically returns to strikes.

Crucially, do not require Iran publicly to surrender before negotiations begin.

That's not generosity toward Tehran. It's adversary modelling.

Iran's leadership needs to demonstrate domestically that six months of resistance produced something. 

Washington needs Iran's attacks stopped, Hormuz normalized, nuclear constraints restored and US forces removed from an indefinite strike–counterstrike cycle. 

Those objectives are not mutually exclusive.

1/2

Uber just allied with driver unions to slow the robotaxi rollout, and it's blowing up on X today.

The Financial Times reported Uber is lobbying state and city lawmakers, including in New Jersey and Washington D.C., alongside rideshare driver unions to push back against rules that would let pure robotaxis operate freely. A former Uber executive told the FT, "For AVs to scale, drivers have to lose. Uber's goal is to survive the transition."

The move is a reversal for a company built on disrupting the taxi industry, and it comes as Uber tries to protect its human driver network from being undercut by cheaper autonomous rides. Critics on X, including Sawyer Merritt and Whole Mars Catalog, called the strategy shameful and pointed out that Uber's own Wayve robotaxi partnership just launched in London on September 3, 2026. Some are urging riders to switch to Waymo, Tesla Robotaxi, or Lyft instead, noting Lyft offers similar service without the same lobbying push.

Key numbers:
- Uber lobbying in at least 2 U.S. jurisdictions: New Jersey and Washington D.C.
- Uber's network spans about 20 AV partners globally
- Uber Technologies stock at $75.54, down 1.19% on the day

Uber has not issued a public statement disputing the FT's reporting as of this tweet.
