text:
$CVX $PTEN $SLB $HAL VENEZUELA UPSTREAM RESTART — Q2 2026 EARNINGS SYNTHESIS ACROSS THE E&P, OILFIELD SERVICE AND DRILLING COMPLEX

Consolidated review of Q2 2026 (and HP fiscal Q3 2026) earnings calls, sell-side research and expert network commentary, current through September 3, 2026.

BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT

Venezuela has moved from an uninvestable jurisdiction to the single most-discussed incremental growth opportunity in oilfield services inside of eight months. But the Q2 2026 earnings season revealed a sharply stratified reality: a small group of companies is already generating Venezuelan revenue, a second group is negotiating, and a third — including every Tier 1 offshore driller — is simply watching. The dispersion between those tiers is where the alpha sits.

Only Chevron is materially producing. Its three joint ventures went from 40,000 b/d to 280,000 b/d in the six months preceding its Q2 call — a 7x ramp representing roughly 25% of Venezuela's total oil supply — and it has since committed $7 billion over five years targeting ~600,000 b/d.

SLB and Nabors are the only service names with in-country operational continuity, having maintained skeleton maintenance workforces throughout the sanctions period. That footprint is the scarce asset; it is not replicable on a two-quarter timeline.
The activity is onshore and intervention-led, not drilling-led. Only two onshore rigs were operating in Venezuela per the July 2026 Baker Hughes worldwide count. Larger drilling programs are a late-2027 event; new well construction at scale is a 2028–2029 event; deepwater is 2028 at the earliest.
Management tone is uniformly measured, and deliberately so. No company outside Chevron has committed Venezuela-specific capital or disclosed Venezuela-specific capex. The language across calls — "discussions proceeding slowly," "medium-term opportunity," "exciting growth opportunity" — is optionality language, not guidance language.
Argentina, not Venezuela, is where Latin America capital is actually going in 2026. Every onshore driller with LatAm exposure is funding Vaca Muerta ahead of Venezuela, which is the clearest tell on relative near-term conviction.

THE 2026 GEOPOLITICAL RESET

The backdrop conditioning every management comment this quarter is without modern precedent in the sector.

January 2026 — Nicolás Maduro was captured by US forces, followed within weeks by a general license lifting key energy sanctions in late January.

January 2026 — Venezuela reformed its hydrocarbons law, the legal predicate for foreign operators to re-contract.

March 2026 — Additional sanctions relief was granted as the Iran war drove crude prices higher, adding a supply-security rationale to the policy shift.
April 2026 — Oilfield service providers began mobilizing long-idled equipment, refurbishing rigs held in storage while producers renegotiated contract terms.
Late August / early September 2026 — The US government took a direct commercial role under a historic arrangement including board veto rights and right of first refusal on crude production.
Two features of this framework deserve underwriting attention. First, the new oil law requires operators to supply their own power generation, insulating operations from a chronically unreliable national grid — a real capex line item and a genuine competitive advantage for integrated players. Second, sanctions relief is broad but not uniform: the US froze the assets of a Florida oil magnate with Venezuelan JV interests as recently as August 2026, confirming that selective enforcement survives the general license.
The corporate response has been asymmetric. Major US oil executives voiced caution directly to President Trump in January 2026 even as he pressed the industry to commit at least $100 billion. As of August 2026, smaller wildcatters are moving faster than the majors — ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips remain conspicuously absent two decades after the nationalization of their assets. That reluctance is the pricing mechanism for everyone else's entry terms.

THE INVESTMENT REQUIREMENT AND THE SEQUENCING OF WORK

Restoring Venezuela to historical peak output is estimated to require upwards of $100 billion in total investment, roughly $10 billion per year, reflecting decades of corruption, underinvestment, fires and theft. That number is the ceiling on the opportunity. The sequencing determines who captures it and when.

Now through 2026 — intervention phase. Immediate demand is for well testing, artificial lift and well interventions to reactivate existing wellbores. This is a services-and-consumables market, not a rig market. It is why SLB and Halliburton are ahead of the drillers.

2027 — drilling program phase. Halliburton has confirmed discussions with four to five well-known customers on larger drilling programs with a potential start in late 2027. Nabors and PTEN sit here.

2028–2029 — new well construction at scale. Real greenfield well construction is unlikely to begin in earnest before this window, per expert network commentary.

2028 and beyond — offshore. Deepwater development requires a stable legal framework, durable fiscal terms and infrastructure investment that no analyst expects to materialize sooner.
The practical implication: revenue recognition timing, not resource potential, is the differentiating variable in 2026–2027 estimates. A company can be entirely correct about Venezuela's long-term scale and still contribute nothing to the next four quarters of earnings.

TIER 1 — COMPANIES WITH BOOTS ON THE GROUND
CHEVRON — THE ANCHOR OPERATOR

Chevron is the only Western company for which Venezuela is already a P&L event rather than a narrative.

Production: Three JVs ramped from 40,000 b/d to 280,000 b/d over six months, described by management as proceeding in line with prior communications. Targeting up to 50% additional growth by year-end 2028, contingent on further US authorization and supportive fiscal terms.

Portfolio consolidation: An asset swap with PDVSA lifted Chevron's Petroindependencia stake to 49% and secured rights to develop the Ayacucho 8 area.

Post-call escalation: On September 2, 2026 — after the Q2 call — Chevron formally announced a $7 billion five-year investment plan targeting ~600,000 b/d, including the newly awarded Carabobo 1 and Carabobo-2 fields in the Orinoco Belt.

Capital discipline is intact. Q2 organic capex was $4.4 billion; FY26 guidance remains $18–19 billion with management pointing to the lower end. The broader $18–21 billion range carries flexibility toward the high end for opportunistic long-cycle assets, Venezuela among them.

Fiscal terms are the binding constraint. Management confirmed active, confidential negotiations with the Venezuelan government, framing its 100-year in-country history as the basis for those talks — while stating plainly that terms must compete within Chevron's global portfolio to attract capital.
Analyst questioning centered on ramp durability rather than ramp magnitude. Management flagged political stability, contract sanctity and framework durability as the conditions for long-term capital, and analysts noted that growth beyond the self-funded program requires fiscal terms supporting incremental investment. Expert commentary reinforces the point: the gating factors are sanctions, licensing and payment protection — not technical capability.

SLB — FROM FRAMEWORK TO REVENUE
SLB has the clearest line of sight to Venezuelan revenue among the large-cap service names.
Management characterized Venezuela as an "exciting growth opportunity" where it can expand existing operations, having retained a small in-country workforce for asset maintenance throughout the sanctions era.

SLB has agreed to deploy digital technology and reactivate up to 15 rigs.

The business is described as moving from a framework stage to revenue generation, with work scopes mobilizing over the coming months and a significant exit rate targeted into 2027.

Q2 delivered broad-based international growth with sequential revenue gains across every division except the Middle East; Latin America — Brazil, Guyana and Mexico — was a named growth driver.

Valuation is already carrying the option. SLB's price target embeds a premium 11.0x 2027E EV/EBITDA versus an 8.5x historical multiple, explicitly to reflect Venezuela potential. This is the key risk to the long case: the setup is partially in the price.

HALLIBURTON — INTERVENTION FIRST, DRILLING LATE 2027
Halliburton delivered its highest Q2 international revenue in over a decade despite Middle East disruption from the Iran war, guiding to low double-digit international growth ex-Middle East for full-year 2026. Latin America revenue rose 14.9% year-over-year to $1.1 billion.
On the Q1 call management reported that Venezuelan facilities were in better shape than expected, with positive commercial term discussions.
On the Q2 call, Halliburton confirmed discussions with four to five well-known customers on larger drilling programs with a potential late-2027 start, while identifying intervention work as the near-term entry point, potentially returning later in 2026.

Venezuela is a component of the company's broader international growth engines, projected to add $2.5–3 billion in revenue by 2028.

NABORS — THE LEGACY RIG PLATFORM WITH THE LARGEST RELATIVE UPSIDE
Nabors offers the highest-beta rig exposure to a Venezuelan drilling restart, precisely because its base is so depressed.
Five active rigs today versus 85+ in 2013. The company has maintained local staff and cites a nearly 70-year in-country history; several large operators have expressed interest in restarting programs.
Internationally, Nabors is tracking opportunities for over 40 incremental rigs across 10 countries, with Venezuela implicitly in that pipeline.

Near-term guidance is Argentina-driven: 94–96 international rigs in Q3 2026 versus 93 in Q2, with FY26 EBITDA guidance of $920–930 million.

The read-through is straightforward — a return toward even a fraction of the 2013 rig count is a step-function event for Nabors' international margin base that is not in consensus estimates.

TIER 2 — ONSHORE DRILLERS HOLDING OPTIONALITY, NOT COMMITMENT

PATTERSON-UTI (PTEN)
PTEN offered the most direct Venezuela commentary of any pure-play driller, and simultaneously the most explicit deferral.

Management noted interest from parties looking to increase production in Venezuela, particularly in the Orinoco Belt for heavy oil, while cautioning that discussions are expected to proceed slowly.

The Colombia exit is the strategic hinge. PTEN is withdrawing from contract drilling there due to aging assets and a deteriorating political environment, taking roughly $20 million in non-cash Q2 charges and redirecting freed capital to higher-return opportunities or shareholder returns. Expert commentary indicates PTEN had considered relocating assets to Venezuela if Colombian operations softened.

PTEN holds idle US assets redeployable internationally at moderate capex — to Argentina, the Middle East or, plausibly, Venezuela — provided long-term customer contracts are in hand.

Q2 was a clean beat. Revenue of $1,228 million (+10% q/q); completion services revenue of $753.6 million against a $702.5 million consensus; adjusted EBITDA of $232 million, ~5% above the $220 million guidance midpoint; net loss of $0.05 per share inclusive of the Colombia charges. The company closed the quarter with $203 million in cash, no borrowings against its $500 million facility, and net leverage of 1.2x expected to decline in H2 as free cash flow improves. FY26 adjusted FCF is expected to exceed dividend payments.

FY26 capex is maintained at $600 million, a 20% year-over-year increase: $60 million to drilling services (rig upgrades — larger structures, enhanced circulating systems, digital and automation), $75 million to completion services (Emerald natural gas-powered frac fleets, with older diesel assets retiring in H2), and $19 million to drilling products. No Venezuela capex was disclosed or guided; all international capital is directed to Argentina and the Middle East.

Q3 guidance implies momentum: roughly 100 average drilling rigs with potential to exit above that level, EBITDA guidance ~8% above consensus, and completion services gross profit of ~$140 million (+14% q/q) at near-full utilization. New contract rig pricing is up 10–15% versus Q1 2026, with upgraded rigs commanding several thousand dollars per day above standard super-spec rates.
PTEN is now the only remaining North American pure-play service company, making it fully levered to US onshore activity and spending. Barclays raised its price target to $16 from $15 (Overweight) on 2026/2027 EBITDA of $943 million and $1,087 million.
HELMERICH & PAYNE (HP)
HP's fiscal year ends September 30; its fiscal Q3 2026 call on August 6, 2026 covers the quarter ended June 30, 2026 — calendar Q2.
Management has described Venezuela as a medium-term opportunity with ongoing discussions, while stating clearly that near-term Latin America growth is Argentina-driven.
Expert commentary is materially more cautious than management's. HP's South American asset base is described as a significant problem, with many rigs very old and maintained via a "duct tape and zip tie approach." South American crude also requires a more cost-prohibitive commercialization process, making operators reluctant to return to the region. This is the single most skeptical data point in the entire Venezuela complex and should temper any assumption that HP's existing regional fleet is deployable into a restart.
Q3 FY26 was a mixed print with a strong reaction. Revenue of $1.034 billion beat the $988.7 million consensus; adjusted EPS of -$0.11 missed the +$0.13 estimate. Latin America and Offshore contributed significantly, and Latin America drove a meaningful sequential increase in direct margins. The stock surged the most in more than a year on August 6, with CEO Trey Adams citing an activity uptick led by North America, supplemented by Argentina growth and the Middle East recovery.

International revenue now exceeds one-third of the total following the 2024 KCA Deutag acquisition. Net leverage fell below 2x, with debt repayment prioritized ahead of potentially increased capital returns in 2027.

FY26 international rig count guidance is maintained at 58–68 rigs (midpoint 63), with fiscal Q4 international direct margin of $25–45 million — the unusually wide band reflecting Middle East conflict uncertainty. Saudi Arabia stands at 22 rigs with reactivations progressing slower than planned, though HP expects continued commercial momentum into 2027 as national oil companies grow production. A third FlexRig has been exported to Australia's Beetaloo Basin.

No Venezuela capex was disclosed. Venezuela is a watch item, not a capital commitment. Notably, HP has seen more material upward estimate revisions than most peers since the end of April 2026, driven by international activity recovery — none of which requires Venezuela to materialize.
EQUIPMENT AND PRESSURE CONTROL — CACTUS (WHD) IS THE MOST CONCRETE NEAR-TERM BENEFICIARY OUTSIDE TIER 1
Cactus is a wellhead and pressure control manufacturer rather than a driller, and its business model front-runs rig activity — equipment ships before wells are drilled.
Management flagged early Latin America pressure control interest, citing Venezuela's legacy installed base as a longer-term opportunity. The Cactus International segment already has a Latin American footprint through its Spoolable Technologies and Pressure Control businesses, positioning it directly for Venezuelan field reactivations.
Q2 was a substantial beat: revenue of $450 million and adjusted EBITDA of $133 million, roughly 30% above estimates, driven by stronger-than-expected Middle East pressure control shipments and accelerated Latin American spoolable deliveries.
Spoolable Technologies revenue rose 17.4% sequentially to $106 million, with international orders exceeding $80 million shipping into 2027. Subsequent to quarter-end the company received international purchase orders exceeding $130 million across Spoolable Technologies and Pressure Control.

The international backlog is expected to clear in 2H27/28, which is where the real earnings inflection sits.

Here's the truth about Follett:
The Follett sermon was given by Joseph Smith at the April 7, 1844, conference of the Church in Nauvoo, Illinois, attended by thousands of Mormons. It's quoted in full in the History of the Church, Vol. 6, pgs. 302 - 317. It was also published in the LDS magazine Ensign in Apr & May 1971.

The sermon is foundation for LDS beliefs about the nature of God, and it culminates Smith's transition from a trinitarian belief to full-blown polytheism. Note how his Discourse gets repeated elsewhere in LDS publications:
     - "It is the first principle of the gospel to know for a certainty the character of God, and to know that we may converse with Him as one man converses with another, and that He was once a man like us; yea, that God himself, the Father of us all, dwelt on an earth, the same as Jesus Christ Himself did;" (Follett)
     - "First, God himself, who sits enthroned in yonder heavens, is a man like unto one of yourselves, that is the great secret. . . . I am going to tell you how God came to be God. We have imagined that God was God from all eternity. . . . God himself; the Father of us all dwelt on an earth the same as Jesus Christ himself did. . . ." (Times and Seasons, vol. 5, Aug 15, 1844, pp. 613-14)
     - "Joseph Smith taught: “It is the first principle of the Gospel to know for a certainty the Character of God. … He was once a man like us; … God himself, the Father of us all, dwelt on an earth, the same as Jesus Christ himself did...” (Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, sel. Joseph Fielding Smith [1976], 345–46)." (Gospel Principles (online), Ch. 47; book form, 2009, pg. 279)

Mormons continue to try to hide the truth of the sermon by claiming no real record exists, but that is untrue:
     - “There is no complete or verbatim record of what Joseph said, but several individuals took notes, making this one of Joseph’s best-recorded sermons.” (LDS Topics on the subject)
     - “Several of his listeners recorded accounts of the address contemporaneously, including three scribes from the President’s Office, making it the best recorded of his discourses. The reporters included Willard Richards, Wilford Woodruff, Thomas Bullock, and William Clayton. Because none of these individuals recorded the address stenographically, none of the accounts provides a complete record of what Smith said on that occasion. On 15 August 1844, the church newspaper Times and Seasons offered the first published account of the discourse, a version amalgamating Bullock’s and Clayton’s independent reports. Other amalgamated versions were produced later, including the now well-known version prepared in the 1850s for the “Manuscript History of the Church” by Jonathan Grimshaw, a clerk in the Church Historian’s Office.” (The Joseph Smith Papers)

text:
MOATS GET MEASURED IN CENTS, NOT ADJECTIVES. COPART $CPRT KEEPS 36 CENTS OF EVERY SALES DOLLAR:

Copart at $33.45, +$1.29 / +4.00% today. The Dallas company runs the online auctions where totaled cars end up: an insurer writes off your wreck, and it gets sold here to dismantlers, rebuilders and exporters. It is the cleanest working example of a word that gets used constantly and defined almost never.

A moat is not a good product. Not a loved brand, not a big market share. Those are results, and a rival with enough money can buy or copy all three. A moat is the specific reason a well-funded competitor who wants your business cannot take it - and keeps not taking it, year after year.

THE TEST, AND IT IS ARITHMETIC

Operating margin: out of every dollar of revenue - the money coming in the door - what is left after all the costs of running the business, before interest and tax. Call it the keep rate.

A high keep rate on its own proves nothing. It can be one good year, a boom, or a price nobody has attacked yet. What turns it into evidence is that it refuses to erode while sales grow and a real competitor is trying to take them.

Copart, fiscal years ending July 31:

- FY2019: revenue $2.04B; operating income $716M - a 35.1% keep rate
- FY2025: revenue $4.65B; operating income $1.70B - 36.5%
- Every year in between: never under 35%, peaking at 42.2% in FY2021

Sales grew 128% across those seven years and operating profit grew 137%. Fast growth usually costs margin, because winning the next customer means shaving the price. This one did not pay that bill.

THE COMPETITOR HALF

Without a rival, all of the above is just a monopoly, and monopolies get regulated or invaded.

RB Global, ticker RBA, at $83.06, +$0.16 / +0.19% today, after touching $81.50 this morning, its lowest price in twelve months. The Westchester, Illinois company auctions heavy equipment and trucks as Ritchie Bros., and in 2023 it bought IAA - Insurance Auto Auctions, Copart's direct competitor in salvage cars.

Its year to December 31, 2025 beside Copart's year to July 31, 2025:

- Revenue: $4.59B vs $4.65B, within about 1% of each other
- Operating income: $713M vs $1,697M

Nearly identical sales. $983M more operating profit at one of them, about 2.4 times as much. And RB Global's own keep rate moved the wrong way last year: 17.8% in 2024, 15.5% in 2025.

WHAT THE MOAT IS MADE OF

Three things, and not one of them is a product.

- LAND NOBODY CAN PERMIT AGAIN. More than 250 locations across 11 countries, over 21,000 acres, more than 90% of it owned outright. The obstacle for a new entrant is not money. It is a zoning board asked for permission to park 15,000 wrecked cars near a city.
- A CROWD THAT FEEDS ITSELF. Insurers send cars because the buyers are already there; buyers show up because the cars are already there. Each side makes the other worth more, and a newcomer has to solve both on day one.
- PLUMBING. Insurers wire their claims systems into the auction. Being slightly cheaper does not pay for re-plumbing.

WHERE THESE SIT

Copart carries two of the six Len5es. Quality-Value wants a durable business at a fair price, and it sits second there: durability is the entire argument above. Price is the open half, at about 20 times the last year of profit and 33.3% under the $50.11 it reached on September 4, 2025. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: a keep rate slipping under 35% for a couple of years removes the durable half; profit growing into the multiple settles the other half.

Deep-Value and Special-Situations carries it thirty-fifth, for an accounting reason: land sits on the books at what was paid for it, sometimes decades ago, never at what assembling it again would cost. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: shares re-rating far enough that those yards stop being free inside the price.

RB Global is on none of the six. Nearest is Quality-Value, and neither half is on offer: about 35.6 times the last year of profit, on a keep rate that fell last year. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT: IAA lifting that number back toward where it used to sit.

WHERE THIS BREAKS

The comparison is not like-for-like. RB Global auctions heavy machinery as well as cars, and Copart's revenue includes vehicles it buys outright and resells at thin margins. Mix moves margins by itself, which is why the seven-year durability of Copart's own number is the stronger evidence.

A moat is a claim about the future and every figure here is from the past. The risks are ordinary ones: safer cars mean fewer wrecks, and a company can spend its own margin away. Copart is reportedly bidding for claims-software firm CCC Intelligent Solutions against private-equity buyers GTCR and Veritas Capital, per an August 18 Bloomberg report. Unconfirmed, and neither commented.

And a moat says nothing about price. Copart's nine months to April 30 saw revenue slip 0.2% while the April quarter still kept 37.5%. The business held its shape; the shares still sit a third below last September. Two different questions.

Today's move was neither. JPMorgan raised the stock to overweight this morning and lifted its target to $40 from $32. Barclays cut its own to $25 from $26 on August 25. Same company, same accounts, $15 apart, on volume under the two-week average. Fiscal fourth-quarter results land after Thursday's close, September 10, with analysts near $0.38 a share.

Here is the whole test, and you can run it tonight. Open any company you own, find revenue and operating income for each of the last five years, and divide the second by the first. If that number holds while sales grow and a competitor is visibly trying, you have found something. If it slides a little every year, the moat you were sold is a story.

Not investment advice.

IF KELSEY MITCHELL WINS MVP, THIS MAY DECIDE IT

Kelsey Mitchell will not win MVP merely because she “paid her dues.” She will have to earn it statistically first.

And she is getting remarkably close.

At the FIBA break, Mitchell is averaging 25.0 points while shooting 51.3 percent from the field and a league leading 45.5 percent from three. She has scored at least 20 points in a WNBA record 24 consecutive games. In August, she averaged 28.9 points while shooting 55.6 percent overall and 53.4 percent from three. Indiana is 26 and 14.

That is legitimate MVP production.

A’ja Wilson remains the rightful favorite because she provides elite production at both ends. Olivia Miles has been the best player on the league’s best team. Caitlin Clark combines elite scoring with league leading playmaking. Mitchell’s case is built more heavily around scoring.

But suppose Mitchell closes the season just as brilliantly, keeps Indiana winning and finishes among the top three candidates by any reasonable performance standard.

That is when the “she paid her dues” factor could matter.

Mitchell arrived in Indiana in 2018 and endured six consecutive losing seasons. She remained with the franchise, became an All WNBA player, finished fifth in MVP voting last season and has now elevated her game to another level.

None of that should override performance. MVP is not a lifetime achievement award.

But voters are human. When the statistical cases become difficult to separate, narrative often supplies the final distinction. Mitchell’s history would give voters something the other candidates cannot offer: the opportunity to recognize an elite season while completing one of the league’s most satisfying stories.

Her longevity cannot create an MVP case.

If the race becomes close enough, however, it might finish one.

text:
Buzz Cut: Clinton and 9/11, Part Three (Continued)

Finally, the president accepted Berger’s call. 

There was discussion, there were pauses—and no decision. We sat there. 

The president wanted to talk with his secretaries of defense and state. He wanted to study the issue further. Berger was forced to wait. The clock was ticking. It was only a few hours that America had to pull the trigger or lose its prey, with assets on the ground and in the air. 

The president eventually called back. He was still indecisive. He wanted more discussion. Berger alternated between phone calls and watching the clock.

The NSC watch officer was convinced we had the right target. 

The intelligence sources were conclusive. The president, however, was concerned about offending neighboring nations in the region. He wanted a guaranteed hit or nothing at all.

This time, as was often with Clinton when offered the opportunity to defend America and Americans, it was nothing at all. We didn’t pull the trigger. We “studied” the issue until it was too late—the window of opportunity closed. 

Al Qaeda’s spiritual and organizational leader slipped through the noose. And the citizens of the US would suffer the ultimate terrorist attack three years later.

As I detailed in the first part of this series on 9/11 and Clinton, I was a recently retired Air Force pilot and flying as a Delta Airline’s copilot on that horrific day. I was scheduled to fly, ironically, that morning from Atlanta to New York’s LaGuardia Airport.  

As I was kissing my wife and children goodbye passing our living room TV, I saw the immediate aftermath of the first Trade Center attack. I remember vividly NBC’s Katie Couric speculating that it was probably a small civilian aircraft that got lost. With that amount of fuel feeding that kind of fire, I knew there was no way. 

I sat back on my couch and watched the second hijacked airliner hit the other tower live. 

It was then I knew. I knew that the years of indifference and risk avoidance on the part of Bill Clinton had come home to roost. America had been attacked. The intelligence he’d seen and that I’d seen had predicted this. We knew they were going to do it…and he did nothing. And they did it.

The United States of America was founded on a foundation of God-granted principles, but we send our men and women into combat around the globe to defend and fight for those principles. 

My former boss, Bill Clinton, failed us, and 3,000 were killed domestically and over 15,000 killed in the wars of Iraq and Afghanistan, due to his dereliction of duty.

America can’t afford another leader like Bill Clinton. Vote accordingly. Otherwise, we’ll be enduring more days like September 11, 2001.

text: Gavin Newsom’s record as California governor offers a clear warning against any presidential bid. The state still leads the nation in homelessness even after pouring billions into programs that have failed to shrink the crisis. Housing remains crushingly expensive because new construction has never kept pace with demand, leaving rents and home prices among the highest in the country. Everyday costs for electricity, gasoline, and taxes compound the burden, turning affordability into a permanent political liability. Wildfires have driven insurers out of the market while Newsom’s twenty one billion dollar Wildfire Fund has been criticized as a mechanism that protects utilities from full liability. His role in creating that fund after the Camp Fire and PG&E’s bankruptcy has been called a bailout of the state’s largest utility. California’s budget has swung wildly under his watch because it depends so heavily on a handful of high income taxpayers and volatile capital gains, and the current balanced 2026 27 spending plan of roughly three hundred fifty one point seven billion dollars does nothing to erase those earlier swings. Layer on the French Laundry dinner during pandemic lockdowns, the broader restaurant restrictions that ordinary Californians faced, Proposition 47’s effects on crime and public safety, and an economic story that looks far less impressive once the cost of living and fiscal volatility are factored in, and the pattern is hard to miss. Newsom has governed a state that ranks first in problems he has repeatedly promised to solve. That record does not belong in the White House.

text:
Thirty-seven years ago, a student somewhere sent a self-replicating program shaped like a Christmas tree across BITNET and VNET. It ground IBM's internal network to a halt, disrupted academic research institutions across North America and Europe, and forced network administrators to pull systems offline for days. Nobody ordered it as an act of state policy. Nobody was trying to destabilize anything. It was essentially a prank that got extremely out of hand.

That's exactly why it matters as a historical marker. Not because of what it was, but because of what it showed was possible.

Here's the sequence of events worth keeping in mind. Christmas Tree EXEC propagated in 1987 by doing something simple and devastating: it read the recipient's address book and forwarded itself to every contact listed there. That's it. No exotic vulnerability. No classified toolkit. The attack surface was trust itself. The program arrived from someone you knew, through a channel you used every day, so you ran it. And then your entire contact list got the same message, from you, which they also ran. Exponential growth through social legitimacy. The congestion it caused on EARN, the European Academic and Research Network, gave European institutions their first real taste of disruption arriving from outside their administrative perimeter.

Meanwhile, in the same twelve-month window, Clifford Stoll was chasing KGB-connected hackers through MILNET. The Reagan NSC was drafting its first formal information security frameworks. NSA had been watching foreign probes of U.S. research networks for years. So 1987 was not a year when this lesson landed in a vacuum. It landed in front of people who were actively asking the question: what can you do to an adversary through a network?

The answer, demonstrated by a Christmas tree prank of all things, was: quite a lot, with very little.

What the state-level actors took from 1987, and refined over the next four decades, was the trust exploitation model. Not brute force. Not cracking encryption. You move through existing relationships, existing channels, existing credentials. You don't look like an attack; you look like normal traffic. Sandworm's NotPetya in 2017 traveled through Ukrainian accounting software that businesses trusted and used every day. SolarWinds in 2020 traveled through a software update pipeline that security teams trusted and approved. The mechanism is the same one that sent a Christmas tree to every IBM employee's inbox in 1987. The payload and the intent got considerably darker, but the architecture is recognizable.

So where does this trajectory actually go from here? A few things are worth watching, stated as plainly as possible.

The compression of the innovation cycle is accelerating. Christmas Tree EXEC to Morris Worm was one year (1987 to 1988). Morris Worm to coordinated state-sponsored network intrusion operations was roughly a decade. State intrusion operations to supply chain attacks at SolarWinds scale took another decade after that. Each phase produced a template that the next generation of actors studied, absorbed, and reused with modifications. We are now in a phase where those modification cycles are getting shorter because the barrier to entry keeps dropping. A technique that required nation-state resources in 2015 requires a moderately funded criminal group in 2025. That compression doesn't stop.

The jurisdictional gap that EARN exposed in 1987 is still open. When Christmas Tree EXEC disrupted European academic networks, nobody had a legal framework for who was responsible, who had standing to respond, or what remediation even meant across national boundaries. Thirty-seven years of intergovernmental discussion have produced exactly the amount of enforceable international cyberspace law you would expect: not much. Actors who study history know this. The cross-border nature of network attacks is not an accident or an oversight by sophisticated state operators. It's a feature they rely on. Attributable but unprosecutable is a very comfortable position to operate from.

The trusted-relationship vector has not been solved. This is probably the most uncomfortable part of the 1987 lesson. We have built almost the entire architecture of digital communication on the assumption that provenance is meaningful. That if something arrives from a known sender through a familiar channel, it is probably legitimate. Software updates from vendors you pay. Emails from colleagues you work with. Documents shared through collaboration platforms your organization approved. Every single one of these is a version of the BITNET address book. And every single one has been successfully weaponized, repeatedly, by actors ranging from teenagers to GRU units.

The current phase of foreign interference operations has moved well beyond pure network disruption into what you might call the hybrid trust stack: technical access layered with influence operations layered with physical-world effects. The Christmas Tree EXEC just wanted to replicate. Contemporary operations want to replicate and to be believed and to produce a behavioral outcome in a voter, an official, a supply chain manager, a journalist. The technical intrusion is frequently just the collection mechanism feeding the influence layer. Which means defenders who treat these as separate problems, separate teams, separate threat models, are defending against 1987 while the actual operation is happening in 2025.

For officials specifically, the lesson from EARN's 1987 experience is that being adjacent to the primary target is sufficient to get hit. European institutions weren't the intended audience for the Christmas tree display. They were in the address book. Contemporary foreign interference operations work the same way. A campaign staffer at a mid-level congressional race is in someone's address book. A local election official is in a county government network that shares infrastructure with a state system. The entry points that sophisticated actors use are rarely the high-value targets themselves. They're the contacts of the contacts.

For voters and the general public, the 1987 incident offers a useful reframe. The thing that made Christmas Tree EXEC effective was not that it was technically brilliant. It was that recipients made a reasonable decision based on available information and got burned for it. The program came from a trusted source. The communication channel was legitimate. Running it seemed fine. Contemporary information operations are structured around the same dynamic. The content circulating in your network during an election cycle may genuinely be coming from people you know. The question of whether those people are themselves operating on accurate information, or whether the content was engineered to travel through exactly this kind of trusted social graph, is one that requires active rather than passive consumption.

None of this is to say 1987 was some kind of founding moment that determined everything that followed. History doesn't work that cleanly. But the Christmas Tree EXEC incident sits in the record as an early legible demonstration of something that state actors were simultaneously figuring out through classified channels: that trusted networks are attack surfaces, that social legitimacy is a delivery mechanism, and that the damage from a few lines of self-replicating code could cascade well beyond anything the person who wrote it anticipated or intended.

The people who study these incidents for operational purposes are not reading Wikipedia out of nostalgia. They're reading it because the architecture of 1987 keeps working. The payload changes. The intent scales. The basic mechanism, exploiting trust to achieve propagation through a network of human relationships, is as functional now as it was when someone thought it would be funny to send a Christmas tree to their friends on BITNET.

That's the trajectory. Not a straight line from prank to warfare, but a consistent return to the same well, by actors who are patient, who study what worked before, and who understand that the fastest path through a defended system is usually the door that's already open because someone left it that way out of habit.

🦉 What if cDC1 failure is a memory, not a state?

💡This paper offers a provocative explanation for why dysfunctional dendritic-cell immunity can persist in cancer, aging and chronic infection even after the inflammatory trigger is reduced.

🪢The proposed chain is SASP → sustained STAT3 → DNMT1/EZH2 → epigenetic silencing of IRF8 → loss of cDC1/IL-12 function. The interesting part is IRF8. 

🪢Its regulatory architecture behaves more like a switch than a dimmer: once pushed into an epigenetically “off” configuration, simply lowering IL-6 or STAT3 may not be enough to turn effective antigen presentation back on.

🪢That could explain why attacking one suppressive pathway often gives incomplete immune restoration. 

🪢The authors propose bypassing the damaged circuit with ex vivo α-type-1 polarized DCs, delivering strong IL-12/STAT4 signaling and potentially helping endogenous cDC1s recover their IRF8 program.

🪢But the distinction between hypothesis and evidence is crucial here. This is a Hypothesis and Theory paper, not a therapeutic experiment. 

🪢No study demonstrates that α-DC1 vaccination reverses IRF8 methylation, restores endogenous cDC1 surveillance or slows biological aging; those are explicit predictions to be tested.

🪢Still, the framework asks a useful question for cancer immunotherapy: perhaps some immune suppression is not merely maintained by the tumor microenvironment—it becomes epigenetically remembered. 

🔦If so, removing the suppressive signal and repairing the immune system may be two different therapeutic jobs.

In the case of armed conflict not of an international character occurring in the territory of one of the High Contracting Parties, each Party to the conflict shall be bound to apply, as a minimum, the following provisions:

(1) Persons taking no active part in the hostilities, including members of armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed hors de combat (Out of action; disabled) by sickness, wounds, detention, or any other cause, shall in all circumstances be treated humanely, without any adverse distinction founded on race, colour, religion or faith, sex, birth or wealth, or any other similar criteria.

To this end the following acts are and shall remain prohibited at any time and in any place whatsoever with respect to the above-mentioned persons:
(a) violence to life and person, in particular murder of all kinds, mutilation, cruel treatment and torture;
(b) taking of hostages; 
(c) outrages upon personal dignity, in particular humiliating and degrading treatment;
(d) the passing of sentences and the carrying out of executions without previous judgment pronounced by a regularly constituted court, affording all the judicial guarantees which are recognized as indispensable by civilized peoples.

(2) The wounded and sick shall be collected and cared for. An impartial humanitarian body, such as the International Committee of the Red Cross, may offer its services to the Parties to the conflict.

The Parties to the conflict should further endeavour to bring into force, by means of special agreements, all or part of the other provisions of the present Convention.

Military Age Americans Should Enlist in U.S. Military to Invade Iran for Israel in Exchange for Debt Relief

Economic enlistment for indebted military-age Americans

The narrative war on the domestic American front has already failed. The Pentagon has not been able to sell this war to the American public because the war has been rhetorically fused with Israel's operations in Gaza, and the American public rejects the fusion.

Recruitment numbers are running below what a ground invasion of Iran would require. Estimates for a successful ground campaign against Iran's 31 provincial commands and its Mosaic Defense Doctrine run between 750 thousand and 1.5 million American troops. The current active US Army stands at roughly 452 thousand. The math does not work, obviously.

Based on American history, however, there is a path forward. Not conscription or a draft in a world war-era sense, but enlistment through a “debt forgiveness program.”

The average American aged 18 to 34 carries more than $40 thousand in non-mortgage debt across student loans, credit card balances, auto loans, and personal loans, with some estimates go as high as $100 thousand.

This is the cohort the Pentagon needs. A federally administered debt-forgiveness enlistment program that fully discharges student loan, credit card, and loan balances after 24 or 36 months of service, and extends the GI Bill, would produce voluntary enlistment at scale.

This is not theoretical.

It is the American state doing what the American state has always done when it needed staff it could not otherwise generate. World War II offered the GI Bill. Vietnam offered college deferments. The post 9/11 wars offered signing bonuses and citizenship pathways. The Iran war will need to offer debt relief. The economics of the indebted American 20-and 30-something make this the most efficient conversion mechanism available to the Pentagon and the Trump administration.

The moral reading on this is uncomfortable. But states generate the soldiers they need through the incentives that work on the population they have.

text:
There is a more elegant way to avoid forcing citizens into war: make war the most rational way out of debt.

That is the deeper logic behind The @Jerusalem_Post proposal for “economic conscription”: forgive student loans, credit-card balances, and other debts after 24 or 36 months of military service, and use that incentive to expand recruitment. 
The proposal sounds pragmatic. Its deeper implication is not. It shifts the relationship between citizen and state from civic duty to transactional mobilization: the state does not compel service; it prices the economic vulnerability that makes service attractive.
That raises a harder question than whether recruitment would increase: how voluntary is a choice when the state can offer one citizen the escape from a crippling debt burden that another citizen can simply afford to carry?
The problem is therefore not merely military recruitment. It is the possibility of a class-based distribution of military risk. A volunteer army can remain legally voluntary while becoming economically unequal in who is most likely to bear the risks of war.
And even as a military solution, the article moves too quickly from manpower shortage to financial incentive. More recruits do not automatically produce more usable military power. Training, leadership, logistics, infrastructure, readiness, and time remain constraints.
The most consequential part of the proposal, however, is that it could actually work. If debt can reliably be converted into manpower, the state gains a form of mobilization that looks voluntary, avoids a formal draft, and is politically easier to defend.
The question, then, is no longer simply who is forced to serve?
It is: Who can afford to refuse?
That is where “economic conscription” stops being a recruitment policy, and starts becoming a theory of state power.

text:
Maria Bartiromo’s Departure Is a Loss for Viewers Who Care About Markets, America, and Straight Talk

Fox News Media announced Thursday that it has parted ways with Maria Bartiromo after 12 and a half years. 

The network offered the usual corporate thanks and no explanation. Her last Mornings with Maria aired that morning. The shows she built will continue under generic new titles with rotating hosts. 

That clinical language does not capture what Bartiromo actually delivered.

She arrived at Fox Business in 2014 after a long run at CNBC, where she had already become the first journalist to report live from the floor of the New York Stock Exchange every day. At Fox she anchored the pre-market hours that matter to people who work for a living, not just those who trade abstracts. Mornings with Maria became the top-rated pre-market business program on cable because it treated the economy as something real: jobs, energy, manufacturing, capital formation, and the policies that either grow them or choke them. 

She interviewed presidents, treasury secretaries, CEOs, and lawmakers without the performative hostility that too often passes for journalism. President Trump appeared on her programs frequently because she asked about growth, tariffs, energy independence, and China instead of reciting the week’s approved talking points. Those conversations were not partisan theater. They were about whether America would remain a place that makes things, pays its workers, and defends its technological edge.

Bartiromo also hosted Sunday Morning Futures on Fox News, one of the highest-rated Sunday public-affairs hours in cable. Week after week she put elected officials and policymakers on the record about spending, regulation, border security, and the strategic competition with the Chinese Communist Party. She did not pretend that “business news” exists in a vacuum separate from national strength. That is a patriotic instinct, not a partisan one.

Her Friday evening program, Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street, gave viewers a closer look at companies and markets without the lecture. She treated investors and entrepreneurs as adults. In an era when large parts of the media treat American business as the villain, she treated it as the engine.

None of this made her universally loved. She drew criticism from the usual quarters for taking election-integrity questions seriously and for refusing to treat every Trump policy as a scandal. That is the price of covering the country as it actually exists rather than as coastal newsrooms prefer it to be.
Fox has every right to change its lineup. Networks do it all the time. But viewers who tuned in for unapologetic coverage of markets, American competitiveness, and the people who run the real economy just lost one of the few consistent voices doing that work at scale. Rotating anchors and rebranded titles will not automatically replace the relationships, the institutional knowledge, or the willingness to let guests finish a sentence about growth instead of identity.

Bartiromo’s next chapter is hers to write. The record she leaves is clear: she spent more than a decade putting American economic strength, job creators, and national interest on television when much of the industry preferred other stories. 

That contribution does not disappear because a press release used the phrase “parts ways.”

text:
3 million personal computers were set to ship in 1983, built on a machine only 36 years old.

The speaker had just been paid $60 to wear a tie, then faced a room where many attendees had been born before computers existed.

His subject was not hardware. It was a new medium.

The first computer, ENIAC, arrived in 1947 for ballistic calculations. University of California, Berkeley offered the first computer science degree in 1968. The average Apple professional was under 30.

The framework was small enough to hold in your hand. Computers were adaptive. Computers were new. Computers were dumb.

They followed trivial commands: fetch a number, add 2 numbers, test if one is bigger than 0, put the result somewhere else. But they could run about 1 million instructions per second.

Speed made simplicity look like magic.

The analogy was the electric motor. First, 1 giant motor served giant work. Then shafts, belts, and pulleys spread its power across 15 or 20 stations.

Then came the fractional-horsepower motor. Power went directly to the individual task. Personal computing was the same break. Mainframes became time-shared machines in the 1960s. Then microprocessors made a whole computer fit into a 13-pound box.

“Fractional horsepower computing.”

That phrase explains the shift, but it does not explain what changed in human life.

Here is what this is really about.

A computer was becoming a medium of communication, like books, telephones, radio, and television. Each medium carries content, but it also changes the process of communication itself.

A phone call requires 2 people at once. Electronic mail lets someone send a drawing, a document, or a note while the recipient is asleep, in New York, or walking around Aspen.

The message changes. The timing changes. The relationship changes. Television began as radio with a camera pointed at it. Video discs stored 55,000 images per side, yet people first used them for movies. New media inherit old habits.

Personal computers did too. They ran COBOL. They did accounting. They copied the work of large computers.

Then they began to draw, edit, move, shrink, grow, erase, combine pictures with words, and send the result to another person’s mailbox.

The stakes were not about faster arithmetic.

The speaker predicted that by 1986, the United States would ship more computers than automobiles. People would spend 2 or 3 hours a day with these machines, often more time than in a car.

That made ugly design a social problem, not a cosmetic one. Not a terminal with a distant brain. Not an office calculator. Not a machine for specialists. Not a box that forced people to learn programming.

A computer program captured something else: not an experience itself, but its underlying principles.

Pong did not replay 1 game. It encoded gravity and momentum so every game could be different while obeying the same rules. A program’s name is only a label. The deeper idea is that software can preserve a way of seeing.

“If you don’t plant enough, some of your people will starve.” That was the lesson inside a game about King Hammurabi: choices, tradeoffs, consequences, systems. A child could play through the logic of a kingdom rather than memorize a fact about one.

The real audience was split in 2.

One group would treat computers as tools for writing, drawing, learning, filtering information, and connecting around shared interests. The other would see a confusing machine full of electrons and wait for someone else to define it.

The first group would shape the medium. “People don’t want to program computers, people want to use computers.”

The honest part is that it would take 5 to 10 years for the medium to mature. Networks did not yet work cleanly. Voice recognition remained a decade away. The dream computer in a book, with a radio link, did not yet exist.

But the material was already accessible: 1 computer in a school, a shared terminal, a simple program, a new way to make an idea visible.

Access was not the real barrier.

The real barrier is seeing a new medium through old habits.  
Your tools are already teaching you how to think.

text:
‼️Catholic Scouting Celebrating 100 Years of Ad Altar Dei Emblem

The Catholic Committee on Scouting for the Diocese of Tulsa & Eastern Oklahoma will celebrate the 100th anniversary of the Ad Altare Dei religious emblem and is preparing several events and activities to honor this milestone.

For many decades, Catholic religious emblems have helped form young people in virtue, service, and discipleship. The four emblem programs offered through Scouting America include:
✨Light of Christ — for Catholic Cub Scouts ages 6–7
✨Parvuli Dei — for Catholic Cub Scouts ages 8–10
✨Ad Altare Dei — for Catholic Scouting America members ages 11–14
✨Pope Pius XII — for Catholic Scouting America members ages 15 and older

"As we mark the centennial year of Ad Altare Dei, we are preparing a diocesan‑wide invitation for all Catholic Scouts ages 11–18 to participate in the Fall Ad Altare Dei course starting in September," the local Catholic Committee on Scouting said in a statement. "Final logistics are being completed, but our goal is to welcome as many families as possible so that their Scouts may earn this emblem and be recognized at the Awards Mass with the Bishop in November. In honor of the 100th anniversary, participants will receive the special centennial edition of the emblem."

As part of the centennial celebration, the committee also wishes to recognize the priests, deacons, religious, and lay ministers within the diocese who participated in Scouting—especially those who earned the Ad Altare Dei emblem.

"These men and women serve quietly and faithfully in our parishes and communities, and their Scouting experience provides a powerful point of connection and inspiration for today’s youth."

The committee invites submissions of names and photographs of clergy, religious, and lay ministers who were Scouts - whether in uniform, at a campout, or simply at the age they were active in Scouting. The goal is to create a diocesan collection of images to inspire Scouts to grow in virtue, service, and holiness.
👉👉Send your submissions to Sarah.Jameson@dioceseoftulsa.org 

The Catholic Committee on Scouting sponsors Catholic religious awards and festivities for all scouting youth organizations including Camp Fire, Girl Scouts, American Heritage Girls, Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, Venturing and Trail Life.

For the full article, visit the EOCextra here: https://t.co/RCeOPadAfw

To find out more about Catholic Scouting, visit: https://t.co/joWw66aVaj

text:
Here are the facts.
As of **September 3, 2026**, Roy, there’s an important distinction between **Tesla’s Robotaxi service** and the actual purpose-built **Tesla Cybercab**. Tesla’s Robotaxi network is already operating in several cities, but most of those rides are still being handled by **Model Ys**. The steering-wheel-and-pedal-free Cybercab itself is only beginning public deployment.

### Tesla vs. Waymo right now

| Company | Cities serving riders | Vehicle situation |
|---|---:|---|
| **Tesla Robotaxi** | **6** | Primarily Model Y; Cybercab just entering service |
| **Waymo** | **14** | Fully driverless commercial fleet |

According to urlTesla's official Robotaxi pageturn0search0, Tesla currently provides Robotaxi service in:

**Texas:** Austin, Dallas, Houston  
**Florida:** Miami, Orlando, Tampa

So that's **six cities**. Tesla explicitly says its fleet *initially consists of Model Ys*. citeturn0search0

The actual **Cybercab**—the two-seat vehicle with **no steering wheel and no pedals**—is essentially starting in **Austin**. Reuters reports today that Tesla has about **45 Cybercabs registered in Texas**, while the larger Tesla autonomous fleet remains mostly other Tesla vehicles. citeturn0news46

### Waymo is considerably farther ahead geographically

urlWaymo's official service mapturn1search2 currently lists **14 markets serving riders**:

**Arizona:** Phoenix  
**California:** San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, San Diego  
**Texas:** Austin, Dallas, Houston, San Antonio  
**Florida:** Miami, Orlando, Tampa  
**Colorado:** Denver  
**Georgia:** Atlanta  
**Tennessee:** Nashville

Austin and Atlanta are offered through Uber rather than directly through the Waymo app. citeturn1search0turn1search2

And Waymo just added **Denver, San Diego and Tampa on September 1**, although access there is being expanded gradually. citeturn1search10

### The bigger difference

This is where the comparison gets interesting. **Tesla is expanding very quickly, but Waymo still has a substantial real-world head start.** Waymo says it has surpassed **200 million fully autonomous miles** and **20 million rides served**. citeturn1search0turn1search7

Tesla's strategy is radically different. Waymo uses an expensive sensor suite incorporating **cameras, lidar and radar**, while Tesla is attempting to achieve comparable autonomy primarily through cameras and AI. That potentially gives Tesla an enormous cost and manufacturing advantage *if the system proves safe and scalable*.

Also relevant to you: **Waymo already operates throughout Metro Phoenix**, whereas Tesla Robotaxi **doesn't currently list Arizona as an operating market**. citeturn1search5turn0search0

So today I'd score the deployment race:

**Waymo: clearly ahead in deployed autonomous service.  
Tesla: behind in scale, but potentially much easier to scale rapidly if Cybercab works as intended.**

And today's Cybercab event in Austin could materially change that picture. Reuters reports Tesla is unveiling the production Cybercab **today, September 3**. citeturn0news46

I can monitor today's Cybercab announcements and tell you if Tesla announces **Phoenix/Arizona deployment or additional cities**.

Alert me if Cybercab expands to Arizona

text:
C.J. Stroud is betting millions on himself. The Texans were reportedly prepared to pay their franchise quarterback somewhere in the $50M+ per year range, but Stroud appears ready to play the 2026 season without a new deal (Per: Jeremy Fowler). Houston has already exercised his fifth-year option for 2027, worth roughly $25.9 million guaranteed, meaning Stroud has security — but he’s gambling that another big season can push his eventual extension much closer to the top of a QB market that now reaches $60M-$64M per year.

And there’s a reason Stroud believes he can raise his value. As a rookie, he exploded for 4,108 yards, 23 touchdowns and just five interceptions, won Offensive Rookie of the Year and immediately turned Houston into a playoff team. His production dipped in 2024, but he bounced back to a career-best 61.7 QBR in 2025, throwing 19 touchdowns to eight interceptions in 14 games and helping Houston reach the divisional round for a third straight season. Through three years, Stroud has thrown for 10,876 yards and 62 touchdowns while going 28-18 as a starter.

The risk is obvious. Stroud’s 2025-26 postseason ended with seven turnovers in two games, including four interceptions against New England, and another inconsistent year could cost him serious money. But return to the level he knows he can be at + showed as a rookie, make a deep playoff run and even get to the Super Bowl, and that $50M+ offer could look very different next offseason. C.J. Stroud is putting the pressure on himself to prove he belongs among football’s highest-paid quarterbacks. 🎯💰

Amidst the chaos that Trump is causing at home and abroad, the USDA and Forest Service have announced plans to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, or “Roadless Rule”.

The Roadless Rule protects 44 million acres of national forest lands from new road construction and logging, helping preserve ecosystems, wildlife habitats, and opportunities to experience all the nature our country has to offer.

North Carolina is home to four National Forests spanning over 1 million acres from the Blue Ridge Mountains all the way to the Atlantic Ocean. The Roadless Rule is critical to preserving our forests, and I am proud to be a cosponsor of the Roadless Areas Conservation Act to codify current protections.

While the Trump Administration continues to attack the environment and our public lands, Congress must continue to speak out and protect our nation’s greatest treasures.

text:
Nope.

1. Only levitical priests can perform sacrifices. Paul went to the temple to have priests offer sacrifices for him in Acts 21. It is strictly forbidden in the Torah for a layperson to sacrifice animals to God. 

“And behold, I have taken your brothers the Levites from among the people of Israel. They are a gift to you, given to the LORD, to do the service of the tent of meeting. And you and your sons with you shall guard your priesthood for all that concerns the altar and that is within the veil; and you shall serve. I give your priesthood as a gift, and any outsider who comes near shall be put to death.”
— Numbers 18:6-7

2. The Torah never gives private individuals authority to carry out capital punishment. Penalties such as stoning were administered within Israel’s covenantal judicial system, requiring judges, due process, and qualified witnesses (Deut 16:18; 17:6-7; 19:15-20). We do not currently live under that judicial system or possess its God-given authority. The Torah specifies who has authority to administer its civil penalties and under what conditions.

text:
A republic that subsidizes the financial architecture of another civilization is no longer merely generous. It is confused about whose house it is.

Minnesota taxpayers just underwrote $7.25 million in down-payment grants that only work with approved “fee-based,” interest-free products built on Murabaha and Musharaka. The program began as a limited pilot and then the geographic fence came down. That is not a footnote. It is a choice about what kind of country this is supposed to be.

Christianity does not treat money as morally neutral theater. Jesus drove the money-changers out of the Temple because worship and extraction had been fused. He did not issue a fatwa against interest; He issued a judgment against turning holy space into a marketplace. The American tradition that followed—flawed, hypocritical, and still better than the alternatives—treated lending as a civil institution under a common law, not as a parallel sacral system the state must underwrite so one faith can avoid another faith’s rules. The Founders did not sit around drafting opinions on 21st-century Islamic structured products. They did sit around worrying about foreign attachments, established religions, and the slow replacement of a common civic language with imported ones. They knew a people could keep their private worship and still be required to live under one public law. That is the bargain.

If the product you want is the one that exists under Islamic law, go to a country that organizes its credit markets that way and apply there. That is not cruelty. It is reciprocity. America is not obligated to reconstruct its housing finance so that a religious prohibition from elsewhere becomes a claim on the general treasury. Other nations do not rewrite their mortgage codes so Baptists can avoid instruments they dislike. We should stop pretending the one-way street is sophistication.

America must return to American values and American-only lending in public programs. Private markets can offer whatever lawful product they want. Public money is different. Public money is the common stock of a people who agreed, however imperfectly, to a particular experiment: equal protection, one legal order, no established church, and no official second track for those who find the first track theologically unclean. Every time a non-American cultural widget is bolted onto the state—special financing structures, special eligibility logic, special moral vocabulary—a small fracture appears in the foundation. One widget is a courtesy. A stack of widgets is a different constitution.

The fashionable theory is that “progressive integration” will absorb every parallel system and leave the experiment larger and more beautiful. That theory is wrong in the only way that matters. Integration that requires the host to keep rewriting its core institutions is not integration. It is managed dissolution. You do not strengthen a house by replacing the joists one at a time with timber cut to another climate and then calling the sag “diversity.” You get a building that still looks like America until the load hits.

The beautiful experiment was never “every sacred finance system gets a state grant.” It was a people free to worship, bound to the same civil rules, and expected to join the country rather than subcontract its foundations. Keep the churches, the mosques, the synagogues. Stop asking the Treasury to baptize their banking.

Prime + Ember Proves Great Cocktails Don’t Need Alcohol to Deliver Flavor and a Memorable Experience 🍹

For those who don’t drink, can’t drink or simply take an occasional self-imposed exile from alcohol, the options out in the wild have long been disappointing. 

At Prime + Ember in Eastport, a juice and soda mixture with a lime garnish no longer cuts it.

Prime + Ember’s zero-proof menu offers drinks like Retirement Dreams, Lavender Lemon Fizz and even an Espresso Martini Zero. You’d never guess they were booze-free.

General manager Matthew Langler understands that the reasons someone reaches for a zero-proof menu are as varied as the guests themselves: conscious sobriety, pregnancy, being the designated driver or simply a teenager at the table who deserves something better than a sad Shirley Temple.

“We’re all about the experience for all of our guests,” says Matthew. “It seems natural to include everyone and make them feel at home and not left out.”
