text:
Caution with the word "cure" is right, but incomplete if building trust and conquering cancer are paramount.

In the AI ecosystem, Jensen Huang has described Nvidia's role as funding what venture capitalists will not and building what no one else will.

Nvidia and the frontier AI labs could play a similar role in the cancer ecosystem. With global stature and expansive networks of capital and talent, they can reshape the landscape like few organizations can.

They can attack gaps left by misaligned incentives, question old assumptions the field has molded itself around, and anchor startups and investors with a public roadmap.

Today, AI is bolted on rather than assigned a central role. What if we reimagined the ecosystem around what humans and AI each need and where each excels?

This essay reflects five years of researching cancer from the outside and aims to start a discussion about where we can go from here. It is long because cancer is a systemic problem and needs an interdisciplinary perspective.

AI and cancer research share surprising parallels. In both fields, many ideas sound compelling in theory but die in reality. In cancer, findings may not translate to patients while AI methods may not transfer across models. Even success can be contextual.

Pancreatic cancer illustrates the gulf between progress and cure.

Over the past year, a drug from Revolution Medicines has invigorated oncologists by demonstrating unprecedented efficacy against RAS, a protein family implicated in roughly 20% of cancers and historically deemed undruggable. Small molecules usually need a pocket, a contoured groove to wedge into and hold, but RAS proteins are smooth globes with shallow ridges.

The drug is a genuine breakthrough and can buy patients more time with loved ones, another birthday or graduation, or maybe the birth of a grandchild. Everyone who contributed deserves our gratitude for years of devotion.

Nonetheless, progress is measured in months, not years or decades. The Phase 3 trial reported a median overall survival of 13.2 months against 6.7 months on chemotherapy. A gain of 6.5 months.

Curing cancer is hard because no one fully understands human biology. Many aspects remain inscrutable despite centuries of remarkable insights, and even clarity at the population level may not impart understanding at the individual level.

Humans are devilishly heterogeneous. What helps Shaq may not help you. What triggers lung cancer in an Asian American woman who never smoked may not affect a young man in Europe.

As Stanford geneticist Michael Snyder puts it, a sick you is closer to a healthy you than to a sick me. His longitudinal study of 109 people found many health measurements stay stable within a person and vary widely between people. Population ranges matter, but your baseline may matter more.

Cancer itself is heterogeneous. It is not a single disease but a set of them, varying by tissue of origin, oncogenic drivers, and the immune context of each patient. What succeeds against a blood cancer like leukemia may fail against a solid tumor like pancreatic cancer.

Many cancers arise from genetic damage accumulated with age or through exposure to carcinogens such as tobacco smoke and ultraviolet radiation. Viruses and other pathogens cause an estimated 10% of new cases worldwide.

Technology should accelerate our understanding of cancer, but AI fatigue in the life sciences is warranted. Countless deaths and failed experiments already condition scientists and doctors to distrust breezy optimism. On top of this, past efforts often exacerbated workloads instead of freeing time for patients.

Skepticism has been amplified by crypto bros and growth marketers who breathlessly hype AI news, but also by AI experts who fixate on flaws.

The worst critics are right about the wrong things. In tech, the classic pitfall is being right about limitations but wrong about their permanence.

No technology is perfect, particularly one endeavoring to emulate an entity as opaque as the human mind.

By fixating on flaws, you will find plenty but also miss how primitive AI models could morph into sophisticated systems, transforming the world and producing trillions in market value.

The consolation prize is playing 3D chess in the Hall of Infamy with Paul Krugman, who in a 1998 essay titled "Why most economists' predictions are wrong" proclaimed that the Internet would not have a greater impact on the economy than the fax machine. He won the Nobel Prize in economics ten years later.

Pessimism is natural but frequently conflates difficulty with impossibility. It underestimates the rate of innovation and how small improvements can compound.

Surrendering to the problem as impossible merely guarantees no solution. Goals, especially audacious ones, demand belief.

This mindset empowered us to invent the airplane and put a man on the moon, despite declarations of impossibility.

Of course, we accomplished both before curing cancer for a reason.

All three require discovery and engineering, but machines can be simulated, reset, and retested. No two patients are the same. No patient can be reset.

Impossible metamorphoses into possible with belief, a refusal to accept demoralizing evidence as final without first exhausting every creative route. Belief is the enzyme, even if the transformation stays slow and encumbered by setbacks.

Tech needs to give our life science colleagues more reason to believe. No one understands the constraints better than the clinicians and scientists who devote themselves to easing suffering and prolonging lives.

Earning trust demands openness, not guardedness.

The strategy, as with any seemingly impossible task, is to speak plainly and honestly about where we want to go, where we are, and what we must do.

In the best case, the mission is to cure cancer, even after it has spread. In the worst, the goal is to reduce every cancer to a manageable condition, the way chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is now largely controllable with a daily pill instead of killing most patients within five years.

Today we stand far from such a world.

Cancer kills nearly 10 million people each year, with the most aggressive cases stealing our friends and loved ones within months of diagnosis.

Towering mountains and deep rivers block the way. Promises of a cure are deceptive because the probability of failure is staggeringly high.

There can only be pursuits, not promises. But CML and breakthroughs like PD-1/PD-L1 immunotherapy hint that the terrain is not impassable.

Similar leaps are what we seek. The path is forged sometimes by serendipitously connecting to an old trail or wandering long enough to discover one, other times by methodically chipping away, but always by pressing forward, stone by stone and plank by plank.

It is reasonable to say the odds of curing cancer are infinitesimal. It is reasonable to say AlphaFold changed the world but did not solve protein folding. It is reasonable to say virtual cell models, at this time, fall short of the hype and may not even represent the right cells in the tumor microenvironment. It is reasonable to say AI models do not capture the biochemical and biophysical dynamics of one human organ system, let alone the whole body.

It is reasonable to say AI trained on animal models and immortalized cell lines may not learn the reality of patients. It is reasonable to say small, unstratified studies may obscure human heterogeneity.

It is reasonable to say much of clinical work is deciding what to ignore, but vignettes and multiple-choice questions spoon-feed scenarios where most details count. It is reasonable to ask whether models overfit to benchmarks rather than reason clinically.

It is also eminently reasonable to say AI today covers a sliver of drug discovery, that no magic AI wand can wave away clinical trials. That beautiful binders for the wrong targets are worthless. Or that even if we develop a cure, we cannot designate it as such until years pass without signs of relapse.

Daphne Koller details many of these issues in a superb essay, "Drug Discovery Has No Magic Wands." She decomposes drug discovery into three stages: disease-to-mechanism, mechanism-to-drug, and drug-to-patient, and argues AI largely concentrates on the second.

My primary quibble is the decoupling of an interdependent system, illustrated by rocatinlimab. The antibody modulated the OX40 pathway as intended, but the mechanism may have let HHV-8, a typically dormant herpesvirus, escape immune control and cause Kaposi sarcoma in some patients.

Koller, a distinguished expert in AI biology, later covers the systems-level principle in the essay, and the three-stage abstraction is valuable for conceptualization. But it sidesteps a core tension: when is it logical to separate the disease from the patient?

Yes, the reasons to disbelieve are numerous. But stark differences separate today from yesterday and support grounded optimism.

AI is more sophisticated than ever. Yes, it may hallucinate and sound no smarter than a babbling child, but it has also achieved superhuman feats in math, cybersecurity, and weather forecasting. In chip design, AlphaChip from Google DeepMind has produced novel layouts that now ship inside the hardware training frontier models like Gemini.

In healthcare and biology, progress remains tangible even when verification is delayed and expensive. In early 2026, The Lancet published results from a randomized trial of over 105,000 Swedish women. AI-supported mammography raised sensitivity nearly seven points to 80.5% without reducing specificity. Computer-aided detection could not do this well a generation ago.

EAGLE, a model developed by researchers at Memorial Sloan Kettering and Mount Sinai, predicts the presence of EGFR mutations from routine pathology images. EGFR status helps determine treatment in lung adenocarcinoma, the most common histologic subtype of lung cancer. In a prospective silent trial published in Nature Medicine, an EAGLE-assisted workflow would have reduced rapid EGFR testing by up to 43%, with predictive performance comparable to the existing rapid test.

While AlphaFold did not solve protein folding, its database of over 200 million predicted structures helps scientists sharpen hypotheses and prioritize experiments on a scale infeasible with prior approaches.

Rentosertib marks another milestone. AI helped both identify TNIK, a kinase previously investigated in cancer, as a fibrosis target and design the compound. Phase 2a results were published in Nature Medicine last year, and a 320-patient Phase 3 is now registered to test efficacy.

The rate of innovation is accelerating. A jar of peanut butter enjoys a longer shelf life than frontier models. The field is also expanding. Billions in capital have flowed into AI-native startups, and researchers worldwide are contributing to cancer research and drug discovery.

Cancer is a systemic problem, yet careers reward specialization. Frontier models can now track research and draw connections across fields, allowing specialists to answer questions and explore ideas outside their expertise.

The reasons to doubt are many, but the reasons to believe are not few.

Ultimately, we are all allies. No one wants to stay trapped in this world of cancer, not even the staunchest AI critic. Not believing is reasonable. The burden of proof belongs with the optimists. Meanwhile, we can all help enumerate key gaps and draw the map:

- Which feedback loops between models and the real world remain neglected?

- Which promising targets lack assays fit for automated screening?

- What verification systems are missing?

- What new modalities and instruments do we need?

- Which datasets could help us understand and stop metastasis?

- Which dogmas are most likely wrong?

The cancer ecosystem is rich with expertise and infrastructure. Cancer Grand Challenges, for example, funds interdisciplinary teams to tackle intractable problems. Open Targets integrates genetic, transcriptomic, and clinical evidence into scores ranking target-disease associations.

The opportunity is to complement these initiatives by designing for humans and AI from the outset. People thrive when creating and deciding, but dislike rote tasks. AI can automate menial work and analyze across domains, but needs supervision.

The open secret of AI is how data and evaluations can dictate performance more than model architecture. Without data, you cannot train AI. And without evaluations, you cannot steer it.

Some proposals:

1. Pilot an AI reference design in five rare cancers.

Reference designs are blueprints for building complex systems. Nvidia develops them so partners can deploy and customize AI infrastructure without solving the same problems from scratch.

Similarly, Nvidia and frontier labs can give disease foundations the template and resources for connecting talent, knowledge, and experiments into a learning system accelerated with AI.

More than 300 million people live with roughly 7,000 rare diseases, over 95% of which lack an effective treatment. Piloting in five rare cancers focuses effort and tests what transfers.

Chordoma is a bone cancer diagnosed in about one person per million each year. The Chordoma Foundation provides much of what the reference design could emulate and extend.

The foundation supplies tumor tissue, disease models, and wet-lab capabilities such as target validation and drug testing. It curates priorities, resources, and knowledge, lowering the barriers for researchers to contribute.

It fills gaps left by academia and industry and shares nonconfidential results, including negative ones. Models, like humans, trained only on success may struggle to learn what fails.

Concretely:

- Build the disease knowledge graph. Frontier labs seed it with claims from the literature, each linked to evidence and work reliant on it. The graph maps open questions, foundation priorities, and assets such as cell lines. People access it through ordinary AI assistants or AI-generated personalized interfaces.

- Frontier labs donate compute and embed engineers. Foundations oversee implementation and tailor each graph using a shared schema and canonical identifiers. Corrections can then propagate across cancers and organizations.

- Grant access. Model Context Protocol, or MCP, connects AI assistants to the graph, data, and tools the foundation permits. The foundation's priorities, judgment, and resources can then guide research.

- Attract ideas with prizes. In tech, competitions can efficiently concentrate energy. ARC Prize drew 1,430 teams with a $1M purse. The Chordoma Foundation created a $500K challenge for binding TBXT, a key driver of chordoma, and included free biophysical evaluations. Anthropic and AWS backed a $50K hackathon for one child's rare disease. Frontier labs can supply compute and awards.

- Turn hypotheses into experiments. The design specifies how an idea moves from the graph through expert review to an assay or disease model. Labs run the experiment and return results to the graph.

2. Seed open validation.

The WHO says more than 7,000 rare diseases exist while the FDA says more than 10,000.

How many are there?

When experts disagree, how do people determine the truth? How about machines?

In science, facts are born as claims and mature into truth through validation. Most truths endure while others are refined or overturned as new data, methods, or cohorts emerge.

Consider MDA-MB-435, a melanoma cell line mistakenly used to study breast cancer before cell line authentication became more common. The origin was contested for years. By the time it was resolved, decades of breast cancer findings based on melanoma cells had already accumulated.

Outdated or overstated claims can misdirect years of research, and the risk rises with automated scientific loops.

Humans, however, are rewarded for novelty and not for the unglamorous work of validation.

As such, we lack a public system and incentive structure for tracing what supports each claim and what depends on it, and for propagating updates through the literature.

Open source offers a precedent, where code has a public history and unresolved problems remain visible. The frontier labs could seed open validation, starting in the same five cancers. The knowledge graph gives models and researchers a place to check claims.

- Machines analyze, humans judge. Models revisit claims as evidence changes, trace dependent work, and highlight conflicts. They flag studies missing key controls or details needed to assess or replicate the work. Experts decide what the evidence supports and what merits retesting. Selected items become open issues in the graph.

- Version control each claim. The graph preserves how a claim and its evidence change over time. Models can see what earlier work relied on and what the evidence supports now.

- Fund validation. Pilot one validation per cancer, prioritized by what depends on it. Foundations can later apply to validate others. Frontier labs provide the capital. Publish every outcome, including negative and inconclusive ones, plus time and cost, and update the graph.

- Standardize claim checks. AI assistants learn to query the graph before relying on a claim, recording the version used.

3. Scale up biological datasets.

Koller sees a data chasm between what we can measure in patients and how drugs act inside cells. The average adult has roughly 30 trillion cells across hundreds of types and many states, each of which may respond differently to the same intervention. A TBXT drug may work in one state, for instance, yet not another.

The chasm is enormous. As she writes, "The largest cell atlases assembled to date, now spanning hundreds of millions of cells, remain orders of magnitude too small to cover this space."

The answer is not always data, though. In glioblastoma, a beautiful drug against the right target can still fail unless it crosses the blood-brain barrier.

The answer is also not indiscriminate scale. One billion pulse readings cannot explain why lung cancer develops.

The answer is creating and scaling the right data.

For causal understanding, Koller argues for perturbational experiments to measure how a living system changes after an intervention.

Observational datasets offer a pragmatic complement, though cannot alone establish causality. Drawn from patient tissue, blood, and other specimens, they help scientists identify patterns across tumors, generate hypotheses, and design experiments.

While not the whole problem, data remains a central bottleneck because gaps can hide mechanisms and risks.

Addressing this means scaling data both up and out. Scaling out, or integrating more of what exists, might have connected OX40 modulation to the risk of Kaposi sarcoma sooner.

Yet gaping holes remain in cancer datasets. The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), a landmark molecular map completed in 2018 and spanning 33 cancer types, demonstrates what scaling data up can achieve. It reshaped cancer genomics and has enabled thousands of researchers to deepen our understanding of cancer.

These gaps puzzled me, but the explanation became clearer the more I studied biomedicine. It mirrors a pattern in AI, where research incentives and interests favor discovery over dataset construction.

Practical burdens also hurt. Specimens are difficult to obtain, clinical records are messy, and assembling multi-site cohorts can take years. This leaves disease foundations and others to fill the void.

As a result, many valuable datasets remain unbuilt.

Take lung cancer in never smokers (LCINS).

LCINS accounts for up to a quarter of lung cancers worldwide and would rank as the fifth-leading cause of cancer death on its own. In the US, up to 20% of lung cancers occur in never smokers, or people who have smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lifetime.

Among Asian American women with lung cancer, more than half are never smokers, and the figure nears 80% among Chinese American women.

Proteins perform and regulate cellular activities, but some can drive tumor growth and survival when dysregulated. Many cancer drugs target such proteins. Yet most LCINS datasets stop at DNA and RNA, both imperfect proxies for protein abundance. RNA, the closer of the two, poorly predicted the abundance of more than one-third of 13,000 proteins across eight cancers.

Proteomics, the measurement of many proteins, can reveal molecular subtypes while nominating prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets not inferable from DNA and RNA alone.

In colorectal cancer, proteomics helped reduce a broad set of driver candidates to the most promising ones. In a 406-tumor lung adenocarcinoma atlas, protein patterns marked a group at higher risk of recurrence, including stage I tumors whose biology resembled advanced disease.

Armed with proteomic insights, the field can enhance treatment strategies based on protein tests. Certain subtypes of lung cancer, for example, can overexpress the c-Met protein without corresponding DNA alterations. As a result, genomic profiling may fail to identify patients who could benefit from a c-Met-directed drug.

LCINS is not a single disease. Beyond tumor biology and treatment, patients vary in genetic susceptibility and carcinogen exposure.

Capturing this heterogeneity requires both scale and representative sampling.

The 406-tumor atlas included 242 tumors from never smokers, but only seven came from the United States, leaving little power to resolve subgroups within American LCINS. Dedicated proteomic LCINS cohorts typically profile about 100 tumors and top out at 150.

At those sizes, a subgroup representing 5% of LCINS patients yields about five to eight patients, compared with fifty in a cohort of 1,000. Recurrence analyses are constrained further because only a subset will recur, leaving perhaps just a few events. This also assumes the cohorts capture real-world heterogeneity, which may not hold.

A 1,000-tumor atlas of LCINS adenocarcinomas linked to outcomes is better scaled for subgroup analysis. Focusing on one histology prevents cross-histology differences from dominating protein clusters. Adenocarcinoma is the most common form of LCINS and already has extensive genomic datasets and tissue collections.

Unlike many missing oncology datasets, this atlas could rely mostly on archived specimens, decreasing the need for new biopsies.

What remains is largely capital and execution: auditing specimens for sufficient tissue and consented use, standardizing workflows, and linking each tumor to treatment, recurrence, and survival.

Nvidia and frontier labs have both the footprint and the motive to scale datasets across borders. International atlases fit awkwardly within national mandates, but AI models expected to generalize across human heterogeneity need global data.

They also have the capital and could share costs across public datasets. The OpenAI Foundation, for example, plans to invest at least $1 billion over the next year across four areas, including life sciences and curing diseases.

Given the disease burden of LCINS, frontier labs could start with this atlas, then ask disease foundations which molecular, imaging, and longitudinal datasets they need but cannot build alone.

4. Make clinical trials cheap, fast, and informative.

In pharma, Koller observes an aversion to failure and a herd mentality. Novel targets per year have dropped from roughly 100 in 2015 to about 30 in 2024 while 37 targets each carry more than 50 programs.

My diagnosis differs. When bets can run $100 million or more, caution is rational. Every pharma executive aspires to cure cancer, but must worry about job security like all of us.

Evidence-based thinking cuts both ways. As CEO, are you promoting the executive who blew $100 million on an unproven target, or the one who shipped a profitable program against de-risked biology? As a patient, do you prefer the trial backed by human evidence or the untested one?

As Koller points out, we cannot engineer around disease progression. To get 24 months of follow-up, we must wait 24 months.

Cost, however, is different. We can make trials faster to launch and cheaper to run while maintaining robust ethical guardrails.

Decades of tech history prove what falling costs make possible. More people can create and participate, and innovation blooms.

More trials mean more ideas tested, perhaps more of them designed for human heterogeneity. Failures are inevitable, but learning from them could deepen our understanding of cancer.

Twitter unfortunately cut this idea short, so the next essay will flesh it out. I believe certain labs could benefit from building public health infrastructure the way governments built highways.

In the end, not overpromising is the right first step.

State the mission, flag the gaps, and do what others will not.

Stone by stone, plank by plank, it is possible.

text:
Two people get the same job offer. One negotiates and gets $7,000 more. Thirty years later that person is earning $100,000 a year more than the one who didn't. Same offer, same start, one conversation.

Margaret Neale teaches negotiation at Stanford's Graduate School of Business, and Stanford put her talk online for free. her first move is to take the whole thing away from you and hand it back differently.

most people treat negotiation as a fight, and avoid it because they are afraid of looking greedy or demanding or difficult. she says it is not a fight. it is problem solving, and problem solving is collaborative.

then she corrects the goal itself. the goal is not to get a deal. the goal is to get a good deal. and to tell one from the other you need three numbers before you walk in.

your alternative. what actually happens to you if this falls apart. the research on this is not subtle - whoever has the better alternative does better.

your reservation price. the exact point where saying yes and walking away feel identical.

your aspiration. an optimistic read of what is genuinely achievable. she says this is the one almost everyone skips, and it is the one that sets the ceiling.

four steps after that. assess. prepare. ask. package.
the last one is where most people lose money.

most of us negotiate issue by issue. salary. then start date. then title. and she says that is a terrible strategy, because when you take issues one at a time, every single one becomes a win or a loss. there is nothing to trade.

put them in a package and suddenly you can trade across them. if I give you this, then I get that.

she ran it on her own dean. he emailed the faculty that everyone was moving from five courses a year to six, because the provost wanted contact hours to match course credit. so he had changed the credit to match the hours.

she worked out what he actually wanted - the provost off his back - and proposed the reverse. change the contact hours to match the credit. her specialty classes already ran three and a half to four hours regularly. so make them four-hour courses on paper. she stays at five.

he told her he had never thought of it. she was the only faculty member to get an exception, and everybody had received the same email.

two reasons, she says. she decided to negotiate. and she arrived with something that left him no worse off.

then the line that stays with you. every bad deal you have ever taken, you agreed to. which means you need the capacity to say no, and you will never learn whether they would have come back unless you are willing to walk.

her homework is deliberately small. go to a shop, find something you want, and negotiate for it. low stakes, real practice.

Stanford filmed it and left it up.

the talk is free. working out how much you have already paid to avoid the discomfort of asking is the part nobody hands you.

Breaking News
Seattle police union sounds alarm after city axes officer hiring bonuses amid staffing shortage

The department is hundreds of officers short of staffing goals, while nearby Bellevue police offer $30,000 signing bonuses

Seattle's police union is sounding the alarm after the city eliminated lucrative hiring bonuses for new and experienced officers despite the department remaining hundreds of cops short, warning the move could make it even harder to compete with neighboring departments for recruits.

"Public safety should be the cornerstone of every city budget," Seattle Police Officers Guild President Kent Loux told Fox News Digital after the city ended incentives that had offered $7,500 to new recruits and as much as $50,000 to experienced officers willing to join the Seattle Police Department. 

"Unfortunately, Mayor Katie has proven time and again that public safety is not a priority, but rather an inconvenience to be addressed after tragedy strikes.

"The decision to eliminate hiring incentives is baffling. Seattle has still not recovered from the consequences of the defund-the-police movement that began in 2020, and we remain hundreds of officers short. Now is the time to be aggressively recruiting qualified officers, not eliminating one of the tools that helps us compete for them. Keith Ellison’s office did not invent compassion. It invented a rule that disagreement is “intolerance” and that a parent who will not affirm a child’s confusion may need supervised visits. That is not care. That is the state taking a child’s tantrum and calling it law.

There are two sexes. Male and female. That is not hate. That is biology, language, and the created order Christians have named for two thousand years: “male and female He created them.” Jesus did not heal people by baptizing their delusions. He told the truth and then bound up the wounded. Gender dysphoria is real suffering. Treat it as a mental and developmental disorder: protect the body, refuse irreversible harm to minors, offer therapy and community instead of a costume and a court order. Love the person. Do not hand them the scalpel and call it dignity.

The Founders wrote a Constitution for a people capable of self-government, not a nursery. They knew factions, zealots, and fashionable errors. They would not have let a loud sliver of the population rewrite sex, silence religious conscience in a public law office, or instruct lawyers to “deal with” colleagues who still believe what every generation before 2010 believed. They built walls against the mob and against the magistrate who confuses mercy with surrender.

A child will scream and nag until Momma says yes. A healthy mother does not say yes to every demand. She loves the child enough to say no. America has spent a decade saying yes to every identity, every disorder recast as a right, every demand for affirmation as if attention were medicine. That is not inclusion. That is enabling. Caring for every person means refusing to give them everything they ask for—especially when the ask is that the rest of us deny reality.

Ellison’s office is not protecting the vulnerable. It is pandering to a small, very loud segment and training public lawyers to treat dissent as an HR emergency. Stop. Be resolute. Two sexes. Religious liberty. Parental authority. Care without capitulation. The tantrum ends when the grown-ups stand up.

text:
His organizations absolutely have done some good. But that no way excuses the incredible harm he has inflicted on our nation and in fact our world over decades. 

1. He taught the country that Christian morality is a weapon, not a standard.

In 1998 he told America that a president’s private sexual sin was public business, that lying to a wife predicted lying to the nation, and that confession without spin was required. Two decades later, hush money to a porn star was “nobody’s business,” Clinton’s impeachment was “a great mistake,” and Trump was a man God placed in office. Same category of conduct. Opposite rule. The only thing that changed was the team.

That is not a private inconsistency. It is a public lesson. Once a leading evangelist says character is essential until it costs a Supreme Court seat, everyone else learns the real doctrine: morality is for out-groups. Secular critics already suspected that. Graham confirmed it from the pulpit of American evangelicalism. David French put it plainly: the double standard “seared the consciences of the culture and the church” and handed opponents a permanent argument that the piety was never sincere.

A society needs some people who will apply the same rule to their friends. Graham models the opposite and calls it faithfulness.

2. He fused the Graham name with partisan power and called the result providence.

Billy Graham built a reputation, however imperfect, as a preacher who wanted a hearing across parties. Franklin used the inheritance as a political asset: God put Trump there because he “offended everybody” and still won; America is “morally rotten” because of gay marriage and transgender people; “Christian nationalism” is just a media slur; opponents are destroying the country. He has preached God as a “God of war” at the Pentagon, blessed candidates as if elections were salvation history, and treated criticism of Trump as spiritual warfare.

The social cost is not that Christians vote. It is that a billion-dollar ministry tells believers their political tribe is the church. That makes compromise look like apostasy and neighbors look like enemies. It also trains non-Christians to hear “Jesus” and think “this faction.” You do not need to like secularism to see why that is a civic problem. A large religion that cannot criticize its own champion cannot restrain him either.

3. The charities make vulnerable people a mission field.

Samaritan’s Purse does surgeries, water, food, and disaster rebuilds. It also runs Operation Christmas Child as explicit evangelism. Graham’s own line: every shoebox is “an opportunity to reach one more child with the Gospel.” Boxes go out with a gospel presentation; children are steered into a 12-lesson conversion course. Schools and parents in donor countries are often sold a simple “toys for poor kids” story. Recipients in poor or religiously different communities get a gift that is hard to refuse and a follow-up that is not neutral. Critics have called that gift-wrapped pressure. Save the Children has warned against mixing humanitarian work with a conversion agenda. UK chains and services have dropped the program over it.

You can believe evangelism is good and still see the problem: need becomes leverage. That is a bad precedent for every faith and every NGO. It also means a large share of the “charity” budget is not development. It is a distribution system for a religious product.

The same pattern showed up in New York in 2020. A field hospital in Central Park treated COVID patients. Staff had to affirm a statement of faith that defines marriage as one genetic male and one genetic female. Graham has said gay people face “the flames of hell,” that Satan drives LGBTQ rights, and that Pete Buttigieg should be ashamed, not praised. Patients were told they would not be turned away. Staff were told they must share the creed. In a pluralist city in a plague, that is not just “religious liberty.” It is a public institution of last resort branded by a man who has spent years telling a class of patients they are detestable. Even if every patient was treated, the signal was: your body may be saved here; your dignity is conditional.

4. He uses compassion as a shield for contempt.

This is the mechanism that makes the rest work. When you criticize the politics, the answer is Ukraine food tonnage. When you criticize the theology of exclusion, the answer is hurricane rebuilds. When you criticize the hypocrisy, the answer is “we’re all sinners” — a sentence he did not offer Clinton in 1998 and does not offer gay Christians now.

That is a bad bargain for society. It teaches donors that good works purchase moral immunity. It teaches targets of the rhetoric that the hospital tent and the denunciation come from the same hand. And it teaches the broader public a brutal civics lesson: if you deliver enough sandbags, you can say almost anything.

The books reinforce the insulation. Samaritan’s Purse takes in well over a billion dollars some years, sits on multi-billion-dollar assets, and paid Graham about $945,000 from that organization alone in 2024, plus an undisclosed BGEA salary. BGEA stopped filing a Form 990 after being classified as a church. Both groups left the Evangelical Council for Financial Accountability. None of that proves theft. It does prove that the brand is built to be hard to audit and hard to separate from the man. A private political actor with a charity halo is harder to check than either a pastor or an NGO director would be alone.

5. The net cultural product is fear plus exemption.

Add the rhetoric: Islam as “evil and wicked,” “true Islam” impossible in America because it means beating wives; Obama “born a Muslim”; praise for Putin’s anti-gay laws; America “completely sick with sin” over gender and sexuality; violence in video games as national decay; God intervening to spare a politician. Then subtract the one thing that would make that preaching costly: applying it to the leader he needs. What remains is a public religion of panic about out-groups and amnesty for in-groups.

That is a negative influence even if you grant every crate of water. Societies get meaner when moral language is used that way. Churches get emptier among people who notice the split. Politics gets more apocalyptic. Charity gets more suspected. The Graham name, which once signaled a big-tent invitation to “come to Christ,” now signals a societal wedge. Franklin Graham’s organizations do enough genuine good that people excuse a leadership project that makes American religion less honest, American politics more sacralized, and American charity more conditional. The planes and field hospitals are not the rebuttal. They are the reason the rest of it spreads.

text:
The AI and space industries shifted hard today.

OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra and called it a new frontier in computer and browser use. The model navigates spreadsheets, websites, and desktop apps, writes code, and hunts vulnerabilities. OpenAI also touted its ability to find zero-days. But the model uses opaque recurrence reasoning, which obscures chain of thought and alarms safety researchers. Greg Brockman said he personally thinks AGI is here.

Nvidia confirmed it acquired Hugging Face for $12.93 billion. The platform hosts three million models, one million applications, and serves over 18 million developers. It was clocking $150 million in annualized revenue and rejected a $500 million offer from Nvidia last year.

Accel is in talks to lead a $1 billion round for Thinking Machines at a $40 billion valuation. The startup was founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati and now has over $100 million in annual revenue. Its last round was $2 billion at a $12 billion valuation.

Microsoft released MAI-Transcribe-2 at ten cents an hour, down from $0.36 five months ago. That is a 72 percent price cut. The model runs ten times faster than OpenAI's GPT-Transcribe and supports 60 languages. For a large bank processing 100,000 hours of call audio a year, costs drop from $36,000 to $10,000.

Google shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash, its third Flash model in six weeks, alongside a Cyber twin built specifically to hunt software vulnerabilities. The releases show Google racing to make its models the default runtime for AI agents.

SpaceX is planning to invest as much as $100 billion into a massive Louisiana spaceport. The project would become one of the largest aerospace infrastructure bets ever and a direct bet on Starship launch cadence.

NASA is quietly redesigning its lunar spacesuit because the Artemis IV timeline is slipping, while China delayed its critical Moon launch to 2027 after one of its workhorse rockets exploded in flight. The setbacks are slowing the lunar race and giving the US breathing room.

That is the daily roundup.

Paul Harvey’s 1965 radio commentary “If I Were the Devil” and Ion Mihai Pacepa’s 2013 book Disinformation (co-authored with Ronald J. Rychlak) are not directly connected. Harvey never cites Soviet intelligence, and Pacepa does not discuss Harvey. The useful correlation is thematic: both describe a strategy of internal moral and institutional corrosion aimed at the United States rather than open military conquest. Harvey presents it as a spiritual allegory. Pacepa presents it as documented (in his telling) KGB “dezinformatsiya” and active measures.

Harvey’s piece is a short, rhetorical warning. Pacepa’s book is a longer insider account of how Eastern Bloc services tried to weaken the West by attacking religion, rewriting history, and using Western media and churches as unwitting carriers. The overlap is strongest on targets and methods, not on proof that Harvey was describing KGB operations.

Shared pattern: attack the moral and religious foundation first

Harvey opens by saying he would “subvert the churches first” with a “campaign of whispers”: “Do as you please,” the Bible is a myth, man created God, what is bad is good and what is good is “square.” The old would be taught to pray “Our Father, which art in Washington.”

Pacepa and Rychlak argue that Soviet intelligence treated Christianity—especially the Catholic Church—as a primary obstacle because it supplied an independent moral authority that competed with the state and with Marxist ideology. They describe campaigns to smear church leaders (most famously the multi-decade effort to recast Pius XII as “Hitler’s Pope”), to promote Liberation Theology as a Marxist-compatible Christianity that would split churches and turn them against the United States, and to influence bodies such as the World Council of Churches.

Both accounts treat religion not as a side issue but as the first line of defense. Harvey calls it the devil’s opening move. Pacepa calls it a systematic intelligence priority.

Moral inversion, youth, and family

Harvey’s devil whispers to the young that traditional faith and restraint are outdated, then predicts families, churches, and nations “at war with themselves.” He adds lurid literature, dirtier entertainment, narcotics, alcohol, tranquilizers, and schools that refine intellect but neglect discipline.

Pacepa’s framework is ideological subversion: replace traditional Christian ethics with relativism or politicized substitutes, amplify existing social tensions, and let Western institutions do much of the work. The book ties this to longer-term goals of reducing the West’s cohesion and its will to resist. Media is central in both pictures. Harvey says “mesmerizing media” would fan the flames for ratings. Pacepa says disinformation only succeeds when respected Western outlets treat planted stories as independent reporting.

Government as substitute authority

Harvey’s line about praying to Washington is a compact image of the state replacing God. Pacepa’s book repeatedly returns to the same substitution: weaken the church’s independent standing so that political ideology and the state fill the vacuum. Both treat this as a feature, not a bug, of the strategy they describe.

Important limits of the comparison

Harvey is preaching a moral warning in 1965. He does not name the KGB, communism, or any intelligence service. His “devil” is a literary and theological device that also functions as social criticism of trends he already saw in American life.

Pacepa is making specific historical claims about operations he says he participated in or observed (framing Pius XII, Liberation Theology, anti-American and anti-Zionist campaigns, later efforts in the Islamic world). Those claims are influential in some conservative and Catholic circles and contested by many historians, especially the assertion that Liberation Theology was essentially a KGB invention.

Correlation is not causation. 

Mid-century secularization, the sexual revolution, changes in media, and domestic political conflict had many sources. Pacepa’s argument is that Soviet active measures accelerated and steered some of those currents, particularly around religion and anti-American narratives. Harvey simply lists the symptoms as if they were a coordinated plan.

Pacepa’s later chapters expand into post-Cold War and Islamist-related disinformation. Harvey’s 1965 text does not.

How the two texts complement each other
Read together, they offer two languages for the same pattern:

Harvey supplies the inside-the-culture diagnosis: what it would look and sound like if America’s religious and moral habits were being systematically loosened.

Pacepa supplies an intelligence-history diagnosis: how a hostile state actor tried to produce some of those effects through fronts, forgeries, recruited or influenced clergy, and media operations that were meant to look homegrown.

The tightest overlap is not “Harvey predicted the KGB” but this: both treat the United States as uniquely valuable (“the ripest apple”) and both argue that the decisive battlefield is churches, families, schools, and the stories people believe about good, evil, and authority—not tanks or missiles. Harvey frames the agent as the devil. Pacepa frames one historical agent as the KGB’s Service A and its sister services. The methods they describe—whispers, inversion of values, internal division, media amplification, displacement of God by the state—line up closely enough that many readers who take both seriously treat Harvey’s monologue as a folk summary of the kind of campaign Pacepa later documented from the other side.

Not only is Trump NOT paying for the ballroom — he’s given the business to a buddy… AGAIN. And they know what they’re doing is wrong, because they’re trying to keep it secret!

Trump’s White House secretly awarded another no-bid contract worth up to $500 million for the construction of the East Wing ballroom — routing it through the Executive Residence LAST YEAR, an office that is exempt from rules that require federal agencies to solicit competitive bids and disclose details to the public. 

The office is typically responsible for routine repairs, entertainment expenses, and the purchase of furniture, art and other items for the executive mansion.

The confidential contract with Clark Construction, along with related correspondence and records obtained by The Post, reveal for the first time how the Trump administration bypassed norms last summer as it set the ballroom project in motion.

Records also show that Trump was directly involved in negotiating some costs for the East Wing project.

The East Wing contract is the latest example of the administration turning to no-bid deals to hasten a Trump-style makeover of the nation’s capital, which has included handpicking firms to upgrade Lafayette Square next to the White House and to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Competitive bidding is generally required at most federal agencies. Experts said the Executive Residence is exempt from those rules, and the president has legal authority to hire companies of his choosing to make changes to the executive mansion and the surrounding grounds. Those experts said soliciting bids would have ensured the best price for taxpayers, especially given the size and cost of the East Wing project.

The estimated East Wing construction cost has tripled since last July, when the project was first announced, with half expected to come from taxpayers, The Post previously reported.

Trump has repeatedly claimed that the ballroom would be paid for by private donors and once said that Clark executives offered to build it for free.

📸: The Washington Post

text:
📚Canadian nationalism rises as US threatens sovereignty📚

Ahmed Adel

The trade war between Washington and Ottawa has escalated from a tariff dispute into an aggressive campaign against Canadian sovereignty and identity. United States President Donald Trump recently signed an order renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” a move that has no legal force in Canada but is a national insult. Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the change outright, noting that the indigenous Wendat word Ontari’io is more than four centuries old and that Canadians will continue to call the lake what it has always been. Trump’s renaming of the lake came only days after trade talks collapsed and new American duties took effect, further straining relations between the two North American neighbors.

The US, Canada, and Mexico were required to conduct a joint review of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement in 2026. Although Ottawa and Mexico City sought to lock in a fresh 16-year term, Washington declined to renew the pact in its current form, leaving the existing agreement in force until at least 2036. Canada has sought relief from sectoral tariffs imposed by the US on steel, aluminum, autos, and lumber, and has offered concessions on dairy access, provincial alcohol listings, and automotive content rules.

In mid-August, Trump briefly claimed a deal had been reached and paused a new 50% tariff, but the deal collapsed a few days later, leading to sanctions and reciprocal measures. This has hurt Canada more because more than two-thirds of Canadian merchandise exports head to the US. Therefore, Canada’s commercial diversification will be a long and difficult process, especially since other countries diversified earlier.

Trump’s attempts to interfere with Canadian sovereignty and cultural identity — including pressure on the French language, annexation talk, and symbolic gestures such as the lake renaming — are rekindling nationalism among Canadians. The US president has repeatedly claimed he could absorb Canada as an American state. Combined with the tariffs and a citizen-led boycott of some US goods and travel, these actions have reignited nationalist sentiment among Canadians.

US pressure on Canada started during Justin Trudeau’s prime ministership. By the end of his government, Washington’s stance had become more assertive, with discussions of annexation for the first time. Carney’s rise indicated that public opinion supported a tougher approach to the US while still leaving open the possibility of a future trade agreement. That harder line now includes a pivot toward large markets outside the US orbit.

In January, Carney visited Beijing and announced a strategic partnership with China focused on energy, agriculture, and trade. The agreement included an initial plan to cut Chinese tariffs on Canadian canola seed to about 15%, down from nearly 85%, affecting a market worth approximately $4 billion for Prairie farmers. Canada also agreed to allow up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at the most-favored-nation rate of 6.1% and to aim to increase exports to China by 50% by 2030. China already ranks as Canada’s second-largest trading partner, and officials believe that trade volume there is crucial for Canada to double its non-US exports within ten years. However, there are questions and fears that Canada is simply replacing one dependency with another.

Carney has also made India a key partner. After years of diplomatic coldness between India and Canada due to Trudeau’s meddling in India’s domestic affairs, Carney and Prime Minister Narendra Modi revived negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. Both countries aim to finalize the agreement by the end of the year and to more than double bilateral trade to $70 billion by 2030. New Delhi announced a strategic energy partnership covering LNG, LPG, uranium, solar, and hydrogen, as well as memoranda on critical minerals, technology, talent, and defense. Canadian energy and mining ministers view India as a natural buyer of Canadian LNG and high-grade minerals as New Delhi expands nuclear capacity and manufacturing.

Canada is also turning to its trade agreement with the European Union, under which merchandise trade has grown sharply; the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership; critical-minerals partnerships with European and Indo-Pacific countries; and talks with ASEAN and Mercosur. Ottawa’s stated target is to double non-US exports within ten years and to build trade corridors that extend beyond the Americas.

Predicting such a sharp decline in bilateral relations would have been unthinkable in recent times, given the historically deep political, economic, and social ties between Americans and Canadians. However, increasing unpredictability in White House domestic politics under Trump is causing tension with traditional partners like Canada, which are seeking to reduce their dependence on the US. This shift once again points to a major reorganization of the bilateral relationships between the White House and former allies. Canada cannot exit the American market but is under pressure and diversifying its trade partners to ensure it is no longer solely reliant on the US.

text:
Israel's Jerusalem Post has published a proposal every American should read. The argument runs like this: the war on Iran cannot be sold to the American public. A ground campaign would need somewhere between 750,000 and 1.5 million troops. The active Army has about 452,000. So the gap should be closed by offering to erase the student loans, credit-card balances and car notes of Americans aged 18 to 34 in exchange for two or three years in uniform.

Look past the fact that a foreign newspaper is calculating how many American families should bury a child. Look at the mechanism. The author has identified a population under financial pressure, priced the relief, and concluded that an indebted young American can be bought for about forty thousand dollars.

At $40,000 a head, 750,000 recruits costs $30 billion. The full 1.5 million costs $60 billion.

Now set that against the bill Americans are already paying. The White House has sent Congress an $87 billion supplemental request for this war, on top of direct military operations already estimated at up to $42 billion. The Pentagon told the House Armed Services Committee the figure was $25 billion; Democratic members and outside economists put the cost to the American economy between $630 billion and $1 trillion. Independent trackers put the first 108 days alone above $113 billion.

The war has already consumed more money than every debt the author proposes to forgive, several times over. The supplemental request by itself would clear the balance sheets of more than two million young Americans.

Then there is the standing line item. Israel receives roughly $3.3 billion a year in Foreign Military Financing plus $500 million for joint missile-defence programmes. Cumulatively, the United States has provided Israel about $352 billion in aid, including $263 billion in military assistance, in inflation-adjusted terms. That sum, had it stayed home, would have discharged the non-mortgage debt of some six million Americans in exactly the cohort the Post has now marked for enlistment.

So there is a simpler version of the author's own proposal. Cut the aid to Israel. Cut it completely and cut it now, and apply the money to the debt. The young American gets the debt relief without having to sell his life for it. His government can stop asking him to pay for someone else's war with his blood.

Weird how you never hear about any of this in the news...... TRUMP DOES THE UNTHINKABLE...
I've never heard anything negative about the man until he announced he was running for president.
• He's never even tried alcohol or tobacco. He doesn't do drugs.

• His work ethic is beyond unparalleled as a hardworking businessman.

• He's one of the most generous celebrities in the world with a heart filled with more gold than his $100 million New York penthouse.

Since the media has failed so miserably at reporting the truth about Trump, I decided to put together some of the acts of kindness he's committed over three decades which has gone virtually unnoticed or fallen on deaf ears.

• In 1986, Trump prevented the foreclosure of Annabell Hill's family farm after her husband committed suicide. Trump personally phoned down to the auction to stop the sale of her home and offered the widow money. Trump decided to take action after he saw Hill's pleas for help in news reports.

• In 1988, a commercial airline refused to fly Andrew Ten, a sick Orthodox Jewish child with a rare illness. The boy had to travel with an elaborate life-support system. Trump contacted the grief-stricken parents after hearing this and didn't hesitate to send his own plane to take the child from Los Angeles to New York so he could get his treatment.

• In 1991, 200 Marines who served in Operation Desert Storm spent time at Camp Lejune in North Carolina before they were scheduled to return home to their families. However, the Marines were told that a mistake had been made and an aircraft would not be able to take them home on their scheduled departure date. When Trump got wind of this, he sent his plane to make two trips from North Carolina to Miami to safely return the Gulf War Marines to their loved ones.

• In 1995, a motorist stopped to help Trump after the limo he was traveling in got a flat tire. Trump asked the Good Samaritan how he could repay him for his help. All the man asked for was a bouquet of flowers for his wife. A few weeks later Trump sent the flowers with a note that read: We've paid off your mortgage.

• In 1996, Trump filed a lawsuit against the city of Palm Beach , Florida, accusing the town of discriminating against his Mar-a-Lago resort club because it allowed Jews and blacks. Abraham Foxman, who as the Anti-Defamation League Director at the time, said Trump put the light on Palm Beach not on the beauty and the glitter, but on its seamier side of discrimination. Foxman also noted that Trump's charge had a trickle-down effect because other clubs followed his lead and began admitting Jews and blacks.

• In 2000, Maury Povich featured a little girl named Megan who struggled with Brittle Bone Disease on his show and Trump happened to be watching. Trump said the little girl's story and positive attitude touched his heart. So he contacted Maury and gifted the little girl and her family with a very generous check.

• In 2008, after Jennifer Hudson's family members were tragically murdered in Chicago , Trump put the Oscar-winning actress and her family up at his Windy City hotel for free. In addition to that, Trump's security took extra measures to ensure Hudson and her family members were safe during such a difficult time.
• In 2013, New York bus driver Darnell Barton spotted a woman close to the edge of a bridge staring at the traffic below as he drove by. He stopped the bus, got out and put his arm around the woman and saved her life by convincing her to not jump. When Trump heard about this story, he sent the hero bus driver a check simply because he believed his good deed deserved to be rewarded.

Dear members of the American press!

Steve Jobs once said, "If you can convince the press of your technology, and the press convinces us, we'll pay attention."

That's why I'm reaching out to you.

For years, the development of personal devices has been driven by advances in smartphones, tablets, and virtual reality technologies. However, all of these solutions still require people to adapt to the device. I've developed a concept based on the opposite principle: the device should adapt to the user and interact with them as naturally as possible.

I believe this technology has the potential to be the next major step in the development of consumer electronics. It offers a fundamentally new way to interact with the digital environment and has the potential to replace many existing devices that accompany people in their daily lives today.

If my assessment is correct, this isn't just another gadget, but a platform capable of transforming the market in the same way that the personal computer, iPod, and iPhone once did. Such opportunities arise extremely rarely, and that's why they deserve independent attention and objective assessment.

I believe Apple has the experience, engineering culture, and vision necessary to turn this idea into a world-class product. Moreover, the successful implementation of such technology could strengthen the leadership of the American tech industry at a time when global competition is becoming increasingly fierce.

I'm not asking you to take my word for it. I'm asking only one thing: help draw Apple's attention to this development and give it the opportunity to be considered by those capable of objectively assessing its potential.

If the technology truly represents the value I see in it, ignoring it could be a missed opportunity. If not, that will become clear after a professional evaluation. But in either case, the idea deserves to be heard.

Thank you for your attention.

Sincerely,

Alexander.

text:
Just had an incredible conversation with Heather Cowap, MS, MEd, RSM about the future of early childhood education and why schools should be run from top to bottom on Agile and Scrum frameworks. And our conversation had insights too good not to share.

We dug into the massive misunderstanding around accountability in our school systems. Too often, we conflate accountability with "getting in trouble," when it really just means owning your choices and commitments. We also explored the double-edged sword of EdTech and AI.

Yes, technology is a powerful tool, but it cannot replace the human connection that makes learning meaningful, nor should it become a crutch that robs students of the grit required to do hard things.

Ultimately, frameworks are just tools. You have to learn the rules before you break them—take what works for your classroom and throw out what doesn't.

How are you balancing rigid frameworks with real human connection in your own teams or classrooms? Let me know below.

Key Ideas Summary:
Agile Frameworks in Schools: Educational institutions could benefit from operating as agile, scrum-frame worked programs from top to bottom.

The Necessity of Human Connection: EdTech cannot be the sole method of education, as students unanimously dislike 24-7 virtual learning. People need one-on-one conversations and the immediacy of human connection.

Tech as a Tool, Not a Crutch: EdTech offers amazing capabilities, like helping a third grader read grade-level content via translation. However, AI becomes a problem when students offload difficult tasks, avoiding the hard work necessary to develop grit and live fulfilling lives.

Reframing Accountability: The concept of accountability is currently misconstrued across the education system. People are not taught that taking accountability is distinct from getting in trouble.

Choice and Consequence: True accountability looks like allowing students to choose how they spend their time (e.g., talking about a football game instead of working) while ensuring they understand the natural consequence is completing the work over the weekend to stay on track.

Flexible Application: It is crucial to learn the rules of a technique before breaking them. Rigid structures can become crutches; educators should reflect on their tools, use what is usable, and leave behind what does not fit their specific circumstances.

•Providing Honest, Unfiltered Perspective: Public figures are often surrounded by people who only say what they want to hear. True friends offer a safe space for candid, grounded conversations that are completely detached from his public persona or corporate status.
•Listening Without Judgment: Sometimes the best support is simply letting someone vent without offering immediate strategies or solutions to their problems.
•Monitoring for Burnout: Close friends are often the first to notice signs of extreme exhaustion, sleep deprivation, or severe stress, and they can gently encourage stepping back to rest.

text:
Tonight,
the cosmos is quiet on purpose.

Not because life has gone still.

Not because love has disappeared.

But because something beautiful
is trying to reach you
without having to shout.

So breathe.

Let the noise fall away
for one sacred moment.

Let your heart hear
what the universe has been gently saying
all along:

You are wanted here.

Deeply.

Truly.

Beautifully.

Not for what you give.

Not for how strong you are.

Not for how much you carry, fix, offer, or endure.

But for the simple miracle
of you still being here.

Dear God, angels, universe,
and all loving light
surrounding this night,

Please lift every heart
that finds these words.

Let them feel lighter
than they did a moment ago.

Let peace return to their body.

Let hope rise in their chest.

Let a soft smile find them
for no other reason
than the soul remembering
it is loved.

May tonight become a little opening.

A little sign.

A little spark
that reminds us
beautiful things are still moving toward us.

May the quiet not feel empty.

May it feel full of presence.

Full of guidance.

Full of the unseen love
that has been walking beside us
through every uncertain step.

Dear loving light,

bring fresh energy
to the tired.

Bring warmth
to the lonely.

Bring courage
to the ones beginning again.

Bring joy
to the places in us
that forgot life could still surprise us.

May we wake tomorrow
with softer thoughts,
brighter eyes,
and a heart more willing
to believe good things are coming.

Because they are.

Love is still finding its way in.

Light is still gathering around us.

The path is still opening.

And our story
still has so much beauty
left to reveal.

Tonight,
the cosmos is quiet on purpose.

So we can hear the truth
beneath everything:

We are loved.

We are wanted.

We are guided.

We are not finished.

And something beautiful
is still coming for us.

Amen.

text:
THE GLACIER THAT REFUSED TO READ ITS OWN OBITUARY

PETERMANN WAS DECLARED DEAD IN 2012, AND IT HAS SPENT THE LAST DECADE POLITELY IGNORING THE PAPERWORK

TK: There is a particular kind of confidence required to declare a several-hundred-metre-thick slab of Arctic ice dead, and an even more impressive kind of confidence required to keep insisting it is dead once satellite imagery shows the thing has advanced thirty kilometres since the funeral. Back in 2012, journalists across several continents took one look at Greenland's Petermann Glacier, decided it was "hemorrhaging," and confidently informed the public it would be gone soon, using the same tone people usually reserve for describing a terminal diagnosis. The glacier, apparently not having received the memo, has spent the years since quietly rebuilding the exact section that was supposed to have sealed its fate, advancing back out into the fjord by almost twenty miles. This is roughly the ice-sheet equivalent of showing up to your own wake, helping yourself to the sandwiches, and asking everyone why they look so surprised.

What makes this particular episode worth dwelling on is not merely that one prediction turned out to be wrong, because predictions turn out to be wrong all the time and nobody owes anybody an apology for honest uncertainty handled honestly. What makes it worth dwelling on is the tone. Nobody in 2012 wrote that the glacier "might" retreat, or that current trends, "if they continued," could produce a certain outcome by a certain date. The language was hemorrhaging, irreversible, soon, the full vocabulary of an emergency room drama rather than a field that deals, by its own admission, in probabilities and margins of error. When the confident language turns out to describe the opposite of what actually happened, the appropriate response is not to quietly move on to the next confident prediction as though nothing occurred, yet that does appear to be the industry standard.

The glacier, annoyingly for the narrative, is not behaving like an isolated eccentric either. It fits neatly into the wider and rather less dramatic story of Arctic sea ice extent, which has remained essentially stable for the better part of two decades now, a fact that sits awkwardly alongside roughly twenty years of increasingly specific predictions about the exact summer in which the Arctic Ocean would finally go ice-free. Various dates have been offered with great confidence and then quietly retired without ceremony once they passed without incident, in the manner of a psychic revising the date of the apocalypse after the previous one fails to arrive on schedule. At some point, a reasonable observer starts to notice a pattern, and the pattern is not "the ice is collapsing." The pattern is "the predictions keep needing new deadlines."

None of this is an argument that the Arctic is some frozen fortress entirely unbothered by a changing climate, because ice sheets are large, complicated, regionally variable things that do genuinely gain and lose mass depending on a tangle of factors well beyond a single headline's capacity to explain. It is an argument for a certain basic humility that seems to have gone missing somewhere between the original research paper and the front-page graphic, the humility to say "here is what the data currently show, and here is how confident anyone reasonably ought to be about extrapolating it forward," rather than reaching immediately for hemorrhage and soon. Petermann did not save anyone from having to think seriously about environmental change. It simply demonstrated, rather pointedly, what happens to confident short-term predictions dressed up as long-term certainties: sooner or later, the ice comes back, and somebody has to quietly delete the old headline.

text:
⚠️ 🇺🇸 One Holdout Stands Between Lindsay Clancy and a Verdict After She Strangled Her Three Children

A Massachusetts jury that has already spent more than thirty-five hours over six days is stalled by a single juror who, according to the rest of the panel, will not follow the judge’s instructions on reasonable doubt in the case of a mother who admits she killed her three young children.

Lindsay Clancy, 36, of Duxbury, faces three counts of first-degree murder for the January 24, 2023, killings of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months. She strangled them with exercise bands in the basement of the family home while her husband Patrick was out running errands, then slashed her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window. She is paralyzed from the waist down and appears in court in a wheelchair. She has never denied the acts. The only question left for the jury of nine women and three men is whether she was criminally responsible.

Prosecutors spent six weeks arguing that the killings were a choice. They pointed to the timing, the method, the photos she sent her husband that afternoon of a “good day” building a snowman, and a pattern of not taking prescribed medication while shopping providers. They noted that no clinician had documented psychosis before that day and that she reported hearing a commanding voice only once, on the afternoon she killed the children. The defense answered with postpartum psychosis and bipolar disorder and asked the jury to find her not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.

Deliberations began August 27. On September 1 and again on September 2 the jury sent notes saying it could not reach a unanimous verdict. Judge William Sullivan read the Tuey-Rodriguez instruction, Massachusetts’ last-ditch “dynamite charge,” and sent them back. On Thursday, September 3, a new note arrived. The foreperson reported that one juror was holding out and “refuses to listen to the law” on reasonable doubt. Sullivan questioned the jurors one by one at sidebar, received assurances they could follow the law, reinstructed the whole panel on the Commonwealth’s burden, and sent them out again. Defense lawyer Kevin Reddington exploded. He asked the judge to remove the holdout and seat an alternate. The judge refused. Reddington later told reporters the inquiry of that juror would happen Friday morning and that he did not want a mistrial because, in his words, the defense had “kicked the s*** out of their case.”

What the holdout is thinking cannot be known from outside the room. The only facts available are the note itself and the reaction it produced. Eleven jurors appear ready to accept the defense theory that mental illness erased criminal responsibility. One juror is not. That juror is treating the legal standard of reasonable doubt as something other than a permission slip. Three children were found dead with exercise bands around their necks. A parent planned the moment her husband would be gone. A diagnosis offered after the fact does not unstrangle them. A single juror who still sees the bodies instead of the paperwork is, for now, the only person in the room applying the law as it was written rather than as it is being sold.

If that juror holds through Friday, Sullivan is expected to declare a mistrial. Prosecutors have already signaled they would retry the case. The children will still be dead. The only open question is whether one adult in Massachusetts is still willing to say so out loud.

text:
VIRGINIA IS THE MODEL FOR DATA CENTERS!

Virginia Is the Canary in the Coal Mine When It Comes to Data Centers: The Canary Is Singing!

Opponents of the data center boom have taken to calling Virginia the canary in the coal mine, and the geography is fair. 

If these buildings drain local water, drive household power bills through the roof, and leave counties poorer than they found them, the damage should already be visible in the state that has hosted the densest cluster on earth since the mid 1990s. 

Northern Virginia has lived with that concentration for thirty years, and the wreckage the models keep announcing has not shown up in the bills, the taps, or the tax rate.

Virginia now hosts roughly 385 operating data center buildings, totaling on the order of 75 million gross square feet. 

Measured by square footage, that is about 5 times what Texas has, roughly 7 times California, roughly 7 times New York, and roughly 10 times Florida.

Adjusted for population, the gap widens. 

Virginia has nearly 5 times as many data centers per resident as Texas, 6.2 times as many as California, 5.9 times as many as New York, and 8.5 times as many as Florida. 

Northern Virginia is the largest data center market in America and the largest in the world, and Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties alone account for roughly 80% of the Commonwealth’s inventory. 

Other states are still arguing from models of what might happen if a campus were to arrive. Virginia already has the record of what did happen after the campuses arrived in force and stayed.

The water claim is the one that travels fastest. 

Critics say the facilities will drain a community’s supply and then poison what remains with their discharge. 

A large share of Virginia’s data center buildings do not use meaningful quantities of water after the tanks are filled. 

About 40% are exclusively air- or dry-cooled, meaning they reject heat mechanically and consume almost no energy once the system is charged. 

Another 35% are hybrid, running dry through most of the year and switching to evaporative assistance only in the hottest stretches of summer. 

That leaves roughly 25% that depend on water. The phrase “data centers use water” treats those three machines as a single entity.

Virginia’s fleet consumes about 2.1 billion gallons of water a year, of which roughly 780 million gallons are discharged. 

The fair test is what the same land and the same 75 million square feet would demand as ordinary offices.

Federal Energy Star benchmarking puts median office water use at about 14.48 gallons per square foot per year. 

Multiply that out, and you get roughly 1.086 billion gallons of annual use and roughly 619 million gallons of annual discharge. 

The data center stream is larger by volume, somewhere in the range of 16% to 26% depending on which assumptions you carry through the arithmetic.

Electricity was the prediction offered with the most confidence. 

If concentrating this much computing load in one state drives residential rates through the roof, Virginia should post the highest household bills in America.

Households there paid an average of 16.69¢ per kilowatt-hour through mid 2026, 8.1% below the national average of 18.16¢. 

Virginians pay roughly 49.7% less than Californians, 44.5% less than Massachusetts residents, and 43.7% less than Mainers. 

California, Massachusetts, and Maine are not data center hubs. 

They are states that have spent years treating energy abundance as a problem to be managed rather than a condition of growth.

Learned this structure from @CreateNotesOnRE today.

Numbers & scenario just for illustration.

Seller wants $15M.

We think the market will bear more like $7.5M.

We'll never agree on price.

Is there a deal here?

There's $1M debt on the property that the seller wants to clear.

Offer:

We buy it for $1M. That clears the debt & solves the seller's immediate problem. 

Seller can continue to operate the property and keep the cash flow. 

Seller has an option to buy the property back on an increasing price scale: 
$1.5M within first 6 months
$2M between 6 mos-1 year
$2.5M between 1 year-1.5 yrs
$3M between 1.5 yrs-2 yrs
$3.5M between 2 yrs-2.5 yrs
$4M between 2.5 yrs-3 yrs

If they don't exercise their option within 3 years, we keep the property and get control of operations.

The structure creates a deal for us regardless of if or when within the buyback window the seller exercises their option.

The seller gets their debt cleared now, which is what they want, and preserves the opportunity for them to get a windfall if they find a buyer at their price. 

And if they do find a buyer at a price that makes them happy, cool, they can buy it back and then sell it to their buyer.

The structure incentivizes the seller to do that as quickly as possible, but we're happy either way.
