text:
Google has been found liable for monopolization by federal judges twice now. Both times, however, the judges have allowed the company’s monopoly to remain intact. The rather dire message this sends to would-be monopolists is that their business model will be protected even if they are found to have broken the law. It’s an ominous development as the tech industry seeks to shift its dominance into artificial intelligence, even as enforcers find more ways that platforms are abusing their power.

We don’t yet know everything about the latest ruling because it will be under seal for a couple of weeks. But we know the important thing: Google will be allowed to continue to run all sides of the advertising technology stack, including the “sell side” where advertisers make bids, the “buy side” where publishers offer inventory on their websites, and the “ad exchange” where both sides come together in real-time auctions. For years, this integration enabled Google to extract billions of dollars from publishers and advertisers in a market it controlled. It was found guilty of this, yet will not have to give up any of those pieces.

Yesterday, Judge Leonie Brinkema rejected the divestiture of AdX, the ad exchange part of the architecture, as well as the Justice Department’s proposal that source code for the publisher tools be made public, with the option of breaking that piece of Google’s business off if competition didn’t improve.

The judge did accept a series of “behavioral remedies,” which we don’t have the details for yet. But Google is already declaring victory. “We’re very pleased the court rejected the DOJ’s proposal to break apart tools that help small businesses reach new customers and grow,” Lee-Anne Mulholland, a Google vice president of regulatory affairs, said in a statement. https://t.co/w4tFfU3SmL

text:
The more I work my way through this, the more I think that the SEC's complaint is subject to dismissal. The federal jurisdiction is being manufactured as a First Amendment problem where there is none. Who is forcing any association with LSU? There is no Ken Paxton letter like we had with the Big 12. A state officer threatening a conference with antitrust liability for exercising its associational rights is a First Amendment injury. I get that. That letter manufactured the controversy and the federal jurisdiction.

But LSU recruiting football players? Lane Kiffin putting them at practice? LSU threatening to play them? That is precisely what the complaint offers as the coercion. SEC Compl. ¶ 70. Two of those are speech and one is a football practice. The complaint then has to insist that the defendants went "beyond mere public statements," which tells you the drafters saw the problem coming. Compl. ¶ 75. All of it may be brazen. It may violate the SEC's bylaws. It may constitute an anticipatory breach of the governing compact. But none of those things, without considerably more, explains how Louisiana has used sovereign power to compel the SEC to associate with anybody.

There is an antecedent problem too: What is the constitutionally protected association being impaired? Dale was an expressive-association case, and the complaint leans on it hard. See Compl. ¶¶ 55, 66, 70. But the First Amendment does not create a generalized right for every private organization to avoid dealing with people it dislikes. The SEC is principally an athletic and commercial joint venture, and its own pleading says so, complaining of harm to its brand and its media partnerships. The complaint needs to explain why LSU rostering a football player infringes a protected expressive association rather than simply violates the rules of the league.

And notice what is actually alleged. Not forced association with a member. Forced association with conduct. Dale protects against compelled membership. Being adjacent to conduct you disapprove of is a different thing, and no case the SEC cites makes it a constitutional injury.

Rumsfeld v. FAIR, 547 U.S. 47 (2006), forecloses most of what is left. (Citation to cases in a complaint is disfavored, but note that a pleading with room for Roberts, Dale, Wooley, and Barnette somehow found none for FAIR.) The Court rejected an expressive-association claim even where federal law required law schools to permit military recruiters onto campus, reasoning that recruiters were outsiders who came to hire students rather than to join anyone's expressive association. Id. at 68-70.

Compelled interaction is not compelled expressive association. If a genuine federal mandate backed by the loss of every federal dollar does not state that claim, a member's breach of a private bylaw cannot. And here nobody mandated anything. Which leaves the SEC on a fork of its own making. If the objectionable association is with the players, FAIR controls, because they are outsiders and not SEC members at all. Compl. ¶ 12. If it is with LSU, then this is a member breaching an agreement it signed, and Dale has never supplied a cause of action for that.

Then comes Section 1983. Yes, LSU officials are state actors. Agreed. That gets you halfway. Section 1983 requires state action and the deprivation of a federal right. The complaint does a reasonably good job identifying Louisiana officials. It does a much less persuasive job identifying what those officials have done with the sovereign power of Louisiana that deprives the SEC of a constitutional right. Recruiting a tight end is not an exercise of sovereign authority.

The assertion that "[e]ach Defendant is a 'person' within the meaning of Section 1983" is simply wrong. Compl. ¶ 69. LSU and its Board are arms of the State of Louisiana, and arms of a State are not persons at all under Section 1983. That has been the law for 37 years. Will v. Michigan Dep't of State Police, 491 U.S. 58 (1989). LSU does not become a statutory person by ipse dixit. The official-capacity defendants survive, but a complaint that gets the elementary point wrong as to two of five defendants does not inspire confidence in the rest.

The invocation of Ex parte Young also makes no sense. Ex parte Young exists to stop state officers from enforcing unconstitutional law. What law is at issue here? None. Ex Parte Young, probably the most inconsistently applied case of all time, is not a vehicle for enforcing a private association's bylaws.

And the SEC's own allegations make the supposed compulsion harder to understand with every page. By its telling, the Conference can declare these players ineligible, sanction LSU, strip its championship recognition, bar it from conference events, withhold its revenue distributions, suspend it by a two-thirds vote, and ultimately expel it. All of that sits in Articles 3 and 4 of Exhibit A, attached to the complaint by the SEC. So the constitutional theory is that the SEC is being compelled to associate with an institution it voluntarily admitted, voluntarily retains, and possesses the contractual authority to expel?? Ultimately, it sounds like one hell of a conference-governance dispute.

None of which changes my view of LSU and Kiffin. I am Team SEC on the merits. Conferences have to be able to define the product they offer. They can distinguish college football from professional football. They can establish eligibility rules and sanction members that seek unilateral competitive advantages by blowing through them. LSU apparently voted to reaffirm these rules and then, days later, decided Lane Kiffin could treat them as advisory. See Compl. ¶¶ 7, 45, 48, 51.

LSU's conduct is outrageous. But outrageous conduct by a public university is not ipso facto a constitutional tort. The SEC has identified state actors, an impending violation of its rules, and a spectacular governance crisis. What it still needs to identify is the juridical alchemy by which all of that becomes compelled association under the First Amendment.

text:
FPC Asks Federal Court to Block Louisiana's Ban on Gun Carry Permits for 18-to-20-Year-Old Adults

Firearms Policy Coalition (FPC) announced today that it has filed a motion for preliminary injunction in its Pool v. Besson lawsuit, asking the United States District Court for the Western District of Louisiana to immediately block Louisiana's ban on handgun carry permits for 18-to-20-year-old adults.

The lawsuit is brought by Louisiana residents Ella Pool, Christian McDuffie, and Charles Matthews, along with FPC. Each individual plaintiff is a peaceable adult between the ages of 18 and 20 who is legally eligible to possess firearms and would apply for a Louisiana concealed handgun permit, but is prevented from doing so because of the State's age restriction.

Louisiana generally allows adults 18 and older to carry a concealed handgun without a permit. But the State still prohibits 18-to-20-year-old adults from obtaining a Louisiana concealed handgun permit. That ban has significant real-world consequences, including restrictions on carrying within 1,000 feet of school grounds under federal law and the denial of legal protections Louisiana grants to permit holders.

But this lawsuit could have been avoided if Louisiana had simply fixed the constitutional problem when FPC first raised it.

In April 2025, while FPC was working with Louisiana officials to resolve constitutional problems raised in its Mate v. Wescott litigation to end the State's non-resident carry permit ban, FPC's counsel warned Louisiana Solicitor General Ben Aguiñaga that the State's carry laws also violated the rights of 18-to-20-year-old adults, and provided Louisiana with proposed legislative language addressing both problems. The proposal would have allowed nonresidents to obtain Louisiana permits and lowered the minimum carry permit age from 21 to 18.

Instead, despite having FPC's proposed language in hand, Louisiana moved forward by addressing the non-resident carry permit ban while leaving the 21-year-old permit restriction intact. The State then let another legislative session come and go in 2026 without fixing the constitutional violation. Meanwhile, Louisiana continues to enforce a law that denies peaceable 18-to-20-year-old adults rights and legal protections available to other adults.

"We told Louisiana about this constitutional problem and gave them a simple way to fix it in early 2025. And by then, the Fifth Circuit had already made clear in our Reese v. ATF victory that the rights of 18-to-20-year-old adults are protected under the Second Amendment. Louisiana had ample notice, a perfect solution, and two legislative sessions to act. They refused. That's on the State," said FPC President Brandon Combs.

FPC's motion argues that Louisiana's ban cannot survive the Supreme Court's Second Amendment test. The Fifth Circuit has already held in FPC's Reese win that 18-to-20-year-old adults are part of "the people" protected by the Second Amendment and that there is no historical tradition supporting categorical firearm restrictions against them. FPC is asking the court to immediately block enforcement of Louisiana's 21-year-old minimum age requirement while the case proceeds so that 18-to-20-year-old adults can apply for a carry permit.

"We offered to resolve this issue with a consent decree and settlement, but the State refused. Our plaintiffs are being denied their rights today, so we have no choice but to seek relief," said Combs. "When we tell you there's a constitutional problem, you should take it seriously. If you have an unconstitutional law on the books—red state, blue state, or purple state, it doesn't matter—we're coming for it. Government officials do not get to knowingly violate constitutional rights and then tell the people they are harming to wait for politicians to maybe fix the problem someday."

FPC also made clear that it is eager to help states clean up unconstitutional laws before litigation becomes necessary. Earlier this year, FPC launched the FPC State Freedom Index, where gun owners and policymakers can explore an interactive map, compare states, and identify laws that should be repealed.

"We're always looking for opportunities to work with states to identify unconstitutional laws and craft legislation to eliminate them. But the Second Amendment is not a second-class right, and refusing to act is not an option. Someone's lawyers are going to fix these laws—either yours or ours. We hope states will take us up on our offer and work together to get this important work done," concluded Combs.

The motion and other case documents in Pool v. Besson can be viewed at https://t.co/3dS1oQBzcQ.

Something about the Pennsylvania governor polling is starting to bother me.

Most of these polls keep asking voters some version of the same question: Josh Shapiro or Stacy Garrity?

Meanwhile, look at what is sitting outside those two names.

The latest Bravo poll has Shapiro at 56% and Garrity at 25%, with 19% listed as “Other.”

The latest Franklin & Marshall poll has Shapiro at 50% and Garrity at 25%. That leaves a full 25% of voters outside those two choices.

Twenty-five percent.

At what point does “Other” get big enough that pollsters actually start asking voters who those people are?

Ken Krawchuk is the Libertarian candidate and is actually on the November ballot, yet he still isn't being offered by name in most of these polls. I'm running statewide as a write-in candidate and haven't been offered either.

And here's the part that made me laugh. Tony Dastra was actually broken out at 2% in one poll, even though his ballot petition was later successfully challenged and he was removed from the November ballot. Meanwhile, Ken Krawchuk is actually on the ballot as the Libertarian candidate and still isn’t being named in most polls.

I'm not claiming that any of it belongs to me. Some are undecided, some may support Ken, some may support another candidate, and some may ultimately vote for Shapiro or Garrity.

But that's exactly the point.

We don't know because nobody is asking.

If you're going to poll Pennsylvania voters and tell us what the race looks like, maybe give them the actual choices instead of deciding ahead of time that this is only a two-person race.

When as much as one-quarter of the electorate isn't choosing either major-party candidate, “Other” deserves a little more attention than a footnote.

text:
Here are the options they’ve been given:

Guilty of first-degree murder
They find she was criminally responsible and that the killings were either premeditated or committed with extreme atrocity or cruelty. That carries a mandatory life sentence with no parole.

Guilty of second-degree murder
They find she was criminally responsible and acted with malice, but not the extra elements required for first-degree. That is also a life sentence, but with the possibility of parole.

Guilty of manslaughter
They find she was criminally responsible but that the killings were unlawful without malice—wanton or reckless rather than intentional murder. Maximum is twenty years per count.

Not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility
This is Massachusetts’ version of an insanity verdict. Prosecutors have the burden to prove she was criminally responsible. If they fail—if the jury finds a mental disease or defect left her unable to understand the wrongfulness of her actions or unable to control her conduct—she is acquitted of the crimes. She would not simply walk free. The court can order a psychiatric evaluation and then commitment to a secure hospital, which can be renewed and can last for years or life.

Not guilty
A traditional acquittal: prosecutors failed to prove she committed the acts. Legal observers say this is unlikely because the defense has not contested that she killed the children.

If they still cannot agree after the judge’s final instruction, the judge can declare a mistrial.  Prosecutors could then retry the case, offer a plea, or drop it.

The central fight is not “did she do it.”  It is whether the state proved she was legally responsible at the time. Each child’s count is decided separately, so mixed verdicts are possible in theory.

In theory, the one juror can be taking any of these positions contrary to what the 11 are concluding. I’m not arguing for the defense, I think she’s guilty AF although the one holdout could be opining on manslaughter for all we know. It sounds like the defense is simply trying to avoid a mistral based on what he said yesterday that Lindsay is not up for that emotionally. 
What do I know though? 🤷🏽

🚨🕵️‍♂️The $10 million everyone agrees was stolen, that no one will be charged for.

A Florida grand jury just concluded that the DeSantis administration misappropriated $10 million in taxpayer money. 

Not “raised questions.” Misappropriated. Their word.

Here is the trail. The state settled with Centene, its largest Medicaid contractor, over alleged overbilling. Centene offered to pay the full $67 million back to Florida. 

Instead, $10 million got peeled off and sent to Hope Florida, the charity run by the governor’s wife. From there it flowed to two nonprofits, then to a political committee staffed by the governor’s own chief of staff, and finally into the campaign to defeat the 2024 marijuana and abortion ballot measures. Money meant to insure low income kids ended up funding the governor’s political priorities.

Everyone can see what happened. The grand jury said so plainly. So why is no one charged?

Because the scheme was built so no single person owns the decision. The grand jury’s own explanation: nobody will take responsibility for deciding the money should go to Hope Florida. 

That is not exoneration. That is a confession that the structure worked exactly as designed. Diffuse the decision across enough hands and you can misappropriate eight figures in daylight and have it be no one’s crime.

Then came the burial. The report was filed under seal in January and kept hidden for seven months. The people named in it, including the sitting attorney general, fought in closed proceedings to keep it from the public. Court clerks told reporters they had no records of a case that plainly existed. It only surfaced because a journalist obtained a copy. And the administration’s response to the leak was to call the disclosure the real crime.

Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. A few key details:
•Who was invited: Rabbi Aaron Teitelbaum and Rabbi Zalman Leib Teitelbaum, leaders of rival Satmar Hasidic communities; the Skverer rebbe; the Bobov rebbe; the Vizhnitzer rebbe of Monsey; and Rabbi Malkiel Kotler, a leading figure at Beth Medrash Govoha, a major yeshiva in Lakewood, New Jersey.

•Main topic: The question of Israeli military service is expected to feature prominently, as Israel’s long-standing exemptions for many full-time yeshiva students have become a major domestic political and legal issue, with court rulings and public pressure pushing the government to increase haredi enlistment.

•Timing: it was arranged ahead of Rosh Hashanah, and one source told Israel Hayom the official purpose was to offer Rosh Hashanah greetings, with the draft issue not formally on the agenda — though it was expected to come up anyway.
It’s drawn criticism in some corners of the American Jewish community given Satmar’s ideological rejection of Zionism and the State of Israel’s legitimacy.

text:
I built 2 directory websites in 6 months.
18,158 business listings. ~14,000 visits last month. ~100 people phoned in looking for a local pro.
I sold 3 of those calls.
Here’s the mistake, because it’s the one nobody teaches about programmatic SEO:
Everyone talks about traffic. Nobody talks about collection.
The stack: Next.js on Vercel, Neon Postgres, Outscraper for the listings, a Twilio tracking number on every state and city page, a ping-tree that auctions each inbound call to buyers in real time, Journey by Mediavine for ads, Stripe for the guides.
The plumbing works. A caller hits a state page, taps the number, my server pings the buyer network, the highest bid wins, the call forwards.
Except an offer only goes live when three environment variables exist for it. I set them for the highest-ticket service type. I never set them for the three routine ones.
The routine ones are most of the calls.
So for three months, 99 out of 102 calls went to an unsold voicemail. At the network’s median of $32 a call, that’s about $3,000 that never happened — on sites making a few hundred a month from ads and guides.
Three lessons I’d have paid for:
1.Directories don’t make money from pages. They make money from the 1% of visitors who call or fill a form. Instrument that path before you write article 200.
2.Every monetisation rail needs its own dashboard row: calls, accepted bids, voicemails. If a number is zero for a week, something is broken.
https://t.co/kC2cLbdPNJ, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo sent 83% of one site’s traffic last month. Google sent 105 visits. “The Google update killed my site” is only true if you only count Google.

Follow along if you want the unglamorous version of pSEO, numbers, stack, mistakes. No “$50k in 30 days” nonsense

text:
Here's my hardtech brief for September 3rd, 2026

U.S. HARDTECH:
- The Army gave AeroVironment $464.8 million for LOCUST X3, the first time a laser weapon has moved from prototype into real production in the US. It's a 30-kilowatt beam that burns drones out of the sky for under $5 a shot, and it rides on trucks and pallets instead of needing a fixed site.

- The Pentagon is building around 50 mobile SCIFs, the accredited rooms where classified work legally has to happen, and putting them within reach of smaller suppliers. The stated reason is that plenty of companies with useful technology can't get into a secure space at all, which has quietly kept startups out of classified programs for years.

- Hermeus picked Anduril's Lattice for the Quarterhorse Mk 2, its high-speed uncrewed aircraft. Lattice is the software layer that fuses sensor feeds and makes flight decisions, and testing starts next year.

- GE Aerospace booked $2.9 billion for parts for the F414, the engine in the Navy's Super Hornet, and the same day won a Defense Innovation Unit award for a hypersonic test vehicle. DIU is the Pentagon's commercial technology buying shop, so that's a legacy sustainment deal and a frontier one landing together.

- Oshkosh offered the Marines an interim supply of JLTVs, the Humvee replacement, while AM General works through delays on the newer A2 version. The Marines have until October 31st to take it.

- York Space Systems is facing an investor class action alleging it concealed the termination of a Space Development Agency contract. The company went public in January and raised $629 million.

- A group of senators and a House member want the Army to explain why it's dissolving its 600-soldier Unmanned Assault Battalion in Europe and turning it back into regular infantry. The unit was stood up in November specifically to absorb what Ukraine learned about drone warfare, and lawmakers want a briefing by the 21st.

ALLIED HARDTECH:
- The UK certified Open Cosmos as a supplier on TacSys, a framework worth up to £8 billion running through 2034. A framework isn't a guaranteed order, it's a pre-approved pool the Ministry of Defence draws task orders from, and Open Cosmos is pitching a low orbit constellation with laser links between satellites so data can move without touching a ground station.

- Spain's iPronics raised a $125 million Series B led by Maverick Silicon and Light Street, with Nvidia and Bosch Ventures joining. The Valencia company builds a rack-mounted optical switch that reroutes light paths inside AI data centers on the fly, which keeps more of a cluster's chips busy instead of idle.

- Germany's TKMS handed Israel the INS Drakon, the last of its Dolphin-class submarines. Its unusually tall sail, the tower on top of the hull, is widely believed to hold vertical launch tubes, which would give Israel a submarine-launched ballistic missile for the first time.

That's today's. Follow for more!
